12422-journal-of-a-residence-on-a-georgi:
Frances Anne Kemble published her Journal of a Residence on a Georgian Plantation, covering 1838 to 1839, after her marriage to a slaveholder. Kemble, an English actress, kept the journal on her husband plantations and later published it as an abolitionist document.

The journal quotes Alexander Stephens on slavery as the chief corner stone of the Confederacy, then records Kemble own encounters with enslaved people, overseers, and her husband anger. A mid-book scene has her husband forbid her to bring more complaints, saying the people had done very well without an advocate. Kemble writes with moral fury and literary skill. The journal is a primary source for American slavery, told by a witness inside the master house.
15916-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, number thirty-nine, dated August 5, 1897. Five cents bought news, science, and stories in words young readers could follow. Four new subscribers earned a pocket Kodak, measuring two and a quarter by two and seven-eighths inches, making pictures one and a half by two. The paper mixed learning with prizes.

This number turns to the week's events abroad and at home, with nature notes and serial tales beside. Editors explain treaties and inventions in short, clear paragraphs. Picture items keep young eyes moving. Seen now, the issue captures high summer 1897 for American children: cameras as prizes, and the world arriving weekly.
33841-history-of-ambulance-company-numbe:
The men of Ambulance Company Number 139 wrote this brief unit history while waiting for sailing orders home, in barn-loft billets at Aulnois-sous-Vertuzey in France. It follows the company from camp life and training at Camp Doniphan, across the Atlantic, through England and France, to action on the Wesserling sector and in the Meuse-Argonne offensive.

Chapters recall the march from Luneville to Benney, work with the kitchen in the Argonne, citations and losses, and furloughs at Grenoble and Aix-les-Bains. The tone is plain and comradely, written while memories were fresh. The book preserves one small unit's Great War in its own words.
5942-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Galleys and defeat fill chapters sixty-three through sixty-six of this Don Quixote portion. Chapter sixty-three treats the mishap that befell Sancho through the visit to the galleys. It also treats the strange adventure of the fair Morisco. Quixote reflects profoundly on the enchanted head's reply without hitting its secret. Chapter sixty-four treats the adventure that gave Quixote more unhappiness than any, and chapter sixty-five reveals the Knight of the White Moon.

Chapter sixty-six treats what readers will see, as defeat's consequences unfold. Readers get Barcelona's climax, where a disguised friend defeats Quixote and imposes a year's retirement. The part suits readers following volume two to its turning point, since the White Moon's victory sends the knight homeward toward shepherd dreams and death.
arxiv-2412-00339:
Conrad Zimmerman and Jenna DiVincenzo unify program logics in two thousand twenty four. Gradual verification blends static checks with runtime checks smoothly. It was built before on overapproximating logics like Hoare logic. Underapproximating logics, such as incorrectness logic, find real bugs instead.

They define gradual exact logic from exact logic directly. Static verification inside gradual verification links to both logic families. Hoare logic and incorrectness logic both restate in the new terms. Gradual verification itself also falls out of the definition. Tools may now serve verification and bug finding together.
arxiv-2412-04439:
Luis Lozano and co-workers mapped a special shock face for three-phase flow underground in a paper printed in 2024. Oil, water, and gas moving through porous rock obey conservation laws whose answers can jump across shocks. Undercompressive shocks are exotic jumps certified by having a viscous profile rather than by the usual Lax inequalities. The authors construct the face of such shocks for two models of the diffusive effects: a simple identity spread. The capillarity matrix that properly encodes capillary pressure.

The shock face's form turns out similar for both diffusions, a reassuring robustness. The capillarity choice still steers which answer the Riemann problem, the basic building block of flow mock run, selects. Reservoir simulators inherit those choices.
arxiv-2412-05439:
Abdulkadir Canatar and SueYeon Chung apply physics methods to a classic learning algorithm in this two thousand twenty-four paper. The algorithm is support vector regression, used to decode signals such as neural activity. The authors treat the learning problem as a physical system and compute its average behavior. Their focus is how geometry of the data shapes decoding precision. Neural noise plays a central role in the analysis.

They find a sharp phase change in training error as data load grows. The balance between a tolerance setting and noise drives the shift. Test error shows a double descent, falling, rising, then falling again. These patterns mirror puzzles seen in deep learning. The work links neuroscience decoding to the theory of learning curves.
arxiv-2412-05739:
James Dylan Douthitt and James Oxley classify binary matroids by excluded induced minors in two thousand twenty-four. Matroids distill the core idea of independence in math. A class can be pinned by the small matroids it bans as induced minors. Past work handled bans of one or two named matroids.

Here every pair from a set of four matroids gets its class worked out. The pairs are drawn from cycle, complete graph, and Fano type cases. Classes with neither member of the pair are determined in full. Extra lemmas push toward the class that bans the complete graph case alone.
arxiv-2412-07439: Rawat and Roy proved a fractional Hardy inequality for half spaces in the Heisenberg group in twenty twenty-four. Hardy's inequality bounds a weighted average of a function by its smoothness energy. Fractional versions use far off gaps in place of rates of change. The Heisenberg group is an odd space. In it, a move to the side and a move up shape each other, so the two cannot be treated apart.
arxiv-2412-08139:
Jiaming Lv, Haoyuan Yang, and Peihua Li swap the standard distance in knowledge distillation for the Wasserstein distance. Their paper from twenty twenty-four reviews the classic setup, where a small student learns from a big teacher. The usual Kullback-Leibler score compares matching class odds only. It cannot weigh cross-class links, and it breaks on layers whose spreads do not overlap.

Their WKD line comes in two forms. WKD-L distills output odds with a discrete Wasserstein score, which reads cross-class ties in full. WKD-F distills mid-layer features with a continuous score over modeled spreads. Image sorting and object detection tests favor both. The logit form beat strong KL variants. The feature form beat KL rivals and top peers. Code is public for reuse.
arxiv-2412-09739:
Johnson, Meegan, Lowry, Oudemans, and Dana build a vision framework for tracking cranberry ripening in twenty twenty-four. Growers need hard numbers on how berries ripen to compare varieties and spot disease. The team imaged bogs from drones and with handheld cameras. Fixed markers let them follow the same patch all season.

Aerial shots give distributions of surface brightness across whole bogs. Ground shots track single berries as their appearance changes. Vision transformer features describe each berry in rich detail. A two dimensional map of those features makes ripening paths visible. Ripening rates can then be measured and compared. Four cranberry varieties were compared with the method. Both data sets were released publicly.
arxiv-2412-16739:
Long Zhou and five co-authors remove hand-tuned knobs from few-shot learning. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Transductive few-shot methods judge a whole test batch at once. Their behavior hinges on settings like how balanced the predicted classes should be. Those settings are found by grid search on validation data. The best values shift with each dataset and base model. Searching is slow and still suboptimal.

Their method, UNEM, unrolls an optimizer into a neural network. The base is a generalized expectation-maximization routine. Unrolling lets the system learn the right settings itself. Learning to optimize replaces the grid search. The approach adapts per task without manual tuning. Few-shot classification becomes cheaper to deploy on new problems.
arxiv-2412-17339:
Yu, Shen, Na, Chen, and Li build an AI agent for finding minerals from satellite data in twenty twenty-four. Mineral exploration from remote sensing needs deep geological knowledge. General multimodal language models lack that expertise and struggle with many images at once. Their MineAgent framework structures the reasoning in layers.

Judging and decision modules work hierarchically to combine spatial and spectral clues. The team also built MineBench, a benchmark for this specialty. It uses geological and hyperspectral data to grade model performance. Experiments showed the agent improved results on exploration tasks. The authors see domain frameworks as the way to make AI useful in geoscience. Long context limits remain a challenge they explicitly target.
arxiv-2412-17739:
Ermo Hua and nine co-authors rethink how language models mark word position in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Models need position signals to read order. The standard trick, rotary position embedding, helps models stretch to longer texts, but only so far. The authors trace the failure with signal processing theory. They show the method works by a hidden Fourier transform, and that other model parts damage the needed spectrum.

Linear layers and activations smear the frequencies, and short training starves some of them. Their fix, Fourier position embedding, repairs the spectrum on purpose. Models using it extend to longer contexts more cleanly. The paper serves researchers who push models toward book-length inputs. It reframes a practical trick as a signal design problem.
arxiv-2412-17839:
Wijesinghe and five co-authors present a paper from twenty twenty-four on goal-oriented communication with high spectrum efficiency. Traditional systems prize exact data copying at the receiver. Goal-oriented systems instead send what the receiver's task needs. Their design pairs a latent diffusion model with a quantized image network. A shared feature codebook is trained for the receiver side. Tests show better perceived quality than leading rivals. Downstream task accuracy also improves in their runs.

Bandwidth use drops sharply against state-of-the-art systems. Smart delivery suits edge computing and device networks, they argue. Generative tools power the compact message encoding. The authors frame the system as a quality-of-service advance.
arxiv-2412-18339:
Li, Cárdenas-López, Lupascu, and Motzoi designed control pulses for qudits in this paper from twenty twenty-four. A qudit is a quantum unit with more than two levels, packing extra information into each site. Higher levels lose their quantum state faster, so gates must be quick and clean. Methods that work for two-level qubits do not extend easily.

The authors give a recipe for pulses that rotate any two neighboring levels. The analysis squeezes errors into a four-level window, counting two leakage levels as well. Their pulses suppress several error types at once and beat prior schemes. Tests on transmon circuits showed strong gains toward very low error rates. The approach should transfer to other ladder-like quantum systems.
arxiv-2412-18839:
Neil Shah, Shirish Karande, and Vineet Gandhi wrote this paper, listed in two thousand twenty-four, on turning non-audible murmurs into speech. A murmur is a silent mouthing of words that sensors can pick up, used when sound cannot be made or heard.

Past methods leaned on paired whispers to fake true speech, but the speech was often hard to grasp and weak on new speakers. The team instead learns sound unit alignments from whispers and text, then works straight from murmurs, and adds lip video through a diffusion method. They also release MultiNAM, a data set with close to eight hours of murmur, whisper, video, and text from two speakers, and test all methods on it.
arxiv-2501-07239:
Ankita Dargad, Urban Larsson, and Niranjan Balachandran compute the temperature of a take-from-the-rich game called Robin Hood. Their paper from twenty twenty-five sits in cumulative games, a bridge between classic game theory and economics. Each heap holds tokens tied to both players' wealth. A move takes tokens from one heap, capped by the mover's wealth, and cuts the rival's wealth by the same count.

Temperature gauges how urgent the first move in a part is. Most Robin Hood spots run hot. On one large heap, the curve splits by the wealth ratio. Inside a golden-ratio band, temperature grows in a straight line with heap size. Outside it, temperature stays flat, and mean values mirror each other. A twist ends the tale: the hottest part is not always the best first play.
arxiv-2501-08239:
Riva and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about friction felt by a particle crossing through a crystal. As the particle moves, it excites sound waves called phonons in the crystal. Those waves carry away energy, slowing the particle like friction. The team treats the weak interaction with linear-response theory. That many-body method yields explicit formulas for the friction force. The formulas show how friction depends on the particle's speed.

They compare the formulas against computer simulations of the same system. Agreement between theory and simulation was remarkable, they report. The model covers crystals in two and three dimensions. Weak coupling keeps the math controlled and transparent. The results give a clean baseline for nanoscale friction studies. They also show sound emission alone can brake a moving particle.
arxiv-2501-13739:
Vitalii Vertogradov built a collapse model in twenty twenty-five that forms a black hole with no singularity inside. Standard collapse ends in a singular point, and avoiding it normally requires matter that violates the strong energy condition — gravity that repels. What physical matter could do that is unknown. His model uses just dust and radiation.

Alone, those ingredients still collapse to a singularity. But if dust and radiation exchange energy, with the exchange growing toward the cloud's center, a regular center becomes possible. Vertogradov identifies the conditions for regularity and gives an explicit example of the interaction producing it. The model offers a concrete, simple route to singularity-free black holes without exotic ingredients.
arxiv-2501-15139:
Gui, He, and Zeng use holography to picture the Einstein ring of a charged black hole with quantum corrections. Their setup rests on the AdS/CFT link between gravity and field theory. A wave source sits on the boundary of the space. The response that appears on the far side is then captured. A virtual lens system turns that response into a ring image on a screen.

Moving the observer turns the neat ring into an arc, then a bright point. The ring also shrinks as the quantum correction grows. Higher temperature and chemical potential shrink it as well. The study ties ring size to black hole traits in a testable-looking way.
arxiv-2501-18439:
Yan Sun, Yutong Lu, and colleagues predict molecule properties with a graph model that reads long-range structure in a 2025 study. Drug discovery needs fast guesses about how a molecule will behave, and graph networks over atoms and bonds are the usual tool. Those networks, though, often miss influences between distant parts of a molecule.

Their framework pairs graph features with an extended long short-term memory design at two levels, and a mixture of expert heads shares the work. The dual-level reading aims to capture both local chemistry and global shape. Interpretability is a stated goal, so chemists can see which structures drive a prediction.
arxiv-2502-02139:
Yukun Zhang and six co-authors survey quantum algorithms for molecules in a twenty twenty-five review. Solving how molecules behave is hard for classic computers, since the math grows fast with size. Quantum computers that can fix their own errors, even in early form, offer a new path.

The review covers how molecule problems are encoded, how their energy changes are simulated, and how ground state energies are found. It notes gains like shallower circuits and fewer spare qubits. It also weighs the limits set by classic methods that mimic quantum ones. The authors close with next steps toward real tests on hardware.
arxiv-2502-03639:
Yunuo Chen and colleagues teach video generators some three-dimensional common sense by annotating training videos with moving points in space. Current models morph objects and break physics because they lack shape awareness. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team augments ordinary clips with three-dimensional point trajectories, aligned to the pixels. A latent diffusion model fine-tuned on the enriched set learns to track flat objects with true spatial coordinates. On top of that, shape and motion regularization penalizes non-physical deformation in the output.

Contact-rich scenes are the showcase. When solid objects interact, the spatial information keeps hands and tools coherent. The method plugs into existing video diffusion models rather than replacing them. The authors frame plausibility as a geometry problem: give the model points to respect, and the pictures behave.
arxiv-2502-04739:
Pramodh Senarath Yapa, Xinyu Guo, Joseph Maciejko, and Frank Marsiglio study odd superconductor states in this two thousand twenty-five physics paper. The symmetry of the superconducting gap bounds what pairing route can be at work. That makes it a key test. The team shows how phases that mix singlet and triplet pairing can rise below the critical temperature. They show this in a tight-binding model, looking at the one-dimensional case first, then the two-dimensional case.

In both, shifts that break symmetry below the critical temperature turn out to be common. To link with tests, they work out the density of states, what spectroscopists read, at temperatures below the shift. Its form near the critical temperature can stand far from its form near zero. The warn: a full picture of a superconductor's symmetry calls for reads across the heat range, not just at the cold point.
arxiv-2502-07239:
Liu and five co-authors generated speech-matched gestures on video in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Avatars feel alive when their hands move with their words. Older systems miss the exact beats or meanings that should trigger a gesture. Their framework attacks the problem in three parts.

A chronological alignment links the speech and motion streams in time. Gesture tokens are then distilled with speech context baked in, so patterns carry meaning. Finally, a structure-aware step reconnects keypoints along the body's edges for cleaner video. Experiments showed realistic, well-synced gesture videos. Long sequences and later editing of gestures were also supported. The authors aim the system at lifelike avatars and interfaces.
arxiv-2502-07739:
Yuzhu Chen and six co-authors study how fine-tuning starts, in a twenty twenty-five paper. They work with LoRA, a popular way to adapt large models by training only small low-rank parts. Their analysis shows the final result depends heavily on the starting values. A poor start can trap the method in a weak outcome.

A good start would point toward the main directions of the change the model needs. But that change is not known ahead of time in real use. Their method, HRP, first trains briefly at a higher rank. It then uses the main directions found to set the start for the main run. Tests showed gains over a random start, growing with the warm-up rank.
arxiv-2502-08739:
Avner Bensoussan, Gunel Jahangirova, and Mohammad Reza Mousavi sort real faults found in systems that mix quantum and classic parts. Their study is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such mixed systems are now in wide use, but they fail in their own ways, and checks must fit those faults. The team mined open code sites for fixed faults. From more than five thousand closed reports, they kept a sound set and tagged just over one hundred faults by sign and source. Two authors cross-checked each tag. Talks with eleven builders then tested the sort, which grew as checks went on. The result is a map of real faults, with data, for those who test such systems.
arxiv-2502-08839:
Ping, Lin, Tan, and Cong introduce a benchmark for quantum layout tools in twenty twenty-five. Layout synthesis maps a quantum program onto real hardware. It inserts SWAP gates so that linked qubits sit close enough to interact. Prior benchmarks used circuits that need no SWAP gates, so they miss a key cost.

The new benchmark, QUBIKOS, has circuits with proven optimal SWAP counts. It lets researchers measure how far top tools fall short of optimal. The best tool, from IBM, used sixty-three times the optimal count. Other leading tools showed gaps well above one hundred times. The authors also dissect one weak case to guide better design. They argue the field needs major advances in layout methods.
arxiv-2502-09639: Brito and co-authors link a class of minimal surfaces in a three-sphere to special vector fields on a punctured two-sphere. The surfaces are genus one Lawson surfaces inside S3(2). The fields are unit vector fields that minimize area, defined on the unit sphere with both poles removed. The team proves a one-to-one correspondence between the two objects. As a payoff, they derive a stability relation for Lawson cylinders in the same space, tying surface geometry to field theory in a precise way.
arxiv-2502-10239:
Mohamed Aboelenien Ahmed, Kilian Pfeiffer, and three colleagues fine-tune language models across many small devices without moving private data or burning device resources, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Federated learning trains on data where it lives, but full fine-tuning is far too heavy for phones and edge hardware.

Their route is zeroth-order optimization, which estimates gradients just by evaluating the model under small random nudges. That needs only forward passes, so memory stays at inference level and communication stays low. The catch is slow convergence and the cost of many nudges. The authors introduce a more efficient variant that cuts the number of perturbations needed while keeping the estimate useful. Task alignment steers the process toward the target job. The method aims to bring federated fine-tuning within reach of resource-constrained devices. Privacy is preserved because raw data never leaves the device.
arxiv-2502-10939:
Chen and Li study how to draw sound claims from trials where groups start a treatment at staggered times. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such trials need methods that can track effects that change over time. They must also deal with groups that may act early, and with group sizes that are not alike.

The pair study regression tools that use data from single persons, group means, or scaled group totals. Some tools adjust for other traits, and some do not. They show when each tool stays on target as samples grow. Their work finds an edge for scaled group totals with trait adjustment. It gives clear advice on which tool to pick.
arxiv-2502-11639:
Pietro Barbiero and seven others set out a way to build deep learning systems whose reasoning can be checked. Interpretability claims are usually verified case by case, and direct verification explodes in cost as variables multiply. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team anchors their structure in inference equivariance, the demand that a model's logic transform in a fixed pattern when its inputs are relabeled. They show the verification burden eases when interpretability is treated as a Markovian trait, passed step to step, and when networks are rebuilt to expose that structure.

On that foundation they propose a design pattern: neural parts generate, interpretable parts execute. Systems built this way, which they call neural interpretable reasoners, aim to keep deep learning's expressiveness while making each inference auditable. The structure is offered as a general design habit for clear AI, beyond any single design.
arxiv-2502-12639:
Mohammed El Azar and colleagues studied electrons scattering off graphene quantum dots under light and magnetic flux in a 2025 paper. Graphene dots confine Dirac electrons into tiny islands whose states can be tuned, a playground for quantum electronics. The team solved the energy spectrum when a circularly polarized laser and a magnetic flux thread the dot together, then computed how incoming electrons scatter.

Light polarization emerged as the master switch, steering how strongly electrons scatter and how tightly they localize near the dot. Raising light intensity or flux encouraged quasi-bound states, while an electrostatic potential thinned the scattering states and fine-tuned coupling to the dot. The knobs suggest new ways to control electronic states in graphene devices.
arxiv-2502-13039: Melvyn Nathanson gives a construction of finite sets of integers and lattice points known as B_h sets. In such a set, all sums of h elements are distinct, a property prized in additive combinatorics problems. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Nathanson builds these sets using nothing more than rational independence. He chooses elements that are independent over the rational numbers as vectors. He then maps them into integers and lattice points. The one-page-style argument is notably elementary for a construction that usually requires heavier machinery.
arxiv-2502-14339:
Zhang and five co-authors analyzed spin waves in ferrite films in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Magnetostatic waves carry signals in microwave devices, launched by metal transducers. Engineers usually judge devices by impedance spectra alone. The authors instead tracked how the waves actually propagate, including uneven magnetic fields inside the film.

Their analysis pinned high-frequency losses on the metal nature of the transducers. Dips and ripples at low frequencies came from interference among multiple width modes. Commercial simulations confirmed the picture closely. The authors say propagation physics, not just spectra, must guide design. The work aims at better magnetostatic devices inside microwave systems.
arxiv-2502-16539:
Möller and Schmitt wrote in twenty twenty-five about how energy model errors affect predictions of nuclear fission fragments. When a heavy nucleus splits, the masses of the pieces follow patterns models try to predict. A Brownian motion method walks the nucleus through shapes toward splitting. A past study using it predicted a new region of uneven splitting for certain nuclei. Most experiments agreed, except one case involving iridium. The authors revisit whether energy surface errors explain that miss.

They argue such errors connect to errors in calculated ground-state masses. The paper gives a fuller discussion of that link. It also checks whether similar misses could occur in other regions. The work helps judge where fission predictions can be trusted. That matters for nuclear data used in science and energy.
arxiv-2502-20739: Yunxiang Wang and Hong-Wei Zhang prove that a sparse-maximal operator built from spheres stays bounded on hyperbolic spaces of every dimension, for a far larger set of radii than Euclidean space allows. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Maximal operators are basic measuring tools in harmonic analysis. Lacunary versions sample only a thin sequence of radii.
arxiv-2503-00739:
Wu and a large team build radon sniffers fine enough for dark matter hunts in twenty twenty-five. Radon gas and its kin foul rare event searches like PandaX. Two rigs were built, one for small samples and one that traps radon cold for big loads. The trap form runs thirty times keener than plain counting.

Surface care drove the blank rate down hard. Smoother steel, epoxy coats, and foil wraps each cut the gas seeping from walls. Coat and wrap gains ran near ninety and sixty percent. The systems now vet parts before they enter the deep labs.
arxiv-2503-02139:
The CMS Collaboration reports a study of charmonium in proton lead collisions in two thousand twenty-five. Charmonia are bound states of charm and anti-charm quarks. The team tracks the ratio of an excited state to the ground state. The ratio is read as a function of how many charged particles the crash makes.

Data came from the CMS detector at a set energy per pair. The ratio is split into prompt and nonprompt parts. For the first time, the prompt ratio shifts with particle count in this kind of crash. No clear trend with angle was seen. A model with talks among near particles is used for contrast.
arxiv-2503-02539:
Yiyun Zhou, Zheqi Lv, Shengyu Zhang, and Jingyuan Chen aim to free tutoring software from a bias that skews how it judges students. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Such software tracks what each student knows to pick the next task. When some topics appear far more than others, strong students get too little work and weak ones get too much.

The team traced the skew to a hidden factor: each student's past success rate across topic groups. Their model, DisKT, splits what a student knows into familiar and new ground. It then strips the hidden factor out of the student profile. A further part shields the model from guesses and slips in the data. Tests on many data sets show less bias and sharper calls than past tools. The model's picks can also be read in plain terms.
arxiv-2503-03139:
Jinwoo Lim, Suhyun Kim, and Soo-Mook Moon use a new lens to compare federated learning methods. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, studies training split across many devices. Each device holds data that differs from the rest. A backward error view asks what hidden extra term each method really follows as it trains.

For the basic method, that hidden term pushes each device's steps away from the group mean. That spread slows the shared model down. Two rival methods cut that bias in part or in whole at the first level. At the second level, one bias stays. The lens thus explains both the strengths and the limits of each method.
arxiv-2503-03739:
Mark Alaverdian and six co-authors take a deep look at spin in gravity in a twenty twenty-five paper. When two heavy bodies fly past each other, we can measure how their paths and spins change. Past work showed these measures can depend on more than the spin arrow alone.

The paper works out those extra parts in full. They come from the full spin tensor, a richer object than the spin arrow, and they can even change how large the spin is. The team gives the wave form, the push, and the spin kick to high order. They also build two-body Hamiltonians and show the extra parts are required, not optional, for a full account.
arxiv-2503-04239:
Christos Papalitsas and five co-authors apply quantum optimization to molecular docking in two thousand twenty-five. Docking finds how a drug binds best to a target protein. The search is hard for large biomolecular systems. Quantum approximate methods offer a fresh angle on it.

Their Digitized Counterdiabatic QAOA runs on a GPU cluster. Test cases reach fourteen and seventeen node instances. Those exceed the largest published docking cases they cite. Binding interactions match the expected exact solution in results. Compute time climbs steeply as instance size grows, though. The trade off frames where the method helps today.
arxiv-2503-10239:
Cai and co-authors expose a privacy leak in super-apps: the history of which mini-apps a person used and how. Super-apps bundle many mini-apps for chat, pay, shopping, and more. Because mini-apps run on web tech, the host can log use with no extra tracking code. Use history covers which apps were opened, how often, and in what mix. Action history covers clicks, drags, and image views. The team reviewed 30 papers and checked 31 super-apps by hand.

They show these histories can reveal private traits of the user. A tool built on the histories demonstrates the inference risk. The leak needs no breach; it sits in normal platform logs.
arxiv-2503-12939:
Nicolò De Ponti, Giacomo Enrico Sodini, and Luca Tamanini wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It proves that the Hellinger-Kantorovich distance is the metric infimal convolution of the Hellinger and Wasserstein distances.

That split was guessed by Liero, Mielke, and Savaré. The proof runs through unbalanced optimal transport, by way of a side problem called the marginal entropy-transport problem. That problem is one step in the build of an infimal convolution. The authors give sharp bounds and study what happens as the count of steps grows without end. They do this both for the named distances and for abstract distances in general.
arxiv-2503-13339:
Martín Richarte and Júnior Toniato test scalarized Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet theories in a physics paper from twenty twenty-five. Their tool is the parametrized post-Newtonian formalism. That framework measures small departures from general relativity. The focus falls on two parameters that track how the theories bend light and slow time.

Data from the Cassini mission set tight limits on those parameters. Lunar laser ranging and geodetic measurements around the Sun add more bounds. Mercury perihelion measurements from MESSENGER combine with the Cassini results for one model. Galaxy strong-lensing systems give still another check. Readers learn which versions of these gravity theories survive real solar system tests.
arxiv-2503-13439:
Wu and co-authors present Amodal3R, a model that rebuilds full 3D objects from partly hidden 2D images. Most rebuilders assume the whole object is visible, yet real scenes hide parts behind other things. Their model starts from a foundation 3D generator and extends it for occlusion.

A mask-weighted cross-attention step comes first, then a layer built to use occlusion cues directly. Those priors steer the model toward plausible hidden geometry and appearance. Training used synthetic data alone, yet the model handled real scenes well. It beat pipelines that first fill in the 2D image and then rebuild, setting a new benchmark.
arxiv-2503-13639:
Matthew Hamil classified families of representations in a 2025 algebra paper. He works with Lie superalgebras, which mix ordinary symmetry with a signed, odd part, and studies their representation categories up to a stable equivalence that ignores easy pieces. The goal is to list all thick subfamilies that respect the tensor product and allow limits, called localizing subcategories.

Hamil proves a layering result that yields that full list, under stated conditions on a smaller detecting subalgebra and on how supports are realized. Newer tools based on homological spectra and a broader layering theory do much of the heavy lifting. The result extends his earlier joint work on the detecting subalgebra alone.
arxiv-2503-14439:
Kyriakos Stylianopoulos, Panagiotis Gavriilidis, Gabriele Gradoni, and George Alexandropoulos rebuild hidden surfaces from scattered radio waves using learned physics. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. RF imaging inverts scattered fields measured at spread-out receivers. The inversion is a notoriously hard problem. Data-driven solvers are fast but need good training data. The authors first build that data from real equations.

Electric field integral equations supply a quick forward model. A neural network then learns the inverse mapping. Graph attention feeds the system geometry into the network. Residual convolutional layers extract object features. A UNet head paints the final image. Two synthetic test sets check quality in numbers and pictures.
arxiv-2503-17239:
Aladin Djuhera and four co-authors present SafeMERGE, a way to keep language models safe after fine tuning in two thousand twenty-five. Fine tuning adapts a broad model to a niche task. It can also wear down the safety training set in place. Past fixes use complex steps or hurt task skill.

SafeMERGE runs after fine tuning and is light to use. It merges layers from the tuned and safe models by choice. A layer is merged only when it drifts from safe acts, judged by a match score. Tests on four models show fewer harmful outputs than rival guards. Task skill stayed flat or rose a bit.
arxiv-2503-19239:
Jiaqi Liao, Hong Liu, and Guiying Yan extend a classic result about sets of binary strings, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The result limits how large such a set can be when no two strings differ in too many places. The classic result is Kleitman's theorem on binary vectors.

Kleitman showed that a family of binary vectors with diameter d can be no larger than a Hamming ball of radius half of d. In plain terms, the roundest shape is also the biggest one allowed. The authors prove the matching statement for vector spaces over finite fields, the q-analog of the binary case. Sets of vectors take the place of sets of strings, and subspaces play the role of balls. The result settles how the old bound carries over to this broader setting.
arxiv-2503-20939:
Horacio Thompson, Maximiliano Sapino, Edgardo Ferretti, and Marcelo Errecalde work toward interpretable depression risk detection in two thousand twenty-five. Early risk checks on the web aim to flag users in need fast. Large language models solve many language tasks well, but domain reasoning needs proof. Their texts here are in Spanish.

A specialist style reasoning rule guides how users are read. In-context learning applies that rule to the Gemini model. Scores are checked in both counts and quality terms. Apt calls came with clear reasons that humans can follow. The method opens a path for language models in early risk work.
arxiv-2503-21039:
Héctor Chang-Lara and Sergio Zapeta-Tzul build a dynamic model of traffic congestion. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, revisits a classic route choice problem from the nineteen fifties. Two given distributions of travelers must move across a graph's nodes. The best routes are shortest paths, but congestion itself sets the distances, and both change over time.

Their dynamic version of the Beckmann problem yields equations for the flow's evolution. Those equations let them bound how many edges carry flow at once. Simulations show how efficient equilibria behave when interactions reach across the network. The work bridges static traffic theory and live flow.
arxiv-2503-21139:
Shifra Mandel and eleven co-authors hunt high-mass X-ray binaries in the galactic center with NuSTAR. Their paper from twenty twenty-five starts from thousands of X-ray points charted by Chandra in the core region. Chandra's soft band left their classes murky. NuSTAR's hard X-ray survey found a smaller set that could hide the rare high-mass systems among magnetic white dwarf pairs and low-mass binaries.

Bright near-infrared partners are the tell for a high-mass system. Seven NuSTAR sources have such partner candidates at the right brightness. Chance alignment odds clear the bar for two of them, making them strong candidates. Joint spectra from three telescopes fit the high-mass reading for both. One was already known as a red supergiant host. Infrared spectroscopy must confirm them, the team notes.
arxiv-2503-23639:
Ralph Howard wrote this mathematics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, proving a broadened form of the Gronwall inequality. That classic inequality bounds how far apart two solutions of a differential equation can drift, given how their starting points and rules differ.

Howard's version works in any Banach space, with solutions moving through an open convex region. One solution follows one rule, the second another, and the second rule is Lipschitz with a fixed constant. The gap between the two rules along the path is capped by a known function of time. The conclusion is an explicit bound: the drift at any time is at most the starting gap plus the accumulated rule gap, both scaled by an exponential factor. Such bounds are workhorses for proving that equations behave well.
arxiv-2503-24039:
E. Tempel, J. Laur, and colleagues present a code that estimates galaxy distances from colors alone in a 2025 astronomy study. Spectroscopic redshifts are exact but slow, so large surveys lean on photometric estimates fitted against template spectra. Their code, built at Tartu Observatory, was applied to a major galaxy survey catalogue with photometry in nine bands.

Estimated redshifts are checked against the spectroscopic values available for the same galaxies. Accuracy statistics tell cosmologists how much weight the photometric distances can bear in studies of galaxy evolution. Reliable cheap distances multiply the value of every wide imaging survey.
arxiv-2504-07239:
Vitorio and four colleagues design a unit vector controller for uncertain systems with saturating actuators in twenty twenty-five. Actuator saturation limits how much control force can be applied. The systems considered have several inputs and polytopic uncertainty in their parameters. The goal is a controller that drives the system to its origin in finite time.

They give matrix inequality conditions to compute the control gain. Those conditions guarantee finite time stability of the closed loop system. An optimization problem enlarges the estimated region from which trajectories still converge. That region accounts for the saturation limits explicitly. Numerical simulations illustrate how the method performs. The authors present it as a robust design tool for constrained control.
arxiv-2504-10939:
Krynski and co-authors model how barium stars form, focusing on the orbits their birth leaves behind. Barium stars' spread in period and orbit shape has resisted explanation for over thirty years. Simulations show a disk can form around the pair as the giant star sheds mass. Dust in that wind changes how much spin the system loses. It also changes how much mass the companion gains through wind overflow.

The team updated a binary evolution code with these effects. A disk is switched on when wind overflow starts. Its pull on the pair follows standard resonance theory. The richer physics aims to match the stubborn orbit pattern at last.
arxiv-2504-12739:
Runyi Hu and seven co-authors watermark images in a way that can be found and read locally. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A watermark proves ownership and exposes tampering. Global marks are easy to wash out of a small edited region. Local marks survive better but are harder to build. Their MaskWM framework offers both modes.

One variant embeds globally yet extracts from masked local areas. Masking during decoding teaches the system to localize marks. That supports tamper detection on edited photos. The second variant embeds locally for finer protection of small regions. Masks guide both encoding and decoding there. Training follows the classic encoder, distortion, decoder pattern. Image protection gains a flexible, region-aware tool.
arxiv-2504-17739:
Lorenzo Simone, Mauro Giuseppe Camporeale, Vito Marco Rubino, Vincenzo Gervasi, and Giovanni Dimauro detect Parkinson's disease early from speech, and show their work. The disease erodes movement and more, and the voice falters among its first signs. A detector that explains itself earns more trust than a black box. Their deep learning system points to the vocal segments behind each call.

Those highlighted segments are tied to features of articulation, the mechanics of forming sounds. Such links hint at the underlying muscle and nerve damage. The team tested on an Italian voice database of eight hundred thirty-one recordings from sixty-five people, patients and healthy speakers alike. Accuracy rivaled the best known methods. The added clarity sets this approach apart. Doctors can see which sounds drove the verdict and judge whether they fit the patient.
arxiv-2505-00039:
Hudson de Martim wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It builds a search-and-answer system for law that respects how laws are ranked, change over time, and cause later change.

Plain text search is blind to that shape, so it can serve stale or out-of-date law. The design stores norms in a graph that splits the broad work of a law from each dated version of its parts. Law-making acts are nodes too, so cause can be traced. A planner then guides queries for point-in-time lookup, spread of change, and proof of source. A case study on the constitution of Brazil shows the setup gives dated, checkable ground for language models.
arxiv-2505-04739:
Kais Ammari, Vilmos Komornik, Mauricio Sepulveda, and Octavio Vera studied stabilization in twenty twenty-five. Their case is a model of two porous rigid solids mixed as one. Porous mixes such as bone, soil, or engineered foams bend in coupled ways. Plain elasticity misses those ways. The authors study the system's initial boundary value problem with numeric tools. They ask when vibrations die out. They ask how fast they die.

Their tests probe strong stabilization and polynomial decay of solutions. They do so with varied damping at work. They vary key parameters. They watch which ones rule the dynamics and the decay rate. The goal is firm rules that ensure stabilization, with rates you can state in numbers. The results guide how porous composite structures can be built or held in check. The wish is that bad shaking fades at a pace you can foresee.
arxiv-2505-05139:
Shruthi Patil, Noah Pflugradt, Jann Weinand, Jürgen Kropp, and Detlef Stolten map local energy use in two thousand twenty five. Fine grained energy and emissions data guide local climate plans. Small municipalities often lack data at their own scale. Their study builds local level datasets for Germany and Spain.

National data are split down with open sources and statistics. XGBoost fills missing values in the input records. District and province figures steer the stepwise disaggregation. Confidence ratings mark how reliable each local value is. The open approach scales to other regions needing local plans.
arxiv-2505-05739:
Akira Onuki, writing alone in twenty twenty-five, builds a full theory of how polar fluids line up in electric fields. The theory tracks two kinds of alignment at once. One kind comes from how each unit turns, and the other comes from charge shifts inside the fluid. A shared term in the free energy links the two kinds.

Onuki works out both still and time-based forms of the theory. The math gives back known results from Onsager and Kirkwood, plus the known Debye form for field response. One key find is that swings in total alignment hinge on bench setup. Fixed charge and fixed voltage give quite distinct results.
arxiv-2505-06639:
Joseph Hahn and co-authors used computer models in 2025 to ask how narrow, eccentric planetary rings keep their sharp edges. Ring thickness should slowly spread a ringlet outward, yet rings such as Saturn's stay thin. The standard account invokes shepherd moons whose gravity confines the ring. But spacecraft findings of Saturn's rings found no such shepherds for some ringlets, which undermines that story.

The models test an other: the ringlet's own gravity confines it. Across many starting conditions, the ringlet's gravity effect on itself grew the outer edge's eccentricity at the inner edge's expense. This pushed a nonlinearity measure past a threshold. Past that point, the outward flow of angular momentum from thickness and self-gravity cancels to zero. With no net transfer, the ringlet stops spreading, a self-confining state reached without any moon.
arxiv-2505-09839:
Venkatesan Guruswami and Shilun Li prove a density form of a classic sphere theorem. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The Frankl-Rödl theorem concerns pairs of vectors kept at one fixed distance. On a sphere, distance translates to a fixed inner product. The density version asks about large regions of the sphere. Random pairs inside such a region should often hit the set distance.

The authors set lower bounds for that chance when the region is big enough. They widen the result to whole configurations with prescribed pairwise products. A class they call inductive configurations includes simplices with any allowed inner product. As a payoff, all such configurations are sphere Ramsey. Combinatorics on spheres gains a robust density toolkit.
arxiv-2505-12939:
Roy, Maiti, and Laroze study electric currents in a tiny ring of atoms in twenty twenty-five. A magnetic flux through the ring can drive a persistent circular current. Their ring follows a dimerized pattern with two alternating link strengths. Site energies vary slowly around the ring in a cosine pattern.

They treat both free electrons and electrons that repel each other on the same site. A mean field method handles the interacting case. Both the strength and shape of the site pattern shape the current in key ways. Surprisingly, a stronger pattern can help electrons spread out, unlike in disordered rings. They also study ring size, filling level, and spin currents. Possible lab realizations of the system are briefly described.
arxiv-2505-13139:
Fotopoulos, Karachalios, and Koukouloyannis study how long neat wave forms can last in a grid form of a classic wave equation for cold gases. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

They match the grid form to a near twin that can be solved in full. A trap that holds the gas makes the twin need care in weighted spaces. The team bounds the gap between the two systems' paths for broad start data, and maps how that gap can grow. For the grid form, the bounds mean small bright lump waves, driven by the twin's known path, last a long time. This holds even with a weak trap in place. Worked runs back the claims.
arxiv-2505-18139:
Gordon Dai and Yunze Xiao argue that clashing measures should be welcomed in responsible AI work in a 2025 position study. Fairness definitions conflict with each other, and accuracy trades against privacy, so no single metric suite can be made fully consistent. The usual instinct is to treat that inconsistency as a defect to engineer away.

The authors contend the opposite. Keeping contradictory metrics preserves the range of moral views held by different stakeholders, a benefit they call normative pluralism. Treating metrics as divergent objectives, rather than one score, forces honest negotiation about trade-offs. The piece is an argument, offered to shift how teams judge responsible systems.
arxiv-2506-00739:
Chiyu Zhang and colleagues release DefenderBench, an open toolkit for grading language agents on cybersecurity work. Agents powered by large language models reason well in words, but their security skills were untested. The bench covers offense, defense, and knowledge tasks. Its arenas include network intrusion, malicious content detection, code flaw analysis, and security quizzes.

The design stresses low cost and easy access alongside fair, strict scoring. Several leading models, open and closed, took the bench through one standard agent harness. The top score went to a recent Claude model, with its reasoning variant close behind. The best open model trailed only modestly. Custom models and tasks slot into the modular bench easily. The authors aim to make security agent comparisons reproducible across labs.
arxiv-2506-00839:
Pedro Figueiredo, Qihao He, and Nima Khademi Kalantari teach rendering software where to aim its light rays. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Monte Carlo rendering traces random paths to build an image. Guiding those paths toward bright directions cuts noise. Neural guides learn such direction maps. Old maps were either fast or expressive, never both.

Their trick splits the two-dimensional directional map into two one-dimensional ones. A network estimates each at fixed points, with interpolation between. Training maximizes how well the learned map matches the true one. A second network caches incoming light to steady the learning. Experiments show cleaner images for the same effort. Movie and game rendering gain efficiency.
arxiv-2506-01139:
Pollner and a team including Török and Pósa pushed a tiny switch circuit in twenty twenty-five past one hundred mega-hertz, for use in brain-like nets that solve by sync. Such nets let physics settle hard problems as their parts lock step. The switch gear is a vanadium oxide chip that flips fast between states.

Layout tweaks to chip and circuit lifted the beat more than ten-fold. They also timed how set and reset slow under beat use versus lone pulses. Those times cap how fast the nets can run. The step opens fast, low-power wave nets, they say.
arxiv-2506-02339:
Jiawen Huang, Felipe Sousa, and three co-authors adapt speech recognizers to transcribe song lyrics over full backing tracks. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, tackles automatic lyrics transcription. Singing strains models trained on plain speech, and accompaniment makes it worse. They fine-tune a foundation speech model with a low-rank method.

Training on isolated vocals alone does not carry to mixed audio. Mixing both domains naively also disappoints. Their fix adds a consistency loss tying the vocal and mixture views together. Gains are modest but steady across tests. The trick avoids a separate vocal separation step. Music tools gain a simpler path to usable lyric drafts.
arxiv-2506-02439:
Shuang Li and four co-authors use words to help match people across camera types in video. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The task is person re-identification between visible and infrared footage. Night cameras see heat, not color, so the same person looks quite different. Sequence-level traits must be pulled out that stay stable across both views.

Language offers a shared description of a person's traits in both modes. The team uses the CLIP model to build video-level text prompts. One module crafts prompts that ignore the camera mode. Another weaves in space and time cues from the frames. Together they guide learning toward features both modes share. The framework is simple in design but strong in tests. It targets security and search uses for video.
arxiv-2506-03939:
Junqi Gao and six co-authors send a team of agents to walk knowledge graphs for better answers. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Graph-based retrieval grounds language models in structured facts. Single-agent systems follow fixed loops and gather shallow evidence. Preset reasoning schemes cannot adjust depth on the fly. Semantic slips go uncorrected. Their Graph Counselor answers with collaboration.

An adaptive extraction module reads text, structure, and degree signals at many levels. Agents divide the exploration work and cross-check each other. Reasoning depth flexes with the question's difficulty. Semantic correction happens during the walk, not after. Specialized domains with rich graphs benefit most. Factual accuracy is the metric the design chases.
arxiv-2506-04039:
Jiulong Wu and seven colleagues propose EMPO, a method for reducing hallucinations in large vision-language models, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Such models sometimes describe things that are not in an image. Causes include misalignment between image and text, plus habits inherited from the underlying language model.

Earlier preference alignment methods tuned answers to human taste while ignoring modality alignment. That neglect left models leaning too heavily on language. EMPO instead aligns preferences around entities in the image. The team automatically built preference data from open instruction datasets, covering image, instruction, and response quality. On five hallucination benchmarks, the method cut error rates sharply. One benchmark's hallucination rate fell by about eighty-six percent.
arxiv-2506-05439:
Takishita and co-authors test if word cores in sight-word tools make up for weak sight codes. Sight-word tools oft build on CLIP sight codes, which bear known flaws. Three CLIP-based tools took a probe task built for the test. Self-focus cuts in set spots form the probe's core move. Finds show CLIP codes still give the word core clean sense facts. Those facts sit ready to read for the word side in tools.

When sight codes lose tale depth, the word core can fill in. It claws back most of the lost score in those runs. That split of work is live and shifts by case in the tools. Next builds could push more sight work to the word core. Lean sight codes may thus cost less than past tales said.
arxiv-2506-05839:
Steven Libby, a solo author, presents a study from twenty twenty-five on how a compiler for the Curry language runs its code. Curry mixes logic and function styles of coding. Past work built the compiler, named RICE. What was missing was a clear account of how its programs run step by step.

Libby sets out the cuts made to the FlatCurry form of the code so it can run. He then gives rules for each step, in a style drawn from a known model of lazy run order. Last, he proves these rules match the standard rules for Curry. The result ties the compiler's real runs to the language's formal sense. It gives later builders a firm base to check their work against.
arxiv-2506-06539:
Yijie Hao, Haofei Yu, and Jiaxuan You name a failure mode of large language models in twenty twenty-five. When a query has many conditions, models often answer only part of it. They may skip some conditions or invent parts that were never asked. The authors call this intent hallucination, since the model's grasp of intent goes wrong.

They built a benchmark, FAITHQA, to measure the problem in a set way. It holds just over twenty thousand problems, across many topics and levels of difficulty. It covers plain queries and cases where the model also retrieves outside text. Early tests found intent hallucination to be common across models. Readers get a tool that looks past wrong facts to wrong aims.
arxiv-2506-06739:
Andrew Cropper, Filipe Gouveia, and David Cerna wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on making logic-based learning faster. Inductive logic programming searches a space of rules for one that fits examples plus background facts, and that space is huge.

Their idea is to shrink the space before the search starts. Using background knowledge alone, the method finds rules that can never belong to a best answer, like rules that would call an even number odd. Those dead ends are cut away with an answer set programming tool. In tests on visual reasoning and game tasks, ten seconds of this trimming cut learning from over ten hours to two seconds in one case. Accuracy stayed the same. The authors frame preprocessing as cheap insurance against wasted search.
arxiv-2506-09539:
Alvaro Garcia Murga and Manuele Leonelli use Bayesian networks to sort out what drives home prices in three Spanish cities. Price work needs models that both predict well and stay clear to read. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team built chance based maps from a huge pool of geo-tagged home listings in Madrid, Barcelona, and Valencia. Each city showed its own logic. Madrid split by access to perks, Barcelona by home type and class, and Valencia by place and build traits. The maps let users test what-if cases and weigh which factors matter most, which the authors link to fair city policy.
arxiv-2506-11139:
Namhoon Kim and Sara Fridovich-Keil deliver a humbling benchmark for implicit neural representations, the networks that store a signal as a function instead of a grid. Such representations compress images and volumes elegantly, but their capacity and scaling were murky. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the pair test many variants on two- and three-dimensional signals, real and synthetic, across bandwidths. Tasks cover memorization and generalization: tomography, super-resolution, and denoising. Results are sorted by model size and signal type.

For dense signals, a plain regularized grid with interpolation often trained faster and matched or beat every implicit network at equal parameter count. Implicit models won mainly on binary signals like shape contours. The authors aim the conclusion at practitioners: choose the representation the signal deserves, not the fashionable one.
arxiv-2506-11639:
Hassan Mortada and four co-authors present Recursive KalmanNet, a neural network that boosts the classic Kalman filter for state tracking with sound error bounds. The Kalman filter is best for straight systems with clean bell shaped noise, but real cases break those terms. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The network is shaped by the filter's own steps and spreads its error bounds with a classic exact formula. Training tunes it by a likelihood score for bell shaped error. In tests with non bell shaped white noise in the reads, the model beat both the plain filter and a top deep learning rival. Gains held for both state exactness and trust in the error bounds.
arxiv-2506-13739:
Guy Laban, Micol Spitale, Minja Axelsson, Nida Itrat Abbasi, and Hatice Gunes draw lessons from studies of robots for mental wellbeing in a 2025 review. Social robots are being tried as helpers for emotional health outside clinics. Results so far mix promise with pitfalls, and the field lacks settled guidance.

Six insights structure the discussion. Wellbeing has no single objective measure, and robots need not play companion to help. Virtual contact is gaining ground, clinicians should join design work, and one-off meetings differ from long relationships. The authors weigh evidence from trials and real deployments. Their cautions aim to keep enthusiasm honest as robots enter care settings.
arxiv-2506-14339:
Azuki Onaya and Hiroki Tanaka hunt, in a 2025 preprint, for brain wave signs of struggling to hear speech in noise. Some listeners test normal on hearing checks yet cannot follow talk in a room. No diagnosis exists for that gap. Ten Japanese-speaking students took listening tasks under EEG recording. Conditions ranged from rest to attending a lecture over background noise, to attending the noise itself. The team tracked alpha wave power and peak rate, the long-range patterning of alpha rhythms, and delta wave power.

Alpha power dropped when students attended against noise, a sign of heavier mental load. Its peak rate barely moved, so it reads as a poor gauge. The long-range patterning rose under attention tasks, while delta power stayed flat. Alpha power in noise also tracked screening scores for listening difficulty, in the negative direction. The authors propose it as a candidate indicator.
arxiv-2506-16239:
Michael Parfenov builds a theory of integration for quaternions modeled closely on complex integration, in a two thousand twenty-five mathematics paper. Quaternions extend complex numbers to four dimensions and appear in physics and engineering. Complex integration, by contrast, is a mature theory with famous theorems.

Parfenov extends earlier representation ideas for holomorphic functions to integration itself. He introduces the notion of an H-plane, generalizing the complex plane. On that foundation he adapts the central results one by one. The complex Taylor theorem, Cauchy's theorem, and Cauchy's integral formula all get quaternionic versions. Laurent series and the residue theorem follow the same path. The paper is a systematic translation of a classical theory.
arxiv-2506-19239:
Guillaume Graciani and Marcel Filoche predict that random light inside a mirrored cavity can measure tiny changes with great precision. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The setup uses Lambertian reflections, which scatter light in a soft, even way. The light field inside is random, yet its interference pattern responds in a measured, repeatable way. Small shifts in wavelength, refractive index, or shape all leave marks.

The predicted sensitivity matches experiments that tracked deformations down to the picometer scale. That is a trillionth of a meter. Such reach usually demands carefully controlled laser setups. Here randomness itself becomes the measuring tool. The theory gives the scheme a firm base. It may guide cheap, rugged sensors for labs and industry.
arxiv-2506-20539:
Alberto Padovan leads a team of six on this software paper from two thousand twenty-five, which appeared in SoftwareX. It presents resolvent4py, a Python package for the study, slimming, and control of huge linear systems.

Such systems can hold millions or billions of degrees of freedom. The package feels like numpy or scipy to write, yet runs in parallel across machines. It leans on MPI through three bridge libraries that wrap PETSc and SLEPc. That mix lets short, clear Python code chew through very large jobs. The tool serves fluid and solid mechanics, graph theory, and molecular dynamics, among other fields.
arxiv-2506-21139:
Taylor Baird, Rodolphe Vuilleumier, and Sara Bonella published a computational physics paper in 2025 on lattice vibrations. Vibrations, or phonons, reveal a material's heat and light behavior. Light atoms and cold conditions add strong quantum effects. Including those effects in simulations is usually very expensive.

The authors combine two methods to cut that cost. A quantum thermal bath adds nuclear quantum effects cheaply. A newer correlator method then extracts vibration frequencies from the motion data. Together they give phonon patterns across a crystal. Tests began with simple one-dimensional systems. The team then applied the scheme to solid neon. They report strong efficiency and accuracy, with clear limits noted.
arxiv-2506-22139:
Shaojie Zhang and four co-authors present Q-Frame, a way to pick video frames for language models by the question asked. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Video models that take frames at even gaps miss key moments tied to the query. Long videos also flood the model with data.

Q-Frame scores frames with a text-image match network and picks the ones that fit the query, with no training needed. It also scales frame detail to the content, so more frames fit in the same budget. On bench sets for long and general video tasks, it beats even sampling and past pick methods. It plugs into many video models as an add-on.
arxiv-2506-22839:
Hannah Wakeford, Laura Mayorga, and a large group of contributing authors lay out a science case for a planned space telescope. The document appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The Habitable Worlds Observatory is meant to study planets around other stars in new depth. This case focuses on planets that cross in front of their stars.

The team wants to track how such planets spin by watching their light shift across each orbit. Those curves reveal how air moves, what it holds, and where haze sits. The telescope could reach cooler planets on wider orbits than current tools can touch. Its wide color range would catch both reflected light and heat glow. Light wobble measures would also help sort the haze types. The case argues these steps would sharpen our picture of distant air and weather.
arxiv-2507-00039:
Lucas Potin, Rosa Figueiredo, Vincent Labatut, and Christine Largeron compare ways to judge patterns in graphs in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Graph classification sorts networks by their structure, for tasks from social analysis to biology. Pattern-based methods classify by which subgraphs appear, and the patterns can be read and explained afterward. A quality measure scores how well each pattern separates the classes. Dozens of such measures exist, and picking one is guesswork.

The authors test the measures head to head, with attention to how the data are prepared first. Preprocessing turns out to matter, not just the scoring rule. Their results guide practitioners who want interpretable graph classifiers. The work serves data mining researchers who mine subgraphs for meaning.
arxiv-2507-02539:
John Campbell builds algebras whose representation sizes are counted by a special kind of tableau in a 2025 mathematics study. A famous identity for the symmetric group ties a factorial to the squares of tableau counts, reflecting that algebra's semisimple structure. Campbell seeks the same pattern with standard immaculate tableaux, tableaux built on compositions rather than partitions, in place of the classical Young kind.

Starting from the counts of those tableaux, he constructs a semisimple algebra, a direct sum of matrix algebras, whose module dimensions realize the numbers. The construction extends a beloved piece of algebraic combinatorics to a newer tableau family.
arxiv-2507-04639:
Annu Bura and eight co-authors weigh small jets from rejoin of pull fields, called nanojets, in two kinds of sun flare. They use sharp far light shots from the Solar Orbiter trip. They look at one flare that bursts out and one that stays held in. They find fifty-nine jets in all. Forty-four are in the burst flare and fifteen in the held one.

The two groups stand far apart. Jets in held flares move more slow and hold low strength on a small scale. Jets in burst flares are more fast and reach a step up in strength. Maps of pull fields out from data show the burst zone has a more sheared arch. It is more twirled and holds more strength per bulk. The team takes this to mean the pull zone near a jet rules how strong such small jets grow.
arxiv-2507-08139: Leung gives faster algorithms for a classic number theory task in twenty twenty-five. A theorem of Erdos, Ginzburg, and Ziv says any long enough sequence of integers holds a subsequence of a set length whose sum is divisible by that length. Finding such a subsequence quickly is the problem. The best known method took time growing as n log n. Leung offers a simple practical method that is faster, and a theoretical method that is faster still. Both rest on a faster variant of boolean convolution.
arxiv-2507-09139:
Dewen Zhang, Tahir Hussain, Wangpeng An, and Hayaru Shouno wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It improves language-guided pose estimation, where a model finds body joints from a written description, by upgrading the bridge between images and words.

Older systems passed joint locations as fixed priors, so new poses broke them. A recent language-based system freed the joints but joined vision and text with a simple linear layer, too weak for fine placement. PoseLLM swaps in a small two-layer network with a curved activation, letting the two data types mix in richer ways. Trained only on the COCO dataset, it edged its predecessor on that test set. It also kept its skill on art images and another pose set it had never trained on. The authors say connector design, not model size, was the bottleneck.
arxiv-2507-09839:
MohammadReza Davari and three co-authors improve automatic tuning of prompts for language models reached through black-box services, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Such tuning often learns only from failed answers, which makes prompts unstable and prone to drifting off course. Good parts of a prompt can be lost along the way.

Their framework also learns from correct answers, drawing a steadying signal that protects what already works. Both signals are noisy, so they sample each several times and merge them into one clear directive. They also define the practical task of moving an expert prompt to a new model version without losing key instructions. Tests show higher accuracy, faster settling, and less damage during such moves.
arxiv-2507-10039:
Steven Palayew, Bo Wang, and Gary Bader ask, in a 2025 preprint, how language models can partner with specialist models of single-cell data. Foundation models like scGPT read gene activity in single cells and do well on many tasks. But much biological knowledge lives in text, which they cannot use. Language models can, and they rival the specialists on some tasks. Rather than swap one for the other, the authors combine them. Their model, scMPT, fuses both kinds of representation.

The team first probed which biological insights drive the language model's success. Then they built the fused model on scGPT plus those text-based features. Across datasets, scMPT beat both parents and, just as key, was steadier. The two parents often swung far apart from dataset to dataset. Other fusion styles were also tried. The study argues the two model families cover each other's blind spots.
arxiv-2507-11239:
Janovská and seven co-authors used ultrasound to probe stress inside cold-sprayed nickel in twenty twenty-five. Cold spraying builds metal parts by blasting powder at a surface, leaving high compressive stress locked inside. Measuring that stress without cutting the part is valuable.

Nickel is magnetic, and its elastic softening near its Curie temperature depends strongly on stress. Using contactless resonant ultrasound, the team tracked stiffness and internal friction as two nickel deposits heated through that point. The softening's size revealed the stress level. The method also watched recrystallization, where strained grains regrow, and checked stress evenness through the deposit's thickness. A room-temperature version of the probe was proposed and tested as well.
arxiv-2507-11939:
Yichen Xu and five co-authors build the first large test of how well vision-language models answer questions about charts in many languages. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Charts carry data across borders, yet past tests stuck to English. That leaves most of the world's readers unmeasured.

Their bench holds more than twenty thousand charts and even more question-answer pairs across ten languages. A pipeline built the set by translating data and reusing chart code, with model help and strict checks. Top models scored far worse outside English, above all in low-resource tongues. A matched training set lifted scores a lot when used for fine-tuning. Gains held across model sizes and designs. The authors offer the bench as a base for truly global chart readers.
arxiv-2507-12239:
Alessandro Codenotti wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It proves fixed point theorems for flows of automorphism groups of Fraïssé structures, in the null and tame cases.

The proof leans on a broad form of the Kechris-Pestov-Todorčević correspondence, due to Nguyen Van Thé. That bridge links Ramsey-type traits of a class of finite structures to fixed points of group actions. When the age of the structure is a free joint embedding class, every null flow has a fixed point. When it is a free amalgamation class, every tame flow has one. The paper sits in topological dynamics and logic.
arxiv-2507-14839:
Ruwanga Konara and four colleagues propose a quantum blockchain that encodes classical data in phases, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Blockchains lean on classical cryptography for security. Large quantum computers running algorithms like Shor's could break that cryptography within the coming decade.

Two earlier quantum designs point in different directions. Time-entangled GHZ state chains offer physics-based tamper detection, while quantum hypergraph chains offer scalability. The new framework merges features of both. Data goes into quantum registers using phase encoding rather than plain copying. Any undetected measurement attack should disturb the states visibly. The authors aim for information-theoretic protection with better efficiency than the entangled design alone.
arxiv-2507-16239:
Sleeba Varghese, Pierre Illien, and Benjamin Rotenberg test a view of polar fluids in twenty twenty-five. Polar fluids sit at the base of salt fluids and life based media, so how they move counts. The view they build, stochastic density functional theory, tracks how charge lean shifts with time. Their test case is the Stockmayer fluid: Lennard-Jones grains, each with a point dipole set in.

From Langevin laws for slow, drag bound grains, they work out forms for the scatter curves. The curves split by wave path into parts that run with the wave and parts that run across it. Runs of the same fluid give the check on those forms. The view gets the with wave part right in full. The across wave part comes out less well in the test. The piece names the strong side and the weak side of the view.
arxiv-2507-16439:
Gunnar Larsen, Carol Wong, and Anthony Peruma test language models on code naming in twenty twenty-five. Scientists now write much of their own research software. Good method names aid comprehension, but naming quality in scientific code is little studied. Language models offer a new way to appraise and improve such names automatically.

The team evaluated four popular models on four hundred ninety-six method names. The names came from Python code in Jupyter notebooks. Models analyzed grammar patterns and suggested better names. They were somewhat effective and mostly followed good practice, such as starting names with verbs. Their handling of domain-specific terms was inconsistent, though. Readers learn where automated naming help is ready and where it still stumbles.
arxiv-2507-16739:
Jackson Barnes, Stephen Schwartz, and Seth Jacobson model how small worlds form from falling pebble clouds. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses gravity to pull a cloud of large grains into solid bodies. Older models merged grains on contact and puffed up their size. That hid the shapes, spin, and tight orbits of the worlds that form.

Their method lets grains rest on each other with real contact forces. Grains keep their true size and do not just merge. One cloud can yield many paired worlds this way. The team can now track each world's shape, spin rate, and orbit in fine detail.
arxiv-2507-17439:
Byeonghee Lee and four co-authors build a statistical estimator for treatment effects that resists bad data, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their setting is observational data with many variables but few cases, as in gene studies. Stray outliers and wrong model guesses can easily wreck standard estimates.

The method guards both sides of the problem at once: how outcomes are modeled and how treatment chances are balanced. It sits inside a likelihood framework with a penalty that selects variables. Theory shows it stays consistent even if one model side is wrong, picks the right variables, and keeps normal behavior. A custom interval method avoids relying on large-sample shortcuts. Tests on gene data beat rival methods on bias and interval accuracy.
arxiv-2507-18039:
Ahmad Suleiman, Yiming Tang, and Daqing Hou survey eighty computing faculty on what helps or blocks project-based learning in their classrooms. Learning through projects promises motivated, collaborative problem-solvers. Adoption, though, is patchy. The mixed-methods survey quantifies barriers and enablers with closed questions and mines an open question for themes.

Faculty value the approach but adopt it selectively. Planning and managing the learning process, designing suitable projects, and thin institutional support for time, funding, and assistants are the chief drags. Peer collaboration, professional development, and institutional incentives predict who adopts and persists. Projects themselves are sourced from research, industry partnerships, and colleagues' shelves. The findings give departments a concrete support list. Project-based learning succeeds, the data say, when institutions treat it as infrastructure rather than individual heroism.
arxiv-2508-01439:
