Lulu Zhang and a large team of colleagues prepared diagnostic guides in 2025 for the James Webb Space Telescope. The telescope sees mid-infrared glow lines from gas near feeding black holes in galaxy centers, lines that older tools could barely detect. Which lines reveal heat, pressure, and radiation strength in that gas needed a careful map.

Using a standard photoionization code, the team modeled over twenty lines and tracked how each reacts as conditions change. Lines from highly charged argon and neon stood out as strong tools for reading the gas near active black holes. The guide helps observers turn Webb spectra into physical facts about galaxy cores. It systematizes line choices before precious telescope time is spent.
arxiv-2508-03239:
Mirco Bussmann and six co-authors ask whether a giant impact once struck Venus, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Huge collisions were common early in the solar system's life. A big hit on Venus could have changed its spin and its heat history. The team ran computer simulations of such impacts. They used a method that tracks countless particles of rock and metal.

Their model Venus has an iron core and a rocky mantle. The impactors vary in mass, speed, and angle, from head-on to glancing blows. Starting spin and inner heat also vary. The team then checks the spin periods and debris discs that result. They look for cases that match Venus as it is today. The work helps sort out how Venus got its slow, backward spin.
arxiv-2508-05939:
Engh studies how people choose when paying attention is costly in twenty twenty-five. Classic models assume a shopper weighs the hidden state of the world but knows each option's traits. In real life, traits such as quality are unsure too, and learning them costs time and thought. His model charges for both kinds of learning under one cost rule.

He shows a best pattern of choice odds exists and is the only one of its kind. It gives every trait combo some chance, even ones that turn out poorly. Costly trait learning pulls choice toward common traits, while costly state learning flattens choice. A seller can lift welfare by shifting what shoppers see, with no need to know their tastes.
arxiv-2508-06039:
Hongliang Jiang and De-liang Zhong compute a string scattering amplitude in a curved background with extra internal modes, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The background pairs anti-de Sitter space with a sphere, a classic holography setup where a string amplitude mirrors a correlation function in a boundary quantum theory.

The amplitude is the Virasoro-Shapiro amplitude extended to Kaluza-Klein modes, the tower of states from the compact directions. The authors want its first correction from the curvature of the background. They start from a special case, matching guessed formulas built from special polylogarithm functions against the boundary theory's expansion. Then a Mellin-space formalism generalizes the answer to arbitrary mode numbers. The final formula is an integral over the Riemann sphere, echoing the flat-space original but dressed with richer functions. Such amplitudes test holographic duality beyond its simplest limits.
arxiv-2508-06239:
Tova Holmes and Lawrence Lee estimated event rates for a proposed ten tera-electron-volt muon collider in a 2025 document. A muon smasher would smash muons at energies far beyond present machines. Its sensors must survive an unusual flood of background and signal processes. This short document surveys the rates of a wide range of processes expected at such a machine. Giving a first look at what will fill the sensor and how often the interesting events occur.

Those rates drive hard engineering choices: how the readout electronics keep up. Whether a trigger system can select events in time, and how luminosity, the machine's delivered intensity, gets gauged. It is planning groundwork for a smasher still on the drawing board.
arxiv-2508-08939:
Eduarda Caldeira, Fadi Boutros, and Naser Damer detect face morphing attacks with a foundation model never trained for the task. Morphing blends identity facts from two people into one face image. Recognition systems may verify that image as belonging to both people. That is a grave security threat. Multimodal foundation models like CLIP offer strong zero-shot skill. But past biometric work mostly fine-tuned them. It neglected direct use that can spread to new cases.

Their method, MADPromptS, is pure zero-shot. CLIP is used with no extra training or fine-tuning. The gain comes from the design and pooling of many text prompts for each class. Pooling embeddings of varied prompts aligns the model's forms with the task better. It catches richer cues of real versus morphed samples. Results show prompt pooling lifts zero-shot scores a lot.
arxiv-2508-14639:
Greene, Welker, and Wille study shape counting for sets built from triangles and cubes with added symmetry in twenty twenty-five. Such sets are used to model spaces in a form computers can handle. Symmetry maps let the same piece be reused in flipped or turned forms. The team asks how the counting rules, called homology, treat these maps.

They look at the chain of sums used to compute the counts. With number fields of a mild type, they show a big chunk of that chain adds nothing at all. Dropping it gives the same counts with less work and cleaner structure. They also give cases that show the claim fails for broader number rings.
arxiv-2508-15439:
Yogesh Kumar, Uday Agarwal, Manish Gupta, and Anand Mishra present MATR, a model that finds a moment in one video by using another video as the query. Their twenty twenty-five paper tackles video-to-video moment retrieval. A user gives a clip of an event, and the system must find the matching stretch in a target video, with no labels to guide it.

MATR is a transformer that aligns the two videos in two stages, at the level of frames and of meaning. It then marks which frames are foreground and where the moment starts and ends. A self-taught pre-training step, finding random clips in videos, warms it up. Tests on two data sets beat past methods by clear margins.
arxiv-2508-16139:
Keon-Woo Roh, Yeong-Joon Ju, and Seong-Whan Lee introduced XLQA in twenty twenty-five, a benchmark for multilingual question answering that respects locale. Most QA tests are English-first and assume the right answer is the same everywhere. In truth, questions about holidays, laws, or customs have answers that vary by place and culture.

XLQA starts from three thousand English seed questions expanded into eight languages, filtered for semantic consistency. Human-verified labels mark which questions are locale-sensitive and which are not. Testing five leading multilingual models exposed clear failures on the sensitive ones, with gaps between English and other languages traced to missing locale knowledge. The authors offer the benchmark and its method as a resource for fairer multilingual evaluation.
arxiv-2508-18739:
Chang Wang, Siyu Yan, and colleagues generate advertising headlines that vary as well as persuade in a 2025 study. Headlines must be good enough to earn clicks and varied enough to reach different audience segments. Tuning models only for quality or click rate tends to produce many near-identical lines, wasting that variety.

Their framework optimizes a language model for diversity and quality together. A semantic design first spreads candidate headlines across meanings before ranking them. Joint training then keeps the spread without giving up click appeal. More varied headlines let advertisers test fresh angles and speak to segments that a single style would miss.
arxiv-2508-19339:
Kristoffer Hansson and eight co-authors compute how strongly common atoms stick to the dust grains found between the stars. Their study, from two thousand twenty-five, uses a fast quantum-based method.

How atoms bind to dust shapes how grains grow and what reactions run on their skins. The team used a model face of a mixed rock dust, with many spots where an atom can sit. They tested ten common atoms, from carbon to nickel. Each atom showed a wide range of binding strength by spot. Some, such as silicon, stuck hardest on the whole, while magnesium stuck least. The work aids models of how dust and gas change in deep space.
arxiv-2509-00039:
Yuqi Li and eight co-authors present AMMKD in 2025, a method to shrink vision-language models for phones without losing search skill. Such models match images with text, but their size and cost block use on mobile gear. Distillation trains a small student model to copy a large teacher. Here many teachers and both data modes are used at once.

A fusion network first merges sharp traits from image and text. Two CLIP teachers are pre-trained, and text traits are stored ahead as class vectors to save time. The student learns to match teacher outputs through a tuned loss that adapts as training proceeds. The result aims for light models that still retrieve image and text pairs well.
arxiv-2509-00139:
Obasho M, Shambhavi Jaiswal, Santanu Das, and Krishna Mohan Parattu use a generative network in 2025 to clean maps of the cosmic microwave background. That faint glow holds key clues about the early universe. To read it, teams must strip foreground glow from our galaxy, tool noise, and the blur of the telescope beam.

Their generator is a U-Net, a convolutional design with a bridge shape, set inside an adversarial pair that pits maker against critic. Training maps mimic Planck satellite views, with real beam shape, scan paths, and uneven noise. Rebuilt maps differ from the truth by less than one percent outside the galaxy's band. Sharp cleaning sharpens tests of how the universe began.
arxiv-2509-00239:
Felipe P. Abreu and Welles A. M. Morgado analyze heat fluctuations in a small driven system in 2025. Mesoscopic systems, between atom and bulk scale, are key to biology, tiny engines, and particle cooling. They study an underdamped Brownian particle, a jittering grain with inertia, held in a harmonic trap while temperature swings in a sine wave.

Analytic work and simulations reveal resonant links between position and velocity at set drive rates. The heat distribution turns non-Gaussian and asymmetric, in line with the Fluctuation Theorem, a law that relates forward and reverse chance. Inertia damps the response and slows settling into a periodic steady state. Rhythmic heating could thus steer energy flow at the nanoscale.
arxiv-2509-01139:
Some predictions change the very data they aim to predict, as when a forecast shifts behavior. Guangzheng Zhong, Yang Liu, and Jiming Liu study this setting, called performative prediction. Past work often assumed the loss changed in tightly bounded ways and stuck to linear cases, which rarely match real data with complex curves.

Zhong and the co-authors relax those hard assumptions and extend the method to nonlinear cases. They frame the loss with a maximum margin approach, a way of keeping a wide safety gap, and use kernel methods to handle curved spaces. To measure shift, they compare prediction errors across the old and new distributions. Their design aims to keep sound theory while fitting real, nonlinear problems.
arxiv-2509-01339:
Cheap embedded systems often talk chip to chip over a single wire, saving pins, but older one-wire protocols are slow and fragile. Bochen Ye, Gustavo Naspolini, Kimmo Salo, and Manil Dev Gomony present LinkBo, a single-wire protocol built for low delay, higher throughput, and fault tolerance over varied distances. It adds a hardware interrupt so urgent messages are not stuck waiting.

At the protocol level, high-priority messages with error detection arrive in about fifty microseconds, at least twenty times faster than the commercial 1-Wire option and several times faster than UNI/O. The team built the hardware design and tested it on two FPGA boards. LinkBo held up over wires as long as fifteen meters at three hundred kilobits per second, and reached seven and a half megabits per second over a short eleven centimeter wire.
arxiv-2509-01539:
The force between two nucleons, a proton or a neutron, can be described by a potential, and rebuilding that potential from scattering data is an inverse problem. Ayushi Awasthi, with three co-authors, proposes a physics-guided neural network for that construction. The network is steered by inverse scattering theory rather than left to fit data blindly.

The framework joins the phase function method with a two-stage supervised network model. Synthetic phase shift data are generated by solving the phase equation with a high-order numerical method, keeping the training data physically consistent. One network predicts the attractive strength of a standard potential form, the second its repulsive strength, and a range parameter is set by minimizing phase shift errors. Tests cover low-energy proton and neutron scattering states, with gains in stability and accuracy over conventional inversion.
arxiv-2509-01739:
Benjamin Doerr, Martin S Krejca, and Simon Wietheger speed up a well known optimizer that juggles two goals at once. Such optimizers keep many candidate answers to hold all best trade-offs, called Pareto optima. Large fixed groups slow the search, and picking the group size is a key choice. Their variant starts small and doubles the group after a set number of tries.

Proofs show the growing group finds the full trade-off front much faster on a standard test problem. A second test with a gap also runs faster than the fixed version. A tweak that lingers longer at small sizes does slightly better still. Running copies side by side removes the need to set sizes by hand.
arxiv-2509-02039:
Chul Moon and Soohyun Ahn introduce generalRSS, an R package for ranked set sampling and inference. Ranked set sampling ranks cheap auxiliary data to pick informative samples, beating plain random sampling on efficiency. Balanced designs split samples evenly across strata, while unbalanced designs shift weight where it helps most. Skewed distributions benefit most from the unbalanced form.

Existing software leans heavily on balanced designs, leaving gaps the package fills. Tools cover data generation, smart allocation for unbalanced designs, and inference for both forms. Two medical examples using national survey data show the workflow. One estimates a single mean, the other compares curve areas between groups. The package aims to make ranked set methods routine in applied analysis.
arxiv-2509-02339:
Federica Capellino and four co-authors wrote a 2025 nuclear physics paper applying topological data analysis, a way of studying shape in data, to heavy-ion collisions. Such collisions create quark-gluon plasma, an extremely hot fluid of basic particles.

The team built persistent homology observables, which track features that survive across scales, inside the Trajectum simulation model. They predict values for lead-lead and oxygen-oxygen collisions, carrying uncertainty from model settings fitted earlier. A dictionary then links the new measures to familiar ones such as particle counts and elliptic flow. The new observables mostly mirrored known behaviour and added little extra sensitivity. Even so, the paper proves topology tools work reliably in this setting.
arxiv-2509-02439:
Partha Kumbhakar and Varadharaj Ravi Srinivasan wrote a 2025 paper in differential algebra on when solutions of a paired differential system stay internal, meaning they can be recovered inside a controlled extension. The system couples one equation driven by a rational function with a second, multiplicative equation.

The authors prove two results that generalise earlier theorems of Jin and Moosa about this internality question. Both driving functions depend on a single variable. Internality matters in model theory of differential fields, where it controls how new elements relate to a base structure. Results of this kind feed classification work for differential equations. The note stays at the level of the two theorems and their proofs.
arxiv-2509-02739:
Enric Florit-Simon and Joaquim Serra proved a 2025 mathematics result about the Allen-Cahn equation, a model for how two phases of a material meet. They studied calm, stable patterns in four-dimensional space. In such patterns, the value slides smoothly between two extremes, much like a boundary layer between regions.

Their finding says any stable pattern with limited energy growth must in fact depend on just one direction. In plain terms, the pattern is flat and one-dimensional beneath its surface detail. That kind of rigidity result has weighty side effects in geometry. It supports sharp estimates for how phase boundaries curve. It also feeds into open conjectures about counting and classifying minimal surfaces, which are surfaces that locally use the least area.
arxiv-2509-03039:
Vahid Asadi and 6 co-authors used machine learning in 2025 to sort galaxies into quiet and star-forming groups. Quiet, or quiescent, galaxies have largely stopped making stars, so telling the two apart traces how galaxies age. The standard fitting method is slow and can miss subtle patterns in galaxy colors.

The team trained a boosting classifier on simulated galaxies whose true types were known, using colors from eight bands of light. They cleaned missing values, added realistic noise, and applied brightness and distance cuts to match real survey data. On test data the classifier scored far above the standard method, especially at finding quiet galaxies. Applied to a major catalog, it found more quiet galaxies at every distance range than older rules did.
arxiv-2509-03339:
Khyodeno Mozhui, Tithi Dwary, and K. V. Krishna settled a question about word-representable graphs in 2025. A graph is word-representable when a word over its vertices can encode its edges: two vertices are linked exactly when their letters alternate in the word. Some graphs admit no such word, and earlier examples left open whether their line graphs always fail too.

A line graph turns the original edges into vertices, linking those that shared an endpoint. The authors study Mycielski graphs of odd cycles of length at least five, a known family of non-word-representable graphs. They prove the line graphs of these graphs are word-representable after all. That single family answers the open problem in the negative: failure does not always pass to line graphs.
arxiv-2509-03439:
Yunfan Zhao established concentration inequalities for heavy-tailed random tensors in a 2025 probability paper. Concentration inequalities bound how far a random quantity can stray from its average, and they underpin much of modern statistics and machine learning. Tensors, multi-way arrays of numbers, bring extra structure and difficulty.

Zhao treats simple random tensors whose coefficients follow sub-Weibull distributions, a heavy-tailed family indexed by a parameter between one and two. The bounds show a phase transition: moderate deviations behave as in the light-tailed Gaussian world, while large ones follow heavy-tail rules. The proof rests on a new maximal inequality for products of heavy-tailed variables. A martingale analysis using Nagaev-type inequalities, classic tools for heavy tails, completes the argument.
arxiv-2509-03539:
A 2025 research paper from Chatipat Lorpaiboon and two co-authors examines the committor, a key quantity for rare transitions. For a system that can settle in either of two stable states, the committor gives the odds it ends in one rather than the other. It is usually fitted from trajectory data by minimising a rate expression.

The authors show the standard expression is minimised by the true committor only for a single-step lag time, biasing practical estimates. Their replacement uses the actual entry times into each stable state, called stopping times, instead of a fixed lag. Their new formula recovers the true committor for every lag choice. Benchmark tests show estimates far less sensitive to lag choice. Combining two lag times improves the transition rate further.
arxiv-2509-03739:
April Horton and twenty-two co-authors reinterpret two gaseous arms flowing around the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, in a 2025 research paper. As the Cloud travels through the Milky Way's halo, tidal forces and ram pressure disrupt its gas. The study traces material in front of the Cloud near the 30 Doradus star-forming region.

Radio data from two surveys join ultraviolet absorption data from the ULLYSES programme, along eight sightlines. Gas tied to both arms appears in neutral, low, and medium ionisation states. Line widths for lower-ionisation gas reflect both heat and other motions. The more ionised phase is shaped mostly by non-thermal motion. Decomposition of the hydrogen emission extends both arms beyond earlier predictions. The arms likely converge and partly cross in front of the Cloud. Two rival origins stay open: swept-back outflow, or stripped inflow fuelling new stars.
arxiv-2509-04239:
Arturo Valdivia and one co-author, Paolo Burelli, propose a structured way to judge game stories co-written with artificial intelligence in a 2025 research paper. Generative tools can draft plots and dialogue quickly, but studios lack a shared yardstick for quality. Their method borrows the Delphi structure, where narrative design experts answer in rounds until views converge. Quality dimensions drawn from literature and expert input form the basis of the evaluation.

Those dimensions are then mapped into the Kano model, a framework that sorts features by how they drive customer satisfaction. Results show which story qualities players treat as basic, which delight them, and which barely matter. Developers can prioritize effort when creating narratives alongside AI.
arxiv-2509-04339:
Valentina Biagioni and five co-authors derive a shortcut for gas flowing through repeating channel shapes under strong pressure drops in a 2025 engineering paper. Periodic channels, built from one single cell, rival packed columns in chemical analysis and processing. Liquids are easy: solve the flow in a single cell. Gases squeeze as pressure falls, so flow patterns stop repeating and whole-channel simulation becomes hugely costly.

Their two-scale method gives a local pressure-drop curve from an incompressible single-cell solution. Integrating that curve along the channel then yields pressure and speed profiles by formula. Different gas laws give quite different profiles. Full computer runs in several channel shapes confirmed the predictions. Designers gain fast estimates for long periodic devices.
arxiv-2509-04539:
Kenzo Ishikawa and one co-author, Osamu Jinnouchi, take a systematic look at wave packet sizes in quantum scattering in a 2025 physics paper. Quantum particles travel as wave packets, spread-out waves with a finite coherence length, rather than as points. Transition probabilities between states depend on those packet sizes, yet the sizes are not universal constants. Surroundings and experimental conditions set them, so estimating them accurately is essential for correct predictions.

Propagating packets take their size from environmental coherence lengths. Bound states, by contrast, inherit size from their own wave functions. The analysis sorts both cases carefully. Scattering calculations across particle physics depend on getting these humble parameters right.
arxiv-2509-04739:
A single atom interacts more strongly with light when a cavity confines that light tightly and cleanly. Qian Bin, lead author with five co-authors, propose a way to raise that interaction sharply in a 2025 quantum optics paper. Their cavity design uses strongly localised modes and a special geometric symmetry.

By widening the cavity wings, interference raises the quality factor exponentially without changing the mode volume. That breaks a usual trade-off in subwavelength cavities. The stronger cooperativity supports very long vacuum Rabi oscillations and strong photon blockade. The authors point to uses in quantum communication networks, sensors, and algorithms.
arxiv-2509-05039:
Turbulence can be described through the chance spreads of the flow, but the equations for those spreads contain unclosed terms. Qian Huang and one co-author study approximations to such conservation laws in a 2025 applied mathematics paper. Their setting is scalar hyperbolic balance laws, a simpler model for turbulent transport.

They show those terms stay important even as viscosity vanishes, and they keep probability densities from going negative. A sampling-based estimator, built from runs of the underlying solutions, approximates those terms. Error bounds link guess quality to estimation error. Tests on solvable problems confirm the guess converges as samples increase.
arxiv-2509-05139:
Digital rights policies need a precise meaning before software can check or compare them. Jaime Osvaldo Salas, lead author with five co-authors, give a formal semantics for the Open Digital Rights Language in a 2025 paper. That language is the standard for governing access and use of digital resources, but a comprehensive formal semantics was missing.

Their semantics is based on query answering and aligns with the latest published specification. Building on it, they define policy comparison: detecting when two policies are equivalent, or one is more restrictive or permissive. Data sharing scenarios motivate the comparison problem.
arxiv-2509-05739:
Reasoning models can be poisoned through their thinking steps, yet often shake the poison off, Hanna Foerster and six co-authors report in a 2025 machine learning security paper. Data poisoning hides backdoors in training, and chain-of-thought reasoning gives attackers a new place to hide them.

Their decomposed reasoning poison alters the reasoning path alone, keeping prompts and final answers untouched, and splits the trigger into harmless-looking pieces. Planting such poisons works, but reliably firing them to change final answers proves surprisingly hard. Models often recover from a backdoor triggered mid-thought, helped by the separation between reasoning and answer generation. An emergent robustness, not a designed defence, appears to be at work.
arxiv-2509-05839:
Building a queueing model usually takes an expert who specifies arrivals, service rules, and routing by hand. Daksh Mittal and three co-authors propose in 2025 to learn that model straight from event records instead. Their framework treats a service system as a stream of events whose next type and timing can be learned like a sequence.

Transformer-style sequence models, the design behind modern language AI, learn those event patterns from tables of past activity, with no hand-specified arrival or service laws. The learned model then acts as a simulator for the system. Tests on event data from varied queueing networks show the simulators can support uncertainty estimates and what-if comparisons across service domains. The authors present this as a step toward automated pipelines that widen the use of queueing models.
arxiv-2509-05939:
Biharmonic maps that move one curved space into another are sorted out in a special case by Shun Maeta and Miho Shito in a 2025 paper. A Riemannian submersion is a map that drops dimension while keeping lengths sideways. Biharmonic maps extend harmonic ones, and earlier work showed that in three dimensions, from spaces of constant curvature, biharmonic submersions onto a surface must be harmonic.

Maeta and Shito extend that result to all dimensions for codimension one. Building an adapted orthonormal frame, a moving grid fitted to the map, they make the biharmonic equation simpler and use the curvature structure. Their theorem says such a submersion is biharmonic exactly when it is harmonic. They note the result echoes Chen's conjecture, a long-standing question about biharmonic submanifolds.
arxiv-2509-06239:
Hardware that is correct by construction, generated from plain English, is the pipeline Proof2Silicon in a 2025 paper by Manvi Jha and two co-authors. Language models write code readily but often fail formal verification, which hardware and safety-critical work demand. The system embeds PREFACE, an earlier framework that repairs prompts by reinforcement learning until a frozen model emits verifiable Dafny code.

Verified programs then translate automatically into high-level C and onward to chip-ready RTL through high-level synthesis. On a one-hundred-task benchmark, prompt repair lifts verification success by up to about a fifth across models, and the full pipeline reaches a hardware synthesis success rate above seventy percent. The authors present a scalable bridge from specification to silicon.
arxiv-2509-06539:
Defending a computer network against attacks, in a benchmark game called CAGE-2, is modeled formally by Duc Huy Le and one co-author in a 2025 cybersecurity paper. Many learning methods have been tried on this benchmark, but without a formal model it is hard to know what the best possible defense looks like.

The authors rebuild CAGE-2 as a partially observable Markov decision process, a standard framework for acting under uncertainty about the true state. That model lets them define an optimal defender strategy and a practical way to learn it. Their method, BF-PPO, extends a known learning algorithm and uses a particle filter to tame the huge state space. In the CybORG test environment it beats CARDIFF, the top-ranked earlier method, on both defense quality and training time.
arxiv-2509-06839:
Cutting anime characters out of their backgrounds, a job general tools do badly, is the specialty of a 2025 computer vision paper by Matteo Muratori and one co-author. State-of-the-art background removal shines on realistic photos. Anime images bring fine hair strands and transparency effects that trip those models up.

The authors collected and annotated a custom dataset of over twelve hundred high-quality anime images of characters and objects, then fine-tuned the open-source BiRefNet model on it. Accuracy on their new pixel accuracy metric rose from about ninety-five percent to about ninety-nine and a half percent. The fine-tuned system is called ToonOut. Code, model weights, and the dataset are all open-sourced, so other builders of anime tools can start from a model that already understands drawn hair and translucent details.
arxiv-2509-07239:
Max Asselmeier and 4 co-authors extend gap-based motion planning to moving obstacles in a 2025 book chapter. Gap-based planners steer robots through open regions called gaps in their sensor view. In busy settings, other planners often rely on luck or tuned habits rather than proof for avoiding collisions. The new planner, called dynamic gap, handles moving obstacles directly.

Gaps are tracked over time and their motion is estimated, then future gap positions are projected with new propagation methods. Pursuit guidance theory, borrowed from missile steering, generates local paths that are provably collision-free under ideal conditions. A fallback handles scenes with no gaps at all. In benchmarks against classical and learned planners, dynamic gap beat every baseline in every test setting. Trials on a real TurtleBot2 robot confirmed the avoidance behavior in practice.
arxiv-2509-07339:
Longer chains of thought are often taken as proof that a language model is thinking harder. Vardhan Palod and 3 co-authors test that belief in a 2025 research paper. They train small transformer models from scratch on traces of the A* search algorithm solving mazes. In those traces, problem difficulty is known exactly, as the number of steps the search truly needs.

Even on trivial open mazes, the models often produced overly long traces and sometimes failed outright. On harder, unfamiliar problems, trace length only loosely matched true difficulty. Where a match appeared, the problems sat close to the training data, suggesting recall rather than fresh reasoning. The authors warn against reading long outputs from reasoning systems as automatic evidence of real thinking effort.
arxiv-2509-07639:
Martijn Brehm and 1 co-author construct fast good codes with fast good duals in a 2025 paper. An error-correcting code protects data by adding redundancy. Good codes balance rate against error tolerance near the Gilbert-Varshamov bound, a classic benchmark. The dual code is built from all vectors at right angles to the code. Duals matter in tasks such as secure computation of an encrypted matrix-vector product.

Their rate one-half binary code and its dual both approach the GV bound. Both can be encoded in linear time. The construction is inspired by repeat multiple accumulate codes. It alternates accumulation steps and discrete derivative steps, each with a random permutation. The two steps are inverses of each other. That makes the dual look much like the code itself. The authors open the study of such pairs, with wider uses in mind.
arxiv-2509-07739:
Dessislava H. Kochloukova's 2025 paper, with 1 co-author, describes the structure of HNN extensions of Lie superalgebras. Lie superalgebras extend ordinary Lie algebras with a grading. The grading mixes commuting and anticommuting parts. Such algebras underpin supersymmetry in physics. An HNN extension, borrowed from group theory, adjoins a new element that forces two substructures to become conjugate.

The authors give bases in full for these extensions. The extension splits as a direct sum of two parts. One part is the original superalgebra. The other is a free Lie superalgebra, whose free generators are described in full. They apply the structure to finite generation of ideals in finitely presented ones. A key tool is a Gröbner-Shirshov basis theory built for this setting. Its normal form theorem is stated through admissible bracketings. Such normal forms make work in this field routine.
arxiv-2509-07839:
Faster wireless channel estimation is the goal of a 2025 paper by Florian Strasser and 2 co-authors. Before a MIMO system, which uses many antennas at once, can send data well, it must estimate the radio channel from pilot signals. Score-based generative models do this job accurately but can be too slow for real-time use.

The team redesigns the noise schedule and skips steps during sampling, cutting the number of denoising steps the model must run. An extreme version uses a single denoising step guided by signal-to-noise information. On synthetic city-like channel data, latency drops sharply without hurting accuracy. Speed of this kind decides whether a clever estimator can leave the lab and run inside live networks.
arxiv-2509-08139:
Wireless networks that plan ahead need a model of how channels evolve, and Ke He with 6 co-authors adapt language models to that job in a 2025 communications paper. Future AI-native networks aim at agentic decisions: sensing, predicting, and acting as radio conditions change quickly. Predicting channel state several steps ahead gives the lookahead such agents require.

Feeding radio time series into a language model is not straightforward, because adapters must expose the spectral and temporal patterns that matter. Their spectral-attentive design targets exactly that interface. Language models are general sequence learners, and if they can forecast channels reliably, network controllers gain a reusable prediction engine instead of a shelf of narrow, hand-built forecasters.
arxiv-2509-08639:
Hadrien Notarantonio introduces DDE-Solver, a Maple software package, in a 2025 paper. The package solves discrete differential equations, which link a power series to its special values in an extra variable. Such equations arise when counting maps and other combinatorial objects.

Earlier theory showed that fixed point cases give algebraic series, with a method to find their defining polynomials. Newer algorithms compute those witnesses faster. DDE-Solver automates the whole process for working combinatorialists. The paper compares timing for all the algorithms on equations from the literature. Users gain a ready tool instead of building each solution by hand.
arxiv-2509-09039:
Tomoyuki Arakawa and 3 co-authors work out fusion rules for boundary W-algebras in a 2025 paper. W-algebras extend the symmetry algebras of field theory. Their characters and modular data tell how representations, the basic building blocks, combine.

The team prove that q-characters and modular data match between certain boundary cases. From that match, fusion rules for the exceptional W-algebras in type A are largely fixed. Fusion rules list what comes out when two blocks are merged. Worked cases and uses are given as well. The paper is pure math, tied to conformal field theory, the study of scale free fields.
arxiv-2509-09339:
Tiny vesicles are the body's own delivery parcels, carrying proteins and RNA between cells. Steering them could target drugs precisely. Mohammad Zoofaghari and 3 co-authors study how electric fields might steer them, in a 2025 research paper. Vesicles carry surface charge, so fields can push them. The question is whether extremely low-frequency fields give real directional control.

The team built a theory on the Fokker-Planck equation and solved it on a computer. Computer runs varied the field's phase, frequency, and strength and tracked vesicle paths. Low frequencies with moderate field strengths produced strong directional control. Multi-part fields improved directivity further. The authors frame the result as beamforming for nanoparticles, borrowing the antenna idea for molecular communication. The theory lays groundwork for targeted vesicle delivery in nanomedicine, pending lab proof.
arxiv-2509-09439:
John Alistair Kressel and 2 co-authors present μFork in 2025, a design that brings POSIX fork to operating systems where kernel and programs share one address space. Such systems are light, but fork normally assumes separate spaces for parent and child, so multiprocess POSIX programs cannot run as written. Earlier fixes gave up lightness, compatibility, or isolation.

μFork copies a process's memory to a fresh location inside the shared space, then repairs the child's pointers and guards its boundaries with CHERI hardware features. Trials covered Redis snapshots, multi-worker Nginx, and function worker warm-up. The system beat earlier approaches while keeping the three goals the authors refused to trade away.
arxiv-2509-09839:
Andrea Sante and 4 co-authors test how well a clustering algorithm can excavate the Milky Way's merger past in a 2025 galactic archaeology paper. Stars swallowed from smaller galaxies should still cluster in motion and chemistry space, and HDBSCAN is a popular tool for finding such groups. Its real reliability inside a messy cosmological history, though, had never been fully measured, so the team turns to the Auriga simulation suite.

Their recipe uses twelve features mixing chemistry, dynamics, and stellar ages, then tunes the search using each cluster's internal structure to stop groups shattering. Purity and completeness came out well across varied accretion histories, and merged groups were matched back to their true parent galaxies. Contamination from home-grown stars does erode the recovery, a limit the authors chart.
arxiv-2509-09939:
Noel Brady and 2 co-authors measure how hard it is to fill loops inside a broad family of groups in a 2025 geometric group theory paper. The Dehn function of a group counts the cheapest way to fill a closed word, a yardstick for the difficulty of deciding when two expressions name the same element. The groups in question sit inside direct products and project onto a free abelian group, a pattern that includes the classic Stallings-Bieri examples and far more.

A new bookkeeping device, the n-split of such a projection, organises the estimate. With it the authors bound Dehn functions for these coabelian subgroups in terms of the pieces they are built from. The framework widens older results considerably, giving one lens for a whole landscape of product subgroups.
arxiv-2509-10139:
Santiago Montiel-Marín and 4 co-authors present CaR1, a camera-radar fusion system for self-driving cars, in this 2025 paper. Cameras read rich detail but judge distance poorly. Radar gives sparse yet solid position and motion data. Joining the two is cheaper than lidar and can be more robust, which makes the pairing attractive for production vehicles.

Built on the BEVFusion design, CaR1 encodes radar points onto a bird's-eye-view grid and blends the two sensors with a fusion step that adjusts its weighting on the fly. On the nuScenes benchmark it reached segmentation quality on par with leading methods. The authors released the code in public, offering the system as a baseline for later fusion work.
arxiv-2509-10539:
F. Minotti and G. Modanese study a modified law of charge conservation in this 2025 paper. The question is when approximate quantum calculations can live with it. In many-body quantum mechanics, the continuity equation is standard. It ties the change in charge density to the flow of current. Their variant scales the current term by a factor. Such an equation fits the extended Aharonov-Bohm electrodynamics. It does not fit Maxwell's theory.

The authors test two kinds of approximations against the modified equation. One kind uses non-equilibrium Green functions. The other solves the Dyson equation approximately. Then they turn to molecular junctions, simulated with density functional theory. A redefinition of local current density, proposed by Wang and collaborators, enters the discussion. That redefinition also suits the extended electrodynamics. A numerical modeling question thus ties to a deep one. Which electrodynamics does nature use?
arxiv-2509-10739:
Mobina Pournemat and seven co-authors probe whether large language models can reason about chance in this 2025 evaluation study. Models ace many language tasks yet behave inconsistently when probabilities enter. The authors give models explicit discrete probability distributions and test three skills: spotting the most likely outcome, estimating likelihoods, and generating samples that match the distribution.

The pattern is clear and uneven. Larger models clearly out-reason smaller ones, and their sampling ability surprises. But performance sags badly, by over sixty percent, as the context grows longer, and merely changing the notation used to write outcomes down swings the results. Queries about joint distributions and their conditionals expose the same fragility. The study gives the field its first detailed map of where LLM probability reasoning stands and where it breaks.
arxiv-2509-10839:
Arpan Dutta and Josnei Novacoski study how far apart the conjugates of an algebraic element can sit in this 2025 paper. Their setting is a henselian valued field. Such a field carries a valuation, a way of measuring size. A separable algebraic element a extends the field. For each conjugate of a, they record the valuation of the difference. The collection is a set of distances. Its size is what they aim to bound.

They characterize the elements whose distance set is a single value. They connect the set to the notion of depth. For minimal extensions, the set is always a singleton. A stronger result holds at depth one. Examples show their bounds are strict. The motivation reaches beyond the distance set itself. In depth one Galois cases, its size matches counts of ramification ideals. The authors describe those ideals in detail, extending known theory.
arxiv-2509-10939:
Bibhabasu De is the sole author of this 2025 particle physics paper, which asks why underground detectors keep failing to see dark matter particles directly. He studies an extension of the Standard Model built on an extra symmetry that treats muons and taus differently from electrons.

The model adds new heavy particles, the lightest of which stays stable and serves as the dark matter candidate. De shows that the signals for dark matter scattering off electrons and off quarks can cancel almost exactly, which would explain the empty detector results. The same setup shifts lepton magnetic moments and certain Z boson decay rates, and measurements of those decays tightly limit the model's parameters. With three heavy neutrinos included, the model can also reproduce the known neutrino masses and mixing patterns.
arxiv-2509-11039:
Zixi Chen, Yumin Xu, and Ruixun Zhang wrote this 2025 paper on stochastic approximation. These algorithms update two sets of variables at different speeds. They learn from noisy data. Earlier theory mostly assumed the noise stays bounded. Real problems often break that assumption.

The authors let the noise depend on the current state or on time. They track a Lyapunov function, an energy-like measure of error. They prove it shrinks at a polynomial rate. The rate depends on the noise parameters. When state noise settles fully to its limit, the rate improves. It becomes exponential. Two examples show the theory at work. One is stochastic gradient descent with averaging. The other is stochastic bilevel optimization.
arxiv-2509-11339:
Philipp J. di Dio, writing alone, simplifies a known result about representing sequences in this 2025 mathematics paper. A theorem from 1989 says every complex sequence indexed by multi-indices can be written as the moments of a smooth, rapidly decaying function supported on the positive orthant. The result is often described as a generalization of a 1964 theorem of Sherman about representing sequences by complex measures.

Di Dio shows, using convolution of sequences with measures, that the newer result in fact follows from Sherman's older one almost immediately. The short proof is then used to widen the smooth-function result, showing how much freedom there is in choosing the representing function. The note is a tidy lesson in how an old theorem can contain a newer one.
arxiv-2509-11939:
Shuning Zhang and 7 co-authors present PrivWeb in a 2025 paper on privacy for web agents, the programs that browse and act on web pages for users. Agents need access to what is on the screen, and that access can expose private details. The authors start from the user's point of view, which they say earlier work has largely missed.

A small study with 15 people showed that users often misunderstand what agents collect and want quiet, clear control over their data. PrivWeb answers with a local language model that hides private information on a page according to user choices. It pauses a task only for highly sensitive details and uses gentler notices for the rest. In tests with 14 people, it lowered felt privacy risk without adding mental effort.
arxiv-2509-12439:
Entropy inequalities govern what information theory allows, and the hunt for new ones runs through a few known machines. In a solo 2025 tutorial-style survey, Laszlo Csirmaz explores the entropic region by comparing three methods for generating such inequalities and mapping their limits.

The Copy Lemma, distilled from the construction behind the first non-Shannon inequality, anchors the discussion, with its iterated form, symmetrization tricks, and ties to polyhedral vertex counting. A maximum-entropy method contains the lemma as a special case yet seems no stronger. The Ahlswede-Körner method, by contrast, hides a copy step inside and proves strictly weaker. Open problems close the tour.
arxiv-2509-12639:
Jun Ye and Jun Yong Khoo present EmuPlat in a 2025 paper on emulating quantum hardware. Quantum programming systems and hardware-certain pulse control systems often live in isolated software stacks, creating an interoperability gap. A researcher writing circuits in one system may struggle to run them through another system's low-level controls.

EmuPlat gives a unified, system-agnostic platform that integrates ecosystems including CUDA-Q, Qiskit, and Qibolab. Its transpiler-to-pulse pipeline transforms abstract circuits through four validated stages. These are decomposition to a minimal native gate set, virtual phase optimization, connectivity-aware routing with automatic swap insertion, and deterministic pulse compilation respecting hardware timing. A modular adapter-based architecture supports adding further model run tools. The design aims at seamless integration across diverse quantum computing settings.
arxiv-2509-13139:
Kushal Bose and Swagatam Das read in 2025 how self-loops and twin edges shift graph learning on mixed-link graphs. Message nets falter when neighbors differ in kind. Smooth filters blend unlike notes and lose class cues.

Adding self-loops lowers graph pitch values; twin edges raise them. Tests on mixed benchmarks show filter skill can rise or fall with each add. Trends link back to spectra, which encode clumps, sparsity, and degree. Reading trends lets users gauge spectra without costly splits. Theory backs the pitch shifts. The work ties cheap graph edits to deep traits.
arxiv-2509-13239:
Tianxu An, Flavio De Vincenti and three co-authors train legged robots with arms to pick and place loads together in 2025. Long tasks from approach to release strain standard learning. One robot and paired robots are both in scope.

A staged reward that shifts with the load guides one policy through sub-goals. Training runs faster by more than half. Run time falls by near a fifth in fake tests. Paired robots learn to watch distinct parts at distinct stages, which aids joint work. Real ANYmal D trials back both solo and paired runs. Full joint pick tasks are claimed as a first.
arxiv-2509-13339:
Ming Jin and Hyunin Lee argue in 2025 that AI safety must grow antifragile, gaining strength from shocks over time. Static benchmarks miss evolving settings. Unchallenged models drift to reward hacks, overfit, or skill loss as settings shift.

Antifragile safety uses current doubt to prep for larger future doubt. Rare and out-of-norm events are training fuel, not edge noise. Limits of static tests span scenario range, hacks, and over-alignment. The plea is to recalibrate measures, benchmarks, and steady improvement. Ethics and practice guides for a community shift close the position and frame next steps.
arxiv-2509-13439:
Zeno Capatti, Mathijs Fraaije and four co-authors compute in 2025 photon-fusion heavy-quark pair cross sections at NNLO QCD with local unitarity. Local unitarity joins loop and phase-space integrals so infrared poles cancel before integration. Local ultraviolet fixes allow direct Monte Carlo in four dimensions at any order.

Over a hundred forward diagrams with photons on heavy quarks alone are included. NLO electroweak terms and Coulomb resummation at next power join the QCD core. State-of-art predictions cover top, bottom, and charm in ultraperipheral hits and electron colliders. Forward methods push precision frontiers.
arxiv-2509-13539:
Alisa Kanganis and Katherine A. Keith released Op-Fed in 2025, a dataset of just over one thousand human-annotated sentences from Federal Open Market Committee transcripts. The committee sets United States monetary policy, and its members' opinions and stances are often buried in long discussions where most sentences stay neutral.

Building the dataset meant handling two problems: non-neutral stances are rare, and most sentences need surrounding context to interpret. The team used a five-stage labeling scheme and active learning, letting a model pick the most useful sentences to annotate, which roughly doubled the positive cases. Tests show a top closed model labels opinion well but stance toward monetary policy far below human accuracy.
arxiv-2509-13939:
Gia Khanh Nguyen, Yifeng Huang, and Minh Hoai test whether AI models count what users mean in a 2025 computer vision paper. Counting sounds simple. Asking for objects of one specific type inside a cluttered scene is a sterner test. The types may differ only in shape, size, color, or meaning. Fine-grained understanding is what gets measured.

Their benchmark, PairTally, holds several hundred high-resolution images. Each image contains two object categories. The settings cover clearly distinct pairs and closely related subcategory pairs. They ran exemplar-based counters, language-prompted models, and large vision-language models through it. Despite recent progress, every family struggled to count the intended category reliably. Ambiguous cases hurt most. PairTally becomes a diagnostic tool for a basic skill models still lack.
arxiv-2509-14139:
Víctor Mayoral-Vilches, Andreas Makris, and Kevin Finisterre detail how a humanoid robot doubles as an attack platform in a 2025 security paper, a systematic assessment of the Unitree G1. Entry, they show, can come through the Bluetooth provisioning protocol, where a command injection flaw plus hardcoded encryption keys shared across all units yield root access through rigged Wi-Fi credentials.

Two case studies carry the argument. First, the robot acts as a trojan horse, quietly sending multi-modal sensor and service telemetry to outside servers every few minutes without operator notice, in tension with European privacy law. Second, a resident cybersecurity AI agent pivots from reconnaissance to preparing attacks, including against the manufacturer's own cloud. Partial reverse engineering of the proprietary encryption exposed how the pieces fit together.
arxiv-2509-14239:
Arash Azizi, writing alone in 2025, gives a physical source for a family of quantum states called the kappa plane wave vacuum. The thermal behaviour of those states, meaning how hot they look to a detector, was well known. What produced them in a real setup was not.

Azizi shows the vacuum matches the state made by a mirror that speeds up along the Carlitz-Willey path, judged far away where light escapes. Three checks line up: the same squeezing values, the same thermal patterns in field correlations, and the same response from a standard particle detector. The match ties the abstract parameter kappa to the scale that sets the mirror motion, grounding a formal construction in a concrete moving mirror model.
arxiv-2509-14639:
Richard Beals and Jacek Szmigielski widen the Euler-Bernoulli beam problem in 2025 and link it to multi component Camassa-Holm dynamics, a wave family from shallow water theory. The beam starts life as a matrix string problem whose density is a matrix. Here the density takes values in a Clifford algebra instead.

For discrete densities, the linked matrix Weyl function gains a Stieltjes type continued fraction form with Clifford valued parts. Moving the problem from a finite span to the whole real line shows the Camassa-Holm link in a direct way. The wave system that comes out is a vector form, left unchanged by any orthogonal group action. One worked dynamic case shows the theory in play. Spectral links between beams and waves keep yielding new solvable systems.
arxiv-2509-14839:
Miriam Louise Carnot leads a team of six authors evaluating MapAnything in a 2025 computer vision paper. City governments keep databases of street assets such as traffic signs and trees, plus problems such as graffiti and road damage. Keeping those records current takes heavy manual work. MapAnything aims to locate such objects from a single street-view photo.

The pipeline uses metric depth estimation models, which predict real distances from one image, to compute each object's map coordinates. Camera distance estimates are combined with geometry and known camera details to place objects in three dimensions. The team checked accuracy against precise LiDAR point clouds in complex city scenes. Their validation shows how far single-photo mapping can be trusted for updating city asset records.
arxiv-2509-14939:
Hao Zhang, Zhen Kan, Weiwei Shang, and Yongduan Song introduce DART for manipulating hinged and jointed objects in a 2025 robotics paper. Opening doors, drawers, and lids requires finding the right contact points and motion, and generalizing across object categories is still hard. DART strengthens a diffusion-based policy with two extra ingredients.

Linear temporal logic descriptions give the policy a clear representation of task semantics, the ordered steps a job requires. Affordance learning identifies the best places to interact with each object. An optimization step based on interaction data then refines the proposed actions, going beyond what demonstration-trained diffusion policies usually achieve. Experiments show DART ahead of most existing methods on manipulation success, generalization to new categories, and transfer of reasoning between tasks.
arxiv-2509-15539:
Ta Tang leads a team that sharpens blurry spectra from short simulations. For strongly linked materials, mock runs over time can predict how electrons leave a sample. Short runs and small samples blur both the energy and the direction detail. The team wanted finer detail without paying for much longer runs.

They propose a cheap learning method that extends short time and short range results. It uses a linear model that predicts later values from earlier ones. They apply it to two models of linked electrons, one far costlier than the other. The sharper spectra reveal traits tied to electrons coupled with lattice shakes, traits the blur had hidden. The method adds reach at low cost.
arxiv-2509-15739:
Reza Sanayei leads a team that tests whether language models can judge debates. Debates branch like graphs, with arguments attacking and backing each other. Linear reasoning tests miss that shape. The team use a formal semantics that scores each argument's standing from its attack and support links.

Models see only the debate as dialogue, with no graph shown. They must rank the arguments on their own. Several models are tested with strong prompt styles, such as step by step reasoning and examples in context. Scores track the formal ranks moderately well. Long inputs and shuffled order hurt the match. Strong prompts cut biases tied to argument length and place.
arxiv-2509-15839:
Zhongze Luo leads a team that builds a Chinese benchmark for physics reasoning by multimodal models. Such models have grown strong at reasoning, yet physics exposes gaps. Past tests cover few subjects, skip the steps of reasoning, and lean on English. The role of images in the answers also went untested.

Their set holds over fourteen hundred multiple choice questions with images, across eleven high school physics subjects and five levels of difficulty. Twenty models are graded two ways: on the final answer and on the soundness of each reasoning step. The team also vary whether images are included, to gauge their weight. Data and code are open. The set gives a fine tool for probing model reasoning.
arxiv-2509-15939:
Michael Greenacre and Maurizio Vichi group the categories of survey style data. Their data hold many variables, each with its own set of categories. Grouping splits into two problems. Within one variable, merging categories shrinks the data while keeping its key traits. Between variables, the goal is a few clusters of categories that typify the cases.

Order matters in the first problem: for ranked categories, only neighbors may merge. The second problem bars merges inside one variable but is otherwise free. Results come as two tree diagrams stacked together, which they call a bi-dendrogram. The pair of trees shows both levels of grouping at a glance. The method aids simpler reads of complex surveys.
arxiv-2509-16039:
How strongly the top quark couples to the Higgs field is a basic test of the standard model of particle physics. The ATLAS Collaboration measures this coupling from proton collision data taken at the Large Hadron Collider between 2015 and 2018. Near the point where top quark pairs just form, their mass pattern bends in ways that depend on the Higgs link.

The team rebuilds pair events with one charged lepton and at least four jets. The measured coupling agrees well with the standard model value. They also set an upper bound on its strength, in line with what the data could reach. It is the first ATLAS result of this type.
arxiv-2509-16139:
When a shock wave hits a porous or latticed material, tiny pores collapse and hot spots form in ways that are hard to predict. M. Giselle Fernández-Godino and six co-authors train a deep learning model that tracks seven linked fields at once, such as pressure, heat, density, and speed. It learns from detailed physics runs across complex inner structures.

The model captures odd effects like density drops after a shock and stays stable over long rollouts. Its errors stay near one percent, and it beats single-field models by a wide margin on structure. It also runs about a thousand times faster, which aids design work.
arxiv-2509-16239:
Most logic systems treat a contradiction as a failure that breaks the whole system. Jhet Chan builds a formal system in the Lean 4 proof tool that treats paradox instead as a signal that drives new structure. Self-referential loops are packed into safe nodes and re-entered in a fixed cycle, so they fuel growth rather than collapse.

The mechanized proofs show these paradoxes stay contained and resolve into fresh structures. The loop runs by design and never needs to halt. Chan argues the calculus could ground agents that fix their own inner conflicts. It offers a rare case where non-ending recursion is a feature, not a bug.
arxiv-2509-16339:
Predicting rare but harmful events from table data is hard when the rare cases are outnumbered a thousand to one. Josias K. Moukpe, Philip K. Chan, and Ming Zhang tackle such lopsided regression tasks, with solar particle storms as a driving use case. Standard error loss ignores how well forecasts track the true values, and common weighting tricks are too rigid.

Their method adds a tracking term, a new form of importance weight, and sampling that keeps rare cases in each training batch. On five data sets it beat recent rivals on error and tracking. Its tracking term also boosted other methods when added.
arxiv-2509-16439:
Tensor networks that store mixed quantum states can waste resources, since the same state admits many encodings of varied size. Amit Jamadagni and Eugene Dumitrescu study the key case where noise washes a state toward the fully mixed one, a limit labs meet often. They test two numerical tools and one analytic method for trimming the encoding, and they map how the tools relate.

Closed forms for the trimming step come from the state's symmetry and injectivity traits. Away from the fully mixed limit, the trim threshold glides smoothly between known results and the new ones. Cheaper encodings could push tensor methods to larger quantum systems.
arxiv-2509-16839:
Yu Yao and co-authors pool language models into a roundtable for science in a 2025 paper. Several models can reason together and beat a single model. Past schemes used votes, debates, or complex protocols. Their policy weights each model's voice by its confidence. Consensus then forms in a clear, structured way.

Tests show clear gains on complex, mixed science tasks. The method needs only black-box access to each model. Its steps stay uniform and easy to read, unlike opaque convergence. Structured pooling could help labs tackle questions that mix fields. Confidence weighting keeps strong voices from being drowned by weak ones.
arxiv-2509-16939:
Taehyoun Kim, Duksan Ryu, and Jongmoon Baik predict software reliability with synthetic data in a 2025 paper. Growth models forecast failures from defect records during testing. Early testing and safety-critical work yield few records, so forecasts wobble. The team generate deep synthetic cross-project data to fill the gap.

Their approach borrows patterns from other projects to enrich scarce local data. Too much synthetic data, though, hurt forecasts in tests. A naive mix of fake and real data also hurt. Balance between the two proved key. With care, synthetic help could give early projects reliability estimates that managers can act on sooner.
arxiv-2509-17039:
Gang Yang, Zixuan Yang, and Shenggui Zhang solve saturation problems for matchings in a 2025 graph paper. A graph is saturated for a pattern if it avoids the pattern, yet adding any missing edge creates it. Here the pattern is a matching, a set of disjoint edges. A regularity condition adds that every vertex has the same degree.

The team find the exact regular saturation number for matchings of each size, in all cases. As a counterpart, they find the most edges a regular graph can have while avoiding such a matching. Exact values close a question left open in earlier work on constrained saturation.
arxiv-2509-17139:
Reinhold Hübl, Craig Huneke, Sarasij Maitra, and Vivek Mukundan wrote a 2025 arXiv article in algebra about valuations on a special kind of local ring. The ring is one dimensional, complete, and reduced, and it sits inside its own integral closure. The paper looks at the values tied to the smallest set of generators of the ring's maximal ideal.

The authors give a way to set those values in a unique fashion. Their result extends the better known case of numerical semigroup rings. Along the way, the paper fills gaps in proofs found in the older literature. Some of those gaps touch results linked to a long-standing conjecture credited to R. Berger.
arxiv-2509-17239:
Armando de la C. Rangel-Pantoja, M. Napsuciale, and Carlos A. Vaquera-Araujo wrote a 2025 arXiv paper in theoretical physics. Their subject is a class of massless fields that live in a stated symmetry representation of the restricted Lorentz group. They ask whether theories built from these fields can still be made finite and consistent at one loop.

The authors work with a broad model that covers the whole class of parity-even, self-interacting massless theories in that setting. Its free part folds in three older theories as special cases, named for Joos and Weinberg, for Shay, Good, Hammer, McDonald, and Pursey, and a Klein-Gordon-like variant. The interacting part holds every allowed self-interaction of the right size. The model turns out to be renormalizable, which keeps the class alive for further study.
arxiv-2509-17339:
Robert D. Cousins, writing alone, posts a comment on a recent review of confidence intervals for the Poisson distribution. The review, by Frank Porter, surveys a long and varied history that runs beside the history of intervals for the binomial case. Cousins calls much of the review enlightening, but he argues that one part of it is flawed.

The dispute centers on intervals that Cousins built with Gary Feldman from a likelihood ratio test. At issue is whether a likelihood function can exist in a region where the statistical model itself does not exist. Porter says yes, while Feldman and Cousins say no. The comment focuses mainly on that point and what follows from it. A few smaller remarks on other parts of the review round out the piece.
arxiv-2509-17439:
Yangxuan Zhou and six co-authors borrow a brain trick to keep EEG decoders learning without labels. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles continual decoding of brain signals, where new people arrive over time and each brain differs. A fixed decoder decays, but retraining with labels for every newcomer is impractical.

Their framework, SPICED, copies synaptic homeostasis, the process that keeps the brain both stable and plastic. A synaptic network grows as adaptation proceeds, driven by three bio-inspired mechanisms: reactivating key memories, consolidating synapses, and renormalizing them. The interplay strengthens traces tied to the task and weakens harmful memories. Helpful traces get replayed when a newcomer resembles past users, which aids adaptation. Harmful replays are suppressed, which curbs catastrophic forgetting. Tests on three EEG data sets back the design.
arxiv-2509-17539:
Athanasia Gkogkou, Guilaine Lagache, Matthieu Béthermin, and Abhishek Maniyar stress-test a standard tool of cosmology. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses the halo model with occupation prescriptions to read the cosmic infrared background. That background's patchiness links star-forming galaxies to large-scale structure, and the models claim to recover how efficiently halos form stars.

The team fits a current model to mock data from the SIDES-Uchuu simulation, where the true answers are known. The model fits the mock sky well yet fails to recover the true parameters, above all the halo mass where star formation efficiency peaks. A second, simplified simulation matched to the model's own assumptions shows the same trouble, which points below the surface ingredients. Bias and matter clustering, the model's deep parts, may be at fault. The warning is plain: a good fit is not proof of true values.
arxiv-2509-17639:
Jose Pedro Gaivao and Benito Pires settle a dynamics problem posed in 1999. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies multidimensional contracted rotations, maps that rotate a unit cube while shrinking it and wrapping the overflow around. Bugeaud and Conze asked about such maps in Acta Arithmetica, and the one-dimensional case was understood first.

The pair prove that for an invertible linear contraction, the map is asymptotically periodic for almost every shift vector. In plain terms, nearly every orbit settles into a repeating cycle in the long run. They also give a family of examples in higher dimensions that cannot be reduced to products of one-dimensional maps. That example matters: it shows the new theorem is a genuine extension, not a corollary of the old one. The result closes a question that had stood for over two decades.
arxiv-2509-17739:
Rudi Coppola and 4 co-authors build a way to shrink a live system into a small, finite copy. Their 2025 paper deals with systems that change in smooth steps but must be checked for safety. The copy keeps error bounds that can vary from place to place.

Some systems get such a copy even when older fixed-error ways fail. The authors prove copies exist for a wide class of calm systems. A loop that learns from failed checks makes the grid finer where needed. Tests show copies up to half as small as grid methods, with tighter error bounds.
arxiv-2509-17839:
Michael Farber, Amit Kumar Paul, and Lucile Vandembroucq measure how hard motion plans get when terms change. Their 2025 paper deals with robots that must move with no crashes while outside terms shift. The cost scale for such plans is called parametrized topological complexity.

Past work solved the scale for some bundle types, such as sphere bundles. Here the team takes up bundles of real projective spaces, built from vector bundles. They set sharp upper bounds for the scale. For lower bounds, they build tools from a classic class of shape traits. Pairing the bounds, they work out many cases in full.
arxiv-2509-17939:
Simone Billi and 3 co-authors test when a symmetry of a surface lifts to a maximal one on its point schemes. Their 2025 paper uses a classic bound: the fixed set of a flip cannot have more mod-two shape count than the whole space. A flip that meets that bound is called maximal.

For point schemes of a smooth surface, they give an exact test for when the lifted flip is maximal. The test rests on the surface flip itself and on how it acts on a key shape group. For one large class of hyper-Kahler spaces, they show no maximal flips exist at all.
arxiv-2509-18239:
Milena Crnogorcevic, Tim Linden, and Annika H G Peter hunt gamma rays from active nuclei in dwarf galaxies. Their 2025 paper deals with small galaxies whose centre black holes sit in a mid-mass range. Such holes can teach us how huge centre holes first grew, yet no gamma signal had been tied to them.

Fifteen years of space telescope data cover dozens of X-ray picked dwarfs. No single source cleared the bar for detection. A joint look at all of them shows a faint excess, at low trust, with a very soft spectrum. That hint may track hole mass, but the authors do not claim a find.
arxiv-2509-18339:
Some shapes in algebraic geometry come in linked families, where one shape quietly defines another. Corey Brooke, Laure Flapan, Sarah Frei, and Lisa Marquand study such links for Peskine sixfolds in this 2025 paper. These six-dimensional shapes can pair with K3 surfaces and with cubic fourfolds, shapes cut out by a degree-three equation. The team works out when such pairings can occur.

They derive number-based conditions that a pairing must meet. In the first case where a cubic fourfold appears, at discriminant 24, they name the cubic in full. In that case they also prove a neat match: the shape formed by all lines on the cubic is the same as the paired Debarre-Voisin fourfold. That fourfold is a hyperkähler shape, a class prized in geometry. The results tighten the map of how these shapes relate.
arxiv-2509-18739:
Insurers cannot investigate every suspicious claim, so they rank claims by predicted fraud risk and check the top. Christos Revelas, Otilia Boldea, and Bas J. M. Werker show that habit can corrupt the learning itself. Their 2025 paper argues the checked claims are not a random sample. Models retrained on them can drift into inconsistency.

The team frames claim selection like a multi-arm bandit problem, where each choice shapes future data. They formalize selection inside a binary regression model. With the right accounting, updating the model can proceed as if claims were picked at random. They define what a consistent selection strategy means and conjecture conditions that ensure it. Simulations show the standard top-risk strategy can be inconsistent. Their randomized alternative stayed consistent. A classic bandit heuristic, Thompson sampling, learned rare fraud rates inefficiently by contrast.
arxiv-2509-18839:
Naming the saint in a religious painting is a specialist skill, built on symbols and dress. Gianmarco Spinaci, Lukas Klic, and Giovanni Colavizza test whether general vision-language models can do it in this 2025 study. They benchmark such models on Christian iconography sorting. Three data sets built on the Iconclass system supply the test images.

Models were tried three ways: with class labels alone, with added class descriptions, and with five example images. A fine-tuned classic network served as the baseline. Two big commercial models beat that baseline. On one data set, a smaller open model scored best, hinting at sensitivity to image size and metadata fit. Added descriptions generally helped zero-shot scores. Example-based learning, oddly, helped little. The authors see these models as plausible helpers for curating heritage metadata.
arxiv-2509-18939:
Kaushick K. Parui and ten co-authors study a mineral called ktenasite, whose copper atoms carry spin one-half. The mineral's structure is messy: copper and zinc atoms swap places at one key site. The team asked how that disorder changes the way the material orders magnetically at low temperature.

Using neutron beams and heat and magnetism tests, they find two magnetic states living side by side. One is a long-range ordered state that sets in below about four kelvin, with a pattern that does not match the crystal grid. The other is a frozen, glassy state of small spin clusters at a slightly lower temperature. The mixing also reshapes flat spin sheets into one-dimensional chains, a rare change driven by disorder alone.
arxiv-2509-19039:
Rubén Izquierdo-López and three co-authors extend a classic embedding theorem across a whole zoo of geometric settings. The original result, by Gotay, says a pre-symplectic manifold can be embedded, in a structure-preserving way, into a larger symplectic one. Settings like that arise when a physical system has constraints or leftover symmetries. The authors carry the theorem to cosymplectic, contact, and several multi-versions of those geometries.

One generic method drives all the cases, which the authors stress is the point: a uniform proof travels well. The payoff is practical as much as theoretical. Embedding theorems underlie the regularization problem, where singular Lagrangian systems in mechanics and field theory are replaced by smoother ones that are easier to solve. By settling the embeddings across settings at once, the paper lays groundwork for those applications in mechanics and classical field theory.
arxiv-2509-19239:
Oscar Cavichia and five co-authors rebuild a distance ladder for planetary nebulae, the glowing shells shed by dying stars, and use it to map oxygen across the Milky Way. Nebula distances were long the weak point of such studies. The team recalibrated a relation between a nebula's hydrogen-alpha surface brightness and its radius, now anchored to Gaia satellite parallaxes. That yields distances for more than a thousand nebulae, hundreds of them tied directly to Gaia.

With better distances, they fit the oxygen gradient for 231 disk nebulae under three models. Segmented fits bend near the Sun's radius: flatter or slightly rising inward, steeper outward. The bend may reflect the galactic bar or the spiral arms' corotation zone changing how efficiently stars form. A two-dimensional map shows modest asymmetries, with richer oxygen near the bar. The results constrain how our galaxy built its elements.
arxiv-2509-19339:
Mohammad Sadegh Khorshidi and five co-authors evolve programs in many cooperating groups to sort data with huge, mixed feature sets. Their method, MEGP, splits the input traits into roughly free-standing views. A separate group evolves for each view, side by side. Each program carries several genes, and a smooth weighting layer blends their outputs. That keeps the final choice adaptive, and parts of it stay readable. Fitness is judged alone and in the team, so groups help each other without losing spread.

Across eight test sets, MEGP beat a standard baseline on speed of improvement and on new data. Tests confirmed gains in loss, precision, recall, F1, and AUC scores. The groups kept their diversity through the runs, and fitness climbed faster. The authors pitch it as a step toward learning systems that scale and stay readable.
arxiv-2509-19639:
Factories that also repair returned goods must balance cost, emissions, and energy in one plan. I. B. Wadhawan and M. M. Rizvi build an inventory model for that mixed world of new and remade products. Production and repair rates shift with lot sizes and cycle counts. Demand and quality differ between the two product streams, and returns flow back at a set rate.

Their framework optimizes several goals at once: low inventory cost, low greenhouse gas output, and low energy use. The math mixes whole-number choices with smooth ones, a hard class of problem. Test cases from earlier literature check the model, and sensitivity runs show which settings matter most. Both exact and heuristic solvers are applied. The work gives managers a greener way to set lot sizes.
arxiv-2509-19939:
Pose estimation systems assume two arms and two legs, and fail people whose bodies differ. Hyunjin Cho, Giyun Choi, and Jongwon Choi build AJAHR, a mesh recovery system aware of limb loss. A body-part amputation classifier trains jointly with the mesh network, flagging which limbs are absent. The system then reconstructs a mesh that respects that anatomy.

Because real data is scarce, they also built a synthetic dataset of amputee poses in wide variety. Performance on non-amputees stays competitive while amputee results set a new best, the authors report. Inclusive vision matters for rehabilitation tech, prosthetics fitting, and media tools. The dataset may prove as influential as the model, since it lets others train for bodies the field ignored.
arxiv-2509-20239:
In a 2025 arXiv paper, Andrea Della Vecchia and Damir Filipovic study how errors grow in dynamic programming for stochastic control. Such problems ask for the best sequence of decisions under uncertainty over time. Solvers estimate a value function step by step, mixing regression with Monte Carlo sampling.
