Small errors at late steps can compound as the calculation runs backward.

The authors set up a general framework for discrete-time control and decompose the total error into natural parts. Each part is bounded rigorously at every time step. Their analysis then tracks how those errors propagate from the final stage back to the start, an aspect earlier work rarely treated. Regression runs inside reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces with a classical kernel ridge method. The theory lands on a flagship application: pricing American options, which can be exercised at any time before expiry.
arxiv-2509-20339:
Account takeover fraud, where criminals hijack bank customers' accounts, is the target of a 2025 arXiv paper by Mohsen Nayebi Kerdabadi and three co-authors. Banks usually score each login session alone with tree-based models. That misses the shared devices, addresses, and timing patterns that betray coordinated fraud rings. Their framework, ATLAS, rebuilds detection around those links.

ATLAS turns sessions into a directed graph that respects time, connecting accounts, devices, and internet addresses they share. Rules on time windows and recency keep the graph causal, so no future information leaks into a score. Graph learning models then classify nodes, using only labels available at scoring time. At Capital One scale, the graph held over one hundred million nodes and about a billion edges. Detection accuracy rose by over six percent while customer friction fell by more than half.
arxiv-2509-20439:
Some quantum field theories have no Lagrangian, yet their spectra can still be probed. Yiwen Pan and Peihe Yang compute the Schur index for two such families in closed form in a 2025 arXiv paper. The index is a counting function tied to the theory's states and dualities. Their targets are Argyres-Douglas theories built by gauging pairs of matter theories.

They classify several infinite families and note central charge relations echoing a famous supersymmetric pattern. For two chosen families, flavored and unflavored indices, including line indices, come out in compact form. The large-size behavior matches special limits of a known gauge theory index. A generalized integration formula also yields closed forms for two exceptional theories. The results hint at a universal structure linking integration residues, loop indices, and algebra modules.
arxiv-2509-20639:
Defending language model applications cannot wait for the next attack to be understood. Adam Swanda and five co-authors describe a production defense platform in a 2025 arXiv paper. Novel attacks cannot be prevented outright, they argue, any more than novel malware can. Protection instead means layered defense, strong observability, and fast response, the formula that matured in malware protection.

Three components carry the design. A threat intelligence unit converts emerging threats into concrete protections. A data platform aggregates and enriches signals while supporting monitoring and model operations. A release platform ships detection updates safely and quickly, without disturbing customer workflows. Together they also generate training data that improves the detectors over time. The paper evaluates the system end to end, where earlier work usually graded single detection models in isolation.
arxiv-2509-20939:
Some vision models shrug off image noise while others collapse, and the difference lies in design choices. Bum Jun Kim and three co-authors hunt for those choices in a 2025 study of more than eleven hundred pretrained vision models. They focus on robustness to additive Gaussian noise.

Four design patterns consistently help. Larger stem kernels and smaller input resolutions improve robustness. Average pooling beats sharper alternatives, and supervised vision transformers beat their CLIP-trained counterparts. The gains reach large rank improvements and clear accuracy boosts under noise. The authors back the empirical rules with theoretical analysis explaining why each pattern helps. Their rules are deliberately simple, so model builders can apply them without exotic techniques.
arxiv-2509-21039:
Scientific code must run fast on graphics processors from rival vendors without being rewritten each time. William Godoy and seven co-authors test the Mojo language for that job in a 2025 paper for an SC25 workshop. Mojo is the first language built on the MLIR compiler infrastructure, with Python interoperability.

The team ports four scientific workloads to Mojo: a stencil, a memory benchmark, and two compute-heavy codes, including a Hartree-Fock chemistry kernel. They compare performance against vendor baselines on NVIDIA and AMD flagship GPUs. Mojo matches CUDA and HIP on memory-bound workloads, the authors report, while compute-bound cases are harder. The study gauges whether one language can realistically span the GPU ecosystem for high-performance science.
arxiv-2509-21639:
Shmuel Friedland, a mathematician, shows how tensor math can describe quantum entanglement in this 2025 paper. Entanglement links particles so they behave as one system. Telling entangled states apart from separable ones is a core question in quantum theory. The paper is set to appear in Communications in Mathematical Physics and pulls known and new results into one frame.

Friedland ties measures of entanglement to two sizes of a tensor, its spectral norm and its nuclear norm. States with no entanglement are exactly those whose nuclear norm takes one fixed value. Checking that value is hard in general. For systems of identical particles, such as bosons, he shows the values can be computed in fast polynomial time, which makes those cases practical to test.
arxiv-2509-21739:
Drum transcription is usually a sorting task over spectrograms, but a generative reframing may work better. Michael Yeung and 4 co-authors present a diffusion system for it in a 2025 paper. Noise to Notes transforms audio conditioned Gaussian noise into drum events with velocities. Diffusion offers a flexible speed hit rate trade off and strong inpainting. Binary onsets plus non stop velocities challenge standard diffusion training.

An annealed pseudo Huber loss enables working joint optimization of those mixed outputs. Traits from music base models augment low level spectrogram traits. Those traits capture high level semantic information and improve robustness to out of distribution audio. Automatic drum transcription from recordings is the end task. The generative approach redefines how drum events can be produced.
arxiv-2509-21939:
Waves in the upper atmosphere, called gravity waves, push on the air flow and shape the climate of the middle atmosphere. Tobias Kühner, Georg Sebastian Voelker, and Ulrich Achatz examine what standard shortcuts in modeling those waves leave out. Their 2025 paper, submitted to the Journal of Geophysical Research, lists three gaps: the flux form used, the assumption that wave patterns settle instantly, and the ignoring of sideways wave travel.

The authors run a wave model that makes none of those assumptions inside a global weather and climate code. Turning each aspect on shows all three change the results. Transience and sideways travel matter most. The changes reach the average winds high above all latitudes, and they also alter the daily solar tides, both the parts that follow the Sun and those that do not. Comparisons with satellite readings favor the runs that include both key aspects.
arxiv-2509-22239:
Andrew Duncan, Murray Elder, Lisa Frenkel, and Mengfan Lyu prove a closure result about a family of formal languages in this 2025 paper. Multiple context-free languages sit between context-free and context-sensitive languages in expressive power, and they matter for modeling natural language syntax. The question is whether scrambling all the words of such a language, in every possible order, stays inside the family. That operation is called permutation closure.

The authors prove that it does: the permutation closure of a multiple context-free language is again multiple context-free. The result extends earlier work that settled the weaker operation of cyclic shift for the same family, and it parallels older results for several other language classes. Where the cyclic shift proof worked with grammars, this proof runs through restricted tree stack automata, a machine model for the family.
arxiv-2509-22339:
Arman Akbari and eight co-authors present CircuitSense, a benchmark testing whether multimodal language models can read engineering diagrams as engineers do. Design work moves through levels of abstraction, from system plans down to single components, and each level needs visual understanding joined with math. Their 2025 benchmark holds more than eight thousand problems, from component schematics to system block diagrams, generated by a pipeline that also derives the symbolic equations automatically, giving exact labels.

Six leading models, closed and open, were evaluated across the full workflow of perception, analysis, and design. The closed models scored very high on perception tasks like recognizing components and tracing connections. On deriving symbolic equations and analytical reasoning, though, every model fell to low scores. That gap between seeing a circuit and reasoning about it mathematically is the paper's central finding.
arxiv-2509-22539:
Idweep J. Gogoi and 3 co-authors split a graph's energy down to single vertices, for a Randić version. Graph energy sums the magnitudes of a matrix's eigenvalues and is used in chemical graph theory. A 2018 idea assigned each vertex its own share of the total energy. The team extends that idea to the Randić matrix, which weights edges by the degrees of their endpoints.

They define the Randić energy of a vertex and study its traits with combinatorial tools. Upper and lower bounds are derived. Among connected graphs, the center of a star graph scores highest, while leaf vertices score lowest. A Coulson-type integral formula and its uses round out the results.
arxiv-2509-22739:
Sasha Cui and Zhongren Chen automate activation steering, a cheap way to adjust a language model after training. Steering adds a vector to the model's internal activations to shift its behavior. It beats fine-tuning on cost and prompts on control, but older methods need hand-built prompt pairs or laborious feature labels. Their family of methods, PAS, builds the steering vector from any labeled data set with no human steps.

Tests covered three open-weight models and eighteen tasks. PAS reliably improved behavior tasks, though not intelligence-oriented ones. An introspective variant gave the strongest causal effects on bias, morality, and alignment measures. PAS also stacked gains on top of in-context learning and fine-tuning.
arxiv-2509-22839:
Ibrahim Delibasoglu and Fredrik Heintz build a forecasting model that shows which time periods drive its predictions. Explainability in time series matters for decisions, but pinpointing important times is harder than ranking features. Post-hoc saliency methods are also expensive. Their architecture, CrossScaleNet, mixes patch-based cross-attention with multi-scale processing. Attention sits inside training, so saliency comes out as a built-in product, not an afterthought.

They validated it on synthetic data with known saliency and on public benchmarks. The model found the right time spans and forecast as well as or better than most transformer rivals. The authors note many models that claim explainability fail on standard benchmarks. CrossScaleNet aims to deliver both at once.
arxiv-2509-22939:
Rob McConkey and Luke J Seaton study how a knot invariant called theta acts under satellite operations. Satellites build new knots by embedding one knot inside a pattern around another. The pair first prove theta adds up under connected sum. They then build a code tool that makes twisted Whitehead doubles.

With that tool, they probe untwisted Whitehead doubles in depth. They propose a conjecture for how theta behaves on those doubles. Checks on the first two thousand nine hundred seventy-seven prime knots all agree with the claim. Theta pairs with the Alexander polynomial as a joint invariant. The authors suggest more work on cables and general satellites.
arxiv-2509-23139:
Implicit neural representations store signals in network weights, but their setup is chosen by guesswork. Sipeng Chen, Yan Zhang, and Shibo Li turn that setup into an optimization problem. Choices include activation type, start scales, and per-layer tweaks, all tangled together. Their framework, OptiINR, searches the joint space with Bayesian optimization. Activation families span sinusoidal, wavelet, and variable-periodic types.

The search replaces grid hunts and hand tuning with one data-driven process. The authors claim globally optimal configurations within the searched space. Those settings aim to maximize performance across signal tasks. The work lays a principled base for designing such representations.
arxiv-2509-23239:
Weighted conditional type operators get a full classification for two isometry-like classes here. Y Estaremi, M S Al Ghafri, and S Shamsigamchi study m-isometric and quasi-m-isometric cases. The stage is the Hilbert space of square-integrable functions. They characterize which such operators fall in each class. For normal operators of this type, the two subclasses turn out to coincide.

Multiplication operators get special results as a clean subcase. For order two or more, such an operator is m-isometric exactly when it is isometric. The quasi version follows the same pattern. Examples illustrate the boundary cases of the theorems.
arxiv-2509-23339:
Restoring damaged faces means searching a huge space of plausible outputs, and artifacts creep in. Bin Wu and 4 co-authors apply online reinforcement learning to blind face restoration. Their LRPO framework samples candidates and learns from their rewards. Good outputs grow more likely over time. Plain RL, though, drifts too far from the true face.

Three strategies keep quality and fidelity in balance. A composite reward is tailored to face restoration traits. Ground-truth guided likelihood regularization anchors the outputs. Noise-level advantage assignment credits the right steps. Across experiments, restoration quality beat baselines and hit top-tier scores.
arxiv-2509-23539:
Abstract algebra over a quantum plane raises a basic question: what counts as a local piece of the space? Anar Dosi, the sole author, studies localizations, in Taylor's sense, of the algebras tied to a contractive quantum plane. These Arens-Michael-Fréchet algebras encode the formal geometry of the noncommutative analytic space. Structure sheaves over open sets give candidate local algebras.

Dosi shows every algebra from those sheaves is indeed a localization. That homology property of the sheaves then drives key facts about Taylor and Putinar spectra. The spectra concern left Banach modules over the algebra of global sections. The paper links the sheaf picture to spectral theory for the q-plane.
arxiv-2509-23939:
Some hard problems ask for the point where the sum of two curved-space costs is least. D. R. Sahu and 2 co-authors speed up a splitting method, Douglas-Rachford, on Hadamard manifolds. These are curved spaces where the method's steps still make sense. They give two forms of the method, one with inertia and one without. Both are proved to converge, with rates, under stated terms.

Forms that run in parallel handle sums with many parts. The test case is the Heron problem on such spaces, a least-sum-of-distances task with many target sets. Tests there show the new forms work as claimed.
arxiv-2509-24039:
Nearby brain cells that respond to sound tend to act alike, forming smooth maps. Haider Al-Tahan and 3 co-authors ask if that layout also shapes how sound facts are stored. They built TopoAudio, a sound model trained on a flat sheet where close units are pushed to tune alike.

The added layout rules did not hurt scores on speech and everyday sound tasks. The model also matched brain scans from listeners about as well as plain models did. Its inner parts were tighter, though, and they lined up more closely with parts drawn from human brain recordings. Layout, the team argues, helps models store facts in a brain-like way.
arxiv-2509-24239:
Chess punishes sloppy strategy, vague rules, and lost track of the board, which makes it a sharp test of language models. Jincheng Liu and 7 co-authors built ChessArena, a testbed where models play each other under four modes. They tested thirteen models over more than eight hundred games, probing rule knowledge, move choice, and puzzle solving.

No model beat an amateur-level chess engine, and some lost even to random play. A fine-tuned mid-size model from the team did much better, nearing far larger reasoning models. The gap suggests current models lean on pattern matching more than genuine strategic thought, the authors argue.
arxiv-2509-24339:
Waves from gravity leave a lasting mark called memory, a fixed shift in the shape of space after the wave passes. Anthi Voulgari Revof and Shubhanshu Tiwari compute that effect for a cosmos with a positive cosmological constant, known as de Sitter space. The standard flat-space account ties radiation to symmetry at null infinity. With a positive constant, future infinity is spacelike and fields fade in a different way.

The pair derive leading corrections for both displacement and spin memory. The size of each correction grows in direct proportion to the cosmological constant, stated through flux-balance relations. As expected, they are far too small for any current or planned observatory to detect.
arxiv-2509-24439:
Electrons in the Hubbard model can line up into spin stripes, patterns that matter for cuprate superconductors. Ruslan Mushkaev and 3 co-authors map spin-stripe order on the square lattice as doping and temperature change. They solve the Bethe-Salpeter equation with a local vertex taken from dynamical mean field theory, working both inside and outside the antiferromagnetic phase.

Broad regions of horizontal and vertical stripes appear at low temperatures, with or without next-nearest neighbor hopping. The stripe wavelength shifts with hole doping in a nonlinear way. It is also highly sensitive to the ratio of nearest to next-nearest hopping, a knob that tunes the pattern.
arxiv-2509-24539:
Robots that copy animal motion usually train with an on-policy method that values stability over sample thrift. Nayari Marie Lessa and 2 co-authors swap in Soft Actor-Critic, an off-policy algorithm, paired with adversarial motion priors for imitation learning. Replay-driven learning and entropy-guided exploration promise more natural motion from fewer samples.

They test the pairing on quadruped gaits across several reference motions and terrains. The framework kept task execution stable while earning higher imitation rewards than the widely used on-policy pairing. Robustness improved as well. The findings make a case that off-policy imitation deserves a central place in robot motion generation.
arxiv-2509-25639:
Auriane Egal, Paul Wiegert, Danielle Moser, and a wider team wrote this astronomy paper, published in 2025. It predicts the 2025 October Draconid meteor outburst, when Earth plows through young dust trails shed by a comet.

The Draconids are famous for rare, fierce storms that can top ten thousand meteors an hour, though most years are quiet. In 2025 Earth was set to cross trails the comet shed in 2005 and 2012. Three independent models, tuned on past outbursts including new ones in 2019 and 2024, all foresaw a burst on October 8. The meteors would be faint, seen best by radar, peaking in the mid-afternoon by world time. The team urges radar stations across the Northern Hemisphere and cameras in Asia to watch, so the forecasts can be checked and the comet's dust better mapped.
arxiv-2510-00139:
Daryl Funk, Angus Matthews, and Dillon Mayhew wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the limits of logical description. They ask which families of gain-graphic matroids can be captured by sentences in a counting logic. Matroids generalize the idea of independence in graphs and vector spaces. Gain-graphic ones arise from graphs whose edges carry labels from a group.

The authors build a Myhill-Nerode style test that can prove a family is not definable in that logic. Applying it, they show non-definability whenever the label group fails a finiteness condition. They also define a conviviality graph for a group and use its infinitude as a second route to the same verdict. The tools are meant to serve future constructions in matroid theory. Such negative results matter because they mark where formal description must stop.
arxiv-2510-00639:
Halpern and Toda present this paper, published at the ACM Multimedia Asia Workshops in December 2024, on scoring the severity of disordered speech without any reference recording. Clinicians now rate such speech by hand, which is slow, costly, and subjective. Many automatic systems need a clean reference sample or transcript, which real clinic visits rarely provide.

Their method, SpeechLMScore, uses a language model built from acoustic units to judge how natural speech sounds. They also release NKI-SpeechRT, a new dataset for severity research. Across two datasets, SpeechLMScore beat traditional acoustic feature methods and held up well under noise. The gap to reference-based scoring remained, but the reference-free approach proved strong enough for practical triage support.
arxiv-2510-01039:
Dwivedi, Schiassi, Sigovan, and Sixou present Gated X-TFC in this 2025 arXiv paper on scientific machine learning. Some differential equations develop boundary layers, razor-thin regions where the solution changes almost vertically. Physics-informed neural networks handle such sharp gradients poorly unless the domain is split, and splitting adds messy interface penalties. The X-TFC method avoids multi-objective training by enforcing boundary conditions exactly, but it stays slow and resists decomposition.

Gated X-TFC replaces hard subdomain borders with a smooth logistic gate that widens or narrows radial basis kernels across the domain. On a one-dimensional convection-diffusion benchmark, it cut error by an order of magnitude versus standard X-TFC. It also used eighty percent fewer collocation points and shortened training time by about two thirds. A meta-learning layer predicts good gate settings for new problems.
arxiv-2510-01239:
Lee and co-authors at Qualcomm AI Research stop a phone's language model from rereading the whole conversation for every side errand. Multi-turn assistants constantly spawn sub-tasks like rewriting queries or summarizing, and naive handling recomputes everything. Their system, CIFLEX, branches off the main conversation instead.

Sub-tasks run in isolated side paths that reuse the main task's cached context. When a sub-task finishes, the model rolls back to the untouched main path. A hierarchy of yes-or-no classifiers picks sub-tasks in a way small models can handle. Experiments showed large cost savings with task performance intact. Cache reuse is the whole trick, since prefill dominates on-device cost. Binary decomposition turns one hard choice into several easy ones. Query rewriting and summarization are the everyday sub-tasks named. Rollback keeps the main thread pristine after each errand. Phones gain assistant range without cloud bills.
arxiv-2510-01339:
Spagnoletti, Almansa, and Pereyra restore high-definition video with a solver that respects time instead of treating frames as strangers. Image restoration models achieve stunning stills, but frame-by-frame application flickers and smears motion. Their solver, LATINO, builds on video consistency models that internalize temporal causality.

A plug-and-play Bayesian design enforces measurement consistency without expensive automatic differentiation. Few function evaluations per reconstruction keep the method practical. Moving objects and camera shake, the classic failure cases, were handled convincingly in tests. Perceptual quality and physical faithfulness arrive together rather than trading off. As few as eight evaluations can complete a restoration pass. A frame-wise consistency module and smoothing regularizer support the prior. Zero-shot use means no retraining for each new degradation. Bayesian framing keeps uncertainty part of the answer. High definition is where temporal errors become impossible to hide on screen.
arxiv-2510-01539:
Vashishtha and co-authors build a stricter test of counterfactual reasoning for language models, using code that can actually run. Asking what would have happened takes three steps: infer hidden values, change one, then predict the result. Many benchmarks skip the first step, which flatters the models being graded.

Executable problems force all three steps and scale to many difficulty levels. Accuracy fell sharply once the hidden-value step could no longer be dodged. The gap between intervention questions and full counterfactuals reached tens of points. Training on the generated problems then helped smaller models improve at the complete skill. Code makes each hidden value checkable, since the program itself fixes the ground truth. Difficulty knobs let test makers stress one step at a time. High-stakes fields need this honesty, because skipped inference hides real risk. The framework doubles as a training data factory.
arxiv-2510-01639:
Truong, Lau, and Qi test whether language models can read road maps by asking them to reconstruct masked GPS trajectories. Navigation is a clean probe of geospatial reasoning that text-trained models were never explicitly taught. Their dataset holds over four thousand real trajectories across regions and transport modes.

Given the road network as context, models generate valid connected paths with no routing tools. They beat specialized trajectory-recovery systems and off-the-shelf baselines, generalizing zero-shot. Fine-grained analysis finds strong coordinate comprehension alongside systematic regional biases. Preference-aware rerouting shows the flexibility that structured reasoning unlocks. Schema-constrained prompting keeps generations valid and connected. Enterprise navigation performance is approached without any engine. Structured map topology is the key eliciting ingredient identified. Transportation-mode biases join regional ones in the gap analysis. User preferences bend routes flexibly once language reasoning is in charge.
arxiv-2510-02239:
Gruntkowska and co-authors argue that training should skip most layers at each step. Their 2025 machine learning paper challenges a deep habit. Standard optimizers update every layer on every step. The Muon optimizer, a recent leader, follows that rule. The team shows full updates can be provably wasteful. Their method, Drop-Muon, updates a random subset of layers per step. A randomized schedule decides which layers move. Layer specific geometry still guides each update. The design merges progressive training thrift with modern optimizer quality.

Theory gives convergence guarantees for the scheme. The guarantees cover smooth and rougher loss surfaces. They also cover noisy stochastic gradients. Cost analysis shows full updates win only under a rare condition. Controlled image experiments backed the theory in practice. Drop-Muon trained faster at equal quality. Updating less can truly converge faster.
arxiv-2510-02339:
Zhou and co-authors ask which uncertainty method works best inside argument based language models. Their 2025 paper studies ArgLLMs, systems that decide through structured debate. Each claim in such a system carries a confidence score. That score steers the final verdict, so its quality matters. The team plugged several known uncertainty methods into the framework. They then graded claim verification performance for each method. The test itself offers a fresh way to judge uncertainty tools. Tricky and contentious claims make the grading demanding.

Plain direct prompting won the comparison clearly. Asking the model for its confidence beat far more complex methods. Among the complex options, one LUQ implementation placed best. Semantic entropy and eccentricity methods trailed behind it. Simple verbal confidence also suits long, disputed statements. Explainable decision systems gain a cheap, effective option.
arxiv-2510-02539:
Wang organizes document search as a walk down a tree of concept prototypes. His 2025 information retrieval paper adapts a framework called Cobweb. Neural search usually scores a flat cloud of vectors. That flatness wastes corpus structure and hides its reasoning. Cobweb sorts sentence embeddings into a prototype hierarchy. Internal nodes act as concept summaries at many scales. Search proceeds from coarse concepts to fine matches. Two rankers use the tree in different ways. One runs a guided best-first search. The other sums scores along the retrieval path.

Tests used MS MARCO and a large question pairs corpus. Encoder and decoder embeddings both entered the trials. With strong encoders, tree search matched plain dot product scoring. With weak GPT-2 vectors, dot product search collapsed badly. The tree methods still retrieved relevant documents there. Retrieval paths double as readable explanations. Robustness to embedding quality is the headline gain.
arxiv-2510-02739:
Thomson reports sky maps of ultra-high energy cosmic rays from the Telescope Array. His 2025 astroparticle physics talk covers two medium scale excesses. The array is the largest such observatory in the Northern Hemisphere. Cosmic rays at these energies arrive as rare air showers. Surface detectors record the shower footprints across the desert. Two patches of sky hold more events than chance suggests. One hotspot sits near the Ursa Major constellation. Another excess points toward the Perseus-Pisces supercluster. An oversampling analysis re-examines the features in the data.

Medium scale patterns may betray the sources of these particles. Magnetic deflections blur smaller scale pointing badly. Hotspots survive as the readable clue at these energies. The talk presents significance estimates for both regions. Comparing hemispheres sharpens the origin question further. Local large scale structure may be steering the arrivals. Each added year of exposure firms up the maps.
arxiv-2510-02839:
Pamshetti, Zhang, and Sun tackle battery health forecasting. Knowing when a battery will fade matters for safety and cost. Real batteries degrade in messy ways. Capacity drops, stalls, and sometimes briefly recovers. Pure data-driven models often miss the long trend. The team's model is called Karma. It blends deep learning with stored knowledge about how batteries age.

Karma first splits the battery signal by frequency. One stream tracks the slow, long-term decline. The other tracks fast, short-term wiggles. A knowledge layer then guides the forecast. It forces the trend to follow a double-exponential aging curve. A particle filter tunes that curve and reports uncertainty. Tests used the standard NASA and CALCE battery data sets. Karma cut average error by about half on the NASA set. It also beat rival methods on the CALCE set by a wide margin.
arxiv-2510-03139:
Gitika and co-authors tune a gravitational wave detector made of pulsars. Pulsar timing arrays clock many spinning neutron stars at once. Shared delays in those clocks can reveal nanohertz waves. The team hunted the noise sources that cap sensitivity. MeerKAT data on eighty-nine millisecond pulsars formed the base. Pulse jitter, a wobble in each tick, was measured anew.

Twenty pulsars gained their first jitter values in this work. Over half the sightings of eleven pulsars are jitter-ruled. The brightest pulsar is jitter-ruled every single time. Forecasts for the future SKA-Mid telescope followed. Its best twenty-nine pulsars would hit the same jitter wall. Gas between stars adds a second noise source. Modeling it as a smooth random process handled it best. A lower radio band could lift wave sensitivity slightly. Focused, frequent looks at the best pulsars help most, they find.
arxiv-2510-03339:
Ennadir and colleagues from industry labs present a 2025 arXiv paper on pooling, the step that squeezes a transformer's token outputs into one fixed vector. Pooling choices shape what a model can express, yet papers rarely study them closely. The authors build a theory that bounds what pooled models can represent and tell apart. They test pooling styles on vision, language, and time series tasks to see how the theory plays out.

The results split by task type in a consistent way. Pooling that smooths tokens worked best when a task needed broad context. Pooling that expands detail did better when fine contrasts mattered. Learned pooling settled toward the best balance when training data and time were plentiful. No single method won everywhere, the team stresses. Their bounds give designers a principled way to pick pooling by task instead of by habit.
arxiv-2510-03439:
Boldt and Mortensen present a 2025 arXiv paper on finding the building blocks of languages that AI agents invent. In emergent language studies, agents develop their own codes to talk about shared scenes. Human languages build words from morphemes, the smallest units that carry meaning. Their algorithm, CSAR, hunts for such units in agent corpora. It scores form and meaning pairs by mutual information, picks the best, removes it, and repeats the cycle.

Tests on generated data sets showed the method recovers planted units well against rival baselines. On human language data, its guesses looked reasonable to the authors. The team then turned CSAR loose on several real emergent languages. It measured how much synonymy and polysemy those codes carry, two traits that shape how learnable a language feels. Tools like this help linguists judge whether agent codes grow true grammar or stay simple signal lists.
arxiv-2510-03539:
Van Heijningen presents a 2025 arXiv paper on Rasnik, a three point optical alignment sensor born in particle physics. The system reads position from coded masks with absolute values, so readings never drift by accumulation. Purely optical sensing makes it immune to electromagnetic noise. Working distances span from fifty millimeters to fifteen meters. New software called RasCal processes camera images in real time and steers several cameras at once with thread safe control.

Live tests hit processing rates above three hundred frames per second on consumer hardware at best settings. Displacement sensitivity reached five picometers per root hertz in a gravity lab setup. Trials covered a Watt's linkage for dynamic checks and thermal vacuum testing of photoreceiver mounts for the LISA space mission. Multi day runs held absolute tracking without drift. Gravitational wave detectors and space instruments both need cheap, relentless precision, and Rasnik now ships with software to match.
arxiv-2510-03639:
Wang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper teaching speech recognition without paired audio and text, by working at the syllable level. Unpaired training would open speech technology to the languages lacking transcribed recordings. Phoneme based systems need grapheme to phoneme converters and train unstably where phoneme boundaries blur. Their system, SylCipher, leans on masked language modeling over syllable units, avoiding both problems. The team evaluated it on English benchmarks and on Mandarin, where phoneme methods have struggled.

On LibriSpeech, the syllable approach cut error rates by up to forty percent relative to the best unpaired systems. It generalized to a caption data set. On Mandarin it reached a phoneme error rate of about thirteen percent, in a setting where phoneme based rivals failed to converge. The authors admit universal tokenization remains unsolved for scripts that omit vowels. Still, the results widen the map of languages that speech tools can reach.
arxiv-2510-04039:
Lei and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on helping AI agents click the right button on a crowded screen. Interface agents must ground a text instruction to an exact on-screen element before they can act. On complex, high-resolution screens that grounding step is unreliable, and one wrong click can derail a whole task. The authors train a model that reasons about the image.

Their system, GUI-Spotlight, calls specialized tools to narrow its focus onto smaller screen regions iteratively. Each round refines the search area until the target element is pinned down. On the ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark, the model set a new accuracy high among compared systems. It did so with strikingly little training data, using tens of thousands of samples where rivals used millions. That data efficiency suggests iterative focus, not brute scale, is the missing ingredient for precise grounding.
arxiv-2510-04139:
Johansson, Bakkenes, and Wang present this 2025 arXiv course project report on adapting a language model to an underrepresented language. Large models train mostly on English, so they underperform elsewhere and risk accelerating digital language death. The team set out to improve Google's Gemma 2 for Swedish and to document a reusable recipe. Their approach combined curated culturally relevant data with two standard techniques.

LoRA fine-tuning adjusted the model cheaply on the prepared dataset. Retrieval-augmented generation supplied current information at answer time and reduced off-topic responses. Together, the methods improved question answering, summarization, and translation for Swedish. The authors are candid about limits: small datasets, overfitting struggles, and evaluation by only two judges on few prompts. They suggest larger curated datasets, better target-language embeddings, and human-feedback training as next steps. The report doubles as a roadmap for other communities adapting open models to their own languages.
arxiv-2510-04639:
Iraci and a large international team wrote this 2025 paper on merging low frequency radio data into a pulsar timing array. Timing arrays listen for gravitational waves by watching the clockwork pulses of spinning neutron stars. Signals from interstellar gas add noise that mimics or masks the waves. Low frequency observations feel that gas noise most strongly, so they can measure and remove it. The team folded LOFAR and NenuFAR data into the European array for the first time.

The combined set, called DR2low, holds twelve pulsars watched for about eleven years. Its frequencies span a wide band from thirty megahertz to twenty five hundred megahertz. Noise models built on the wider band sharpen the data set from new receivers. Cleaner noise models raise the odds of spotting the background hum of gravitational waves. The work is a step toward the third international data release, which aims at a detection.
arxiv-2510-05139:
Hamed Jelodar and three co-authors benchmark small language models on describing code in this 2025 arXiv paper. Natural language description turns structured material like source code into readable text. Teams assume the biggest model writes the best descriptions. Nobody had tested that assumption systematically across model families.

Their framework, NLD-LLM, evaluates Qwen, DeepSeek, Phi, LLaMA, and Mistral models under one protocol. Standardized prompts and clear task guidance keep the comparison fair. An iterative refinement loop then improves each model's outputs step by step. Semantic and structural metrics showed prompt design mattered enormously. Smaller models often performed competitively, sometimes beating larger ones, when prompts were well crafted. The findings favor task-specific, efficient models over defaulting to the largest.
arxiv-2510-05239:
P. Tiwari and ten co-authors analyze the fading light of gamma-ray bursts across the whole spectrum in this 2025 arXiv paper. They assembled 31 bursts observed between 2008 and 2024. Swift and Fermi data together span from soft X-rays to high-energy gamma rays. The goal is to pin down how relativistic shock waves radiate.

The team modeled each afterglow with a forward shock producing synchrotron and synchrotron self-Compton light. A self-Compton-dominated model in a wind-like medium fit the data best. That medium matches expectations for long-duration bursts from massive stars. The fits demand a notably low fraction of energy in magnetic fields. The model also explains why soft X-ray and TeV bands carry comparable energy. These benchmarks refine the microphysics used in future burst studies.
arxiv-2510-05339:
Abrar Faiyad and Ashlie Martini simulate doped molybdenum disulfide with machine learning in this 2025 arXiv paper. Doping tunes the layered material for electronics, optics, and low-friction coatings. Accurate quantum calculations are far too slow for large doped systems. A learned interatomic potential promises quantum-level accuracy at classical cost.

The team applied Meta's Universal Model for Atoms to MoS2 doped with 25 elements. Benchmarks against density functional theory showed formation-energy errors near 0.37 electronvolts. Heating and cooling runs on 3,100-atom cells revealed four dopant behaviors. Some metals cluster and fracture the layers, while others diffuse between them. Reactive non-metals form stable compounds inside the matrix. The open workflow enables fast screening of dopant candidates.
arxiv-2510-05539:
Emas and a large collaboration validate a flagship cosmology analysis before trusting its results. The analysis joins galaxy clustering data from the DESI instrument with weak gravitational lensing surveys. Such joint studies can test the standard model of the universe with fresh precision. Modeling errors could quietly bias the answers, so checks must come first.

The team designs scale cuts that drop data where modeling gets shaky. With those cuts, key parameters shift by less than a third of the statistical error. Lensing data come from the KiDS, DES, and HSC surveys, which overlap the DESI survey skies. They also run shear ratio tests, which compare lensing signals across galaxy samples. The same cosmic model fits those ratios well, supporting the internal consistency of the data. The study clears the ground for the coming full parameter analysis of these datasets.
arxiv-2510-05739:
Zhang bounds the higher cumulants of a random variable using only one moment. Cumulants measure non-normality and drive tools like Edgeworth expansions and concentration bounds. Controlling their size usually demands strong assumptions about the distribution. Zhang's 2025 inequality needs only a single finite absolute moment.

The bound comes from the combinatorial structure of the moment-cumulant formula. Its coefficient grows like a factorial divided by an exponential factor. Classical bounds grow far faster, on the order of n to the n. Zhang's rate is therefore an exponential improvement for large orders. Ordered Bell numbers set the general constant, tied to the log of two. Fewer contributing partitions tighten the bound as assumptions grow. Centered and symmetric variables earn still sharper constants. No generating function or dependence structure needs checking first. The same control extends to joint cumulants in several variables.
arxiv-2510-05939:
Skowronski and colleagues upgrade the BGO detector at the underground LUNA site. Radiative capture reactions for nuclear astrophysics have tiny cross sections. Total absorption setups need high capture rates plus very low background. Their 2025 upgrades target both with a split BGO detector.

Three-layer shielding cuts the high-energy background rate about fourfold. Higher summing capture rates come with that background cut. The setup enables the first direct reading of a sixty-five keV resonance. That resonance sits in the oxygen-17 proton capture reaction. Splitting the detector also spots and cuts beam-made signals faking the sum peak. The deep site already cuts cosmic background many times over. In-situ activation readings of unstable products form a second new use. Nitrogen-14 capture making oxygen-15 shows the activation method at work. Complex gamma chains gain most from the split design. Stellar reaction rates are what the work pins down.
arxiv-2510-06239:
Gupta presents OpenStaxQA, a multilingual question answering benchmark built from open textbooks. College-level education needs evaluation data that is rigorous and legally reusable. OpenStaxQA draws on forty-three open-source textbooks under a permissive Creative Commons license.

The textbooks span English, Spanish, and Polish, so the benchmark is multilingual from the start. Gupta fine-tunes models of roughly seven billion parameters using quantized low-rank adapters, the cheap method called QLoRA. He evaluates the tuned models and runs a zero-shot check on the AI2 reasoning challenge. That test asks whether textbook training transfers to other reasoning tasks. The paper also discusses broader impacts of openly licensed educational datasets. For tutoring system builders, OpenStaxQA offers evaluation grounded in real course material, not scraped trivia. Its license keeps the data shareable for research and teaching.
arxiv-2510-06339:
Cui and five co-authors combine vision and touch so robots can manipulate articulated objects in a 2025 robotics paper. Opening doors, drawers, and lids requires knowing hidden kinematics. Vision alone estimates them imprecisely on unfamiliar objects, while touch needs accurate initialization.

Vi-TacMan pairs the two senses in their natural roles. Vision proposes grasps and coarse directions, seeding a tactile controller for precise execution. Surface normals serve as geometric priors, and directions use von Mises–Fisher distributions. The tactile controller refines coarse visual estimates through real-time contact regulation. Remarkably, the system needs no explicit kinematic model. Gains over baselines were large and highly significant. Tests covered over fifty thousand simulated objects plus diverse real-world items. Performance generalized robustly across categories. Coarse visual cues suffice for reliable manipulation when touch closes the loop.
arxiv-2510-06539:
Zui Tao, Jonah Haber, and Jeffrey Neaton study excitons, which are pairs of an electron and a hole that move together through a solid. Their 2025 paper presents a new method for measuring how spread out an exciton is. The method works inside a standard physics framework called the Bethe-Salpeter equation. They test it on acene crystals, a family of materials built from rows of carbon rings.

The method breaks each exciton into small, localized building blocks called Wannier functions. That gives clear measures of where the electron and hole sit, at low computing cost. As the crystals grow from naphthalene to pentacene, the excitons become steadily more spread out. Their charge-transfer character and average electron-hole distance both grow as well. The approach also reveals hidden glide-mirror symmetries that standard methods miss.
arxiv-2510-06939:
Rukdee leads a team measuring the radiation around K2-18 b, a planet in the search for habitable worlds. Their 2025 paper characterizes the high-energy output of its host star, an M dwarf. The planet sits near the boundary between super-Earths and sub-Neptunes. X-ray light from the star can strip a planet's atmosphere over time.

The team combined X-ray data from eROSITA, Chandra, and an XMM-Newton look. They fitted the star's plasma emission with a thermal model. The star turns out relatively inactive, with low X-ray luminosity despite flares. Its activity ratio runs about ten times the Sun's level. The authors estimate how fast the planet's atmosphere evaporates under this radiation. They also model the atmosphere's structure with hydrodynamics. A quiet star helps explain how K2-18 b kept its atmosphere close in. Such measurements sharpen habitability judgments for planets around small stars.
arxiv-2510-07239:
Ziakas, Loo, Jain, and Russo present Red-Bandit, a system that adapts its attacks while probing a language model for weaknesses. Their 2025 paper works in automated red-teaming, the practice of stress-testing models before release. Red-Bandit trains a set of small expert modules, each tuned to one attack style. Styles range from manipulation to slang-laced prompts. A safety model rewards experts whose prompts slip past the target's guardrails.

During a live audit, a bandit algorithm picks which expert to deploy next. It balances trying new styles against pressing styles that already work. The system set new best results on a standard attack benchmark given enough tries. Its prompts also read more naturally than rivals, with lower perplexity scores. The bandit's choices double as a diagnosis, revealing which styles a given model fears most. Auditors can use that map to target fixes.
arxiv-2510-07439:
Ding, Lin, Yang, and Zhang present QFAMES, a quantum algorithm that reads the fine structure of a system's energy spectrum. Their 2025 paper targets eigenvalues and their multiplicities, the counts of states sharing one energy. Such detail reveals phases of matter and topological order. Extracting it with tiny error is provably hard in the worst case. The authors sidestep that barrier with physically motivated assumptions about which energy clusters dominate. Their filter isolates clusters of closely spaced leading eigenvalues one by one.

For each cluster, the algorithm counts how many states it holds. It also estimates measurable quantities restricted to that cluster's states. Numerical demonstrations cover two benchmarks. In the transverse-field Ising model, the method characterizes distinct quantum phases. In the two-dimensional toric code, it recovers the ground-state degeneracy that signals topological order. Rigorous guarantees accompany the simulations.
arxiv-2510-07939:
Elmer and Kadr wrote this 2025 representation theory paper on modules over elementary abelian p-groups. In characteristic p, even simple groups have wild representation theory. The authors study a family built from a two-dimensional indecomposable module by taking symmetric powers and duals. Tensor products of these modules are the focus. One basic product splits neatly into two neighbors in the family, whenever an index avoids multiples of p.

At multiples of p, the same product refuses to split and stays indecomposable. That contrast drives formulas for general products in the range below p. The formulas hold up to a correction term built from projective-like summands. The authors conjecture the formulas extend across the whole range and offer supporting evidence. Their work generalizes classic results of Almkvist and Fossum for cyclic groups. Even in wild territory, symmetric powers keep a surprisingly orderly multiplication table.
arxiv-2510-08239:
Chris Fields and colleagues argue in a 2025 arXiv paper that no lab test can certify that a system is purely classical. Tests do exist that certify entanglement, the quantum link between particles, when it is present. The open question was whether a test could certify its absence, called separability. The authors work in a topological representation, a math frame based on shape and connection, not on any one reading of quantum theory.

Within that frame, they prove that no operational protocol can certify separability. Any hands-on test sequence, however clever, leaves the classical label unproven. This supports Niels Bohr's old view that classicality is a practical notion, not a provable property. The result limits what device-independent checks can promise in quantum work. It also matters for claims about decoherence, where quantum effects fade into classical behavior.
arxiv-2510-08539:
Joe Suk and Yaqi Duan build a theory of why reward-based fine-tuning of language models works, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards uses simple binary feedback, right or wrong, to post-train models. It succeeds in practice, but a principled account of its dynamics was missing. The authors analyze training at both whole-response and token levels.

Their central quantity, the Gradient Gap, formalizes the pull from low-reward toward high-reward responses. Convergence depends critically on aligning updates with this gap, they prove. They derive a sharp step-size threshold set by the gap's size: below it learning converges, above it performance collapses. Theory predicts how the safe step size scales with response length and success rate. This explains why length normalization stabilizes training in practice. Controlled bandit simulations validated the predictions.
arxiv-2510-08739:
Yikai Zhao and Jiekai Ma explain complex ensemble time series forecasts with simpler stand-in models in a 2025 arXiv paper. AutoML tools like AutoGluon build ensembles that forecast well but hide their logic. Users cannot tell why a forecast says what it says, or how far to trust it. The authors tackle two linked problems: explaining the model, and judging how forecastable each series is.

A LightGBM stand-in model is trained to copy the ensemble's forecasts closely. SHAP values on the stand-in then explain the ensemble in terms of input features. Feature injection tests checked these explanations against known true effects, with very high faithfulness. A second tool scores each series' forecastability from its spectrum, against pure noise baselines. On the M5 data set, higher scores tracked better accuracy and closer stand-in fidelity. The scores also serve as trust filters for forecasts and their explanations.
arxiv-2510-09639:
Ahmad Zueter, Ahmad Dalaq, and Mohammed Daqaq test ventilation powered by folding geometry in a 2025 arXiv paper. The stack effect moves air naturally: warm air rises through a tall vent, pulling fresh air in below, but its strength is hard to control. Their system retrofits chimneys and exhaust risers with expandable origami units that change height and vent area on demand.

The units modulate the geometry to regulate buoyancy-driven airflow without relying on wind or sunshine. Using a three-dimensional computational model, the authors study how the deployable stack's design and the surrounding atmospheric conditions shape the volumetric airflow in expanded and contracted states. The ventilation rate rose by up to twenty-five percent each time the origami stack's height doubled. The authors pitch the concept for underground mines and buildings, especially energy-hungry or remote off-grid sites where adaptable passive ventilation saves power.
arxiv-2510-09839:
Johnathan Kowalski and Liangbo Liang build a library for identifying layered materials by their vibrations in a 2025 arXiv paper. Janus transition metal dichalcogenides are single-layer crystals whose two faces differ, breaking out-of-plane symmetry and adding new functions. Making and checking them is hard, so a fast in situ check is valuable, and Raman spectroscopy is the standard non-destructive tool for the job.

The authors compute a Raman digital twin library for many monolayer Janus materials in two phases. The set covers the group-six compounds of molybdenum and tungsten with sulphur, selenium, and tellurium, plus their Janus variants. Using first-principles density functional theory, they calculate vibration patterns and predict a distinct Raman fingerprint for each material. The signatures reflect each crystal's symmetry and composition, enabling clear naming and quality control.
arxiv-2510-09939:
Adil Kabylda and co-authors release QCell in this 2025 arXiv paper in computational chemistry. QCell is a quantum-mechanical dataset covering diverse fragments of biomolecules, the small building blocks of proteins, sugars, and other cell components. Such data trains machine learning force fields, fast models that mimic quantum accuracy.

The authors note that good force fields for living systems are held back by scarce, narrow quantum data. QCell spans all major classes of biomolecules found in cells, computed at quantum-mechanical quality. That breadth matters because a field trained on one class often fails on another. With richer reference data, the team aims to make learned simulations of biomolecular systems both faster and more trustworthy.
arxiv-2510-10239:
Boucksom gives lecture notes on hybrid analytic spaces in this 2025 arXiv text in algebraic geometry. The notes introduce non-Archimedean geometry, a geometry built on unusual notions of distance, as a tool for studying how complex algebraic varieties degenerate along a parameter.

Hybrid spaces fill in a one-parameter degeneration by attaching the Berkovich space, the non-Archimedean shadow of the family, as a central fiber. The notes are self-contained and move from amoebas, the logarithmic shadows of varieties, toward pluripotential theory on these hybrid spaces. That theory links complex analysis with the combinatorics of degeneration. The text is meant to bring new readers into a fast-growing meeting ground of geometry and analysis.
arxiv-2510-10339:
Rismani and co-authors connect AI ethics evaluations to real system risks in this 2025 arXiv paper on responsible AI. Over the past decade, many measures have appeared to judge the social and ethical effects of AI systems, guided by high-level principles. They are built and used in fragmented ways.

The authors argue that evaluations are rarely tied to the attributes of the system being tested, or to the specific hazards and harms that matter. A fairness score means little if it is not linked to who can be hurt and how. Their framework situates each measure inside the system and its context. Better-situated evaluation should tell builders which tests to run and what a passing score actually promises.
arxiv-2510-10639:
Haemin Choi and Gayathri Nadarajan test modern machine learning methods for predicting how satisfied students feel with their learning, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Student satisfaction has been studied widely, but newer methods have barely been tried on it. The authors compare several state of the art approaches. They find that automatic piecewise linear regression, a recent model pairing boosting with interpretability, fits the data best among the methods tested.

Reading the model's numerical and visual explanations, three factors stood out with the strongest positive impact: students' time management and focus, their perceived helpfulness to classmates, and participation in offline courses. Surprisingly, involvement in creative activities did not positively affect satisfaction. Because the model explains contributions at the individual level, educators can see which factors drive a particular student's satisfaction. The authors suggest this lets teaching be tailored to student profiles, rather than relying on group averages.
arxiv-2510-10739:
Shivani Shukla and Himanshu Joshi model conversations with language models as a system buffeted by noise, in this 2025 arXiv paper. When users iterate with a model toward several goals at once, the goals can interfere. The team's framework uses stochastic differential equations, which describe quantities that drift and diffuse randomly. An interference matrix captures how the competing goals push against each other during repeated interactions.

They validate the framework on iterative code generation, a proof of concept use. They analyzed 400 sessions across three goals: security, efficiency, and functionality. The results showed strategy dependent convergence, with rates ranging from 0.33 to 1.29 across the approaches tried, and a fit score, R-squared, of 0.74 for balanced strategies in their tests. The authors conclude that this style of analysis is feasible for multi goal model interactions, with code generation as an initial test bed.
arxiv-2510-11139:
Do the biggest firms in an industry lift the productivity of their smaller rivals, or crowd them out? Mohammad Zeqi Yasin asks this question for Indonesian manufacturing in a 2025 arXiv economics paper. He studies superstar firms, those holding the top market share in their industry. He measures how exposure to them affects the output dynamics of other firms between 2001 and 2015.

Yasin finds that superstar exposure raises both the output level and the output growth of other firms, working through horizontal channels within a sector and province and vertical channels across sectors. Foreign superstars lift output except through the horizontal channel, while domestic ones generate positive spillovers through both channels. The negative side of growth comes mainly from reshuffling within groups, evidence of misallocation among surviving firms. Top firms look efficient but grow slowly, suggesting possible stagnation.
arxiv-2510-11239:
Filling in a smooth field over a curved surface, such as pollution levels over the Earth, is harder than interpolating on a flat map. Charlie Sire, Mike Pereira, and Thomas Romary develop such a method for general curved domains in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their approach covers spline interpolation on compact Riemannian manifolds beyond the standard Euclidean and spherical cases.

The method exploits the equivalence between spline interpolation and kriging, the geostatistical interpolator. The authors approximate random fields on the manifold with finite elements, using Gaussian Markov random fields and a discretization of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on a triangulated mesh. Domain deformation lets the model express local anisotropies, directions in which the field varies faster or slower. Tests on the sphere, including a pollution study, match the classical spherical harmonics method, and experiments on a cylinder surface show the generality of the approach.
arxiv-2510-11739:
Muhammad Hamza, Rizwan Jafar, and Muhammad Sharjeel ask whether a celebrity's traits can be inferred from fans' posts. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that most celebrity profiling work uses English text. Yet many celebrities and fans in the subcontinent write in Urdu. The authors built the first corpus for this task from Urdu tweets, taking posts from ten followers of each celebrity.

They trained both classic machine learning models, such as logistic regression and support vector machines, and deep learning models, such as convolutional and recurrent networks. The goal was to predict each celebrity's age group, profession, gender, and fame level. Gender proved the easiest trait to predict from followers' words. Profession was the hardest. Age and fame landed in between. The modest scores show that followers' language carries real but limited signals about the people they follow.
arxiv-2510-11839:
Yu-Hsiang Wang and Olgica Milenkovic introduce WaveletDiff, a method for generating synthetic time series. Real time series data are scarce in fields like healthcare and finance, yet models hunger for them. Earlier generators worked purely in time or purely in frequency, and both miss the multi-scale structure of real signals. Their 2025 arXiv paper trains a diffusion model directly on wavelet coefficients instead. Wavelets split a signal into layers from slow trends to fast wiggles.

A dedicated transformer handles each decomposition level, and cross-level attention lets the layers exchange information through adaptive gates. Energy constraints drawn from Parseval's theorem keep each level's spectrum faithful during generation. Across six real datasets drawn from energy, finance, and neuroscience, WaveletDiff beat the best time-domain and frequency-domain rivals. Its discriminative and Context-FID scores ran about three times smaller than the second-best method on average.
arxiv-2510-12039:
Jit Wu Yap counts the nearly invisible points of rational maps. In arithmetic dynamics, a rational map's canonical height measures a point's arithmetic complexity under iteration. Points of tiny height are rare and structurally important. His 2025 arXiv paper proves a uniform bound for rational maps over number fields, where uniformity means the constants depend only on the map's degree.

Specifically, consider a map with at most s places of bad reduction. The points below a small-height threshold number at most a constant times s times the logarithm of s. The result is a uniform version of a theorem of Baker. It also generalizes earlier work of Benedetto and Looper from polynomials to all rational maps. The engine is Luo's theory of degenerating sequences of rational maps, recently formalized by Favre and Gong using Berkovich spaces.
arxiv-2510-12539:
Zhao and co-authors tune vehicle to everything radio settings to balance road safety against energy use in rural areas, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Connected braking lets vehicles warn each other over 5G sidelink links, reducing fatal collisions. Rural roadside units are sparse and often power constrained or off grid, so every transmission setting carries an energy cost.

They study three control factors: subcarrier spacing, the modulation and coding scheme, and transmit power. Safety is measured by the packet receive ratio at the minimum communication distance. In heavy traffic, raising transmit power and choosing a low rate coding scheme at the middle spacing sustained high reliability at that distance, at higher energy cost. In light traffic, lower power with low coding levels gave a favorable reliability energy trade off. They conclude that rural vehicle networks need adaptive, energy aware configuration.
arxiv-2510-12639:
Srinivasan and Slotine analyze the continuous time flow behind the Sinkhorn algorithm, which matches two probability distributions, in a 2025 arXiv paper. In the limit of vanishing step size, this flow was shown to be a mirror descent on the space of such measures. How fast it contracts, and how its entropy behaves, were only partly understood.

The authors give contraction tests in two time dependent metrics given by the mirror Hessian, reducing them to coercivity of certain operators. They derive a precise identity for the entropy production rate, earlier known only to be at most zero. The flow creates a reversible Markov dynamics on its target marginal. They prove a Poincaré inequality giving its spectral gap as positive whenever the penalty is positive. Entropy decay is exponential exactly when a logarithmic Sobolev inequality holds. Two uses are sketched: designing latent spaces for generative models and stopping discrete algorithms.
arxiv-2510-12739:
Obeed and Jian replace the single large neural network inside a radio receiver with several small networks that cooperate, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Deep learning receivers for orthogonal frequency division multiplexing, the modulation used in WiFi and cellular systems, beat standard receivers in detection. But the usual models, adapted from vision models, are heavy, slow, and memory hungry, and shrinking them costs notable quality.

Their collaborative network design runs multiple small convolutional subnetworks in parallel, each viewing the signal from a different angle, such as channel correlations or interference patterns. The subnetworks fuse their outputs through interaction steps like element wise multiplication, which strengthens it. In tests the design greatly outperformed standard residual network designs in bit error rate. At equal size and compute cost it also reduced inference delay. The authors aim the design at resource constrained devices where full size vision style models cannot fit.
arxiv-2510-13039:
Oblomkov and Rozansky categorify a quantum supergroup action in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Categorification lifts algebraic structures into richer categorical ones. Numbers become spaces and equalities become explicit maps. Their target is the quantum group of the smallest super Lie algebra. It acts on repeated tensor powers of its two-dimensional vector representation, where one part is even and the other odd.

The authors realize the algebra's two generators as Fourier-Mukai functors. These are geometric transforms between derived categories of coherent sheaves. They act on total spaces of semi-parabolic vector bundles built over Grassmannians, the spaces of fixed-size subspaces. Earlier categorifications by Sartori and by Tian used symplectic methods instead. A diagrammatic approach covered the positive half. Oblomkov and Rozansky's build is algebro-geometric. It follows a path used before for the ordinary rank-two quantum group.
arxiv-2510-13539:
Nadeem and co-authors design a smart interface for a rescue wearable that guides first responders during emergencies. Their 2025 arXiv paper comes from the KIRETT project, which aids rescue operations with artificial intelligence. The wearable reads live patient data such as pulse, blood pressure, and ECG traces. It then suggests step-by-step treatment drawn from local rescue protocols.

The design is informed by a treatment knowledge graph built for the project. Graph transitions map directly onto interface elements: prompts, options, and screen changes. The authors gather requirements specific to knowledge graph solutions. They also gather the direct requirements of health professionals working under time pressure. The resulting interface aims at fast, situation-aware information delivery in chaotic settings. Warnings and alarms flag drastic changes in the monitored patient data.
arxiv-2510-13639:
Beale and Tlupova derive high-order formulas for taming nearly singular integrals over surfaces. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves boundary integral methods, which rewrite flow and Laplace problems as surface integrals. The kernels blow up at the surface, so plain numerical rules fail nearby. Accurate values near surfaces are needed when two surfaces almost touch.

Their regularization smooths the kernel so standard quadrature works without special care. They treat single and double layer integrals for harmonic functions and for Stokes flow. Errors shrink at high order as the smoothing radius narrows, with three accuracy levels derived. Tests show the predicted convergence rates in practice. A companion technique spreads accurate near-surface values to all grid points efficiently. Demonstrations include a harmonic function set by interface conditions and flow around a moving spheroid.
arxiv-2510-13839:
Zhang, Conia, and Rago extract part-whole product ontologies from raw customer reviews using large language models. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets meronymies, structures listing which parts belong to which products. Such ontologies organize catalogues and power review aggregation, yet building them by hand is slow and costly. Most automated work chases is-a taxonomies instead of part-of relations.

Their fully automated method prompts language models to mine meronymic structure from review text. No manual annotation pipeline stands between raw reviews and the finished ontology. An LLM-as-judge evaluation compares the output against a BERT-based baseline method. The language model ontologies won that comparison, the authors report. The study is early groundwork rather than a finished product tool. It suggests large models can shoulder ontology extraction well beyond products. E-commerce is the motivating case, with travel and movies as neighbouring domains.
arxiv-2510-13939:
Tuhin Chakrabarty, Jane C. Ginsburg, and Paramveer Dhillon test whether AI writing trained on copyrighted books can match expert human writers, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The question feeds directly into lawsuits over training data, and into the legal test of whether AI output harms the market for the original works.

In a preregistered study, writers with Master of Fine Arts training and three frontier AI models wrote short excerpts imitating fifty award-winning authors. Expert readers strongly disliked AI text produced by prompting alone, rating it low on style and quality. Fine-tuning a model on an author's complete works reversed the verdict: both expert and general readers preferred the fine-tuned AI writing, and detectors rarely flagged it as machine-made. The median fine-tuning cost was eighty-one dollars per author, far below typical writer pay.
arxiv-2510-14239:
Siqi Guan, Shangbin Yang, and Xiao Guo estimate the gravitational waves produced when flux tubes rise through the Sun's convection zone and erupt into sunspot-forming active regions, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The buoyant emergence of these magnetic bundles drives solar activity, and any moving mass-energy distribution radiates gravitational waves, however faintly.

Adopting parameters for a moderate-sized active region, the authors estimate the wave strain could reach ten to the power of negative twenty-nine. That assumes the signal were stacked and detected about one solar radius from the surface. The frequency sits near the high-frequency end of the pulsar timing array band, the technique that times pulsars to sense gravitational waves. The amplitudes remain orders of magnitude below the sensitivity of current and foreseeable detectors. Shortening pulsar timing observations to two-hour cadence would raise the reachable frequency enough to cover the signal's component.
arxiv-2510-14439:
Satyaranjan Pradhan, Abhishek Senapati, and Madan Mohan Soren analyze the convergence of two families of sampling operators, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The operators approximate functions from their values at exponentially spaced points. The operators are max-product and max-min variants of the Durrmeyer-type exponential sampling series, nonlinear cousins of approximation schemes that suit signals with product-type structure.

The authors establish pointwise and uniform convergence for both operators on the space of bounded, logarithmically continuous functions. They then quantify the speed of convergence using the logarithmic modulus of continuity, a measure of how wiggly the target function is. They also examine the errors from a variety of kernel functions, the weighting profiles at their heart. Illustrations demonstrate the convergence behavior of both families. This rounds out a treatment aimed at approximation theorists working with exponential sampling.
arxiv-2510-14539:
García Escudero, in a 2025 arXiv paper, works on a question in algebraic geometry about how rough a surface can be. An algebraic surface is the shape cut out by a polynomial equation. Its singularities are points where the surface is not smooth, and type A points are the simplest, best understood class of them. Researchers want to know the largest number of such points a surface can carry.

He builds surfaces that carry a large number of these type A singularities. The constructions reuse bivariate polynomials, meaning polynomials in two variables, that earlier work developed for nodal surfaces. Certain families of Belyi polynomials also feed into the constructions. In some cases he obtains fully explicit formulas, written with the classical Jacobi polynomials. Because each construction is a concrete example, the counts it reaches give lower bounds for the maximal possible number.
arxiv-2510-14839:
Dong and co-authors describe, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a small binocular telescope built to watch the infrared sky from the coldest, driest observatory site on Earth: Dome A, Antarctica. Infrared time-domain surveys lag far behind optical ones, and Antarctic conditions offer exceptionally steady infrared viewing. Their instrument, AIRBT, pairs two identical fifteen-centimeter telescopes with indium gallium arsenide cameras, one filtered for the J band and one for the H band.

The paper characterizes the cameras in the laboratory, measuring bias, readout noise, dark current, and response curves. These sensors behave distinctly from the charge-coupled devices astronomers know, with noise that depends on temperature and grows with exposure time. On-sky tests in October 2022 then measured real performance. A single three-second exposure reached limiting magnitudes of 11.2 in J and 9.7 in H, and the best photometric precision hit twenty millimagnitudes for bright stars.
arxiv-2510-15339:
Hong Ting Tsang and seven colleagues train a language model to build knowledge graphs that are useful, not just tidy, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Knowledge graphs feed retrieval-augmented generation, where a model answers questions by consulting the graph. The catch is that graphs are usually built without regard to the questions they will serve, so their structure can miss what the task needs.

Their framework, AutoGraph-R1, uses reinforcement learning: the model builds a graph, the graph is used in a real question-answering pipeline, and the score becomes the reward. Two new reward functions handle graphs acting as knowledge carriers and graphs acting as knowledge indices. Across several question-answering benchmarks, graphs built this way gave significant gains over task-agnostic baseline graphs. The authors argue the work closes the loop between building a graph and using it.
arxiv-2510-15439:
Feifei Zhang and four colleagues rethink how deep learning models learn to outline organs and tumors in brain scans. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that standard end-to-end training converges slowly and hungers for large labeled datasets, Their predictive-corrective paradigm splits the job into a rough first guess and a focused fix-up.

The resulting network, PCMambaNet, starts with a module that exploits anatomy's bilateral symmetry to draft a focus map of suspicious asymmetric regions. That draft anchors the search at low cost. A corrective network then learns only the leftover error, spending its capacity on hard regions and precise pathological boundaries. On high-resolution brain MRI tests the system reached state-of-the-art accuracy while converging within one to five training passes. The authors argue that baking in domain knowledge simplifies the learning problem itself, easing data scarcity and overfitting.
arxiv-2510-15739:
Lorenzo Satta Chiris and Ayush Mishra present AURA in a 2025 paper. AURA is a framework for judging the risks of autonomous AI agents. It works before and during deployment. Firms are giving agents more independent work. The authors see gaps in alignment, governance, and risk control. These gaps threaten wider adoption. So they built a scoring system meant for real operations.

AURA scores risk with a gamma-based method. The method balances accuracy against computing cost. It runs for one agent or many. It can work interactively or on its own. Human overseers stay in the loop. Agents report self-assessments through set protocols. Overseers can then judge and reduce risks in a repeatable way.
arxiv-2510-15939:
Shreya Gopalan and Sundar Narayanan audit AlphaFold3 on proteins that have no fixed shape. Intrinsically disordered proteins make up a large share of the human proteome and drive transcription, signalling, and disease, yet their floppy regions defy the folded structures predictors handle best. The pair test seventy-two such proteins curated from the DisProt database.

Predictions run across several random seeds and ensemble outputs, and per-residue confidence scores are compared with experimental disorder labels. About a third of residues disagree with the record, counting cases where the model invents order in disordered stretches or the reverse. A further share shows context-driven mismatch, and residues tied to biological processes hallucinate at a notable rate. The findings warn drug and disease researchers to treat predicted order in such regions with care.
arxiv-2510-16039:
Xiangyuan Peng, Xingsi Dong, and Si Wu compress action and observation sequences with a code inspired by grid cells in the brain. Vector quantisation usually squeezes static inputs into discrete codes.
