They treat key and value signals as damped, driven oscillators, and they expand queries in waves of sine form. In that picture, attention acts like resonance between waves, and the maths has a direct closed-form answer. The team proves the design keeps the broad power of continuous-time attention, and it beats rival scores on uneven time series tests while running far faster.
arxiv-2602-12439:
Hyperkähler manifolds sit at a rich meeting point of geometry and moduli theory, and Fujita's conjecture asks when a polarisation gives enough sections to map the manifold well. Alessandro Pilastro works alone here, studying general base point freeness and very ampleness for moduli spaces of polarised hyperkähler manifolds of Hilb^n(K3)-type and Kum^n-type. The polarisation has square 2d and divisibility t, parameters that shape the whole picture.

The paper provides cases where these moduli spaces are connected, and a formula characterising when the spaces are non-empty. That formula tells readers exactly which parameter choices give non-empty spaces, so they can test Fujita's conjecture in the standard series without guessing. Readers get a precise advance on Fujita's conjecture for general hyperkähler manifolds in the standard examples.
arxiv-2602-12639:
Legal text from large language models can usually achieve fair factual hit rate, but it often fails to follow the special style norms of legal writing. Yiran Rex Ma led this work with two co-authors, giving CLASE, a hybrid method for Chinese legal style scoring. Reliable scoring is a crucial first step toward improving style quality.

Manual metric growth by legal experts is impractical, since hidden style needs are hard to turn into explicit rubrics. Old auto methods also fall short: reference-based scores mix meaning hit rate with style faithfulness, and LLM-as-a-judge scores suffer from over-generosity and inconsistency. CLASE mixes reference-based scoring with LLM judgement in a hybrid frame, matching expert ratings on Chinese legal texts better than either approach alone.
arxiv-2602-12839:
Quasars shine through both an accretion disk and a dusty torus, and the relation between optical and infrared light could serve as a cosmological probe if it is calibrated well. Mateusz Rałowski and four co-authors study nearly 400 quasars across redshifts 0.7 to 2.4, fitting full spectral energy distributions with the CIGALE code and comparing against simpler photometric estimates. Host-galaxy light, polar dust, and stellar emission all contaminate the measurements.

For disk luminosities above 10^45 erg per second, photometric estimates agree with full fits, and the authors propose two empirical calibrations of the optical-infrared relation. Polar dust barely changes luminosity but shifts fitted torus geometry, while stellar emission dominates optical contamination. In the high-luminosity regime, the optical band traces the disk and the infrared traces the torus, making simple methods reliable.
arxiv-2602-13039:
Sparse resultants extend the classic resultant to few-term polynomials, and their theory and math have grown a lot. Carles Checa, Ioannis Emiris, and Christos Konaxis survey those gains. They first examine the Canny-Emiris formula, a ratio determinant-style form, and prove its build with care.

Next, they compare that formula with a Koszul-complex formula built from nef parts in a toric variety. Finally, they cover methods for finding the Newton shape of those. For readers in machine algebra and shape, the survey orders a spread writings into a tidy story, from forms to shapes.
arxiv-2602-13139:
Language identification underpins multilingual web datasets, but existing tools stumble on closely related languages and on telling real language from noise, contaminating low-resource subsets. Mariia Fedorova and six co-authors extend the OpenLID classifier into OpenLID-v3, adding training data, merging troublesome variant clusters, and adding a dedicated noise label.

Development focuses on three hard groups: Scandinavian languages; Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian; and Romance varieties across northern Italy and southern France, with new evaluation datasets where old ones fall short. Tested against GlotLID, ensemble approaches lift precision but sharply cut coverage for low-resource languages, a trade-off dataset builders must weigh. OpenLID-v3 is publicly available for reuse.
arxiv-2602-14139:
Zhihan Zhu and two co-authors diagnose a 2026 arXiv flaw in the classic projected subgradient method. For nonsmooth convex optimization, the method can fail after a single step when no valid subgradient exists at a boundary point. Under standard step sizes, that failure can occur with probability near one, even on simple problems.

The fix, called the subgradient gliding method, stays well defined without boundary subgradients and avoids early termination. It contains the classic method as a special case and widens the allowed step-size designs. The authors prove optimal ergodic rates: order 1 over root t for convex problems, and order 1 over t for strongly convex ones. Extensions to stochastic settings need only mild control on subgradient growth, not global Lipschitz continuity.
arxiv-2602-14439:
Ruike Wu and two co-authors study a 2026 arXiv portfolio problem: how ESG constraints affect large mean-variance portfolios. A positive definite penalty matrix is placed on the sample covariance matrix, in a large-size setting where guessing error matters. The paper derives asymptotic results for the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio, quantifying both the ESG-level constraint effect and the error from estimating assets' ESG scores from sample means.

To study regularization choices, the authors develop an estimator for the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio, with asymptotic properties established via random matrix theory. Simulations show the estimators perform near oracle level. Numerical study of varied regularization matrices on the Sharpe ratio gives practical guidance, helping investors weigh sustainability constraints against risk-adjusted returns in large portfolios.
arxiv-2602-14539:
Marthin Toruan and four co-authors probe a 2026 arXiv ease gap in post-quantum cryptography APIs. Quantum computing threatens data guarded by current public-key code systems, and the security world has pushed post-quantum codes, built to resist quantum attacks on old machines. NIST has set several post-quantum methods and plans to retire RSA and ECDSA by 2035.

Despite that push, take-up stays slow, often due to thin builder skill. APIs are meant to bridge the gap, yet prior work on old security APIs shows poor ease can lead builders to add flaws. The ease of post-quantum APIs had not been studied step by step. This research offers a real-world probe of how builders truly meet those APIs, a first step toward safer post-quantum migration.
arxiv-2602-14739:
Paolo Lorenzoni and others work out when a first-order and a third-order Hamiltonian pair fit well. Such pairs give a bi-Hamiltonian frame to many tame wave laws, from Korteweg-de Vries and Camassa-Holm to water waves, Dym, and WDVV.

Strikingly, the full fit rules are pure algebra, with no calculus left in them. The first member is then fixed in full by sets of kept laws that fit the third member's frame. New WDVV cases show the rules at work. Tame wave laws thus gain a clean fit test, built from algebra alone.
arxiv-2602-15039:
Hill and Ryoo present GRACE, a simulation-native agent for experiment design in high-energy and nuclear physics. Given a plain-language prompt or a published paper, the agent extracts a structured account of the setup. It builds a runnable toy simulation. It then explores design changes on its own using first-principles Monte Carlo methods. Unlike agents built for operational control, GRACE tackles upstream design.

It proposes non-obvious changes to detector geometry, materials, and layouts that lift physics performance within physical and practical limits. Candidate designs are judged through repeated simulation, physics-motivated utility functions, and budget-aware escalation from fast parametric models to full Geant4 runs. Reproducibility and provenance tracking stay strict. On past setups, the agent finds upgrade directions matching known priorities from baseline inputs alone. A benchmark shows it can recover setups and propose improvements from varied prompts, with or without a source paper.
arxiv-2602-15239:
Porras-Valenzuela and colleagues study size-transferability of graph transformers with convolutional positional encodings. Such models succeed widely, motivating graph transformers as focus-based designs for graph-structured data. A key design choice is graph neural network-based position codes that add shape information. The team views such models through manifold limit models for graph series and shows a theory link between them with such codes and manifold neural networks.

Building on size-transfer results for graph neural networks under limit meeting, they show such models inherit size-transfer pledges from their position codes. Notably, models trained on small graphs provably carry over to larger graphs under mild assumptions. Tests on standard graph benchmarks show scaling behavior on par with graph neural networks. A real-world build for shortest path distance gauging over terrains further shows the speed of movable models, suggesting usable paths for lean training at large scale.
arxiv-2602-15939:
Bacchini and colleagues review and improve methods to add shearing, expansion, and escape to particle-in-cell simulations of astrophysical plasma. Particle-in-cell methods are widely seen as simple and flexible tools for collisionless plasma physics in fully kinetic sims. Yet the standard algorithm often needs extension to cover macroscopic effects in microscale sims.

For plasmas under shearing or expansion, shearing-box and expanding-box methods bring global effects into the sim. For plasmas under local acceleration in confined regions, a leaky-box method lets closed-box sims cover particle escape from the accelerator region. The work gives numeric details for solving Maxwell equations and particle motion equations in each case. It introduces generalised Boris-like particle pushers to solve the momentum equation under extra forces. It aims to serve as a comprehensive reference for implementing shearing-box, expanding-box, and leaky-box algorithms in particle-in-cell work.
arxiv-2602-16239:
Sandeep Kumar and coauthors tackle a practical space-weather problem: estimating how a coronal mass ejection travels when only two viewpoints are available. Stereoscopic study of CME kinematics once used three viewpoints, but STEREO-B was lost in 2014. When the separation angle between them is small, uncertainties grow large. The authors show how that limitation can be addressed for the CME of April 21, 2023, observed by the two spacecraft separated by a small ten-degree angle.

Using the Graduated Cylindrical Shell model near the Sun and the Advanced Drag-Based Model in the heliosphere, they estimate arrival times at different locations. They compare those estimates with actual arrival times measured by BepiColombo, STEREO-A, and Wind. Directional uncertainty from two viewpoints runs about twenty degrees, which significantly affects arrival-time prediction. The actual chronology of arrivals at STEREO-A and Wind proves essential for resolving directional ambiguities.
arxiv-2602-16439:
Taras Mel'nyk, Sorin Pop, and Christian Rohde study nonlinear reactive transport in a layered porous medium split by a very thin, highly heterogeneous fracture whose aperture and obstacle pattern vary periodically. In the bulk, moving species obey parabolic reaction-diffusion equations, joined to a fracture problem of convection, diffusion, and reaction, with nonlinear wall and obstacle reactions and a very large Peclet number.

Through multiscale analysis as the fracture thickness tends to zero, the fracture collapses to a flat interface. The authors then derive a new homogenized model: bulk diffusion-reaction equations coupled through nonlinear conditions plus a first-order semilinear hyperbolic system on the interface. They settle well-posedness and regularity for the limit system, then build a multiscale approximation, adding boundary-layer correctors, and work out quantitative error estimates in fitting energy norms. The paper thus gives a rigorous upscaled model for reactive transport in fractured media.
arxiv-2602-16839:
Zeliang Zhang and co-authors bring in Progressive Thought Encoding. It is a lean fine-tuning route for training large reasoning models well under fixed-size caches. Reinforcement learning training of reasoning models needs long rollouts for outcome-based rewards. In those rollouts, step-by-step decoding eats most time and memory. Sliding-window cache tricks bound memory but disrupt long-context reasoning and hurt scores.

The new route encodes middle reasoning bit by bit into fixed-size vector codes. That removes the need to backpropagate through full-cache rollouts. It holds memory steady at inference. Tests on three models across six hard math benchmarks show steady gains. Lifts over low-rank fine-tuning are large. Lifts over unfine-tuned reasoning models are large too. The biggest accuracy jumps come on AIME 2024 and 2025 under tight cache budgets.
arxiv-2602-17039:
Elise Fuller led a large team studying how the energy output of active galactic nuclei shapes the growth of massive galaxies. These bright galactic cores drive gas outward, but astronomers debate what pushes that gas: light pressure on dusty gas, or hot winds sweeping cooler gas along. The paper uses spectra from five nearby obscured quasars, taken with the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph, to tell those two drivers apart.

By pairing optical line measures with highly ionized ultraviolet lines, the team could judge whether radiation or hot wind pressure ruled the gas clouds near each core. Three of the five targets fell in the radiation-led range, a fourth showed both pressures at work, and the faintest object hinted at a hot wind role without a firm verdict. The result points to radiation pressure as the main driver, with hot winds mattering in some cases.
arxiv-2602-17439:
Heng Lin led a three-author team on the nonlinear non-Hermitian skin effect. The team studies a continuum Hatano-Nelson model with saturating nonlinear nonreciprocity, analyzing its stationary states through phase-space flow. They uncover a scenario steered by a subcritical Hopf bifurcation and a saddle-node of limit cycles. Together these create a coexistence window.

Inside that window, skin modes and extended states are stable at a fixed energy. They are separated by a nonlinear basin separatrix in phase space, not by a spectral mobility-edge mechanism as in a system. An averaged amplitude equation predicts the limit-cycle branches and the saddle-node threshold. Building on the basin geometry, the authors introduce a basin-fraction order parameter. It jumps sharply at the threshold. The findings show attractor-basin geometry offers a powerful lens beyond linear spectral concepts, for steady states in nonlinear non-Hermitian systems.
arxiv-2602-17539:
Xiuhe Yan led a three-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on a dense raft of millimeter-sized grains floating at a shaken air-water interface. As vibration amplitude, frequency, and packing fraction change, the raft shows a rich mix of wave patterns and particle motion. Over part of the range, the classic parametric instability with standing waves still appears. But wave dispersion readings point to a growing role for the raft's emergent elasticity.

At higher packing, the surface tension falls while the bending modulus rises, marking the raft as an elastic sheet. At higher frequency and lower amplitude, standing waves vanish, and grains show thermal-like motion. Transport crosses from diffusive to sub-diffusive as packing grows, with patchy heterogeneity like that of supercooled liquids. Push the amplitude higher still, and a cavity opens, its size and shape set by frequency and energy.
arxiv-2602-17839:
Edson Leonel and Diego Oliveira present a unified, physically grounded exploration of scaling invariance, a bridge between geometry, motion and criticality. Scale invariance orders effects from edge conduct in stats physics to transport and chaos in nonlinear motion systems. The paper builds intuition through simple shape builds, math arguments and model motion systems, rather than pure abstraction.

It begins with simple, doable examples governed by a single control parameter, showing how power-law conduct arises when typical scales vanish. It then extends to nonlinear systems with local splits, where two scaling variables control settling toward still states through powers, cross-over effects and critical slowing down. That groups systems of varied size into shared classes. Finally, it addresses continuous phase shifts in chaotic systems, including tame to wild and bounded to unbounded spreading, interpreting them through order parameters, responses, balance breaking, kicks and shape defects.
arxiv-2602-17939:
Daniel Killough and team ask how well existing 3D accessibility guidelines support extended reality building. While guidelines exist for 3D games and virtual worlds, their fit for extended reality exchange styles such as spatial tracking and motion-based exchange stays new. Extended reality workers need usable guidance to apply guidelines under real-world limits.

The team presents the first review of existing 3D guidelines applied to extended reality work. It rests on semi-structured talks with twenty-five workers across workplaces. They assess twenty agreed guidelines from six major resources across visual, motor, thinking, speech and hearing domains. They compare worker practice against guideline fit. Guidelines prove highly strong when designed as change sparks rather than checklists, yet basic clashes between existing 3D guidelines and extended reality needs create use barriers and design gaps. The work offers insights toward guidelines and support tools matched to extended reality traits.
arxiv-2602-18039:
Lauri Valkonen and Juha Karvanen estimate what one extra night does to a traveller's total spending. Tourism shapes the economies of many countries, and the causal link between overnight stay length and expenditure helps stakeholders map spending profiles and design marketing strategies. That link works differently for personal and work-related travel, since the two kinds of trips follow different drivers and constraints.

The authors model causal mechanisms with context-specific independence relations, using trip purpose to define contexts, and identify the causal effect of stay length on expenditure. Drawing on survey data on foreign visitors to Finland, they fit a hierarchical Bayesian model estimating the posterior distribution of counterfactual spending from extending a stay by one night. A Bayesian sensitivity analysis checks how omitted variable bias might shift the estimated effect.
arxiv-2602-18139:
L. C. R. Patell and one co-author ask how the United States could calm fears that its lead in powerful AI threatens other nations. Their 2026 paper warns that even if an American power shift is not technically possible, rivals who see it as a grave threat might strike first to prevent it. A policy of restraint could lower that risk, if rivals believe it.

Drawing on work about how states make believable promises, the authors sketch steps Washington could take to show it will not use advanced AI to threaten other nations' survival. The hardest case is a certain one-sided lead, where trust is hardest to earn, though layered policy effort plus technical advances might still make it credible. With real doubt about American aims and powers, restraint grows more workable. The paper urges weighing restraint against rival plans for a tense AI transition.
arxiv-2602-18239:
Alvise Pizzella and seven co-authors derive and test the signal strength math for LISA, the space gravitational-wave antenna. Their 2026 paper treats beam tilt at the photodiodes, which can reach one milliradian and saps signal strength while raising readout noise. The team builds on an earlier framework of minimal approximations for two-beam interferometers with round photodiodes.

They derive an exact response for an endless detector, plus a closed-form approximation covering finite ones, checking both against simulations and lab runs on a LISA-like testbed. The model then measures how tilt-driven signal loss amplifies phase noise, finding that mismatched beam curvature worsens it greatly. A new noise feature from that mismatch is both predicted and seen in the lab for the first time. Controlling curvature mismatch in the test-mass interferometer is essential, and the models apply to any tilted interferometer with pivots on the detector plane.
arxiv-2602-18439:
Suraj Prasad and Anubha Pant retest a federated learning method to see whether its claims hold up. Their 2026 paper replicates FedTPG, a text-driven prompt generation network that creates prompts conditioned on class names. It aims to improve generalization to unseen classes in federated settings where private data stays local.

The team tests the pre-trained model across six diverse vision datasets, from Caltech101 and Oxford Flowers to FGVC Aircraft, Oxford Pets, Food-101, and DTD. Results land within two-tenths of a percent of the original paper's reported accuracies, averaging about seventy-five percent on seen classes and seventy-six percent on unseen classes. The replication confirms both core claims. Text-driven prompts beat static prompt learning on unseen classes. Federated training keeps performance high across domains without sharing private data.
arxiv-2602-18539:
Supriya Khadka and two co-authors design privacy-preserving checks on Ethereum. Their 2026 paper notes digital identity checks often force a privacy trade-off, making users reveal sensitive data to prove simple eligibility rules. As blockchain apps join regulated settings, over-disclosure creates serious risks of data breaches and surveillance.

The team proposes a Selective Disclosure Framework on Ethereum, designed to split attribute checks from identity. Using client-side zk-SNARKs, the framework lets users prove eligibility rules without revealing identity papers. A case study, ZK-Compliance, runs a Grant, Verify, Revoke lifecycle for age checks. Early results show strict rules can be met with tiny latency, under two hundred milliseconds, while keeping blockchains pseudonymous.
arxiv-2602-18939:
Nonstabilizerness, often called magic, is a necessary resource for universal quantum computing. Yet quantifying it usually demands a huge number of tests and doubly huge classical post-processing. J. M. Varela, with five co-authors, shows in 2026 that magic can be witnessed and quantified from far fewer measurements, provided the set contains anti-commuting pairs.

A general frame projects the stabilizer polytope onto the subspace defined by chosen observables. A method estimates magic from Pauli expectation values, with runtime growing fast with test count and slowly with qubit count. Relating the problem to a stabilizer-restricted quantum marginal problem proves that deciding membership in the reduced shape is NP-hard. Unless P equals NP, no method with runtime slow in test count can solve it in full generality. The frame is also applied to Hamiltonian ground states beyond the reach of existing techniques. Few tests can still reveal magic.
arxiv-2602-19239:
Large language models can carry out long procedures yet stumble on a trivial last step: reporting a value they computed moments earlier. The paper calls this procedural hallucination, a failure to carry out a clear, checkable instruction even when the right answer sits in the model's own context. Ahmed Karim and five colleagues study it with long-context tasks where the correct answer is a single known token.

They find that many mistakes happen at readout, when the model must fetch and state its result. Some failures are gating errors, where the model never switches into answer mode at all. Others are binding errors, where it enters answer mode but picks the wrong candidate. Splitting the failure this way matters, because each kind points to a different fix for making models follow procedures they already understand.
arxiv-2602-19339:
Offline tests of recommender systems can be swayed by quiet choices in data prep. Anna Volodkevich and five co-authors introduce SplitLight, an open-source toolkit for exploring those choices and making them easy to measure, compare, and report. Filtering, repeat handling, cold-start treatment, and splitting plan can reorder model rankings, so the toolkit helps researchers building pipelines and reviewers checking outside data sets alike.

Given an interaction log and derived splits, SplitLight studies core and time-based statistics, repeat use patterns, and timestamp oddities. It checks whether splits are valid, flagging time leakage, cold-user and cold-item exposure, and distribution shifts. Side-by-side tests of splitting plans, with combined summaries and interactive charts, yield audit notes that justify evaluation rules.
arxiv-2602-19639:
Evacuation choices shape disaster policy, yet how household talk sways the choice to leave or stay is poorly mapped. Made Krisnanda and three co-authors build an agent-based model where household agents weigh leaving against staying. The agents compete for limited shared resources, property recovery funds and coordination services, under evolutionary game theory. They test four scenarios that rank access to government incentives differently.

The incentive's pull fades as funding value rises and as prioritization tightens, pointing to an optimal support level past which more money stops helping. Overall evacuation rates hinge on the social network shape, jumping when prioritization crosses node degree. Backing community influencers lifts total evacuation sharply, while backing low-connectivity households can slow the collective exit.
arxiv-2602-20039:
Sub-terahertz wireless channels vary over tiny distances in theory, but in practice they may stay similar over much larger spans, which would slash ray-tracing costs for beyond-6G design. A 2026 arXiv paper by Hossein Amininasab and six co-authors measures spatial consistency experimentally in an indoor hall.

A large measurement campaign in a band around one hundred forty gigahertz characterized the channel at separations from a few millimetres up to a metre. Delay spread and angular delay spread, plus K-factor, shift only slightly over spans of many tens of centimetres. That implies the simulation mesh can span tens of wavelengths along stable line-of-sight directions, while finer resolution is needed where line of sight does not dominate. For coarser grids, advanced interpolation is needed to capture rapidly varying scattered components. The study thus quantifies how far ray-tracing grids can be stretched.
arxiv-2602-20139:
Time-of-flight devices measure arrival times. Cherenkov light is prompt, making it ideal for pushing those devices toward their built-in timing limits. A 2026 arXiv paper by a large team led by Liliana Congedo develops precise time-of-flight devices from solid Cherenkov blocks with high light-bending index, read out by silicon photomultipliers.

A thin radiator with high refractive index produces a nearly instant signal from particles past the Cherenkov threshold. Reaching the best possible time resolution took careful tuning of radiator makeup and shape, plus good optical coupling to the sensors. Monte Carlo models mapped the factors limiting time resolution, and beam test data checked the models. Small-scale prototypes used various Hamamatsu silicon sensor arrays, with pitches from about one to three mm and windows of fused silica and fluoride at various depths. They passed beam test campaigns.
arxiv-2602-20239:
Stars blow winds, and how strong those winds are should depend on how much metal the star's atmosphere holds. Testing that idea needs wind measurements in galaxies of different metal content, done the same way. A 2026 arXiv paper by T. Alkousa and twelve co-authors measures twenty supergiants of late-O and B type in the Small Magellanic Cloud. Ultraviolet and optical spectra are fitted together with the CMFGEN code.

The team then compares with a matching study of the Large Magellanic Cloud, built from a similar sample, similar data, and the same modelling tools. From the pair, they derive a recipe for wind momentum that varies with metal content and holds across the sample's range of brightness and temperature. Wind momentum turns out to depend strongly on metal content, mostly because the mass-loss rate does. Readers gain a wind recipe checked in two galaxies, not one.
arxiv-2602-20539:
Self-driving tree pruning needs true per-branch three-dimensional rebuilds, but dense depth-gap maps from stereo matchers stay too noisy for single branches in thick treetops. Yida Lin and four co-authors build a stepwise chain joining DEFOM-Stereo depth-gap guesses, SAM3 branch masking, and multi-step depth tuning to give sturdy per-branch point clouds. From a plain start, they fix three error kinds.

Mask edge spill is fixed with shape-based erosion, refined by a spine-keeping form that guards thin-branch shape. Mask errors are eased with LAB-space color checks plus cross-branch overlap calls. Depth noise, the most stubborn source, falls first to outlier removal and median cleanup, then to a sturdy five-step cleanup. On Radiata pine images from a UAV in Canterbury, New Zealand, mean per-branch depth spread drops by eighty-two percent while edge match holds.
arxiv-2602-20639:
Large language models show promise for scientific discovery, yet they struggle to connect theory with proven physical simulation. Bo Zhang and five co-authors note that current systems run a passive execute-then-respond loop with no runtime sensing. That leaves agents blind to transient glitches such as number wobble or runaway swings. Their system, EmbodiedAct, turns known research software into active embodied agents.

It grounds language models in actions through a tight sense-and-act loop. Agents sense and respond as runs proceed. The paper builds the system within MATLAB and tests it on complex design and research modeling tasks. Broad tests show it clearly beats current rivals, reaching state-of-the-art scores, staying steady and stable in long-horizon runs, with better hits in research work.
arxiv-2602-20839:
Editing images with diffusion models usually needs training, and text prompts alone miss fine detail like face shape and surface texture. Niki Foteinopoulou, Ignas Budvytis, and Stephan Liwicki propose a training-free alternative in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their method, Concept Distillation Sampling, anchors edits in pretrained LoRA adapters instead of words alone.

A stable distillation backbone with ordered timesteps, regularization, and negative-prompt guidance combines with dynamic weighting to compose several visual concepts at once, without clashes between them. Identity survives the edit without reference samples of the target. Tests on two standard benchmarks show the method beating existing training-free editing and multi-LoRA composition approaches.
arxiv-2602-21639:
András London alone authors a paper on the maximum number of spanning trees in connected C4-free graphs. For projective-plane orders n equal to q squared plus q plus 1, the paper determines the spanning-tree count of every polarity graph. Polarity graphs with exactly q plus 1 absolute points maximize that count within the polarity family. They attain n to the power (n minus 3) over 2 spanning trees.

Combined with a stability theorem of He, Ma, and Yang, that yields the same exact upper bound for all sufficiently dense C4-free graphs in the known polarity stability regime. For arbitrary C4-free graphs at these orders, a global upper bound implies a growth law. Log of the maximum count equals (n minus 3) over 2 times log n plus an error of order square root of n. That pins down the growth rate of spanning-tree maxima in C4-free graphs.
arxiv-2602-21739:
QU-fitting reads radio spectrum data by tying them to real models, yielding magnetic field values for the Milky Way, galaxy clusters, and radio jets. Lindsey Oberhelman and eleven co-authors test its power and limits across the ASKAP POSSUM survey bands, 800 to 1088 and 1296 to 1440 megahertz. They model Faraday simple, Burn slab, internal and outside turbulence, and two-part sources.

Results show reliable fitting depends on the model. In set value regions, model selection, and thus reading of the medium, turns unclear. The Bayes factor, drawn from the edge odds, beat older goodness-of-fit metrics such as BIC, AIC, and chi-squared for model choice. The team also maps edges where models cannot be told apart and gauges how well QU-fitting gets back values and error bars for point and wide sources.
arxiv-2602-22039:
Speech recognition for languages with little transcribed audio is a stubborn problem, and Taiwanese Hokkien is a clear case: its TV dramas abound, but subtitles usually come in Mandarin only. Cheng-Yeh Yang and five co-authors build TG-ASR, a system that leans on translation to guide recognition. It feeds multilingual translation embeddings into the recognizer, letting meaning from better-resourced languages steer the Hokkien decoding.

At the core sits a parallel gated cross-attention mechanism, which blends embeddings from helper languages while keeping training stable and cross-language interference low. The team also introduces YT-THDC, a new research resource drawn from online drama material to support further work. For low-resource languages, the approach turns the world's subtitled video into a training asset rather than a dead end.
arxiv-2602-22139:
Wild plant-eaters must balance food against the risk of being eaten, and that trade-off shapes how they live and group. Tomás Ignacio González and two co-authors model one striking outcome in camelids: polygyny, where females gather in family groups around males. Their individual-based stochastic model lets females move between groups as conditions change, each aiming to maximize her own fitness.

The simulations show female choices alone can generate group-level patterns, including group size and the spread of fitness across the population. The model thus links private decisions to social structure, showing how harems can emerge without any central plan. For ecologists, it offers a testable bridge from foraging trade-offs to the shape of camelid society.
arxiv-2602-22239:
Cancer leaves mutation patterns that reveal the body processes behind a tumor, but reading those patterns well has been hard. Ida Egendal and four co-authors introduce VAE-MS, a new model that pairs a lopsided autoencoder design with probabilistic methods. It aims for truer estimates that better capture how tumors vary.

The model is tested against three top rivals, including the factorization gold standard and two autoencoder variants. By mixing lopsided design with probability, VAE-MS targets the twin flaws of past methods: accuracy and honest uncertainty. Doctors gain a signature tool built for the messy variation of real tumor data.
arxiv-2602-22339:
Most people assume hardware choice decides a device's power draw, but Harry Cheon and six co-authors argue user behavior matters just as much. They analyze Intel telemetry data on package power consumption, comparing patterns across countries with a focus on the United States and China. Exploratory analysis comes first, followed by a simple linear model of power use.

The model confirms the exploratory patterns and highlights how user behavior shapes consumption, pointing to where stakeholders like Intel can cut environmental impact. The paper's message is practical: efficiency is not only a chip-design problem but a behavior problem. Understanding how people actually use devices becomes part of saving energy.
arxiv-2602-22439:
Vortex threads are tight, spinning strands in fluids that support several kinds of wave motion. Elio Sterkers and Giorgio Krstulovic study them with computer simulations of fluid flow in three dimensions. They first tackle Kelvin waves, spiral waves traveling along the thread, measuring wave speeds that match Lord Kelvin's old predictions well.

Inspired by the link between vortex-line motion and an integrable system, the authors then show by simulation that solitons can travel along vortex threads, and they study crashes between two solitons. Finally they propose a lab test for making vortex solitons, showing by simulation that such solitons could work in practice. The work links old fluid threads to soliton physics.
arxiv-2602-22539:
Mohammad Hossein Shokouhi and one co-author propose an agent team for running open radio networks by operator intent. A supervisor agent turns plain intents into an optimization goal plus minimum data-rate promises. A user weighting agent pulls past experience from memory to set priority weights for precoding. When saving energy is part of the intent, a radio-unit management agent picks which units stay on using deep reinforcement learning.

A monitoring agent watches user rates and works with the others to hold the promised minimums. One language model serves every agent through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, cutting memory use by 92 percent against separate agents. In simulations the system switched off about 42 percent of radio units in energy-saving mode against three baselines, while still meeting rate promises.
arxiv-2602-22839:
Hao Zheng and nine co-authors build slide-deck agents that learn from what they see. Making slides demands deep research, tidy visual design, and repeat polish, yet past agents follow fixed workflows and forms. DeepPresenter instead plans, renders, and revises middle drafts on its own, tuning to varied user intents.

Key to it, its review is grounded in the setting. Rather than trusting internal thinking traces, it bases making on seen draft states such as drawn slides. It catches and fixes slide flaws during run. On diverse slide cases, it reached leading scores, and its fine-tuned nine-billion-weight model stayed strong at far lower cost.
arxiv-2602-22939:
Yosuke Inoue and one co-author steer steady-state spread with sparse frame meddling. For linear moving systems, the goal is shaping the steady-state spread toward a target Gaussian. The problem becomes shrinking the Kullback-Leibler gap between steady-state and target Gaussian spreads.

The solver, a nearby gradient-based method, pushes thinness in the meddling through L1 penalty inside a nearby gradient frame. Its main result is a plain gradient formula for the KL gap with respect to the meddling matrix. That formula is stated through answers of two Lyapunov rules tied to the state spread rule and its adjoint. Tests show the method finds sparse, frame-wise bounded meddlings that steer spread exactly.
arxiv-2602-23039:
Jakob Kramp and two co-authors develop a shifting mean-field theory for neural scaling laws in random feature fitting. Training large networks exposes scaling laws for test-skill error, pointing to shared conduct across large designs, lasting even in oversized networks and the neural-network Gaussian-process limit.

Their setup unifies Bayesian reasoning on Gaussian processes, slope flow with or without decay, and random Langevin training shifts. Using tools from physics of large systems, the unified setup yields a working picture of tiny-scale network conduct in terms of lower dimensional order parameters. Group training shifts split into N solo modes, whose growth rules link only through group response functions and shared working noise. The approach explains in numbers the shifts of test-skill error by linking spectral and shifting properties of learning on power-law spectra, including effects such as neural scaling laws and early stopping.
arxiv-2602-23339:
Tilemachos Aravanis and four co-authors ask whether a few examples can bridge the supervision gap in open-vocabulary segmentation. Open-vocabulary segmentation extends vision-language models' zero-shot recognition to pixel-level prediction for arbitrary text-specified categories. It still trails fully supervised methods, for two reasons: coarse image-level supervision in vision-language training, and the semantic ambiguity of natural language.

The authors add a few-shot setting that pairs text prompts with a support set of pixel-annotated images. On top of it, a retrieval-augmented test-time adapter learns a lightweight per-image classifier by fusing textual and visual support features. Unlike prior methods with late, hand-crafted fusion, the approach learns fusion per query for stronger synergy between modalities. It supports growing support sets and fine-grained tasks such as personalized segmentation, narrowing the zero-shot to supervised gap while keeping open-vocabulary ability.
arxiv-2602-23739:
Xiang Deng and seven co-authors present U-Mind, a unified method for real-time multi-modal chat. Multi-modal chat is central to bodied agents. Current systems are limited to single-mode making or suffer weakened thinking and poor cross-modal matching.

U-Mind is the first system for multi-modal chat, building language, speech, motion, and video making within a single live loop. At its core, a Unified Matching and Thinking Method tackles two hurdles: lifting cross-modal syncing via segment-wise matching, and keeping thinking through practice-driven learning. During use, a text-first reading line performs internal chain-of-thought planning then time-synced making. A video drawing method tied to pose and speech gives lively, synced feedback. Tests show state-of-the-art scores on multi-modal chat tasks: question answers, order obeying, and motion making.
arxiv-2602-23839:
A. Yu. Korchin studies spin effects in tau-lepton pairs that could reveal anomalous magnetic and electric dipole moments, signs of physics beyond the Standard Model. The 2026 solo paper focuses on tau-pair production at collider energies, where such moments would shift tau polarization and pair spin correlations.

The author examines electromagnetic and weak dipole contributions in two production channels: photon-photon fusion and quark-antiquark annihilation, both observed in proton and lead collisions at the LHC. Extensions of the Standard Model amplitudes that include tau dipole moments are built into the TauSpinner simulation program. Examples show how spin-correlation observables could expose dipole signatures. The work gives collider analysts concrete handles for probing tau moments through spin measurements.
arxiv-2602-24039:
Hidemasa Ishii and Hiroshi Kori study how degree heterogeneity shapes noise-induced escape in networks of diffusively coupled bistable elements. The 2026 paper generalizes earlier results for fully connected populations, where three distinct escape mechanisms appear as coupling strength varies. It extends those results to networked systems where nodes differ in how many neighbors they have.

Networks of noisy bistable elements offer a minimal model for abrupt transitions in complex systems, from power grids to ecosystems, but nonlinearity, network interaction, and noise jointly complicate analysis. Extending an annealed network approximation, the authors derive three effective one-dimensional descriptions of collective escape and validate predicted mean escape times by direct simulation. The validity and quantitative behavior of those reduced descriptions depend on degree heterogeneity as well as coupling strength. In short, the shape of the web changes how fast the whole flip comes.
arxiv-2603-00039: Zhao's team presents CARE, a confounder-aware aggregation method for LLM-as-a-judge panels. Standard voting and mean-taking assume independent judge errors. In practice judges share confounders such as verbosity, style tastes and training quirks, so plain pooling can amplify system-wide mistakes. CARE models scores as latent true quality plus shared bias factors. It separates the two without ground-truth labels, offers identifiability and finite-sample promises, and cuts error by up to about twenty-seven percent across twelve benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-00339: Benameur, Elhechmi, and Benhenda prove a new result about the Laplace problem with exponential Robin boundary rules on the unit disk. They show one answer exists and is unique when the boundary data stay small. Their method joins an iterative scheme with periodic Sobolev embedding results. In this setting, the unknown function is harmonic inside the disk, and its boundary values obey an exponential law.
arxiv-2603-00539: Jin and Chen find that language models overcorrect when judging whether code meets natural language requirements, marking correct code as non compliant. More detailed prompts, especially those demanding explanations and proposed fixes, raise error rates further. The team probes the reasons behind these failures and tests judgements that require reasons. Their Fix-guided Verification Filter treats a proposed fix as executable counterfactual evidence, checking original and revised code against each other to restore reliability.
arxiv-2603-00839: Badahmane extends tensor Krylov subspace methods with a random Einstein product approach for large multi-way image and video systems. Older tensor global GMRES uses Frobenius inner products, which grow costly at large sizes. He adds a sketched Einstein inner product from per-mode random sketches and a randomized Arnoldi process. The new RTG-GMRES method cuts that cost while keeping convergence under subspace embedding rules. Error bounds, perturbation study, and projected Tikhonov smoothing follow, giving an efficient method for ill posed image and video restoration.
arxiv-2603-01239: Harshavardhan names self-anchor tuning drift, the guessed lean for language models to shift shown trust when building on their own prior answers across multi-turn chats. Testing three frontier models on 150 questions under single-turn, self-anchor, and solo-rerun setups, the study finds a mixed pattern by model. One model's trust falls under self-anchor, a second model's rises on open-ended items, and a third shows no trust drift. Self-anchor appears to block the tuning gain reruns alone would bring.
arxiv-2603-01339: Overman, Shirani, and Bayati study causal effects on humans in mixing human-AI groups where unit types and the contact network are hidden. A human-AI prior gives each unit a human odds, letting the team compute average human mix within large groups. Through a causal message passing plan and sample-mean results across groups, they show groups varying in mean human mix and treatment doses can always recover human causal effects. The work maps when spread knowledge of mix works for ID, tested on a mock human-AI platform.
arxiv-2603-01539:
Warming Mars on purpose, often called terraforming, would stir its water cycle in large ways. Ashwin Braude, Edwin Kite, Mark Richardson, and colleagues model that stirring in this 2026 study. Recent work claims injected particles could warm the surface enough for liquid water in local habitats.

Using a three-dimensional Mars climate model, the team tests how such warming moves ice and vapor. Each step of warming lifts far more vapor into the air as north polar ice turns to gas. Clouds then warm low areas at night but cool mid-latitude zones by day in winter. Ice shifts from the north polar cap edge toward the south cap, and shallow buried ice grows less stable. The authors stress that gaps in Mars weather knowledge still block any firm plan.
arxiv-2603-01939:
Sari Ghanem proves global existence and decay for a coupled system of tensorial wave equations in this 2026 work. The system covers the dynamical Einstein equations linked to nonlinear matter sources that break the classic null condition. Small-data global existence for weak-null systems has stayed largely open, with no decay theory for this class.

Her technique decouples the higher-order energy estimates for tangential components from all other components. Working at the level of Lie derivative norms, the decoupling holds up to a harmless factor. That split generalizes her prior results to nonlinearities absent from the Einstein-Yang-Mills system in Lorenz gauge. Classic energy estimates that powered older breakthroughs fail here, so the new decoupling fills a real methodological gap for relativistic wave systems.
arxiv-2603-02739:
Judah Unmuth-Yockey probes phase changes in the O(2) model, a standard toy system for magnetism, in this 2026 paper. The tool is a twisted partition function, a summary of system states computed with a built-in symmetry twist. Tensor renormalization group methods can compute these quantities efficiently on a lattice.

In three dimensions, the twisted function clearly detects the spontaneous breaking of the model's continuous symmetry. In two dimensions, it directly gives a stiffness measure at a fixed twist, letting the author pin down the famous BKT transition point. The method also extends to a generalized two-dimensional model. There it correctly separates the ferromagnetic, nematic, and paramagnetic phases from each other.
arxiv-2603-03139:
Peter Keevash and Peleg Michaeli prove a Ramsey theorem that survives damage to the host graph. Ramsey theory asks how large a structure must be before a colored pattern becomes unavoidable. The Cockayne-Lorimer theorem fixes the multicolor Ramsey number of matchings, sets of disjoint edges, in a complete graph.

Their robust version shows a far-from-complete graph can behave almost identically. The only demand is a weak connectivity property: the graph's complement avoids a certain dense pattern, with the missing slack growing slower than the graph itself. The loss versus the complete graph is merely additive and provably tight. The proof adapts a compression algorithm from the authors' earlier work on Ramsey-Turán problems, built on a classical decomposition of graphs.
arxiv-2603-03239:
Miguel Espinosa, Eva Gmelich Meijling, Valerio Marsocci, and colleagues generate Earth observation data that admits more than one right answer. Satellite products mix optical, radar, elevation, and land-cover layers, and the same inputs can match many plausible outputs. Deterministic models average those possibilities away, losing the uncertainty tasks like data completion need.

Their system, COP-GEN, is a latent diffusion transformer that learns the joint distribution of all modalities at their native resolutions. It translates between sensors in any direction with no task-specific retraining, fills missing spectral bands, and works from partial inputs. On a large global dataset, outputs stayed diverse yet physically consistent, with uncertainty growing sensibly as conditioning thinned. The authors urge evaluation methods that respect that spread.
arxiv-2603-03339:
Joseph Walusimbi and three colleagues design a tutoring system for classrooms where the internet barely reaches. Most learning tools built on large language models assume constant cloud access, which excludes bandwidth-poor schools. Their 2026 system, Arapai, runs everything on the local machine instead. Compressed models are chosen to fit the hardware at hand, including old computers with no graphics card.

Arapai gives curriculum-aligned explanations and structured study support through plain conversation. Answers adapt to four levels, from simple English through lower and upper secondary to technical. The team tested it with one hundred twenty students and nine instructors under limited connectivity. It ran stably on legacy hardware, answered typical questions within a few seconds, and users rated it positively for supporting self-directed learning.
arxiv-2603-03639:
Nguyen H Le, Florian Mintert, and Eran Ginossar tame the crosstalk that poisons large quantum computations. Neighboring qubits interact parasitically, and the damage grows exponentially with system size while its strength stays unknown. Their 2026 method fights back with many-body robust control: control pulses designed to work across a whole ensemble of possible noise conditions, not one guessed condition.

Tensor network simulations make the many-body design tractable, the GRAPE algorithm shapes the pulses, and random sampling over noise ensembles keeps the search efficient. The team demonstrates high-fidelity parallel gates on a chain of fifty qubits, a thirty-qubit entangled GHZ state, and the ground state of a twenty-qubit Heisenberg model. With crosstalk present, robust control improves fidelity by about an order of magnitude at large sizes.
arxiv-2603-03939: Radia Daci and others present CMDR-IAD, an unsupervised method for multimodal industrial anomaly finding. The method pairs bidirectional 2D-3D cross-modal mapping, models appearance-shape consistency, with dual-branch reconstruction capturing texture and shape structure. Fusion then combines a reliability-gated mapping anomaly with a confidence-weighted reconstruction anomaly for stable precise localization. On the MVTec 3D-AD benchmark it reaches leading results without memory banks, including 97.3% image-level AUROC, and its 3D-only variant proves strongly effective on a real polyurethane cutting dataset.
arxiv-2603-04239: Yang and others present DiverseDiT, towards diverse representation learning in diffusion transformers. To support their capture of meaningful internal pictures, recent works like REPA use external pretrained encoders for picture match. However, core steps behind picture learning within diffusion models are not well understood. To this end, the authors first study picture motion in depth of diffusion models.
arxiv-2603-04339: Saporiti and colleagues fix errors in noisy quantum simulations of time varying dynamics. NISQ hardware noise limits such simulations, so good mitigation is in demand. Their rule samples fixed choices using a polynomial subset of extended BBGKY hierarchy equations. For good Hamiltonians that subset keeps classical and quantum overhead polynomial. On the Schwinger model's chiral magnetic effect, real time dynamics return from noisy runs, with more constraints giving stronger noise cuts. Noise thus falls as more constraints are used.
arxiv-2603-04639: Dai and colleagues benchmark memory for robotic generalist policies with RoboMME. Memory matters for long-horizon, history-dependent manipulation, like counting repeated actions. Recent vision-language-action models add memory, yet evaluations stay narrow and non-standard. That limits understanding, comparison, and progress measurement. RoboMME offers a standardized benchmark for VLA models on long, history-dependent tasks. It holds 16 manipulation tasks covering temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory. Fourteen memory-augmented VLA variants on a shared backbone explore memory representations. Memory representation value varies strongly by task.
arxiv-2603-05339: Oswin Aichholzer and colleagues study colored k-gon and empty k-gon questions of Erdős and Szekeres. With n planar points, each red or blue, a k-point structure is a geometric graph with edges spanned by some points. Monochromatic means all k points share a color. For k 4, open problems include whether large bichromatic sets contain convex empty monochromatic quadrilaterals. The authors study five monochromatic 4-point structures. They improve lower and upper bounds on the threshold size for bichromatic sets to contain those structures.
arxiv-2603-05739: Sriraman and Block revisit Best-of-N sampling. It samples N tries and selects the highest forecast reward. Recent theory called it second-best and open to reward hacking, where models exploit flaws for high reward without gains. Earlier studies focused on mean true reward, but authors look into win-rate. Under minimal rules, well tuned sampling is optimal in compute and stats for win-rate, in part showing real success. Because it remains open to reward hacking, they propose a version wiping out hacking with proof while keeping scores.
arxiv-2603-05839: Debnath and team analyze how a large language model shows trust inside. Trust lets teamwork and guides decisions, yet models' grasp of it remains little known. Using paired prompting, the authors make firing-space vectors for two-way trust and related traits. They find trust concepts from five human trust models, then set a threshold from likeness across 60 feeling concepts. The model's trust picture aligns most closely with the Castelfranchi model, followed by the Marsh Model. The findings suggest models encode social-mind ideas supporting matching and teamwork design.
arxiv-2603-06139: Button asks which finitely generated groups admit proper actions on finite products of locally finite simplicial trees, and offers evidence favoring hyperbolic surface groups. He also constructs one completely concrete embedding for the closed genus 2 hyperbolic surface group, placing it inside SL2 over F_p(x, y) for every prime p. The result supports the case for hyperbolic surface groups acting properly on such products.
arxiv-2603-06339: Ancona-Flores and his team explore CNN inference of physical parameters for simulated galaxy galaxy lens systems with a Singular Isothermal Ellipsoid profile. They build 76396 synthetic lensing images from the China Space Station Telescope catalog, training an AlexNet to predict Einstein radius, axis ratio, and ellipticity components. Tests under dropout setups show dropout is key for precision and robustness of those values under 4-fold cross validation. With dropout, determination coefficients reach up to about 0.96 for most of them and signal to noise ratios reach about 37 decibels.
arxiv-2603-06439: Favorito tests a two-loop dark-matter trispectrum part, using math that stays infrared-safe. Around a fixed reference cosmology, the target spectrum is recast as its rescaled base plus a small difference for stepwise expansion. At third order, cutoff already matches the full number result to sub-percent accuracy across the scales studied. Higher orders stay tiny, and the reshuffle needs fewer cosmos-free blocks than direct basis breakdowns. That yields a faster route to higher-loop, higher-multiplicity correlators in large-scale-structure effective field theory.
arxiv-2603-06639: Zhang brings RECAP, a strategy for robust image classification coupling raw reservoir dynamics to a self-ordering Hebbian prototype readout; the name expands to Reservoir Computing with Hebbian Co-Firing Prototypes. The method bins tank responses into activation levels, builds a mask over tank unit pairs catching co-firing, and updates class-wise template matrices through a Hebbian-like growth-decay rule. Inference proceeds by overlap-based template matching, skipping error backpropagation and suiting template updates. On MNIST-C, RECAP remains robust under damage without exposure to training samples.
arxiv-2603-06739: Wang and colleagues present ResearchEnvBench, a benchmark for a skill other agent tests assume away: building a runnable setup for research code. Given a repo, its docs, and a target setting, an agent must sort out dependencies, align hardware and framework versions, and configure execution so the code runs. Tests on varied repos show a large gap in top agents. Failures center on missing dependencies and fragile version ties.
arxiv-2603-07039: Legel and colleagues build DeepEarth, a self-supervised multi-modal world model, around Earth4D, a planetary-scale 4D space-time encoder. Time joins its three-dimensional multi-resolution hash encoding, letting the system span the whole planet across centuries at sub-meter, sub-second precision. Training pairs multi-modal encoders with Earth4D embeddings through masked reconstruction. On an ecological forecasting benchmark, it reaches the state-of-the-art mark, and learnable hash probing lets it outdo a multi-modal foundation model trained on substantially more data.
arxiv-2603-07339: Ravi and colleagues present Agora, a platform that trains consensus-finding with AI personas voiced from real human views on policy. Deliberative skill is learned by practice, yet citizens' assemblies reach only a few people. Agora lets users propose and revise recommendations, hear both sides and see how changes shift predicted support. In a small student study, voice explanations beat bare support numbers at lifting perspective-taking and multi-sided statements.
arxiv-2603-07439: Schvöllner, Pastine and Jaume show that any two forests or pseudoforests sharing a degree sequence connect through 2-switches without ever leaving the family. Every intermediate graph in the sequence stays a forest or pseudoforest. The 2-switch operation also perturbs classic integer parameters only minimally within such families. From that stability the authors conclude the parameters have the interval property there.
arxiv-2603-08239: Li and colleagues present Fibration Policy Optimization, a method for training large language models as mixed systems spanning many domains, expert partitions, and agentic pipelines. Common proximal objectives work at a single scale. They lack a clear way to couple token-level, trajectory-level, and higher-level stability control. The authors derive the Aggregational Policy Censoring Objective, the first exact unconstrained reformulation of sample-based TV-TRPO. It shows that clipping-based surrogate design and trust-region optimization can be unified across scales.
arxiv-2603-08539: Tianyu Jiang and colleagues link two combinatorial worlds that at first look far apart. They show generalized tropical oriented matroids match subdivisions of root polytopes one to one, where each root polytope sits inside a product of two simplices. They also extend a matching-based model of Oh and Yoo to the case of triangulations.
arxiv-2603-08639: Simone Carnemolla and colleagues open up closed vision models using only their output odds. Modern vision systems hide weights, gradients, and training data behind closed APIs, blocking audits for bias and failure. Their UNBOX frame asks language and image models to hunt for plain words that fire each class hardest, rivaling white-box explanation quality on ImageNet-1K, Waterbirds, and CelebA tests.
arxiv-2603-08739: Xianzhe Zheng and colleagues tune tiered storage for language-model KV caches across cost, speed, and delay. Cache behavior resists neat formulas, with tangled couplings hiding the best trade-off frontier. Their Kareto optimizer prunes the setup space by diminishing returns, adapts tuning per group from eviction and access patterns, and beats fixed setups on throughput, latency, or cost as chosen.
arxiv-2603-09139: Claude Zeller shows that multilayer Kubelka-Munk theory is, in exact terms, what remains when the full transport equation is projected onto two hemispheric basis functions. Under steady, plane-parallel, symmetric assumptions, that rank-2 step discards angular detail no stacking of layers can restore. He derives the Kubelka-Munk coefficients as hemispheric moments and gauges the error across scattering media. A reduced optical thickness governs accuracy, which explains why layered models work so well for printed media.
arxiv-2603-09239: Yoon-Hyun Ryu and the KMTNet team begin a systematic hunt for planets in the 2023 Korea Microlensing Telescope Network data, focusing on low mass-ratio candidates. That season's photometry was fully re-reduced before the anomaly search, which may raise sensitivity. They report three strong low-q planet candidates and examine two further ambiguous ones. One candidate's bright foreground star yields a spectrum fixing its mass and distance, clarifying the lens either way.
arxiv-2603-09339: A. M. Hollinger and colleagues reveal the hidden Vela supercluster through the first hybrid reconstruction mixing galaxy redshifts with peculiar velocities. Dust and stars along the Milky Way's plane hide about a fifth of the extragalactic sky, blurring cosmic flow maps. They combine tens of thousands of CF4++ velocity distances with thousands of new redshifts near the southern Galactic plane, including deep MeerKAT HI data. Vela emerges as one of the largest mass concentrations known, rivaling Shapley.
arxiv-2603-09439: Corentin Fierobe proves Bialy's conjecture, which says two ellipses whose Mather beta functions agree at two nonzero rotation numbers must be the same ellipse. One rotation number even suffices if the two ellipses share a perimeter. He also draws consequences for local extremizers of the beta function, using a recent result by Baranzini, Bialy, and Sorrentino. The work bears on spectral rigidity among ellipses.
arxiv-2603-10339: L-P Kubushishi and P Capel model how beryllium-11, a one-neutron halo nucleus, breaks up in the Coulomb field of a heavy target. Their coupled-channel calculation lets the beryllium-10 core be excited, going beyond a frozen-core picture. Researchers often read a core-halo spectroscopic factor off such breakup data. Their result confirms a caveat: with the asymptotic normalization coefficient held fixed, changing that factor leaves cross sections unchanged, so the data alone cannot pin it down.
arxiv-2603-10439: Jihua Yang studies how many zeros a sum built from the three complete elliptic integrals can have. He first discusses linear independence of the integrals K, E, and Pi, then bounds the zero count for polynomial-weighted sums of them on a set interval. One coefficient may be a rational function of the variable. As an application, he turns to a Hamiltonian system whose phase portrait is a triangle bounded by three invariant lines. Small piecewise smooth perturbations there are where such counts feed Melnikov analysis.
arxiv-2603-10639: Mohsen Ghaffari and Christoph Grunau give massively parallel algorithms for orienting and coloring graphs by subgraph density, in the strongly sublinear memory regime. Their methods run in very few rounds, a poly-log-log count that breaks a long-standing square-root barrier. The orientation keeps maximum outdegree low, scaled by the density of the densest subgraph, and the coloring uses a matching number of colors. The result improves on the best prior density-dependent orientation algorithm and a pattern common to many scalable MPC methods.
arxiv-2603-10839: Benedikt M Reible, Somayeh Ahmadkhani, and Luigi Delle Site link the Lindblad equation to path integral molecular dynamics for open quantum systems beyond equilibrium. The Lindblad equation governs an open system's density operator but is practical only for small models. PIMD gives quantum averages for thousands of atoms at equilibrium, yet cannot follow direct time evolution toward a steady state. The authors show PIMD can compute that evolution of ensemble averages out of equilibrium, without solving the Lindblad equation. A formal link also argues PIMD keeps the density operator positive.
arxiv-2603-10939: Jalen Macatangay and Alejandro Strachan ask how much nuclear quantum effects change the thermal decomposition of the energetic crystal TATB, a multi-step reaction inside a solid. They compare path integral molecular dynamics, where each atom is a string of bead replicas, with a quantum thermal bath method and with plain classical dynamics. The path integral runs decompose faster, helped by early hydrogen transfers. The thermal bath method makes the quantum acceleration look too large, as it also does in simpler systems.
arxiv-2603-11239: Haihua Luo and coauthors make lifelong editing of large language models reversible, packaging each edit as its own frozen low-rank adapter that semantic routing switches on only for matching inputs. Existing editing schemes drift semantically or forget as updates accumulate, because edits share parameters or clusters keep moving. Freezing each adapter and routing by meaning avoids both failure modes. Removing an edit's routing key revokes it and restores the model's original behavior, a rollback the authors call a first.
arxiv-2603-11339: Arun Vignesh Malarkkan and coauthors present FinRule-Bench, a benchmark testing whether language models can audit real financial statements against explicit accounting principles. Earlier benchmarks leave this skill unclear. Four statement types pair with human-curated rules across three tasks: verifying one rule, naming the rule that was violated, and diagnosing several violations at once down to the record. Models handle single-rule checks well. They fall sharply on discrimination and multi-violation diagnosis. This exposes weak spots in high-stakes reasoning.
arxiv-2603-11439: Baek and co-authors split dense video captioning into two jobs that no longer fight each other. One set of queries finds where events sit in a video; a second set writes the captions. Shared queries in older systems caused clashes between the two tasks and repeated event spans. Contrastive alignment keeps each query pair saying the same thing. A new loss also punishes overlap between event spans, and a small module adds core event concepts to enrich the text. Tests cover YouCook2 and ActivityNet Captions.
arxiv-2603-11539: Bore, Persson, and Sveinsson settle an old question with fresh simulations: why is ice so slippery? Nanoscale runs alone overstate friction and miss how it changes with speed. The missing piece is frictional heating, which warms the contact toward the melting point. Heat thickens the premelting film tenfold and cuts its viscosity a hundredfold. Friction then drops with velocity, matching experiments. Premelting forms the film with no sliding or heating, yet slipperiness itself hinges on that heating, as Bowden and Hughes proposed in 1939.
arxiv-2603-12139: Liu, Yu, Velasco, and Zhu optimize stellarators that mix omnigenity with its piecewise form. Inside the OOPS framework, a new mapping squeezes general fields toward the piecewise kind on the high-field side. The runs yield designs across varied field periods and aspect ratios. Each design stays compatible with a magnetic well. Transport and bootstrap current traits look favorable, while the strict demands relax in part. The authors flag these designs as reactor candidates.
arxiv-2603-12739: Hongyang Shang and co-authors speed up spiking neural networks with an SRAM compute-in-memory design. Spiking networks save energy, but updating every neuron state one by one slows them down. Matrix work is already parallel in memory, so state updates became the bottleneck. Their neuron uses linear decay, which turns costly multiplies into simple adds. An in-place scheme then decays all states inside the SRAM array at once. Benchmark tests cut energy sharply with negligible accuracy loss.
arxiv-2603-12839: Aleksandra Ardaševa and co-authors model how cells wrinkle the soft surfaces they pull on. Traction forces can buckle a compliant substrate into clear patterns. Their thin film model couples Föppl-von Kármán elasticity to a phase-field view of one cell. Contractile stress size, spread, and symmetry set when wrinkles start and which form they take. Predicted forms shift between radial, circumferential, and anisotropic layouts. Scaling rules for wavelength and height match gel experiments well.
arxiv-2603-12939: Yuzhi Huang and co-authors give vision-language robot planners a persistent memory of space and action effects. Step-by-step planners re-read raw pixels at each move and forget what past actions changed. Errors then pile up, and hidden objects are lost for good. Their RoboStream binds visual evidence to 3D traits in spatio-temporal fusion tokens. A causal graph records how each action shifts the scene state. Long-horizon tests beat rival planners by wide margins, with no extra training.
arxiv-2603-13439: Ahmed Karam Eldaly, Matteo Figini, and Daniel C. Alexander propose a Bayesian framework for MRI reconstruction with uncertainty quantification. The task is posed as a Bayesian linear inverse problem from under-sampled k-space data. They place a total variation prior on the image, taken to be sparse in its spatial gradient. A Markov chain Monte Carlo method, based on a split-and-augmented Gibbs sampler, draws from the joint posterior. Tests on single- and multi-coil data beat compressed sensing methods. Uncertainty maps tracked error maps closely.
arxiv-2603-13639: Joseph Damouni, Wadia Tanus, and Naomi Unkelos-Shpigel present an adaptive virtual reality museum that reacts to its visitors. Static VR content for cultural heritage can overload visitors or bore them. Their closed-loop interface sets content depth from real-time behavior, sensed in an implicit, multimodal way. Gaze dwell, head motion, and locomotion feed a rule-based classifier that infers engagement. An LLM then adjusts how complex each explanation is, without breaking exploration. In a museum proof-of-concept, reading engagement rose 2 to 3 times versus static content.
arxiv-2603-13939: Renshaw introduces a new totient function tied to variants of groups. The idea grows from semigroup variants and their use in discrete logarithm problems and cryptography. The function relates to Euler's totient and to a generalization by Schemmel from 1869. The focus is on how to compute its values in practice. The number theory needed is at times technical but kept accessible. Natural generalizations are flagged for readers who want to push further.
arxiv-2603-14439: Golshani and co-authors give the covariant phase space formalism a parallel geometric treatment on its two spaces. It builds symplectic structures and surface charges for theories free of coordinate choice. It works on spacetime and on the solution space at once, where slicing changes, long overlooked, are defined and studied. The standard Wald-Zoupas test for charge integrability turns out to depend on that slicing. A Frobenius theorem on that space yields a slicing-free test, plus definitions of its connection, torsion, and curvature.
arxiv-2603-14539: Cao, Deng, Hacon and Paun answer a question of Campana on local system monodromy. They give a test for when nilpotent local systems have two-step nilpotent monodromy. The test covers quasi-projective varieties. As an outcome, any complex local system on a Campana special variety has virtually two-step nilpotent monodromy. The same holds for h-special varieties. That claim sharpens an older theorem by Cadorel, Yamanoi and Paun. The proof builds a deformation theory for local systems on quasi-compact Kähler manifolds.
arxiv-2603-14739: Peng, Zhang and Zheng predict pedestrian paths from a moving camera with TrajMamba. Egocentric forecasting must untangle walker motion from camera motion. Two Mamba encoders read the two streams apart. One takes pedestrian movement, the other takes ego-vehicle movement. A guided decoder then fuses them with ego features as cues. Relative motion sits at the center of the decode step. Future paths roll out from time-stamped decoded features. Tests on PIE and JAAD reach state-of-the-art scores, they report.
arxiv-2603-14939: Choplin and Meynet test rotating massive star models against fluorine in a metal-poor CEMP-no star. The target star, CS 29498-043, is the first fluorine-rich case of its kind. A 20 solar-mass model spins at rates up to seven tenths of critical. Rotational mixing boosts light element yields in the hydrogen-helium layers. Fluorine-rich ejecta always come out nitrogen-rich in the models. The best fit spins at six tenths of critical speed. Tuned reaction rates pull the value down toward the data.
arxiv-2603-15639: Baxi sets out a formal design for AI agents that hold real economic power. Agents now trade, spend, negotiate, and spawn sub-agents, yet checks rest on skill tests. His Comprehension-Gated Agent Economy caps each agent's rights by audited robustness. Audits cover rule compliance, epistemic integrity, and behavioral alignment. A weakest-link gate maps audit scores to economic tiers. He proves bounded exposure, honest incentives to invest in robustness, and stable safety as the economy grows. Decay and random re-audits guard against drift.
arxiv-2603-15739: Zigdon links worldsheet conformal theories to target-space wormholes. His examples show strings moving through wormholes that join two separate regions. The worldsheet view reaches past supergravity methods. It covers throats as small as the string scale itself. Strongly coupled theories describe these stringy wormholes. The cases include Euclidean wormholes, double cones, and Einstein-Rosen bridges. One conformal manifold even mediates a change between closed universe and wormhole. The work widens the known map of string backgrounds.
arxiv-2603-16139: Sun, Xie, and Lin pretrain image generators on images alone to cut costs. Unified multimodal models need scarce paired text-image data. Their IOMM frame splits training into two stages. Stage one trains the visual part on unlabeled images. Stage two mixes images with a small paired set. Alignment and quality rise in the second pass. The biggest model holds 3.6 billion parameters, trained in roughly 1,050 H800 GPU hours. On GenEval it reaches 0.89 against BAGEL-7B at 0.82, and on WISE it ties BAGEL at 0.55, topping BLIP3-o at 0.50.
arxiv-2603-16239: He and Cai take their neural pushforward method to curved spaces. The target is the Fokker-Planck equation on compact embedded manifolds. The solution is a distribution over the manifold. A neural map stands for that distribution. A retraction layer keeps each point of the map on the surface. This holds by construction, so mass is conserved too. Training uses a weak adversarial test with plane-wave functions. The needed formulas come in closed form from the embedding. Tests on a two-sphere double-well problem captured multimodal steady states.
arxiv-2603-16339: Byun, Lee, and Oh derive large deviation formulas for elliptic Ginibre matrices. They cover the real, complex, and symplectic symmetry classes. As matrix size grows without bound, they find the upper tail behavior. Targets are the spectral radius and the rightmost eigenvalue. More broadly, they price the chance of an eigenvalue landing outside the elliptic law's support. Sharp one-point function asymptotics drive the proofs.
arxiv-2603-16439: Lee and co-authors harden object detectors against domain shift with CD-FKD. A detector trained on one domain often fails under new weather or light. Their method distills features from a teacher into a student. The teacher sees clean source images. The student trains on downscaled and corrupted copies. Matching happens at both global and instance levels. Tests on hard scenes beat prior methods on new domains. Source-domain scores also improved.
arxiv-2603-16839: Ananda Kumar and Arunachalam train an agent to make slide decks with reinforcement learning. Their environment lets a language model research a topic, plan content, and build HTML slides through tools. Rewards mix structure checks, render quality, aesthetic and content scores. One reward is novel: a second model tries to recover the original brief from the slides alone. They fine-tune Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with GRPO on expert demonstrations. On 48 business briefs, the tuned 7B model reached 91.2 percent of Claude Opus 4.6 quality. It also improved 33.1 percent over its base model.
arxiv-2603-17039: Householder and co-authors report the first direct sightings of stars stably accreting from substellar companions. Brown dwarfs near a host star are usually expected to be engulfed and destroyed. Theory allows stable, long lived mass transfer in some cases, but it had never been observed.
