Heating to 650 degrees Celsius drives them between graphene and its buffer layer into ordered islands. Microscope checks, light-based checks, and calculations confirm a stable structure with robust interfacial magnetism and preserved graphene bands.
arxiv-2604-21839: Nogay models electric arc welding stability with a Hidden Markov framework built from physically interpretable spectral features. The welding current signal passes through a Short-Time Fourier Transform, yielding energy, entropy, and centroid descriptors as observations. The model infers three dominant regimes: transient, stable, and extinction. Stable arcs show rising spectral energy and falling entropy, meaning less variability. Despite partial feature overlap, the inferred state sequence stays temporally coherent, with high persistence and low transition rates.
arxiv-2604-22039: Jin and five colleagues study many-body light states in a tiny pumped Kerr ring that leaks light. They show a Mott insulator to superfluid transition from local Kerr interactions. A crystal gap cut into the ring controls mode links while keeping Kerr links. Growing the gap cuts mode links, reaching the Mott-insulator phase with a flat comb. Shrinking it restores links and drives a superfluid state with linked phases.
arxiv-2604-22439: Yang and five colleagues refine noisy 3D semantic fields for Gaussian splatting, a scene-rendering method using Gaussian blobs. Vision models give inconsistent multi-view features, and lifting them into 3D Gaussians yields a noisy field that hurts later tasks. Earlier methods either fix features first or improve optimisation, at the cost of time or compute. The authors instead use a variance-aware conditional MLP on the Gaussians, correcting semantic errors from geometric and appearance attributes. Experiments show their method enhances lifted semantics efficiently, giving robust semantic Gaussian splatting.
arxiv-2604-22639: Hrdonka and Jureček survey prior Linux ELF malware work and build a new adversarial malware generator for the ELF format. Despite intensive Windows PE research, minimal work exists on Linux Executable and Linkable Format files. Evaluated with varied metrics, their generator reaches an evasion rate of 67.74 percent while shifting detector confidence downward on average. MalConv serves as the target classifier, and the most successful modifications used strings typical of benign files as a data source. Experiments show the target classifier appears sensitive to strings anywhere within the executable.
arxiv-2604-23139: Niam, Kosar, and Nine cut energy use in distributed graph network training, where remote fetching wastes power through fixed-cost calls. Static caches fail: under shifting congestion they can raise energy by up to 45 percent, since a fixed rebuild schedule cannot react. GreenDyGNN treats cache windows as a sequential choice, rebuilding inside epochs with a Double-DQN agent trained in a congestion-randomized simulator. Under congestion it cuts energy by up to 43 percent over Default DGL and 4 to 24 percent over the best static policy, nearly matching the clean optimum.
arxiv-2604-23439: Charalambous, Guvercin, and Djouadi build a dynamic programming method for decentralized control problems where agents share information only after a delay. Their approach recovers the classic properties of centralized dynamic programming by splitting each agent's knowledge into a private belief and a shared common belief, each updated by its own rule. The result settles a long-standing open problem for delayed-sharing patterns.
arxiv-2604-23639: Ivanov proposes the Functional Proximity Law for multilayer nets: hub scores persist more between functionally similar layers than dissimilar ones. He tests it in 31 pre-registered trials, with 25 confirmations, and names six failure conditions. One is an inversion effect in fan-out clustering. The law extends from particle physics to legacy banking code and a neural replication across some 600 million years.
arxiv-2604-23739: Cui, Zhang, Huang, and Fu work out the kaon distribution amplitude from functional QCD plus large-momentum effective theory. They start from quark correlation functions and the kaon Bethe-Salpeter amplitude in Euclidean space. Extending the quasi-amplitude gives a single-peaked, asymmetric shape. They report its first two moments, with errors from the fit range and ansatz.
arxiv-2604-23939: Wang and Wu study rigid shrinking Ricci solitons. A noncompact one has scalar curvature k over two, nonnegative Ricci curvature, and sectional curvature capped at one over twice k minus one. It is a quotient of Euclidean space times a sphere in parts n minus k, k. With scalar curvature n minus two over two and zero Weyl curvature, it is a quotient of 2D Euclidean space times an n-minus-two sphere. This extends Cheng-Zhou's 4D result upward, since Weyl curvature vanishes on level sets at n=4.
arxiv-2604-24139: Gatti and twenty colleagues show that electrons in single-layer transition metal dichalcogenides are dressed by phonons from the nearby hexagonal boron nitride slab. Photoemission spectra reveal replica bands, a clear fingerprint of long-range electron-phonon coupling across the interface. A modified Fröhlich model matches the spectra roughly. The authors argue remote coupling is generic at hBN contacts, with effects on mobility, superconductivity, and moiré phases.
arxiv-2604-24339: Wu and four colleagues present ForeSight, a reasoning framework for vision-language models. It lets models see further with low-level cues and think deeper with feedback, feeding fine-grained detail into the reasoning chain. Mask feedback lets the model re-examine answers. Driven by reinforcement learning, ForeSight learns when to call tools and verify answers, using accuracy as reward. Their 7-billion-parameter model, tested on Character and Grounding SalBench, beats same-scale rivals and surpasses closed-source leaders on some metrics.
arxiv-2604-24439: Farah and three colleagues extend an earlier direct-forcing immersed boundary method so it can handle bodies that move freely in a flow. Earlier versions handled only fixed or preset motion. They link flow equations with rigid-body motion equations and add a steady coupling scheme for strong interface effects, while dropping costly predictor and corrector steps from the pressure solver. Tests on standard cases show the method stays stable and fast across hard fluid-solid cases.
arxiv-2604-24839: Erramilli develops and adapts extremal flows for a wider class of flows showing apparent discontinuities, as an alternative approach to solving bootstrap constraints numerically. He focuses on taking gap-maximization solutions for the spinning modular bootstrap from low numerical order to high. The method applies more broadly to bootstrap constraints and flows. It presents nontrivialities and nuances reflecting the richness of bootstrap solutions. The result is a prototype that improves solutions for a simple small-scale test case.
arxiv-2604-25039: Chatterjee, Patil and Ramesh propose Dual-Track CoT, budget-aware stepwise guidance for small language models. Large models reason via chain-of-thought, but smaller models of about 7 to 8 billion parameters struggle under tight budgets. Existing methods like self-consistency and Tree-of-Thoughts improve performance but cost many tokens and lack step control. The project asks whether small models can reason reliably with the same or fewer tokens. Process supervision and simple controls, such as rejecting redundant steps and token budgets, might substitute for model scale.
arxiv-2604-25139: Basarkar and four colleagues use conformal prediction to forecast conflict, treating a country's future war status as a sequence of states from a discrete-state Markov process. A single point prediction is risky because a wrong call carries extreme costs. So they compare conformal prediction sets with a likelihood-based strategy, seeking uncertainty quantification that stays valid when the model is misspecified. The paper gives real forecasts across several countries and notes limits for Markovian data, where exchangeability breaks down.
arxiv-2604-25239: Kwong proves that compact quotients of real semisimple groups with regular complex structures cannot carry two prized metric types at once. No such quotient can be both balanced and pluriclosed, a clash read off from Vogan diagrams that encode the underlying structure. The same study also fixes errors in the earlier list of regular complex structures for these groups. In short, the diagrams decide which metric type, if either, a given quotient can support.
arxiv-2604-25439: Ameen, Zhang and Schwarz show pattern learning can emerge in cellular tissue. Using a 3D vertex model, they train packings to realise set stress patterns via contrastive learning on shape indices. Learning is collective, needing coordinated shifts. Tissue rigidity steers exploration versus exploitation: fluid regimes explore more, rigid regimes favour set configurations. As target-cell share or load rises, learning slows and leans on rare rearrangements. Sequential training gives a sturdier but slower route than parallel training. Results point to a phase diagram set by load, rigidity, and protocol.
arxiv-2604-25539: Yanagi and Suzuki study the electronic structure of the inversion-symmetry-broken spin-orbit-coupled metal PbRe2O6 from first principles. Their work reveals Fermi surfaces from d-yz and d-zx orbitals with strong one-dimensional nature, explaining highly anisotropic charge transport seen in tests. Also, d-x-squared-minus-y-squared orbitals on each Re hexagon form Eg states. They yield nearly flat bands close to the Fermi level. Quasi-1D surfaces plus flat bands may explain successive phase transitions in PbRe2O6.
arxiv-2604-25939: Snyder, Poursiami, and Parsa present qFHRR, a quantized-phase form of Fourier Holographic Reduced Representations. Standard FHRR encodes structure in complex hypervectors using floating-point arithmetic. That limits efficiency on constrained hardware. In qFHRR each dimension becomes a discrete phase index. Integer-only binding, unbinding, similarity, and bundling follow through modular arithmetic and lookup tables. The quantized form keeps FHRR algebra while cutting bits per dimension from 64 to as few as 3 to 4. Quality stays high at low bit-widths, and spatial matches under fractional binding survive.
arxiv-2604-26439: Agundez and Cernicharo surveyed the QUIJOTE line survey of TMC-1, a cold dark cloud whose known molecule count has more than doubled in recent years. QUIJOTE scanned the Q band with the Yebes 40-metre telescope, joining the GOTHAM program in driving the boom. The review sums up the cloud's current observational status and weighs chemical models against its composition. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons stand out: their origin remains far from understood.
arxiv-2604-26539: Roussilhe, Dromard, and Mitra counted the own goals in the ICT sector's troubled relationship with oil and gas. Environmental debate has stressed the sector's footprint while ignoring added emissions from digitizing carbon-heavy activities. Input-output data from 2000 to 2022 show about 2 percent of annual ICT financial flows heading to oil and gas. In 2022, each dollar ICT sent to renewables and nuclear drew over 4 dollars to oil and gas. Two case studies estimate added emissions from digitizing oil work, and the paper links GPU success to early oil-and-gas ties.
arxiv-2604-26739: Basak, Rao, and Abdulla study charge flow across a Weyl semimetal and layered Chern insulator junction under a perpendicular field. The topological mismatch forces interface Fermi arcs to reconnect through the zone boundary instead of ending at Weyl nodes. Current through interface states rises in line with field at low fields. Beyond a key field, it levels off to a constant free of interface coupling, arc geometry, and lattice details. This saturation reflects topological charge pumping from the Chern layers rather than breakdown between arcs.
arxiv-2604-26839: Zhang and thirteen colleagues propose Walk with Me, a map-free system guiding robots that assist people outdoors over long distances. It uses GPS context and public-map points of interest to turn spoken intentions into destinations and waypoint routes. A high-level vision-language model handles coarse planning and hard cases such as crowded crossings, while a low-level vision-language-action policy drives routine segments and pauses when unsafe. The split lets the robot follow social norms without costly prebuilt high-definition maps.
arxiv-2604-27039: Zhang and thirteen colleagues introduce LenVM, a token-level framework for remaining length at every decoding step for autoregressive models. Framing length as value estimation with a constant negative reward per token, it predicts a bounded discounted return that tracks the remaining horizon. The setup gives annotation-free, dense, scalable training signals. On LIFEBench-token it lifts exact scores sharply in one pass, and higher still with LCG. Near 200 tokens on GSM8K it keeps about 63 percent Pass@1, versus 6 percent under a hard token budget.
arxiv-2604-27139: Beyene and thirteen colleagues report three very-near-Earth reconnection events inside one 12-hour storm main phase, the first such trio seen together. THEMIS inner probes caught tailward-retreating field lines between magnetic local times 23 and 24 at 12 to 13 Earth radii, inside a thin current sheet under one Earth radius thick. Satellite data show particle injections and field dipolarizations earthward of geosynchronous orbit, suggesting such events can be frequent and important.
arxiv-2604-27239: Jiaru Zhang and four colleagues propose Analytical Bias Correction, a closed-form plug-in adjustment from in-batch statistics, as the answer to subsampling bias in drifting models. Those models are one-step generative models that learn by following a drifting field, a blend of attractive and repulsive softmax-weighted centroids over data and generator distributions. In practice, each minibatch holds only n samples per distribution, so every centroid must be estimated. That empirical centroid is biased: softmax self-normalization leaves a pointwise bias that shrinks inversely with batch size.
arxiv-2604-27439: Ramadhan and five colleagues analyze Indonesian student views on artificial intelligence in higher education, comparing TF-IDF machine learning with transformer-based deep learning. Their dataset holds 2,295 labeled samples, mixing 1,154 student views with extra lexical sentiment data. Among machine learning models, a support vector machine performs best at about 82 percent test accuracy and F1 score, while DistilBERT leads overall at about 85 percent on both measures. The authors conclude that transformer models capture context better, though the support vector machine remains a competitive, efficient alternative.
arxiv-2604-27639: Pach answers a question of Simon Griffiths about how much of a graph k neighborhoods can cover, for any fixed k of at least two. For a graph with n vertices and average degree a fraction c of n, some k vertices have neighborhoods covering at least a share set by c and k. The result is essentially tight, meaning no substantially stronger general guarantee is possible. It settles how large a part of such a graph k neighborhoods can always be made to cover.
arxiv-2604-27739: Karan and three colleagues propose an orbital angular momentum sorter based on a wave twister, in the line of wave spinners like the Dove prism. Unlike a Dove prism, which merely turns a wave, the twister's twist varies linearly with radial position. After a lens, the twister sends each mode to a ring of its own radius at the lens back focal plane, with tiny overlap between modes. The scheme scales to many-mode sorting while keeping round shape, aiding real orbital angular momentum uses.
arxiv-2604-27839: Chalmoukis, Meda, Papageorgiou, and Santagati study a twist on a classic maximal operator on Damek-Ricci spaces, swapping balls for half balls. Oddly, the half-ball form behaves better than the classic one. It stays bounded for every exponent above one, while the ball form needs exponents above two. It also meets a limiting spread inequality for inputs in a log-weighted class, and that end-point result is sharp, failing for any wider Orlicz class.
arxiv-2604-27939: Achammer, Hetzl and Schmidt extend the SCAN algorithm, a saturation-based method for removing second-order quantifiers from formulas. Their version does more than produce an equivalent first-order formula: it also finds a witness for the quantified parts that yields that formula. A prototype implementation shows the extended method working in practice.
arxiv-2605-00339:
Xiangdong Ji, Gerald A. Miller, and Chen Yang present evidence about one of the deepest facts of nuclear physics: quarks cannot be seen alone. This confinement is unique to the strong force, and while experiments support it broadly, no one has proved it from the theory of quantum chromodynamics. The authors take a measurement-based route instead of a purely mathematical one.

They show how to define and measure the force acting on quarks inside the proton using available experimental data. The force they extract is attractive and stays constant across a wide range of quark positions, behavior they present as direct evidence of confinement. A constant, never-fading pull is exactly what would stop quarks from escaping. The work also aims to guide experiments at future Electron-Ion Colliders toward a sharper, quantitative grip on confinement and the origin of nuclear mass.
arxiv-2605-00439:
Pascal Auscher and Sebastian Bechtel prove results about quasilinear partial differential equations started from rough initial data. Weak solutions are the flexible notion of solution such problems usually allow, and the question is whether a single, well-behaved one exists for all time. Their data is critical, meaning it sits at the borderline scale where standard methods can fail.

The authors establish existence and uniqueness of global, bounded weak solutions when the initial data is bounded and uniformly continuous, and they investigate those solutions' properties. They also prove existence of bounded weak solutions when the initial data is merely bounded, a weaker starting point that gives up uniqueness. The paper is a piece of pure analysis: it secures the basic well-posedness facts on which any later study of these equations, numerical or applied, ultimately rests.
arxiv-2605-00539:
Wenxiang Lin and 7 co-authors cut the memory cost of training large language models across many graphics processors. Quantizing activations and gradients to fewer bits should shrink memory, but at the aggressive settings that matter, four-bit activations and eight-bit gradients, existing methods converge slowly or lose accuracy. Their system, AGoQ, introduces two techniques to hold quality at those settings.

A layer-aware algorithm assigns each layer's activations a bit-width suited to its type and pipeline stage, achieving near four-bit storage overall. A gradient method stores gradients in eight bits and communicates them in a precision-preserving eight-bit form, cutting both memory and transfer time. In experiments across up to sixty-four processors, AGoQ cut memory by up to about half. It also trained up to a third faster than leading systems, with comparable downstream accuracy.
arxiv-2605-01039:
Ziyuan Lin and three co-authors analyze how removing options affects active hypothesis testing, where a decision maker gathers evidence step by step to identify the true option with fixed confidence. Such problems arise in safety-critical settings. Their pruning-augmented Track-and-Stop algorithm prunes active opponent sets for each champion over time and reallocates sensing effort toward surviving alternatives.

The analysis gives a non-asymptotic upper bound on expected stopping time. Finite-sample gains from pruning appear in the non-leading term, through tighter tracking and concentration on the reduced set. An aggressiveness setting trades faster pruning against weaker confidence guarantees. Experiments on synthetic Gaussian instances confirm the theoretical predictions.
arxiv-2605-01339:
Yannik Schnitzer, Alessandro Abate, and David Parker tackle safety checks for Markov decision processes whose move odds must be learned from data. The usual fix wraps each move in its own uncertainty range, but that ignores links between moves that share hidden causes.

Their route learns a parametric model, where move odds are formulas over a shared set of parameters. Doubt from observed counts is then mapped into parameter space, giving a sound uncertainty set that respects how moves hang together. Such models are hard to solve, so the team builds a ladder of safe box-like over-approximations of the set. In tests, the method gives much tighter uncertainty bounds than the classic per-move approach, which should yield policies that are robust without being needlessly timid.
arxiv-2605-01439:
Akira Kawano, Ilia Soroka, and Greg J Stephens tune reservoir computing, a fast learning scheme where a fixed random network is driven by input and only a readout is trained. The hard part is climate: matching a system's long-run statistics, not just its next few steps.

Short forecasts can look sharp for several characteristic times and still drift to the wrong long-run pattern. So instead of tuning for forecast length, the team tune the reservoir to match the spread of states the system visits, a target read straight from data. The tuned models recover the chaos rates of test systems such as the logistic map and the double pendulum, even from partial views. Memory in the reservoir turns out to matter only when views are partial. Applied to the posture record of a small worm, the method rebuilds its chaotic behavior pattern, given one extra stability constraint.
arxiv-2605-01639:
Anuar Idrissov and six co-authors ask how spin and squashed shape bend two classic relativistic effects around a compact star. The Shirokov effect splits the period of orbiting test particles, and the Shapiro effect delays signals that graze a mass. Both are read here in the Hartle-Thorne spacetime, the standard outside field of a slowly rotating, slightly deformed body.

Geodesic deviation equations track how neighboring paths oscillate. The period split in the weak field turns out to be ruled by the body's Newtonian quadrupole, its plain squashedness, rather than the relativistic mass term Shirokov first named. For the time delay, dragging from spin alone keeps the effect for either spin direction, while a static squashed source delays more as it grows more oblate and more distant. Full numerical runs without the weak-field shortcut confirm the picture and expose how spin and shape can mimic each other.
arxiv-2605-01739:
Asrul Arifin, Hussain Ahmad, Yiyao Zhang, and Diksha Goel automate the triage of software vulnerability alerts, a queue that buries security teams in raw scanner output. Their multi-agent framework, AgenticVM, mixes rule-based processing, a BERT module that predicts missing severity scores, and language-model agents with defined security jobs.

Feeds from the United States and European vulnerability databases ground the pipeline. Agents detect, assess, rank, and report, with human oversight kept in the loop by design. In trials the system cut raw findings down to compact action queues. At best it shrank nearly four thousand findings to eighty-two top items, a reduction of about ninety-eight percent. It also filled missing severity attributes with accuracy near ninety percent. The authors stress design lessons, how to split agents and wire tools to models, alongside the scores.
arxiv-2605-01939:
Yongrui Chen and colleagues build StressEval, a way to make fresh tests for language models from the models' own failures. Fixed tests grow stale as models train on them, and harder tests can become unfair or unclear. StressEval starts from a failed item, records which reasoning step broke and why, and uses that card to guide new items.

New items target both gaps in knowledge and breaks in reasoning, while keeping the core difficulty. A gate then keeps only items that are grounded and have a single clear answer. From several source sets, the team builds Dynamic OneEval, a focused suite that separates leading models more sharply than the original tests.
arxiv-2605-02339:
Zhong-Nan Dong and colleagues describe the design, testing, and commissioning of an 80-centimetre infrared telescope for Sun Yat-sen University. The new facility at the Lenghu site on the Tibetan Plateau, at about 4,100 metres, is dedicated to time-domain astronomy and serves as a testbed for near-infrared cameras. It uses a reflective Cassegrain design with two Nasmyth foci for the J and K bands.

Commissioned in October 2024, the J-band system first used a commercial indium gallium arsenide camera and was upgraded in June 2025 to a larger, science-grade cooled camera. It reaches background-limited performance, with deep stacked exposures and millimagnitude precision for bright variables in on-sky tests. Early observations since commissioning are reported in the paper.
arxiv-2605-02639:
K. Ackley and fifty-six co-authors report follow-up observations by the ENGRAVE Collaboration of a bright transient found during a gravitational wave search. The candidate wave event was one of few in the network's fourth run classed as a possible binary neutron star merger above a low threshold. Its sky region was huge, and a search there found a fast-fading, featureless transient.

That transient drew wide attention because its place and timing fit the wave alert. ENGRAVE ran a broad multi-wavelength campaign with the Very Large Telescope and partners. Spectra classified the source as a type IIb supernova, an exploding star unrelated to the wave event. The paper details observing strategy, data handling, and interpretation. The case shows both the promise and the false alarms of counterpart hunting.
arxiv-2605-02739:
Yudong Liu and fourteen co-authors present Latent Bridge, a small model that makes dual-system robot controllers run faster. In such systems, a large vision-language backbone must run at every control step, yet its features change little between steps. That redundancy is the cost Latent Bridge removes, by predicting how the backbone's output will change.

The action head then runs on predicted outputs, and the costly backbone is called only from time to time. The bridge is shown on two distinct robot systems, one in feature space and one in cache space, so the idea is not tied to a single design. A task-agnostic training pipeline moves across benchmarks unchanged. Tests kept nearly all task performance while cutting backbone calls by half or more, for a clear net speedup.
arxiv-2605-02839:
Dmitry Treschev discusses the algebra and combinatorics of Hamiltonian normal forms, a tool for simplifying the equations of motion near a special point. Normal form theory rewrites a system in its cleanest local shape, but the standard route is a step-by-step normalization procedure that can hide the final formula's link to the original system. Treschev's aim is the opposite: an explicit formula.

For systems with one degree of freedom, the normal form is computed as an explicit nonlinear functional applied directly to the original Hamiltonian, with no procedure in between. In higher dimensions the formulas grow more complex but stay explicit. The paper is a compact theoretical account, aimed at readers in dynamical systems who need closed forms rather than algorithms.
arxiv-2605-03039:
Joydeep Chandra proposes a compact voice system that separates stable speaker traits from volatile agitation states in bipolar disorder. Constant checks must run on cheap edge devices, and mixing who a person is with how agitated they sound can spoil both privacy and accuracy.

The method, MP-IB, uses numeric precision itself as a bottleneck: a wider trait head holds identity, while a narrow state head holds agitation. On a large voice dataset it beat strong baselines, kept identity leakage near random, and ran in real time with a tiny footprint on very cheap hardware.
arxiv-2605-03239:
Daehyun Choi and fourteen co-authors show that a squid's funnel times its elastic recoil to boost each pulsed jet. Squid swim by jet pulses across a huge size range, and the soft funnel nozzle was thought too slow to matter within a single pulse.

Tracking skin markers in two species, they found the funnel widens and recoils with a steady lag while the mantle still contracts, even after denervation. Models, simulations, and silicone nozzles agree the impulse can reach about four times the rigid value at the observed timing. Tuned synthetic nozzles launched jets farther and drove a boat more cheaply.
arxiv-2605-03339:
Tong Guo, Caishun Chen, and Yew Soon Ong automate the design of solvers for very large vehicle routing problems, where hundreds to thousands of stops defeat even strong solvers. Splitting the problem helps, but crafting the split logic and tuning sub-solvers takes deep expert labor.

Their LaF-MCTS framework uses language models inside a flexible tree search, organized in three decision tiers for split policies and sub-solvers. Semantic pruning drops redundant code, while branch regrowth restores diversity. On CVRPLib tests, the system built split-enhanced solvers that beat several state-of-the-art routing solvers without hand design.
arxiv-2605-03439:
Nabila Zakiyah Zahra, Salwa Farhanatussaidah, Nasywa Nur Afifah, Luluk Muthoharoh, Ardika Satria, and Martin C. T. Manullang benchmark classic machine learning against IndoBERT for sentiment analysis of Indonesian product reviews. Tokopedia reviews offer a large, skewed three-class task where satisfaction signals matter to sellers at scale.

With word-frequency features, logistic regression, linear SVM, and naive Bayes served as baselines, while a fine-tuned IndoBERT used a custom weighted loss for imbalance. The linear SVM won clearly on accuracy and macro F1 in their setup, a gap the authors trace mainly to sampling: baselines saw the full corpus, the transformer only a subset. A Gradio app deploys the final model.
arxiv-2605-03639:
Zhuoyue Zhang and six co-authors introduce Diffusion Masked Pretraining, a self-supervised method for learning from dynamic point clouds, sequences of 3D point sets that move over time. Masked reconstruction dominates the field but leaks ground-truth positions into the decoder. It also supervises motion with single fixed targets, discarding uncertainty about plausible paths.

DiMP applies diffusion modeling to both problems. Masked tube centers are noised and then predicted from visible context, removing the positional leakage. Inter-frame motion is also learned as a noise-prediction task, so the encoder targets the full distribution of plausible motions instead of one average. Broad experiments support the design over masked reconstruction baselines.
arxiv-2605-03839:
Weiming Feng, Yucheng Fu, Minji Yang, and Anqi Zhang study how hard it is to compute the total variation distance. The distance is between two mixtures of product distributions over a discrete domain with n coordinates. It measures how far apart two distributions are. Mixtures of product distributions are a basic model in statistics and machine learning. Each mixture combines a set of component distributions.

The authors give a randomized algorithm that approximates the distance within a small multiplicative error, running in time polynomial in a term set by the total number of components. For the special case of mixtures of Boolean subcubes, they give a deterministic exact algorithm. They also show exact computation becomes counting-hard when the number of components grows linearly with dimension.
arxiv-2605-03939:
Rory Barnes and six co-authors reconstruct how much extreme ultraviolet radiation the exoplanet GJ 1132 b has absorbed over its lifetime. The planet is an Earth-sized world orbiting the small M dwarf GJ 1132 every day and a half. Cumulative high-energy flux decides whether such a planet can keep an atmosphere, so the star's history matters as much as its present brightness.

The team compares two quiescent XUV evolution models. It also simulates flare contributions from TESS observations and a Kepler re-analysis. Only four flares appear in the star's TESS light curve. That suggests an age of many billions of years. All model permutations give the planet at least a ninety-five percent chance of having received over fifty times modern Earth's XUV flux. That makes it a strong candidate for permanent atmospheric loss.
arxiv-2605-04039:
Sebastian Wind and eleven co-authors show that safety and accuracy follow different scaling laws in clinical large language models. Medicine punishes a few confident, high-risk errors more than average benchmark scores suggest, so the common assumption that bigger, more accurate models are safer by default is incomplete. The authors introduce SaFE-Scale, a framework for measuring how safety changes with model scale, evidence quality, retrieval strategy, context exposure, and inference-time compute.

Its testbed, RadSaFE-200, is a radiology safety benchmark of two hundred multiple-choice questions with clinician-defined clean and conflicting evidence and option-level labels for high-risk errors. Thirty-four locally deployed models were evaluated under six conditions. Clean evidence gave the strongest improvement, raising mean accuracy a lot while sharply reducing high-risk errors, evidence conflicts, and dangerous overconfidence.
arxiv-2605-04239:
Véronique Defonte and three co-authors tackle gaps in satellite image records caused by clouds and the edges of a satellite's path. Their focus is the Sentinel-2 mission, whose optical images are widely used for farming, climate, and land studies.

Most methods only fill gaps inside the time already observed. Their learning framework can also forecast images at future dates, by combining optical data with radar data from Sentinel-1, which sees through cloud. They pay special attention to how unsure each generated image is, so users know how much trust to place in a filled or forecast view.
arxiv-2605-04339:
Hossein Nemati and four co-authors ask how a varied environment changes the fate of a beneficial mutant in a population spread over a lattice. Depending on the setup, variation can either help the mutant take over or hold it back, and past results seemed to conflict.

Their unified framework lets the fitness of mutants and residents depend on the local environment. Two principles emerge: which genotype the environment affects decides the direction of the effect, while how mixed or clustered the environments are decides its size. Together these principles reconcile earlier findings and give criteria for predicting outcomes in new settings.
arxiv-2605-04539:
Qiming Bao and three co-authors tackle a weakness in a popular fine-tuning method for language models: the preference signals it learns from tend to reward fluent, lengthy answers over logically correct ones. In knowledge-heavy subjects, that leaves models that sound good while their answers are rarely entailed by the facts.

Their system builds preferences automatically by fusing a natural-language inference model's signal with a verifier model's score, needing no human annotation. Across five academic domains and three base models, it raised entailment scores substantially over standard fine-tuning in most settings. It also improved answer coverage. On one compact model it ran faster at inference time as well.
arxiv-2605-04939:
Erel Shtossel and Gal Kaminka propose a modular way for cooperative robot swarms to learn how to work together. Each small robot can only interact with a few neighbours and cannot see how its choices affect the whole group's goal. Earlier learning methods forced each robot to track a huge number of combined interaction states, straining tiny memories.

Their alternative splits the spatial state into features, with a separate learning procedure handling each feature and the results combined afterwards. Simulated swarms carrying out foraging tasks show the approach works well across many experiments. It offers swarm designers a memory-light route to coordinated behaviour in simple robots.
arxiv-2605-05039:
Akinari Hoshi and Kazuki Kanai study generalised Jacobi sums and cyclotomic numbers inside Thaine's framework, proving new multiplicative identities between them. Their main result extends a classical lifting theorem of Davenport and Hasse from single prime powers to products of prime powers. Jacobi sums are basic objects in number theory with deep links to counting points on curves.

As applications, the authors construct multiplicative forms of higher degree on complete intersections of such forms in algebraic geometry. That places a classical theory of multiplicative quadratic forms inside a broader setting on affine varieties, where new phenomena appear. On a dense open part of the variety, the form also fits an algebraic torus structure and its group law.
arxiv-2605-05239:
Jianhao Yang builds a variational framework for quantising gravitational fields based on an entropy-based action principle, aiming to avoid a classic puzzle of canonical quantum gravity. The usual route turns momentum into an operator, which creates ordering ambiguities. Yang instead extends the stationary action principle with an added term built from the relative entropy of field fluctuations.

An ensemble version on superspace carries that added term, and the refined scheme treats the quantum step and constraints together, settling the long-standing ordering question between them. The Wheeler-DeWitt equation emerges without operator promotion. Applied to gravity coupled to a massless scalar field, it yields a Schrödinger equation for the scalar wave function with an extra small quantum term.
arxiv-2605-05339:
When several drones carry one load on cables, a snapped cable can doom the flight. Hadi Hajieghrary and Paul Schmitt study that failure for teams of unmanned aircraft flying a shared slung load. The load shifts at once, and there is little time to diagnose the fault or plan a fix.

Their answer is a passive design that feeds each drone's measured cable tension straight into its thrust command. Control layers around it keep the load steady and limit swing. In simulations with five vehicles and a ten-kilogram load, the system recovered within one swing period, even when two cables broke.
arxiv-2605-05839: Maxim N. Demchenko studies the characteristic problem for the ultrahyperbolic equation, a wave-like equation with extra time-type directions, posed in Euclidean space. The data are given on a characteristic hyperplane, a surface aligned with the equation's own wave directions. He asks how smooth the solution is and how it behaves far away, tracing it along lines that cross the starting plane at an angle. The work connects to scattering questions: what a solution looks like at infinity records how it met the starting data.
arxiv-2605-06239:
Masatsugu Yamada and Mahito Sugiyama ask whether graph language models learn real structural rules or just memorize training graphs. Standard fidelity scores cannot separate the two, since a model that copies can score as well as one that generalizes. The authors build a calibrated diagnostic protocol to pull memorization and structural alignment apart.

Their method joins frequent subgraph mining, a graph level bootstrap baseline, and three level frequency stratification. At small scale, fidelity proved largely indistinguishable from verbatim recall under the diagnostic. At large scale, with millions of graphs, verbatim memorization dropped sharply while rank correlation stayed near ceiling. High frequency patterns were reproduced well at every scale, while rare patterns stayed poorly covered.
arxiv-2605-06339:
Zhaoyang Jiang and six co-authors develop a regime theory for choosing how a deployed model should decide what to do with each input. On every request, a language or vision language system can answer directly, fetch evidence, defer to a stronger model, or abstain. Common sense says more expressive per input controllers should win, but strict cross validation shows different benchmarks preferring different controller classes, a finite sample effect the paper sets out to explain.

Controllers form a nested lattice of four classes, from fixed actions up to prior gated designs. The theory converts three measurable bottlenecks into a class choice, with matching lower bounds on what any method can achieve. Across four benchmarks the predicted class matched the empirical winner. A prior gated controller also won a visual question task where OCR text supplied a free prior.
arxiv-2605-06639:
Apurva Gandhi, Satyaki Chakraborty, Xiangjun Wang, Aviral Kumar, and Graham Neubig introduce Recursive Agent Optimization, a reinforcement learning method for agents that can spawn copies of themselves. A recursive agent delegates sub-tasks to fresh instances of itself, giving a divide-and-conquer way to scale past one context window and toward harder problems at inference time.

RAO trains models to use that ability well: when to delegate, how to split work, and how to communicate results back. Agents trained this way learn more efficiently, handle tasks longer than a single context, and generalize to problems much harder than their training tasks. They can also finish faster in wall-clock time than single-agent systems by working branches in parallel.
arxiv-2605-06939:
Fiedler examines a quiet flaw in a popular way of grading language models, where one model is used as a judge of other models. Raw judge scores are systematically biased. Researchers correct them with calibration data, but corrections are only as good as the judge behind them. Sharing one calibration across compared models looks efficient, yet it can badly distort the comparison, even flipping which model appears better while looking highly confident.

Through analysis and simulations that vary judge quality and calibration drift, the author maps when corrected estimates go wrong. A real data MMLU-Pro case study shows an actual sign reversal. He proposes two diagnostics, judge quality J and cross model calibration shift, called delta J, to flag comparisons that are likely unreliable. He closes with reporting guidance so judge based evaluations state their uncertainty instead of presenting a biased score as a clean measurement.
arxiv-2605-07039:
Minghao Yan and thirteen co-authors improve how language-model search agents learn during a search itself. Most evolutionary search systems sample new candidates from a fixed policy, which adapts poorly when evaluations are costly. PACEvolve++ instead trains a smaller advisor model at test time to guide the search.

The advisor proposes, judges, and selects hypotheses, while a stronger frontier model turns chosen ideas into working candidates. Training shifts strategy as the search matures, from broad group feedback early to frontier-focused feedback later. Across load balancing, recommendation, and protein tasks, the system converges faster than a leading framework and keeps test-time training stable.
arxiv-2605-07139:
Jialin Yang and five co-authors fix a quiet problem in teaching small language models to reason: teacher examples are inconsistent. For similar problems, a large teacher may show wildly different solution styles, burdening the student with noisy supervision. Their method constrains the teacher to a small bank of reusable reasoning paths.

For each question, the system retrieves the closest path and has the teacher follow it, keeping style consistent yet varied across problem types. Theory ties bank size to coverage, pointing to a best middle size that experiments confirm. Across five reasoning benchmarks and two student models, the method beats standard distillation approaches while using fewer tokens.
arxiv-2605-07239:
Hongyu Cheng and three co-authors count how many samples stochastic optimization needs when variables must be whole numbers. Intuition might say integer problems are always harder than their continuous versions, but the picture depends on the objective's shape and the constraint set. The authors map out where each direction holds.

For Lipschitz objectives over box-shaped regions, mixed-integer complexity exactly matches plain linear optimization. Over round regions, integer problems can need strictly fewer samples in one regime. For strongly convex, smooth objectives, they need far more, with a lower bound that beats the classic continuous rate. New continuous results fill gaps along the way.
arxiv-2605-07439:
Mutian He and six co-authors release CA-DEL, a public benchmark for learning drug activity from DNA-encoded library screens. Such screens generate huge datasets, but their main signal, sequencing read counts, is a noisy stand-in for true binding strength. The benchmark covers screens against three closely related carbonic anhydrase enzymes, focusing on selectivity among near-identical targets.

Unlike benchmarks built only on noisy enrichment scores, CA-DEL adds a validation set of experimentally measured binding affinities from a public database. Models train on the noisy screens and are tested on high-fidelity measurements, a sim-to-real setup. The authors present it as a tougher, more realistic test for drug-discovery models.
arxiv-2605-07639:
Lorenzo Lamazzi and six co-authors address a stubborn problem in knowledge engineering: much of expert know-how is tacit, held in habits and judgments that never get written down. Procedural work runs on such knowledge, so pipelines that only handle explicit instructions miss what makes experts succeed. Their goal is machine-readable knowledge graphs that capture it.

They propose a neuro-symbolic framework pairing logic-augmented generation with an active-inference-inspired method for ontology-grounded graph construction. In a manufacturing case study, assembly-style repair procedures drawn from instructional videos served as the test domain. The approach improved both the completeness and the semantic quality of the extracted knowledge, a step toward knowledge engineering that can reuse real industrial expertise.
arxiv-2605-07739:
Eric Jacob and eight co-authors revisit the Emery model, the standard theoretical description of cuprate superconductors. Emery's original version included only one hopping term between oxygen and copper sites; later work added nearest and next-nearest oxygen-oxygen hoppings. Whether those three parameters suffice for a quantitatively correct picture was the open question.

Using the dynamical vertex approximation, the team does find a superconducting dome consistent with real cuprates. But matching the phase diagram quantitatively, and getting a proper d-wave order parameter, required long-range hoppings beyond the three conventional parameters. The result says the textbook model is qualitatively right but quantitatively incomplete, and names the missing ingredient.
arxiv-2605-07839:
François Pachet generates sequences that obey hard structural rules exactly, joining variable-order Markov models with regular constraints. The Markov side conditions each symbol on the longest matching stretch of history; the constraint side is an automaton expressing fixed positions, forced endings, metrical patterns, or banned copied fragments. Exact belief propagation already handled constraints for first-order chains, but not for variable-order generators.

Pachet pinpoints why: a first-order layer merges histories that a variable-order generator deliberately keeps separate, corrupting the future probabilities. The fix is to run the machinery on the observed context state instead, then take the product with the constraint automaton. Inference stays linear in sequence length for a fixed setup, and the same interface supports reversible data augmentation by inverse count lookup.
arxiv-2605-08139:
Gopal Krishna Shyam and Priyanka Bharti propose a stability-first autoscaler for distributed cloud systems. Ordinary scaling rules react to load spikes and can oscillate, repeatedly adding and removing virtual machines because network delays hide the true state. That flapping wastes money and hurts performance.

Their framework, C-SAS, converts noisy telemetry into a safety envelope on the complex plane using the argument principle and Rouché's theorem, and computes a real-time analytic stability index. Operations that would push the system toward oscillation are suppressed. In experiments, the method cut virtual machine flapping by ninety-four percent and reached ninety-six percent resource efficiency, beating PID and learned baselines.
arxiv-2605-08239:
Viktor Danchev, Alex Dyer, Sebastian Grau, and Guillaume Vazeille make the case for building particle colliders in space. The Large Hadron Collider has confirmed the Standard Model to high precision, yet dark matter, the hierarchy problem, and force unification stay open. Planned ground machines reach about one hundred teraelectronvolts, far below the scales where grand unified theories should show themselves.

From the scaling law for circular proton colliders, the authors estimate that rings thousands to hundreds of thousands of kilometers across are needed for the next energy frontier. Only orbital infrastructure offers that room, they argue, and space machines bring further practical benefits for reaching unification energies.
arxiv-2605-08339:
Shivam Singh Kushwah computes charge transport in a holographic model of hot quark-gluon plasma. The setup is a top-down M-theory background with quartic curvature corrections, extending the usual gauge-gravity dictionary into a non-conformal, higher-derivative regime closer to real thermal plasma.

Direct-current and Hall conductivities come from the Dirac-Born-Infeld action of probe flavor branes, using a reality condition method from earlier literature. Kushwah also works out pair production with and without an external magnetic field and identifies where thermal pair creation outweighs transport by existing charge carriers. The results carry earlier AdS/CFT transport findings into a richer class of plasma-like theories.
arxiv-2605-08439:
Natalie Seah, Danielle Bitterman, Daphna Spiegel, and Thomas Hartvigsen test whether language models can list the side effects of breast cancer radiation accurately enough for survivorship care. Patients deserve complete, clear toxicity information at consent and beyond, but clinician knowledge gaps and fragmented records make that hard in practice.

The team built paired clinical scenarios for twenty-one patient profiles that differ only in the radiotherapy regimen, then asked seven instruction-tuned models for side effect lists under several prompting styles. Comparing the outputs against the regimen differences forms a deployment-oriented stress test. The study probes how much trust oncology teams can place in model-generated counseling material.
arxiv-2605-08539:
Annan Yu, Dongwei Lyu, and N. Benjamin Erichson ask whether sequence models that claim roots in continuous time actually behave smoothly as time steps shrink. A model counts as continuous when its outputs settle toward one smooth path under finer time sampling. They also build a score for how continuous a dataset's own time structure is.

One state space model, S4, behaves steadily, while Mamba's core can react sharply to input size and selective dynamics. Across test sets, matching model continuity to task continuity tracks better results. Finer sampling tricks can then boost both speed and quality. Sequence modeling gains a clear law linking smooth time behavior to real gains.
arxiv-2605-08839:
Zhen-Hao Xie and five coauthors unify two hard learning problems: adapting to new domains and learning new classes without forgetting old ones. A driving system trained on sunny city roads may later face rural highways in rain, needing both shifts handled at once. Their CORF framework refines training samples by spatial contribution maps that highlight informative regions, and weighs samples by prediction confidence to favor domain agnostic features.

For memory, a cascaded distillation scheme transfers relational knowledge between samples across several feature levels from earlier tasks. The framework plugs into existing incremental learning methods and lifts their results across benchmarks. Systems that must keep growing in changing worlds gain one tool for both pressures.
arxiv-2605-09039:
Timo Kleger and four co-authors build SeasonScapes, a way to make large 3D landscapes that change with the seasons and can be lit anew. Their data comes from webcams in the Swiss mountains: more than eighty-five thousand images from thirty-two spots, taken at thirteen times across a full year.

The team projects the webcam images onto a 3D mesh of the terrain, which spans over fifty by sixty kilometers. Gaps from blocked views and missing data are filled with a diffusion model that paints directly on the mesh. The finished seasonal landscapes can then be rendered again under new lighting with standard tools, giving researchers a rare record of how a whole region changes through the year.
arxiv-2605-09239:
Venkatesh overturns the usual explanation for language model failures at counting repeated tokens. Counting failures are commonly blamed on weak internal count tracking, but linear probes recover the correct count almost perfectly at every layer. That holds even where the wrong answer crystallises, even as the model outputs an incorrect count.

No collapse appears in attention patterns over repeated tokens, and tokenisation artefacts explain none of the failure. Rather, a format triggered MLP block overwrites the correct count with one fixed wrong answer at roughly 88 to 93 percent depth. The prior triggers on repeated word tokens in space separated lists, is absent for digit tokens, and is suppressed by commas in bigger models but survives in smaller ones. The pattern holds across Llama-3.2 and Qwen2.5 models at the same relative depth. Counting failure is a routing failure, not a representation failure, and the two demand different interventions.
arxiv-2605-09439:
Meidler and two colleagues tackle a design problem that ordinary inverse design does not cover. Generative models sample outputs from a learned distribution, and inverse design finds an input that yields one desired output. Many goals, however, are distributional: the designer wants the whole spread of possible outputs to take a target shape, including its uncertainty. Their new problem class, conditional distribution matching, formalizes that goal in two variants, one for sampling and one for optimization.

Their solver, MLGD-F, combines a pretrained diffusion model with a fast conditional sampler at inference time. It needs no extra training or fine tuning. Single step conditional sampling keeps gradient computation tractable, memory light, and fast. Tests on synthetic benchmarks, structured image changes, and generative editing show reliable recovery of inputs whose output distributions match varied targets, from discrete mixtures to continuous low rank shapes.
arxiv-2605-09739:
Badhe and two colleagues fixed a quiet flaw in how language models are forced to pick from a short list of labels. Standard constrained decoding throws away probability the model gave to synonyms of each label, a loss the authors call the Silent Vote. The discarded mass creates fake overconfidence, a distortion named Renormalization Bias, and weakens calibration.

Their fix, Semantic Softmax, is an inference-time layer that gathers the scores of each label's semantic neighbors before deciding. Tests on Qwen-3 and Phi-4-mini, using the GoEmotions and Civil Comments sets, showed lower calibration error on both Expected Calibration Error and Brier Score. Discrimination improved too, on AUROC and Macro-F1. Counting near-meanings, the paper shows, makes zero-shot labels both steadier and sharper.
arxiv-2605-09839:
Park and Matsumoto introduced the Free Energy Manifold, a score-trained conditional energy network for hybrid Bayesian networks, which mix discrete and continuous variables. One learned object plays four roles. It gives discrete posteriors and samples by annealed Langevin. It composes leaves by energy addition. It also handles sparse data over high-cardinality discrete parents via prototype embeddings.

The paper also names a mode-bridge artifact. Network smoothness creates a low-energy ridge between modes of the same class, causing overconfidence at off-distribution interior points. A simple valley regularization fixes it, with an optimal strength following a non-monotonic three-phase pattern. On synthetic anti-correlated multimodal benchmarks, FEM cut KL divergence 60 to 172 times versus the best non-FEM baseline at the standard setup.
arxiv-2605-09939:
Wei, Peng and Vougioukas take on self-driving tractor-trailer rigs in cluttered farm settings, where articulated bodies and nonlinear dynamics make collision avoidance hard. Older methods trim the vehicle shape or lean on pre-made distance maps that assume a known field, both poor fits for dynamic, partly unknown orchards and vineyards. Their system reasons from raw laser scans instead.

A shape-based neural encoder gauges gaps between the full tractor-trailer body and LiDAR points quickly and accurately, with no map required. Those distances feed a Model Predictive Path Integral control scheme, which weighs true articulated geometry when scoring trial paths. Tests show the system producing dynamically feasible, safe trajectories through cluttered and complex agricultural scenes.
arxiv-2605-10239:
Mingwei Xing, Xinliang Wang, and Yifeng Shi offer a strikingly small fix for a hard 3D problem. They rebuild a scene from a few photos. Their 2026 paper presents AdaptSplat, a method for feed-forward 3D Gaussian splatting. That technique renders new viewpoints from sparse views by picturing a scene as many soft 3D blobs.

Instead of redesigning the whole pipeline, the authors add a single adapter of just 1.5 million parameters. Called the Frequency-Preserving Adapter, it pulls direction-aware, high-frequency detail from the shallow layers of a vision foundation model and feeds it back in. This sharpens edges and complex surfaces that deep networks tend to smooth away. Across standard benchmarks the method reached leading feed-forward reconstruction scores and generalized steadily across domains.
arxiv-2605-10339:
Konstantin Zaitsev improves how chat systems recall personal facts about users. Chat systems pile up facts such as tastes and ties, but past labeling schemes, notably PeaCoK, limit tidy storage and quality filtering. His 2026 paper offers a wider labeling scheme for personal fact sorting, with new groups and traits for carrying a chat forward.

The scheme adds Demographics and Possessions as groups, plus Duration, Validity, and Followup as traits. That enables tidy storage, quality filtering, and spotting facts fit to continue a chat. Zaitsev hand-labeled 2,779 facts from Multi-Session Chat and trained a multi-head sorter on transformer encoders. With the Gemma-300M encoder it hit 81.6 percent macro F1, beating the best few-shot language-model baseline, at 72.92 percent, by nearly 9 points while using far less computing power. Data and sorter are public.
arxiv-2605-10439:
Yu Zhe and four colleagues address a copyright risk hiding inside shared AI customizations. Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, lets users inject new visual concepts or styles into diffusion models through light weight updates. Platforms hold huge libraries of user-uploaded LoRAs. Yet LoRAs can memorize training images, reproducing copyrighted or sensitive content. Their 2026 paper proposes Base-Anchored Filtering, or BAF, a fix needing neither training data nor pipeline access.

BAF sorts LoRA updates into spectral channels and checks how far they line up with the main subspace of the pretrained backbone. Channels strongly aligned with that subspace are kept as generalizable adaptations. Weakly aligned channels are damped down as likely carriers of memorized content. Tests across multiple datasets and diffusion backbones show BAF steadily cuts memorization while keeping or even improving generation quality, giving hosts and users a post-hoc tool for deployed LoRAs.
arxiv-2605-10639:
Regina Gugg and three colleagues study bias in toxic benchmarks for language models. The rapid rise of language models highlights the risks of using them safely. It reveals a gap in sound testing of toxic benchmarks. As firms rely on benchmarks to approve models for apps and auto review, hidden testing tilts could lead to bad launches.

Their 2026 paper studies the strength of current benchmark setups. The authors study how to measure missed built-in tilts, such as those tied to model choice, metrics, and task types. Tests uncover gaps in benchmark conduct when testing setups are altered. Shifting from text writing to digests makes benchmarks flag content as harmful more often. Certain benchmarks fail to maintain steady conduct when the input domain is changed. The authors also observe model swings, showing a need for more robust and full safety evaluation frameworks.
arxiv-2605-10839:
Paul Kairys and Phillip C. Lotshaw study synthetic twist defects in the surface code, a 2026 quantum error-correction design in which defects can mimic particles with non-Abelian statistics, the kind needed for braiding-based computing. Such defects are usually treated as fixed lattice features, but theory suggests local nudges to the underlying state could create and move them.

The authors build the defect model in both spin and Majorana pictures, uncovering hidden symmetries that simplify the math and a direct link to Kitaev's Majorana chain. Numerical work then traces the energy spectrum and points to where the phase change that births the defects occurs. Experimentalists get a concrete map of the conditions under which these useful defects should appear in finite, realistically perturbed devices.
arxiv-2605-11239:
Zhenhuan Sun and Shahrokh Valaee extend the kernel trick to influence functions with a dual representation that scales in cost with dataset size rather than model size. In theory and in tests, this representation gives a cheaper stand-in for original influence functions when estimating how removing a data point shifts parameters, model outputs, and loss. This holds when model size is large versus dataset size or when parameter-space evaluation is infeasible.

The dual route is limited to linearizable models, whose behavior can be approximated by linearizations throughout training. It also needs a matrix whose size scales with model output dimension times dataset size. Interpretability researchers get a dataset-sized route to influence estimation, with its limits stated plainly.
arxiv-2605-11539: Angel, Ray and Spinka study a noisy min-max game on trees. Each d-ary tree edge carries a cookie worth plus or minus 1. Two players alternate choosing a child, collecting cookies into a jar won by the first player, paid by the second. The value stays tight for d equals 2, converges in distribution from d equals 3, and almost surely from d equals 15. The analysis mixes percolation arguments for large d, with iteration and interval arithmetic for small d. For d equals 2, a continuum of fixed points exists.
arxiv-2605-11639: Yao and six colleagues present a machine learning-based ensemble Kalman filter for high-accuracy data assimilation with limited ensembles. Data assimilation merges forecasts with observations for state estimation, but ensemble methods depend heavily on ensemble size, trading accuracy against cost. Their multilayer perceptron predicts the covariance gap between a limited ensemble and a large one. That gap enters the filter through element-wise scaling, yielding an amended covariance matching true uncertainty better. Tests on Lorenz-63 and Lorenz-96 beat standard EnKF at the same limited size with higher accuracy.
arxiv-2605-11739: Yuchen Cai and eleven colleagues explain why on-policy distillation trains large language models so efficiently. They argue its speed comes from foresight: early in training it settles on a stable update path, concentrating changes on reasoning-critical modules and aligning dominant update directions with the final ones. Building on this, they propose EffOPD, which adapts its step size along the current direction and trains about three times faster with comparable final quality.
arxiv-2605-11839: Patrizio Dazzi and three colleagues compare ways to find AI agents spread across cloud, edge, and machines that link up only at times. Within one shared control plane they test Chord, Pastry, and Kademlia on 4096-node steady and churn benchmarks. They track how often agents are found, how startup goes, and how much control traffic each overlay adds. The tests clarify the trade-offs each overlay offers for agent indexes from edge to cloud.
arxiv-2605-12039: Xiaoyuan Li and six colleagues arrange agent skill stores as changing graphs instead of lone entries. Their SKILLGRAPH system shows skills as nodes in a linked graph, with typed edges for must-come-first, boost, and joint-use links. For a new task it fetches an ordered skill subgraph to guide multi-step choices, changing the graph often from runs and RL feedback. Tests on ALFWorld, WebShop, and seven search-aided QA tasks showed state-of-the-art results, above all on multi-skill tasks.
arxiv-2605-12139: Du Cheng, Serdar Kadioglu, and Xin Wang build BoolXLLM, a hybrid system joining large language models with Boolean rule learning. Rule-based models like BoolXAI give faithful, compact accounts of model behavior, but non-experts struggle to pick meaningful features and read formal rules. BoolXLLM uses language models at three stages: picking domain-relevant features, suggesting meaningful cut points for numbers, and shrinking rules into plain-language accounts at global and local levels. Early tests show the language-model help lifts clarity while keeping predictive performance competitive.
arxiv-2605-12239: Bogdan Banu gives harness engineering a theory via categorical architecture. The harness, the layer of prompts, tools, memory, and orchestration around a model, is central for agents. Banu maps the ArchAgents triple onto harness parts: memory as state, skills as composed objects, protocols as wiring, and the harness as the whole. Guarantees like integrity gates and escalation checks become Know certificates preserved by replay. A build with compilers for Swarms, DeerFlow, Ralph, Scion, and LangGraph preserves three certificate types. An escalation test confirms the control path is model-parametric.
arxiv-2605-12339: Nguyen and five colleagues simplify safety tuning for language models by recasting it as matching density ratios. Current pipelines juggle separate reward and cost models plus online reinforcement learning, while simpler preference methods bolt safety on with ad-hoc margins. They show the optimal safe policy's likelihood ratio splits in closed form. Minimising Bregman divergences between data and model ratios yields BSO, a single-stage family of losses with one extra hyperparameter. Safety benchmarks show a better safety-helpfulness balance.
arxiv-2605-12639: Suri, Ringel and Sonnewald bring OceanCBM, the first concept bottleneck model for ocean forecasting and mechanistic diagnosis. Good forecasts alone do not reveal real drivers, and opaque machine learning offers limited fidelity to ground-truth physics. OceanCBM predicts mixed layer heat content, a leading sign of marine heatwaves, while routing information through prescribed concepts from geophysical dynamics plus one free concept. That structure imposes soft real constraints without making the model too tight, and the free concept regularises predictions while capturing residual processes.
arxiv-2605-13139: Guan and ten co-authors present SWE-Cycle, a benchmark of 489 cases for code agents across the full issue resolution cycle. Current benchmarks hide friction with ready-made environments and static parsers that fail on autonomous trajectories. SWE-Cycle tests environment rebuild, code writing and verification test writing separately, plus an end-to-end FullCycle task in a bare repo. Its SWE-Judge pairs static review with dynamic testing to verify correctness reliably. Results show a sharp drop from single tasks to FullCycle, exposing cross-phase dependency bottlenecks.
arxiv-2605-13339: Gilg and colleagues probe how language models hold preferences across adopted personas. They train linear probes on internal activations of two large models to predict pairwise task choices. One genuine preference direction tracks shifting choices and, on one model, steering along it causally changes choices. Preference signals partly transfer across personas, even to an evil persona whose tastes run opposite to the helpful assistant.
arxiv-2605-13639: Ishaq Hamza and Zaiwei Chen establish final-iterate rates of convergence for off-policy actor-critic methods within reinforcement learning. Under a single-loop single-timescale setup and a broad class of policy updates, they prove the first tilde-O sample complexity guarantee for epsilon-optimal policies. The rate is epsilon to the minus two. That needs only an irreducible Markov chain policy. Their analysis uses a coupled Lyapunov drift framework, proving actor convergence and tilde-O of one over T critic convergence, combined via a cross-domination property.
arxiv-2605-13839: Wenrui Bao and five colleagues study another multi-agent word model talk link. It packs a sender's hidden states into a brief target weight nudge instead of adding the sender's message to the target's notes. They present TFlow, a weight-space talk frame for a known and fixed target design. With three Qwen3-4B agents, TFlow improves over a solo target by up to 8.5 hits across five tests. It keeps rival hits on four of five tests.
arxiv-2605-14139: Ali and four co-authors model how opinions and epidemics shape each other with graphon math. Chats between people drive opinion change, which alters how disease is seen and thus how it spreads, for instance through uptake or rejection of preventive measures. Contact patterns also steer spread. The paper builds a math model for the coupled motion of opinion formation, disease spread and physical contacts, using graphon networks that capture the varied, large-scale links of realistic social structures.
arxiv-2605-14239: Long and five co-authors propose IFGNet, an implicit frequency-geometry fusion network for hyperspectral and lidar data. Hyperspectral sorting struggles in complex scenes with spectral ambiguity, varied ground, and tight coupling between material traits and geometric shapes. Lidar adds complementary elevation data, yet most fusion methods use CNNs or MLPs with fixed activations and linear weights. IFGNet instead uses Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with spline-based functions that learn to capture highly nonlinear links across spatial and frequency domains.
arxiv-2605-14439: Monemzadeh and Tazimi investigate a Kapitza-inspired process where rapid oscillations in heavy-quark interactions create short-range repulsion in diquark-antidiquark potentials. The inverse-fourth-power term prevents short-distance collapse and creates a stable minimum. With a modified Cornell-type potential and Gaussian variational method, they compute binding energies, radii and mass spectra for charm and bottom tetraquarks. The model reproduces the X(3872) mass and predicts a deeply bound T-bb state matching lattice QCD. Kapitza dynamics unifies molecular-like and compact tetraquark pictures as a robust stabiliser.
arxiv-2605-14539: Ren, Lou, Cao, Wen, Lin, Han, Sun, Yu and Lu turn a language model's own failed reasoning attempts into training signal. Their Correction-Oriented Policy Optimization adds correction samples drawn from failed trajectories to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, aiming to sharpen credit assignment where binary rewards are sparse. Across eleven mathematics and coding benchmarks, the method is claimed to beat strong baselines on reasoning and self-correction.
arxiv-2605-14639: Sharma studies localisation plus spectral topology in a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic lattice of Su-Schrieffer-Heeger type, with Rashba spin-orbit coupling plus spin-dependent hopping. As the non-Hermitian parameter grows, the system is claimed to swing from extended to localised and back to extended, with a matching real-complex-real spectral switch. Adding spin-dependent hopping splits two spin loops into four spin-resolved branches with distinct winding numbers.
arxiv-2605-14939: Alasdair Ross and nine others build neural-network emulators that give tokamak plasma controllers virtual circuits in real time. Virtual circuits untangle coupled shape controls so each shape trait can be steered alone. The team trained on over a million model equilibria spanning much of the MAST Upgrade operating range. Tests show the emulated circuits stay accurate and near-orthogonal across diverse equilibria, replacing fixed schedules of precomputed circuits.
arxiv-2605-15139: Sudipta Saha, Shoumik Debnath, and Md Kawsar Alam propose a single silicon microring sensor for breath markers of disease. An anisotropic beryllium sulfide cladding lets two light modes, transverse-electric and transverse-magnetic, probe orthogonal permittivity parts, yielding two solo readouts from one device. Five markers were tested in simulation with first-principles optical constants. The electric mode shifts evenly as a concentration reference, while the magnetic mode shifts by analyte, with a distinctive amplitude flip for benzene. The dual response fingerprints all five without an array.
arxiv-2605-15239: Yu Fu and six others tackle the safety tax, the reasoning ability lost when safety alignment trains on outside demonstrations. It trains on demos from humans, other models, or fixed traces, not the model's own rollouts. Their on-policy self-distillation, OPSA, lets the model generate its own rollouts. Dense per-token supervision comes from a frozen teacher copy with a privileged safety context. A teacher flip rate measures how often privileged context turns unsafe responses safe, guiding context search. Across model families, OPSA improves the safety-reasoning tradeoff.
arxiv-2605-15739: Jun Zou and fourteen colleagues build a cosmic-ray detection module from liquid scintillator and wavelength-shifting fibers. Cosmic muons bedevil neutrino physics and rare-event searches, and must be spotted and rejected. Cost control with good performance is also hard for a large detector array. Their module offers reasonable cost and performance. Prototype tests with muons show a good photoelectron response. The study suggests strong potential for cosmic-ray observation and underground rare-event detection, giving a viable option for future observatories.
arxiv-2605-15839: Seyoon Kim, Antonio Matas-Gil and Robert G. Endres ask how evolving systems find the narrow parameter regions where Turing patterns form. They couple a reaction-diffusion system to a common biochemical limit cycle, such as a genetic feedback loop, so the system sweeps dynamically through Turing-permissive regimes and produces transient spatial patterns. An entropy-based measure in Fourier space quantifies pattern formation, showing cycles improve detectability and robustness. Coupling to positional gradients further increases reproducibility, suggesting a route from oscillations to stable developmental programs.
arxiv-2605-16239: Wang presents a motion-level mark for flow matching models, placing the mark in the learned speed field rather than weights or outputs. The method frames marking as random coding over an ongoing channel: a keyed tweak added during training is read back at check time from black-box queries. The tweak is built to leave the made spread the same. Tests on MNIST and CIFAR-10 confirm reliable message readback, kept output quality, and chance-level decodes without the secret key.
arxiv-2605-16539: Jalbert-Desforges presents vega-mir, an open-source Python toolkit bundling nine information-theoretic and statistical measures for symbolic music. Across fourteen MAESTRO composers, the PageRank of the gravity-centre chord node tracks marginal KL distance at rho 0.61 in their test, a moderate link. The centre's identity itself shows no such link. In a 247-piece Bach corpus, Gould's rubato is small but structured in time. His median dominant period is 66 beats, against 102 for Schiff and 104 for Richter.
arxiv-2605-16739: Mohammed, Gu and Fang present EmoMind, the first end-to-end system that decodes affective captions directly from fMRI brain signals. It first finds a neutral scene description from brain-decoded visual features, then rewrites it with a 34-dimensional emotion vector decoded from the same recording. Guidance during training balances content preservation against feeling. Across two emotion fMRI datasets, EmoMind beats label-prompted GPT-4 on all three validation axes, with the largest gains on person-specific feeling structure.
arxiv-2605-16839: Song and colleagues propose CompactAttention, a chunked-prefill method for long models with block-union selection. Sparse methods suit one-shot prefill but falter when chunks limit query length or pattern search repeats over the cache. CompactAttention treats 2D block-sparse masks as selection signals, converting them into group block tables via block unions. Blocks are read in place without compaction. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, it nearly matches dense RULER accuracy, running up to 2.79x faster than dense attention and 1.25x faster than FlashPrefill at 128K.
arxiv-2605-16939: Jakšić, Teofanov and Vučković study whether a Cauchy problem for the general Laguerre operator is well posed and link it to the global harmonic-oscillator problem. They analyse continuity of the associated propagator in detail and connect several integral transforms, including the fractional Fourier and fractional Hankel transforms. Their results highlight the role of Pilipović spaces on positive orthants for problems that involve the Laguerre operator.
arxiv-2605-17039: Chen's team builds a private federated framework for generation fraud in distributed home solar grids. Unlike theft checks, solar fraud checks face uneven generation, while distributed systems challenge central checks on scale. Each community runs a local check fusing solar and weather feeds through joint focus to spot discrepancies. The framework pools parameters and prototypes, sharing global knowledge locally while preserving privacy, and prototype alignment counters imbalance. Tests on real home data beat leading methods, scale with community size, and stay robust to imbalance.
arxiv-2605-17239: Hao Li introduces the handling of control-system uncertainty as a core aspect of advanced control theory for practical use. Control theory, he argues, matters both for why systems behave as they do and for how engineers build them. The article frames methodology in mathematical terms as the heart of control science, spanning hardware, software, operation, upkeep, cost and social concerns, and treats uncertainty handling as its featured topic.
arxiv-2605-17639: Volodymyr Ovcharov tests whether co-citation gives stable retrieval signal, building UA-StatuteRetrieval over 20 snapshots of Ukrainian court records.
