Using a leave-one-out protocol, Adamic-Adar rank falls 33 percent on a fixed set and 47 percent under a temporal split, confirming genuine decay, not a shifting mix. Decay is uneven: criminal procedure holds stable patterns, while civil law degrades around the 2017 reform. Hub items resist decay, but mid-frequency ones lose half their predictability. A BM25 baseline decays faster at 31 percent, and embedding drift reveals a semantic shift.
arxiv-2605-18039: Soyeon Yoon and two colleagues propose SGSoft, a unified pipeline for dense matching across deformable 3D shapes that bend and change. It builds a geodesic field on a canonical template, learns dense codes from semantic priors with field supervision, and finds correspondences in one pass via nearest-neighbor search. This setup gives stable guidance under pose variation, structural differences, and remeshing, so matches stay steady. SGSoft tops inter-category generalization, and runs near real-time without alignment or refinement.
arxiv-2605-18139: Zhenhao Wang's 2026 study maps the ground-state shapes of a two-part dipolar condensate trapped in a flat round box. Varying the trap depth, the imbalance of forces, and the mix of the two parts yields a rich cast: near-flat pancakes, pancake-droplet mixes, ring mixes, droplet arrays, and concentric rings. The shapes mirror phase patterns in diblock copolymers, with the population mix playing the role of volume share. Pattern spacing grows in step with trap thickness, but the round box forces it into discrete jumps.
arxiv-2605-18239: Dylan Marx's 2026 study tests whether multi-turn chats in low-resource African languages can slip past large language model safety guardrails. Single-turn translated prompts fail, but multi-turn conversations in Afrikaans, Kiswahili, isiXhosa, and isiZulu succeed at high rates across ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, and Grok. English harmful-response rates run from 52.7 percent to 83.6 percent by model, with similar spreads in Afrikaans and Kiswahili. Human red-teaming pushes rates higher still, and the authors find translation quality is the key factor limiting jailbreak success.
arxiv-2605-18639: Fabio Benatti and two co-authors challenge, in a 2026 paper, complete positivity as a requirement for open quantum dynamics. They weigh its physical motives and limits, including plans to limit non-completely-positive maps to matching initial states. Using isotropic states as a test case, they show domain limits tighten fast as system size grows. The study exposes a built-in flaw in the matching-based approach to non-completely-positive dynamics.
arxiv-2605-19339: Nhu, Son, Sang and Duy study control of a heat-like equation with exponential growth and point sources, where the control is a summable sequence. The control-to-state map can fail to have a direction, so standard calculus breaks down. They first prove direction-based differentiability on finite-dimensional slices, then define a generalized derivative as the limit when slice size grows. From that plus Taylor-type estimates, they derive first- and second-order optimality conditions for box-limited controls.
arxiv-2605-19439: Hoang, Busch and Fogarty study charging for a one-dimensional many-body bosonic quantum battery fed by a harmonic-oscillator charger. In weak coupling the dynamics reduce to an effective two-level model that predicts resonance, best charging time, stored work, extractable work and charging power. Tuning the charger to the interaction-shifted resonance gives full energy transfer and maximum extractable work. Adding particles shortens the quantum speed-limit time and lifts power with square-root scaling, while stronger coupling can boost power further at low excitation cost.
arxiv-2605-19539: Zhu and team present Trust3R, an uncertainty method for feed-forward 3D reconstruction from raw images. Current feed-forward models give rough scores with no probabilistic meaning, often hiding where shape can be trusted. Trust3R pairs gated mean refinement with a Normal-Inverse-Wishart evidential head, yielding a Student-t distribution for per-point uncertainty. It lifts risk ranking and sparsification over MASt3R and rivals, with 25 percent lower AURC and 41 percent lower AUSE on ScanNet++, giving later workflows a reliability signal.
arxiv-2605-19639: Wang and team benchmark and evolve Reason-Reflect-Rectify for review-based visual generation. Single-pass text-to-image models struggle with complex prompts needing repeated fixes. The authors define the Reason-Reflect-Rectify loop and offer R^3-Bench, over 600 expert-labeled cases. Tests expose a sharp gap: leading models spot output errors yet fail to produce usable fix steps. Their R^3-Refiner, a dual-stage framework using group relative policy optimization and a hierarchical reward mechanism, lifts reflective verdict scores by 12 percent and rectification scores by 9 percent.
arxiv-2605-20239: Farokhnaz Hosseinifar and five co-workers introduce a rotating Kaluza-Klein black hole with massive vector and scalar fields. They map horizons and parameters, separating black hole solutions from naked singularities. Heat study shows a phase shift: Hawking temperature marks a critical point, while off-shell free energy places it in a universal group. They also study ergosphere shape, spin, shadow size and thin disk features. Extra-dimensional shifts move phase shift points and change shadow size, yet the topological class stays stable, for telling gravity models apart.
arxiv-2605-20339: Singam and two co-workers map phase diagrams of charge-conserving fermions in the trivial, so-called featureless phase. Topological families such as charge pumps texture those diagrams, visible through Berry phases and higher analogues. The texture yields robust edge modes ending at bulk diabolical points, and at finite chemical potential those modes need no fine-tuning in two or more dimensions. In one dimension the edge modes sit estranged, appearing at different parameter values per edge.
arxiv-2605-20539: Ipsita Bhar and four colleagues answer a scarcity of real seismic data for machine-learning underground mapping. The best surveys stay private, which limits training and testing. Their OpenSeisML collection draws on public surveys from the UK National Data Repository. An automated pipeline turns raw surveys and well logs into matching velocity models for generative training.
arxiv-2605-20639: April Tran and three colleagues speed up design problems where the rules are given by time-dependent partial differential equations, the maths of fields that change over space and time. High-fidelity runs need repeated forward and sensitivity solves, which grow too costly in many-query design and control. Their weak-form latent-space method compresses solution paths into a low-dimensional latent form and learns its dynamics without explicit numerical differentiation. That improves robustness to noisy data, and they derive direct and adjoint gradients for the reduced problem.
arxiv-2605-20839: Jeffrey Wang, J. Gregory, and G. Chrysos show that pointwise activations and exponential softmax are not needed in MetaFormer-style vision models. They design activation-free polynomial options for three core parts: MLPs, convolutions, and attention. Hadamard products replace standard nonlinearities in their design. Their PolyNeXt models match or beat standard rivals on ImageNet, ADE20K segmentation, and out-of-distribution robustness tests. The work shows a simpler path to strong vision results.
arxiv-2605-21239: Hongrui Zhang and colleagues survey emotion recognition from mixed inputs with large language models. The field has moved from small task-specific models to general models. The survey groups prior work by three hard problems: scarce labeled emotion data, gaps in feeling across inputs, and opaque interpretation. Responses include data augmentation and better alignment of inputs. The survey aims to guide future work toward more general emotional intelligence in machines.
arxiv-2605-21439: Dianrui Mu and co-authors present a low-complexity, model-free, output-feedback controller for unknown nonlinear systems with unknown input constraints. The controller hits preset accuracy before saturation and keeps flexible accuracy after saturation. This extends linear-manifold constraint methods to nonlinear manifolds and varied constraints, achieving preset accuracy in finite or fixed time via an error-driven flexible constraint.
arxiv-2605-21539: Xuyang Zhong and co-authors propose DualOptim+, bridging shared and split optimizer states for machine unlearning. It adds a base state holding common patterns shared by forgetting and retaining goals. Delta states keep goal-specific leftovers. The optimizer flexibly bridges shared and split states based on direction clash between forgetting and retaining gradients. They also introduce DualOptim+ 8bit, a quantized variant cutting memory cost without harming performance. It shows a better trade-off across unlearning, safety alignment, and multi-task learning in wide tests across fake and real tasks.
arxiv-2605-21639: Cynthia Curtis, Kendra Ebke, and Kate O'Connor determine weights of essential surfaces in two-bridge knot complements. Work on ideal points in the character varieties of knot spaces has produced important invariants for three-manifolds. Building on Ohtsuki's 1994 count of ideal points for two-bridge knots, they map in full the structure of a Serre tree for each key surface from the knot diagram. His 1996 paper made the methods more concrete. From these trees they derive a formula for the number of ideal points linked to each incompressible surface.
arxiv-2605-21739: Lubrano and colleagues introduce AttuneBench, a benchmark for emotional intelligence in language models. It rests on two hundred genuine multi-turn conversations, with turn-by-turn notes on feelings, model conduct, and wanted replies. Across eleven models, rankings on emotion recognition, behavior classification, preference prediction, and response quality prove largely independent. Emotional skill thus splits apart. Predicting the reply a user wants in context tells models apart far more sharply than labeling emotions correctly.
arxiv-2605-21839: Jigme Zangpo, Hirokazu Kobayashi, and Ryo Yasuhara simplify phase-edge imaging with a 4f system and an off-axis q-plate. Earlier work needed four q-plate shifts. Their method needs only two shifts along plus and minus x, with linear polarizers at forty-five and one hundred thirty-five degrees. Halving the count doubles acquisition speed. Theory shows the intensity equals the phase gradient squared, with amplitude-object contributions removed. Tests on two phase-amplitude samples cut amplitude edges by up to ninety-seven point six percent.
arxiv-2605-22039: Prajwal Panth presents a secure, parallel framework for determinant work on large matrices in edge settings, where limited clients delegate heavy work to edge servers. Determinant work matters for control, cryptography, and machine learning, yet cubic complexity makes classic methods unfit for real-time use. His framework adds privacy and integrity guarantees with minimal client burden, plus two checks: Q2, a probabilistic scalar check, and Q3, a deterministic simple check. Analysis shows strong privacy and security, low overhead, and easy rollout for scalable, real-time determinant work.
arxiv-2605-22139: Xu and co-authors present EventGait, gait recognition with event streams. Gait recognition identifies people at a distance, but conventional cameras suffer in uncontrolled environments from illumination and motion sensitivity. Event cameras offer microsecond timing and high dynamic range, capturing robust dynamic cues while cutting static noise. Event-based gait recognition matches camera-based results under normal conditions and beats it in low light. The method sets a new state of the art on lab and real-world event-based gait benchmarks, with code and datasets released.
arxiv-2605-22339: Dumas and colleagues report a bulk source of entangled photon pairs at 810 and 1550 nanometres, fed straight into single-mode optical fibres. The pair of wavelengths suits hybrid quantum networks. The longer wavelength travels well in fibre, while the shorter one suits free-space links and detection. The source uses down-conversion in a lithium niobate crystal inside a Sagnac interferometer, giving built-in stability. Measured visibilities reach 0.995 for polarisation and 0.991 for energy-time entanglement.
arxiv-2605-22939: Parashar and seven coauthors propose LIFT, a fine-tuning method for diffusion language models that respects what tokens are learnable, and when. Standard supervised fine-tuning ignores learnability: rare tokens resist learning when most input is masked, while common tokens teach little when most input is visible. LIFT instead learns easy tokens under heavy masking and hard tokens with more context. It beat existing fine-tuning baselines on six reasoning benchmarks, with up to threefold relative gains on AIME tests.
arxiv-2605-23039: Guo, Wu, and Yiu study how language models learn what not to say, testing statistical preemption against entrenchment in one converging design. Across four experiments with 120 English verb-construction pairings, model surprisal tracks human acceptability at r equals 0.79. The patterns follow rival-form frequency, not overall verb use. Preemption sensitivity grows as a power law with model size. A fine-tuning intervention causally shifts preemption by manipulating rival-form frequencies, with reverse controls ruling out mere rate sensitivity. Neural models, they conclude, learn negative knowledge through distributional competition.
arxiv-2605-23239: Lee and Park propose a self-supervised cleaning tool for graph networks. Defense needs balancing accuracy and toughness, mishandled by attack training mixing conflicting goals in one classifier. They separate toughness from the classifier with a cleaner that cleans input data. Unlike cleaners, they propose GPR-GAE, a graph auto-encoder cleaner trained, adapting to graph shapes. Multiple Generalized PageRank filters let GPR-GAE capture shape codes for robust cleaning. Tests across datasets and scenarios show top toughness for GPR-GAE as a plug-and-play cleaner.
arxiv-2605-23739: Li and colleagues present a wavelet pipeline for narrowband technosignatures in FAST observations of 33 exo-world systems. The pipeline uses a Multi-Scale Wavelet Net for a picture, then a setting gauge for endpoints. Rather than drift searches, it recasts detection as wavelet-guided pulling, endpoint fitting, shape-aware filtering, raw-data checks, and multi-beam veto. Applied to FAST data, it finds typical events from prior studies and gives veto-ready candidates. The workflow preserves interpretability, low complexity, and open threshold control, moving to other radio surveys.
arxiv-2605-23839: The cloe-org maintainers present cloelib, a Python library for computing cosmological observables in the Euclid era. Galaxy surveys now map the sky in fine detail, and theory must keep pace. Its modular design pairs with established Boltzmann solvers and JAX automatic differentiation, so gradients flow through theory predictions. It covers background evolution, perturbations and nonlinear structure. It also covers photometric and spectroscopic large scale probes, plus cross correlations with the microwave background and clusters. The goal is to anchor Euclid's first cosmological release.
arxiv-2605-24339: Liang and Han present IsaacIPC, a robotic sim tool coupling GPU contact physics with IsaacSim and IsaacLab. IsaacIPC maps deformation between sim and visual meshes, giving live lifelike visuals for data and policy tests. For tactile sensing, the mortar contact rule sets a barrier over contact samples on touch surfaces, resolving pressure patterns better. The authors test the rule on contact benchmarks and show IsaacIPC on rigid-soft sims including a four-legged robot, a dexterous hand, and a gripper.
arxiv-2605-24439: Yang and three co-authors show that cavity vacuum fluctuations can drive triplet superconductivity in a singlet superconductor. The vacuum field reshapes the band structure with polarization, altering the Fermi surface and the contest among pairing channels. Once light-matter coupling passes a critical value, the leading instability changes from singlet to triplet pairing, producing a state. That vacuum-driven symmetry change alters the gap and the low-energy quasiparticle spectrum. The results establish cavity vacuum engineering as a route to unconventional phases and stable triplet states relevant to superconductivity.
arxiv-2605-24739: Pinheiro and Almeida study how chiral fermion localization fades as two domain walls merge in braneworld models. In the Jackiw-Rebbi framework, left- and right-handed zero modes approach and hybridize. Chiral asymmetry drains away as the walls close. The gap between chiral zero modes obeys a universal power law in the merging limit, its exponent set solely by the Jackiw-Rebbi topological index. Tests across wall models sharing index one give exponents just below one, and a closed-form overlap integral explains the sub-unit value.
arxiv-2605-24939: Ziyue Chen, David \Ši\ška, and \Łukasz Szpruch study policy gradient converging globally for entropy-regularized Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions. They use log-linear softmax policies with linear function approximation, extending the tabular class. Under value-function realizability, they prove a non-uniform Polyak-\Łojasiewicz inequality from policy geometry degeneracy. Two feature regimes bound the constant: full-affine-span and simplex-valued features, each giving radial unboundedness and eigenvalue lower bounds. These imply global linear convergence, extending tabular theory beyond its original setting.
arxiv-2605-25039: Zhifeng Wang, Jason Jingshi Li, Kaihao Zhang, and Ramesh Sankaranarayana build AstroRAG, a PageRank retrieval pipeline for astronomy questions. It uses token-aware chunking and indexes each instance ephemerally in Elasticsearch, so no data leaks across tasks, with no training needed. Retrieval runs in two stages. Maximal marginal relevance picks a small diverse set, then PageRank re-ranking over a similarity graph selects a context within a token budget. On AstroQA, a retrieval-enhanced Mistral-7B reaches 79.49 percent accuracy and F1, nearly doubling its counterpart.
arxiv-2605-25239: Manan Kharwar presents FusionCore, a ROS 2 package fusing inertial, wheel-encoder, GPS, and visual SLAM data into one 100 hertz odometry stream. A 23-state unscented Kalman filter carries gyroscope and accelerometer biases as states. Its 23rd state tracks the wheel encoder's yaw rate bias, learned from GPS heading and subtracted during GPS blackouts. Outliers pass a chi-squared gate, and noise adapts from innovations. On twelve NCLT sequences it beats robot_localization on ten, while the rival filter diverges on all twelve.
arxiv-2605-25339: David Flynn presents ionized-carbon motion data for 31 star-forming galaxies from roughly 12 to 13 billion years ago, as a unified corpus. From the ALPINE survey, the High-z Kinematic Corpus Z1 gives maps and motion measures for galaxies near the reionization era. Eight rotators carry per-ring rotation curves with mass estimates, while the remaining carry classification only. Every entry adds stellar mass, star formation rate, disk criteria, and geometry. A 2026 correction fixes a formula slip, so the eight rotators show positive rotation values and the sign reversal is withdrawn.
arxiv-2605-25539: Taketo Tominaga and Ryo Onishi test whether particle clustering in shifting turbulence can be treated as if it settles at once. Their direct simulations of uniform turbulence under unsteady forcing show lag and hysteresis once the forcing period passes several large-eddy turnover times. For the heaviest particles, clustering at one dissipation rate takes two far apart values. A finite-time relaxation model then cuts the worst prediction error from 49 percent to 10 percent, with a similar gain on a fresh validation case.
arxiv-2605-25639: Wei and colleagues mine anomalies from drone state-estimation logs, where failures are rare and scattered across uneven PX4 telemetry streams. Their AeroTSBoost lines up multivariate flight logs and turns each window into deterministic descriptors of distribution shifts, quantile shape, endpoint drift, local dynamics and lag correlation. It then trains a class-balanced LightGBM detector for the task. On UAV-SEAD, it leads all baselines on AUPRC and holds the lead under chronological and leave-log-out checks. It also scores strongly on ALFA fixed-wing fault logs.
arxiv-2605-25739: Lovén and colleagues prove a reinforcement learning policy with confidence-gated autonomy cannot reach help, optimal calibration and autonomy at once, when tasks exceed skill. The block is shape-based: adding a non-affine incentive to a proper scoring rule destroys its strictness. A rewarded agent then pumps up its stated self-ratings on tasks below the pass bar. Their Perturbation Lemma sizes the bloat and spotting costs. No affine oversight rule wins in the open regime. A test confirms five claims with large effect sizes.
arxiv-2605-25939: Alba and Lopez-Rubio ask whether training biases can make hidden neurons in a tiny network specialise. Specialised neurons would each cover a distinct part of the training data. They compare three added losses against plain fitting on one-dimensional data. The losses reward coverage, separation between prototypes, and low overlap of responses. Coverage wins at every size, giving the lowest rebuilding error and the most specialised neurons. Separation helps unevenly, while overlap penalties harm by driving prototypes outside the input range.
arxiv-2605-26039: Paxton, Cheon, Geelen and McQuarrie speed up quadratic manifold learning, a way to shrink nonlinear systems. Quadratic manifolds add bend terms to a reduced basis, but bases from top principal components suit straight fits, not curved ones. Greedy basis hunts improve fits yet cost too much for large bases. FastQM instead treats basis choice as smooth optimisation on the Stiefel manifold, turning the basis inside a span of candidate singular vectors. Tests on a turbulent airfoil wake show strong curved fits learned fast.
arxiv-2605-26139: Akhmedov and Milovanova show directly that radiation from a charge in steady speed-up escapes outside the Rindler wedge. The wedge is the region open to a speeding-up observer. Inside the wedge, flux through infinity vanishes in both the Minkowski and Rindler frames. That holds even though the frame change is awkward at infinity. The paper settles a point that coordinate quirks had left murky.
arxiv-2605-26339: Preetam Sharma and Kacper Dobek's 2026 codec, QAM-W, quantizes language-model weights jointly in two dimensions instead of one coordinate at a time. Each row is normalized, rotated, paired into two-dimensional coordinates, and quantized against a single codebook, with activation-aware scaling. At five point five bits per weight, the activation-aware variant stays within zero point four percent of BF16 perplexity on every model, matching SmoothQuant quality at thirty-two percent fewer weight bits. Joint two-dimensional coding beats polar coding by two to fifteen points.
arxiv-2605-26739: Cignarale introduces the Deontic Action Model Logic, a system for reasoning about what agents must do in multi-agent settings. It builds on epistemic Action Model Logic and rates actions by how good and how likely their results are. An action counts as obligatory when it tops the expected deontic value among the agent's choices. He gives axioms for the logic, proves it sound and complete, and tries it on the Miners' Puzzle.
arxiv-2605-26839: Gravgaard, Kristensen, and Hančl prove positive lower bounds on the Hausdorff dimension of sets of reals given by infinite reciprocal sums with growth conditions on their terms. As a consequence, some irrational numbers from Erdős's 1976 construction are shown not to be Liouville numbers, numbers that are extremely well approximated by rationals. The bounds give new metric information about expressible sets defined by such series.
arxiv-2605-26939: Rogers and Briozzo show that a class of nonlinear moving boundary problems admits exact solutions. The problems come from a new extension of a two-component mKdV system, solved with a hybrid Ermakov-Ray-Reid and Painlevé II symmetry ansatz. The mKdV system itself arises from reducing a coupled nonlinear Schrödinger system with de Broglie-Bohm potential terms. The symmetry reduction thus turns a hard moving-boundary problem into one with exact solutions, linking the new system back to its nonlinear Schrödinger roots.
arxiv-2605-27039: Xiao and six co-authors present EnvMem, a controlled multi-turn benchmark for acoustic memory in large audio language models. While these models handle speech well, they struggle to retain non-speech sounds across turns. EnvMem probes failures at representation level, in latent embeddings, and at retrieval level, in attention allocation. Results point to representational trajectory drift as the key failure mode, with attention allocation playing only a limited role. The work offers a systematic framework for improving non-linguistic memory.
arxiv-2605-27239: Abdulmumin and co-authors study why agreement between annotators fades during a long labeling campaign. They built a Setswana sentiment set of 3565 tweets labeled by three native speakers in eight batches. Overall agreement looks excellent, yet batch scores fall by more than 32 points over time. The key driver is timing: tweets labeled within a minute agree almost perfectly, while tweets labeled over a day apart agree far less. Label mix-ups cluster at the negative-neutral border, and two labelers show drift toward autopilot labeling.
arxiv-2605-27439: Will Jack, Noah Lehman, Keller Maloney, and Sarah Xu audit tens of thousands of AI brand recommendation runs across five prominence tiers in 19 sectors. Top brands appear almost everywhere but win only a quarter to two fifths of slots reached, while mid-market brands mark the inflection point. The smallest brands face catastrophic invisibility, with about half never surfacing at all.
arxiv-2605-27739: Tolga Dimlioglu, Kristi Topollai, and Anna Choromanska show that worker disagreement in Local SGD exposes sharp directions in loss shape. The worker-average gap covariance reflects gradient noise and Hessian curvature, so gaps between workers trace bend-sensitive sharp directions. Worker-average gaps therefore give a cheap Hessian-free gauge of the dominant subspace, catching much of the gradient in that eigenspace.
arxiv-2605-28139: Lin and colleagues show compact speech recognition can be taught far more cheaply with a strong teacher. Their on-policy distillation recipe lifts a small audio-language model past supervised fine-tuning alone and past a same-size rival on four of five test sets. The gain comes on a hundred thousand hours of speech, a fraction of the largest rivals' audio budgets.
arxiv-2605-28239: Cao and colleagues teach image-labeling models to draft their own training labels where human labels run thin. Their Learning to Label loop starts from multimodal hints, then rewards picks of high-value pixel labels, tuning model and labels together. Label trust climbs step by step, beating rivals on standard phrase-grounding tests.
arxiv-2605-28339: Mohamedou Ould Haye and Anne Philippe study time series with long memory and nonstationarity, deriving joint limits for discrete Fourier transforms across a range of memory strengths. At the boundary case known as 1/f noise, logarithmic corrections keep the sample mean and variance limits meaningful, yielding chi-square-type distributions. They combine mean, variance, and low-frequency spectral measures into a test that distinguishes nonstationarity from long-memory stationarity without tuning parameters.
arxiv-2605-28739: Tirtharaj Dash presents BIRDNet, mining and encoding Boolean implication knowledge graphs as interpretable deep neural networks. Tabular data in knowledge-rich domains often hides Boolean implication links between feature pairs, mined with a sparse-exception binomial test. The mined typed graph becomes the connectivity of a layered network where each hidden unit stands for one mined rule for its two features. BIRDNet lands near 0.02 AUROC of the strongest dense rival using up to 95-fold fewer active parameters, and its first-layer rules match known biological signatures across cancer subtypes.
arxiv-2605-28839: Ali Holmov and three colleagues ask whether edits share a common mechanism. Despite fact-specific changes, ROME and MEMIT target the same weights critical to maintaining edits. To isolate this subset they train a compact binary mask over edited weights. The mask reverses 80 percent of training-set edits and over 70 percent of test-set edits, confirming diverse edits share structure. Injecting the mask drops success from 98 percent to 38 percent, showing this mechanism is necessary for success. Edits suppress rather than overwrite knowledge, so related facts fail to update.
arxiv-2605-28939: Lukas Ebner and colleagues track how entanglement evolves in holographic conformal theories after a quench, using mutual information between intervals. In the large-central-charge limit, mutual information jumps at critical times, forming six phases, each ruled by a different conformal block or geodesic layout. A D4 symmetry on the interval endpoints governs whether mutual information appears, breaking to a smaller subgroup at its onset. Spin-chain checks show finite-size effects soften them, though transitions in and out of mutual information stay non-analytic.
arxiv-2605-29239: Rajat Goswami and Safvan Palathingal study midpoint-fused arches and their structural bistability. Arranging several arches in a circle and fusing them at their midpoint yields a shape with two distinct, force-free stable states. Starting stress-free, the structure can invert into a stressed, toggled state reminiscent of an umbrella's ribs. The authors model a pinned-pinned setup under a mid-span load by minimizing total potential energy. Tests on two-arch and three-arch cases, checked against simulations and experiments, show close agreement.
arxiv-2605-29439: The maximal length of maximum distance separable codes built from elliptic curves is settled for its open cases by Haojie Chen and three colleagues. Earlier work bounded this length and reached the bound for odd dimensions over odd square fields. Even dimensions, non-square fields, and characteristic two remained open. For codes supported on rational points, they show the bound drops by one for even dimensions. Without that restriction they construct codes reaching the full bound, and they give exact maximal lengths for both parities of the governing count.
arxiv-2605-29639: Boyu Tan and colleagues built RTP-LLM, an inference engine built for speed in language-model deployment across Alibaba. It speeds loading with file-ordered input-output overlapping communication. A prefill-decode disaggregation design separates compute-heavy prefill from memory-bound decode, paired with cache management for reuse. Modular speculative decoding, adaptive cache quantization, and multi-level parallelism complete the design. Against leading engines, it loads models faster and cuts first-token latency by about a third. It more than triples cache reuse and improves throughput and batch latency.
arxiv-2605-29739: Arianna Armanetti and four colleagues model questionnaire answers as interacting items, not reflections of hidden traits. Past energy-based models handled only binary answers, two-way links, and approximate fits. The team infers three generalized-spin models for ordinal Likert-type answers, proving the likelihood fit concave and gauge invariance for two, fitted by stochastic gradient ascent. Across eleven psychometric and sociological datasets, the Blume-Emery-Griffiths model beat factor analysis and spin rivals, catching average-extremist styles. Only spin models capture the peaked factor histograms of polarizing questionnaires.
arxiv-2605-29839: Joris Kirchner and Ioannis Diamantis introduce the Topological Stability Index, a variance-based scalar for barcodes. Unlike persistent entropy, which uses only weights, the index captures spread across varied scales. The team proves its properties: scaling, invariance under lifetime shifts, and update rules for added or deleted bars. A second quantity, the Topological Signal Index, captures typical scale, and a normalized version links to Rényi entropy. Tests on synthetic sets and stochastic series show the index complementing entropy, staying calm under trends while reacting to random swings.
arxiv-2605-30139: Andronikos Paliathanasis introduces Cosmo-PINN, a physics-informed network that rebuilds the dark energy equation of state from late-time observations. Standard Gaussian process and neural rebuilds follow data but need not respect physics. Cosmo-PINN embeds constraints into its loss function so rebuilt quantities obey physical laws. Training uses DESI baryon acoustic oscillation data, cosmic chronometers and supernova compilations. The rebuilt equation of state crosses the phantom divide around redshift one half, matching the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder model, and hits the standard limit in the past for quintessence.
arxiv-2605-30339: Tingle Li and eight co-authors introduce FlatSounds, auditing the physical reasoning of video-to-audio models. It uses counterfactual pairs varying one factor, and single-video tests probing consistency. Evaluation reveals a trade-off: models lean more on captions than on the visual stream for physics and semantics. Captions improve physical and semantic accuracy, but degrade temporal alignment. Results highlight moving beyond audio quality toward learning physical processes from pixels. Physics-based metrics track human preference tests closely.
arxiv-2605-30439: Aideen Fay proves no Z/2-birational map links a very general complex symmetric Verra fourfold to projective 4-space. She uses the theory of atoms, from Katzarkov, Kontsevich, Pantev, and Yu, in the equivariant setting of Cavenaghi, Katzarkov, and Kontsevich. The result shows that a generic member of this symmetric family cannot be mapped to projective 4-space by a birational map respecting the twofold symmetry. The argument carries the involution through the theory of atoms. This places a sharp limit on symmetric birational models of Verra fourfolds.
arxiv-2605-30639: Jiang tackles a gap in embodied AI: reaching a target's area does not prove the agent found the right instance, since details like floral versus striped patterns demand close inspection. He formalizes Active Instance Verification: an agent picks viewpoints around a candidate to judge whether it matches a detailed description. His PInVerify benchmark offers thousands of episodes across many categories, with captures, six sectors, trap views, and unreachable sectors. The best multimodal baseline beats the embedding baseline, active viewpoint choice shows no gain, and a fine-tuned agent scores high.
arxiv-2605-30839: Khan, Lee, and Singh propose and analyze a new two-field form for Biot's consolidation model, with solid displacement and fluid pressure as the main unknowns. They first prove the new form is well-posed, then show an optimal control exists and is unique when fluid sources act as the control. They also prove prior error bounds for a fully discrete scheme using backward Euler time steps and a variational control approximation. A numeric test backs the scheme's performance.
arxiv-2605-30939: Wang and colleagues improve night road segmentation for self-driving cars, when standard methods fade badly. Many fusion methods let weak night camera features bleed into the fused view, ignoring how light changes sensor trust. Their IAF-Net adjusts camera and geometric fusion weights with illumination, and adds a brightness-tuned decoder to pick low-light features. They build two new test sets, night driving scenes and simulated varied weather, and report state-of-the-art night results.
arxiv-2605-31239: Amoukou, Mishra and Veloso fix split selection in online decision trees with anytime-valid inference. Hoeffding trees, the base learners of Adaptive Random Forests, test splits with fixed-sample bounds even though stopping rules depend on the data, voiding the guarantees and risking wrong splits. The new method controls false splits at any time, even on shifting streams, commits in finite time when a real advantage exists, and improves risk monotonically on stationary data. Tests show better performance with substantially smaller trees.
arxiv-2605-31539: Choudhary and team present a pipeline that predicts risk of postoperative pancreatic fistula from CT scans taken before surgery. This fistula is a serious complication after pancreatic resection, raising morbidity, hospital stay, and costs. The pipeline runs from pancreas segmentation to sorting, testing a lightweight 3D CNN baseline and two ResNet variants. It shows good results, offering a valuable tool and a benchmark for pancreas-specific CT classification.
arxiv-2606-00039:
Singh and co-authors examine how text-to-image models reproduce caste discrimination in this 2026 arXiv paper for a fairness and accountability conference. Prior work documented caste stereotypes in images but treated caste as a simple identity category, often a binary split. The authors study caste as a relation: how hierarchy and moral ordering operate between groups. Their audit combines algorithmic testing of generated images with discourse analysis, guided by a frame challenging Brahminical normativity, the assumption that upper-caste norms define the default.

In their corpus, prompts about people in particular places produced images where caste appeared outright and through an invisible order shaping cleanliness, dress, and setting. Bias thus outlived simple categorical representation. The gains are twofold: showing the mechanics of caste bias, and proposing an anti-caste approach to fairness efforts in AI. The authors argue that fixing representation counts will not undo the normative patterns.
arxiv-2606-00239:
Recabal and co-authors show how twin baths can push a quantum pair off the heat norm. A famed law, the Redfield form, tracks small systems tied loosely to baths. In its trimmed form, it keeps states sound and leads to Gibbs heat spread. Terms cut in that trim are most often brushed aside.

The team keeps those terms for two linked wave units, each with its own bath. Both baths share the same heat. When the units are damped at lopsided rates, end counts stray far from Gibbs spread. A flow of kicks, born of bath-made links twixt near-tied levels, drives the stray. They map when Gibbs spread comes back. They also hint at lab signs that could spot the effect.
arxiv-2606-00439:
Venkatesh and co-authors build a world model that can be asked odds on any part of a scene. To grasp things, a model must learn how parts form wholes and push each other. Past forms can not state odds for one trait given the rest. Their class of chance-based world models can.

Such models train well through plain line-by-line fits, they show. From raw clips, rich grasp of things springs up in the model. It rolls out more than one sound future for a scene. Shared move traits across those futures bare things and their joint parts. Known things can then be steered in 3D space in the model. Links twixt things can be read off for tasks like a block-stack game.
arxiv-2606-00539:
Kong and co-authors guard low-grade chat model training with a live risk gauge. Cheap low-grade paths can spark brief math risks at a few steps. Those sparks can spoil a long train run in a flash. Their gauge, GNMR, tracks slope size next to its past mean.

Each fix-able unit gets a risk mark from that gauge in real time. A twin gauge flags sharp jumps in a short span. Marks map to bounded fix acts under a hard cap and brief lock. Form, core math, and back-end plan stay as they were. Tests span stress runs, a DeepSeek-style run, and a LLaMA fine-tune. Risk acts stay sparse and capped while grade holds high.
arxiv-2606-00639:
Frolkina solves how the shadows of a tight set shift under a typical bend of its space. Her sets are compact, shut and bound in flat space of N dims. Casts of such a set onto flat walls form the quarry. A 1947 build by Borsuk gave a Cantor set with vast casts.

That set's cast on any wall one dim down holds a full ball. A yet stronger form can grow from any Cantor set by a tiny space sway. Frolkina asks what casts look like for a typical sway or bend. Typical is read in the Baire sense in her work. She solves that ask in full for both sway types. New marks for tame and wild Cantor sets fall out of the solve.
arxiv-2606-00739:
Cheng, Lin, and Yang ask how to curb false output from language models in this 2026 paper. Models can state false claims even when the right answer sits in their own weights. Extra compute at run time can draw that knowledge out. But the best tricks need a trained checker.

The team maps a grid of four scores and three ways to decode. Scores rate each draft answer, and decoders pick or build the final one. They test each cell on the MATH500 set with two Qwen3-1.7B models. One score, self-verification, has the model judge its own answer. It works well in most cells, helped by a training-free prompt trick. Yet no score wins on its own, they find. Its worth turns on the decoder paired with it and on the skill of the base model. Score and decoder must be picked as a pair.
arxiv-2606-01039:
Zhao and co-authors fix a quiet bias in how students learn from teachers in this 2026 paper. On policy distillation trains a student on its own rollouts, scored against a teacher. The reward hangs on the student's own likelihoods. For stability, most work stops the gradient through part of that score. The team asks if that stop is sound.

They frame the task with f-divergence between student and teacher. The math says the stop gradient habit biases both the reward estimate and its gradient, for general divergence choices. Their fix, OPD+, removes the bias and keeps the freedom to pick a divergence. The classic KL version is one special case. On math reasoning and tool use benchmarks, OPD+ beats the KL baseline, they report. The paper is a caution and a repair kit for a widely copied training trick.
arxiv-2606-01139:
Liu and co-authors improve agent skills by revising them against real execution in this 2026 paper. Skills are procedural artifacts that let agents run workflows and recover from failures. Self evolving methods refine skills from past runs. In cold starts, only one flawed skill exists, written by an expert or spat out in one model pass. One shot skills can read well yet act weak.

Their framework, SkillRevise, repairs such skills in a loop. It diagnoses defects from execution evidence. It pulls repair principles from a general memory store. Edits are anchored in what execution showed, then candidates are re-run and scored. The best seen skill is kept within the revision budget. Across three main benchmarks, two domain studies, and six models, the method beats one shot baselines by a wide mark. Success rises from 36.05 percent to 61.63 percent on the SkillsBench tests.
arxiv-2606-01239:
De Magistris, Romano, and Maturo group survival data by risk over time. Most tools group by the chance of survival to a date. They shift focus to instant risk, the hazard rate. Smooth log-hazard curves act as functional objects here. A principal component step cuts each curve to key scores. A 95% variance rule picks how many scores to keep. Clusters then form on those raw scores.

Tests cover hard cases like crossing hazards and outliers. Uneven group sizes also appear in the tests. Two real clinic sets ground the work. One tracks German breast cancer cases. One tracks a liver disease cohort. The method gives a clear view of how risk shifts over time.
arxiv-2606-01539:
Yin and co-authors estimate rare-event risk in long health records, faster. Causal effects of time-varying treatments on survival are hard to estimate. Large observational studies make the computing heavy. Rare outcomes at each time point add class imbalance. That imbalance destabilizes logistic models and slows convergence. G-formula tools like the ICE estimator are principled but costly. Bootstrap variance estimation drives much of that cost. Their fix is a subsampling and reweighting strategy.

The strategy applies to a range of existing estimators. It cuts computing burden while preserving consistency. Stability in rare-outcome settings improves as well. Simulations test the method across settings. A large EHR cohort study validates it in practice. That study links social factors to suicide risk over time.
arxiv-2606-01739:
Katz, Kuhlemann, and Kutateladze document Marx's shifting view of infinitesimals. Marx first took a favorable stance on infinitesimals. That view rested on his study of Sauri's textbook. Later, under Boucharlat's textbook, he reversed to an unfavorable stance. He then called belief in infinitesimals a chimera. Engels, by contrast, endorsed infinitesimals in his writings. The contrast between the two thinkers is a focus here. Scholar Carchedi casts Marx as differentiating with a dialectician's eyes. That reading misses Engels' endorsement, they note.

Struik linked Marx to Abraham Robinson's nonstandard analysis. The link runs through Fermat's adequality technique, they argue. Emil Gumbel was the first editor of Marx's math manuscripts. That fact is missing from the Soviet editions, they observe.
arxiv-2606-02139:
Lentfert and co-authors study how spin waves that travel through a thin magnetic film can be made stronger . The film is yttrium iron garnet, cut into tiny waveguides at the nanoscale, and the method is parametric amplification. As the field of magnonics moves toward new kinds of computing, ways to boost spin waves while keeping their phase intact grow more important. Local flaws in the film turn out to play a key role in how the boosting works.

Detailed simulations show an effect that was not expected in large pump regions, where only adiabatic amplification should occur. Scattering centers in those regions supply extra linear momentum, and that momentum opens the door to the non-adiabatic form of amplification. The coherence of the process is not harmed by the scattering, and waves that travel together raise the effective gain. Lab measurements confirm what the simulations predict.
arxiv-2606-02339:
Nielen and co-authors study a failure that hits medical image models when data shifts. Models adapt at test time by lowering entropy, a measure of doubt. That habit can end in collapse, where all outputs fall into one class. The authors trace the cause to a skew they call prediction bias.

Under shift, clusters of like cases merge in the model's feature space. The class boundary stays fixed, so some classes gain and others fade. Entropy training then tightens the wrong clusters. The team proposes DSBR, a fix that balances each predicted class in the loss. Tests span four medical image sets plus ImageNet-C. The authors report that DSBR keeps adaptation stable. It blocks collapse and matches or beats top rival methods. The fix runs at test time only.
arxiv-2606-02439:
Alanis-Cantú and Ortiz-Ambriz study a model system called artificial colloidal ice. Tiny particles sit on a lattice and feel mutual push and pull. Frustration keeps them from settling at once. The setup lets researchers watch every particle in real time. A flat magnetic field now changes the game. It makes the particle links anisotropic, or direction-dependent.

The new regime has a clean ground state. It is a checkerboard of fully charged vertices. Yet Brownian dynamics simulations never reach it. The system freezes in disordered metastable states instead. No quenched disorder is needed for this freeze. The cause is local. The field raises the energy barrier for a particle to cross. That barrier locks particles into place. The result shows how a field can drive a system into a frozen state.
arxiv-2606-02739:
Li and co-authors unify audio tokenization for both understanding and generation. Audio tokenizers bridge continuous sound and audio language models. Reconstruction codecs keep acoustic fidelity but lack semantics. Semantic tokenizers split into separate streams, causing redundancy or misalignment. EntangleCodec learns caption-aligned representations before quantization. Captions carry more than transcripts. They encode content, speaker identity, emotion, prosody, and scene.

A single compact token stream results. A flow-matching diffusion decoder rebuilds high-quality audio from it. Speech, music, and general audio are all covered. Reconstruction rivals specialized codecs. Understanding beats all codec-based baselines, by up to 7.4 percent on MMAR. Text-to-speech and text-to-audio generation both work in the same frame. A 0.6 billion parameter model surpasses continuous-representation models over 13 billion parameters. At 8 billion parameters, new state-of-the-art results appear. Representation quality, the authors argue, rivals model scale.
arxiv-2606-03339:
Bason and Valandro study boundary conditions for circular quiver gauge theories in string theory. The theories are four-dimensional with N=2 supersymmetry, built from D4-branes hung between NS5-branes on a circle. The boundary conditions at stake keep half of the supersymmetry. They arise when the D4-branes end on a boundary D6-brane sent to infinity.

A single-pole ansatz turns the BPS equations into a constrained algebraic problem. A winding phenomenon shows up that has no analogue for linear quivers. Several cases are solved in closed form. A brane-duality argument points to the S-dual of the pure Neumann boundary condition inside this class. The residual gauge symmetry can be discrete only under a condition set by tracelessness. Then it is the center group Z_N. Solutions with that trait exist for every N and K, the authors show.
arxiv-2606-03739:
Agyemang and co-authors cut token waste in language model pipelines with Entropy Gate. Pipelines burn budget on repeated context, verbose replies, and boilerplate. Entropy Gate applies entropy quenching, a process borrowed from thermodynamics. Low-energy tokens freeze out step by step while meaning stays intact. Each token gets an information energy from statistical, structural, and positional factors.

A cooling schedule lowers the temperature over time. Tokens whose survival chance falls below a threshold are removed. A fidelity gate halts compression if weighted similarity drops too low. Theory shows the selection rule maximizes expected meaning preserved. Achievable compression nears the information-theoretic limit. A heuristic phase reaches 40 to 60 percent compression across five prompt types. Similarity stays above 0.80. Deduplication of repeated blocks saves far more. Combined with external memory, agentic workloads shrink by up to 96 percent. The tool is stateless and deploys as a proxy.
arxiv-2606-03839:
Han and co-authors condense text-attributed graphs while keeping training accuracy high. Such graphs pair each node with a text description. Models train a graph network and a language model jointly, at high cost. Condensation shrinks the graph before training starts. Their method, TAGSAM, compresses both texts and topology.

For texts, a selection step merges representative chunks from related descriptions. It maximizes mutual information while doing so. For topology, matching training trajectories suffers from high variance. Attribute similarity matching steadies it by aligning stable similarity matrices. Six state-of-the-art baselines face TAGSAM in tests. At equal compressed size, accuracy tops the best rival by about five points on average. Even at one percent of the original size, training accuracy stays competitive. Code is public for graph learning teams.
arxiv-2606-04239:
Nilay Kant designs a state observer in 2026, a tool that infers a system's hidden state from its outputs. His design carries a hard promise: the output error must never exceed a bound fixed in advance.

Classic observers, such as the Luenberger design, promise only that errors shrink over time. Kant's design keeps the error inside a set tube from the start. The proof uses a Lyapunov function, the standard energy-like check for stability. Tests in simulation showed the bound held even under strong disturbances. The trade-off is a more complex design step. For safety-critical systems, the authors argue, a bound that holds at every moment beats one that holds only in the limit.
arxiv-2606-04339:
Cathy Liu presents in 2026 a design pipeline for epilepsy brain stimulation that optimizes for the worst-off virtual patient rather than the average one. A protocol that helps on average can still fail the patient whose network tolerates stimulation least, and that failure is the clinically important one.

The pipeline mines the published literature for hypotheses, simulates a standard virtual brain epilepsy model across sampled patients, and lets a language-model-guided optimizer search stimulation settings against a worst-case objective. Tuning internal model parameters improved the worst case by about forty percent. The clinical-style external stimulation search, though, gained under two percent, and a twenty-patient cohort showed no overall benefit despite individual responders. Liu frames the work strictly as in silico proof of concept.
arxiv-2606-04439:
Fu, Luo, and Ni settle a question in Ramsey theory, in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. The authors study graphs, which are networks of points joined by edges. The edges are colored with several colors. A size Ramsey minimal graph is a smallest graph that forces a one-color copy of a target pattern. This holds no matter how its edges are colored. Their targets are uniform star forests. These are sets of separate star shapes, each with the same number of edges.

Earlier work in 1978 and 2025 described the minimal graphs for these targets in the basic setting. Fu and colleagues now give a complete description for the multicolor case. In that case, edges may use many colors at once. They pin down exactly which graphs reach the minimum size. Those graphs still force a star forest in a single color.
arxiv-2606-04539:
Singh, Goswami, and Sahoo study how heat, charge, and particle flows influence each other inside dense quark matter, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. In coupled transport, a temperature gradient can drive particle diffusion. This is the Soret effect. A chemical potential gradient can drive heat flow. This is the Dufour effect. The authors compute the coefficients of these cross-effects across the phase diagram of strong-force matter.

They work within the 2+1 flavor Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model. This is a standard model of quark interactions. They solve the relativistic Boltzmann transport equation. They use a relaxation time approximation and temperature-dependent cross sections. They track the scaled Soret and Dufour coefficients against temperature and quark chemical potential. The coefficients prove sensitive to the chiral phase transition. That is the point where quark matter changes character. The work gives the first systematic map of cross-coupled transport in dense quark matter.
arxiv-2606-04839:
Boeche and colleagues give the open star cluster NGC 2509 its first thorough characterization, in a 2026 arXiv astronomy paper. The cluster is distant, about two and a half kiloparsecs away, little studied, and of imprecisely known age. Using the FLAMES spectrograph on the Very Large Telescope, the team observed 132 stars, at moderate and high resolution.

They provide parameters and, for the first time, abundances of 21 species. The cluster's average radial velocity is 58.6 kilometers per second, its metallicity mildly supersolar, and its age is about 1.26 billion years. Its narrow turnoff is explained by stellar rotation: rotational velocities cluster around 80 kilometers per second with little dispersion, and its chemistry follows normal thin-disk trends.
arxiv-2606-05139:
Luca Thale-Bombien, Jan Ewald, Ralf König, and Aaron Klein introduce BBOmix in this 2026 arXiv paper, a tabular benchmark for tuning unsupervised representation learning on omics data. Modern sequencing produces large omics datasets, and autoencoders are widely used to compress them into useful representations. Autoencoders are highly sensitive to architecture and hyperparameters, though. The usual tuning signal, reconstruction loss, may poorly reflect downstream usefulness, while exhaustive tuning is expensive.

BBOmix is the first open-source tabular benchmark for this setting, holding 105,000 stored evaluations across four autoencoder designs and seven omics data types drawn from the TCGA and SCHC datasets. Because every run is already tabulated, new tuning methods can be compared cheaply. The authors quantify how reconstruction loss tracks downstream task performance. They also evaluate single-fidelity, multi-fidelity, and transfer learning tuning methods, establishing a rigorous baseline for future work.
arxiv-2606-05239:
Hongfan Gao, Wangmeng Shen, Bin Yang, and Jilin Hu propose HyFAD in this 2026 arXiv paper, a hybrid time-frequency diffusion model for filling in missing values in time series. Diffusion models generate data by removing noise, and they perform strongly on time series, but current versions struggle with frequency-sensitive denoising and high-frequency detail. HyFAD couples two diffusion processes on the standard DDPM framework.

The reverse denoising runs from the time domain to the frequency domain, giving a coarse-to-fine generation. The time-domain process captures low-frequency global trends first, and the frequency-domain process then refines the high-frequency spectral components. A frequency-aware step embedding exploits the relationship between diffusion steps and spectral components, supplying step-dependent spectral guidance for band-wise reconstruction. Across multiple benchmark datasets for imputation, HyFAD achieved the best performance, and the authors release the source code.
arxiv-2606-05739:
Minoru Kishi and co-authors ask whether speech models judge voice likeness as people do in a 2026 arXiv paper. Listeners grade how similar two voices sound on a smooth scale. Speech foundation models instead embed each voice as numbers, and distance stands in for likeness. Whether that distance tracks human judgment was unknown. The team compared model distances against human similarity scores at scale.

More than forty models entered the comparison. Their embeddings were scored against the same human ratings. The study then varied model design choices to find what drives agreement. Architecture and training factors were weighed for their effect on human-like spacing. Findings point to which configurations yield embeddings that mirror perception. The authors offer the results as guidance for building speech models whose voice space feels human. Such grounding matters for search, casting, and voice conversion tools.
arxiv-2606-06139:
Ilyass Taouil and colleagues introduce MotionDisco in this 2026 arXiv paper on humanoid robotics. Loco-manipulation means a robot walks and handles objects at the same time, using its whole body. Long tasks are hard to design by hand because each new contact with an object multiplies the possible motion sequences. MotionDisco discovers such motions from scratch, without teleoperation by a human or retargeting of recorded human movement.

The system couples a language-model-guided evolutionary search over contact sequences with a kinodynamic optimizer, which checks both geometry and physical forces. A pruning stage quickly discards plans that cannot work, and feedback from failed plans guides the next round of search. Across eight long-horizon tasks, the search beat a single-call state-of-the-art language model on both success and motion cost. Tracking policies trained on the discovered motions then ran on a real humanoid robot.
arxiv-2606-06539:
Yucheng Chen stress tests a backpropagation alternative and finds its ceiling in this 2026 arXiv paper. Forward Forward learning, proposed by Hinton, trains each layer locally on a goodness score instead of sending gradients backward through the whole network. Recent results on small thirty two pixel benchmarks made it look nearly competitive. Chen built DTG FF, with dynamic temperature goodness, decoupled normalization, and multi layer fusion, pushing the family to its best real data results.

Then he used it as an audit instrument. On identical backbones, a matched backpropagation baseline beat it by two point four points on CIFAR 10. On CIFAR 100 the margin was five point nine three points, and the gap grows with class count. At full resolution it managed only forty nine point four percent, far below typical backpropagation. On synthetic tasks the ranking reversed. Synthetic benchmarks, he concludes, flatter layer local training in ways real images do not.
arxiv-2606-06739:
Population geneticists model how gene variants drift over time with a diffusion, a smooth random wandering of variant frequencies. Ethier revisits the classic infinitely many neutral alleles model in this 2026 arXiv paper, a short note in mathematical genetics. The model imagines endless possible variants, none favored by selection, with new ones arriving by mutation at a steady rate.

The note connects two versions of the model. In the labeled version, variants carry names, and the process is a Fleming-Viot process spread over a space of types. In the unlabeled version, only the ranked shares of the variants matter. Ethier derives the transition function, the rule giving the odds of each future state, for the unlabeled model from the labeled one, following the form Zhou published in 2015. His route slightly simplifies the earlier derivation by Feng, tightening a small but foundational piece of the theory.
arxiv-2606-07239:
Franke and co-authors introduce Morph, a generative model that designs molecules without fixing their size in advance, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most molecule generators built on diffusion or flow methods must decide the atom count before generation starts. That is limiting because many useful properties, such as solubility, depend strongly on size. Morph instead inserts and deletes atoms during generation, letting size and structure evolve together toward target properties.

The method pairs graphs of different sizes using unbalanced optimal transport, a matching technique that tolerates unequal totals. On a standard drug-like benchmark, Morph's molecules showed near-perfect atom stability and full uniqueness across 10,000 samples per run. Molecular stability lagged the best fixed-size rival, a trade-off the authors acknowledge. The clear win was flexibility: Morph generated sensibly in size regimes where fixed-size models fail, and it could decorate existing molecular scaffolds.
arxiv-2606-07539:
Neumann, Sargeant, and Singh question whether governing AI through its prompts can work, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Generative systems are steered by language instructions at every level, from system prompts to developer specs, and stakeholders treat those texts as governance tools encoding constraints and compliance rules. Policymakers now treat system prompts as intervention points, assuming they control behavior. The authors examine it from two directions, looking at how researchers discuss them and how policy documents deploy them.

Their analysis probes whether they behave consistently and predictably across contexts and under adversarial pressure, the properties a governance tool needs. If a system prompt's effect varies with phrasing, task, or attack, then regulations written against it rest on sand. The paper works through implications for accountability: who is responsible when an instruction fails to constrain a model. It warns regulators not to treat prompt inspection as the same as auditing behavior.
arxiv-2606-07639:
Wang and a team present a video model built for live interaction rather than after-the-fact answers, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Real-time understanding means perceiving frames while replying, revising answers as evidence arrives, and staying silent when nothing needs saying. Their claim is that perception must never be blocked by generation. The architecture feeds features through cross-attention instead of inserting them into the text sequence, so seeing and speaking proceed on non-blocking pathways.

A data pipeline converts video captions into real-time question-answer material revised to match what has been perceived so far, and an offline model is specialized on it. The authors prioritize feasibility over leaderboard performance and report that the model trails a 7-billion-parameter baseline, which they attribute to data and scale rather than architecture. It stayed competitive on video tasks and robust on the temporal reasoning that live use demands.
arxiv-2606-07739:
Fuyuto, Manzari, and Murayama propose hunting axion-like particles in old collider data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Axion-like particles are hypothetical light particles that could solve puzzles the Standard Model leaves open, including the strong CP problem. The team targets particles that couple to photons and weigh a few GeV, a range poorly covered by other searches.

Their idea uses ultra-peripheral collisions of gold nuclei at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider, where the nuclei miss each other but their photon clouds collide. Two photons can fuse into an axion-like particle that decays back into two photons, and heavy nuclei boost this rate enormously. Simulating the existing PHENIX dataset, the authors find sensitivity to masses between about two and five GeV at couplings down to a few ten-thousandths per GeV. That region is previously unexplored, and larger datasets would extend the reach further.
arxiv-2606-07839:
Lamperski bounds the spectral gaps of non-reversible Markov chains in this 2026 arXiv paper, motivated by temporal difference learning. Those learning algorithms rely on a Markov chain whose eigenvalues decide whether learning settles or blows up. Reversible chains are well understood, but the chains arising in learning are typically non-reversible, and their gaps are harder to control.

Lamperski generalises the known sufficient conditions for stability and bounds the relevant values through the chain's Dirichlet spectral gap. One clean result is that a positive absolute gap forces a positive Dirichlet gap. For discrete-time linear Gaussian systems, he gives fully explicit bounds for both gaps. He also builds a cautionary example: a chain that converges fast from every start, in the uniform geometric sense, yet has a Dirichlet gap of exactly zero. The example warns that some stability intuitions fail without reversibility, and the bounds give practitioners usable checks.
arxiv-2606-08039:
Manan Tayal releases an open-source simulator for training swarms of tiny drones, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Aerial robotics develops control algorithms and reinforcement learning policies in simulation, but existing quadcopter environments trade off physical fidelity, multi-agent support, and the speed modern training pipelines need. MuJoCo-Drones-Gym, built on the MuJoCo physics engine and compatible with the Gymnasium interface, targets all three.

The environment supports any number of Bitcraze Crazyflie nano-quadcopters. Users can swap the physics model, from rigid-body simulation to lighter dynamics with optional ground effect, blade drag, and downwash. Actions range from raw motor speeds to waypoint commands, and observations from state vectors to camera images. A multi-agent wrapper makes it a drop-in reinforcement learning environment. Seven bundled tasks, hovering, velocity tracking, waypoint navigation, formation flight, and gate racing among them, demonstrate the interface's breadth for single and swarm research.
arxiv-2606-08339:
Xinye Chen, Hilaire, and Jézéquel present a tool that finds the lowest safe number precision for a program, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reduced-precision math can improve speed, memory use, and energy use, provided accuracy survives. Their work goes beyond standard formats. It allows custom floating-point formats, with user-defined sizes for the exponent and the significand, the two parts of such a number. This framework can emulate emerging low-precision formats and explore non-standard setups.

The method, implemented in the PROMISE autotuning tool, combines numerical validation with a structured search. The search generates program variants that meet user-defined accuracy requirements. Because exploring many variants is costly, a containerized framework runs setups in parallel. The tests cover numerical programs including linear solvers and Rodinia applications. Custom precisions open savings that fixed choices miss.
arxiv-2606-08739:
Jamie Portsmouth, Raab, Belcour, and Francis Liu make rendered materials bounce light back the way safety gear does, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Retroreflective materials, such as road signs and safety clothing, return light toward its source rather than scattering it. Physically based rendering models surfaces with microfacet models, which treat a surface as a field of tiny mirrors. Standard models do not retroreflect. Their Minimal Retroreflective Microfacet model turns any microfacet shading model into a retroreflective one by a single substitution. Replace the view direction with its reflection about the surface normal.

Built on the published back-vector formulation, the change requires only minimal code edits. It has been adopted in the OpenPBR and MaterialX material standards. The authors prove the model is reciprocal and conserves energy, under a reflection-symmetric normal distribution. They validate the model against measured retroreflective material data.
arxiv-2606-08839:
Koide and Nicacio generalize Brownian motion theory and test whether heat flows through it sensibly, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Brownian motion models particles jostled by their surroundings, with noise and friction usually added only to the momentum equation. Their model adds such terms to the position equation too, a change needed for consistency with the quantum GKSL equation. Because the usual heat-current definition breaks down here, they derive a new formula from stochastic energetics.

The steady-state heat flow they obtain obeys Fourier's law, the rule that heat current grows in proportion to the temperature gradient. The model also produces thermal boundary resistance, like Kapitza resistance at interfaces. Numerically, position and momentum trace continuous but nowhere-smooth paths, unlike the standard model. When the particle interaction switches on, an instant heat flow appears, its direction fixed by whether the interaction attracts or repels.
arxiv-2606-09139:
Zibin Liu and colleagues recover a camera's pose and velocity from an event camera's sparse stream, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Event cameras take no pictures; pixels fire on brightness changes, giving microsecond timing for fast motion. Earlier geometric methods mostly estimated velocity. Absolute pose matters just as much for navigation and augmented reality, and joint recovery was open.

The framework exploits scene lines and the events they trigger. Two constraints do the work: a line is orthogonal to its event plane's normal, and each event is collinear with the projected line. From these come linear and polynomial pose solvers, the latter globally optimal for rotation, plus solvers for angular and linear velocity. Only 3 event-line correspondences suffice for the 6-degree-of-freedom pose or velocities. Simulation and real-world tests gave state-of-the-art accuracy at better efficiency, and the demo code is public.
arxiv-2606-09339:
Rui-Chun Xiao and his co-authors work out the symmetry rules governing Raman scattering in magnetic materials in this 2026 arXiv paper. Raman spectroscopy shines light on a material and reads the scattered colours to reveal vibrations and magnetic excitations. In magnetically ordered samples, time-reversal symmetry complicates the Raman tensor, the mathematical object that encodes which signals are allowed, and earlier treatments left puzzles unresolved.

Instead of the usual approach, the authors impose the constraints through the Onsager reciprocity relation, a fundamental symmetry of microscopic dynamics. With a direct-product representation method, they generate Raman tensor tables for all magnetic point groups and a complete account of the selection rules. Their results match earlier experiments well. They also resolve a standing puzzle in Raman readings of the layered magnet CrSBr.
arxiv-2606-09939:
Morgan Jones extends a basic measure of quantum similarity into settings where usual geometry breaks down, in a 2026 arXiv paper on mathematical physics. Fidelity measures how much two quantum states overlap, and standard theory defines it for density operators, the matrices that describe quantum states, in ordinary Euclidean spaces. Krein spaces instead carry an indefinite metric, a distance rule that can return negative values, governed by a symmetry operator called J.

Working with J-states, the Krein-space version of quantum states, Jones defines an analogous notion of measurement for them. He shows that a fidelity notion still holds in this setting and that a counterpart of the Fuchs-Caves measurement result, a theorem about optimal state discrimination, also survives. He then extends the definition to U-quantum states on S-spaces, a further generalization. The same geometric motivation, tied to geometric means of operators, holds across all three settings.
arxiv-2606-10339:
Bridges provides a constructive version of a cornerstone theorem of optimization theory, in a 2026 arXiv paper on math logic and analysis. Ekeland's variational principle says that a suitable function on a complete metric space nearly attains its lowest value at a point that exactly minimizes a slightly perturbed version of the function. Constructive mathematics demands proofs that, in principle, compute their conclusions, and many classical theorems need restating there.

Building on early results about lower sections of real-valued functions on metric spaces, Bridges supplies a constructive twin of Ekeland's theorem on the approximate minimizing of real-valued functions. The constructive version carefully states what can be located and pinned down, avoiding appeals to excluded middle or dependent choice. Such work matters beyond the basics: variational principles underlie proofs across optimization, control theory, and economics, and knowing which parts survive constructively clears up their practical content.
arxiv-2606-10439:
Lin and his team improve multilingual speech recognition built on large language models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on speech technology. Their projector-based framework connects an audio encoder to a language model through a learned projector. Two components do the heavy lifting: a mixture-of-experts architecture, where specialized sub-networks handle different inputs, improves cross-lingual adaptability. A continuous integrate-and-fire mechanism performs dynamic downsampling that aligns speech frames with text tokens.

Dynamic downsampling matters because languages and speaking rates vary widely, so a fixed compression of the audio stream wastes capacity on some inputs and starves others. Mixture-of-experts routing lets the model allocate specialized capacity to language-specific patterns without growing total active computation proportionally. The authors present the method as a step toward more accurate, robust, and generalizable language-model-based recognition across many languages.
arxiv-2606-10539:
Belhadjoudja designs controllers for a class of flow-like systems in this 2026 arXiv paper in control theory. The systems are coupled first-order hyperbolic partial differential equations, describing quantities transported through space, as in traffic or pipelines. They live in several space dimensions, where the backstepping method for boundary control was long confined to one dimension. The paper treats velocity fields that are collinear: every field points along one common direction, differing only in speed and sign.

A change of variables built on characteristic curves, the paths along which information travels, converts the system into a family of one-dimensional systems. A backstepping controller is designed for each independently. Provided travel times along characteristics stay bounded, the system is stabilised in finite time. The collinearity assumption is restrictive, and the work is framed as a first step toward the general case.
arxiv-2606-10739:
Chanu and colleagues report an X-ray line from a neutron star binary in this 2026 arXiv paper. GRS 1747-312, in the cluster Terzan 6, was observed 40 kiloseconds by AstroSat during the decay of its 2017 outburst. Fitting the spectrum with Comptonisation, disc reflection, and plasma accounts for most features, including a broad iron line near 6.4 kiloelectronvolts. But a line appears near 4.19 kiloelectronvolts, unexplained by standard components.

The proposal: it is the iron line again, reflected off the neutron star's surface, dragged down by gravity. Shifting the iron line from its rest energy to the observed one needs a redshift of about 0.6, matching a non-spinning star of 1.4 solar masses and ten-kilometre radius. If confirmed, the line would measure gravitational redshift and constrain the mass-to-radius ratio, hence the equation of state of dense matter. Caution: a neighbouring source could contaminate the spectrum, so the detection stays potential.
arxiv-2606-10939:
An and colleagues slim down a detector of hidden messages in images in this 2026 arXiv paper. Steganalysis spots information embedded in pictures, and the residual Transformer PENet detects it well but costs too much for small devices. PENet+ keeps the attention design and streamlines the classifier instead, narrows the filter front end, and swaps in a MobileNetV2-style backbone.

A balanced front end of 31 high-pass filters, 16 Gabor and 15 SRM, matches or beats heavier setups. Against the PENet baseline on ALASKA2 images, PENet+ cuts parameters by up to 45.5 percent and floating-point work by about 97 percent, with negligible accuracy loss. Swapping ReLU for PReLU also helps, since it keeps the faint negative responses where stego traces hide.
arxiv-2606-11039:
Climescu, for the SHiP Collaboration, presents a new CERN experiment in this 2026 arXiv paper. SHiP, the Search for Hidden Particles, is a beam dump approved in 2024 for the SPS's ECN3 hall. Protons slam into a target, and detectors watch for feebly interacting particles that standard searches miss. The target mass range runs from about 100 megaelectronvolts to a few gigaelectronvolts.

Over some fifteen years the facility will deliver six times ten to the twentieth protons on target. The setup targets heavy neutral leptons, dark photons, dark scalars, axion-like particles, and light dark matter, with leading sensitivity across most such models. The intense neutrino flux also enables roughly a thousand tau-neutrino events per year.
arxiv-2606-11139:
Dong, Ouyang, and Wei settle a family of extremal combinatorics problems in a 2026 arXiv paper.
