The classic oddtown and eventown problems bound how large a family of subsets of an n-element set can be. Set sizes and intersection sizes must obey parity rules, odd or even. The authors generalize: fix a binary pattern for every intersection level, up to k sets at a time. An alpha-town is a family whose every i-wise intersection has the prescribed parity.

They determine the sharp asymptotics, the exact growth rate, of the maximum family size for every pattern, answering questions of Johnston and O'Neill and of Wei, Zhang, and Ge. They also study a symmetric variant, where the parity condition uses intersection size plus union size. The results complete a picture begun by Berlekamp and Graver, whose sharp bounds for the original problems modeled this line of restricted-intersection work.
arxiv-2606-11339:
Sarkar, Raghuvanshi, Chakrabarti, and Baranwal study distributed optimization under finite-bit communication in a 2026 arXiv paper. Agents optimize together using stochastic gradients, communicating through random unbiased quantization. They propose q-PDGD, a quantized primal-dual method, and analyze it under relaxed global geometry.

Under the restricted secant inequality, constant steps contract linearly to a small region set by gradient noise, rounding distortion, and connectivity. A diminishing step size achieves an order one-over-k rate without a shared minimizer. Under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality, they obtain the same linear-to-neighborhood result in the same setting. Their rates match the best-known central ones. The point: finite bits and noise need not destroy fast convergence if the relaxed setting still holds across the network.
arxiv-2606-11639:
Catherine Bao, Maneesha Rani Saha and Neal Patwari test speech recognition for demographic bias in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most bias studies examine systems that output ordinary spelling. This study looks at phoneme-based systems, which transcribe speech in the International Phonetic Alphabet, a symbol set for sounds across all languages. Such systems increasingly support multilingual and low-resource language tools.

The authors evaluate two open-source systems, WhisperIPA and ZIPA, on multilingual collections and English collections labelled by speaker traits. They score output with phoneme error rate, and with a new Soft version that forgives substitutions between similar sounds. Performance varies across languages and across groups defined by gender, accent, ethnicity and age. The disparities persist even under the forgiving metric, so they are not explained by near-miss sound choices. The authors argue the findings should guide fairer, more robust phoneme-based recognition.
arxiv-2606-11739:
Evgeny Gorelik leads a team releasing a dataset for watching inside buses in this 2026 arXiv paper. In-cabin monitoring tracks who is inside a vehicle, where they sit and how they move. It supports passenger counting, boarding checks and emergency detection. Cabins are crowded and cluttered, and existing datasets usually offer one camera view.

The team fitted a digitised German city bus with four inward-facing cameras recording colour and depth, plus a rotating LiDAR, a laser scanner measuring distances. The dataset holds over nine thousand synchronised, annotated samples. An automatic labelling pipeline produces three-dimensional pose estimates and oriented boxes for occupants. Benchmarks of representative multi-view detection models are provided as baselines. The authors note the automatic labelling can still merge or split identities. The dataset and its tools are openly released for other teams to use and build on.
arxiv-2606-11839:
Kacper Darowski, Sebastian N Peters and Lukas Lautenschlager audit the cybersecurity of Europe's rail signalling standard in this 2026 arXiv paper. The European Rail Traffic Management System unifies train control across the EU and enables automatic operation, but security was an afterthought in its design. Which threats matter most had never been systematically ranked.

The authors translate the specification documents into an abstract system model, then estimate risks with a structured framework across current and future configurations. The verdict is concerning. Legacy components, especially EuroBalise track beacons and the GSM-R radio system, are the primary source of risk. Their weaknesses persist even in deployments with optional safety measures and in planned future versions. Jamming and denial-of-service attacks rank among the highest risks. The single biggest improvement identified is fully transitioning to the second level of the European Train Control System, paired with the next-generation railway radio.
arxiv-2606-12239:
Mnich and co-authors show that stacking switches a carbon sheet between two spin regimes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The stack wraps graphene between tantalum disulfide monolayers in a charge density wave phase, where electrons settle into a repeating pattern. Layers imprint spin-orbit effects, twists of electron spin tied to motion, onto the graphene. Two stackings are compared: offset AA and mirrored AA-prime, which preserves a horizontal mirror plane.

In AA stacking, fields from both faces add up, giving a radial Rashba pattern whose special response beats the conventional one 35-fold across a wide energy range. In AA-prime stacking, a persistent spin texture points out of plane. The orbital Hall effect, sideways current from orbital motion, dwarfs the spin Hall effect a thousandfold. Inside the induced energy gaps it holds a plateau while the spin Hall signal vanishes. Stacking choice alone selects the conversion regime.
arxiv-2606-12339:
Wang and co-authors teach a robot to judge how far away a sound is, using one small microphone, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Knowing a speaker's distance shapes natural robot interaction, but most systems need microphone arrays. Arrays demand synchronization, calibration, and space that robots lack. Echo-filled rooms make the single-microphone version harder still. Their Fast-SDE framework splits the sound spectrum into subbands, narrow frequency slices, instead of processing the whole band at once.

A shared encoder turns each subband into a compact representation, learning how acoustic structure maps to time-frequency patterns. A light regression head fuses the pieces into a distance estimate. Experiments test the design across room setups. Error grows as acoustic environments diversify, marking the generalization challenge. Wall distances, the gap between source, microphone, and walls, also sway the estimates. The open-sourced system runs in real time on limited hardware.
arxiv-2606-12439:
Wen and co-authors warn that optimizing content for AI answer engines is creating risks nobody is governing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Search is shifting from ranked links to synthesized answers. Generative Engine Optimization, GEO, targets the evidence pool and generation process of answer engines, not just rankings. Unlike old search optimization, its influence hides inside the final prose a user reads. The authors formalize the GEO pipeline to locate exactly where optimization acts.

Three risks emerge. First, concentrated influence: low contestability and system sensitivity let small manipulations sway many answers. Second, undisclosed commercial influence can embed itself in evidence and reasoning, invisible as advertising. Third, academic and industry blind spots diverge, because offline evaluations cannot see deployed behavior. The position paper calls for answer-level governance: stronger contestability, precise disclosure, black-box auditing of material influence, and metrics tracking how long manipulated exposure persists.
arxiv-2606-12639:
Bisht and Agarwal show that the scoreboard, not the models, decides who wins at predicting drug responses, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task: predict how a cell's activity answers a compound it has never seen, tested on THP-1 cells under a scaffold split. Their study starts with dumb baselines: the untreated profile and the average training response. It then adds retrieval from compounds, and a fusion model.

On a synthetic control, retrieval shines when chemistry is shared and collapses under the scaffold split; fusion recovers it. On the real data, the ranking flips with the metric. Under a proxy score, a linear model on fingerprints appears to win, beating deep models and retrieval. Under the contest's active-set metric, the order reverses. Deep models win, fusion beats the linear model, and the proxy's champion becomes the worst chemistry-aware predictor. The lesson: benchmark conclusions can be artifacts of the ruler.
arxiv-2606-12739:
Korolev provides a guide to estimating flexible fixed-effects panel data models with the mgcv package in R, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Panel data follow the same units, such as firms or households, over time, and fixed effects control for each unit's constant unobserved traits. Semiparametric and nonparametric versions let some relationships take an unknown smooth shape rather than a straight line, which standard software handles awkwardly.

The guide covers implementation choices in detail: absorbing fixed effects through unit indicators, first differencing, or penalised unit effects. It also covers specifying smooth terms, and computing cluster-robust standard errors that allow correlated errors within each unit. Monte Carlo experiments compare the mgcv bam estimator against linear models and fixed-series spline estimators. The simulations suggest penalised splines adapt well to unknown smoothness and estimate smooth components accurately, making mgcv workable for applied researchers needing flexible panel models.
arxiv-2606-13339:
Liu and Wang work in information-based complexity in this 2026 arXiv paper, the field measuring how much information an algorithm needs to solve a problem to an accuracy. They study linear tensor product problems, where a high-dimensional task is built from one-dimensional pieces. The question is weak tractability: whether the information grows mildly rather than explosively as dimension and accuracy demands increase. Their variant, algebraic weak tractability, allows an algebraic growth rate as accuracy varies.

Working in the worst-case setting under the error criterion, the authors focus on the case where the one-dimensional singular value exceeds one. That case had a gap in prior work: earlier results did not characterise when tractability holds. The paper supplies necessary and sufficient conditions phrased in terms of the one-dimensional singular values. The answer completes the picture for this class of problems.
arxiv-2606-13639:
Mandl, Chaturvedi, and Van Gerven tune an agent-based predator-prey simulation toward classic ecological cycles in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agent-based models simulate many individuals under local rules, capturing adaptive behaviour that equations miss. Their weakness is fragility: many parameters interact, and small changes can cause runaway growth or collapse. The authors study a predator-prey system where sheep and wolves are agents with local sensing, internal energy, and recurrent neural network controllers. The question is whether environmental parameters can be tuned so the dynamics resemble Lotka-Volterra cycles, the classic oscillation of predator and prey.

They optimise parameters with a feature-based loss rewarding oscillations, the correct phase lag, bounded populations, and persistence. Tuning proceeds first for random controllers, then for evolved ones in a more natural setting. The study offers a recipe for disciplining agent-based ecology into regimes comparable against a century of theory.
arxiv-2606-13839:
Chen and Nordling examine whether the explanations given for a heart-rate AI can be trusted. The model, RhythmFormer, uses remote photoplethysmography, which reads tiny skin color changes in ordinary video to estimate pulse without touching the body. Explanation tools highlight which image regions drove a prediction, but pretty heatmaps may not reflect real reasoning. Their 2026 arXiv paper adapts four such attribution methods to this model and scores them with hard numbers.

One new score measures how much highlighted area falls on real skin. Another, adapted from classification work, measures faithfulness by checking whether hiding highlighted regions truly changes the output. A leakage effect appears: some methods restore links that sparse attention had cut. The Beyond Intuition method scored best, with median skin coverage of zero point eight three against zero point five seven for plain rollout. Its faithfulness score reached zero point nine two on the UBFC-rPPG dataset.
arxiv-2606-13939:
Uhlmann and Zimmermann ask how much of an unknown nonlinearity boundary measurements can recover. Their equation is the Monge-Ampère equation, a nonlinear relation arising in geometry and optimal transport. The inverse problem mirrors Calderón's classic question. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines a nonlinear Cauchy data set and studies recovery of that term, linearizing around strictly convex backgrounds.

They first prove local well-posedness near a background solution, with smooth dependence on boundary data. The first variation of the nonlinear measurements then equals the data of a linear elliptic operator built from the background. An Alessandrini-type identity reduces the problem to an anisotropic Calderón-type one. Under uniqueness assumptions for the linear problem, the method recovers the first derivatives of the unknown term along the background. Higher-order steps can recover its full Taylor expansion. For transport cases, the equilibrium version reduces to the classical conductivity equation.
arxiv-2606-14039:
Roohi surveys machine learning for gases so thin that ordinary fluid equations fail, and asks what evidence would make results trustworthy. In rarefied gas transport the Knudsen number, the ratio of molecular free path to device size, is no longer tiny, so kinetic theory replaces fluid equations. Such flows drive vacuum systems and re-entry vehicles, but simulations can consume thousands of CPU-hours. His 2026 arXiv paper, a Perspective, classifies methods by what is learned: equation solving, operators, collision physics, closures, surrogates, and gas-surface models.

The central charge: most evidence is solver-facing. Models usually prove fidelity to a teacher simulation, not to experiment. Roohi separates soft physics penalties from structure-preserving designs. He proposes reporting standards: extrapolation tests, noise-aware metrics, end-to-end cost accounting, and a three-level validation hierarchy. For hypersonic flows the durable near-term contribution will be inference from sparse data, not prediction.
arxiv-2606-14139:
Min and Ma untangle a shotgun wedding between seismic inversion and image priors. Full waveform inversion recovers subsurface velocity from seismic records, but the problem is ill-posed and nonconvex, prone to cycle skipping. Diffusion priors add realism yet force a fragile trade-off between data fit and prior. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes Decoupled Latent Optimization. A quadratic penalty splits a physical variable from the latent code. The data gradient then acts in the model's own space; the sampler contributes only a decoded prior sample.

The standard smoothed start of classical FWI is preserved, with no backpropagation through the solver-sampler chain needed. On OpenFWI it beat classical and existing diffusion methods under clean, noisy, and missing-trace data. Trained only on seventy by seventy OpenFWI models, the prior transferred unchanged to the much larger Marmousi and Overthrust benchmarks, recovering complex faults robustly.
arxiv-2606-14239:
Gao and co-authors improve AI agent instruction packs without any answer key. Skills, structured packages guiding frozen agents in pro workflows, decay after deployment as edge cases and tool changes accumulate. Existing methods need privileged feedback: hidden test scores, rewards, expert responses. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces SkillAudit, whose core trick is paired trajectory auditing: run each task with and without the candidate skill, letting the contrast signal what to edit.

A cluster of evaluators, PACE, maps trajectory divergences to diagnostics tied to specific skill passages: process adherence, artifact evidence, consistency, effectiveness change. A fixed verifier checks constraints and rolls back harmful updates. Edits route two ways: Refine trims noisy guidance; Repair replaces conflicting passages. Across eighty-nine containerized tasks in eight domains, SkillAudit reached seventy-three point nine percent average task reward, versus forty point nine without skills and fifty-six point seven for the static expert skill.
arxiv-2606-14339:
Swinarski wrote a 2026 arXiv paper in algebraic geometry. This field studies shapes set by polynomial equations. In the nineteen eighties, Mukai built models of moduli spaces. A moduli space has one point for each curve, or for each K3 surface. K3 surfaces are a special class of smooth shapes. His models come from a quotient method that keeps track of symmetry.

Little was known about the edges of these spaces. Odd, singular curves and surfaces sit there. Swinarski gives a fast way to compute certain invariant values tied to these quotient problems. With that tool he shows several singular curves and surfaces are semistable. That means they belong inside Mukai's models. A final part gives a counting rule for one invariant.
arxiv-2606-14439:
Guo and co-authors compare two plasma physics tools in a 2026 arXiv study. Plasmas are hot ionized gases. Their wave behavior is captured by dispersion relations. These link wave frequency to wavelength. Two solvers, BO and ALPS, can now compute these relations for any particle speed distribution. But their agreement had never been tested broadly.

The team ran both solvers on several test cases. The cases included kappa, ring-beam, shell, and proton core-beam forms. The solvers agreed on unstable modes for large kappa values. They also agreed on the beam-type cases. BO became unreliable when kappa dropped below four. For a case taken from real data, the two gave similar wave speeds. But their growth rates differed a lot. The gap came from imperfect fitting inside BO. BO is still faster, finding all roots in one run. So the authors advise using both tools together.
arxiv-2606-14539:
Papamanthou settles a conjecture about graph orientations in a 2026 arXiv note. An st-orientation directs the edges of a biconnected graph so everything flows from one source vertex to one sink. Two algorithms, MaxSTN and MinSTN, were designed to produce orientations with long and short longest paths respectively, and experiments on graphs up to five thousand nodes suggested the long version always won.

Papamanthou, a co-author of those original algorithms, now disproves the conjecture outright. He exhibits a single biconnected graph on just nine vertices where MaxSTN produces a longest path of length six while MinSTN produces one of length seven. The reversal holds no matter how ties are broken inside either algorithm, so the experimental pattern was an artifact of the tested graph families.
arxiv-2606-14639:
Hugo Daumain and co-authors harden synthetic-speech detectors in a 2026 arXiv paper. As generated speech sounds ever more natural, anti-spoofing systems struggle. They struggle most with synthesis methods absent from training. The authors convert a self-supervised speech model into a mixture-of-experts design. Several specialist networks share the work.

They replace feed-forward blocks in selected encoder layers with multiple experts. A layer-wise gating mechanism steers the experts. The experts capture complementary acoustic patterns. The pretrained representations stay intact. The team analyzes which design choices matter. They also study how experts activate in practice. Across fourteen spoofing datasets, the change cut the macro equal error rate. It fell from about five point five percent to about four point eight percent. That is a relative gain near twelve percent over the baseline.
arxiv-2606-14739:
Papandroulidakis, Agwa, and Prodromakis build a neural classifier in memory hardware in a 2026 arXiv paper. Edge devices, especially safety-critical ones like autonomous navigation systems, struggle to run modern machine learning within tight energy budgets. Their design uses metal-oxide resistive RAM, memory cells whose resistance stores values, arranged as analog content-addressable memory for metric-based classification.

The building block is a custom template pixel cell acting as a configurable receptive-field neuron with a radial basis activation, which measures how far an input sits from a stored prototype. Arrays of these cells compare a high-dimensional input against all prototypes at once, performing fast, energy-efficient similarity search, and the receptive fields can be retuned on the fly to track domain shift. Simulations reached about eighty-nine percent accuracy on the MNIST digit benchmark at extremely low energy per operation.
arxiv-2606-15339:
Maciá and coauthor study how close the nearest leaf sits to a typical point in a random tree, in a 2026 probability paper. The trees are simply generated: each vertex's number of children follows fixed weights, and the tree is conditioned on its total size. The distance to the nearest leaf, and a related protection number based on a vertex's own subtree, describe how exposed vertices are to the tree's edge.

The authors prove a uniform exponential tail bound for these quantities, valid for every choice of offspring weights. One bound serves all tree sizes. As a consequence, the quantities are uniformly integrable of every order, so all their averages converge to those of the limiting infinite tree. Earlier work had settled such convergence only under extra analytic assumptions; the new probabilistic argument handles the three natural variants, root, random vertex, and protection number, in one sweep.
arxiv-2606-15539:
Ding and colleagues introduce a two-variable parity polynomial for virtual knotoids in 2026, adding a sharper tool to knot theory. Knotoids are open-ended knot diagrams, and their virtual versions allow crossings that are neither over nor under. The new invariant is built from the parity of classical crossings, classifying each crossing as even or odd and treating the two kinds differently.

The polynomial separates pairs of virtual knotoids that two earlier invariants, the odd writhe and the affine index polynomial, cannot tell apart. The authors also prove it is a Vassiliev invariant of order one, placing it in the standard hierarchy of finite-type invariants. They work out its relationship with the Petit gluing invariant as well. Finer invariants matter because classification is the core business of knot theory: each new distinguisher settles pairs that older tools left ambiguous, and parity-based constructions have repeatedly proved stronger than expected.
arxiv-2606-16039:
Gonçalves and Wong construct new manifolds where every self-map can be deformed to one with no fixed points, in a 2026 topology paper. A homeomorphism is a reversible reshaping of a space. The Nielsen number detects the obstruction: it vanishes exactly when a map is isotopic, meaning deformable, to a fixed point free map in known cases.

The key property is R-infinity, a condition on the fundamental group involving twisted conjugacy classes. Spaces of Jiang type let that algebra control fixed point behavior. Nilmanifolds supplied earlier examples, but they are aspherical, with no higher spherical holes. Gonçalves and Wong build the first known infinite family of non-aspherical closed manifolds with both properties. Every self homeomorphism there is thus isotopic to a fixed point free map. A companion result shows certain quotient spaces lack R-infinity, marking the boundary of the construction.
arxiv-2606-16139:
Anagnostides and colleagues settle in 2026 how hard it is to compute equilibria when teams, not single players, compete. Two-player zero-sum games admit tractable equilibrium solutions by the minimax theorem. In team zero-sum games, each side has several agents who share one objective but cannot perfectly coordinate.

Computing Nash equilibria in team zero-sum games is PPAD-complete, the team proves, as hard as general-sum games despite the adversarial structure. The hardness survives strong restrictions: inverse-polynomial precision, ruling out a fully polynomial approximation scheme unless P equals PPAD. It also survives teams of only two players per side, and polymatrix games, where interactions are pairwise. As byproducts, the work resolves group-wise zero-sum polymatrix games, and shows first-order stationary points in min-max optimization are PPAD-complete even for quadratic objectives.
arxiv-2606-16939:
Yin and colleagues make circuit discovery in language models scalable in a 2026 interpretability paper. Mechanistic interpretability hunts for circuits, small sets of model components that jointly produce a behavior. Raw neurons each serve many meanings, which muddies circuits built from them, while cleaner sparse autoencoder features are so numerous that intervention-based search becomes unaffordable.

Their method, CircuitLasso, replaces interventions with sparse linear regression, a far cheaper tool. On benchmark data its recovered circuits match the structural accuracy of leading intervention methods at a fraction of the computing cost. The circuits expose how human-readable semantic features flow through the model and steer its predictions. As a practical check, insights from the learned circuits reach comparable performance at much lower cost on a domain-generalization task. The work opens circuit analysis to the feature level, where explanations are most legible, without the usual supercomputer bill.
arxiv-2606-17039:
Alencar, Fortunato and Hipólito-Ricaldi test burst emission geometry against a whole population in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes from deep space. One candidate mechanism is curvature radiation, emitted by charged bunches sliding along curved magnetic field lines.

The team fits three templates, point source, one-dimensional bunch and paired-bunch cavity, to thousands of bursts in the second CHIME catalog. All three fit the broad spectral envelope well, with fit values clustered near ideal. Information criteria split: one favors the bunch model for most sources, the other the simpler point source. The catch is in the residuals: only a small minority of bursts pass both the fit test and a residual-independence test. Structured leftovers persist, so extra physics is needed for the fine spectral detail. Repeating and non-repeating bursts differ modestly; inferred coherence scales land at tens of centimeters.
arxiv-2606-17139:
Krawczyk revisits a consistency problem for superheavy gravitinos in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. The gravitino, supersymmetry's spin-3/2 field, becomes troublesome when charged and massive: coupling to electromagnetism usually breaks causality and unitarity. Yet a recent proposal makes fractionally charged, Planck-mass gravitinos the only new fermions beyond the Standard Model.

Deser and Waldron showed gravity itself can cure the problem. Krawczyk rederives their result for a minimally coupled field in an Einstein-Maxwell background, from the constraints and the characteristic determinant. Consistency demands a lower bound on mass in terms of charge and the cosmological constant. What looks like an obstruction becomes a prediction: such particles must sit near the Planck scale, matching the proposal's needs. A Stückelberg spinor reformulation makes the delicate helicity sector explicit and yields a renormalizable propagator. Causality, in this corner of theory, points at the heaviest possible scale.
arxiv-2606-17339:
Bhalla and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper introducing SpeechDx, a benchmark meant to unify the fragmented field of clinical speech AI. Speech engages neurological, motor, respiratory, and vocal systems at once, so many diseases leave traces in the voice. Past work, though, grew in isolated condition-specific studies with mismatched protocols, making results hard to compare and generalisation hard to judge across disorders, data sets, and recording conditions in the clinic.

SpeechDx spans a dozen data sets and dozens of tasks across many health conditions in one framework. Tasks are grouped by the stage of speech production they disrupt, from forming ideas to shaping sounds. Twelve leading audio encoders were evaluated on all tasks, including zero-shot transfer across conditions. Large speech models were the strongest baselines overall, while specialised models helped only on closely matched tasks, and nothing generalised reliably everywhere.
arxiv-2606-17639:
Yang and Fernando present a 2026 arXiv paper introducing ERQA-Plus, a diagnostic benchmark for reasoning in embodied AI, where agents must think from a robot's situated viewpoint. Generalist agents need spatial, procedural, and social reasoning, not just object naming, yet older benchmarks cannot tell grounded reasoning from shortcut pattern matching. The new set holds well over a thousand question-answer items grounded in hundreds of robot-centric images, sorted by a taxonomy of reasoning kinds for fine-grained diagnosis.

Questions were drafted under taxonomy guidance, then judged automatically, revised, and checked by humans for grounding and validity. A spread of vision-language and embodied models was benchmarked on the finished set. The strongest model scored well overall, yet category results expose stubborn weakness in spatial reasoning, procedural reasoning, event prediction, and reading intentions. The benchmark shows which kinds of embodied thought each model can trust.
arxiv-2606-18339:
Gupta and colleagues test a leading quantum algorithm on the ground states of random all-to-all Hamiltonians, in a 2026 quantum computing paper. The Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass and the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model have volume-law entangled ground states. Tensor networks strain against them, and neural quantum states have pushed classical limits. Whether a quantum algorithm can beat those methods here is open.

The team used TETRIS-ADAPT-VQE, which grows its circuit step by step. It prepared ground states of dense and sparse SYK models up to twenty Majorana fermions, with fidelities above ninety-nine percent. For the SK model it reached eighteen sites at far higher fidelity. The split came in the cost. Circuit depth and parameter counts grew polynomially for SK. For SYK, dense or sparse, growth looked exponential. State preparation, they conclude, suits quantum hardware for one model family and not the other.
arxiv-2606-18439:
You and colleagues speed up VGGT, a transformer that rebuilds three-dimensional scenes from many images in one pass, in a 2026 computer vision paper from the University of Pennsylvania. The model's cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the number of images, so long sequences exhaust memory and time.

Their analysis divides the network into three regimes. Shallow layers show little cross-view structure, middle layers do the cross-view alignment, and deep layers are largely redundant for geometry yet still vital for camera pose. RegimeVGGT compresses, merging tokens while protecting geometry- and edge-salient ones, and downsampling attention keys and values while preserving spatial coverage and the pose-critical path. The training-free method ran several times faster than an optimized baseline at matched reconstruction quality on an indoor dataset. The broader lesson is that redundancy in such transformers is layered, not uniform.
arxiv-2606-18739:
Okuyama uncovers an exact bridge between two unrelated models, in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. One is the double-scaled SYK model of quantum gravity. The other is a classical stochastic lattice gas. The double-scaled SYK model is exactly solvable through chord diagrams and a transfer matrix. Curiously, the same transfer matrix governs the asymmetric simple exclusion process. In that process, particles hop asymmetrically along a one-dimensional lattice, under hard-core exclusion.

Okuyama shows the moments of the SYK transfer matrix can be written as an overlap. It is between the stationary state of the exclusion process and a product state. He argues this overlap plays the same role as the strange correlator in topological phases. There, an overlap between a string-net state and a product state reproduces the Turaev-Viro state sum. He develops the parallel between the two correspondences, as a sandwich construction like topological holography.
arxiv-2606-19039:
Rahman and colleagues present a learnable speech-to-spike encoder for spiking neural networks in 2026. Such networks work with discrete spikes, while speech arrives as a smooth sound wave. That mismatch is a core block for brain-inspired speech tools. Fixed encoders force the network to cope with rigid inputs, so the team instead trains the encoder jointly with a recurrent spiking backbone, end to end, for the task itself.

Tests use the Google Speech Commands benchmark in its second version. The full model reaches high accuracy on spoken commands. A compact version still matches or beats prior baselines. Probing shows the encoder does not aim to rebuild the sound faithfully. It learns spike patterns that split classes cleanly instead. The authors also compare a bio-inspired learning rule with standard surrogate-gradient training. The bio-inspired rule scores a bit lower, which quantifies its trade-off.
arxiv-2606-19239:
Nappi and colleagues improve quantum-classical auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo in 2026, pushing the method toward practical use. The hybrid method uses a quantum trial state with classical walkers to compute ground-state energies. Its dominant classical cost per step grew steeply with system size, limiting reach. The team cuts that scaling by a full order through two linked algorithmic changes to the core workflow.

Aitken's block transformation handles singular Pfaffians that arise when estimating overlaps between the quantum trial state and classical determinant walkers. Algorithmic differentiation computes the force bias efficiently alongside it. Together they give a very large estimated speedup for a hundred-orbital system. The workflow is demonstrated on a hydrogen chain from quantum data taken on a superconducting processor, with tensor-network error mitigation. Noiseless tests on longer chains and a lithium-air battery pathway validate scaling.
arxiv-2606-19539:
Spiridon Kasapis leads a large team reviewing machine learning for solar energetic particle prediction in 2026. Solar energetic particle events flood space with fast particles from the Sun. They endanger aircraft crews, spacecraft electronics, and astronauts beyond Earth's magnetic shield.

Physics-based simulations and empirical rules long carried the forecasting load. Machine learning now offers a fresh route to earlier, sharper warnings. The review catalogues the available learning models built for this task. It identifies the datasets each model trains on and compares architectures, inputs, and outputs side by side. Common strengths and gaps across the field come into view through that comparison. Good practices and recommendations for future work close the survey. Better particle forecasts would protect hardware in orbit and crews on deep-space missions alike.
arxiv-2606-19639:
Erhan Bayraktar and Ali Devran Kara study shared hidden state control with scattered observations in 2026. Many decision makers watch one hidden state through identical channels, each seeing only its own data. Costs and dynamics depend on actions only through their empirical distribution.

With infinitely many agents, the problem collapses to a single-agent control task. The lone agent steers the hidden state through the conditional law of actions given past hidden values. Bayraktar and Kara frame this as a deterministic measure-valued control problem with a dynamic programming recursion. Randomising control actions proves necessary for optimality in the limit problem. Mixing over whole policies, by contrast, is not required. Symmetric policies tuned for the infinite case stay near optimal for finite crowds. Error decays like one over the square root of the agent count, while growing exponentially with policy memory.
arxiv-2606-19739:
Lingbin Bian and colleagues, with the Baby Connectome Project Consortium, measure how brain structure and function modules align in infants, in a 2026 study. Brain networks split into modules, clusters of regions with shared jobs. Whether wiring modules match activity modules shifts fast during early development.

Stochastic modules replace hard assignments with chances: each region gets a probability of belonging to each group-level module. That design tolerates modules of unlike sizes across structure and function. It also absorbs how much modules vary from child to child. Against standard coupling measures, the new score shows a sharper drop in structure-function consistency. Scores fall from birth to age five in Baby Connectome Project data. Primary regions like visual areas score highest, while attention, control, and default mode regions score lowest. Development thus reorganises the young brain unevenly.
arxiv-2606-19839:
Ashfaque Ahmad, Sudhir Kumar Gupta, and Abbas Ali bound microscopic black hole masses at the Large Hadron Collider in 2026. The ADD model adds extra spatial dimensions, lowering gravity's true scale toward collider reach. Such collisions might forge tiny black holes that decay in the detectors.

The analysis assumes collisions at fourteen TeV of centre-of-mass energy. A loss parameter captures energy shed during black hole formation. With no loss, black holes below about twelve TeV are disfavoured for three extra dimensions. A higher reduced Planck scale trims that bound somewhat. Stronger formation loss cuts the limits steeply, near seven TeV in the studied cases. Raising the dimension count to seven lifts the bounds again. Null results at the LHC thus fence in extra-dimensional black hole scenarios from several sides at once.
arxiv-2606-20439:
Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur solve the four-digit Kaprekar routine in every odd base above three. The routine sorts a number's digits descending and ascending, subtracts, and repeats; in base ten every nonconstant four-digit string famously ends at 6174. Odd bases turn out to have an unexpectedly rigid structure.

After at most three iterations, every nonconstant orbit enters an explicit triangular region. On that region the Kaprekar map is conjugate to projective doubling, a simple doubling rule in disguise. The conjugacy yields a complete finite description of all nonconstant terminal cycles. Explicit formulas give the length and count of each cycle. A recreational puzzle thus becomes a fully classified dynamical system.
arxiv-2606-20539:
Madhulatha Mandarapu and Sandeep Kunkunuru argue that cloud caches should optimize dollars, not hit rates. Their 2026 paper notes that a cache miss on cloud object storage is billed per request and per byte of egress, not by latency. Classic caching minimizes the miss rate, which is the wrong objective when one expensive object costs thousands of times more than a cheap one.

The authors supply the missing reference. For uniform-size page caches with heterogeneous miss costs, the offline dollar-optimum is exact and computable in polynomial time. It comes from an integral interval linear program, validated against brute force. Deployed heuristics can finally be measured against the true dollar optimum on real cloud prices. A crossover point decides when cost-aware caching pays at all. Cloud bills, not hit ratios, become the benchmark.
arxiv-2606-20739:
Minh Vu, Khang Nguyen, Vu Tran, and Vien Ngo present a unified method in 2026 for robotic inspection routing and configuration. A robot must visit many six-degree viewpoints and reach each one without collision. Older pipelines fix one joint configuration per viewpoint. They then build all travel times and route separately. Their method optimizes visiting order and per-viewpoint configuration together in one global search.

Each viewpoint's self-motion space is described in closed form, so pose limits hold by construction. Travel time uses a fast double-integrator approximation. The tour is encoded with random keys and tuned by a derivative-free optimizer. Only edges on the chosen route receive full trajectory checks for dynamics and torque limits. That cuts trajectory solves from quadratic to linear in viewpoint count. Joint planning could shorten inspection tours for complex robots, where a good route with poor joint choices wastes time.
arxiv-2606-20839:
Lingzhi Yang and three colleagues propose Process-Reward Tactic Evolution in 2026 to make language model agents reliable at long bioinformatics workflows. Agents can write code and call tools. Reliable biology work also needs typed data, provenance, and biological checks over many steps. The setting is Galaxy, a widely used workflow platform. An agent must explore data, build a workflow graph, bind inputs, monitor runs, debug failures, and validate outputs.

During training, agents practice on organized Galaxy tasks in a gym environment. Process verifiers score workflow building, software use, execution, and biological correctness. Successful and failed traces are distilled into a reusable tactic library. At test time, the trained agent uses that library on held-out tasks in isolated settings. Turning verified experience into tactics offers a path to agents that improve at real lab workflows, not only at short coding puzzles.
arxiv-2606-21339:
Wenhan Wang and Zeyu Sun present KBSpec in 2026, a system that helps language models write formal specifications, the precise preconditions and postconditions that let software be verified. Models often fail here because specification languages such as the Java Modeling Language appear rarely in training data, so syntax and meaning both go wrong. KBSpec feeds the model two kinds of knowledge: official documentation, and lessons distilled from verifier feedback on earlier attempts.

A self-evolving knowledge base keeps successful generation and repair traces, growing without any model retraining or labeled data. Tested on Java specification writing with three language model backends, KBSpec raises verification pass rates by ten to twenty-five percent over leading approaches. It also produces the most complete specifications, showing that curated, growing knowledge can substitute for scarce training corpora.
arxiv-2606-21539:
Xuan Mei and Junze Lin study an accounting problem in 2026 for banks: when a suite of credit models forecasts portfolio losses wrong, which component model deserves the blame? Expected loss forecasts multiply together exposure at default, prepayment, default probability, and loss given default, each from its own model, then sum across loans and periods. The industry standard, walk analysis, changes one component at a time, but its answer depends on the order chosen.

The authors adapt two order-independent schemes. One is an augmented Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index method tailored to the expected loss structure. The other is Shapley value attribution, which averages each component's marginal effect over all orderings. Compact formulas keep the extra computation to seconds at portfolio scale. The approach also extends to suites with a Monte Carlo layer.
arxiv-2606-21739:
Sourav Khatua and Sutanu Roy develop the theory of paths in quantum graphs in 2026. A quantum graph replaces a graph's vertex set with a finite-dimensional C-star algebra and its edges with a quantum adjacency operator. Such objects show up as confusability graphs of quantum channels and in work on graph isomorphism. Edges are well understood, but how they concatenate into paths, the data behind the graph's C-star algebras, was an open question.

The authors define path indicators and path correspondences for finite quantum graphs and study their basic properties. They then compute both explicitly in three settings: ordinary classical graphs, trivial graphs, and complete quantum graphs. The explicit cases anchor the abstract machinery, giving future work on quantum connectivity and quantum Cayley graphs a concrete path calculus to build on.
arxiv-2606-21839:
Mune and colleagues test an extended theory of gravity against cosmic observations in 2026. Their model, f(Q,T) gravity, modifies general relativity using the non-metricity scalar, which measures how lengths change under transport, plus the trace of the matter energy-momentum tensor. They add a Dirac-Born-Infeld scalar field, a candidate driver of the universe's late acceleration.

On a flat expanding background, the authors derive the model's field equations and solve them for a simple linear form. They fit the free parameters with Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling, a standard Bayesian method, using Hubble-rate data, DESI survey results, and the Pantheon+SHOES supernova sample. The joint fit stayed broadly consistent with current late-time limits and allowed direct comparison with the standard model. They present it as a viable alternative for probing tensions such as the Hubble constant dispute, not as a settled answer.
arxiv-2606-22239:
Azangulov and colleagues introduce, in 2026, variance-tilted diffusion models for drawing diverse sets of samples rather than independent ones. Many downstream tasks need a candidate set that covers distinct regions, not repeated draws from the same modes. Heuristic repulsive drifts can force diversity, but their target distribution stays implicit and hard to control.

The authors instead specify the target explicitly: a variance-weighted batch distribution favouring collections with large empirical spread after a chosen linear feature map. The sampler is derived exactly, as the Doob h-transform of independent diffusion dynamics. The correction has a compact form with two parts. One term repels the posterior denoised means of the particles from each other. A curvature term moves particles toward regions of higher feature variance. The result is an interacting-particle sampler whose probabilistic target is explicit rather than heuristic.
arxiv-2606-22339:
Singh and colleagues introduce T-IMPACT in 2026, a severity-aware benchmark for manipulated image-text pairs in news-style posts. Generative editing now makes persuasive multimodal misinformation easy to produce. Existing datasets label authenticity, context mismatch, or manipulation type, but rarely say how strongly an edit changes how a post will be read. T-IMPACT grades that contextual impact instead.

The benchmark holds 98,786 examples spanning pristine, image-only, text-only, and joint edits. Each carries a calibrated continuous severity score, coarse low, medium, and high bands, and grounding metadata. The pipeline extracts semantic anchors from a source pair, grounds them in the image, makes localized edits, rewrites captions under constraints, and calibrates impact scores with limited human ratings. Experiments show current models recover some authenticity signal. Severity prediction, though, remains much harder and only weakly aligned with human judgement.
arxiv-2606-22539:
Nabh Singh presents a proof about colouring integer distance graphs in this 2026 mathematics paper. An integer distance graph joins grid points whose separation belongs to a chosen set of distances. Its chromatic number is the fewest colours needed so that no joined pair shares a colour, and finiteness is not obvious when the distance set is infinite.

Singh studies distance sets generated by a lacunary sequence of vectors in two dimensions, meaning the vectors grow very fast, each dwarfing the previous ones. The argument extends the one-dimensional lonely set method upward. A lacunary matrix theorem of Broderick, Fishman, and Kleinbock supplies a satisfactory multiplier vector, a scaling that spreads the points out favourably. From that vector, Singh gives an explicit geometric colouring argument. The conclusion is that every such two-dimensional graph has a finite chromatic number, so a fixed palette always suffices.
arxiv-2606-22739:
Rebecca McCabe, Madison Dietrich, and Maha Haji present a design tool for wave energy converters in this 2026 paper. These devices turn ocean wave motion into power, and designing one means balancing power output, cost, and survival in storms. Existing simulators are either too slow for large design searches or too narrow for integrated studies.

Their framework, MDOcean, combines hydrodynamics, dynamics, structures, and economics in one modular package built on analytical and semi-analytical methods. It includes a mesh-free solver for wave forces, a frequency-domain dynamics engine handling drag and saturation effects, and a structural sizing module checking yield, buckling, storm, and fatigue criteria. A simple cost model supports techno-economic assessment. In validation, MDOcean ran in 151 milliseconds, orders of magnitude faster than leading wave energy tools, while keeping near-numerical accuracy. That speed makes broad early-stage design exploration practical.
arxiv-2606-23339:
Victor Lockwood and colleagues let robots grade their own interactions with people in a 2026 human-robot interaction paper. Evaluation in this field rests almost entirely on human questionnaires. The robot's own perspective goes unexamined. The authors invert the setup: language-model-powered robots fill in the same standardized questionnaires humans use. In the first study, five models rated twenty-five recorded interactions on three standard instruments. Their engagement ratings agreed moderately to strongly with human ground truth, with excellent consistency across repeats.

Lockwood and colleagues uncover one systematic failure, though. On comfort and strangeness, the models' ratings ran opposite to humans', a pattern the authors call the strangeness failure. The models seem to conflate engagement with comfort. A live study with a Nao robot replicated both the agreement and the failure in real time.
arxiv-2606-23739:
Lukhi, Moradiya, Timofte, and Ignatov automate the search for vision models built from four different expert networks, in a 2026 paper on neural architecture search. Mixture of experts models route inputs through specialized networks whose outputs a gating network blends. Mixing four architecture families could combine their strengths, but the possible quartets from twenty nine families run to tens of thousands.

Over a twenty eight day campaign on one graphics card, the pipeline generated more than four thousand candidate models and evaluated about a thousand successfully. A critical flaw surfaced: alphabetical listing anchored the entire explored space, under five percent of the total, to one family, AirNet. The authors pin down the bias, trace it to the generator, and propose stratified random sampling as the fix. Within the covered scope, ShuffleNet and MobileNetV3 pairings score highest.
arxiv-2606-23839:
Zalialiutdinov and colleagues measure a small correction to molecular energies that becomes hard to ignore when atoms and molecules sit inside optical cavities, in a 2026 paper on quantum chemistry. Cavities can strongly couple to matter and reshape chemistry even without any external light source. Most theory work uses the Born Oppenheimer approximation, which freezes the nuclei while solving for electrons. The diagonal Born Oppenheimer correction adjusts for the nuclear motion, and the team asks how a cavity changes it.

Working within a quantum electrodynamics framework that treats light and matter together, they compute the correction for helium, beryllium, hydrogen molecules, lithium hydride, hydrogen fluoride, ammonia, and formaldehyde. The cavity shifts the energy needed to break molecules apart by a few wavenumbers. For several atoms, the correction reaches the sharpness of modern experiments. Finite nuclear mass effects, they conclude, belong in precise studies of such systems.
arxiv-2606-23939:
Zangrando, Venturini, Rinaldi, and Tudisco extend a classic shortcut so it survives the constraints that real data science problems impose, in a 2026 paper on optimization. The method fits models with two variable blocks: once the nonlinear block is fixed, the linear block can be solved exactly and eliminated, shrinking the problem. The classical method assumes nothing constrains what remains. Modern problems constrain the remaining variables with sparsity or non negativity requirements. The authors recast the method as a collapsed bilevel problem.

From that view they derive exact formulas for the reduced gradient, of a kind automatic differentiation can use directly. A conditional gradient method solves the constrained problem, with convergence guarantees under standard assumptions. Experiments on dictionary learning, sparse autoencoding, few shot learning, and blind deconvolution suggest gains in speed and data efficiency over joint baselines.
arxiv-2606-24039:
Bravo-Palacios and colleagues present TurboMPC, a model predictive control solver that runs entirely on graphics processors. Model predictive control plans a robot's next moves by solving an optimisation problem over a future horizon. Robotics increasingly runs simulation and learning on GPUs. A CPU-bound solver therefore becomes the bottleneck. Their 2026 solver stays differentiable, meaning gradients flow through its answers for use in learning.

Sequential quadratic programming forms the outer loop. An alternating direction method handles each subproblem. Implicit differentiation supplies the gradients. A co-designed implementation mixing JAX and CUDA keeps the code usable. Tests cover constrained planning, humanoid imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with neural cost functions. TurboMPC runs many times faster than leading CPU and GPU rivals there. On a full-scale car, batched GPU tuning of control parameters beat a hand-tuned baseline in minimum-time racing. Horizons beyond eighty steps remain practical.
arxiv-2606-24139:
Korsky studies how small a range of integers can host a set whose subset sums avoid arithmetic progressions. Take a finite set of positive integers. Form every sum of a subcollection, including the empty sum of zero. Erdős and Sárkőzy asked for the least upper limit N such that some n-element set inside the range has subset sums with no nonconstant progression of a given length.

For progressions of length three, Korsky proves a lower bound that matches the exact bandwidth of the ternary grid. It is stated through central trinomial coefficients, the middle terms of a three-term polynomial power. For longer progressions he proves a general lower bound with an exponential rate. A carry-free digit construction from nearly regular graphs caps growth from the other side, so the two bounds squeeze the rate.
arxiv-2606-24339:
Li works toward sorting out when a tropical intersection collapses to a single clean point. Tropical geometry swaps algebraic varieties for piecewise-linear fans. Complete intersections there are ruled by mixed volumes of lattice polytopes. Writing alone in 2026, Li bridges two classifications. One is the Esterov-Gusev classification of polytope tuples of mixed volume one. The other is Fink's description of Bergman fans. A conjecture follows, describing exactly when the stable intersection is a reduced point.

The conjecture is then proved in three fundamental cases. Unmixed sequences, hypersurface complete-intersection cycles, and tropical two-cycles. Along the way Li develops some tools aimed at the general case, still open. The paper's point is structural. Rather than settling the classification outright, it welds two fields. It states the precise target, clears the basic cases, and forges tools for whoever ends the job.
arxiv-2606-24539:
Li and colleagues teach a multimodal model to reason geometrically about pointing, before naming what is pointed at. Pointing-based visual grounding asks a system to locate the object a gesture indicates. It decodes spatial relations between scene and hand. Traditional methods encode the image once into static features and reason mostly in language. Perceptual cues and explicit geometry the image plainly contains are discarded.

PointVG-R is a reasoning guided multimodal large language model, built against that cognitive vulnerability in interpreting gestural space. A visual chain of thought has the model work through the geometry stepwise. Spatial reasoning is internalised, rather than bolted on at the output. The framework shares a companion pointing study's conviction that gesture understanding is geometry first. Li's 2026 system aims for precise pointing localisation in scenes where language only reasoning guesses, forcing the model to look, orient, and only then answer.
arxiv-2606-24639:
Thompson, Hughes, and Rotenberg inverse design photonic crystal waveguides that handle pulses, not just steady light. These waveguides confine light below the wavelength scale and control its group velocity, enhancing light matter interaction. Applications need a wide band of low loss, constant velocity slow light, though. Earlier dispersion engineering could not deliver that combination. Their 2026 method pairs inverse design with a fast mode solver and physics-based formulas.

Compute time falls by more than a hundredfold. Waveguides with up to an order of magnitude more bandwidth, and several times lower loss than prior state of the art, are unlocked. Trade offs among bandwidth, disorder induced loss, group index, and dispersion are mapped. Two application studies show the reach. They cover broadband, position tolerant Purcell enhancement for quantum light sources, and compact phase shifters for optical communications. Thompson's team offers the workflow as a general design method for integrated photonics.
arxiv-2606-24739:
Fernando Afonso disproves a conjecture about converse invariant orientations of trees. Count copies of an oriented graph inside every tournament, where each edge of a complete graph gets a direction. An orientation is converse invariant if reversing all its arcs never changes that count. Ai and colleagues had conjectured a full description of such tree orientations. They claimed every example is self converse or built by recursive bridge mirroring from a path.

Afonso classifies the converse invariant orientations of trees of diameter four. The classification turns up examples that are not self converse and do not arise from bridge mirroring, refuting the conjecture. His main tool is a new polynomial. It encodes the difference between copy counts for an orientation and its converse. A formula writes it as a signed sum over subgraphs. The method also yields parity obstructions and fresh proofs that oriented paths and cycles are converse invariant.
arxiv-2606-24839:
Tian Zheng and Kai-Tai Hsu study how reliably automated graders judge an agentic data analysis system. Such agents produce code, numbers, and verbal diagnostics, so grading them is harder than grading a single chat reply. The testbed is LAMBDA, a multi agent analysis system, run on 153 numerical tasks from DSGym. The authors build a three layer grading cascade and measure each layer against human labels.

The cascade runs strict pattern matching first, then a lenient language model grader, then human inspection of snippets. Both automated graders show perfect observed precision, with no false positives in seventy cases. The lenient grader's recall reaches 97 percent. A keyword anchored extraction step lifts the strict grader's recall by sixty points over a naive last number rule. A nudging mechanism raises grading run success from 36 to 97 percent. Re adding the original question to the nudge, they find, gives no extra benefit.
arxiv-2606-24939:
Asad Ali, Saif Al-Kuwari, and four colleagues pinpoint where spontaneous Raman scattering enters shortcut assisted atom optics. The loss comes from a lossy excited state, but adiabatic elimination hides its origin. In the dark bright basis, the optical source rides entirely on the bright state amplitude. Scattering probability is then one functional of that amplitude, a framing that recovers the dissipative STIRAP loss. It also shows what a shortcut does: counterdiabatic STIRSAP cancels the bright state source itself, not the optical decay coefficient.

The cancellation is exact in the three level model at the counterdiabatic point, for any detuning, Rabi frequency, and pulse length. What remains splits into two quadratures: a real shortcut mismatch and an imaginary two photon Doppler term. The authors design a protocol nulling the Doppler part for a momentum class. Their caution: the nulling is never better than chirping the two photon detuning.
arxiv-2606-25039:
Nikhil Abhyankar and four colleagues recover the equations of dynamical systems by letting a language model choose what data to collect next. Finding ordinary differential equations from observations is usually treated as static inference on a dataset. That assumption breaks when trajectories are uninformative: several equations can fit the same data, and the wrong one wins. Their framework, LLM-ACES, closes the loop. A language model proposes operator priors that split the search space into regions. Candidate equations are fitted inside each region. Where candidates disagree, new trajectories are acquired.

Across 122 systems from two benchmark suites, the method achieves the lowest median error, beating baselines by orders of magnitude. Symbolic recovery, the test of finding the equation, reaches about 46 and 52 percent on the two suites. The method is sample efficient too, performing better with a tenth of the data. Abhyankar and colleagues show it stays robust under noise.
arxiv-2606-25139:
Agentic AI could automate much of building engineering work, but most demonstrations stay isolated and hard to reuse. Zixin Jiang and Bing Dong present Buildrix, an open platform for developing, sharing, running, and scoring agentic AI skills in this field.

Three parts make it up. A Python command line package handles creating, publishing, validating, installing, and managing skills and test cases. Its web Hub organises open challenges, reusable skills, reviews, and benchmark results. A local agent harness runs the skills, with skill discovery, tool provisioning, staged context loading, and multi step execution. Skills ship as self contained packages holding instructions, scripts, and dependencies. Test cases checked by domain experts can be promoted to golden status, anchoring reproducible benchmark scores.
arxiv-2606-25239:
Testing a neural network for hidden failures one input at a time is slow, and uniform noise wastes effort on features with very different scales. Guanqin Zhang and Yulei Sui present a batch fuzzing framework in 2026 that tests many specification cases in a single pass. Input limits and output checks are embedded inside the network as fixed layers. Mutation sizes are scaled from each specification's own allowed range, either evenly across all features or feature by feature.

On three benchmarks covering six networks and more than four hundred specifications, the tensor based approach reached up to forty times the throughput of a sequential fuzzer. It also found up to four times as many property violations within the same time budget. Traffic sign recognition was among the tested tasks.
arxiv-2606-25939:
DeformGen comes from a joint robotics effort. Its listed sites include Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Tsinghua University, and the Hong Kong Polytechnic University. The problem is teaching robots to handle soft, deformable objects by imitation. Augmenting demonstrations the usual way fails here: valid poses of a deforming object cannot be reached by small rigid shifts, and a copied trajectory does not follow material points as they move.

Two mechanisms solve the two halves of that problem. Small physical disturbances come first. Forward simulation of the dynamics then yields new plausible states with changed topology. Deformation-field warping then adapts the original manipulation trajectory to each new shape, lifting per-particle motion into a smooth spatial field. On demanding deformable test tasks, policies trained with the added data learn better. They beat policies trained on the raw demonstrations alone. They also beat rigid-style augmentation.
arxiv-2606-26039:
Marco Leitão, José Guilherme Milhano, and Alba Soto-Ontoso compute how quarks and gluons split inside quark-gluon plasma. Jets from heavy-ion collisions probe that hot, dense matter. A parton radiating inside the plasma loses energy in patterned ways. The BDMPS-Z formalism, now nearly thirty years old, describes the radiation. Standard uses of it lean on three approximations at once: soft emission, large colour count, and a harmonic-oscillator medium model.

Numerical solution replaces all three shortcuts. The team reports solving the BDMPS-Z equations numerically, completely, for the first time. Accuracy holds across the whole phase space. Finite-energy effects enter the results. Subleading colour contributions enter too, along with a realistic model of parton-medium interaction. Comparing against the standard approximations reveals substantial deviations across phase space. Sharper splitting functions should tighten jet-based measurements of plasma properties at the high-luminosity LHC.
arxiv-2606-26739:
Abigail Langbridge, Martin Corless, and Robert Shorten generalise a classic method for balancing flows between suppliers and consumers. Optimal transport finds the cheapest way to move resources from sources to sinks. The Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm solves a smoothed version by repeated scaling. Real problems add twists: transport constraints of many kinds, and flexible margins on the supplier and consumer sides.

The authors fold such constraints into the smoothed transport problem. Martingale-type constraints, borrowed from probability theory, are included. They matter when a plan must also be realisable as a fair random process, as in sharing-economy settings. New Sinkhorn-like algorithms are proven to converge for this wider class. Worked examples show the method in action. The result widens a fast, trusted algorithm to problems it could not previously touch.
arxiv-2606-27139:
Buono extends a famous map of possible computational worlds drawn by Impagliazzo. That map sorts worlds by which cryptographic tools exist, from easy problem solving to full public-key secrecy. Every world on the map quietly assumes all parties, even attackers, see the complete input. Buono makes that hidden assumption explicit and relaxes it. A second axis grades how much of the input an observer can actually see.

With a suitably blinded observer, a striking collapse appears: two major problem classes become equal for that observer, yet stay strictly below full power. That collapse holds in all five original worlds without extra assumptions. Blindness and computational hardness thus vary independently. Buono names the resulting Observer World, classifies every world-observer pairing, and adds a graded family for partial violations. Links to thermodynamic, quantum, and cosmological information limits are also drawn.
arxiv-2606-27439:
Zelmer leads a large collaboration building simulation-based inference for galaxy cluster cosmology, so that survey catalogues can be used at full strength. The eROSITA all-sky survey delivers record-size cluster samples. Their pipeline generates realistic mock samples through the survey selection function, calibrated on test suites. In 2026, a set-based neural network reads each cluster directly, and a masked flow turns its encoding into posterior densities for the parameters.

Input universes are recovered within the inferred uncertainties across the mock suite. Calibration tests pass, even with survey biases and scatter included. Matter density is constrained to about eleven percent and the fluctuation size to about four percent, averaged over samples matching the real sample size in the reported analysis. That precision rivals classic analyses using much larger samples.
arxiv-2606-27539:
Predicting how far a social media post will spread matters. Advertisers, creators, and platforms all use such forecasts. Earlier studies, though, used different data and different rules. Their results could not be compared fairly. Utkarsh Sahu and six colleagues respond in 2026 with MMG-Pop. MMG-Pop is a shared benchmark for popularity prediction. It standardises datasets, content types, observation windows, and scoring.

The team also built MMG-PopNet. That model reads text, images, timing, and social interaction graphs together. Tests covered four datasets from Bluesky and Reddit. MMG-PopNet performed best overall. Training across platforms generalised better than training on one platform. Predicting several engagement targets at once also helped. Each content type added useful signal. Large language models alone predicted popularity poorly. Language understanding by itself does not capture how social cascades grow.
arxiv-2606-27739:
Reward models that grade each reasoning step can steer language models well. Training them normally needs costly step-by-step human labels. Outcome-supervised versions learn only from final-answer correctness. That creates a credit assignment problem: which steps caused the outcome? Tianyu Jia and eight colleagues propose LCA in 2026. Their guiding principle is simple: a chain fails at its weakest link.

LCA learns credit assignment and reward modelling together. The problem is cast as multiple instance learning. A new pooling method, Softmax-Weighted-Sum, handles the strong dependence among reasoning steps. The authors prove Bayes consistency of the algorithm under mild assumptions. Experiments span multiple tasks and model backbones. LCA consistently beat state-of-the-art outcome-supervised process reward models. Uniform and causal assignment schemes are the main rivals it displaces. Both fail to anchor credit in step correctness, the authors argue.
arxiv-2606-28039:
Free missions give coarser images than paid systems. Super-resolution models promise to bridge that gap. They are usually trained on synthetically degraded images, though, since no sensor gives true paired data. Dawid Kopeć and three colleagues quantify the resulting domain gap in 2026. Five leading diffusion architectures are evaluated. A large, aligned dataset pairs Sentinel-2 with PlanetScope imagery. A domain-adapted perceptual metric, LPIPS Sat, is introduced.

Two persistent challenges emerge. Models trained on synthetic data degrade sharply on real pairs. Models trained on real pairs face the opposite problem. They show optimisation difficulties and struggle with the physical diversity of real sensors. The gap survives both training routes. The findings expose a key limitation of current super-resolution. Methods that separate SR from domain adaptation are motivated.
arxiv-2606-28239:
Giacomo Brunello, Mario Meo, and Sid Smith compute how a black hole scatters a gravitational wave, a process called gravitational Compton scattering, at a deeper level of approximation than before. The post-Minkowskian expansion treats gravity as weak between encounters while keeping the full speed of light, and each order is harder to calculate.

Working inside a framework called Worldline Quantum Field Theory, Brunello and colleagues obtained the classical scattering amplitude at the fourth order. From it they derived the element that yields the phase shift for gravitational-wave scattering, at the same order. As a demanding check, their result agrees with black-hole perturbation theory, a completely separate method that treats one mass as a small ripple on the other's spacetime.
arxiv-2606-28339:
Marwan Dhuheir, Thang X. Vu, and Symeon Chatzinotas design intelligent control for industrial 6G networks, where factories need connectivity that is fast, reliable, and frugal with energy in cluttered, blockage-prone halls. Their architecture mounts reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, panels that steer radio waves, on drones, working with ground radio units plus a high-altitude platform in an Open-RAN layout.

Dhuheir and colleagues pose the joint tuning of data rates, latency, and energy use as a decentralized decision problem and solve it with several cooperating deep reinforcement learning agents. Simulations showed data rates improving by up to three quarters against strong baselines. Latency fell by about a quarter and energy use by about a sixth, supporting the case for surface-assisted open networks in industry.
arxiv-2606-28439:
Jinhao You, Zan Zhou, Shujie Yang, Yi Sun, Lei Zhang, and Changqiao Xu attack the neural networks that guard computer networks. Intrusion detectors built on deep learning catch malicious traffic well, until an attacker reshapes that traffic to slip past. Attacks borrowed from computer vision often produce traffic that is invalid on the wire or no longer does its malicious job.

You and colleagues generate adversarial traffic packet by packet instead, building features incrementally while monitoring semantic integrity at every stage. The generated packets stay protocol-valid and keep their original attack meaning. Against current detectors on three standard intrusion datasets, their method reached an average evasion rate near ninety-three percent. Careful packet-level construction, they conclude, is what makes adversarial traffic both effective and realistic.
arxiv-2606-28539:
Michael R Doboli, Alessandra R P Maranca, and Noah A Rosenberg rank evolutionary trees. A scheme by Maranca and Rosenberg assigns every unlabeled multifurcating rooted tree, where a node may have many children, its own positive integer, a bijection useful for comparing phylogenies. Which trees sit at the extremes of that ranking was known only for purely bifurcating trees.

For a fixed number of leaves, Doboli and colleagues determine the maximum and minimum ranks in two families: strictly k-furcating trees, where every internal node has exactly k descendants, and at-most-k trees. In both families the maximally balanced tree earns the minimal rank and the least balanced tree the maximal rank, a tidy link between the encoding and tree balance. They derive recurrences for the extreme ranks and pin down how the maximum grows, constants and all.
arxiv-2606-28639:
Jose Pascual Gumbau Mezquita argues, in a solo theoretical paper, that the deepest obstacle to aligning a future artificial general intelligence is not building an aligned system but ever verifying one. He presents two claimed impossibility results, which he calls the Unverifiability Theorem of Alignment and a theorem of finite structural unverifiability. He grounds them at what he terms Trakhtenbrot's Wall.

On his account, defenses built on finite hardware or halting designs cannot escape the logical blocks. Open domains fall to undecidability results in the line of Rice and Gödel. Universal finite checking collapses into incomputability, and bounded settings trap the supervisor in worst cases that cannot be solved in reasonable time. A claimed corollary is a trilemma among soundness, completeness, and tractability. Workable containment plans, he concludes, are forced give-ups of logical expressivity rather than stopgap patches.
arxiv-2606-28739:
Shawn Li and Yue Zhao argue that agent safety has been miscategorized. Chatbot safety trains models to refuse harmful outputs. Practitioners imported that recipe wholesale for agents that call tools, move money, and delete records, accepting the lost capability as an alignment tax. Agentic harm, Li and Zhao contend, does not live in any output at all.

Harm lives in the gap between the authority an action exercises and what the user actually granted, a relation invisible in the text the model reads. Their evidence covers the whole autonomy range. Defense-trained models learn surface patterns, and the training cripples multi-step agents before any attack while leaving them exploitable. Even undefended frontier models exceed granted authority in ordinary use. Safety, they conclude, cannot be built into weights; it has to be enforced as least privilege at the action boundary.
arxiv-2606-28839:
Liu introduces a measurement framework for tracking how the outputs of many interacting language models influence each other. His Contagion Tensor records how output distributions couple across three axes: modalities such as text and image, the agents involved, and time steps. From it he derives the Coupling Amplification Factor, a unitless ratio comparing coupling under a test condition against a baseline, reported with bootstrap confidence intervals.

Four variants measure network, cross-modal, temporal and full-axis coupling. In simulations, an apparent super-linear image effect largely vanished when the image perturbation module was switched off, showing the ablation could separate real coupling from design artefacts. Real tests through commercial model services told a mixed story. With uniform personas, text coupling sat near baseline in both model families tested, while mixed personas pushed toward convergence. On one model, real vision input produced clearly stronger coupling than text, matching the simulation's prediction.
arxiv-2606-28939:
Lin, Shakkottai, Kalathil and Kumar introduce ReGuide, a way for robot policies learned from demonstrations to improve themselves after deployment. Diffusion policies, which generate actions by gradually refining noise, are expressive but fragile: small drifts from demonstrated states compound into failure, a problem called covariate shift. Existing fixes either collect costly expert corrections or steer during use and discard the corrections.

ReGuide instead keeps successful guided runs as reusable recovery data. Its guidance step builds phase-specific targets and steers only when the robot has drifted but can still recover, matching the dynamics model's training conditions. Those runs then fine-tune the policy, or retrain it from scratch on the enlarged dataset. The cycle can repeat. On four Robomimic tasks, ReGuide raised success between about one and a third times and nearly eight times. Matched-data tests showed the gains came from the guided recovery data itself.
arxiv-2606-29039:
Delmond, Korsakova, Oberlin, Marsat, Basset and Dobigeon speed up source analysis for LISA, a planned space mission that will detect gravitational waves at very low frequencies. Galactic binaries, pairs of stars orbiting each other, should be LISA's most numerous sources. Their signals will overlap heavily in time and frequency, making standard Bayesian sampling slow and hard to scale.

The team use simulation-based inference instead. A conditional normalising flow, a neural network that reshapes simple distributions into complex ones, learns to estimate source parameters from simulated data. No likelihood calculation is needed in training or use. Once trained, the estimator produces thousands of posterior samples per second. The authors show results for one source in a narrow frequency band, then wider bands. As a proof of concept, they tackle two overlapping sources, the harder case motivating the whole approach.
arxiv-2606-29639:
