Stool checks remain the starting point, but better methods have raised detection a lot. The aim is a practical test ladder for clinics that cannot afford to miss this quiet parasite.
europmc-pmc3553539:
Pancreatic tumors wall themselves off from drugs, and Paolo P. Provenzano and Sunil R. Hingorani examine the physical side of that resistance in 2013. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma grows a dense, inflamed stroma and few blood vessels, and five-year survival sits under 5 percent.

The review centers on hyaluronan, a water-holding molecule that swells the tumor's matrix and drives interstitial fluid pressure extremely high. Pressure and dense matrix together collapse vessels and block drug delivery. Strategies to restore normal fluid dynamics include a delivered enzyme that digests hyaluronan, reopening the tumor bed. Breaching that sanctuary, the authors argue, could finally let chemotherapy reach cancer cells it can kill.
europmc-pmc3694839:
Edelheit and colleagues mapped a chemical mark on RNA, 5-methylcytidine, across bacteria, an archaeon, and yeast, using bisulfite treatment followed by deep sequencing. The mark was known from transfer and ribosomal RNA, but older methods could only inspect a few abundant molecules at a time.

The survey recovered most known sites and measured marks in sixty-four transfer RNAs, with patterns differing between yeast and the archaeon. The surprise was messenger RNA: the archaeon carried the mark inside its messages, guided by a shared sequence motif. The authors take this as the first evidence that archaea modify their messenger RNA, extending a form of regulation once thought mainly eukaryotic.
europmc-pmc3795039:
Kenneth Matreyek, Sara Yücel, Xiang Li, and Alan Engelman reported a study in PLoS Pathogens in 2013 on how HIV enters the cell nucleus. Lentiviruses such as HIV can infect non-dividing cells, which requires help from the cell's nuclear transport machinery. A pore protein called NUP153 was known to matter, and its partner is the virus's capsid protein.

The team showed a direct interaction between the capsid and the FG-repeat region of NUP153. Several primate lentiviruses and a horse lentivirus bound the same region, and binding tracked with each virus's need for NUP153 in infection. HIV's capsid binding mapped to a pocket that also binds a known drug and a host factor, and those rivals competed with NUP153 for it. Mutations confirmed the shared site. The authors link the interaction to HIV's ability to infect non-dividing cells.
europmc-pmc3821639:
Akinobu Takaki, Daisuke Kawai, and Kazuhide Yamamoto review fatty liver disease in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2013. Their subject is NASH, a severe form of fat buildup in the liver that can scar the organ. No single cause drives it, they argue. Many small hits land at once.

Genes, insulin resistance, and gut microbes all feed the harm. Inside cells, stress in key parts plus oxidative stress, damage from reactive oxygen, push plain fat toward swelling and scarring. Trials show anti-oxidant drugs can calm the liver short term, but long-term gain is unproven. The review highlights molecular hydrogen, which mops up only the most toxic reactive forms. It may offer a sharper way to treat the disease.
europmc-pmc3841239:
Lone Simonsen leads a team, with named collaborating teams, in a modeling study in PLoS Medicine in 2013. They estimate deaths from the 2009 influenza pandemic. Lab-confirmed death counts were low, which led some to call the event mild. The team ask what the true toll was.

Their two-stage model starts from death data in countries with good records, then extends the pattern to the world. Lab counts miss deaths where no test was done, above all in poorer regions. A model-based toll gives a fuller base for judging the pandemic and for planning the next one. The study is part of a project built to standardize such counts across countries, so future pandemics can be sized in a shared way.
europmc-pmc3855539:
Seong-Jun Kim, Mohsin Khan, Jun Quan, Andreas Till, Suresh Subramani, and Aleem Siddiqui study hepatitis B virus in cells in PLoS Pathogens in 2013. The virus causes long-term liver infection and raises liver cancer risk. It also disturbs the cell's power units, and the team trace how.

The virus pushes power units to split apart and cluster near the nucleus. It calls in a cleanup process that eats damaged units, by waking a set of tagging proteins. That cleanup blunts the cell death the virus would else trigger, letting infected cells live on. A dual-color reporter let the team watch the cleanup finish in real time. Blocking the split or the cleanup restored cell death in tests, a hint for drug ideas.
europmc-pmc3923139:
Irina Häuselmann and Lubor Borsig review the sugar coating of tumor cells. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Oncology in 2014. When cells turn malignant, the sugar chains on their surface change shape. Mucin sugars go wrong. Branched sugar trees grow larger. More sialic acid appears. These shifts track with how well a tumor invades and spreads.

Spread needs tumor cells to grip other cells as they travel. Sugar-binding proteins called lectins make those grips. The review focuses on three lectin families. Siglecs sit on immune cells and usually calm immune responses. Galectins help tumor cells survive. Selectins sit on vessel walls. They help wandering tumor cells dock and exit the blood. The authors map how each family aids spread.
europmc-pmc3945939:
Tae-Ho Lee, Hui Guo, Xiyin Wang, Changsoo Kim, and Andrew H. Paterson present SNPhylo, a ready-made pipeline for building family trees from huge SNP datasets, in BMC Genomics in 2014. Modern sequencing produces millions of single-letter DNA differences, and trees built from them underpin genetic and evolutionary studies. But handling that volume reliably, with quality checks, was left to each lab to improvise.

SNPhylo accepts three common SNP file formats and walks the data through cleaning steps: dropping poor-quality markers and thinning markers that travel together, which can distort a tree. It then infers the tree by a maximum likelihood method. The authors aim to let researchers spend their time interpreting trees instead of wrestling data into shape, and the pipeline is offered as a free download.
europmc-pmc3954939:
David E. Harrison and a large multi-site team test four candidate anti-aging compounds in mice in Aging Cell in 2014. The compounds, acarbose, a form of estradiol, nordihydroguaiaretic acid, and methylene blue, were fed to genetically varied mice at three test sites, a design meant to weed out flukes. Lifespan effects turned out to depend strongly on sex.

Acarbose stretched male median lifespan by 22 percent but female by only 5 percent. The estradiol raised male median lifespan by 12 percent and did nothing for females. The third compound added 8 to 10 percent for males at three doses and nothing for females, even at equal blood levels. Methylene blue did not change median lifespan in either sex, though it slightly raised the longest-lived females' span. Weight changes did not explain the sex gap.
europmc-pmc3964739:
Fernando Lizcano and Guillermo Guzmán review the link between estrogen loss and weight gain at menopause in BioMed Research International in 2014. Sex hormones shape where fat sits and how fat cells form, and estrogens also tune sugar and fat metabolism through their receptors. Whether losing estrogens at menopause itself drives the metabolic syndrome and heart risk that rise in those years is disputed, and the review takes up that dispute.

The authors trace estrogen action in fat tissue and in the brain centers that govern appetite and energy use. Menopause does bring a clear shift toward abdominal fat and a changed lipid profile. They also weigh estrogen-like compounds from outside the body, including endocrine-disrupting chemicals, as possible players, and they examine how falling estrogen and rising obesity feed each other.
europmc-pmc3965039:
James R. Cole and colleagues update the Ribosomal Database Project in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. The project supplies aligned, annotated ribosomal RNA gene sequences, the standard identity markers for microbes, plus tools for analyzing new sequences in the same framework. Its users span human health, microbial ecology, environmental studies, and taxonomy, and high-throughput sequencing has swollen their datasets enormously in recent years.

Release 11 adds a new collection of fungal large-subunit ribosomal genes beside the established bacterial and archaeal small-subunit sets, and the project's Classifier and Aligner tools now handle the fungal data. Most tools also accept the paired-end reads modern sequencers produce, and many are released as open-source packages so labs can run them on their own large datasets.
europmc-pmc3985639:
Ron L. Dy, Rita Przybilski, Koen Semeijn, George P. C. Salmond, and Peter C. Fineran unmask a bacterial suicide-defense system in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. Abortive infection systems make an infected bacterium die before its virus invader can multiply, saving the population. Screening such systems led the team to AbiE, which proved to be a toxin-antitoxin pair of an unusual, non-touching kind: the antitoxin calms the toxin without binding it directly.

The two-gene unit regulates itself, the antitoxin switching its own operon off through a DNA-gripping front domain, while its rear domain both represses and neutralizes. The toxin grabs the energy molecule GTP, and breaking its grip motifs removed its toxicity. Family members turn up across many bacteria, so the authors present AbiE as a widespread defense design.
europmc-pmc3986639:
Federica Genovese, Alba A. Manresa, Diana Julie Leeming, Morten Asser Karsdal, and Peter Boor ask whether kidney scarring can be read from the tissue matrix itself, in Fibrogenesis and Tissue Repair in 2014. Scarring of the kidney's interior is the common final path to kidney failure, but its course varies wildly between patients. Today only a biopsy can prove fibrosis, and existing blood or urine markers do not reflect the scarring specifically, leaving doctors short of guidance on who will progress.

The matrix proteins around kidney cells are constantly cut and rebuilt, and the cutting leaves distinctive fragments, neo-epitopes, that escape into blood and urine. Fingerprint assays for those fragments could report the scarring process directly and non-invasively. The review weighs the evidence for matrix-derived markers of diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment response.
europmc-pmc4001039:
Inelia Morales, Leonardo Guzmán-Martínez, Cristóbal Cerda-Troncoso, Gonzalo A. Farías, and Ricardo B. Maccioni set out a frame for Alzheimer's disease centred on brain inflammation, in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2014. Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia in older people. Its triggers stay unclear, which has slowed the search for a working treatment.

Hints came from patients who took anti-inflammatory drugs and showed lower rates of the disease. The authors' theory links nerve damage to a slow immune build-up in the brain. Damage signals, from injury, infection, or clumps of the proteins tau and beta-amyloid, stir two support cell types, astrocytes and microglia. Those cells then pour out inflammatory agents that harm nerves further. The paper weighs that process and rates natural anti-inflammatory compounds, among them curcumin and a new Andean compound.
europmc-pmc4016539:
Oumar Faye, Ousmane Faye, Diawo Diallo, Mawlouth Diallo, Manfred Weidmann, and Amadou Alpha Sall build a fast gene test for Zika virus, in the Virology Journal in 2013. Zika is a mosquito-borne virus found in Africa and Asia. Blood antibody tests confuse it with kin viruses, and growing the virus is slow and needs strict containment.

From a gene stretch shared by African Zika strains, the team designed a one-step test that copies and reads it at once, finishing in under three hours. It caught all thirty-seven Zika strains tried, drawn from across Africa and Asia over decades, and none of the thirty-one other flaviviruses tested. Its detection floor was very low, at a small fraction of an infectious dose. Field-caught mosquitoes yielded clear reads with the method. The authors offer it for places where Zika mixes with look-alike fevers such as dengue.
europmc-pmc4053839:
Dvir Aran, Sivan Sabato, and Asaf Hellman show that methylation at distant enhancer sites tracks gene activity across the genome, in Genome Biology in 2013. Methylation near gene starts was the classic epigenetic signal. The control sites far from genes, the enhancers, had barely been studied in this role.

Working from methylation and expression data across dozens of cell types, the team modelled how promoter methylation relates to activity, then extended the logic genome-wide. They mapped many far-off sites whose methylation matched the activity of distant genes. These sites carry the marks of a known enhancer class and bind their factors in a methylation-sensitive way. One enhancer could set a gradient of activity across many cell types, not just an on-off state. In cancers the pattern broke hard: enhancer methylation shifts lined up with cancer gene misregulation more tightly than promoter shifts did.
europmc-pmc4087039:
Cari M. Kitahara, Patricia Hartge, and colleagues pooled twenty prospective studies to link extreme obesity with death rates. Their analysis appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2014. Class III obesity, a body mass index from forty to just under sixty, had grown fast in developed countries, yet its exact toll was unclear.

People in that weight range died at higher rates overall than people of normal weight. The excess was driven particularly by heart disease, cancer, and diabetes. Extreme obesity already affected about six percent of United States adults and carried a large share of health care spending. Clearer risk numbers, the authors argue, are needed to plan effective interventions and to project future care costs honestly.
europmc-pmc4143239:
Maren Johanne Heilskov Rytter and colleagues systematically reviewed how malnutrition affects the immune system of young children. Their review appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Malnourished children die more often, mostly of infections, and weak immunity is a suspected mechanism that had never been fully reviewed.

From over three thousand papers, two hundred forty-five met their rules, covering children from one month to five years with wasting, stunting, or swelling forms of malnutrition. Malnutrition came with a leaky gut barrier, fewer protective secretions, and low complement protein levels. Lymph tissue, above all the thymus, shrank, and skin test responses faded. Vaccine antibody levels also fell in severe cases. Most studies were old, and the authors demand better modern work.
europmc-pmc4231239:
Siamon Gordon, Annette Plüddemann, and Fernando Martinez Estrada reviewed macrophage variety across tissues in Immunological Reviews in 2014. Macrophages settle in every tissue before birth and stand guard there, with fresh recruits arriving after injury. Each tissue dresses its macrophages differently, yet most knowledge came from cells grown in dishes.

The review surveys what resident macrophages look like and do in their home tissues, from brain to gut to liver, and how the local environment shapes their markers and jobs. This variety underpins both steady housekeeping and the start of disease when the balance breaks. The authors note how little is known about the cells in place, compared with cultured ones, and they set out the open questions for the field.
europmc-pmc4250839:
Joannah R. Fergusson and a team of eleven co-authors profiled a marker shared across T cell families in Cell Reports in 2014. CD161 is a surface protein carried by many human T cells, including the innate-like MAIT cells of the gut and liver. Whether the marker flags a shared program or just a shared coat was unknown.

Using mass cytometry and gene activity arrays in parallel, the team found CD161-high cells from CD8, CD4, and gamma-delta lineages share one gene signature, richest in MAIT cells. All these groups also answered two alarm signals, interleukin-12 and interleukin-18, with the same innate-style response, without needing their antigen receptor. CD161 itself boosted receptor-driven responses rather than steering the shared one. The marker, they conclude, labels a functional type that cuts across T cell lineages.
europmc-pmc4263139:
Shota Nakade, Tetsushi Sakuma, and eight co-authors presented a gene insertion method called PITCh in Nature Communications in 2014. Knocking a new DNA stretch into a chosen genome spot usually relies on homology-directed repair, which is inefficient in many cells and animals. An alternative repair route, microhomology-mediated end joining, needs only very short matching arms.

The PITCh system cuts both the target and a donor plasmid with designer nucleases, TALENs or CRISPR Cas9, and lets the short-arm repair stitch the donor in. It worked in human cells and in silkworms and frogs, animals where standard knock-in is painful. The Cas9 version inserted DNA without dragging plasmid backbone along. The authors offer the method for precise insertions across cultured cells and whole organisms.
europmc-pmc4270739:
R Plomin and I J Deary sum up five findings about genes and intelligence that they judge stand apart. Their review appeared in Molecular Psychiatry in 2015. Intelligence predicts schooling, work, health, and length of life, and it is among the most heritable of human traits.

Among the five: the heritable share of intelligence grows from childhood into old age. Diverse mental skills share much of their genetic base. Spouses also match on intelligence more than on most other traits. The authors draw out what these patterns mean for the search for the genes involved. The piece gives a compact entry point to a large and contested field.
europmc-pmc4320539:
Alison O'Mara-Eves, James Thomas, John McNaught, Makoto Miwa, and Sophia Ananiadou reviewed how text mining software is used to screen studies for systematic reviews. Their review appeared in Systematic Reviews in 2015. The flood of published papers makes finding every relevant study slow and costly, and screening titles and abstracts eats reviewer time.

Text mining can rank or pre-sort papers so humans read the likeliest ones first. The review gathers the scattered evidence on these tools, asks how workload savings were measured, and checks how well the claims hold. Written for non-technical readers, it aims to spur joint work between computer scientists and review teams. The field, it finds, is promising but short on shared evaluation standards.
europmc-pmc4342639:
Clemens Scott Kruse, Katy Bolton, and Greg Freriks reviewed studies on patient portals, the websites that let patients see their records and message their doctors. Their systematic review appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2015. American law was pressing hospitals to offer portals under the Meaningful Use program, on the assumption that engaged patients get better care.

The team searched three databases for data driven studies since 2011 that tied portal use or portal features to quality outcomes, especially for chronic disease. Evidence of outcome gains was thinner and more mixed than the policy assumed, though satisfaction and access measures fared better. The review updates an earlier one and cautions Meaningful Use planners about what portals can yet prove.
europmc-pmc4352739:
Laura Marín, Elisa Miguélez, Claudio Villar, and Felipe Lombó reviewed plant polyphenols in BioMed Research International in 2015. Polyphenols are a large, varied family of plant compounds found in foods, including flavonoids, tannins, and chlorogenic acids. Their review asks how much of these compounds the body can use, how gut microbes change them, and whether the changed forms can kill germs.

Most polyphenols reach the gut tied to sugars, so enzymes and gut microbes must first trim them before they can be absorbed into the blood. From there they pass to the liver and other organs, or leave in urine. Along that path, the compounds and their breakdown products show strong action against viruses, bacteria, and parasites. Which microbes do the trimming shapes which active forms appear.
europmc-pmc4359439:
Amit Deshwar, Shankar Vembu, Christina Yung, Gun Ho Jang, Lincoln Stein, and Quaid Morris presented a software tool called PhyloWGS in Genome Biology in 2015. Tumors are mixes of cell groups, each with its own set of mutations, grown from a single ancestor. Reading a tumor's whole genome gives tangled data from all groups at once. The tool aims to unmix that data and rebuild each group's makeup and family tree.

PhyloWGS uses how often point mutations appear, plus how often larger structural changes appear, across one or more tumor samples. It adds a careful fix for spots where copy number changes would otherwise skew the mutation rates. Tests showed that fix greatly improves rebuilding compared with older methods. The software is free and open source, so other labs can run and adapt it.
europmc-pmc4363839:
Bairen Zhu, Xi Chen, and Xiaodong Cui measured a key energy value in an atom-thin material, in Scientific Reports in 2015. Their material was a single layer of tungsten disulfide, part of a family of thin crystals with strong light effects. In such thin layers, electrons and the holes they leave bind tightly into pairs called excitons. How strongly they bind was the open question the team set out to pin down with light-based tests.

Using two light methods, including two-photon excitation scans, the team placed the exciton binding energy at about 0.71 electron volts, with a small stated error range. That is a large share of the material's energy gap, far above what bulk crystals show. Strong binding in such thin layers shapes how they absorb and emit light. The value helps guide work on thin-crystal light devices.
europmc-pmc4435039:
Anne Davin-Regli and Jean-Marie Pagès reviewed two hospital bacteria, Enterobacter aerogenes and Enterobacter cloacae, in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2015. Both are Gram-negative bacteria that infect patients whose defenses are already weak. Over three decades they became known across Europe, and notably in France, for hospital outbreaks and for resisting many antibiotics.

Several traits make them hard to beat. Layers of control systems adjust the cell membrane so drugs enter less easily, while enzymes that break down or inactivate antibiotics are switched on as needed. The bacteria also pick up mobile DNA pieces that carry further resistance, and they adapt fast to new hosts and settings. The review tracks which species now dominates reports and asks whether shared mobile elements explain the shift.
europmc-pmc4439539:
Roser Sala-Llonch, David Bartrés-Faz, and Carme Junqué reviewed brain network changes in healthy aging in Frontiers in Psychology in 2015. Even without disease, aging brings some loss of mental sharpness. Brain scans during tasks often show older adults lighting up some areas more strongly than young adults, a pattern often read as the brain making up for losses elsewhere.

Newer work looks instead at functional connectivity, how strongly areas act together, often measured while the brain rests. Those studies find extra activity alongside weaker or altered links between networks. The review explains basic concepts and method pitfalls, sums up both task and resting findings, and sets them against models of how the aging brain copes. It closes with directions for research that could separate helpful reorganization from harmful breakdown.
europmc-pmc4443739:
Leslie Chávez-Galán, Maria Olleros, Dominique Vesin, and Irene Garcia argued in Frontiers in Immunology in 2015 that macrophages come in more kinds than the standard two. Macrophages are immune cells that kill invaders or repair tissue. Textbooks sort activated macrophages into M1, the attacking kind, and M2, the healing kind, grown from blood monocytes under different signals.

Two further kinds get full treatment here. CD169-positive macrophages sit at borders where blood and lymph are filtered, while TCR-positive macrophages carry a receptor long thought to belong only to T cells, and their origin is still unclear. Tumor-linked macrophages are also covered. The review details each kind's markers and its part in cancer, infection, obesity, and asthma, urging finer labels to match the cells' real variety.
europmc-pmc4451739:
Nicolas Merle, Sarah Church, Veronique Fremeaux-Bacchi, and Lubka Roumenina explained how the complement system is switched on and kept in check, in Frontiers in Immunology in 2015. Complement is a set of blood proteins that forms a first line of defense against foreign and altered cells. Its chain of reactions must fire only where needed, or it will damage the host's own tissue.

As the first of a two-part review, the article walks through the three starting routes, called alternative, classical, and lectin pathways, and the enzyme complexes they build. It covers the small fragments that draw immune cells and the final membrane attack complex that pierces target cells. Structure-function lessons come from a rare kidney disease caused by faulty control. The authors also discuss drugs that block complement, where careful targeting turns a blunt defense into a treatment.
europmc-pmc4455139:
Yei Hwan Jung and a large team of co-authors built flexible electronics on paper made from plant fibers, in Nature Communications in 2015. Phones and tablets are made largely from non-renewable, non-degradable, and sometimes toxic materials, and they are thrown away often. A greener base for electronics would cut that waste, if devices on it still performed well.

The team used cellulose nanofibril paper, a smooth, bendable sheet made from tiny plant fibers, as the base. On it they built microwave and digital parts that matched the performance of parts on rigid bases while using very little toxic material. Gallium arsenide parts, the workhorse of wireless devices, were made in a thin film that can be transferred onto the paper. Fungi could break the finished devices down, showing a path to electronics that return to nature.
europmc-pmc4456639:
Stuart Cahalan, Viktor Lukacs, Sanjeev Ranade, Shu Chien, Michael Bandell, Ardem Patapoutian, and Jeremy Nathans linked the pressure channel Piezo1 to red blood cell volume in eLife in 2015. Red blood cells are squeezed hard as they circulate, but what those forces do to the cells was unclear. Overactive Piezo1 mutations cause a disease in which red cells lose water and dry out, hinting that the channel controls cell volume.

Stretched red cells let calcium in through Piezo1, the team shows. Mice whose blood cells lacked Piezo1 had swollen, fragile red cells in the dish and in the body. The chemical activator Yoda1 triggered calcium entry and then water loss through a downstream potassium channel. Together the results make mechanically opened Piezo1 an essential governor of red cell volume, tying a physical force to a cell's water balance.
europmc-pmc4515639:
Huanyu Xu, Sen Guo, Wei Li, and Ping Yu studied a circular RNA in insulin-making cells, reported in Scientific Reports in 2015. The loop, called Cdr1as, was already known as a strong sponge for a small RNA named miR-7 in the zebrafish brain. Since miR-7 is plentiful in pancreatic islet cells, and too much of it causes diabetes in mice, the team asked what the loop does there.

Cdr1as levels rose after long treatment with signals that work through two known cell pathways, but not after high glucose. Adding extra Cdr1as to islet cells raised both stored insulin and released insulin. The team found two miR-7 targets behind the effect: Myrip, which helps move insulin granules, and Pax6, which boosts insulin gene activity.
europmc-pmc4595839:
Dane R. Samuelson, David A. Welsh, and Judd E. Shellito published a 2015 review on how gut microbes shape lung immunity. Lung infections and asthma cause huge illness burdens, and new treatments are needed. Evidence has grown that microbes in the intestine affect immune responses far away in the lung. The review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology.

The authors survey studies linking an unbalanced gut community, often called dysbiosis, to worse lung defence and disease. They trace how gut microbes help train immune cells and set inflammation levels that reach the airways. The so-called gut-lung axis may explain why gut problems and lung problems often travel together. Understanding these links could point to treatments that support lung health by way of the gut.
europmc-pmc4649539:
Jian-Ying Liu and colleagues published a 2014 study on MALAT1, a long non-coding RNA, in diabetic eye disease. Their earlier work tied MALAT1 misregulation to diabetic retinopathy, where retinal blood vessels decay. This study asked how the RNA harms the vessel lining. Tests used diabetic rats and mice plus cultured retinal cells. The work appeared in Cell Death and Disease.

MALAT1 levels rose sharply in diabetic retinas. Silencing it in animals reduced pericyte loss, capillary decay, leakage, and inflammation. In cells it also controlled growth, movement, and tube formation. Crosstalk with the p38 MAPK signalling pathway carried part of the effect. Because blocking MALAT1 protected vessels, the authors propose it as a target for treating diabetes-related microvascular complications.
europmc-pmc4699039:
Marco Tafani, Luigi Sansone, Federica Limana, and five colleagues traced how reactive oxygen species drive cancer, in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2016. These reactive molecules, called ROS, are a constant byproduct of cells using oxygen. Cancer cells make extra amounts, and ROS play a part at every stage of a tumor's life, from the first change to later spread. The review sets out to reconcile reports that ROS both harm and help.

Attention centers on three control systems: the oxygen sensor HIF, the inflammation switch NF-kappaB, and the sirtuin family of enzymes. ROS feed into each, linking low oxygen, inflammation, and cell aging signals into one story of tumor growth. The authors fit the known hallmarks of cancer into a step-by-step sequence. Their sketch gives readers a single map of how one chemical force threads through cancer's whole course.
europmc-pmc4702839:
Alex H. Wagner, Adam C. Coffman, Benjamin J. Ainscough, and nine colleagues released DGIdb 2.0 in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. The Drug-Gene Interaction Database gathers claims about which drugs act on which genes, and which genes look druggable, from many scattered sources. Version two drew on twenty-seven sources after heavy hand curation. Nine new sources were added, seven of them tied to clinical trials, more than doubling the interaction count.

Claims about druggable genes rose by thirty percent. Most public sources behind the database now refresh automatically each week, keeping entries current. A new search by drug name joins the older gene-first search, and the programming interface was documented for other software. The result is a practical mining tool for precision medicine: clinicians and researchers can ask which known drugs touch a patient's gene of interest, and how strong the evidence is.
europmc-pmc4752239:
Matthew J. Blow leads a team of twelve authors in a PLoS Genetics study from 2016 on chemical marks placed on DNA in bacteria and archaea. Methylation, the marks at issue, guards these genomes and may also steer gene activity. How wide its reach runs across microbes was poorly mapped.

Using single-molecule sequencing, the team read methylation patterns across 230 species. Nearly all carried marks. They logged 834 distinct marked motifs and tied 620 methyl transfer enzymes to the patterns they write. Almost half the species held active enzymes with no matching cutting partner, which hints at roles in gene control and copying. The survey shows methylation is a near-universal feature of microbe genomes.
europmc-pmc4777539:
Yen-Rei A. Yu leads nine authors in PLoS ONE in 2016 with a standard method for counting immune cells in body tissues. Flow cytometry sorts cells by their surface marks, and it is the workhorse for reading a tissue's immune mix. Yet each lab built its own recipe, and none covered all major cell types across many tissues at once.

Their protocol sets tissue preparation, a ten-color stain panel, and a fixed sorting scheme in one package. It counts eleven major immune cell types in lung, heart, liver, kidney, gut, skin, eye, and breast tissue, healthy or inflamed, with low cell loss. It also cleanly splits two look-alike cell types that labs often blur. Tumor tests showed it can even split tumor-linked cell groups by the tumor line that raised them.
europmc-pmc4817139:
Julian S. Gehring, Bernd Fischer, Michael Lawrence, and Wolfgang Huber present an R software package in Bioinformatics in 2015. Cancer genomes carry patterns of single-letter changes, called mutational signatures, that fingerprint the processes which made them, from smoking to faulty repair. Reading those fingerprints helps trace how a tumor arose.

Earlier tools for the job each used their own file formats, which kept them apart from the standard analysis flow. Their package, SomaticSignatures, brings signature hunting into the Bioconductor ecosystem, the field's shared toolkit. It counts changes with their neighboring letters, applies established pattern-splitting methods, and lets users plug in their own. The authors stress scale and fit: large cross-study runs become routine rather than bespoke.
europmc-pmc4845539:
Michelle A. Sugimoto and four co-authors reviewed what starts the shut-down phase of inflammation, in Frontiers in Immunology in 2016. Inflammation that never resolves can harden into chronic disease. The review stresses that the shut-down program is active, planned, and begins soon after inflammation starts, not after it fades. Signals that drive the attack phase can also switch on the cleanup.

Key steps include falling levels of the signals that call in neutrophils, the first-responder white cells. Those same neutrophils, though attack cells, also help trigger resolution. Mapping these start signals could yield drugs that push the body to finish inflammation cleanly, a field the review calls resolution pharmacology.
europmc-pmc4873939:
M. Isabel Veiga and co-authors showed in Nature Communications in 2016 that common changes in a malaria parasite transporter shift drug response in mixed directions. Malaria care worldwide rests on artemisinin-based combination drugs, and resistance spreads. Using gene editing tools, the team altered the PfMDR1 transporter at two spots in Plasmodium falciparum.

One widespread change, N86Y, raised resistance to the partner drug amodiaquine and to the older drug chloroquine. Yet the same change made parasites more open to lumefantrine, mefloquine, and the active form of artemisinin. Drug choice can thus exploit a fault's trade-offs. Tracking which change dominates in each region becomes a guide for pairing drugs well.
europmc-pmc4917339:
Leandro Quadrana and co-authors charted the mobilome of the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana in 2016: the full set of its jumping DNA elements and their recent moves. Genome reads for 211 plant lines from around the world revealed thousands of fresh jumps, touching half of the 326 known element families. Activity varied widely between lines with climate and ancestry.

Jumps land evenly across the genome but are purged fast from gene-rich zones, since they often break genes. Hot targets, strikingly, are genes that control responses to the environment. Jumping DNA thus acts as a fast, risky supplier of raw variation right where adaptation needs it. Species-level maps change how such elements are judged.
europmc-pmc4938539:
Louise H. Hall and four co-authors review whether staff wellbeing and burnout track with patient safety. Their systematic review appeared in PLoS ONE in 2016. Tired, distressed staff may make more errors, but the evidence had never been pulled together. The team searched four major databases plus reference lists. They kept quantitative studies of healthcare staff that measured wellbeing or burnout alongside a patient safety outcome.

Forty-six studies qualified. Of 27 studies on wellbeing, sixteen found that poor wellbeing went with worse safety, and six more found links on some scales. Of 30 studies on burnout, twenty-one tied burnout to worse safety. One study ran against the trend. The authors conclude that staff wellbeing is part of patient safety, not a side issue. They urge health services to treat work conditions as a safety input.
europmc-pmc4982339:
Karen M. Bussard and four co-authors review tumor-associated stromal cells, the support cells cancers recruit from nearby tissue. Their review appeared in Breast Cancer Research in 2016. A tumor is more than its cancer cells. Recruited stroma includes vessel cells, fat cells, fibroblasts, and marrow derived stem cells. During wound healing, local stroma turns reactive to help repair. Tumor cells hijack that program and push the cells further into a tumor serving state.

These converted cells pour out growth and vessel signals, and enzymes that open paths for invasion. They also help tumors resist therapy. The review catalogs the cell types and their marker proteins, and weighs their roles in spread, immune infiltration, and drug resistance. The authors argue the stroma is a drug target in its own right. Cutting a tumor's support system, they say, may succeed where attacking cancer cells alone stalls.
europmc-pmc5035139:
Anderson M. Winkler, Gerard R. Ridgway, Gwenaëlle Douaud, Thomas E. Nichols, and Stephen M. Smith speed up permutation testing in NeuroImage in 2016. Permutation tests judge brain imaging results by reshuffling data thousands of times. On large datasets that reshuffling can take prohibitively long. The team compared six shortcuts that exploit the math of the standard imaging model.

All six kept error rates exact and power close to the full test. Some shortcuts resample less, some fit a smooth curve to the reshuffle results, and one skips reshuffling entirely by predicting its outcome from the test statistic's shape. That last method was fastest of all where its assumptions hold. Methods differed mainly in resampling risk, the chance of flipping a decision on a rerun. On fake data and a real brain-shape study, the shortcuts gave near-identical maps. The work ships in a free tool called PALM.
europmc-pmc5052039:
Xiao-Ou Zhang and seven co-authors map the splicing variety of circular RNAs in Genome Research in 2016. Circular RNAs form when a gene's building blocks are joined in reverse order, closing a loop. One gene can make many loops by choosing different join points and the same cut-and-keep choices, called alternative splicing, that diversify ordinary RNA. No detailed map existed, so the team built one with an upgraded pipeline.

Across several cell lines, circular RNAs showed splicing patterns distinct from their straight counterparts. All four alternative splicing types appeared inside circles, and some blocks were kept almost only in circular form. Thousands of unknown exons turned up inside the circles, less conserved over evolution than known ones. The join-point choices tracked competing RNA pairing across the loops. All results feed a public database, CIRCpedia, for studies of how circles form and what they do.
europmc-pmc5088339:
Alexander V. Ivanov and six co-authors review oxidative stress in HIV infection in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2016. Reactive oxygen species are normal cell byproducts, but when they outrun the cell's defenses they damage molecules and distort signals. The review gathers markers showing HIV-1 pushes cells into that state, and the mechanisms by which the virus provokes it.

The authors then ask what the stress does to the virus itself, and where the infected cell's defenses stand. They connect the redox imbalance to hallmark harms of HIV. These include brain toxicity and dementia, exhaustion of the CD4 and CD8 T cells the virus targets, vulnerability to lung infections, and some side effects of antiretroviral therapy. Nitrosative stress gets a comparison. Their gaps list points future work at shared control points among the many stress sources, and at how defense systems differ between acute and chronic infection.
europmc-pmc5089539:
Duncan A. A. MacLaren and six co-authors reported a rat study in eNeuro in 2016. They tested clozapine N-oxide, or CNO, a drug used to switch engineered brain receptors called DREADDs on or off. CNO was long treated as inert, yet the body can convert it into clozapine, an active drug.

In male Long-Evans rats, one dose of CNO weakened the startle reflex but left a measure of sensory gating unchanged. Higher doses did not change movement on their own, yet one dose blunted the extra movement caused by amphetamine and cut the related rise in dopamine. Blood tests found clozapine after CNO dosing, so the group urges every DREADD study to include animals given CNO without the receptors.
europmc-pmc5114739:
Yasin Şenbabaoğlu and a large team of co-authors profiled immune cells inside kidney tumors in Genome Biology in 2016. They used gene activity data to estimate 24 immune cell types across 19 cancers. Then they focused on clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the main kidney cancer. It scored among the highest for immune entry.

They sorted these tumors into three groups: rich in T cells, mixed, and bare of immune cells. The immune richness did not track with mutation counts; instead it matched how strongly tumors displayed their antigen-presenting machinery. Certain T cell mixes predicted better survival in two patient groups, while other mixes predicted worse outcomes. Tumors with more immune entry also had fewer subclones, and the gene signatures found may guide prognosis and immunotherapy choices.
europmc-pmc5121339:
Michal Bassani-Sternberg and a large team of co-authors hunted for cancer targets on real tumor tissue, reporting in Nature Communications in 2016. Mutated protein fragments displayed on a tumor's surface could guide immune therapy, but no one had fished such neoepitopes directly out of native human melanoma.

Using advanced mass spectrometry, they catalogued 95,500 peptides shown on patient melanoma tissue, including cancer-testis antigens and modified peptides. Among them sat eleven fragments carrying tumor mutations. Four of the eleven provoked responses from the patients' own T cells, and T cells matching chosen neoepitopes turned up in tumor and blood. The team concludes that direct reading of tumor tissue can supply genuine targets for personalized immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc5189939:
Camille Roux, Christelle Fraïsse, Jonathan Romiguier, Yoann Anciaux, Nicolas Galtier, and Nicolas Bierne ask where one species ends and another begins. They compared genomic data from 61 pairs of animal populations or species at different levels of divergence. Gene flow between each pair was estimated with approximate Bayesian computation. The in-between "grey zone" of speciation, where taxonomy is often disputed, spanned 0.5% to 2% of net synonymous divergence.

That range held regardless of the animals' life history or ecology. By modeling how drift and introgression vary across loci, the team clarified most of the ambiguous cases and uncovered several cryptic species. Semi-isolated species, where only some loci face barriers to gene flow, proved common. The authors stress that drawing species lines inside the grey zone is hard. The reasons are both statistical and conceptual. They argue the zone itself deserves study, rather than being treated as a nuisance.
europmc-pmc5209439:
Vinciane Saint-Criq and Michael A. Gray reviewed the CFTR channel and epithelial function in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences in 2017. Epithelia are the cell sheets that line body surfaces and cavities, and they must move salt and water in a tightly controlled way. CFTR is an anion channel that helps run both fluid secretion and absorption in tissues such as the airways, gut, pancreas, and sweat glands.

Faulty CFTR causes cystic fibrosis, one of the most common life-limiting inherited diseases, and it also plays a part in cholera-type diarrhoea, pancreatitis, chronic lung disease, and asthma. The review explains how CFTR keeps surface fluid at the right depth and acidity, then walks through its work in three settings: the airways, the pancreas, and the sweat gland. It also notes drug approaches that fix or boost the channel and backup channels that might offset its loss.
europmc-pmc5257139:
Edwin Bramwell and W. R. Addis reported four new cases of myotonia atrophica in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1913. The name gathers cases that join myotonia, a stiffness in which muscles relax slowly, the hallmark of Thomsen's disease, with muscular wasting. Whether this pairing is Thomsen's disease plus wasting or a disease in its own right was still unsettled.

Their first case was a 27-year-old former miner and naval reservist. He had always been mentally slow, grew irritable and hard to manage, and began dropping heavy objects as hand weakness set in after a fall. The conclusions stress that myotonia can hide: the telltale electrical and mechanical reactions may show even when stiff movements do not. Myotonic signs usually come long before the wasting. The small muscles of hands and feet waste often, and no fixed map for the wasting has been found.
europmc-pmc5310839:
Dari Kimanius, Björn O. Forsberg, Sjors H. W. Scheres, and Erik Lindahl reported a speed gain for a structure tool in eLife in 2016. The tool, RELION, works out the shapes of tiny cell parts from electron microscope images. That method now reaches near atom detail for many samples. But the math is heavy, and slow runs limit how much work labs can do.

The team rewrote the heaviest steps to run on graphics cards, the chips built for games. Sorting images and refining shapes ran more than ten times faster. Picking particles from raw images ran more than a hundred times faster. Memory needs were cut to fit common desktop cards, and simpler math did not harm the results. A full high detail run can now finish in days on one work station, not weeks on a large cluster.
europmc-pmc5319839:
Chethan Pandarinath and co-authors reported a brain-computer link for people with paralysis in eLife in 2017. Small sensor arrays sit in the brain's movement area and read its signals. A decoder turns those signals into control of a screen cursor and keyboard. For people who cannot move or speak, such a link can restore a way to write and talk.

Three trial participants with paralysis tested the system. All three beat the marks set by past brain links of this kind. One woman typed freely for long stretches at a pace of roughly twenty-four correct letters per minute. The gains came in large part from sharper decoder design, grown out of past animal and human work. The authors argue that this level of speed and control brings daily use closer for people with grave loss of movement and speech.
europmc-pmc5331439:
Wageha A. Awad, Claudia Hess, and Michael Hess reviewed gut barrier harm in chickens in Toxins in 2017. A healthy gut wall is the first shield between a bird and the germs and toxins in its food. The wall is a single sheet of cells, stitched by seams called tight junctions. Those seams block free passage of water and dissolved stuff between cells.

Germs and their toxins can loosen the seams. The result is a leaky gut, where germs and toxins slip through the wall and reach the whole body. That breach upsets gut balance and raises the risk of body-wide infection, long swelling, and poor food uptake. The review sorts the main chicken gut pathogens and shows how each one's toxins pry at set seam proteins. The seams are not mere glue: some of their parts form fine channels of their own.
europmc-pmc5334539:
Kendal McCulloch, Gary J. Litherland, and Taranjit Singh Rai reviewed worn-out cells in joint disease in Aging Cell in 2017. Osteoarthritis is the most common disease of the moving joints. It slowly breaks down cartilage, stiffens the joint, and robs it of use. Age is its top risk factor. Cells that stop dividing for good, called senescent cells, build up as we age.

Cartilage cells in the sick joint show many wear marks: worn gene ends, a marker enzyme, and a brake protein called p16. The soup of signals those worn cells release looks strikingly like the mix seen in joint disease. The review sets out how such cells may seed and feed the disease. It also covers mark-level gene changes shared by aging and joint disease. Grasping the links could open fresh routes to treatment.
europmc-pmc5340039:
Maria I. Fonseca and co-authors hunted the source of a brain defense protein in mice, in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2017. The protein, C1q, starts a defense chain that guards against infection. The same chain prunes nerve links in youth, a needful task that can turn harmful with age and disease. C1q shows up near nerve links, in brain guard cells, and in a set of nerve cells.

The team cut the C1q gene in just one cell type at a time. Cutting it in nerve cells changed nothing in the wider brain. Cutting it in microglia, the brain's own guard cells, left the brain near empty of C1q, bar a few nerve cells. That loss held from youth through old age and in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Liver and kidney levels stayed normal. Microglia, they conclude, supply near all brain C1q.
europmc-pmc5356239:
Gunnar Aronsson led a team that pooled studies of work settings and burnout in BMC Public Health in 2017. Burnout grows as drained feeling, cynicism, and loss of a sense of worth at work. Doctors and insurers need firm proof on which job traits feed it. Many past studies tracked drained feeling alone and skipped the other two legs of the syndrome.

The team screened work factors across studies from Europe, North America, and the South Pacific lands. Only studies that tracked workers for one to five years and checked them again qualified. Twenty-five papers passed the bar. The pooled grades found fair proof that low job control feeds drained feeling, and that low support from the workplace does the same. Thin proof tied justice, demands, workload, reward, and boss support to the syndrome. High support and fair treatment guarded against it.
europmc-pmc5394239:
Yuan Yuan and eleven co-authors report a 2017 Nature Communications study of the spike proteins of two deadly coronaviruses, MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV. The spike sits on the virus coat and locks onto host cells, deciding which tissues the virus can enter. Using a freezing microscope method, the team built sharp three-dimensional views of both spikes in their pre-entry form.

Most of each spike matched spikes of kin viruses, but the part that grips the host cell stood out. That part was caught in two poses, one tucked away and one raised for binding, showing that it swings with ease. Shared stretches across six human coronaviruses mark spots where broad antibodies might strike. The work guides vaccine and drug design.
europmc-pmc5428439:
Rupp and co-authors use CRISPR to knock out the PD-1 brake in human CAR T cells. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. CAR T cells are engineered lymphocytes that hunt tumors. Tumors can wear the ligand PD-L1. That ligand engages PD-1 on T cells. The contact leaves CAR T cells hypo-functional. Tumor clearance then falters. The team asked whether deleting PD-1 restores power.

They built a protocol that pairs two steps. Cas9 ribonucleoprotein editing disrupts the Pdcd1 gene. Lentiviral delivery installs the anti-CD19 receptor. Edited cells killed tumor cells better in dishes. In mouse xenografts, they cleared PD-L1-positive tumors faster. Unedited CAR T cells lagged behind. The work shows editing and receptor delivery can combine. Precision genome engineering may strengthen cell therapies. Checkpoint removal inside the cell is one such upgrade.
europmc-pmc5445139:
Temple and co-authors review the safety of caffeine in food and drink. Their comprehensive review appeared in Frontiers in Psychiatry. Caffeine is the world's most used psychoactive drug. It occurs in coffee, tea, and chocolate. Makers now add it to many new products. Intake patterns have shifted with that spread. Regulators want to know the safe dose. Some groups face higher risk than others.

The review sorts evidence for healthy adults first. For them, intake looks relatively safe. It then turns to vulnerable groups. Pregnant and nursing women need care. So do children, teens, and young adults. People with heart disease or mental illness also rate caution. Harms can touch the heart, sleep, and substance use. The authors weighed trials, surveys, and past reviews. Animal data filled gaps on mechanism. They close with gaps in the proof and research needs.
europmc-pmc5447239:
Kapli and co-authors present a faster tool for drawing species lines from DNA data. Their methods paper appeared in Bioinformatics. Field surveys now collect vast sets of DNA barcodes. Workers must group those reads into species. Older tools use fixed cut-offs or run too slowly on big sets.

The new method, called mPTP, builds on an older tree-based method. It lets each species vary at its own rate. Tests on real data found more true species than rival tools did. The authors report a speedup of at least five orders of magnitude. A free program and web service carry the method.
europmc-pmc546039:
Stewart and co-authors demonstrate aging in E. coli, a bacterium long thought functionally immortal. Their study appeared in PLoS Biology. E. coli divides into two seemingly identical cells. It has no juvenile phase. Theory held that such organisms cannot age. Aging seemed to need visible asymmetry at division. The team followed individual cells by automated time-lapse microscopy. They tracked repeated reproduction cycles cell by cell.

A hidden asymmetry emerged from the data. Each division creates one new pole and keeps one old pole. The cell inheriting the old pole grows more slowly. It produces fewer offspring over time. It also dies more often. The old-pole cell acts as an aging parent. Its sibling counts as rejuvenated offspring. The two products of symmetric division are functionally unequal. The authors conclude no life strategy escapes aging. Immortality may be too costly or mechanistically impossible.
europmc-pmc5573739:
Tyng and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Psychology. Their subject is how emotion shapes learning and memory. Emotion affects attention, perception, reasoning, and problem solving as well. Its grip on attention is key, since focus is limited and must land on the right material.

Emotion can help memory form and later recall can improve. Yet the effect is not always good. Studies report both gains and harm, based on many factors. Brain imaging shows the amygdala, prefrontal cortex, and hippocampus working as a team. The authors map what this means for classrooms and online courses. Readers get a broad, brain-based case for designing study settings with emotion in mind.
europmc-pmc5574139:
Xue and co-authors study hypoxic tumor exosomes in Molecular Cancer. Solid tumors grow in low-oxygen pockets. Bladder cancer cells there shed exosomes loaded with RNA. Whether that cargo drives tumor spread was unclear.

The team grew donor cells under low and normal oxygen. Exosomes from hypoxic cells boosted recipient cell growth. Migration and invasion rose as well. The active cargo was a long non-coding RNA called UCA1. Hypoxic exosomes carried far more of it. In mice, those exosomes sped tumor growth. They pushed cells through a transition tied to spread. Patient blood told the same story. Serum exosomes from bladder cancer patients held more UCA1 than healthy controls. Readers see a candidate blood marker and a growth signal in one.
europmc-pmc5594539:
Tadesse and co-authors map antimicrobial resistance in Africa in BMC Infectious Diseases. Drug-resistant infections threaten every continent. Africa's true burden was poorly measured. This review takes a public-health view of the gap.

The search covered recent studies from 2013 to 2016. It included 144 articles in the final analysis. No resistance data existed for 42.6 percent of African countries. Where data existed, resistance ran high. E. coli resisted amoxicillin at a median of 88.1 percent. Trimethoprim resistance hit 80.7 percent in the same bug. Pneumococcus resisted penicillin at a median of 26.7 percent. Carbapenem resistance was common in two hospital genera. The lab data itself raised quality concerns. Readers get both the resistance numbers and a case for better surveillance.
europmc-pmc5770339:
Alfaro-Almagro and co-authors describe how the first 10,000 UK Biobank brain scans were processed and checked. UK Biobank is bringing back 100,000 volunteers for brain, heart, and body imaging. The brain work spans six scan types. Raw and processed data from the first group are now open to researchers.

The team built an automated pipeline that turns scans into summary measures. Quality control steps catch faults before release. The paper details the pipeline and the scan protocol behind it. It also reports tests used while the protocol and pipeline took shape. Other groups can use the same pipeline.
europmc-pmc5805839:
Singh-Manoux and co-authors track body weight and dementia over 28 years. The Whitehall II study follows British civil servants into old age. Past work tied midlife obesity to dementia, but new claims raised doubts. Timing may be the key.

The cohort holds 10,308 adults, with 329 dementia cases by 2015. Obesity at age 50 nearly doubled dementia risk. Obesity at 60 or 70 showed no such link. People bound for dementia carried extra weight years ahead. Then they lost weight in the eight years before diagnosis. Readers get a long view that separates cause from early symptom.
europmc-pmc5823939:
Cooks and co-authors show mutant p53 tumors reprogramming nearby macrophages. Faulty p53 proteins gain new, harmful powers in cancer. Tumor-linked macrophages usually mark a poor outlook. The team finds the tumor cells actively training those macrophages.

Colon cancer cells with mutant p53 shed tiny vesicles loaded with miR-1246. Macrophages that swallow the vesicles switch to a tumor-friendly state. They calm inflammation and raise TGF-beta activity. Patient data link the pattern to worse survival. Readers get a clear route by which a gene fault recruits the immune system to the tumor's side.
europmc-pmc5834839:
Nasrabady and co-authors argue that Alzheimer's disease is also a white matter disease. Their review appeared in Acta Neuropathologica Communications. The classic picture centers on grey matter plaques and tangles. Imaging now shows white matter breaking down as well.

The focus falls on myelin and the oligodendrocytes that build it. When these cells falter, insulation thins and signals slow. Poor blood flow, oxidative stress, and amyloid toxicity all strike them. Tau damage adds to the load. The review weighs whether this damage merely follows grey matter loss or drives decline itself. Repairing myelin, the authors suggest, could become a real treatment target.
europmc-pmc5862339:
Välikangas and co-authors evaluate normalization methods for label-free proteomics. Their study appeared in Briefings in Bioinformatics. Proteomics data from mass spectrometry carry built-in bias. Sample handling and instruments both add unwanted variation. Normalization aims to make samples fairly comparable. The team tested several popular methods on four datasets. Three datasets used spike-in samples, and one used mouse tissue.

The authors report that variance stabilization cut replicate variation most. It also did well in tests for changed protein levels. Linear and local regression methods also performed well throughout. The team checked global against segmented normalization for analysis. They close with advice on what makes a method suitable. Careful choice protects all steps that follow.
europmc-pmc5896039:
Dai and co-authors analyse the colorectal cancer metagenome across cohorts. Their article appeared in Microbiome. Gut microbe shifts link to colorectal cancer in many groups. Single-cohort noise can distort which bacteria stand out. The team pooled 526 metagenomic samples across five populations. Cohorts came from China, Austria, America, and Germany and France. They hunted for species-level changes shared across all groups.

Seven bacteria were enriched in cancer across populations, they report. Names include Bacteroides fragilis and Fusobacterium nucleatum. Those seven markers split cases from controls with an AUC of 0.80. Enriched and depleted bacteria formed separate mutual networks. The marker set could support non-invasive diagnosis, the authors suggest.
europmc-pmc5949339:
Galié and co-authors review biofilms in the food industry, from health risks to control methods. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Many microbes grow on food and on factory surfaces. That growth can build biofilms along production lines. The review names the main bacteria that start and mature these films. Pathogens such as Listeria monocytogenes and Salmonella enterica feature.

These organisms can cause outbreaks and severe illness through contaminated food. The second half surveys ways to prevent or break up biofilms. Options include coated steel, chemical sanitizers, and enzymes. Bacteriophages, bacteriocins, and plant essential oils also appear. Cell-signalling blockers offer another route to control.
europmc-pmc5993839:
Johnston, Jones, and Manley warn about confounding and collinearity in regression analysis, using British voting studies as cases. Their paper appeared in Quality & Quantity. Voting research leans on regressions with many predictors. Few studies ask how links among those predictors distort results. The authors run three empirical examples to test the risk. Even mild links between variables shifted model outputs a lot, they find. Reading the coefficients against prior hopes then misleads.

Confounded results may be the norm, they argue. Care in model building is the only guard. They introduce an extended principal components method for that care. Worked voting examples show how it is applied.
europmc-pmc6027439:
Aderibigbe and Buyana review alginate in wound dressings. Their article appeared in Pharmaceutics. Alginate is a natural polymer from seaweed sources. It is non-toxic and sits well with body tissue. Those traits make it attractive for wound care.

Dressings made from alginate soak up excess wound fluid. They keep the wound moist while limiting infection. The review covers many material forms. Hydrogels, films, wafers, and foams all appear. So do nanofibres and topical mixes. Results from lab and animal studies are summed up. Added polymers, cross linkers, and antibacterial agents shape results. Readers get a full guide to designing alginate dressings.
europmc-pmc6104739:
Metidji and co-authors show how an environmental sensor guards the gut lining in mice. Their research article appeared in Immunity. The sensor, called AHR, answers dietary and microbial signals. Gut stem cells renew the lining after damage. Their balance is delicate.

Deleting AHR from gut lining cells broke that balance. Stem cells multiplied without control. They failed to mature into working lining cells. Infections with a gut pathogen ran unchecked. Growths began to turn malignant. Switching AHR on with dietary compounds restored order. It raised two brakes on the Wnt growth signal. Readers get a diet-linked shield for the stem cell niche.
europmc-pmc6197739:
Elazezy and Joosse wrote a review in Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal on circulating tumor DNA as a liquid biopsy tool. Liquid biopsy reads cancer markers from a blood sample instead of tissue. Tumor cells shed DNA fragments into the blood. Their mutations reveal the tumor's genetic make-up.

Repeated blood tests could track how a tumor changes over time. Clinicians might then predict and measure drug response or resistance early. The catch is technical. Tumor DNA is scarce, highly fragmented, and swamped by normal DNA. The review compares the detection techniques built to find it, from deep sequencing to targeted assays. Sensitivity limits, especially in early-stage cancer, are laid out plainly.
europmc-pmc6323939:
Mi and co-authors present version 14 of PANTHER, a gene classification resource. Their update appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. PANTHER sorts genes by family history and by function. It spans organisms across the tree of life. Researchers use it to make sense of long gene lists.

More prokaryote and plant genomes joined the family trees. That widened coverage of gene evolution in those groups. Many protein family borders were redrawn with care. The protease families now align with the MEROPS resource. A new PANTHER GO-slim holds four times more terms than before. Enrichment tools now cover over 900 genomes. Updated tests correct for false discovery rates. The overrepresentation test is also offered as a web service.
europmc-pmc6324439:
Mandsager and co-authors link treadmill fitness to long-term survival. Their study appeared in JAMA Network Open. It followed adults who took exercise treadmill tests. Fitness was scored by peak work level reached. The cohort held 122,007 patients at a major center. It is the largest such group reported at the time.

Higher fitness meant lower death rates at every step. Elite performers had the lowest risk of all. They had about 80 percent lower risk than the weakest group. No upper limit of benefit showed up in the data. Even very high fitness kept adding survival gains. The risk from low fitness rivaled smoking and diabetes. The authors call fitness a strong, changeable sign of future health.
europmc-pmc6351539:
Jones and co-authors hunt genes behind being a morning person. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Morningness reflects the body's inner clock. The team combined UK Biobank and 23andMe data. Together they held 697,828 participants. Earlier work had found only 24 linked gene regions.

The new analysis raised that count to 351 regions. Sleep timing data came from activity monitors on 85,760 people. Those with the most morningness variants slept 25 minutes earlier. The genes clustered in clock and signaling pathways. Retina, hindbrain, and hormone gland expression stood out. Gene-based tests suggested a causal benefit. Morningness was linked to better mental health. It showed no causal effect on weight or diabetes risk.
europmc-pmc6387439:
Li and co-authors review hormone signals in plant defense, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Plants meet germs and stress of many kinds during their lives. Hormones such as salicylic acid and jasmonate switch on defense genes in response.

Two main defense paths were long seen as rivals. One suits germs that feed on living tissue, the other suits killers and chewing insects. The review asks how these signals cross-talk and tune each other. Other hormones shade the outcome as well. Work in the model plant Arabidopsis anchors much of the evidence they weigh.
europmc-pmc6399239:
Broido and Clauset test a famous network claim in Nature Communications. Many real networks are said to be scale free. In such networks, node links follow a power law, a pattern with wide effects on how systems behave.

The authors gathered nearly a thousand networks from social, biological, and technical fields. With strict tests, few networks proved strongly scale free. For most, a log-normal curve fit as well as or better than a power law. Social networks were at best weakly scale free. The result urges care before claims about network shape are made.
europmc-pmc6440139:
Heuberger and Schuepbach review protease-activated receptors, a family of cell-surface switches flipped not by free-floating molecules but by enzymes that snip their tips. The exposed end then folds back and activates the receptor itself. Sensing protease activity this way ties the receptors closely to inflammation, which has grown more prevalent with industrialization.

Four mammalian receptors, PAR1 through PAR4, signal through G proteins and also cross-activate neighboring receptors and channels. Clinical and laboratory evidence links them to chronic inflammatory diseases from skin to vessels. Sections weigh drugs that block or tune each receptor, judging PARs as reachable targets whose unusual activation demands unusual pharmacology.
europmc-pmc6470739:
Xu and co-authors review the antioxidant activity of quercetin, a flavonoid rich in kale, onions, berries, apples, and tea, and long used in plant remedies and old Chinese practice. Its effects run through glutathione levels, the work of protective enzymes, and signal paths that answer outside and toxic insults.

Chemists have lately focused on quercetin's metal pairings, which can beat the plain molecule. A stubborn weakness is delivery: it dissolves poorly in water, and the body takes up only about 5.3 percent of it as is, so shape tweaks and new forms aim to raise that share. Reported protection spans osteoporosis, heart disease, and some cancers and lung disease. The review maps both the biology and the bench chemistry for researchers designing better versions.
europmc-pmc6470839:
Réhault-Godbert and co-authors make the nutritional and biomedical case for the humble egg, a complete embryonic food supply whose reputation survived decades of cholesterol warnings. Guidance from 1968 urged fewer than three whole eggs a week; half a century of experimental, clinical, and population studies found no solid link between egg cholesterol and blood cholesterol.

Beyond balanced, highly digestible nutrients at low price, eggs carry bioactive compounds still being catalogued: some 550 proteins are identified in white and yolk membranes, with the function of only 20 characterized. Composition varies by hen species and feed, a variability the review quantifies. Elders, children, and athletes all stand to gain.
europmc-pmc6534539:
Zhao and co-authors report a protein-making circular RNA from human papillomavirus. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Circular RNAs form through backsplicing. Most of their functions remain unknown. Virus-made circular RNAs were known only from gamma-herpesviruses.

Oncogenic HPVs also make circular RNAs. One of them, circE7, carries the E7 oncogene. The team detected HPV16 circE7 by inverse RT-PCR and northern blotting. CircE7 carries m6A marks and sits in the cytoplasm. It joins polysomes and is translated into E7 protein. Breaking circE7 in CaSki cervical cancer cells cut E7 levels. Growth slowed in dishes and in tumour xenografts. CircE7 also appears in HPV-positive cancer data.
europmc-pmc6598639:
Naghavi and the Global Burden of Disease Self-Harm Collaborators map suicide deaths worldwide from 1990 to 2016. Their analysis appears in The BMJ. It covers 195 countries and territories. Rates are broken down by age, sex, and development level. Total suicide deaths rose 6.7 percent over the period. They reached about 817,000 deaths in 2016.

Yet the age-standardised rate fell by about a third. Population growth and ageing explain the split. Men died at higher rates than women nearly everywhere. The sole exception was the 15 to 19 age group. Women's rates fell faster than men's over time. The authors say prevention should target the highest-risk groups.
europmc-pmc6599339:
Waffenschmidt and co-authors ask whether one reviewer can screen studies alone for a systematic review. Their methodological review appears in BMC Medical Research Methodology. Standard practice uses two independent screeners. That doubles the labour on large searches. Rapid reviews need defensible shortcuts. The team searched medical databases for head-to-head evaluations. They compared single screening against double screening directly.

Four evaluations covered 23 single screenings. A median of five percent of studies were missed. Experienced reviewers missed a median of three percent. Less experienced reviewers missed thirteen percent. Missed studies rarely changed results for experienced screeners. The authors conclude single screening is not equivalent. They allow it for rapid reviews when experts screen.
europmc-pmc6614039:
Kievit and co-authors offer a tutorial on latent change score models for developmental neuroscience. Their paper appears in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. The field asks how brain and behaviour change together. Cross-sectional data cannot show change within a person. Latent change score models fill that gap. They formalise growth and coupling between measures over time. The tutorial gives open code and worked examples. It draws on the NSPN adolescent cohort.

Two example findings show the method's reach. White matter change tracked lower processing speed gains. Frontal lobe thinning varied more in males than females. Such models test which change leads the other. They also expose individual differences in development. The authors aim to spread the approach widely.
europmc-pmc6639939:
Wang and co-authors identify a circular RNA that drives liver cancer growth. Their study appears in Molecular Cancer. The RNA, circRHOT1, is sharply raised in tumour tissue. Patients with high levels fare worse. Lab and animal tests show it fuels growth and spread. The team traced how it acts inside cells. circRHOT1 recruits a protein called TIP60 to DNA. TIP60 switches on the gene NR2F6 at its promoter.

Removing NR2F6 stalled tumour cell growth and invasion. Restoring it rescued those abilities after circRHOT1 loss. The work used 100 paired patient tissue samples. Assays spanned blotting, imaging, and mouse xenografts. The authors propose both molecules as prognostic markers. They also suggest them as treatment targets.
europmc-pmc6650939:
Jarosz-Biej and co-authors review how the tumour microenvironment shapes radiotherapy outcomes. Their review appears in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Radiation hits more than the cancer cells themselves. It damages tumour blood vessels and immune cells too. Injured vessels block CD8 T cell entry. Suppressor cells then gather in the tumour. These include M2 macrophages, MDSCs, and regulatory T cells. Hypoxic zones grow as vessels fail. Low oxygen blunts radiation's DNA damage.

Radiation can also awaken anti-tumour immunity. Immunogenic cell death acts like an in situ vaccine. The balance between suppression and activation is delicate. Dose effects on vessels and immunity remain unclear. The authors call this balance the field's game changer.
europmc-pmc6722139:
Zhang and co-authors built a nanoparticle that reprograms tumor macrophages. Macrophages inside tumors usually take a form that shields the cancer and calms immunity. Flipping them to an attacking form could help, but broad attempts inflame the whole body. The team aimed mRNA carriers at these cells alone.

The particles deliver mRNA coding for a transcription factor and its activating kinase. In mouse models of ovarian cancer, melanoma, and brain tumors, infusions flipped the macrophages. The reprogrammed cells sparked anti-tumor immunity and shrank tumors. Repeated doses proved safe in the tests. The approach could one day treat suppressive tumors without disturbing the wider immune system.
europmc-pmc6777939:
Achberger and co-authors built a human retina-on-a-chip by merging organoids with chip technology. Retinal diseases such as Stargardt disease and retinitis pigmentosa still lack cures. Drug development leans on animal models whose results often fail to transfer to people. Retinal organoids grown from stem cells model the layered tissue well. They lack blood supply, though, and miss key cell interactions.

The chip integrates more than seven retinal cell types from human induced stem cells. It adds vessel-like perfusion. For the first time, mature light-sensing segments could interact with the pigment layer beneath them, as in a real eye. Microscopy confirmed inner segments rich in mitochondria. The platform may serve drug testing better.
europmc-pmc6862039:
Huang and co-authors review sepsis in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Sepsis is organ failure driven by the body's own botched response to infection. It strikes more than 30 million people a year worldwide and remains a leading cause of death in intensive care. Its signs vary widely between patients. That variety still frustrates diagnosis and treatment.

The review gathers recent findings on how sepsis unfolds inside cells and the immune system. It covers markers in the blood that might diagnose it sooner or predict its course. Candidate marker families include inflammatory signals such as interleukins and TNF-alpha. A final section surveys drugs aimed at specific targets in the pathway, and how far each has got.
europmc-pmc6871539:
Kyrou and co-authors report a gene drive experiment in Nature Biotechnology. Anopheles gambiae mosquitoes spread malaria. A gene drive is a genetic element that copies itself into offspring, spreading through a population far faster than normal inheritance. This drive targeted doublesex, a gene that controls sexual development. Breaking it in females leaves them unable to bite or lay eggs.

Released into caged mosquito populations, the drive spread as designed. Female fertility collapsed generation by generation. In the reported cages, the populations were completely suppressed, producing no offspring at all. The authors frame the result as proof of principle. Field use would raise ecological and ethical questions far beyond the cage.
europmc-pmc6959339:
Rakita and co-authors present a lab model of healing human skin that needs no animal. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Much is known about wound healing, yet no standard lab model kept the deeper skin layer intact. Their method uses suction to lift a blister, then removes its roof.

The wound bed kept its basement membrane, with skin-forming keratinocytes absent. After six days of culture, one to three layers of dividing keratinocytes covered the wound. By eight to twelve days, a many-layered epidermis had formed, showing normal maturation markers. Immune cells behaved in telling ways: T cells were richer in blister roof skin than in normal skin. Some cell groups appeared in the blister that normal skin lacks, apparently drawn up from deeper layers by the suction.
europmc-pmc6979639:
Wilson and co-authors weigh the promise of FLASH radiotherapy, radiation delivered at extreme speed. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Oncology. Radiotherapy is a mainstay of cancer care, but damage to healthy tissue caps the dose doctors dare give. Higher doses could cure more tumours if side effects fell.

Early animal studies found that ultra-fast delivery cut damage to normal tissue while hitting tumours just as hard. That sparing is called the FLASH effect. So far, a single patient has been treated this way, for skin lymphoma, with full response and minimal harm. Why it works is unsettled; sudden oxygen depletion in tissue leads the hypotheses. The authors examine the tissue evidence, critique each explanation, and judge what stands between the lab effect and routine clinical use.
europmc-pmc7001239:
