Riou and Althaus model how the new Wuhan coronavirus passed between people in its first weeks. Their analysis appeared in Eurosurveillance. China alerted the world to unexplained pneumonia cases on the last day of 2019. Within days a novel coronavirus was named as the cause.

By January 29, 2020, China counted 5,997 confirmed cases, with 68 more abroad. The authors simulated early outbreak paths that match the case pattern. They estimate the basic reproduction number, R0, at about 2.2, meaning each case infects roughly two others. That pace resembles SARS and pandemic flu, and signals risk of global spread. The interval suggests sustained human transmission was already under way. Their figures aimed to guide screening, containment, and emergency decisions at a moment of deep uncertainty.
europmc-pmc7045739:
Liu and co-authors test a ferroptosis blocker against lung injury in Cellular and Molecular Biology Letters. Ferroptosis is a recently recognised kind of cell death, distinct from apoptosis, necrosis, and autophagy. Its role in acute lung injury caused by bacterial lipopolysaccharide, or LPS, had barely been explored. The team examined that role in airway cells and in mice.

LPS lowered the survival of human bronchial epithelial cells and shifted ferroptosis markers in the expected direction: protective proteins SLC7A11 and GPX4 fell, while malondialdehyde, 4-hydroxynonenal, and iron rose with dose. Ferrostatin-1, a ferroptosis inhibitor, rescued the cells. In mice with LPS-induced lung injury, the same drug eased tissue damage and lowered ferroptosis levels in the lungs. The results mark ferroptosis as a driver of this injury and ferrostatin-1 as a candidate therapy.
europmc-pmc7190039:
Huang and co-authors review trials on how cutting dietary salt lowers blood pressure. Their analysis appeared in The BMJ. They gathered randomised trials that compared different salt intake levels in adults. Salt intake had to be measured by 24-hour urine tests. The team followed standard systematic review methods.

The central question was dose: how much blood pressure falls per amount of salt removed. They also asked whether longer interventions work better than short ones. Trials varied in size, population, and duration. Pooling them gives a dose-response picture single trials cannot. The findings feed into guidelines on salt in food. They also matter for food labeling and reformulation debates. Readers get a careful summary of what the trial evidence supports.
europmc-pmc7264239:
Leventhal and co-authors engineer a harmless gut bacterium into a living cancer medicine. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The strain, called SYNB1891, is built from non-pathogenic E. coli Nissle. It is designed to reach tumors and switch on the STING pathway, an alarm system inside immune cells.

Once swallowed up by antigen-presenting cells in the tumor, the bacteria trigger STING and other innate immune pathways together. In mouse tumor models, treatment produced strong anti-tumor immunity and lasting immunological memory. Human immune cells in the lab also responded robustly. Built-in containment features keep the strain from surviving where it should not. The authors present the work as a roadmap for designing living medicines that meet manufacturing and safety rules from the start.
europmc-pmc7312039:
Machlowska and co-authors review gastric cancer, from its worldwide pattern to modern treatment. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Stomach cancer is among the most common malignancies and the fourth leading cause of cancer death. Both environment and genes shape who develops it.

Incidence climbs with age, and the median age at diagnosis is 70 years. About 10% of cases appear at age 45 or younger, and those early cancers are a good model for studying genetic drivers, since young patients have had less exposure to environmental carcinogens. The authors cover classification, genomic features, and risk factors including H. pylori infection, then survey treatment strategies from surgery and chemotherapy to targeted therapy.
europmc-pmc7314139:
Kuo and co-authors test whether the APOE e4 gene variant predicts severe COVID-19 in the UK Biobank cohort. Their study appeared in The Journals of Gerontology, Series A. The variant is famous for raising Alzheimer's risk, and dementia had already emerged as a strong risk factor for severe COVID-19, with an odds ratio of 3.07 in this cohort.

Test results from March 16 to April 26, 2020, when testing was largely limited to hospital inpatients, served as a marker of severe infection. The analysis used participants of European ancestry in England, with the cohort aged 48 to 86 years. Carrying the e4 variant, and especially two copies, was associated with testing positive and with worse outcomes. The authors propose the gene helps explain part of why age and dementia track so strongly with fatal disease.
europmc-pmc7543839:
Islam and co-authors analyze the COVID-19 infodemic and its harm on global social media use. Rumors, stigma and conspiracy claims spread widely during the pandemic months. Tracking them in real time is a hard task for health agencies worldwide.

The team gathered reports from December 31, 2019 to April 5, 2020 across many sources. They found 2,311 reports in twenty-five languages from eighty-seven countries in that span of time. Claims covered illness, spread, control steps, cures and the cause of disease itself. Of the rated reports, eighty-two percent were judged false by the review team. That was 1,856 of the 2,276 claims that had text ratings in the data. False claims can steer people away from sound public health guidance in a crisis. The authors urge live tracking and local work with communities to counter false claims.
europmc-pmc7568239:
Cheng and co-authors argue that part of the SARS-CoV-2 spike acts like a superantigen. Severe COVID-19 can bring a hyperinflammatory syndrome in patients. A similar pattern appears in children as MIS-C.

The spike insert has motifs like a bacterial superantigen. Models suggest it may bind direct to T cell receptors. Patient data showed a skewed T cell receptor mix. That skew appeared in cases with severe hyperinflammation. The motif is absent from other SARS family viruses. That absence may explain the unique syndrome pattern. Toxic shock syndrome offers a close comparison case. The findings link spike structure to runaway immune activation in severe disease.
europmc-pmc7578039:
Cho and co-authors show that 5-FU can promote stemness in colorectal cancer through p53. The drug 5-FU is first-line care for this cancer. Tumors often shrink at first, then return after treatment.

The team found p53 raises WNT3 gene activity. That switch turns on the WNT and beta-catenin pathway. Models included mice, patient tumor organoids and patient cells. Through this route, 5-FU enriched cancer stem cells. Those cells in leftover tumors drive recurrence. A WNT inhibitor paired with 5-FU suppressed stem cells. The pairing also cut tumor regrowth after treatment stopped. The findings suggest a new combination plan for colorectal cancer care.
europmc-pmc7589539:
Anjum and co-authors review spinal cord injury, its mechanisms and routes to recovery. Injury causes major motor, sensory and autonomic loss. Damage unfolds in acute and chronic phases over time.

A cascade follows the first injury event. It includes low blood flow and oxidative stress. Inflammation and cell death pathways add more damage. Movement loss reflects this combined harm to tissue. Many treatment plans aim to limit secondary damage. Others aim to protect neurons or regrow connections. Immune-based and regenerative routes are covered in depth. Success so far is partial and mixed across methods. The review maps molecular links to guide better treatment design.
europmc-pmc7599039:
Mehta and Pandey report a case of rhino-orbital mucormycosis in a patient with COVID-19. Fungal co-infections can complicate COVID-19 care in hospital. Diabetes is a known risk factor for this fungus.

The patient was a 60-year-old man with longstanding diabetes. His test was positive for SARS-CoV-2 on admission. He received antibiotics, oseltamivir and steroid treatment in hospital. Signs of orbital cellulitis developed during his stay. MRI showed swelling around the eye and sinus disease. A nasal biopsy showed broad fungal threads in tissue. Culture confirmed mucormycosis as the infecting fungus. The authors warn that steroids and broad antibiotics may worsen fungal disease. Early watch for such infections is urged.
europmc-pmc7782739:
Lau and co-authors measure neutralizing antibody levels after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Such antibodies are a marker of protection. Data on how long they last were still scarce. The team tested 293 serum samples from 195 confirmed infections. Samples spanned 0 to 209 days after symptoms began.

Of samples taken at least 61 days after onset, 99.1% stayed positive. That held for both the 90% and 50% neutralization endpoints. Severe cases reached higher peak antibody levels than mild or silent cases. Age did not seem to weaken the response once severity was counted. The authors estimate slow decay over many months. They conclude that infection raises strong neutralizing antibody levels in most people.
europmc-pmc7820839:
Bharti and Grimm review best practice for analyzing microbiome data. DNA sequencing opened a deep view of microbe communities. It spans many species and settings. Yet results bend easily under lab and computing choices. New sequencing tools keep adding fresh methods.

The authors cover the main workflow types. These include 16S rRNA studies and shotgun metagenomics. Long-read methods are covered too. Best practice spans study design and sample handling. Sequencing, assembly, grouping, and annotation each get guidance. Display of results is included as well. A ready set of workflows sits on GitHub for reuse. The aim is results that other teams can trust and repeat.
europmc-pmc7846939:
Karmakar and co-authors link social factors to COVID-19 case and death rates across the United States. The team used county-level data. Social risk was scored with the Social Vulnerability Index. The study counted 4 289 283 cases and 147 074 deaths.

Counties with higher social vulnerability saw more infections. They also saw more deaths from the disease. Income, housing, race, and transport all feed the index. The pattern held across the country. The authors argue that root causes must be tackled. Fixing them is part of fair pandemic control. Data of this kind can steer aid to the hardest-hit places.
europmc-pmc7884739:
Echle and co-authors present a review of deep learning in cancer pathology. Cancer care leans on molecular tests to predict how a tumour will behave and which drug may work. Those tests cost time and money and need extra tissue. The review asks what image-based learning can add.

Routine tumour slides already hold rich information that standard review does not use. Deep learning systems can sort, grade, and subtype tumours from those images. More advanced systems go further. They infer molecular features, predict survival, and even forecast response to a therapy. The authors stress that such tools need strict testing in real clinics before they guide decisions. The review gives a clear tour of a field that could reshape how biomarkers are found.
europmc-pmc7913839:
Kowalska-Krochmal and Dudek-Wicher present a review of the minimum inhibitory concentration of antibiotics, known as the MIC. The MIC is the lowest drug level that stops a bacterial strain in the lab. It guides the choice of antibiotic for a patient. A wrong reading can lead to a failed therapy, so the method matters.

The authors discuss the two main ways to measure it: dilution and gradient methods. They explain the factors that can shift a result. Rules for reading and reporting the value are set out with care. The review then shows how the MIC joins with drug exposure measures in practice. Statistical tools can estimate the chance of hitting the right exposure in a given patient. The limits of the MIC close the account.
europmc-pmc7935139:
Middleton presents a biographical essay on William Edmonds Horner, the anatomist who lived from 1793 to 1853. Horner held the chair of anatomy at the University of Pennsylvania. He followed a line of famous holders, from Shippen and Wistar to Physick. The essay was read before a medical history seminar at the University of Wisconsin in 1922.

Beneath a calm surface, Horner fought deep inner turmoil. His private journal records self-reproach and restless doubt. Wealth and honours came fast, yet they gave him little pleasure. The ties of husband and father also failed to settle him. Middleton traces this struggle through the journal entries. The portrait is of a gifted teacher marked by melancholy. It shows how much private pain can hide behind public success in medicine.
europmc-pmc7942739:
DeLint presents a historical study of how abdominal wounds were treated in ancient times. Hand-to-hand fighting made such wounds common in the ancient world. Old surgical writers therefore discussed them at length. DeLint gathers their advice, starting with Hippocrates and Celsus. The core problem was gut that spilled from a cut in the belly wall.

Hippocrates warned that protruding omentum dies without fail. Celsus judged by the colour of the intestines. If they had turned blue, pale, or black, treatment was useless. If the colour stayed sound, the gut had to go back at once, before air killed it. Only the large intestine could be sewn with success, he held. The paper follows the steps in detail, from widening the wound to washing dried gut with water and oil. It shows ancient surgery at its most practical.
europmc-pmc7946139:
Gunther presents a study of the row of books owned by Nicholas Gibbard of Oxford. Gibbard was a medical contemporary of Thomas Lorkyn, another Oxford doctor whose library list is known. Printing the second list sharpens the interest of both, Gunther argues. Gibbard signed himself Gibbert or Gibbarde in some of his books. He entered Magdalen College as a demy in 1555.

He took his arts degrees in 1561 and 1566. His licence to practise medicine came on December 17, 1571. College ledgers show him as a tenant and as master of the almshouse. That post meant opening the door to the poor at all hours and keeping the house's linen clean. The paper then sets out his shelf of books. Such a list shows what a Tudor university doctor read and valued.
europmc-pmc7998239:
Ke and co-authors present a review of the antimicrobial actions and uses of chitosan. Chitosan is a natural product drawn from shells and fungi. It suits living tissue, breaks down safely, and does not poison the user. Its power to kill microbes gives it wide commercial promise. Yet that power shifts with the material's traits and with the microbe it meets. The review sets out what governs the effect.

The authors first cover the base properties of chitosan. They then explain how it attacks microbes, from membrane damage to gene effects. Traits such as chain length and charge shift the outcome. Microbes' own gene responses to chitosan are summed up as well. Uses close the account: nanoparticles and films, often paired with standard antibiotics or antifungal drugs. The review guides makers who want the effect to hold up.
europmc-pmc8058039:
Sabia and co-authors link short sleep in midlife to later dementia. Sleep problems mark dementia, but whether they help cause it was unclear. The team drew on the Whitehall II study of 7,959 participants. Follow-up ran 25 years, long enough to pass the slow build-up of disease. In that span, 521 participants were diagnosed with dementia.

Sleeping six hours or less at age 50 carried a hazard ratio of 1.22. At age 60, the ratio rose to 1.37, against a normal seven hours. The estimate at age 70 was less precise. People who slept short persistently across all three ages faced 30% higher risk. The link held after adjusting for social, behavioral, heart, and mental health factors. Midlife sleep, the authors argue, deserves a place in dementia prevention.
europmc-pmc8080639:
Bhattarai and co-authors trace what follows when ER stress and redox signals collide. The endoplasmic reticulum folds and ships the cell's proteins. About 30% of the proteome passes through it. When misfolded proteins pile up, the unfolded protein response fires. That response aims to restore balance inside the cell. Held too long, it switches to ordering the cell's death.

The review maps the talk between the ER and mitochondria. Redox state shapes how the stress response runs, and the response reshapes redox in return. When that loop breaks, stress answering fails outright. The authors sort the conditions that push cells past the point of return. Calcium shifts, energy shortage, and faulty autophagy all play parts. The endgame is a slide from strain to cell death. Dynamic changes across the whole cell close the account.
europmc-pmc8189439:
Guo and co-authors show that human naive epiblast cells keep an open lineage potential. In mice, naive epiblast cells cannot make trophectoderm, the first split lineage. The human cells behaved otherwise in their tests.

Blocking ERK and Nodal signals drove the human cells to trophectoderm fast. Those cells then formed syncytiotrophoblast and cytotrophoblast types. Gene profiles matched direct trophectoderm formation in the embryo. The result sets human early development apart from the mouse pattern. It reshapes how stem cell models of the embryo should be read. That contrast with mouse cells is the core surprise.
europmc-pmc8249239:
Mezu-Ndubuisi and Maheshwari review integrins in inflammation and new blood vessel growth. Integrins are adhesion molecules that span the cell membrane. Each pairs an alpha with a beta subunit, in many combinations.

These pairs grip ligands outside the cell with varied strength. They steer cell growth, movement, and signal release. That makes them central to tissue repair, infection defence, and vessel formation. The review gathers human and animal evidence on their structure and signals. Signal paths in infants get special emphasis. The authors add findings from their own laboratory work.
europmc-pmc8381139:
Pretorius and co-authors report on clotting problems that persist in Long COVID. Some patients stay ill for months after the acute infection clears. They report fatigue, breathlessness, sleep trouble, and anxiety or depression. The team asked whether stubborn blood microclots explain part of this picture.

The authors used proteomics and fluorescence microscopy on plasma samples. Samples came from healthy people, people with type 2 diabetes, and people with Long COVID. They looked for microclots that resist the normal break-down process. Such clots could block tiny blood vessels and cut oxygen flow. The paper also reports raised levels of antiplasmin, a protein that slows clot removal.
europmc-pmc8441439:
Brabletz and co-authors portray the epithelial-mesenchymal transition, or EMT, as a multi-tool for tumor growth. This program is normal in embryo growth. Cells shed their fixed epithelial traits, gain mesenchymal ones, and start to move.

Cancer hijacks the same program to invade new tissue. The review gathers fresh findings on its wider jobs. EMT also feeds tumor stemness, treatment resistance, and fit to new surroundings. It shapes how cancers start and how they answer therapy. The authors argue that drugs aimed at EMT must face this full range. If they do, one strike could hit tumor growth on many levels at once.
europmc-pmc8494639:
Foster and co-authors map the mouse cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic network in fine detail. This loop is a basic circuit motif of the brain. Its layout shapes thought, movement, and many brain disorders. The classic view split it into just three channels: motor, limbic, and associative.

That view cannot explain the many jobs of the basal ganglia. The team traced outputs from 29 striatal domains through the circuit. They found 14 domains in one relay and 36 in another, plus a direct cortex path. Direct and indirect routes from one domain end on the same target cells. Six thalamic domains complete the map.
europmc-pmc8514339:
Elmarakeby and co-authors build P-NET, a deep learning model shaped by biology, for prostate cancer study. Which molecular traits drive aggressive prostate cancer is a major open question. Machine learning that can be read and explained may help find them.

P-NET sorts patients by treatment-resistance state from molecular data. It beat other modeling approaches in their tests. Its built-in clarity points to the traits that drive each call. Known and new candidates emerged, among them MDM4 and FGFR1. Lab tests backed their role in advanced disease. The authors argue that clear, biology-based networks can serve both discovery and clinical prediction. The frame may fit other cancers too.
europmc-pmc8554139:
Manchia and co-authors review how the long COVID-19 pandemic shaped stress resilience and mental health. The crisis lasted longer than most had hoped. High uncertainty and low control asked much of everyone. A fast-growing literature tracked the mental effects across waves.

The review reads that work with a critical eye. It covers the general public first. It then turns to groups under special strain. Patients with psychiatric disorders, health workers, and children feature. Pregnant women and older people get their own treatment. The authors ask how well people truly held up. Their aim is a sober map of resilience under long stress.
europmc-pmc8657439:
Liu and co-authors map the network that builds flavonoids in plants. Flavonoids aid plant growth and have wide uses in food and medicine. They come from a known metabolic pathway and share a basic ring structure. Research on their assembly has run for decades.

The review lays out the full pathway step by step. It builds a map with eight branches of flavonoid types. Four key middle compounds anchor the map. Branches lead to flavones, flavonols, anthocyanins, and more. The authors sum up what is known about each branch's enzymes and controls. Readers get a base for work on flavonoid roles and uses.
europmc-pmc8740839:
Miles, Ramalli, and Wallace describe DichroWeb, a website that reads protein structure from circular dichroism spectra. This light-based method is widely used to gauge protein shape. DichroWeb turns a spectrum into shares of helix, sheet, and other structures. The tool has served the field for nearly two decades.

The site offers several reference datasets and algorithms. It also gives plots and scores that grade each analysis. This account covers current content, access, and how to use the tool. Many features have been upgraded since the first version. The authors aim to keep a popular tool clear for new users.
europmc-pmc8843739:
Xu and co-authors review β-catenin signaling in hepatocellular carcinoma, the main liver cancer. A growth pathway called Wnt feeds into β-catenin. In this cancer, that pathway is often stuck in the on position. Gene studies find activating or disabling mutations in about 35% of tumors. Such tumors show distinct gene patterns and tissue features. The pathway also teams with other signals to drive growth.

The authors detail how the pathway switches on. They describe what makes these tumors stand out. Sections cover how the signal helps start liver cancer. Drug strategies against the pathway follow. The authors also treat the pathway as a biomarker. It may predict resistance to immunotherapy. The review closes with challenges for personal treatment.
europmc-pmc8996939:
Hossain and co-authors review colorectal cancer from its origins to its care, with a global lens. This cancer is the second most deadly worldwide. Early disease can be cured with surgery and follow-up drugs. Return of the cancer is common, though. Drug resistance drives many failures. Deaths concentrate in rich countries today. Rates in poorer countries are climbing fast. Care access splits along the same line. The review aims to raise public awareness.

Sections cover how the cancer develops step by step. World patterns of cases and deaths follow. Risk factors get a full survey. Diet, genes, and lifestyle all enter. Prevention plans are laid out next. Treatment plans cover chemo and targeted drugs. Natural products earn a brief, careful look. The authors end with recommendations. Early detection is their loudest call.
europmc-pmc9007739:
Lauer and co-authors extend DeepLabCut to track the poses of many animals at once. Pose tracking reads body points from video. Groups break simple trackers. Animals hide each other and look alike. The team added fast assembly of points into animals. They added tracking that survives brief hiding. An identity predictor helps when animals cross. The base tool is open source and widely used. Four test datasets of rising difficulty ship with the work.

The datasets span lab species in social settings. They serve as a shared benchmark for new methods. The authors show the system on each in turn. Grouping points to the right animal is the core trick. Keeping names straight across frames is the second. Social science needs both at once. Parenting, schooling, and flocking studies all wait on such tools. The release aims to standardize how labs build them.
europmc-pmc9181839:
Bukowska and co-authors review benzo[a]pyrene, its presence in the environment, human exposure, and toxic action. This compound is the main representative of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. It turns up in air, surface water, soil, and sediments. It is also in cigarette smoke and in smoked and grilled foods.

The body breaks it down through cytochrome P450 enzymes into a carcinogenic metabolite called BPDE. That metabolite forms DNA adducts that can cause mutations and malignant change. The authors also cover harm to nerves, reproduction, and unborn development. Gene variants in the breakdown enzymes shape each person's sensitivity. The review draws mainly on work from 2017 to 2022.
europmc-pmc9273039:
Cohen and co-authors test a mosaic nanoparticle vaccine against diverse sarbecoviruses in animals. Their particles display spike receptor-binding domains from SARS-CoV-2 plus seven animal sarbecoviruses, mixed at random. The design aims to draw antibodies toward shared, hidden sites rather than variable exposed ones. A matching particle with only SARS-CoV-2 domains served as the control.

In mice and macaques, the mosaic vaccine drew stronger responses to strains not on the particle. It matched control protection against SARS-CoV-2, including Omicron variants. Unlike the control, it also protected against SARS-CoV challenge. Mapping showed more targeting of conserved sites. The authors say such particles could guard against future spillovers too.
europmc-pmc9308039:
Zhu and co-authors give an overview of RNA-based medicines and their prospects. RNA drugs can act on proteins, transcripts, and genes once thought undruggable. Only 0.05% of the human genome is touched by current small molecule and antibody drugs. A defined RNA sequence also makes drug design far more direct.

The review groups RNA therapies by type and explains how each works. Antisense pieces, silencing RNAs, messenger RNA, and aptamers are all covered. Big hurdles include getting RNA into cells and keeping it stable. Fixes for those hurdles are surveyed in turn. Several RNA drugs are already approved for clinical use. A dozen more sit in late-stage trials for rare and common diseases. The field, the authors say, keeps widening fast.
europmc-pmc9527239:
Yang and co-authors uncover a metabolic cross talk between tumor cells and macrophages in liver metastasis. Spread to the liver is aggressive and hard to treat. Macrophages in the tumor setting help suppress immune attack. How those macrophages get reprogrammed was the open question.

The team found the scavenger receptor CD36 raised in metastasis linked macrophages. Deleting CD36 in these cells cut liver spread in mice. The macrophages took up long-chain fatty acids shed by tumor cells in vesicles. CD36 routed those lipid rich vesicles into the macrophages. The lipid fuel then drove their tumor aiding behavior. In patients, high CD36 matched dense M2-type macrophage presence. The authors propose CD36 blockade as a therapy route for liver metastasis.
europmc-pmc9644639:
Raulin and co-authors review ApoE in Alzheimer's disease, from its disease paths to therapy plans. Alzheimer's is the top cause of dementia in the world. The APOE gene is its strongest genetic risk factor. It bears on more than half of all cases.

One gene form, the ε4 allele, raises risk sharply. The ε2 allele guards against the disease by contrast. The three forms differ at just two amino acid spots. ApoE hauls lipids in the brain and body as its day job. The harmful form seeds amyloid plaques early and thick. Isoforms also split on tau, inflammation, and vessel health. That rich biology makes drug design hard, the authors say. Therapy plans span level tuning and shape fixing drugs. Gene therapy and microRNA routes join the list. New tools for cell type work close the survey.
europmc-pmc9868039:
Turner and co-authors sum up a major update to the taxonomy of bacterial viruses. The update covers work from March 2021 to March 2022. It came from the Bacterial Viruses Subcommittee of the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses. Plans made in 2021 were approved and then ratified by vote in 2022.

The old families Podoviridae, Siphoviridae, and Myoviridae were abolished. The order Caudovirales was abolished as well. In their place came a two-name system for species. One order, 22 families, and 30 subfamilies were created, promoted, or moved. So were 321 genera and 862 species. The article gives virus experts a single record of the new scheme.
europmc-pmc9927939:
Mohandes and co-authors map the molecular pathways that drive diabetic kidney disease. Kidney disease is a major cause of death in diabetes. Diabetic kidney disease accounts for close to half of all chronic kidney disease. It tends to arise when poor blood sugar control meets genetic risk.

The review centers on podocytes and endothelial cells in early disease. Proximal tubule changes track closely with filtration rate decline. High glucose strains kidney cells, alters their metabolism, and raises energy demand. Later, mitochondrial faults add oxidative stress and inflammation, driving scarring. Blocking the renin-angiotensin system or sodium-glucose transport slows decline. The authors point to new pathways as sources of needed drugs.
faraday-experimental-researches-vol1-183:
Michael Faraday published Volume 1 of Experimental Researches in Electricity in 1839, gathering his papers of the 1830s. Faraday, a bookbinder's lad turned the Royal Institution's leading worker, reported his trials in numbered series. Volume 1 holds Series 1 through 14.

The series announce a great find: electric current made by moving magnets. That find lies behind every dynamo and transformer since. Faraday also set out the laws of how currents split compounds, and coined terms such as electrode and ion. His style reports each trial so others can repeat it. The volume is a founding record of electrical science.
frus-1861-d139:
From Washington on 26 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton after the Bull Run defeat. The letter is document 139 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Five days after Bull Run, Seward's word to Paris had to admit loss without yielding ground. France must not read the defeat as a reason to back the South. The letter shows that hard balance being struck in real time. France's foreign chief, Thouvenel, heard the Union's case from Dayton in person. In person talks let Dayton press points that paper alone could not carry. Thouvenel heard the same balance in person.
frus-1861-d239:
On 14 June 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. It stands as Document 239 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter comes from the opening months of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d39:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 10 April 1861. Adams was about to sail as the new American minister to Great Britain. The letter is document 39 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

London was the post that mattered most. Britain's mills craved Southern cotton, and its fleet ruled the seas. Seward's letter sent Adams to that post two days before Fort Sumter, with the fate of the Union in part in his hands. Adams carried a famous name: his father and grandfather had both been Presidents of the United States.
frus-1862-d139:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 8 September 1862. It stands as Document 139 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d239:
On 18 September 1862, the day after Antietam, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart of the British legation. The letter stands as Document 239 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Antietam had checked Lee's invasion at terrible cost, and Lincoln would soon issue his emancipation plan. News of the battle was still fresh and partial when Seward wrote. A letter from this date sits at a hinge in the record. The military facts that foreign governments had been waiting for were changing, and with them the odds of outside action. Lyons also reported home on each note, so most of these papers exist in two archives.
frus-1862-d339:
Filed as Document 339 but dated 21 October 1862, this dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. The printers set it after a later Dayton report in the 1862 volume.

The letter belongs with the Seward mail of 20 and 21 October, when Washington was pressing its advantage as the truce plan faltered. Its late filing is a clerical accident of the printed volume. Read by date, it joins the effort to lock in Britain's refusal before France could reopen the question. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d39:
Word from Charles Francis Adams reached Washington on 21 March 1862, in a letter to William H. Seward. It stands as Document 39 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the winter of the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d439:
Gabriel García Tassara wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 October 1862. The note is Document 439 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

By October 1862 the rush of foreign intervention talk had eased, and the Spanish correspondence in Washington settled back toward its standing subjects. Tassara, long posted in the capital, handled Madrid's interests with Seward directly. Those interests touched Cuba, the Gulf, and the French advance in Mexico, which Spain had quit but still watched. His autumn note is one more turn in a long, careful exchange that kept two wary governments on speaking terms through the war.
frus-1862-d539:
On 28 July 1862 Roest van Limburg sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 539 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

End of July 1862 found the Dutch exchange in its regular stride, one note answering another across a few days. Van Limburg wrote for a government whose colonial ports lay close to the war's sea lanes. Those ports stood in the West Indies. American practice there was therefore a standing Dutch concern. His letters are formal by design, which makes them good evidence: what a government puts in a signed note, it means. The document adds another careful layer to the Washington side of the Netherlands file.
frus-1862-d639:
Townsend Harris wrote from Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 July 1861, now addressing the secretary by name. The dispatch is Document 639 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

By July, word of the change of administration had long since reached Edo. Harris's correspondence settled into its wartime form. It consisted of reports to Seward from a post the war could not reach. His health was failing after five years in Japan. His letters of this season carry the strain of the post. He was a man holding a difficult station alone. The dispatch belongs to the last year of the first American mission to Japan. That mission is a story of endurance. The volume preserves it at the edge of its Civil War record.
frus-1863p1-d139:
On 31 March 1863, William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 139 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a month-end letter often tied off the month's loose ends. Seward's second sheet of 31 March sits in that place in the file. With its twin, it closes a March in which Washington wrote to London by the dozen and the score. The pair is a fair end to the thickest month in the printed exchange.
frus-1863p1-d239:
Writing from London on 16 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 239 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

After the Emancipation Proclamation took effect on New Year's Day 1863, the war stood openly as a fight over slavery. That change made British support for the South harder to defend in public. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d339:
The American answer to London on 16 December 1862 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 339 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d39: On 17 October 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote to a Mr. Théron. Benjamin was the Confederate secretary of state in Richmond, and the letter is document 39 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It sits in the group of Confederate papers printed in that volume, alongside Benjamin's letters to the South's envoys in Europe.
frus-1863p1-d439:
The date 2 April 1863 heads a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d539:
On 27 May 1863 a formal note passed from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d639:
Among the day's business on 16 October 1863 was a letter from Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London to Secretary William H. Seward. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

Read in sequence, the London letters show how close the two countries came to open conflict, and how both sides kept stepping back. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1933-39:
This special volume covers Soviet relations from recognition onward. America ends sixteen years of refusal in November 1933. Claims and credits talks follow to fulfill the bargain. They fail by 1935 in a candid file. The Moscow embassy shrinks; its consulate general closes. A trade deal signs that July instead. Moscow's Comintern congress draws a sharp protest. Aiding American Communists breaks the pledge of noninterference. Building the new embassy stalls over terms. Trade terms roll on to 1937 in short deals.

A mid-volume warning concerns a warship sale. If war came and the President proclaimed an embargo, delivery would fail. Vessels of war head the banned list, the Soviet envoy is told. The volume is recognition's rocky first years. Handshakes and protests alternate throughout.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d139: Secretary Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on November 18, 1943, and the letter is Document 139 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hull stayed in Washington while the president traveled, minding the home front of American diplomacy. His letters in the voyage week kept the traveling party tied to the department. The record names the two men and the date. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d239:
From Washington on 20 November 1943, Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a short secret telegram, passing on two reports from Ankara dated 17 and 18 November. Both concern Turkey's slow move toward joining the war.

Ankara reports that Foreign Minister Numan won his party leaders' approval to tell Eden the Turks had decided in principle to enter the war. Military help for Turkey now came first, ahead of the political question of Soviet pledges. The British feared the decision would leak and draw an early Axis attack, and noted heavy losses off Leros. The second report has German ambassador von Papen telling Finland's minister that Turkey would stay out, which the minister read as a lie meant to calm Hitler.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d339:
Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy sent Harry Hopkins a memorandum at Cairo on 30 November 1943. Hopkins was then at Tehran. The memorandum sets out the civil affairs arrangement worked out with the British. He asks Hopkins to approve it, and to phone him.

Four points make up the deal. America will treat the European Advisory Commission seriously and give Ambassador Winant a strong staff. Britain will drop the plan to move the Combined Civil Affairs Committee to London, and its Washington members will be empowered to act. Commission recommendations will pass through the Combined Chiefs of Staff for comment before going to the three governments as final. The chiefs will then write the field directives. McCloy has Hull's and Stimson's approval, and his one worry is speed, since Winant does not strike him as a fast administrator.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d39: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on October 6, 1943, and his message is Document 39 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The letter came as the three powers prepared their first foreign ministers' meeting of the war, set for Moscow later that month. The catalog gives the date and the names only. In the published volume the message sits among the exchanges that turned a hoped-for summit into a dated plan.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d439:
A second set of Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes survives from December 4, 1943, the first day of the Second Cairo Conference. The Combined Chiefs were the top American and British officers who directed the two nations' shared war. The State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume preserves this session next to the day's other meetings.

Formal minutes like these keep the shape of the discussion: the questions put to the chiefs, the views of each side, and the conclusions entered into the record. For students of the war, the value lies in that detail. Grand strategy at Cairo was not declared in speeches; it was argued out in rooms like this one and written down.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d539:
Heaton Stevens, second secretary at the American embassy in China, wrote to his own ambassador, Clarence Gauss, on January 5, 1944. Internal embassy letters carried the frank judgments that formal reports to Washington sometimes softened. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Gauss ran a hard-pressed embassy in Chungking, China's wartime capital, and his junior officers fed him reporting from inside the mission. A letter up the internal chain shows diplomacy's workshop rather than its shop window. For readers, it adds a staff-level Chinese view to a volume dominated by presidents and prime ministers, in the weeks after the Cairo Declaration.
frus-1944-quebec-d139:
George Elsey, assistant to the president's naval aide, prepared this background memorandum on occupying Austria and the Balkans before the Quebec Conference. It traces how a question that seemed settled in May 1944 became confused within weeks. The confusion turned on one word: whether American agreement covered Austria's occupation or only its control.

Roosevelt had approved a policy of no American occupation forces in southern or southeastern Europe, Austria included. Yet Ambassador Winant told the European Advisory Commission America accepted tripartite occupation of Austria. Winant explained he had the president's permission for tripartite control, without committing any force. The Joint Chiefs finally allowed a possible token force, while General Wilson planned to occupy Austria with four British divisions.
frus-1944-quebec-d239:
Alexander Kirk, the American representative on the Advisory Council for Italy, reported from Caserta on September 12, 1944. General Wilson had heard from London that the War Cabinet wanted data on how relief in Italy was being administered. The British Service of Supplies was to report existing arrangements and expenditures to date, and what steps were being taken to restart Italian production.

The War Office also wanted General O'Dwyer's report, which he had carried to Washington, sent back with Wilson's comments urgently for the War Cabinet's use. London knew the report would reach the British through Washington in due course. In the meantime, Wilson was asked for his copy plus any additional pertinent information he could supply.
frus-1944-quebec-d39:
August 31, 1944 brought another Churchill message to Roosevelt. It closed the month's exchange between the two leaders. The State Department placed it in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Churchill spent late August preparing to sail for Canada. Roosevelt would receive him at Quebec. His letters that week stated the British case. The questions awaiting them included Germany's future. They also included the war against Japan. For readers, the message is his final word from London. It came before the conference opened. His written preparation in this file was always thorough and detailed. The conference itself opened days later in Quebec City.
frus-1945-50-intel-d139:
Minutes of the 184th meeting of the Secretary of State's Staff Committee are dated 5 February 1946. The committee's numbered run continues into the new year in the volume's second printing of its records. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

The 184th meeting sat as the central system was being born next door, and the State Department's own intelligence office faced its new neighbor. Committee minutes at such a moment record a department adjusting to a settled fact. Readers who followed the November meetings can complete the arc here. The committee went from fixing a position in a fight to living with the fight's result. The staff committee's paper trail gives the State side of 1946 its steady pulse.
frus-1945-50-intel-d239:
On 11 February 1949, Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter sent a letter to the Speaker of the House of Representatives (Rayburn). Readers meet it as document 239 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The first Dulles Report season had begun: an outside team judged the CIA while the agency and its partners answered back.

A formal letter was a step above a memo: it put a request or a stance on record under the writer's signature. Letters like this one let a reader follow a debate between two offices in their own words. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d339:
A letter from Sherman Kent reached Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 9 February 1948. The State Department prints it as document 339 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. Replies in the same file show the exchange from both sides. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d39:
McCormack, the State Department's special assistant for research and intelligence, wrote to Admiral Leahy, the president's chief of staff, on 31 October 1945. Leahy was the gatekeeper at Truman's door. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Writing to Leahy was a way of writing to the president by the staff door. McCormack, whose office held the old OSS analysts, had a plan for central intelligence centered on State. He needed the White House to hear it. His letter shows the State Department taking its case to the top as the Budget Bureau did the same. Readers can feel the contest tightening: by Halloween of 1945, every claimant had found a path to the president's desk.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d139:
Assistant Secretary of War McCloy laid the Bremen problem before the Secretary of State on 23 January 1945. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume in excerpt, asks for help at the coming conference. The issue is American control of the Bremen area in the British zone.

Ever since Quebec, McCloy writes, Washington has tried to get its hold on Bremen clarified, after giving the northwest of Germany to the British. Halifax backed a proposal that seemed to solve it. London's reply, though, added reservations that go pretty deep. The staff still will not clear ratification of the zones protocol until the matter is straight. If the conference staffs can clear the big snags, local commanders can settle the details.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d239:
Stettinius sent the President a draft answer to Churchill on Iran on 17 January 1945. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, encloses the suggested reply to the prime minister's telegram 890 on the oil concession controversy. The Department's own view comes first.

Iran should be discussed at the coming meeting, Washington agrees. It should be taken up among the three leaders themselves, as signatories of the Tehran Declaration. But no advance notice should be given, since notice would lend the subject undue importance. The draft reply concurs fully in the discussion. It adds a measured judgment. The evidence does not yet prove that Russia means to force a concession now. But her open dissatisfaction with Iran's wartime law stirs apprehension that should be quieted.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d339: Three quick points fill this handwritten note from Harry Hopkins to President Roosevelt, passed during the second plenary meeting on February 5, 1945. France, Hopkins noted, already sat on the European Advisory Commission, the only body then studying German affairs. He advised promising France a zone of occupation. He also advised putting off any decision about the Control Commission for Germany. Together these slips show how the French-zone question was settled in practice: zone now, machinery later.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d39: Roosevelt replied to Churchill on 2 January 1945, keeping their exchange unbroken into the summit month. The message stands as document 39 in the Foreign Relations volume covering the Malta and Yalta conferences. By then the American and British staffs were packing for Malta, where the two Western delegations would meet first before flying on together to the Crimea in February.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d439:
So far agreed: this delegation paper of February 10, 1945, prints the Polish formula as the three foreign ministers had settled it. A new situation, it opens, has been created by the complete liberation of Poland by the Red Army. A broader provisional government is called for.

The government then functioning in Poland should be reorganized on a broader democratic basis. Democratic leaders from Poland itself and from abroad would be included. The new body would be called the Polish Provisional Government of National Unity. Molotov, Harriman, and Clark Kerr would consult in Moscow, first with the present government's members. The text is the Yalta settlement on Poland, caught before the leaders signed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d139:
Acting Secretary Grew answered the London embassy's press question on July 14, 1945. His telegram to Ambassador Winant is document 139 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Winant had said that London newsmen expected a meeting place with the President's party late in the talks.

Grew explains that one man each from the Associated Press, United Press, and the news wire and film pools is traveling with the President. They will not attend the talks. They will wait at a meeting place still to be chosen, which some Washington newsmen may also join. The plan is for American newsmen only, and details will come from the White House through press aide Ross. The press stayed near the story but outside the sealed grounds.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d239:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded the Spanish ambassador's probe about Franco's Spain in extracts of a memorandum dated July 9, 1945. The extracts form document 239 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Ambassador de Cárdenas called that afternoon, speaking, he said, friend to friend and not under instructions.

Cárdenas raised the San Francisco decision. Under it, states whose regimes were set up with Axis military help would be barred from the world organization. The bar would last while those regimes lasted. That formula was aimed at Franco's Spain. He asked whether Grew knew of a proposed move by Chile and Uruguay. The move would apply the provision openly to Spain. He also asked whether Ambassador Armour had spoken on the subject in Madrid. Grew said he had no information on either point. Spain's status did reach the Potsdam table, where the three leaders condemned the Franco regime.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d339:
Germany's ban on all political activity is weighed in Murphy's top secret airgram of June 28, 1945, to Matthews, the director of European affairs. Murphy, the political adviser at supreme headquarters, supplements his earlier report of June 2. He lists the risks on both sides of the ban.

Groups allowed to organize soon, he warns, would likely turn against the American military government, above all if hard times came. Yet the ban itself was negative and suppressive, and it left a political vacuum others would try to fill. Kept too long, it might discourage the faint democratic stirrings he could already see among Germans.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d39:
Churchill quoted his own telegram to Stalin in this message to Truman of May 29, 1945. He would be very glad, he had told the Marshal, to meet him and President Truman soon. The place would be what is left of Berlin. He hoped the meeting might take place about the middle of June. He had repeated the telegram to Truman, he added.

The point had been raised in Stalin's talks with Hopkins, Churchill noted to the Marshal. All good wishes closed the message; he was very anxious to meet soon. The quotation shows London pressing for June while Washington aimed at July — a small gap that shaped the summer.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d439:
Czechoslovakia's formal case for expulsion is made in a note from Under-Secretary Clementis to the American chargé, dated at Prague on July 3, 1945. Before the fighting stopped, he writes, the President and government of Czechoslovakia had sent the allied governments a detailed memorandum. It set out the political necessity of evacuating most of the German and Hungarian population.

In doing so, Clementis says, they spoke for the elemental and unanimous wishes of the Czech and Slovak nations. Those nations, anxious for the state's future, wished to exclude elements that had proved propagators of national hatred. They had been, he charges, willing instruments of hostile propaganda and instigators of dissension within the country.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d539:
Post-war financial talks with Britain cannot wait, a briefing book summary argues. It is important to come very soon to definite understandings with the British on post-war financial questions. There is serious danger, it warns, that otherwise Britain may not ultimately go along with the American program to restore world-wide multilateralism in finance and trade.

The summary suggests the Prime Minister be asked to designate representatives to meet American representatives this summer. They would discuss lend-lease settlement policy, post-lend-lease credits, and post-V-J Day monetary and exchange policies. The talks would join the conversations already under way on foreign trade policy, toward comprehensive post-war arrangements under Article VII of the British master lend-lease agreement.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d639:
Minister Wadsworth reported a French peace feeler in the Levant from Beirut on July 1, 1945. His confidential wire is document 639 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It recounts a proposal passed quietly by the French envoy Ostrorog two days before.

Ostrorog proposed that the Troupes Speciales pass to Syria and Lebanon at once. French troops would then leave the Levant at the same time as British troops. That, he argued, would end the tension and let all sides settle their shared problems in good will. Lebanon's foreign minister Pharaon gave a careful answer. Transfer and withdrawal were main Syrian and Lebanese aims, he said. But the basic shape of future ties with France could be settled only in international talks, not in a private deal.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1039: William Clayton and Emile Despres sent this one-line secret telegram from Babelsberg to Willard Thorp in Washington on July 18, 1945. Both men were working on German economic affairs at the Potsdam Conference. Their question is narrow and practical. They ask Thorp to advise them whether the Soviet Union has been informed of the American proposal for a directive on German coal production and exports. The answer follows in the next document in the volume. The brevity of the cable shows a delegation checking one fact before its next move.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1139:
Arthur Bliss Lane, named as the new American ambassador to Poland, wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on 24 July 1945. Lane had his posting but not yet his post. The Warsaw embassy was not open, since Poland's future was still being fought over at Potsdam.

An envoy in waiting worked his brief from afar. He studied the country, the parties, and the men he would soon deal with. His cable shows that work under way days before the summit settled Poland's fate. It is foreign service in a strange pause: full duties, no embassy. The record keeps few such glimpses.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1239:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff wrote to the President on 18 July 1945. The chiefs' direct channel to Truman was a fixture of the war's last year. Their messages joined military judgment to the summit's bargaining while Germany's peace was drafted.

At Potsdam the chiefs' concerns ran from the forces in Europe to the invasion plans for Japan. A note sent on the talks' second day fed that judgment into the opening rounds. This message is one piece of the written record of the alliance at work. It shows the soldiers' house keeping its hand on the president's brief.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1339:
The acting secretary of state, Joseph Grew, wrote to Secretary of State James Byrnes on 19 July 1945. Byrnes was at Potsdam with President Truman, while Grew held the department in Washington. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

With the secretary abroad, the acting secretary's letters formed the spine of the department for weeks. They carried news, requests, and warnings across the Atlantic so the men at the summit stayed tied to their own government. This letter shows the home office at work during one of the busiest stretches of 1945. How much trust the system placed in the man left behind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-139:
The United States delegation circulated this memorandum at Potsdam on July 30, 1945. With two days left, staff papers carried urgent weight. A memo could lock a position before a plenary session began. This one was filed with the conference papers and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Final-week memoranda reward close reading. They often mark the last point where a view could still change. Writers stated their case in short, plain terms. For readers today, the memo is a dated marker of American thinking at the brink of the final deal. It adds grit to the smooth surface of the agreed texts.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-39:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes record the approval of their 196th meeting's conclusions, held July 19, 1945. The top secret record is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Potsdam papers. It settles the rules for passing war information to the Russians, the dispute aired in volume one.

Two rules were written into the conclusions. On operational information and intelligence, each side may pass the Russians what it wishes, without bargaining. That covers the theaters for which each staff is responsible. On all other information, the two staffs must consult together first. Neither party may pass Moscow anything drawn wholly or partly from the other's sources without that party's consent. The chiefs then took up a draft directive to the Supreme Commander in Southeast Asia, proposed by the British chiefs.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d739:
Benjamin Gerig, the American alternate delegate to the United Nations Preparatory Commission, wrote to Leo Pasvolsky and Alger Hiss on July 26, 1945. Document 739 comes from the building of the new world body. The Commission, seated in London, was readying the first General Assembly. Gerig reported to two of the Department's top planners.

Letters like this one wired Potsdam to the United Nations' birth. The men addressed had shaped the charter at San Francisco. Readers see postwar planning as a single web: summit talks in Germany, organization work in London. The document shows staff keeping both efforts in step during a crowded week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d839:
Document 839 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 22, 1945. Staff drafted it as the conference closed its first week. Working papers at this stage answered points raised in the early sessions. The paper was kept in the delegation files and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A week's-end draft shows learning in progress. The writers had heard the other sides and adjusted. Readers can track the change from the opening papers. The document also shows the staff's rhythm: sessions by day, drafting by night. That rhythm produced the mountain of paper from which the final protocol was cut.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d939:
Soviet Foreign Minister Molotov presented this second definition of war trophies at Potsdam on July 27, 1945. It restates the Soviet claim in two parts. War trophies mean all German military property. That includes gear meant for use by enemy military and paramilitary units, or by their members.

The second part reaches beyond the battlefield. It covers property the enemy used for military purposes. Such property counts even when it was removed from Germany during the war to serve Allied military needs. A later letter in the Pauley Files notes that no formal action was taken on either Soviet definition.
frus-1969-76v39:
European security fills Volume XXXIX of the 1969-1976 Foreign Relations series. Early chapters cover the push for talks on troop cuts and a security conference. The Moscow summit of 1972 forms a bridge chapter. Long chapters then follow the opening of the talks and the U.S.-Soviet talks beside them. Basket III, on human contacts, gets a chapter of its own. The volume ends with the Helsinki summit of 1975 and a final run on troop cuts.

The records show allies arguing over words on frontiers and human contacts. Memos weigh how much freedom of movement to demand from the East. The Helsinki chapters close the main arc.
fundamental-orders-connecticut-1639:
Settlers from Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield adopted the Fundamental Orders in 1639 to govern their Connecticut towns. The document lays out a frame of government made by the settlers themselves. No royal charter stood behind it, which made the act bold for its time.

The orders provide for a general court, elected magistrates, and a governor chosen each year. They set rules for meetings, voting, and the duties of town deputies. Because the plan is written, general, and based on consent, many call it the first written constitution in America. It guided Connecticut until a royal charter arrived in 1662.
gao-gaoreports-b-296239:
A joint venture protested the terms of an Army Corps call for modular buildings in GAO decision B-296239, dated July 19, 2005. The site was Biggs Army Airfield at Fort Bliss, Texas. The complex would house a large combat unit. It held barracks, dining space, shops, and offices. The firm hit the mix of terms in the call.

GAO denied the protest. The call used terms for both build work and supply work. That mix was sound here. The job itself mixed both kinds of work. Line items split the work into clear parts. Many were build tasks and many were supply tasks. The terms thus fit the job.
gao-gaoreports-b-298239:
A joint venture protested an Army Corps award for build work in Colorado in GAO decision B-298239, dated July 19, 2006. The winner was B and M Construction. The call was set aside for firms owned by disabled veterans. Up to three wide deals were on offer for small jobs. The firm said the winner was not a fit firm for the set-aside.

GAO denied the protest in part and cut part. Rank as a fit small firm or as a fit veteran firm is for the Small Business office alone. GAO cannot rule that point. Other marks claims were heard and failed. Status fights must go to the office the law names.
gao-gaoreports-b-299539:
Moore's Cafeteria Services protested an Army award for food services at Fort Campbell, Kentucky. The contract went to the Kentucky Office for the Blind. That office is a state licensing agency for the blind. GAO decided B-299539 on June 5, 2007.

The firm attacked the winner's price as too high. It pointed to a policy text on fair and sound price. That text had not yet been put into rules. So the officer was not bound to use its terms. The officer instead matched the price to rival bids and the estimate. That match backed the fair-price call. The award could stand. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-139:
Department of Homeland Security, GAO-05-139 of March 16, 2005, studies the hard merge of 22 agencies into one new department. The merger ranks among the largest in U.S. history. Each source agency brought its own staff rules, pay plans, and computer systems. Stitching them into one set of tools takes years of care.

GAO finds real gains so far in the merge. It also finds a chance to build on them with one broad, steady plan. The report names where joined-up work can grow, from hiring to tech. It warns that a fix in one corner will not hold if the rest drift apart.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-239:
Bioterrorism, GAO-05-239 of February 28, 2005, sorts a fight over grant cash that sat unspent, or just uncounted. Since 1999, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has funded state and local plans to prep for bio attacks. After the 2001 attacks and anthrax mail, funds rose almost twentyfold. Washington then moved some 2004 cash, on the claim that much sat idle.

Local chiefs said pledged cash was missed in that count. GAO tracks what was spent and what was pledged by set dates. It lists why grants moved slow in some places. It tells what some places did to speed the flow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-339:
Nuclear Regulatory Commission, GAO-05-339 of April 8, 2005, warns that used reactor fuel can go lost on the books. Spent fuel can no longer drive a reactor, but it stays hot and fierce for thousands of years. In 2004, rods were found lost at the Vermont Yankee plant. That find shook trust in how plants track each rod.

GAO grades how plants count and guard their spent fuel. It grades how keen the commission's rules and site checks are. It lists what the commission has done since flaws came to light. The watch must do more to make sure each plant's grip is true, the title holds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-539:
New reporting duties for job training programs are weighed in GAO report GAO-05-539, released on May 27, 2005. The Workforce Investment Act of 1998 tied 17 programs to one-stop centers and set shared outcome measures. The Labor Department proposed a single reporting system, called EMILE, for the measures it oversees. GAO asked how heavy that load would be and how the plan was built.

Most states backed simpler reporting. But 36 states said EMILE, as drawn, would be very burdensome. Many said it would take as much work as the 2000 build, or more. GAO found the department had understated the scale of change and the help states would need. It had built the plan with little state input. One new measure could even deter serving laid-off workers. States had little time before data collection had to start. GAO urged the department to weigh other paths and test the plan for a year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-639:
The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria is audited in GAO report GAO-05-639 of June 10, 2005. The fund, set up in 2002, had signed over 270 grants and paid out more than $1 billion. The United States gave almost one-third of its $3.7 billion. Grants pay in stages, tied to proof of results, with a renewal review at 2 years.

Weak local systems often slowed the work, and missing national treatment guides stalled some grants. GAO found the proof behind funding choices shaky: recipient reports rest on thin local checks, and decisions are poorly documented. The fund is tightening its methods; GAO adds its own recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-239:
The market watchdog's own books are audited in GAO-06-239, a report issued on November 15, 2005. The Securities and Exchange Commission was founded in 1934 to enforce securities laws and guard investors. A 2002 law requires it to file audited financial statements with Congress and the budget office. GAO agreed to run the audit under its own authority. The audit covers fiscal years 2005 and 2004. It asks whether the statements can be trusted in all material respects.

GAO also judged whether the commission kept sound internal control over its reporting. It tested compliance with the laws that bind the agency's money work. An agency that polices the accounts of public firms must keep clean accounts itself. The audit applies the same discipline to the regulator that the regulator demands of firms. Its results feed the yearly audit of the whole government's statements. Readers get a check on the checker.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-639:
Oil and chemical spills in a busy border waterway are covered in GAO-06-639, a report GAO issued on June 7, 2006. The St. Clair-Detroit River corridor links the United States and Canada and sits near drinking water intakes. Spills there have harmed the border area over the years. United States spills are reported to the National Response Center, and Canadian spills to a center in Ontario.

GAO found that spill data were not good enough to pin down the true number or size of spills. Rules for telling the other nation about a spill were not clear on timing or size thresholds. The Environmental Protection Agency's prevention and enforcement work was limited. GAO said better data and targeted prevention could improve spill management.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-839:
Rights to technical data for weapons are examined in GAO-06-839 of July 14, 2006. When the government buys a weapon, it also needs the drawings and data to maintain it. If the contractor keeps those rights, the services can be locked into costly support deals. GAO reviewed how the Army and Air Force fared on fielded systems. GAO asked whether defense policy helps them secure the data they need.

GAO found that both services had hit limits in their sustainment plans. Missing technical data rights blocked changes meant to save money. The gaps also hampered plans to meet legal duties for depot maintenance capacity. GAO said the department should strengthen its policies for judging data needs up front. Data rights, the report shows, are decided at contract signing and paid for decades later.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-139:
Between disasters, the Federal Emergency Management Agency still has daily work to run. GAO found that work poorly tracked in GAO-07-139, a report dated January 19, 2007. The study covers fiscal years 2001 through 2005. In that span, the agency was reorganized four times in 3 years. It also moved into the new Homeland Security Department in March 2003. Programs worth over $1.3 billion flowed in while nearly $1.5 billion flowed out.

GAO said the agency could not fully explain its own resource trends. It lacked solid data on staffing, funding shifts, and grant allocations. It had no strategic workforce plan and no business continuity plans for daily operations. Those gaps left it reacting to change rather than managing through it. GAO advised the agency to define its day-to-day resources first. It also urged workforce planning and continuity plans tied to the disaster mission.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-39:
Most critical infrastructure sits in private hands, so protection runs through joint councils. GAO graded the councils' formation in GAO-07-39, a report dated October 16, 2006. About 85 percent of key assets are privately owned. Each sector was to form government and industry councils. The councils write protection plans under a national framework. GAO checked which councils exist. It asked what helped or blocked them.

Every sector had a government council, GAO found. Industry councils existed for all but transport systems as of August 2006. Ten sectors had organized before the national model appeared. Banking and telecom councils work on strategy. Newer ones, like health and commercial facilities, still recruit members. The nuclear sector's sameness eases teamwork. Health care's diversity makes it hard. A channel for sharing sensitive data with government saw little use. Owners doubted their data would stay protected.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-839:
An Iraq oil contract is faulted in GAO-07-839, dated July 31, 2007. The Army Corps of Engineers gave Kellogg Brown & Root a $2.5 billion deal in March 2003. The Restore Iraqi Oil contract aimed to rebuild Iraq's oil network. It also ensured fuel supplies inside the country. The deal paid the firm's costs plus a fee, with a bonus fee possible. Federal auditors questioned $221 million of the firm's costs. GAO asked how the Defense Department handled those findings.

The department paid nearly all of the questioned costs in the end. It cut about $112 million from the sum used to set the firm's fee, though. That step trimmed the fee by about $5.8 million. Late talks drove the outcome, GAO found. All 10 task orders were settled over 180 days after work began. By then, the firm had spent nearly all the money. GAO urged feasibility checks on bonus fee plans in crisis contracts. The department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-39:
Stabilization and reconstruction work abroad is covered by GAO report GAO-08-39, dated December 6, 2007. The State Department's Coordinator for Reconstruction and Stabilization (S/CRS) is building a framework to plan and coordinate such operations across agencies. GAO also checked plans for three rapid-response civilian corps.

The National Security Council had adopted two of the framework's three main parts, but the planning guide was still unfinished. Roles for each agency were unclear, and partners had no shared definition of these operations. The framework had never been fully used in a real operation, so its worth was unproven.
