Key details for the new corps also stayed open. GAO told the Secretary of State to clear up roles and finish the framework. State partly agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-539:
State pandemic flu planning is covered by GAO report GAO-08-539, dated June 19, 2008. Federal strategy puts states and localities first in a flu pandemic. Congress gave $600 million to states and some localities for planning and drills.

All 50 states have pandemic plans, GAO reports, and the five states and 10 localities visited drew in federal, tribal, nonprofit, and private partners. A federal review still found many major gaps in 16 of 22 priority areas, such as school closure policy and public messaging. All funded states and localities have run drills and folded lessons into their plans, from buying gear to new training. GAO urged joint federal meetings in the five pandemic regions to close the gaps. Both departments agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-939:
The Department of Veterans Affairs owns more buildings than it can use well. GAO-08-939, a September 2008 report, tracks its progress in shedding space it does not need. Many VA sites are old and poorly suited to modern care. GAO asked how much spare space VA has cut, what it costs to keep, and which legal tools VA uses to cut more.

Underused space inside buildings fell from 15.4 million square feet in fiscal year 2005 to 5.6 million in fiscal year 2007, though vacant space held near 7.5 million square feet. GAO estimates VA spent $175 million in fiscal year 2007 running space it barely or never uses. VA does not track those costs building by building, which GAO says blocks further cuts. VA accepted one fix and disputed another.
great-bible-1539:
Myles Coverdale prepared the Great Bible, printed in 1539 as the first English Bible authorized for public use. King Henry VIII ordered a copy placed in every parish church in England. Its huge page size gave it the name Great, and copies were chained to lecterns so anyone could hear or read them.

Coverdale built the text by revising Matthew's Bible, drawing on Latin and German sources where older English ran out. The volume holds the complete Old and New Testaments. It put one shared English Scripture in front of the whole country, and later translators, including the Geneva team, worked from it.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
The first part of chapter five in John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands portrays Alexander Farnese before Antwerp. Parma at thirty-seven has the experience of a sexagenarian, Motley says. The impetuous, hot-headed youth has become pensive, modest, almost gentle. His genius is rapid in conception and patient in combination.

Preparations for the siege of Antwerp fill the chapter: forts, lines, and the great bridge across the Scheldt. Farnese commands a handful of veterans in an infamous cause, and Motley grants them full military virtue. No general in the history receives more respect than this enemy of the republic. The portrait explains why Antwerp was doomed: not Dutch cowardice but a besieger of the first rank. Readers meet the war's most complete soldier, painted by his opponents' historian.
ioannis-aurelij-augurelli-p-ariminensis-:
Giovanni Aurelio Augurello of Rimini wrote Chrysopoeia, a Latin poem on making gold, here joined with Vellus Aureum. The title page says this cleaner text now first comes from an old manuscript. Augurello addresses the poem to Pope Leo the Tenth. He asks leave to reveal his art as a noble virgin lifts a veil.

A tiny powder can convert a huge mass of metal, the poem claims. As a speck of crocus flower colors and scents much water, so the stone works. Spirit enters the dense body and mixes through it, he sings. The poem is alchemy in verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-hayyi: Aaron ben Hayyim, an exegete who lived at Grodno, Russia, in the first half of the nineteenth century, fills this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He wrote Moreh Derek, or He Who Shows the Way. The work traces the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt. It follows their wanderings in the desert and the partition of Canaan among the Twelve Tribes. A colored map of Palestine was appended to the work. The book was published at Grodno in 1836, the entry reports.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-hoshaya-of:
Abba Hoshaya of Turya was a Palestinian wool-washer of the third century. Nothing is recorded of any learning he may have had. His fame rests on piety and honesty, which gave storytellers ground for legends. He was said to have been born on the day a certain Rabbi Abun died.

One tale tells how Abba found jewels a Roman princess had lost and brought them back to her. She told him to keep them, but he refused. The Jewish Law, he said, orders that found goods go back to their owner. At that the princess praised the God of the Jews. A verse from Canticles was later applied to him at his funeral.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abendana-jacob-:
Jacob Abendana was hakam of London, born in 1630 and dead on September 12, 1695. He was the oldest son of Joseph Abendana, and trained at the De los Pintos academy in Rotterdam. In 1655 he took a call as hakam to Amsterdam. That year he spoke in memory of two Maranos burned at the stake in Cordova.

With his brother Isaac he issued the Bible commentary "Miklal Yofi," with his own notes, at Amsterdam in 1660. A bid by Professor Hulsius to convert him, carried on by letter about a verse of Haggai, pushed him to turn Judah ha-Levi's "Cuzari" into Spanish. The version is prized for its care. In 1680 he moved to London, and there, it is said, he finished a Spanish Mishnah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abner-339: Abner was a cabalist and a teacher of Isaac of Acco. The entry dates him to about 1150. Isaac named him as a great authority in mystic philosophy. No work by Abner is listed, and no birthplace or death date is given. His record rests on that link to Isaac of Acco and on his standing among students of mystic thought in his time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-mos: Abraham ben Moses of Regensburg, called the Great Rabbi Abraham, was a German tosafist. He flourished about 1200 at Ratisbon, Germany. His readings of the Talmud and his halakic decisions are found in the Tosafot and in other writings, the entry states. No book under his own name is listed, and no birth or death year is given. His work survives inside the writings of others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-absalom-639: Absalom was one of the five sons of John Hyrcanus. When Judas Aristobulus took the Hasmonean throne in 105 B.C., Absalom was jailed with his mother and two brothers. The king died a year later and freed them. His brother Alexander Jannæus then ruled and gave Absalom high honors. Absalom chose the life of a subject over a claim to the crown. Pompey took him captive when Jerusalem fell in 63 B.C. His line later joined the house of Herod the Great.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-academies-in-ba:
Academies in Babylonia traces the schools of Jewish learning east of Palestine. For four centuries after Ezra the record is thin. Sherira Gaon wrote that public teaching went on, but no school heads were known before the death of Judah I. Nehardea was the chief seat. It had an old synagogue tied by lore to King Jehoiachin. Nisibis also had a strong college.

The turn came when Rab came home in 219. He left Nehardea to Samuel and opened a new age. Sura, Pumbedita, and Maḥuza rose as great schools. For centuries these schools led Jewish learning. The entry tells how their heads taught set texts month by month. At the kallah meets, questions sent from far towns were debated. The head gave the final call. The answers were read out and signed as responsa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-accad-or-akkad-:
Accad, also spelled Akkad, is a city named once in the Old Testament. Genesis x. 10 lists it among the four cities that began the realm of Nimrod. No one knows just where it stood. Clay tablets use Akkad as a city name. An inscription of Nebuchadnezzar I, about 1135 B.C., uses it too. That text gives no hint of the place or its past.

Some critics link Accad with Agade in north Babylonia. Sargon I ruled there about 3800 B.C. The entry says no firm proof backs that link. In royal titles, Accad names the north of Babylonia. Sumer names the south. Kings who used both names claimed rule over the whole land. Jewish lore split on the site. One line of thought made Accad the same as Nisibis. Babylonian sages made it Bashkar instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-bar-huna-93:
Aha bar Huna was a Babylonian amora of the fourth generation. He studied under Rabbah b. Nahmani and under Sheshet. Hisda, another teacher, used him for halakic letters to Raba ben Joseph. Raba in turn saw him as a great and wise man.

In his days, the Persian queen-mother Ifra-Ormuzd sent Raba an animal. She wanted it offered to the Jewish God by ancient Jewish rites. Sacrifice had ceased when Jerusalem fell, so a substitute act was arranged. Raba sent Aha with Rab Safra to burn the animal. They used a pyre of fresh-cut wood on a sand-bank by the sea.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-de-fr: Alexander de Franciscis, called Hebraeus, was an author and a bishop at Forli. He lived in Rome in the sixteenth century. His Jewish name was Elisha de Roma. After his baptism he joined the Dominican friars, where he stood out as an orator. Pope Clement VIII. made him proctor, then vicar-general, and at last bishop of Forli. He held that see from 1594 to 1597. His writings are Hebrew notes on Genesis and Exodus, keyed to the Vulgate, and a book called "De Tempore et de Sanctis."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-iv-po:
Alexander IV. was pope from 1254 to 1261. Before his election he was Count Rinaldo di Segni. He died at Viterbo on May 25, 1261. He set up the Inquisition in France in 1255. His edict of that era names Roman Jews in a papal paper for the first time in about 750 years. The names given are Angelus, Sabbatorius, Museus, Salamon, and Consiliolus.

On February 1, 1255, he freed those Jewish merchants from road taxes across the papal lands. They traded alongside Christian merchants, though they stood outside the common gilds. The entry says the favor owed more to their usefulness than to love. On September 3, 1257, he reissued the order for the Jewish badge. He also told the duke of Burgundy to seize the Talmud, as full of errors and blasphemies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aliyah-1239:
Aliyah means the call to come up to the Law in synagogue. A man goes up to the reading desk for a part of the weekly lesson. Seven men are called on Sabbath morning. Six are called on the Day of Atonement. Five are called on the three chief feasts. A last man reads from the Prophets as well.

Rank sets the order of the calls. A Cohen comes first and a Levite comes next. Joy and grief both shape who is called. A groom or a new father may be called. The entry traces how the reading task changed. By the 1300s the reader read the whole lesson aloud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alvalensi-samue: Samuel Alvalensi was a Spanish author born in 1435. He died in 1487. His father was Abraham Alvalensi of Toledo, a learned man. His teacher was Isaac Campanton. Campanton is called the last Gaon of Castile. Samuel wrote a small work on Talmud method. It treats the rules of one form of proof. The work was printed at Venice in a larger set.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amram-b-simon-b: Amram ben Simon ben Abba left a faint mark on learning. He was the son of a scholar. He was a nephew of Rabbi Hiyya ben Abba. The entry says he won no fame in the world of study. His name hangs on two brief notes. He quotes those notes in the name of Rabbi Hanina. Two Talmud tracts are cited as the places. Nothing more of his life is told.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-animals-of-the-:
Animals of the Bible opens with the Hebrew words for living creatures. In Genesis, animals are called living soul, always as a group, or simply hayyah, living. The entry notes that this word matches the Latin animal well. Yet Hebrew never uses it for man.

Popular Jewish thought, the entry explains, gladly grants animals all traits that humans share with them, life included. Still, biblical writers keep a distance between brutes and their God-given ruler, man. They unite both only under the wide word creature, when viewing all things from the Creator's side. The entry then surveys the animals named across the Bible and their roles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aphrodite-1639:
Aphrodite is the Greek name for the goddess of love. The entry argues that her name cannot be derived from Greek and is in fact Semitic, one with Ashtoret. She was so bound to Syria that she was worshiped there as the Syrian Aphrodite.

Palestine knew a recognized cult of her, the entry says. It names Jaffa, Acre, and Bozrah as centers. At Acre a bath held her painting, yet the patriarch Gamaliel still bathed there, a case the Mishnah records. Under Hadrian, pagan Jerusalem even raised a temple to Venus on a holy site. The entry follows her worship and its clash with Jewish law across such cases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-archives-israel:
Archives Israelites is a French Jewish review founded in 1840 by Samuel Cahen, known for his French translation of the Hebrew Bible. Its first number came out in January 1840, a sixty-four page monthly of history, biography, bibliography, and letters. Early contributors included Solomon Munk, Albert Cohn, and E. Carmoly.

In 1860 the founder's son, Isidore Cahen, became editor and stayed director until his death on March 6, 1902. The paper changed shape and schedule often: monthly, then twice-monthly, then a weekly from 1879. It grew more like a journal of the day than a review of long essays. In 1890 it marked fifty years with a volume of essays and letters called La Gerbe, The Sheaf.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aruk-1839:
Aruk is the Hebrew word for a dictionary, drawn from a phrase in Job chapter 32 meaning arranged words. Solomon ibn Parhon of Aragon used it for a Bible dictionary in the twelfth century. A Talmud dictionary by the gaon Zemah ben Paltai of Pumbedita came at the close of the ninth century, but only traces of it survive.

The Aruk that scholars quote is the great Talmud dictionary of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, finished in 1101. Shorter versions later spread the work to wider readers, glossing hard words in modern tongues. Christian scholars such as Sebastian Munster and Reuchlin used those shorter forms. The entry traces the word, the lost first try, and the Roman work that fixed the name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-assignment-2039:
Assignment, in law, means passing a right or claim to another person. The entry compares common law with Jewish law on this point. Under Jewish law, strictly read, a claim itself cannot be assigned. Only the thing itself can pass to a new holder. The reason lies in the bond between debtor and creditor, which is personal.

Much of the entry turns on the sheṭar, a written note of debt. Such a note could pass only by writing and delivery together. The entry follows the Talmudic debate on that rule, then Maimonides and later codes. It also covers notes tied to pledged land and pledged goods. The rules it traces stand behind the later law of negotiable instruments, the paper of modern trade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-augustus-called:
Augustus was the first Roman emperor to bear that honorary title. He was born on Sept. 23, 63 B.C. He died at Nola, in Campania, on Aug. 19, 14 C.E. His uncle Julius Cæsar had made him his sole heir. Toward the Jews he kept up Cæsar's friendly policy. He paired zeal for Rome's own religion with broad tolerance of other faiths.

Augustus renewed Cæsar's edicts for the Jews of Cyrene and Asia Minor. Those edicts guarded their worship, their Temple gifts, and their sacred books and synagogues. Jews could not be called to court on the Sabbath or its eve. In Rome, needy Jews could claim their corn share the day after a Sabbath distribution. His friendship with Herod began after Actium, on Sept. 2, 31 B.C. He confirmed Herod's throne and restored lands Herod had lost. After Herod's death he split the realm among Archelaus, Philip, and Antipas.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baal-gad-2239:
Baal-gad was a place at the northern edge of Palestine. It stood in the valley of Lebanon, near Mount Hermon. Joshua names it as a limit of the land in three passages. Since the first book of Chronicles gives Baal-hermon as the northern limit of the tribe of Manasseh, many take the two names for one place.

The entry finds that guess sound. It finds a rival guess weaker, the one that makes Baal-gad the later famed city of Paneas. Paneas, it argues, can hardly be said to lie in the valley of Lebanon. Others link the name to a town in the Biḳa' plain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baer-dob-ben-na: Dob ben Nathan Nata of Pinsk was a Russian rabbi of the first half of the eighteenth century. The whole entry is only a few lines long. It names his descent from Rabbi Nathan Nata Shapira of Cracow, author of "Megalleh 'Amukim." It gives one work of his own: "Neṭa' Sha'ashuim," a commentary on some parts of the Talmud, printed at Zolkiev in 1748. No birth or death date, no posts, and no other writings are stated in the text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baneth-ezekiel-:
Ezekiel Baneth was a Hungarian rabbi born in 1773 at Alt-Ofen. He died on Dec. 28, 1854. Son of a learned rabbi, he gave all his spare time to Talmud even while in the wool business and married. Loss of his property forced him to seek office. He served as rabbi at Széchény, then at Páks, and last at Neutra, where he died at the age of 82.

Students came to Baneth from far away, drawn by his fame. He rejected the "pilpul" style then in fashion in Hungary and took the great medieval authors as his models. Questions on hard points of law reached him from far and wide, and he answered them gladly. Yet he kept no copies and wrote no books, on principle. The entry ends with the esteem Jews and Christians held for him, and the tale of a fiery column seen over his grave.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barnett-jacob-2: Jacob Barnett was a Hebrew teacher at Oxford about 1613, instructing students under Richard Killye, regius professor of Hebrew. Isaac Casaubon, visiting that year, was struck by his abilities and carried him off to London to perfect his own Hebrew. There Barnett showed signs of attraction toward Christianity, and preparations were made to receive him into the Church at Oxford. On the appointed day he was not to be found, and the preacher spoke instead on Jewish perfidy. Found and imprisoned, he was released at Casaubon's plea and banished on November 16, 1613.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bassani-isaiah-:
Isaiah Bassani was an Italian rabbi of the first half of the eighteenth century. He served at Cento from 1702 to 1707, was at Padua by 1712, and later moved to Reggio, where he died some time after 1736. Moses Ḥayyim Luzzatto was among his pupils.

The entry calls Bassani a man of vast learning and wide range. His rulings appear in a large legal work by Lampronti. It also notes a poem, two printed letters, and an unpublished manuscript kept at Ferrara. One of his poems marked a medical degree granted at Padua on Aug. 14, 1716, to Zebulon Conegliano.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-august-273:
August Beer was a German mathematician born at Trier on July 31, 1825. He died at Bonn on Nov. 18, 1863. He studied math and science at Bonn under Plücker and later assisted him. A prize essay on optics won him his doctor's degree in 1848.

Beer became a lecturer at Bonn in 1850 and a full professor of mathematics in 1855. His 1854 book on higher optics brought him a wide name. He also wrote many papers for a leading physics journal. A work on electrostatics came out two years after his death. His teacher Plücker kept him close at Bonn as an assistant during those early years of study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belmonte-isaac-:
Isaac Nuñez Belmonte, called Don Manuel, was a Dutch statesman born in Amsterdam, where he died in 1704. From 1664 he was agent general for Spain, and from 1674 its resident in the Netherlands. The emperor made him a count palatine in 1693.

Belmonte worked to keep Spain and the Netherlands on friendly terms. His letters to the Spanish government from 1667 to 1691 rest at Madrid. He also wrote verse, founded two poetic academies, and drew dedications from leading writers. His carved tombstone still stands near Amsterdam. Three writers of his day dedicated books to him in the years 1683, 1689, and 1693, the entry records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benevento-2939: Benevento is a city in southern Italy, about 32 miles northeast of Naples. Benjamin of Tudela came there about 1165 and found 200 Jewish families. Three men, Kalonymus, Zeraḥ, and Abraham, stood at their head as parnasim. The small community grew after the exile from Spain. When King Ferdinand took the kingdom of Naples in 1504, he set up the Inquisition at Benevento. Its target was the Spanish and Portuguese Maranos who had settled there in large numbers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berechiah-berak: Berechiah Berak ben Isaac Eisik was a Galician preacher who died in 1664 at Constantinople. Trained by Nathan Shapira, rabbi of Cracow, he was named preacher of that city and spent most of his life there. At the end he set out for Jerusalem but died on the way. His sermons on the Pentateuch and other texts were gathered in two volumes as Zera' Berak. The first came out at Cracow in 1646, and the set was reprinted more than once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-hirsc: Hirsch Bernstein, a Russian-American editor and publisher, was born on March 25, 1846, near the Prussian frontier. He had the usual Jewish schooling and learned to write Hebrew with ease. In 1870 he came to the United States and settled in New York. That year he started the first Yiddish periodical in America, though it lived only a short time. He also founded the first Neo-Hebraic paper in America, which ran weekly for five years. He wrote often for Hebrew journals in Europe as their American voice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bezalel-a-v-bez:
Bezalel was the chief architect of the Tabernacle. Exodus names him for that task. He was son of Uri and grandson of Hur. He belonged to the tribe of Judah. The entry stresses his many skills. He engraved precious metals and stones. He carved wood and taught many apprentices. He directed the tent, its furniture, and the priests' garments.

Rabbinic tradition adds famous stories about him. Bezalel corrected Moses on building order. First the house, then its furnishings, he said. Moses praised his shadow-of-God insight. Tradition says he was only thirteen then. It also credits him with letter-combination wisdom. That wisdom, it says, mirrored creation itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bistritz-kalman: Kalman Kohn Bistritz was a Hungarian Neo-Hebraic poet. He lived at the start of the nineteenth century. He wrote the Purim drama "Goral ha-Ẓaddiḳim." It means The Lot of the Righteous. It appeared in Vienna in 1821. He belonged to Meïr Kohn Bistritz's family. He is considered a good epigrammatist. Two reference works misname his drama, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonirac-solomon: Solomon Bonirac, perhaps Bon Isaac, was a Spanish translator at Barcelona in the middle of the fourteenth century. He turned Galen's medical work on the crisis from Arabic into Hebrew. Its title, Sefer Buhran, keeps the Arabic word for crisis. The entry explains that he likely had no Hebrew word for it. The Arabic version he used was by Honein ibn Ishak. His version still survives in a Leyden manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brandon-benjami: Benjamin Raphael Dias Brandon was a Dutch Talmudist and Hebrew author. He died about 1750 at Amsterdam, where he was cantor. Two of his books came out there in 1753, after his death. One treats the purpose of the Biblical and Talmudic precepts. The other takes up legal problems raised by his Amsterdam friends. The entry praises his pure and simple language. It also notes his poem for the wedding of the poet David Franco-Mendez of Amsterdam.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brooch-or-buckl: Brooch or buckle renders a Greek word found in First Maccabees, where it names a metal ring set with stones and fitted with a pin. Worn like a modern safety pin, it held an overgarment at the shoulder. Romans gave such pieces as gifts and as army rewards for good service. Gold ones resembled the shoulder pieces of high officers. The entry says that in the East only kings and high dignitaries received them. It also warns that the brooch in Exodus was really a nose ring.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-burglary-3839:
Burglary, in English and American law, means breaking into a dwelling house at night to commit a felony. The entry starts from the Exodus passage on a thief found breaking in. If the thief is killed during the break in, no blood guilt follows. If the sun has risen on him, blood guilt does follow, and the thief must repay or be sold.

Jewish versions and commentators split over that sun phrase. Some read it as daylight, others as the eye of witnesses. The Mishnah counts the housebreaker among grave offenders, judged by his likely end. Talmud debate then asks who may kill him and what counts as breaking in. A courtyard, stable, or roof can qualify. The entry closes with proof of intent, using a father breaking into his son's house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calneh-3939: Calneh is a city name that covers two places in this entry, and both sites stay in doubt. The first Calneh stands in Genesis with Babylon, Erech, and Accad in Nimrod's Babylonian kingdom. Rawlinson matched it with Nippur on a Talmud saying, but the entry calls that basis weak. A match with Ctesiphon also lacks proof. The second Calneh, in Amos, may be Kullani, a town taken by Tiglath-pileser the third. Its modern site lies about six miles from Arpad.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carinthia-germa:
Carinthia, an Austrian crownland, held only a small Jewish population. Jews first settled in Carinthia and nearby Styria late in the eleventh century and during the two that followed. Town names such as Judenburg and Judendorf mark that early presence. Jews first lived in villages, then moved into cities during the fourteenth century.

Legal status forms the core of the account. Charters from 1244 and 1254, and an edict renewed in 1396, set out Jewish rights and a Jewish judge for cases among Jews. Attacks came in 1310, 1338, and 1397. After long pressure from the estates, Jews were ordered out in 1496. Legal equality came only in 1849, and the right to own land in 1867. The census of 1890 counted 179 Jews in Carinthian towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-catacombs-4139:
Catacombs are underground galleries with side niches for tombs, or places where human bones are stacked. The word joins a Greek and a Latin term and means near the sepulchers. It first named one place on the Via Appia near Rome. Since the ninth century it has covered all such burial places in Italy and beyond.

Burial in this form is of Jewish origin, the entry argues. Rock tombs were used in Palestine from early times, from the cave of Machpelah to tombs around Jerusalem. Jews carried the custom to Rome, lower Italy, Carthage, and Cyrene. The Talmud describes bodies laid in niches in underground vaults. Christian catacombs at Rome seem to copy that Jewish practice. The account then turns to the Roman sites, their inscriptions, and their synagogue names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chapman-john-42: John Chapman, an English educationist and communal worker born in 1845, trained at Jews' College, London. He became an assistant master there, then head master of the Jews' Hospital and Orphan Asylum. For many years he ran the Great Ealing proprietary school. Many middle-class Jewish boys were trained under him there. For a time he also served as minister of the Western Synagogue, Haymarket. He served as honorary secretary of the council of Jews' College. He helped found the Ealing Public Library as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohnstein-isido: Isidor Cohnstein, a German gynecologist, was born at Gnesen, Posen, on Aug. 1, 1841. He died at Charlottenburg, near Berlin, on July 25, 1894. He took his medical degree in 1864 after study at Berlin, Prague, and Heidelberg. He began practice in Berlin in 1866 and joined its university as privat-docent in 1868. In 1871 he gave up general work and focused on gynecology. In 1877 he moved to Heidelberg and set up there as a specialist. His books include a textbook of obstetrics and an outline of gynecology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cooking-utensil:
Cooking-Utensils describes the gear of the ancient Hebrew kitchen. Women did most of the cooking and ground the flour each day. Men slaughtered and dressed the meat. Most homes had no set kitchen room. A few stones held the pot over a fire lit on the mud floor, while rich palaces had real kitchens.

The entry names the tools one by one. Hand-mills, large earthen jugs for water and meal, and goat-skins for milk and wine all appear. It lists pots and bowls whose exact uses are now unknown. Temple vessels were bronze, silver, or gold, while home ware stayed plainer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-creizenach-theo: Theodor Creizenach was a German poet and historian of literature, son of Michael Creizenach. Born on April 17, 1818, in Mayence, he died on Dec. 6, 1877, at Frankfort. He studied classical antiquities at three universities. Years in Paris as a tutor in the Rothschild house followed. Back in 1842, he taught at the Frankfort Philanthropin and helped found the Reformverein. In 1854 he left Judaism for Christianity. He later taught history and literature at the Frankfort gymnasium. He edited Goethe's letters to Marianne von Willemer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-czestionev-4839: Czestionev is a village in the government of Warsaw, in Russian Poland. Its claim to notice is a Jewish agricultural college. The college was completed in 1901, with room for sixty students. Its lands cover 1,630 acres, of which 1,090 are arable. The rest is forest and meadow. Students learn farming, gardening, and dairying in a practical way. They also work in wood and iron and repair farm gear. Admission asks Russian and a completed thirteenth year. A preparatory school serves boys not yet ready.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-elija: Elijah's son David was a Hebrew scholar of the eighteenth century, and the entry about him is very brief. Its single fact is his translation work: he rendered the second Targum to the Book of Esther into Hebrew. He gave the translation the title "Leshon Zahab" (A Tongue of Gold). It was published at Constantinople in 1732. The entry names no birth or death dates and no other writings by him, resting on notices in Steinschneider and in Zedner's catalogue of Hebrew books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dedanim-hebr-r-: Dedanim, or Dedanites, were the descendants of the Arabian Dedan, spoken of in Isaiah as a trading people. Two family lines are given for Dedan: son of Raamah, of Cush's line, and son of Jokshan, of Keturah's line. The prophets mention Dedan with Edom, and with Tema and Buz. As a Keturean tribe it seems to have held northwest Arabia. One passage in Ezekiel points instead to South Arabia. The entry suggests the two branches mixed, since Dedan's brother is Sheba in each case.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deutsch-david-b:
Menahem Mandel's son David Deutsch was a Hungarian rabbi and Talmudist born about 1760. He served first at Szerdahely, then, after 1810, at Waag-Neustadtl, where he died in 1830. He ranked among the leading Hungarian rabbinical authorities of his day. Stories of his character still circulated in Hungary long afterward.

Deutsch was famed as a giver. He would hand a poor man money without counting it, and if his purse was empty he gave away any valuable at hand. He was also known for wit, which served him as a preacher. His books were two sets of novellae called "Ohel Dawid" (Tent of David). A friend printed his collected responsa after his death as a memorial.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dizahab-5239:
Dizahab is a name that occurs only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy i. 1. It sits in a list of places east of the Jordan. The entry says its identity has never been firmly fixed. The context gives no real clue to where it lay.

Ancient versions rendered the name as a phrase about gold. Onkelos and Rashi tied it to the golden calf. Ibn Ezra guessed it was another name for a place known differently. Cheyne proposed reading Me-zahab and linking it to a northern Arabian land. Burckhardt's candidate, Mina al-Dhahab, has been dropped by later commentators.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dual-5339:
The dual is a word form that points to exactly two persons or things. Arabic keeps it for verbs and nouns alike. Syriac keeps only faint traces of it. Hebrew keeps the dual for nouns only, with the ending ayim.

Hebrew uses the dual chiefly for things that come in natural pairs. Body parts are the main case, and teeth count as a pair of rows. Made pairs, like tongs and scissors, also take it. So do some time and measure words, and the numbers 200 and 2,000. City names ending in ayim form a special group, and Mizrayim, Egypt, is read as upper and lower lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-lazar-b:
Eleazar ben Jose the First was a tanna of the second century. He was the second of the five learned sons of Jose ben Halafta. He is cited often in the Tosefta, though never in the Mishnah. With Simon ben Yohai he made a trip to Rome. Their aim was to plead against the new bans of Hadrian. The mission won its point, the entry says.

On that trip Eleazar fell dangerously ill but got well and went on. At Rome he saw spoils taken from the Temple by Titus. He names the curtain of the Holy of Holies and the high priest's gold band. At Alexandria he heard grim tales of Jewish bodies built into walls. The entry closes with his stress on good works. Giving and kindness, he taught, plead for Israel. They make peace between God and the people, he said.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-ha-adeni: Elijah ha-Adeni was a rabbi and prayer poet of Cochin. He served the Jews of Cochin in India. His dates of birth and death are not known. He was a native of Aden in Arabia. His name means the man of Aden for that reason. He wrote a poem on the 613 commandments. The Jews of India read it on a set feast day. Cochin's Jews use it most of all, the entry says. Amsterdam printed the poem in 1688.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-errera-paul-jos: Paul Joseph Errera was a Belgian barrister born at Laeken on July 23, 1860. He studied at the University of Brussels and taught law there and at the Ecole des Sciences Politiques et Sociales. He belonged to the Belgian royal academy of archaeology. He acted as counsel for the Congo state and for the Jewish Colonization Association. He also headed the local Alliance Israelite Universelle committee. His named books are Les Masuirs, in two volumes, Les Warechaix, and a sketch of comparative constitutional law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-exodus-lit-way-:
Exodus, as an event, is the departure of the Israelites from Egypt under Moses, and the entry tells it first as the Bible tells it. A new king who knew not Joseph enslaved the growing people in Goshen. Moses, called back from Midian, brought ten plagues on Egypt. Pharaoh at last let the people go. More than 600,000 able men marched out in one night from Rameses.

God led them away from the Philistine road and back toward the sea at Pi-hahiroth. Pharaoh chased them with 600 chariots. The sea split at Moses' staff, Israel crossed dry, and the waters drowned the Egyptian host. A critical section then questions the tale's details. The numbers, it says, are fanciful: 600,000 men would mean at least two million souls in all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-faudel-phillips:
George Faudel-Phillips was lord mayor of London in 1896-97, second son of Sir Benjamin Samuel Phillips. He was born in 1840 and took the name Faudel from an uncle. He studied at University College School, Berlin, and Paris, then joined his father's firm. In 1867 he married Helen Levy, whose brother ran the Daily Telegraph.

He rose through city office: sheriff in 1884-85, alderman in 1888, then lord mayor in 1896. In that year he received Queen Victoria at Temple Bar for the Jubilee service. His term raised about 1,000,000 pounds for famine relief in India and other causes. He left office a baronet with the Grand Cross of the Indian Empire. He also led the Jews' Orphan Asylum and a society for the Jewish blind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-first-fruits-61:
First-fruits were the choicest first yield of field, corn, wine, and oil. They belonged to God, much like the first-born of cattle. Early rules made them a feast offering at Jerusalem. If the way was too far, the gifts could be sold at home. The money then bought a feast at Jerusalem. Other passages give the priest a claim on the first share.

Later law drew a line between two kinds of first share. One went to the Temple chambers, the other in a solemn march to the house of God. Rules cover who must bring them and who is exempt. The rabbis set the amount at one-sixtieth of the whole crop. After the Temple fell, acts of charity took the offering's place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-forstenheim-ann: Anna Forstenheim was an Austrian writer and poet born at Agram on Sept. 21, 1846. She died at Vienna on Oct. 19, 1889. She went to Vienna in 1867. There she founded the Society of Women Writers and Artists. She served as its treasurer. Her works open with a drama of 1875 on Catarina Cornaro. A novel in three volumes followed in 1880. Her later books include a tale of a new princedom in old times and a comedy, both from 1882. An epic poem and a Melusine tale came in 1883.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fraternities-34:
Fraternities are societies for mutual benefit. The friendly society may have begun in all lands as a burial club. Jewish burial societies are named in the Talmud. The burial society in its later form was known early in the fifteenth century. But the modern order, with its insurance features, belongs mostly to the later nineteenth century. The orders gave cheap insurance and ready money benefits. They also served as social centers.

The entry lists the larger orders, most of them based in New York. One order, founded in 1859, had 288 lodges and 42,000 members. An offshoot of it, founded in 1887, had 302 lodges and 56,949 members. Another order, founded in 1849, had 103 lodges and about 11,000 members. England had a few such orders too. Jews also rose high in orders not their own. One Jew was then the top officer of the Knights of Pythias in New York state.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-freidus-abraham:
Abraham Solomon Freidus was a bibliographer born at Riga, Russia, on May 1, 1867. He went to Paris in 1886 and from there to the United States in the autumn of 1889. In March 1897 he joined the New York Public Library as an assistant cataloguer. He was soon put in the department of Hebraica and Judaica. He was still in charge of it in 1903.

That department then held 15,000 volumes and pamphlets. It had become one of the most used Jewish collections in the world. His plan for sorting the Jewish books ran to nearly 500 heads. It may be counted the first full scheme of its kind for library use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-furtado-abraham:
Abraham Furtado, a French politician born at London in 1756, died at Bordeaux on January 29, 1816. His parents came from a Portuguese Marrano family. His father died in the Lisbon quake of 1755. His mother fled to London and openly took up Judaism. The family later settled at Bordeaux, where Abraham was schooled.

In 1789 he sat on a royal group asked to weigh plans to better the lot of Jews. His ties to the Girondists brought exile in 1793 and loss of his goods. In 1806 Napoleon called leading Jews to Paris. Furtado led that Assembly of Notables and spoke for its work in the Sanhedrin of 1807.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-geshem-the-arab: Geshem the Arabian, also called Gashmu in Nehemiah vi. 6, was an ally of Sanballat and Tobiah and a foe of Nehemiah. The second name is held to be more correct, since an Arab tribe named Gushamu is known. When Nehemiah set out to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, Samaritans and Arabs tried to block him. Geshem, likely the Arab chief, joined the charge that Nehemiah plotted revolt against the Persian king.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldberg-albert: Albert Goldberg was a German opera singer born at Brunswick on June 8, 1847. He trained at the Leipsic Conservatorium from 1865 to 1869 and debuted at the Munich court theater. Between 1869 and 1883 he sang in Mayence, Bremen, Neu-Strelitz, Strasburg, Augsburg, and Königsberg, directing the Königsberg city theater for three years. In 1883 he became manager of the Leipsic opera, where he was still engaged in 1903. The Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha gave him the title of court singer. His roles included Don Juan, Wotan, Telramund, and Papageno.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gomperz-benjami:
Benjamin Gomperz was an Austrian physician. He was born at Vienna on Oct. 6, 1861. The Leopoldstädter communal gymnasium and Vienna University educated him. He took his medical degree in 1885. He served as assistant at the university hospital from 1885 to 1900. He then set up in Vienna as a physician. His specialty was diseases of the ear and nose.

From 1897 he was curator of a Hirsch charitable foundation. His essays cover ear anatomy and surgery. Titles named include papers on fibromas and old eardrum gaps. He also wrote for the central journals of therapy and medicine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gumplowicz-ludw:
Ludwig Gumplowicz was a Christian historian and jurist. He was born at Cracow on March 9, 1838. He studied at Cracow and Vienna and practiced law at Cracow. In 1876 he became docent at Graz University. He rose to assistant professor in 1882 and professor in 1893. He wrote a work on jurisprudence. He also wrote on Polish law concerning the Jews.

His Polish study divides the country's history into three periods. In each, king, clergy, and legislature stood in constant opposition. Kings, he held, were mostly friendly to the Jews. The nobility was not wholly hostile. Only in the third period did the clergy gain power to act on its views. Through schooling, the clergy then taught Polish youth to see Jews as the Church's enemies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ha-meliz-lit-th:
Ha-Meliẓ, the oldest Hebrew newspaper in Russia, was founded by Alexander Zederbaum in Odessa in 1860. It began as a weekly and moved to St. Petersburg in 1871. Authorities and money troubles suspended it several times, yet Zederbaum always revived it. It became a daily in 1886.

The paper stood for the progressive haskalah movement throughout its run. A severe critic quoted in the entry still judged it more useful to Jews than other Hebrew papers. It carried more news and discussion than its more literary rivals, which made it popular. Nearly every prominent Hebrew writer of forty years contributed. Collections of its articles also appeared as supplement volumes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-happiness-7239:
Happiness, in the Old Testament as this entry reads it, is life's keynote. Life itself counts as good and blessing. Joy flows from a close relation with God. "Blessed is the nation whose God is Yhwh." "In thy presence is fulness of joy." Love of God makes a man happy. Obedience to His Law does the same. Plain trust in Him does the same. Wisdom is a tree of life to those who hold her.

Worship itself is joyful. Joy must also be shared. The feast command names son, daughter, servant, and Levite. It names the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow too. Asceticism is treated as sinful. Eat your bread with joy. The rabbinical half keeps the optimism under harder conditions. It has sayings like "He who made the day will provide daily sustenance." It also has a run of benedictions over every pleasure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hauser-philipp-:
Philipp Hauser, born at Nadas in Hungary on April 2, 1832, was a doctor and writer on medicine. He studied at Talmud schools, then read medicine at Vienna, Paris, and Bern. He took his degree in 1858 and went to work in Tangier. When war drove Jews from the coast, he ran a relief hospital at Gibraltar.

Hauser later treated Jews in cholera-struck Tetuan and settled at Seville in 1872. From 1883 he practiced in Madrid. His many books deal with child deaths, city crowding, and cholera. Two cholera works won prizes from bodies in Paris and Munich. He died after a long career of public health writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heave-offering-:
Heave-offering is a gift set apart for the Tabernacle or Temple and its priests. The term first meant any tax or gift paid to a higher officer. In Israel such payments mostly kept up the sanctuary, so the word took on that narrower sense. Some gifts were free; others were fixed by law.

Classes of the offering are listed one by one. They include the half-shekel tax on grown men, a dough portion, cakes from peace offerings, and a share of the Levites' tithe. Field, grove, and vineyard yields also owed a part. Only priests in a state of purity, and their households, could eat the sacred share. Rabbinic rules fill out the picture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heller-zebi-hir: Zebi Hirsch Heller, also called Herschele Harif, was a Hungarian rabbi. He served at Bonyhad. In 1834 he was called to Alt-Ofen to follow Moses Munz. He had hardly begun there when he died, on Oct. 28, 1834. His pupils included rabbis of Zolkiev, Prague, and Sniatyn. His book of new readings was printed with the legal answers of his son Menahem. A second work of his came out long after his death, in 1865. One of his answers appears in another rabbi's book as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herzl-siegmund-: Siegmund Herzl, born at Vienna on May 26, 1830, was an Austrian merchant and novelist. He died there on Feb. 9, 1889. The entry lists three books of verse by him, dated 1853, 1874, and 1880. It also says he translated Petöfi's poems. Herzl retired from business in 1885. No family, education, or plot details are given. The short entry rests on one cited source about intellectual Vienna.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-baron-ma:
Baron Maurice de Hirsch, born at Munich on Dec. 9, 1831, was a German philanthropist from a banking family. He married Clara Bischoffsheim in 1855. Through railway work in Austria, the Balkans, and Russia he built a fortune. His Balkan line to Constantinople proved a major success.

Seeing poor schooling among Jews in the East, Hirsch funded Alliance schools heavily from 1873. He offered Russia 50,000,000 francs for Jewish education in 1885, but refused state-only control. He then turned to emigration and founded the Jewish Colonization Association. Its work aimed at farm colonies in the Americas, chiefly Argentina at first. He died in Hungary on April 21, 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hunting-7939:
Hunting was the chase of wild game for food. Bible heroes such as Abraham, Jacob, and David appear as shepherds, not hunters. Hunting feels foreign in the stories. Nimrod is a mighty hunter, and Esau, a cunning hunter, stands against Jacob the quiet herdsman.

Still, game was taken after Israel settled in Canaan. Hart, roebuck, and antelope counted as clean food. Lions and bears were destroyed by pits and nets. Bows, snares, and traps served the hunter. Later ages show little hunting. Talmudic notes are few, and Meir of Rothenberg called dog hunting cruel and un-Jewish. Dietary law also kept Jews from eating much of what a hunt could win.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaiah-ben-abra: Isaiah ben Abraham was a Polish rabbi of the seventeenth century. He wrote "Be'er Heteb," a commentary on the Shulhan Aruk's Orah Hayyim, based on the later casuists and printed at Amsterdam in 1708. In its preface he says he wrote a like commentary on the Yoreh De'ah. Steinschneider and Fürst call him a grandson of David b. Samuel ha-Levi. Fürst adds that Isaiah and his family burned to death, probably by accident, in 1723, while traveling toward Palestine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-moses: Jacob ben Moses ben Abun, called ha-Nabi, the Prophet, headed the yeshibah of Narbonne, in France. Abraham b. David's "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" makes Moses ha-Darshan his son, which places Jacob in the eleventh century. Abraham of Narbonne mentions him as the author of a responsum. The entry closes with a small caution: the title ha-Nabi is an honor, and it was given to other men besides Jacob. No work, date, or ruling of his is recorded beyond that one responsum.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jawlikar-samuel: Samuel Isaac Jawlikar, a member of the Beni-Israel, was born about 1820 in Bombay. He joined the Third Bombay Native Light Infantry in 1840 and rose step by step to subahdar-major in 1869. He fought in the Punjab campaign of 1848-49, at the siege of Multan and the battle of Gujarah, and won the Punjab medal with two bars. Later service took him against hill tribes on the Swat border, to Canton in China, and to Abyssinia in 1868. After retiring he became treasurer of the Thana Synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-bar-hiyy: Joseph bar Hiyya was gaon of Pumbedita from 828 to 833. During a fight over the exilarch's post, one party set aside Abraham ben Sherira and named Joseph gaon in his place. Abraham soon won his seat back, yet both men kept the title for a time. At a yearly meeting in Bagdad, moved by the crowd's tears over the split, Joseph gave up the office on his own and took his old post again. After Abraham died in 828, Joseph became the lawful gaon until his own death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kala-i-mordecai: Mordecai b. Solomon Ḳala'i was a Turkish rabbi and author. He lived in the first half of the seventeenth century. He studied under three teachers named in the entry. He became chief teacher of the Portuguese yeshibah at Salonica. Two of his pupils later won fame as scholars. A great fire swept Salonica in 1625. All his responsa and sermons from before that year were lost. Later writers still cite him in their own responsa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-katzenelson-jud:
Judah Löb b. Israel Katzenelson was a Russian physician. He was born in Bobruisk in 1848. He wrote under the pen name Bukki ben Jogli. He studied at the rabbinical school of Jitomir. He then entered the medical academy at St. Petersburg. He finished there in 1877 and served in the war against Turkey. The czar decorated him twice for that service.

Katzenelson later worked at a St. Petersburg hospital. He wrote on blood disease as the Talmud presents it. He also wrote on anatomy in old Hebrew writing. That study served as his thesis for the doctor's degree. Other pieces treat the purity laws and the Babylonian exile. In Hebrew he published a novel, "Shirat ha-Zamir," at Warsaw in 1895. Most of his press work bears his pen name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kufah-al-9539: Al-Kufah was a ruined city of Asiatic Turkey, 88 miles south of Bagdad on a branch of the Euphrates. Omar founded it in 639 on the ruins of Ctesiphon. Land near it went to Jewish exiles from Arabia. A large Jewish community stood there from the time of the calif Ali, whom the Jews backed against Muʿawiyah. Benjamin of Tudela found 7,000 Jews there at the end of the twelfth century. Tradition placed the tomb of King Jeconiah at the site, with a synagogue before the large tomb building.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lara-isidore-de: Isidore de Lara, an English composer born in London on Aug. 9, 1858, was schooled at Boulogne. He first played piano in public at age thirteen. At fifteen he went to Milan to study composition and singing for three years, winning the grand prize for composition. Back in England he taught at the Guildhall School of Music. About 150 songs carry his name, with four listed as most loved. His operas include The Light of Asia, Kenilworth, and Messalina, first staged at Monte Carlo, then London and New York.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leibzoll-or-jud:
Leibzoll, also called Judengeleit, was a special toll Jews had to pay in most European states. It ran from the Middle Ages into the start of the nineteenth century. It grew out of the Jews' place as crown property in Germany. Kings owed them protection, and safe-conduct on long trips cost a fee.

Over time each local ruler taxed foreign Jews who crossed his land. Towns that had expelled Jews used the toll to keep them out while still taking their trade. The entry notes the toll's shaming forms, its exemptions for some court Jews and makers, and its slow end. Wolf Breidenbach campaigned against it from 1803, and Saxony was the last German state to drop it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-perotti-gi: Giustina Levi-Perotti was said to be a poet of Sassoferrato. A sonnet that opens "Io Vorrei pur Drizzar Queste Mie Piume" was long ascribed to her. Petrarch was said to have answered it with a sonnet of his own. The poem first saw print in 1504, under another woman's name. Later editors gave it to Giustina, and collections kept it until 1885. Morici, the entry reports, concludes that the sonnet came from some sixteenth-century hand. On his view, Giustina never existed at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machado-10239:
Machado, the name of a Marano family that crossed to America, is traced in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. The name appears early in Mexico and the West Indies. In 1600 the Mexican Inquisition charged Isabel Machado and her father Antonio with being Jews. Machados also surface in Martinique and Surinam.

The article centers on the New York branch of the family. David Mendez Machado fled the Inquisition from Lisbon to England, then sailed to Savannah in 1733. He married Zipporah, daughter of Dr. Samuel Nunez, and moved to New York. There he served as cantor of Shearith Israel from 1734 until his death in 1753. His descendants, the entry notes, include Commodore Uriah P. Levy and Mordecai M. Noah. A family tree closes the piece. It preserves the path of one refugee family into American Jewish leadership.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mamon-mammon-10:
Mamon, or Mammon, is examined as a word in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. The term is Mishnaic Hebrew and Aramaic for riches. It is the word Jesus uses in the Sermon on the Mount. You cannot serve God and mammon, the saying runs. The article is signed simply by Joseph Jacobs.

The entry clears away a popular error. No evidence shows that Mammon was ever a Syrian god, the writers state. That idea comes from Milton, who personified Mammon in Paradise Lost as a fallen spirit. The word appears in the Mishnah tractate Abot, where almsgiving is called the salt of riches. Gesenius derived it from matmon, meaning treasure, with a letter assimilated. Scholars also debate the spelling, since the Greek form with two m's is held correct. The short piece is a model of separating a word's real history from poetry's inventions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marshall-louis-:
Louis Marshall was an American lawyer and a Jewish communal leader. Cyrus Adler wrote his profile for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Syracuse, New York, on December 14, 1856. He studied at Columbia College Law School and began practice in Syracuse in 1878. He moved his practice to New York City in 1894.

The entry traces his rise at the bar. In 1890 he sat on the commission to revise the judiciary article of the New York constitution. He also played a part in the state constitutional convention of 1894. The entry then turns to his communal work. It names the Jewish Theological Seminary, Congregation Emanu-El, and the Educational Alliance, plus his push for a protectory for delinquent Jewish children.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-medals-10539:
Cyrus Adler and Albert Wolf catalogue Jewish medals in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The medals run from the fifteenth century to the day of the encyclopedia. The art of engraving medals revived in Italy about 1450, and a few Jewish pieces survive from that age. Their numbers were kept small, the authors say, by the general oppression of the Jews. As conditions improved through the eighteenth century the medals multiplied, and after emancipation they appeared nearly every year.

What follows is a dated list, each item describing obverse and reverse and giving the size in millimeters. It opens with a portrait medal of 1503 and one for Gracia Nasi in 1556. It turns to events: the defense of Buda in 1686 and the Frankfort ghetto fire of 1711. It goes on to the execution of Süss Oppenheimer in 1738 and the Prague expulsion edict of 1745. Private and cabalistic medals are left out by design.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-millaud-moise-p:
Moïse Polydore Millaud, born at Bordeaux on August 27, 1813, was the French journalist and banker who built a press empire from almost nothing. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn tell his story in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A poor Jewish tradesman's son with little schooling, he started as a bailiff's clerk and was publishing his own paper at twenty.

His early Paris ventures failed but taught him the trade, and his court-news paper L'Audience prospered from 1839 until 1845 against the official Gazette des Tribunaux. His La Liberté backed Louis Napoleon and was suppressed after the June rising of 1848. With Mirès he then launched the Journal des Chemins de Fer, which became a power in railway finance and speculation across France.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mommsen-christi:
Theodor Mommsen, the great historian of Rome, was born at Garding on November 30, 1817. He earns his Jewish Encyclopedia entry on two grounds, as Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer explain in 1906. His Römische Geschichte treats the Jews of the Roman empire at length. Its fifth volume has a whole chapter on Judaea and the Jews. In German politics, too, he fought the anti-Semites.

Mommsen sat in the Prussian Diet and the Reichstag as a Liberal. He answered Treitschke's attack with his own pamphlet of 1881. In it he pleaded tolerance. He called the Jewish element in the empire a wholesome one. He was among the first to sign the notables' declaration of November 1880. That declaration branded Jew-baiting a national disgrace. He died at Charlottenburg in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moscheles-ignaz:
Ignaz Moscheles was an Austrian pianist ranked, in his entry's words, the greatest player between Hummel and Chopin. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Prague on May 30, 1794, he played a concerto of his own in public in 1808. After his father's death he made his living in Vienna as a teacher and player.

In Vienna, Moscheles knew Beethoven and helped prepare the piano arrangement of Fidelio. Ten years of concert tours followed, and in London in 1824 he gave lessons to the young Felix Mendelssohn. He settled in London, led the Philharmonic Society, and in 1846 became the first piano professor at the new Leipzig Conservatorium. He died at Leipzig in 1870, leaving concertos, studies, and a school of playing of his own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-samue:
Moses ben Samuel ben Asher was a French Talmudist of Perpignan in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He and his father held great influence in the city. They won from King James of Majorca leave for Jews expelled from France in 1306 to settle at Perpignan.

Moses was a close friend of Abba Mari of Lunel, and his daughter married Abba Mari's son. During the Montpellier controversy over philosophy, the two men corresponded steadily. Moses, the more liberal and peaceable of the two, refused to take his friend's hard line. He defended Abba Mari locally while pressing him for facts, and worked to calm all parties in Perpignan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mourning-10639:
Mourning, the show of grief for the dead, is covered at length in this Jewish Encyclopedia article by Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein. It treats grief for a relative, a friend, a leader, or a whole nation. The Bible's first mourner is Abraham, weeping for Sarah.

The article sorts the customs by period and source. Biblical mourners threw dust on their heads, wore sackcloth, and sat in ashes, though self-wounding was forbidden. Public mourning among the Hebrews never passed thirty days, while the anniversary of the Temple's fall is mourned yearly. Rabbinic law then divides grief into stages of three days, seven days, thirty days, and a year for parents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nataf-isaac-b-s: Isaac b. Solomon Nataf was a rabbi at Tunis around the year 1800. His short entry was written by Solomon Schechter and A. S. Waldstein for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Nataf wrote a book on oaths, printed at Leghorn in 1820. The book treats twenty kinds of oaths and the duties they place on man. The entry also points readers to notes on Tunisian Jewish books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-night-11539:
Night, in the Bible, runs from sunset to sunrise. Wilhelm Bacher and Max Landsberg wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The older phrase for a full day was day and night. Later speech used evening and morning instead. Israel, like Greece, reckoned days from sunset.

The Gauls and old Germans kept the same custom. It likely grew out of the cult of the moon. Yet sacrifice law counts some nights with the day before. Time had no exact measure in early Israel. Stages were named by light: dawn, midday heat, evening breeze. Between the lights named the hour of the evening sacrifice. Three night watches divided the dark in the Temple. Roman practice later made the watches four in number.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oath-11639:
Oath treats the sworn pledge in Jewish law and court use. The entry was written for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its authors were the Editorial Board and Julius Rappoport. Two Hebrew words, alah and shebuah, name the oath. In the Bible the two words are used as one.

Under old Jewish law, courts used oaths in civil suits only. They were not used in crime cases at all. An oath came when proof was weak or lacking. It was laid on the one who was sued, not the one who sued. The oath called God to witness the truth told. A man thought prone to lie was not sworn. The piece traces how later rabbis widened these rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheimer-fra:
Franz Oppenheimer was a German doctor who turned to writing. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Berlin on March 30, 1864. His father was rabbi of the Berlin Reform flock. Franz read cures at Freiburg and at Berlin. He took his medical degree in the year 1885.

In 1887 Franz set up a practice in Berlin. He made throat and nose ills his chief field there. Soon he gave up the work of a doctor in full. He turned to books, to wealth in lands, and to groups. He wrote verse and a drama in his first years. His chief works treat land held in common by men. One treats the great land owners and the needs of the poor. One treats the law of growth in the count of souls.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pacifico-case-1:
The Pacifico Case was a clash of states over one man's claim. Joseph Jacobs wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. David Pacifico was born a British subject at Gibraltar. He was born there in the year 1784. He died in London on April 12, 1854.

Pacifico first set up in trade at Lagos, in Portugal. His goods were seized for his lean to the Liberal side. In time he was made consul of Portugal in Greece. He was cast out of that post in the year 1842. He stayed on at Athens, the chief town of Greece. In 1847 a mob burnt his house down in that town. He claimed a huge sum for his loss in goods. Greece would not treat that great claim with care. So Lord Palmerston sent a British fleet to Piraeus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paternity-11939:
Paternity in Jewish law is the subject of this legal article. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Judah David Eisenstein wrote it. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The stakes are high, since fatherhood fixes inheritance and priestly rank.

The Bible traced descent through the father alone. Census lists were kept by the house of the fathers. A man could deny a child born outside marriage. He could also claim such a child and give him full rights. The rules set a three month wait before a widow remarried. That wait kept a child's father clear in most cases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-periodicals-100:
Jewish periodicals, as this long survey defines them, serve Jewish readers. Richard Gottheil and William Popper wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The term covers both newspapers and magazines. Some are marked Jewish by language, others by subject alone.

Daily papers report the general news of the world. Jewish weeklies focus on matters of Jewish concern. They range from world politics to local community gossip. Magazines split into literary and scientific kinds. Most scientific ones serve the Jewish sciences, like history and philology. Special papers serve cantors, students, and societies too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perles-12039:
Perles is a family of rabbis and scholars from Prague. Gotthard Deutsch and Isidore Singer wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its members spread from Bohemia into Hungary and Germany. Many of them served as rabbis for generations.

Aaron Perles edited a classic work on meat porging. His edition came out at Offenbach in 1722. Baruch Asher Perles taught at Baja in Hungary. He favored plain sense over clever pilpul in study. He sent his son Joseph to the new Breslau seminary. Joseph's son Felix became a rabbi at Munich.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pico-de-mirando:
Giovanni Pico de Mirandola was an Italian thinker and cabalist. He was born in 1463 and died at Florence in 1494. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. At twenty-three he stunned the learned world.

In 1486 Pico printed nine hundred bold new theses at Rome. One held that Kabbalah best proves Christ divine. Johanan Aleman had taught him the Kabbalah himself. Pico rendered three Hebrew cabalistic books into Latin. He tried to wed Plato, Aristotle, and Jewish mysticism. Charged with heresy, he was cleared and retired.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-police-laws-122:
Police laws are laws that guard public peace, health, safety, and morals. The Editorial Board and Julius H. Greenstone wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Their main aim, they say, is to stop crime before it starts. The article asks how far back such laws go in Jewish life.

The writers first ask if Bible towns had a true police force. They note that the book of Deuteronomy orders officers in every town. These officers, called shoterim, worked beside the judges. They made public calls to the people, above all in war. They guarded the king and watched over public works. Later parts of the article trace such rules in later Jewish law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-preexistence-12:
Preexistence means that a thing or soul lived before earthly life. Kaufmann Kohler and Ludwig Blau wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Old Jewish books give such early life to key persons and things. These are things that form part of God's plan. They serve the saving of man or the rule of the world.

One teaching tells of the souls of the righteous. God took counsel with them before he made the world. The writers trace this view to a foreign source. They find it in the Zend-Avesta of Persia. There the holy souls of heroes hold a cosmic place. Their god holds council with them before creation as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rahmer-moritz-1:
Moritz Rahmer was a German rabbi born on December 12, 1837. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Rybnik in Prussian Silesia. He died at Magdeburg on March 2, 1904.

The article traces his study at the Breslau seminary from 1854 to 1862. He then served at Thorn and, from 1867, at Magdeburg. His books treat Maimonides, Jerome, prayer, and the twelve minor prophets. He also edited Jewish papers for many years. Those papers included the Jüdisches Litteraturblatt and the Israelitische Wochenschrift. The entry shows a rabbi who also shaped Jewish reading week by week.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rice-isaac-leop:
Isaac Leopold Rice was an American lawyer, author, and chess player. Cyrus Adler and A. Porter wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born on February 22, 1850, at Wachenheim. His mother brought him to America at age six.

The article says he studied literature and music in Paris. He reported for a Philadelphia paper while there. Back in New York he won fame as a music teacher. He took a law degree from Columbia in 1880. He practiced law and worked in railway affairs. In 1885 he founded the Forum magazine. Later he led an electric storage battery company. He founded America's electric car and boat industries, they say. He also led the Manhattan Chess Club.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salomons-sir-ju:
Sir Julian Emanuel Salomons was an Australian statesman born in Birmingham in 1834. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Called to the English bar in 1861, he emigrated to New South Wales.

Salomons practised with much success before Sydney's Supreme Court, becoming Queen's Counsel. He defended O'Farrel, the Fenian who shot the Duke of Edinburgh in 1868. He served as solicitor-general in two ministries, in 1869 and 1870. Offered the chief justiceship in 1886, he resigned it after a few days. Twice he served as the colony's agent-general in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-phoebus-:
Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel Phoebus ben Nathan Feitel, an Austrian writer of history. He lived in Vienna across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. His book Ṭiṭ ha-Yawen tells of the Cossack uprising under Bogdan Chmielnicki. That revolt swept the Ukraine and Galicia in the seventeenth century.

The book names the cities that suffered in the rising. It lists 140 synagogues that were destroyed. It states that some 600,070 Jews were thought to have been killed. The work first appeared at Venice after 1649. A second edition came out at Cracow in 1892. There it formed part of Gurland's collection on the persecutions of Israel. It remains a grim firsthand-style record of the disaster.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saxon-duchies-1:
Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Saxon duchies. The four duchies are Saxe-Altenburg, Saxe-Coburg-Gotha, Saxe-Meiningen, and Saxe-Weimar. All lie in Thuringia, within the German empire. Saxe-Altenburg held only forty Jews among some 195,000 people. Saxe-Coburg-Gotha held 580 Jews, split between Coburg and Gotha.

Saxe-Meiningen carries the darkest history here. On Good Friday in 1349, a girl claimed she heard Jews plotting an attack. Jews were jailed on her word. On July 17 they were burned at the stake with their families. Their synagogue stood closed for twenty-two years. It then became a chapel. By 1904 the duchy held 1,487 Jews again. Saxe-Weimar's edict of 1823 ended the body tax on Jews. It still barred them from brewing, butchering, baking, and innkeeping.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwarz-anton-1:
Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Anton Schwarz. He was an Austrian chemist. Schwarz was born at Polna, in Bohemia, on February 2, 1839. He died in New York City on September 24, 1895. He studied law at Vienna, then chemistry at Prague. In 1868 he emigrated to the United States.

In New York, Schwarz joined the staff of Der Amerikanische Bierbrauer, The American Brewer. He soon became its editor and then its owner. He did much to improve brewing methods in America. In 1880 he founded the Brewers' Academy of the United States. His son Max succeeded him at both the journal and the academy. Max championed the cause of pure beer in America. He died in New York in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-serene-serenus-:
Serene, also called Serenus, was a false messiah in Syria early in the eighth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. A responsum by Natronai Gaon preserves much of what is known. Serene set up rites that broke rabbinic law in many ways.

He dropped set prayer and loosened rules on food, wine, and marriage. He also let people work on the second holy day. His rise is dated to about 720, under the caliph Yazid II. In Spain, many Jews sold all they owned and made ready to follow him. The entry shows how hope for redemption could sweep whole communities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shelah-13539: Shelah was the youngest son of Judah, by a Canaanite wife, the daughter of Shuah. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was born at Chezib, in Judah's lowland country. When his brother Onan died, Shelah was still very young. Judah used that youth as his reason for delay. He would not let Shelah marry his sister-in-law Tamar, as custom required. Shelah later became ancestor of many families, as Chronicles records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sidon-simon-136:
Simon Sidon was a Hungarian rabbi and author born at Nadas in 1815. Gotthard Deutsch wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied at the yeshivah of Moses Sofer, the famed Hatam Sofer. Settling in his native town, he opened a yeshivah there.

In 1845 Sidon became rabbi of Cziffer in Hungary. In 1856 he moved to the rabbinate of Tyrnau. He held that post until his death in 1891. Though strictly conservative, he tolerated modern ideas in others. In 1860 he sent his son to Breslau's seminary. That choice drew strong opposition from traditionalists around him. His Ot Berit covers circumcision, proselytes, and firstborn redemption. His Shebet Shim'on adds legal notes and special sermons in three parts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-cephas-be:
Simon Cephas, better known as Peter, was the first of the Twelve Apostles. Kaufmann Kohler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Peter was the chief disciple of Jesus and head of the early Church. His second name, Kaipha, means rock in Aramaic. Latin Petrus comes from petra, also meaning rock.

Peter was a fisherman of Capernaum, like his brother Andrew. The Gospels tell of Jesus calling both men from their nets. Peter's house became a center of Jesus' work in Galilee. The sick were brought there to be healed on the Sabbath evening. The article follows these Gospel accounts and the legends that grew around his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solis-sometimes:
Solis was a Spanish and Portuguese family of crypto-Jews. Joseph Jacobs and Emily Solis-Cohen Jr wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Some members served as inquisitors, while others suffered under the Inquisition. Those who escaped to Holland, France, and England professed Judaism openly. In the eighteenth century some crossed to America.

The American branch traced its line to Solomon da Silva Solis. He emigrated from Spain to Amsterdam in the seventeenth century. David Hays Solis aided schools and charities in Philadelphia and New York. He backed Isaac Leeser and the anti-slavery movement as well. Other members served as merchants, lawyers, and soldiers across three continents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-victor-14:
Victor Stern was an Austrian dramatist born at Vienna on May 5, 1837. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He spent a short time in commercial work first. Then he turned to literature as his calling. The playwright Friedrich Hebbel encouraged him from 1861.

Under Hebbel's support, Stern wrote some of his best work. His tragedies include Valentin, printed in 1868. Das Kronenhaus followed in 1872. Calas appeared in 1889, late in his career. Schloss Arnheim came out in 1893. The brief entry lists four stage tragedies across twenty-five years. It gives readers a quick map of a Viennese playwright's output. His work belongs to the German theater of his century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sutro-adolph-he:
Adolph Sutro was an American engineer born in Prussia in 1830. Cyrus Adler and I. George Dobsevage wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Aix-la-Chapelle on April 29. The revolution of 1848 ruined his family's woolen mills. They emigrated to Baltimore in 1850.

Gold drew Sutro to San Francisco that same year. Nevada silver mines next pulled him east to Dayton. His stamping mill there proved a technical success. Deep Comstock shafts grew too hot for miners to work. Sutro planned a tunnel to drain and cool the lode. Congress approved his tunnel company in 1866. Digging began in 1869 at the Carson River valley. He died at San Francisco in 1898. The entry follows the tunnel that bears his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-talmud-10739:
The Talmud is the great record of Jewish tradition after the Bible. Wilhelm Bacher wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Two Talmuds survive from the amoraic age. One comes from Palestinian schools, the other from Babylonian ones. Scholars call them the Yerushalmi and the Babli.

Used alone, the word Talmud usually means the Babylonian work. The name itself comes from a verb meaning to teach. It can mean teaching or learning in older usage. The amoraic period ran from the third to fifth centuries. In that span the schools built both compilations. The Talmud crowns the writings of Jewish tradition. Bacher calls it tradition's most important production historically. The long entry unpacks its name, making, and contents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanna-debe-eliy:
Tanna debe Eliyahu is a midrash in two linked parts. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its final editing came at the end of the tenth century. Part one, the Greater Order of Elijah, holds thirty-one chapters. Part two, the Lesser Order, holds fifteen.

The Talmud ties the work to the prophet Elijah himself. Elijah used to visit Rabbi Anan and recite it. After one ruling by Anan, the prophet stopped coming. Anan fasted and begged forgiveness until he returned. Fear then made Anan hear it from inside a box. Rashi explains the two names from those visits. The greater book holds the earlier lectures. The entry blends textual history with a prophet's legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tugendhold-jaco:
Jacob Tugendhold was a Russian educator who modernized Jewish schooling in Warsaw. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Breslau in 1791, he died at Warsaw in 1871. In 1819 he founded a school for Jewish children there. Its teaching used modern methods and broad subjects.

Conservative teachers fought his plan at every step. In 1820 Russia made him censor of Warsaw's Jewish books. He directed the city's rabbinical school from 1853 to 1862. He also led the Warsaw kahal for years. His efforts built a home for aged and invalid Jews. His books include a Polish defense against the blood accusation. He translated Mendelssohn's Phaedon into Polish as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-van-oven-abraha:
Abraham Van Oven was a doctor who settled in London. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His grandfather had fled Spain early in the seventeen hundreds. The family name came from Oven, in Holland. Van Oven earned his medical diploma at Leyden in 1759.
