Birgit Hasenack and four co-authors study the wish for touch after the COVID-19 years in this twenty twenty-three paper. Longing for touch means wanting more touch than one gets, and it rose when distance rules kept people apart. The team asks whether the feeling faded once the rules ended.

They compared survey data gathered during the crisis in a large group across many lands. They set it beside new data from the Netherlands, taken just after the rules lifted. A third set came when almost no rules were left. The wish for touch was much stronger during the crisis than after it. The paper maps what is known so far and points to open questions for future work on touch and well-being.
pmc-10731039:
Liu and co-authors study a rare muscle fault in thickened hearts with outflow block. In some patients a papillary muscle plugs straight into the mitral leaflet. The team reviewed 157 surgical cases from 2020 to 2023 at one center. Eight patients, or 5.1 percent, had this odd insertion. Most inserts sat at the A3 leaflet segment.

Standard heart ultrasound caught the fault in just two of the eight. A lip-nevus-like sign on scans raised the catch rate to 62.5 percent. All eight had septal trimming plus muscle removal or valve swap. Wall thickness and outflow gradient both fell sharply after surgery. No block or major leak returned over about 26 months of follow-up.
pmc-10731139:
Chen and a large team report a study from twenty twenty-three on support cells that help lung tumors grow. These support cells, found near tumors, come in many types, and their roles were not clear. The team read gene activity cell by cell in samples from sixteen lung cancer patients. They also mapped where each cell type sits in the tissue. Stain tests then checked the maps in more samples.

One support cell type, marked by a protein called POSTN, was more common in late tumors. Those cells sat near a second cell type tied to weak immune defense. Patients with more of these cells did worse over time. The find names a cell group that new drugs might target.
pmc-10738039:
Pamela Elfenbein describes a partnership between a Georgia university and the state aging agency, in a paper from twenty twenty-three. The state struggles to hire and keep staff for hard roles that guard older adults from abuse, neglect, and misuse of funds. The university runs an institute focused on healthy aging.

Together they matched a new state degree to the job needs of those roles. The degree was built to open high-demand careers to more Georgians. The match creates a direct path from study into jobs in adult protection and public guardianship. Elfenbein lays out the needs on both sides and what the joint training approach looks like in practice.
pmc-10739539:
Chen and five co-authors reported in twenty twenty-three on blood markers of inflammation and brain scan measures in the Framingham Heart Study Offspring cohort. Brain shrinkage seen on scans has been linked to risk of Alzheimer's disease and related dementia. The team asked which inflammation markers track with brain size.

They studied six hundred sixty-two adults free of dementia and stroke, with an average age of sixty-two. Blood tests covered sixty-eight markers, compared against eight brain volume measures. Higher levels of eight proteins were tied to smaller total brain volume. Two markers were tied to larger volume, suggesting a possible protective role. The authors say more work must confirm these links and explain how they act.
pmc-10741939:
Kyoung Hyeon Cha and colleagues published a medical study in 2023 on recovery after acute stroke. The autonomic nervous system often malfunctions after stroke. That dysfunction is linked to worse recovery and higher death risk. How strongly its severity shapes outcomes was not well established.

The team reviewed records of twenty-two patients at one center. A standard scoring scale graded each patient's autonomic problems. Recovery was measured with balance, walking, and daily activity scales. Scores were compared between the early stage and follow-up. Patients with worse autonomic dysfunction recovered less well. Statistical checks supported that pattern despite the small sample. The authors suggest autonomic testing should inform stroke rehabilitation planning.
pmc-10748239:
Natalia Shamantseva and four co-authors measure breathing with camera-tracked markers instead of a mouthpiece. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, uses optoelectronic plethysmography. Markers on the chest and belly let cameras infer each breath's timing and depth. The gold standard, spirometry, needs a sealed mouthpiece that can alter natural breathing.

Two analysis methods were built, a sum method and a triangle method. Most readings landed within half a breath per minute of the standard. Belly-based variants worked best in every body posture. Five to nine markers proved enough for full timing detail. That trims setup versus older protocols while keeping accuracy.
pmc-10753239:
Sachini Ranasinghe and colleagues followed women with suspected heart ischemia in two thousand twenty-three. Stress heart tests combine imaging with electrical tracings. Some women show abnormal tracings but normal wall motion. Earlier work linked that pattern to more heart events. This study tracked longer-term outcomes in women specifically. Core labs read all tests blindly.

Participants had no major artery blockages. The parent study enrolled women undergoing heart catheterization. Positive imaging cases were largely excluded here. The analysis focused on the tracing-only abnormal group. Their later heart event risk was the key question. Findings refine risk advice for such women. Normal imaging alone may not fully reassure.
pmc-10759939:
Melike Ozkan and colleagues study risky prescriptions in older patients with gut cancers. Their cohort study from twenty twenty-three reviews one hundred fifty-four patients. Potentially inappropriate medicines are a known geriatric hazard. Cancer care adds more drugs and more chances for harm.

Records captured diagnoses, drug lists, and baseline lab values. A standard stop-list flagged inappropriate prescriptions case by case. About one hundred flagged prescriptions appeared in the group. Common side effects included nausea, vomiting, kidney injury, and pain. The team tested links between flagged drugs and survival. Treatment side effects and disease progression were also examined. Safer prescribing could spare older cancer patients avoidable harm.
pmc-10832039:
Jiayao Lu, Jing Yang, and Xiaofei Cai pool the evidence on whether pneumonia patients admitted on weekends fare worse, in a two thousand twenty-four systematic review and meta-analysis. The so-called weekend effect haunts many hospital services, but pneumonia data were scattered.

Thirteen retrospective studies fed a random-effects analysis. Weekend admission carried a marginally higher in-hospital mortality risk that did not reach statistical significance. Thirty-day mortality, intensive care admission, and readmission risks were all statistically similar between weekend and weekday patients. The authors conclude their findings do not support a weekend effect for pneumonia, while noting the borderline in-hospital signal deserves continued monitoring.
pmc-11523939:
Carlos Fernández Moro and six colleagues wrote this comment in twenty twenty-three about how liver metastases growth patterns should be named. Growth patterns are conventionally classed as replacement or desmoplastic. The two patterns predict clearly different survival outcomes for patients. The authors helped set the current classification in international consensus guidelines.

Because these patterns outperform other prognostic markers, the authors want them used in routine pathology assessment. Careful naming matters before that happens, they argue. They accept keeping the term replacement, since cancer cells truly take the place of liver cells while co-opting blood vessels. Their proposal is to rename the desmoplastic pattern encapsulated instead. Clearer terminology, they suggest, will prevent misunderstandings as the classification enters everyday diagnostic practice.
pmc-11534639:
Mahmoud Sultan, Azad Al Hasan, and Nisreen Khazem report a rare pancreas tumour in a teenage girl. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Neuroendocrine tumours of the pancreas are rare in adults and far rarer in the young. Their vague signs and mixed forms make them easy to miss.

The girl has long spells of belly and back pain, then a sharp pain that runs to the shoulder. Plain tests look normal, but a scan shows spots in the liver and a lesion in the pancreas. A liver sample proves the tumour kind, and a scan lights up the liver spots. She starts a monthly hormone drug. The case urges doctors to weigh this tumour when long signs fit no common ill.
pmc-11535239:
Thomas Juhasz-Dora, Stein-Kato Lindberg, and three colleagues find that stressed green sea urchins quite literally glow differently, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Stress kills urchins in the wild and in aquaculture, costing money and ecosystems. This species was already known to emit complex biofluorescence, but nobody had tracked how the glow answers stress.

Two hundred ten adult urchins were split between controls and groups facing transport-like trials: out of water, or in warm or cool water. The team imaged external fluorescence and analyzed the animals' internal fluid at five time points over twelve hours. Green emissions near five hundred eighty nanometers responded to every treatment, peaking around hour nine. Red emissions behaved differently by condition. A readable stress signal that needs no blood draw could transform urchin welfare monitoring. The glow, in effect, reports how the animal is coping.
pmc-11570639:
Kyle Rauch, Jessica Bennett, Amina Stoddart, and Graham Gagnon test ultraviolet LED disinfection against fish pathogens, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Two bacteria, Aeromonas salmonicida and Yersinia ruckeri, plague salmon farming. Vaccination at scale is expensive and unreliable.

Mercury UV lamps kill these bacteria but are fragile and power-hungry, suiting only closed systems. LED versions are durable, battery-friendly, and adaptable. Three LED wavelengths were tried on both bacteria, in pure culture and in wastewater. All three disinfected effectively. The authors see LED treatment opening UV disinfection to open and remote aquaculture settings. Cheaper, hardier water treatment could cut antibiotic use and fish losses across the industry.
pmc-11573139:
Sofi-Mahmudi and six co-authors audit COVID research data sharing, in work from twenty twenty-four. The FAIR principles say research data should be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. The pandemic produced a flood of papers at record speed.

No prior check had judged whether COVID research data met those principles. The meta research study evaluated data availability and quality across that literature. Fast science can still be poor science infrastructure if data vanish or cannot be reused. The audit gives journals and funders a baseline for enforcing data standards in the next health emergency.
pmc-11582139:
Bromek and three co-authors study a drug's effect on a brain enzyme in rats in this two thousand twenty-four paper. The enzyme, CYP2D, helps process brain chemicals and some medicines. Earlier work from the group hinted that brain glutamate systems can sway this enzyme. Here they test a compound that activates a glutamate receptor pair called mGlu2/3. The compound is known as LY354740.

They measured the enzyme's activity and protein levels in the brain and liver. The drug raised CYP2D activity in the frontal cortex of the rat brain. Such a finding links a mood-related receptor system to local drug metabolism in the brain. That link could matter for how psychiatric drugs act. The work is basic animal research, meant to guide later studies.
pmc-11585639:
Kumar, Kabra, and Cole present a study from twenty twenty-four on a database of material strength data mined from papers. Data-driven materials work needs rich property collections, which were lacking. A chemistry-aware text tool reads the literature automatically. It extracts strength and stiffness values for many materials. Over seven hundred thousand records land in machine-readable files. Key traits include breaking strength, yield point, and stretch. Checks show solid precision and recall for the extraction.

The database is released in public for open use. Engineers and data scientists can mine it for design insight. The authors aim to speed data-driven discovery in mechanical engineering. Automated curation is framed as the scalable path.
pmc-11594639:
Domenico Mallardo and a large team seek a gene marker for when an allergy pill boosts melanoma immunotherapy, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Their earlier work showed patients given the antihistamine cetirizine alongside checkpoint drugs fared better. This backward-looking study hunted for what set the responders apart.

Gene activity scans pointed to one gene, a ligand that switches on a T-cell helper. Higher levels tracked with better disease control when the drug pairing was used. The gene also tracked with a marker of a friendly macrophage type, but only in patients who received the antihistamine. The authors propose the gene as a predictor for who gains from adding the pill.
pmc-11599939:
Davide Stefanutti and eight co-authors run a blinded trial of Spirulina supplements for overweight dogs on a weight loss diet, in a two thousand twenty-four veterinary paper. Obesity disturbs dogs' lipid metabolism and antioxidant defenses, and Spirulina helps other species.

Thirty-two dogs ate the same calorie-restricted, high-protein, high-fiber diet for twelve weeks, half with Spirulina and half with placebo. Both groups lost about eleven percent of body weight. Cholesterol, glucose, and liver enzymes improved in both groups once roughly six percent was lost. Triglycerides fell early only in the Spirulina group, and more of those dogs achieved large triglyceride reductions. The authors credit the diet mainly, with a supplement bonus for blood fats.
pmc-11604539:
Lee wrote a solo review in twenty twenty-four on prosthesis-patient mismatch after transcatheter aortic valve replacement. In that procedure, a new heart valve is placed through a tube rather than open surgery. Mismatch occurs when the new valve's opening is too small for the patient's body size and blood flow needs.

Studies disagree on how much mismatch harms patients after this procedure. A large Western registry found severe mismatch in twelve percent of patients, tied to more deaths and heart failure stays. A large Asian registry found it in under one percent, with no clear link to outcomes. Lee argues that group size, mismatch rates, and follow-up length help explain the clash.
pmc-11605839:
Stone, Miller, and Johnston study men training less than full time in Scottish medicine in twenty twenty-four. Twenty-six men with such training experience sat for deep interviews. Four themes emerged from the talks. Work culture, gender norms, lived experience, and push pull factors framed them.

The ideal worker image still wins peer respect and manly standing, men felt. Part time training reads as a women's path, leaving men feeling odd or stigmatized. Gains in life and work were real but hinged on unit support. Both image and practical blocks slow male uptake. The authors urge fixes across culture, process, and planning.
pmc-11606139:
Min-Ki Kim, Sung-Phil Kim, and Jeong-Woo Sohn tackle tangled brain signals in this twenty twenty-four study. Electrodes near brain cells pick up spikes when cells fire. When two cells fire at once, their spikes overlap and blur, hiding who fired. Sorting such mixes has lacked a firm answer key.

The team first learned the spike shape of each cell from clean parts of the recording. They then made fake tangled spikes from those shapes and trained a sorter on them. Tested on real recordings, the method could pick apart overlaps and recover the hidden spikes. Cleaner sorting sharpens the study of how brain cells talk.
pmc-11607939:
Adam Parker, Blandine French, Madeline Groom, and Charlotte Hall review what helps or hinders clinicians caring for people with tics. Their mixed methods review, from twenty twenty-four, gathers thirteen papers. Patients and families often report that professionals misunderstand tics. The review spans clinician knowledge, attitudes, and daily practice.

Three themes organize the findings. First, knowledge exists but confidence and formal training lag behind. Second, wrong beliefs and stigma lead to misread symptoms and missed diagnoses. Family views about blame shape whether care is sought. Third, communication between clinics and families makes or breaks care. Training reform is the recurring prescription.
pmc-11612139:
Sengsim and co-authors compare survival in adults born with heart shunts who face raised lung vessel pressure. Unrepaired shunts can strain the lungs for decades. Long-term data for borderline cases are scarce. The study covered patients seen from 1995 to 2021. It included 99 adults with Eisenmenger syndrome and 118 with mainly left-to-right shunts. Lung resistance in the Eisenmenger group averaged 21 Wood units.

Nearly all Eisenmenger patients, 97%, received targeted drug therapy. Some shunt patients had a treat-and-repair path instead. Survival was compared across these groups. The results help doctors weigh repair against drug care when pressure sits at the borderline.
pmc-11616239:
Ermiyas Debebe and others checked depression after stroke in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia in 2024. Depression often follows surviving a stroke. It is often missed and not treated. Follow-up clinic patients were surveyed here. Special hospitals hosted the study locally. Rates and risk factors were estimated.

Depression rates ran high versus similar studies. Prior depression raised risk strongly. Heart disease also raised risk clearly. Major body limits added further risk. Employed patients faced lower risk instead. Work may protect mood after stroke. Thorough depression checks are urged strongly. These clinics should screen as a rule.
pmc-11621039:
John Black, Steven Cooper, Thomas Schmidt, and Andrew Weeks plan genetic rescue for a threatened marsupial in this two thousand twenty-four genetics paper. The southern brown bandicoot survives in strongly split groups across south-eastern Australia. Genetic mixing, moving animals between groups, can counter drift and inbreeding, but its long-term effects are rarely modeled. The authors checked genetic gaps among twelve groups, with the first genome check of six of them, and measured diversity with a tailored pipeline.

Groups clustered into four major sets, Adelaide Hills, western Victoria, eastern Victoria, and Tasmania, with more structure inside sets. One group, on Tasmania's Inner Sister Island, was extremely degraded in genetic terms. Simulating fifty generations of mixing into a low-diversity captive Victorian group, the authors compared wild source groups for the greatest diversity gain. The work guides which groups should donate animals for rescue.
pmc-11631839:
William Copenhaver and six co-authors review case reports of a pain syndrome after vaccination in this two thousand twenty-four paper. The syndrome, complex regional pain syndrome, brings lasting pain and changes in a limb. Its link to vaccines has long been debated. Vaccines are the strongest tool against infectious disease, so rare harms need careful study. The team set out to gather all published cases that followed immunization.

They searched case reports using standard review guidelines. For each case they noted the vaccine type, the patient's age and sex, and the time until symptoms began. Reviewing cases side by side can show patterns that single reports hide. The authors aim to clarify how the syndrome appears after shots. The paper can inform doctors who weigh rare risks against vaccine benefits.
pmc-11634539:
Rinie van Beuningen and seven co-authors build a large scale rapid test platform based on LAMP, a DNA copying method, for pandemic readiness. The COVID-19 pandemic showed the need for fast tests at huge scale. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

The gold test method is exact but slow and logistically hard, with supply strain in a surge. LAMP is faster, flexible, and cheaper, and it proved itself for the COVID virus. But test volumes rose a hundred to a thousand fold, so hand work could not keep up. A charity led effort built a robot run, end to end line that cleans RNA and runs LAMP in one step, at high volume.
pmc-11639839:
Sean M Murphy and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four critique of a popular method for estimating wildlife numbers from camera traps. The random encounter model promises counts for animals without unique markings. Its strict assumptions are easily broken in practice.

Using years of data on an unmarked predator and its prey, the team tested two common violations. Cameras placed on trails and borrowed movement speeds both warped the estimates. A review of published studies found the same risks widespread. Most predator-prey density figures from the method, they conclude, should not be trusted.
pmc-11641339:
Tang and a large team map a special antibody found in nurse sharks in twenty twenty-four. The antibody, called IgNAR, is smaller and tougher than most human antibodies. That makes it of interest for future drugs. It was found in nurse sharks more than thirty years ago, but its place in the genome stayed unclear.

The team found three IgNAR sites in the nurse shark genome. Only two of the sites are switched on and used by the shark. Each makes forms with five main parts, though some forms lack two parts. Computer models of the shapes matched the gene maps. The work gives a firm base for drug research using these antibodies.
pmc-11642339:
Ewa Dwojak and a large team reviewed in two thousand twenty-four whether long-lasting inflammation of the womb lining helps explain failed fertility treatment. The review centers on plasma cells, immune cells whose presence in womb tissue marks chronic inflammation. That condition links to infertility and repeated failure of transferred embryos to implant.

Special staining can reveal plasma cells, but doctors still debate how many cells should count as disease. The authors also discuss healing potential in womb stem cells as a future treatment angle. Fertility clinics gain a map of a debated diagnosis, and why standard tests may miss a treatable cause of failure.
pmc-11643639:
Monika Rojewska and four co-authors study how anti-HIV prodrugs meet cell membranes in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Pronucleotides are drugs that turn into active nucleotides inside the cell. The active form can block HIV from copying itself. Getting these drugs across membranes is key to their success. Adding oily groups to the drug helps it interact with the fatty membrane.

The team modeled a membrane as a single layer of a common phospholipid. They spread this film on water using the Langmuir method and added drug analogs. The test drugs were variants of AZT, an early HIV drug. Measurements show how the drugs insert into and change the film. Such insight helps chemists design prodrugs that reach their targets better.
pmc-11644039:
Mohamad Khalil, Hala Abdallah, Maria Calasso, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It surveys how people in three Mediterranean countries used herbal medicine during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The team collected 812 full survey replies from Italy, Lebanon, and Tunisia. Fatigue was the most common symptom everywhere, and lasting post-COVID symptoms hit Lebanon hardest. Herbal use was common in all three places, but the share who took herbs to treat COVID-19 ranged from about a quarter in Italy to two-thirds in Tunisia. In Lebanon, heavy use of za'atar, a thyme-like herb mix rich in plant compounds called polyphenols, tracked with milder symptoms. The authors say folk plant remedies stayed central in the region, and their active compounds deserve closer study.
pmc-11646239:
Avinash Sharma and colleagues pin down a gene that helps plant seeds sleep until the time is right, in this study from twenty twenty-four. The plant is Arabidopsis, a small weed used as a lab model. A hormone called ABA keeps seeds dormant and helps the grown plant ride out drought, and the team studied a gene, PUB41, that makes a protein tagging other proteins for disposal.

Plants with a broken copy of the gene told the story. Their seeds woke too easily, and ABA could not hold them back as it does in normal plants. The same plants also wilted faster under drought. In roots, ABA itself switched the gene on, raising its output. The team reads PUB41 as a booster of the ABA signal: it deepens seed sleep and hardens the plant against dry spells. Such genes matter for crops that must sprout on cue, not before.
pmc-11648539:
Guoran Peng, Beibei Cheng, Rongzhen Ding, and Aiguo Dai published a bibliometric analysis in twenty twenty-four of research linking asthma and depression. The two conditions frequently coexist and worsen each other's toll. Bibliometrics maps a field's structure mathematically rather than summarizing its findings one paper at a time.

Searching a major citation database for two thousand to twenty twenty-three yielded over three thousand papers from nine hundred thirty-seven journals and one hundred six countries. The United States and Columbia University led production. Six themes organized the literature, from quality of life to childhood asthma. Burst detection flagged severe asthma and oxidative stress as rising fronts. The authors offer the map to researchers choosing where to dig next.
pmc-11654339:
Laura Foucault-Fruchard and co-authors offer a 2024 full review of simulation training for talking skills in pharmacy. Talking well with patients and co-workers is core to safe care. Simulation builds hands-on skills reliably, but its effect on pharmacy communication was less written up.

Searches covered four databases up to late 2022. Studies had to train pharmacy students or pharmacists through clinical simulation. The reviewers listed simulation types and measured results. Confidence and self-perceived skill were among the results tracked. Teachers get a sorted evidence base for building communication practice that goes beyond lectures.
pmc-11656839:
Junwoo Yea and fourteen colleagues redesigned electrodes so stretchable piezoelectric generators stop canceling their own output. Buckled structures in three dimensions make stiff devices stretchable. In piezoelectric films, though, strain is uneven. Some regions make charges of the wrong sign, and those charges cancel the rest. The team shaped coupling electrodes to match the local strain direction on curved structures. Circuit design cut cancellation losses still more. Their test material was a high-performance inorganic film.

The generator reached a top output power density of 8.34 milliwatts per cubic centimeter. Models tied mechanical and electrical behavior into one. Tests in cells and in animals probed medical use. At this density, energy from body motion could power implants with no batteries. The design rules reach beyond one device: match the electrode to the strain map, the 2024 study argues.
pmc-11657639:
Ma and six colleagues adapt a childbirth fear survey for Chinese expectant fathers in twenty twenty-four. Fathers' fear of birth is a real concern as their role grows. A standard mother's questionnaire was reworded for men. Over seven hundred fathers took part in the checks.

Expert review backed the items' fit. Factor studies found eight themes covering most of the spread. A follow up model fit the father's version well. Repeat and internal scores showed solid reliability. The tool can now screen fathers' birth fears in China, the team concludes.
pmc-11657739:
Kalaivanan Syasyila, Mohammad Rahim Kamaluddin, and two co-authors review how twisted thinking feeds crime. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, covers cognitive distortions. These are bent beliefs that excuse harm, such as blaming the victim. The team asks which types show up and how they differ by crime.

Twenty-five studies from twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-four passed strict checks. The search spanned five large databases. Distortions not only spark law-breaking but shape its form. Violent, sexual, and theft crimes show distinct thought patterns. The authors say grasping these patterns can sharpen prevention and rehab. Therapy that straightens beliefs is a core tool they highlight.
pmc-11660339:
Luigia Sica and colleagues study how meaning in life, optimism, and a view of the future shaped young adults' well-being in the COVID-19 pandemic. In all, 389 people filled in measures of future time perspective, presence of and search for meaning, life orientation, and well-being parts: anxiety, depression, stress, and aggressive behavior.

A person-centered study of latent profiles found three coping profiles. The largest, about two in five people, showed flattened coping. Two smaller groups of about equal size showed aggressive coping and perspective coping. A model then tested predictors of group place: gender, age, student or work status, and pandemic losses. The results back the team's view: presence of meaning, a positive life orientation, and a positive view of the future acted as coping plans against stress.
pmc-11667039:
Ramin Aslani and six co-authors measure heavy metals, nitrate, and nitrite in bottled water brands sold in Tehran, Iran, and gauge health risk with a Monte Carlo method. These pollutants pose clear public health risks. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

Thirty brands were sampled in winter and summer. Metal reads came from a plasma based tool and nitrate reads from ion sorting. Nitrate spanned a wide range across brands. Two metals were below the catch limit in all brands. In half the samples, nitrate or nitrite topped the label claim. Some brands also held more magnesium or sodium than their labels said.
pmc-11672139:
Lorenzo Casimiro and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study of strong supramolecular gels built from metal-linked polymer chains. Such gels, assembled from the bottom up, could serve in smart materials. Earlier versions were mechanically weak.

Cobalt or zinc ions linked hybrid building blocks carrying two gripping arms each. Charge attraction between the blocks and metal nodes stacked the chains into fibres. The fibres cross-linked into gels above a set concentration. Microscopy, scattering, and flow tests mapped the structure. The gels showed improved strength plus light and magnetic effects, opening uses from optics to responsive devices.
pmc-11672439:
Benjamin Vlad and ten colleagues analyzed spinal fluid from 390 people with multiple sclerosis, focusing on antibody production inside the nervous system. Making IgG antibodies within the spinal fluid is a hallmark of the disease. Most studies only record whether production occurs. The twenty twenty-four study instead measured its intensity using Reiber's formula. Patients were all untreated and had relapsing-remitting disease.

Stronger antibody production correlated with higher white cell counts in the fluid. It also tracked with broader antiviral antibody patterns, the MRZ reaction, against measles, rubella, and chickenpox viruses. Female sex was another correlate named in the title. These links help researchers understand what drives the immune activity that defines MS spinal fluid. Intensity, the authors argue, carries information that a simple yes-or-no result misses.
pmc-11672539:
Qian Zhang and eleven co-authors published a molecular computing study in twenty twenty-four on making DNA computers run steps in sequence, quickly. DNA circuits process information through molecular reactions, and origami registers can pass signals between them. Earlier registers could be written only once and moved signals slowly, throttling any multi-step program.

The new register is solid-state: it compresses a circuit's output from three-dimensional solution onto a two-dimensional surface, and it can be rewritten. A hybrid design linking liquid circuits to the surface register cut transfer time to under an hour. A trace amplifier reads stored signals back into solution. The authors say the design enables faster programs and even visual debugging.
pmc-11673639:
Fangping Gong and a team of co-authors link plant pigments called flavonoids to seed strength in peanuts, in a twenty twenty-four study. Strong seeds sprout well, a key quality trait for this oil crop. The team compared developing seeds of a weak-sprouting peanut type with a strong one. They profiled pigments, hormones, and gene activity side by side.

They found 165 pigment types, with fifty-one differing between the two seed types. The weak type held far less of two key pigments, and its pigment-making genes were all turned down. Hormone levels also differed, tied to the same gene switches. One pigment seemed to guard seeds against rust-like damage. The authors say flavonoids help set seed vigor.
pmc-11674839:
Kleinhans and coauthors test if strong cannabis use in pregnancy shifts birth outcomes. Pregnant women have sparse facts on cannabis effects alone. Alcohol, tobacco, and other drugs cloud most past studies. The team kept those other uses out of their cohort.

Women were recruited in Washington and Oregon from 2019 to 2022. All joined after the first trimester of pregnancy. Cannabis users took it at least three days a week early on. Urine tests checked for other drugs at many points. Dose was scored in milligrams of active compounds per day. Birth weight and timing were the main outcomes.
pmc-11675339:
Maria Carolina Juvêncio Francisquini and seven co-authors published a controlled trial in twenty twenty-four testing whether a twelve-week activity program improves teenagers' psychological symptoms. Exercise is linked to better adolescent mental health, but school-delivered programs need proof. The study adapted an existing program into physical education classes.

One hundred fifty students aged twelve to fifteen took part, and symptoms were measured with the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. After twelve weeks, no measure improved significantly: not emotional or conduct problems, not attention difficulties, not peer problems or overall score. The honest null result, the authors say, should push future studies to test longer programs, different doses, or more targeted groups.
pmc-11675439:
Xiaojiao Cheng and five co-authors measure how cooking changes the digestibility of starch in foxtail millet, in a two thousand twenty-four food science paper. Millet starch digests slowly, which is nutritionally attractive, but cooking's specific effects were under-mapped.

Eight millet cultivars were compared raw and cooked against rice flour. Cooking broke down starch granules and crystals, formed starch-lipid complexes, and raised dietary fiber while lowering lipids and phenolics. Cooked millet still digested more slowly than rice. Digestion speed tracked the amount of starch-lipid complexes and total dietary fiber. The authors conclude interactions among components during cooking, not starch alone, set the digestion rate.
pmc-11676139:
Toshiko Tsuyuki and six colleagues survey Japanese families caring for relatives with dementia through the pandemic, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Five hundred family caregivers answered a cross-sectional questionnaire. Lockdowns in those years cut the services such families lean on.

More than half reported increased caregiving burden in the survey. Longer hours drove that rise in the main. So did reduced public services and restricted social contact for the families. Three quarters of them wanted more comprehensive formal support. Yet close to a fifth of patients used no public services at all. The offerings on hand did not match their needs. Or the families held back from inviting help into the home. Informal supports, like dementia cafes, were well known. But they were not enough to meet the load. The gap between wanting help and accepting its available forms is the core find.
pmc-11678439: Hong-Li Huang and colleagues reviewed ring-shaped sulfone chemistry in 2024. These sulfur-bearing rings form a subset of active ring compounds. Interest has grown in their drug-making potential. New drug ingredients may come from this family. The review hunts for better ways to build them. Ideal methods are simple, mild, and environmentally friendly. They must also run efficiently at useful scale. Catalytic routes receive systematic coverage in the review. The authors weigh the strengths of each route. They close on uses in pharmaceutical development.
pmc-11688239:
Alex van den Berg and four co-authors tested ways to show contact forces to people steering robot arms from afar, in twenty twenty-four. The work used haptic assistance, where the controls push back with guide forces, inside a virtual reality setup. Two aids were tried: drawn cues that picture the contact forces, and a head-mounted display that deepens the view of the scene. Volunteers ran a simulated dross removal task.

Both aids helped task performance, each with its own strengths. The drawn force cues cut peak collision force, a clear safety gain. The head-mounted display also lifted performance in a marked way. Users rated both aids well in the follow-up survey. The authors say showing forces and spatial layout in richer ways can make remote robot work safer and smoother, and they offer both methods for use in industry-style tasks.
pmc-11688739:
Emma Cho, Charlotte Weiss, and George Demiris review how older adults view tech tools made to ease being alone. Their review, from two thousand twenty-four, brings past studies into one clear set of themes.

The team searched four large data sets and kept thirteen sound peer-checked studies from a range of lands. Older adults often liked tools such as video phones, pet-like screen figures, and robot helpers. They said such tools brought more contact, comfort, and a link to town life. But some disliked the style of digital talk, found chats dull, or hit faults like sound lag and hard steps. The authors urge that new tools be built with older adults, not just for them.
pmc-11688939:
Jinyu Liu, Yifan Lou, and Ethan Siu Leung Cheung test a plan that trains former carers of people with dementia to mentor current carers. Their pilot study, from two thousand twenty-four, works in the Chinese American community of a large east coast city.

Thirty-eight current carers and eight former carers took part over three months. Current carers were split by chance into a mentored group and a control group. Those who got a mentor showed bigger drops in feeling alone, in strain, and in low mood. The former carers said the work gave them purpose, growth, and trust in their own skill. The authors see past carers as a strong, untapped source of help.
pmc-11691939:
Amy Webster and seven co-authors report in twenty twenty-four on a new standard note for logging claims of abuse or neglect of older patients. Abuse harms a share of older adults each year in the United States. Yet few health systems log such claims in a set way in the health record. The new note came from a national social work program for veterans' care.

Staff at three sites tried the note and spoke with the team in spring of that year. Most found it quick, clear, and easy to use. Half took five minutes or less to fill it in. The note made it simpler to see that a claim had been made and to plan next care. Staff also raised care for patient privacy and safety.
pmc-11725039:
Amrani and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on blood groups and heart disease in Algerian hospital patients. African data on this link are scarce and mostly cover blood donors. The team review records of near twenty-eight hundred heart patients in Algiers. Type O dominates the group, followed by A, B, and AB. Most patients are Rhesus positive. High blood pressure, blood fats, and diabetes are nearly universal risks here. Acute coronary syndrome is the top diagnosis.

No blood group links to heart conditions or risk factors overall. Rhesus-negative patients show slightly more rhythm problems, a marginal gap. The authors provide rare African genotype data. Their null result counters claims that non-O types raise heart risk.
pmc-11831339:
Małgorzata Konieczyńska, Joanna Natorska, Michał Ząbczyk, and Anetta Undas review what is known about lipoprotein(a) and blood clots, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Lipoprotein(a) is set by genes and is a risk factor for heart and vessel disease. High levels affect about a fifth of Europeans. Its role in venous clots, though, remains in doubt.

The strongest proof supports an antifibrinolytic action. The particle blocks plasminogen activation and so slows clot breakdown. Smaller forms of its key protein are the most potent. Other paths include denser fibrin networks, platelet activation, and inflammation from oxidized phospholipids. Clots in odd sites, like cerebral and retinal veins, are discussed too. New lipoprotein(a)-lowering drugs are now in randomized trials. They might also cut clot risk, an open point the authors flag.
pmc-11888639:
Dinesh Pillai and colleagues survey oral health habits and tobacco use among coal miners. Their study from twenty twenty-four covers two mines in Tamil Nadu. Health behaviour, attitudes, and knowledge shape mouth health strongly. Sugar intake and tobacco both damage teeth and gums.

About six hundred workers answered a pre-tested questionnaire. Smoking cigarettes and bidis was common in both mines. Most workers cleaned teeth with brush and toothpaste. A notable minority still used finger and tooth powder. Worksite health programmes could build on existing brushing habits. Tobacco cessation remains the biggest oral health lever here. The survey benchmarks habits before any intervention.
pmc-11931339:
Archana Shrestha and colleagues check how well eye charts that students use on themselves are working in schools, in this study from eastern Nepal, published in twenty twenty-four. The charts hang in classrooms so children can test their own vision and catch problems early. A regional eye care program placed them in one hundred thirty-seven schools.

Four hundred students answered surveys, one hundred eighty tested their vision, and sixteen teachers sat for interviews. Most students who used the chart liked it and called it useful, and most schools had placed it well. Yet only about half the students had used it at all, and just one in ten used it correctly. Teachers praised the charts but said awareness was low on all sides. The authors urge regular information sessions, motivated teachers, and visits from eye health workers to turn a good tool into a used one.
pmc-12056439:
Roya Sahebi leads a team on breast cancer risk from chest scans in Iran. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with high detail CT scans. Such scans were used a lot in the COVID years.

The group came from a hospital in Shiraz over near three years. A tool worked out the dose each breast received. Risk for life was then guessed with a known model. A quarter of folks had more than one scan in that span. Mean risk per group is given with its range. More scans meant more dose and more risk.
pmc-12247139:
Meng Zhang, Jiafeng Sha, Na Li, and six colleagues trace how an early virus infection can worsen asthma for good in this two thousand twenty-four mouse study. Early infection with respiratory syncytial virus is linked to asthma that starts or flares later, but the path was unclear. The team set up asthma models in mice with an early virus infection and tracked a special set of T cells that stay in the lung.

The virus left asthma worse for at least six weeks, with high levels of allergy-type signals in the lung. The resident memory T cells tracked with how bad the flares and airway swelling were. A gene switch called PLZF proved central: raising it grew more of these cells, while removing its gene cut their numbers and eased the response. The authors say the pathway points to new ways to treat asthma after early viral infection.
pmc-12671339:
Tannus and Cobas published in twenty twenty-five a review of autonomic neuropathy, a nerve complication of diabetes. The condition can strike any branch of the automatic nervous system. Its drivers mix high blood sugar damage, oxidative stress, and inflammation. The heart form is especially dangerous, raising risks of rhythm problems and silent heart attacks. Gut, urinary, and sweat gland problems also burden patients heavily. Despite that impact, the complication is often missed in routine care.

Symptoms are vague and onset is subclinical, delaying recognition. The review blends basic, population, and clinical evidence for practitioners. It focuses on heart, gut, and urinary manifestations in depth. Practical guidance covers suspecting, testing for, and managing the condition. The authors aim to move the disease from overlooked to routinely screened. Better awareness could prevent serious outcomes, they argue.
pmc-12693539:
Shaobo Li and six colleagues published a review in two thousand twenty-five on imaging long-term inflammation with a special receptor target. Somatostatin receptors sit on activated immune cells. Tracers that bind them can light up inflamed tissue on PET and SPECT scans without surgery.

The review gathers lab and clinical studies across diseases such as blood vessel inflammation, sarcoidosis, heart inflammation, arthritis, and thyroid eye disease. It compares the receptor scans with the standard sugar-based PET scan. The receptor method gave cleaner contrast in organs where the sugar scan runs hot, like heart and brain. Evidence so far comes from small studies. The authors list open questions on cost, access, and standard practice.
pmc-12693639:
Bahri and a large team studied essential oils blended from plants and spices in twenty twenty-five. Essential oils are concentrated plant extracts with germ-killing, calming, and cell-protecting effects of interest to medicine. The team tested five blends, each mixing four plants used in folk medicine in Mostaganem, Algeria.

They mapped each blend's chemistry and tested safety in live animals plus activity against germs and viruses. Different blends led on different measures. One blend was the strongest antioxidant and antibacterial mix, while others led against specific viruses or cancer cells in dishes. Key scent compounds differed by blend, such as carvacrol, thymol, and eugenol. The authors say several blends merit further study for drug and medical use.
pmc-12698539:
Lu and seven co-authors investigated a collagen-sensing protein, DDR1, in lung cancer in twenty twenty-five. Non-small cell lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death, and many patients respond poorly to immunotherapy. DDR1 helps tumors grow and hide from the immune system, but its role in this cancer was unclear.

Combining tumor genome data, machine learning, lab experiments, and patient samples, the team found high DDR1 linked to advanced stage, worse progression-free survival, and an immune-suppressed tumor environment. A four-gene signature built by the models predicted outcomes well in outside datasets. Silencing DDR1 in cancer cells slowed growth, migration, and invasion and triggered cell death. Over half of patient samples overproduced the protein. The authors nominate DDR1 as both a prognostic biomarker and a drug target.
pmc-12706639:
Maryam Soltani, Vahid Mofid, Mohammad Rabbani, Seyed Amir Mohammad Mortazavian, and Mahdieh Pabast build a sports drink from whey permeate. The drink carries probiotics and whey peptides. Their food science paper showed up in two thousand twenty-five. The aim is a working alternative to standard electrolyte drinks.

Two Lactobacillus strains plus hydrolyzed whey protein were packed into alginate beads, half of them coated with whey protein isolate. Coated beads shielded the cargo best: antioxidant power after twenty-eight days roughly doubled the uncoated version, probiotic survival in storage rose, and survival through mock digestion improved too. The study shows dairy side streams can become carriers for live cultures and bioactive peptides.
pmc-12712539:
An expert panel of the European Food Safety Authority issued a 2025 scientific opinion on L-valine, an amino acid added to animal feed. The product is made by fermentation with a bacterial strain whose cells are killed but left in the final powder. The European Commission asked whether the additive is safe and effective for all animal species.

The panel found the production strain met the standard presumption-of-safety approach: it carried no genes of concern, and no living cells were detected in the finished product. On that basis the opinion supports the additive's use in animal nutrition, giving regulators an evidence-based answer for licensing decisions.
pmc-12722839:
Ye-Dong Lao and colleagues studied gut barrier damage in eczema patients in two thousand twenty-five. Atopic dermatitis causes severe itchy skin inflammation. A leaky gut barrier may worsen the disease. Blood markers can reveal barrier damage. The team compared patients with healthy donors. Some patients then received washed microbiota transplants.

Patients showed clearly higher barrier damage markers. Transplant patients improved on standard eczema scores afterward. Higher starting damage levels predicted greater symptom relief. That link appeared in exploratory analysis only. Gut microbes shifted after treatment as well. The gut-skin connection deserves larger trials. Baseline testing might someday guide transplant selection.
pmc-12729239:
Xu Zhang and colleagues trace causes of adult-onset epilepsy across twenty-five years in China. Their retrospective study from twenty twenty-five reviews one major hospital. Over five thousand patients from most provinces entered. Cause patterns shifted as imaging and testing improved.

Unknown-cause cases fell steadily, especially after twenty fifteen. Metabolic causes declined in recent years of the record. Immune-related epilepsy rose after twenty twenty-one instead. Structural causes dominated in patients over fifty. Their share varied widely across age groups overall. Better diagnosis explains much of the changing mix. Treatment planning increasingly follows precise cause categories.
pmc-12731839:
Vitores-Calero and four co-authors weighed a plastic-linked chem in spit in twenty twenty-five in folks wearing clear tooth aligners. Aligners sit in the mouth for long hours, so leaks matter. Two groups of twelve wore a top brand set or office-made sets.

Spit levels of the chem jumped half an hour after parts were glued on. By one week the levels fell back to the start mark. Both sets showed the same swing pattern in the week. The office sets shed the peak a bit faster than the brand sets, they find.
pmc-12732339:
Chylinska and co-authors measure small fiber nerve damage in Sjogren disease, an autoimmune condition. Nerve damage, or polyneuropathy, is common in primary Sjogren disease and lowers quality of life. Damage to small sensory fibers, both myelinated A-delta and unmyelinated C fibers, may start before dryness symptoms appear.

The cohort study used the cutaneous silent period, a spinal reflex that pauses muscle activity after skin stimulation. This reflex can reveal small A-delta fiber problems without invasive tests. Finding how common this damage is may push earlier nerve checks in Sjogren care, before pain and numbness grow severe.
pmc-12734839:
Tomaszkiewicz and eight colleagues describe a new way to fix umbilical catheters in newborns in twenty twenty-five. Umbilical venous catheters are common in neonatal care. They can shift position or cause infection if not held well. The new method uses the umbilical cord clamp itself for fixation.

The catheter enters through the side of the cord, which is not cut. A sterile patch then secures the line to the clamp. Tip position was checked by ultrasound every twenty-four hours. The review covered two hundred sixty-four newborns at one centre. The catheter shifted in about nineteen percent of cases, mostly inward, and was repositioned. No bloodstream infections linked to the line occurred. The authors call the method safe, cheap, and simple for one operator.
pmc-12735339:
Hamed and co-authors review carbon capture and cuts for the built environment. Buildings drive about 40 percent of global energy use and carbon output. The review sorts plans into capture, storage, and reduction. Capture paths include plant growth, concrete carbonation, and microbe minerals. Storage paths cover curing, mineral locking, and waste reuse.

Reduction paths swap in industrial waste and bio-based stocks. New direct air capture stocks get a feasibility check. The review weighs carbon uptake across building materials. Gaps in proof and scale are flagged for each path. The authors urge buildings to gain climate jobs beyond shelter.
pmc-12735439:
Sanda Jurja and colleagues reviewed berry compounds for vessel health in 2025. Heart disease still kills most worldwide. Diet strategies may support standard drugs. Blueberries carry rich purple pigments. Honeysuckle berries carry similar pigments too. Both pigment groups are polyphenols.

Evidence covers vessel lining function mainly. Combined berries might add benefits together. Synergy is also possible, they suggest. Support stays mostly preclinical for now. Indirect clinical hints exist as well. The idea is hypothesis-generating only. No practice change is recommended yet. Mechanism-aware trials are the next step. Berries remain a low-risk dietary option.
pmc-12735739:
Dawid Łażewski leads a team of sixteen authors adding bromine atoms to a promising anticancer stilbene and checking whether the trade is worth it. The parent compound, a tetramethoxy stilbene related to resveratrol chemistry, already kills cancer cells. Halogenated relatives were largely unexplored territory.

The team synthesized the bromo analogues, characterized their physical properties, and simulated how the body would absorb and process them. Cancer cell tests showed the brominated versions were not dramatically stronger than the methoxy compounds. Their advantage lay elsewhere: they were gentler on pseudo-normal cell lines. A safer profile at similar potency, the authors argue, makes the bromo series a legitimate new path for stilbene drug development.
pmc-12736939:
Peishan Sun, Mingyang Du, Zhihui Li, Xuan Chen, and Junpeng Shi build a radar mode reader that learns from mostly unlabeled signals. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. Fine-grained radar reading with deep learning normally needs heaps of labeled data, which is costly to make.

Their setup joins three branches in one system. Two contrast methods teach the model to match like signals and split unlike ones, and special steps handle warped pulses. On two hard test sets, the method lifted accuracy by wide margins while using only a tenth of the labeled data. The authors say that sets a new best mark for this task. The work matters for defense and sensing teams that cannot label vast signal stores by hand.
pmc-12737339:
Agnes Carolin and co-authors tracked a shift in where the Omicron coronavirus attacks in 2025, joining patient samples with mouse tests. They sequenced RNA from nose and throat swabs of thirty-seven intensive care patients in Australia. The samples spanned a period when the dominant sublineage rolled from BA.5 through to XBB-like and finally XBC forms. That roll matched the worldwide succession. Viral loads varied enormously between patients, complicating the human contrast.

Restricting the patient study to samples with comparable viral counts. The later XBC virus showed a gene expression and cell-type signature of increased targeting of ciliated epithelial cells. The hair-lined cells of the airway. To test the trend, the team infected mouse strains with either a BA.5 or a XBB isolate. And the XBB virus indeed infected the nasal turbinates and their ciliated cells more heavily. Measured by virus counts and tissue staining.
pmc-12738739:
Zhengyao Liu and colleagues published an open sediment database in 2025 for a major Chinese desert. The Gurbantunggut Desert sits in the Junggar Basin of Central Asia. It is China's second-largest desert. Its fixed and semi-fixed dunes take branching, honeycomb, and mixed shapes. Yet broad grain-size data across dune types were scarce. The team sampled many zones and hundreds of sites. They collected well over a thousand surface and profile samples.

All samples followed standard field protocols. A laser instrument measured grain sizes after careful pretreatment. The data capture how sediment changes by dune type and slope position. They also show change with depth in profiles. The patterns reflect wind, sediment supply, and plant cover at work. The authors offer the dataset as a baseline for dune studies. It can support work on sand transport, climate effects, and desert monitoring.
pmc-12739939:
Yadong Li leads a team that maps inhaled allergy profiles in Fuzhou children. Their study from twenty twenty-five deals with respiratory allergies in kids. Rates of such diseases in children rise each year.

Kids aged zero to fourteen with allergies were screened. One group had allergic rhinitis, the other had asthma. Blood tests used a standard system for inhaled allergens. Two dust mite types topped rates in both groups. A cockroach allergen stood out in the asthma group. Results can guide diagnosis, treatment, and prevention there. Regional spectra had not been mapped before.
pmc-12740939:
Nasima Sultana and nine co-authors link a gene form in SCGB1A1 to COPD in a West Bengal group through low CC16. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. CC16 is a flare guard protein, and its gene form is a known may-be mark for this lung ill. More than two hundred sick folks and near two hundred well folks were gene-typed.

The risk form ran more in sick folks and tied to worse lung flow scores. Gene use and protein both ran low in risk-form folks against other forms. Net probes flag a small RNA and three switch parts as may-be drivers of that drop. The team calls it a first India report of this path.
pmc-12749039:
Ping Yuan and colleagues solve the structures of T cells gripping two favorite targets on the coronavirus nucleocapsid, in this study from twenty twenty-five. The nucleocapsid mutates far less than spike, making it a tempting vaccine target. Yet the T cell response to one short fragment is strangely uniform, cloned from near-identical receptors, while the response to another is a crowd.

Crystallography explained the temperaments. The uniform fragment's shape admits essentially one receptor solution, forcing heavy use of a single gene segment. The crowd-pleaser fragment accepts several distinct docking geometries, so many receptor families can answer. The team also benchmarked AlphaFold's predictions against the real structures, finding promise and clear headroom. The work guides vaccine designers choosing fragments that recruit broad, variant-proof T cell armies.
pmc-12751739:
Vildan Kocatepe, Dilek Yildirim, and Ayşegül Türkmenoğlu published a nursing study in two thousand twenty-five on job safety for nurses. The nurses worked in internal medicine clinics at a hospital in İzmir. The team asked how safe the nurses felt and which workplace factors shaped that view.

Three hundred nurses filled in a standard safety scale and a background form. Over half had either not read the national safety rules for health workers or did not know them. Nurses rated safety as only middling overall. Three factors stood out as shaping the scores: the design and gear of the work area, the quality of protective equipment, and the tools in daily use. The authors urge better training and better equipment.
pmc-12771039:
Takuya Takata and seven co-authors build a scoring system that grades arthritic joint damage from three-dimensional scans instead of tissue slices. Histology, the traditional yardstick in rat osteoarthritis studies, is slow and two-dimensional. Micro-CT gives full 3D joint views but historically scores cartilage poorly.

Arthritis was induced in twenty-four rats' knees with varying doses of a chemical irritant. After twenty-eight days the joints were scanned, divided into ten compartments, and each scored zero to four for degeneration. Two observers agreed excellently on most compartments, and the scan scores were checked against standard histology scores from the same joints. The authors offer the system as a reproducible, less destructive way to grade preclinical joint damage.
pmc-12771139:
Jing Di, Yijia Zhou, and Jingjing Hu reviewed in two thousand twenty-five how molecular science is reshaping care for thymic neuroendocrine tumors. These rare tumors of the chest gland vary widely, and doctors long sorted them mainly by appearance under the microscope. New gene and chromosome studies now offer a sharper sorting.

Recurring changes in a few key genes, plus a chromosome-instability grouping, refine risk estimates and link these tumors to similar cancers elsewhere. Certain drugs show promise, while a radiation-based therapy works less well here. The authors propose blending appearance with molecular type. Oncologists gain a framework for more precise treatment choices.
pmc-12784739:
Dorit Albertsen, Peter Plate, and Suzanne Held assess natural weaning on a suckler beef farm. Their retrospective study from twenty twenty-five covers seven years on one English farm. Farms usually separate calves from mothers at a few months old. Early separation stresses both animals and can harm calf health.

The farm phased out separation herd by herd over time. Yearling calves stayed with their mothers past the next calving. Records tracked whether new calves survived to one year. Colostrum antibody uptake in new calves was also examined. Herds with yearlings present were compared against those without. Chalk downland herds supply the setting. The study tests a gentler weaning model at farm scale.
pmc-12787039:
Carlos Novillo-Sarmiento and seven co-authors present a review from twenty twenty-five that casts phosphate as a driver of harm in kidney disease, not just a marker. Long phosphate overload sparks rust like stress in vessels and organs. The team names the whole picture Phosphatopathy. Its marks are inflammation, vessel crusting, worn cells, and skewed metabolism.

Paths in play run from oxidant bursts to growth signals and a broken hormone axis. A ratio of phosphate to urea nitrogen in urine may flag load more well than blood phosphate. Care ideas span food cuts on added phosphate, binders with no calcium, and mineral add-ons. Boosting the cell's own guard paths is a further aim.
pmc-12818339:
Kanimozhiy Senguttuvan and colleagues reported a rare jaw cyst case in two thousand twenty-five. The patient was a teenage girl with swelling near her jaw angle. Routine dental X-rays revealed pale areas in both jaws. The lesions were an uncommon developmental cyst type. Such cysts were once lumped with a different, riskier type. Experts now class them separately.

Surgeons removed the lesions completely. Tissue study confirmed the diagnosis afterward. Multiple cysts of this type are especially rare. The report reviews earlier published cases too. Dentists gain a reminder to check both jaws. Quiet lesions can hide behind one visible swelling.
pmc-12820139:
Liu and four co-authors studied in twenty twenty-five how to hold back ground stress in a deep gold mine under the sea. Deep digs there face high stress that can harm rock and put staff at risk. They test a new control mode with a scale model and with computer runs.

In the scale test, strain at watch points stayed near a tiny set level as dig went on. The strain trend matched the computer runs, which backs the scale test. A real dig trial at the mine then used the mode in the field. It held the high stress in check well, the team reports.
pmc-12820239:
Uma Venkatesan and Rajiniraja Muniyan test leaf fractions of Acalypha indica, a common weed, against foodborne germs in the lab and on the computer. Extracts were made with three solvents: petroleum ether, chloroform, and ethanol. The ethanol extract won on both fronts. It showed the strongest antioxidant power in two standard assays. It also made the widest kill zones, 24 millimeters against Staphylococcus aureus and 29.3 millimeters against Escherichia coli.

Chemical profiling found eleven main plant compounds in the extract. On the computer, these were docked against key enzymes of the two germs. Two compounds bound most tightly. Those two went on to dynamic simulations to check that the pairing stays stable. The authors used response surface methods to tune the extraction for antioxidant yield. A full lab-plus-computer screen like this is how candidate plant drugs earn a closer look.
pmc-12825239:
Luo and nine co-authors mapped sugar and acid metabolism in ripening Prunus mume fruit in twenty twenty-five. This plum relative is eaten and used in medicine, and its taste hinges on sugars and organic acids. How those compounds build up during ripening was unclear.

Across four ripening stages, sucrose proved the main sugar and citrate the main acid. The hormone ABA rose alongside both. Gene activity data named candidate genes: some switched on to build sucrose and citrate, others switched off to stop breaking them down. Lab assays confirmed one citrate gene makes a working enzyme. Hundreds of regulators and transporters also tracked the compounds. A factor called AP2 emerged as a core regulator, with ABA as the central switch.
pmc-12831939:
Nimra Nabi and colleagues pool the epidemiology on breathing fine particles for years and developing cardiovascular disease, in this meta-analysis from twenty twenty-five. Four studies survived their screening. Long-term exposure to PM2.5, the soot fraction that reaches deep lung and bloodstream, was tied to overall cardiovascular disease with a pooled hazard ratio of about one point two.

The finer outcomes were murkier. Cardiovascular death showed no association, and heart disease and stroke estimates pointed upward without reaching significance, all with wide intervals and heavy between-study disagreement. The authors read the pattern as supportive but unsettled, and use it to argue for stricter air quality standards and better integrated studies. Their candor about the thin evidence base, four studies for a global exposure, is itself a finding.
pmc-12842739:
Flavius-Alexandru Gherasie and four co-authors set drug balls gainst drug stents in heart artery care. Their tale review appeared in twenty twenty-five. Drug balls lay cure drugs in the wall and leave no frame behind. The pair of ball kinds and stents are set side by side in fresh wounds, in sharp chest ills, and in re-tight stents.

In fresh small wounds and high bleed risk, ball cures match stents in most trials. In sharp ills, ball-only runs are fit for picked wounds. For re-tight stents, one ball kind is a top class cure. New ball tech aims to fix drug pass flaws of the first kinds.
pmc-12848839:
Senthilvelan Thenmozhi and Subramanian Girija compared diabetes tests in two thousand twenty-five. Their patients faced elevated diabetes risk already. The glucose drink test is valuable but underused. Blood was drawn fasting, at one hour, and at two hours. Standard markers like HbA1c were compared too. The study ran at a South Indian hospital.

The one-hour reading classified far more people as diabetic. Fasting measures labeled most as merely prediabetic. HbA1c fell between those extremes. Many participants were overweight or obese. Early detection matters most in such at-risk groups. A shorter test could catch hidden diabetes sooner. Clinics might adopt the one-hour checkpoint widely.
pmc-12849639:
Xiao Chen and five colleagues published a brain imaging study in two thousand twenty-five on rumination, the repetitive dwelling on negative thoughts. Rumination feeds depression's onset and return. Past work mostly scanned resting brains or relied on self-report, missing the active state.

Forty-three depressed patients and forty-two matched controls underwent scans while a task induced rumination or distraction. Both groups strengthened links inside the default mode network while ruminating. Controls additionally boosted attention network links, which patients lacked. One attention hub grew more central in patients only, scaling with symptom severity. The authors describe a shared core circuit plus a patient-specific attention twist.
pmc-12854339:
Aruna Jothishanmugam published a survey study in two thousand twenty-five on nursing students' knowledge of palliative care. Palliative care improves life quality in serious illness, and nurses deliver much of it. Student gaps can persist into practice.

One hundred thirty-seven senior students and interns completed a standard palliative care quiz. The average score was about ten of fifteen. Pain and symptom knowledge was strong; psychosocial and spiritual care knowledge was near zero. Most students landed in the satisfactory band, yet wrong ideas about family presence and opioid use were common. Attending any palliative course lifted scores significantly. Year of study alone did not predict knowledge. The author urges curriculum repair in the weak domains.
pmc-12859939:
Jingjing Wang and colleagues build a virus-like particle showing a conserved piece of Akabane virus, for both vaccine and testing uses. Akabane virus causes costly disease in ruminants, with outbreaks of abortion and birth defects. Vaccines are the main defense, but safer, more stable, epitope-based vaccines remain untested. The group's prior work found a neutralizing epitope on the viral Gc protein, kept across genotypes.

They put that epitope into a hepatitis B core antigen scaffold, making a chimeric particle. Construction was checked by gel electrophoresis, antibody blotting, and electron microscopy. The team tested mice for antibodies against the Gc antigen and how well they neutralized the virus. Based on the particle, the team also built a first indirect ELISA for finding Akabane virus antibodies. A conserved epitope is the ideal target, and the same particle doubles as test bait.
pmc-12864639:
Vaishnavi Rajurkar and four co-authors describe an unusual cancer case in this two thousand twenty-five report. A seventy-two-year-old man developed swollen lymph nodes on both sides of his neck and in his groin. He had none of the classic warning symptoms, such as fever or weight loss. Early scans and exams pointed toward infection or spread from another cancer. The true cause turned out to be Hodgkin lymphoma.

A surgical biopsy of the nodes showed the telltale Reed-Sternberg cells of this lymphoma. Marker tests backed the diagnosis. Staging placed him at an advanced stage, and he moved to cancer care for chemotherapy. The authors stress that lasting swollen nodes deserve a biopsy, even in regions where tuberculosis is common. Delay can let a hidden lymphoma advance.
pmc-12872839:
Yuxuan Gu and colleagues report a teenage girl with two rare conditions at once: spinal muscular atrophy and IgA nephropathy. The first is an inherited disorder of nerves and muscles, from loss-of-function variants in the survival motor neuron gene. The disease may also hit kidney function.

The girl was fourteen, with six months of limb weakness, worse in the left lower limb. Her knee and ankle reflexes were absent. Gene tests confirmed spinal muscular atrophy type three. She also had protein and blood in her urine, and a kidney biopsy was done. From her clinical and tissue traits, the final call was both diseases at once. pmc-12876239: Tran Cong Duy Long and eight co-authors published a position paper in twenty twenty-six on split liver transplantation. One donated liver can serve both a child and an adult. pmc-13174139:

pmc-13185039:

pmc-13189939:

pmc-13198039:

pmc-13198639:

pmc-13200539:

pmc-13202139:

pmc-13202439:

pmc-13202639:

pmc-13203939:

pmc-13215439:

pmc-13234739:

pmc-13266239:

pmc-13266839:

pmc-13267039:

pmc-13267539:

pmc-13267939:
Maojiang Lyu and colleagues present a 2026 case report on rebuilding a teenager's thigh bone after infection. Their patient was a 14-year-old girl whose right thigh bone broke in a car crash. pmc-13268139:

pmc-13268639:

pmc-13269039:

pmc-13269839:

pmc-13270339:

pmc-13271139:

The authors say trained patients' home readings, in both positions, are reliable for clinical decisions.
pmc-13271439:
Sneha Vidyasagar is lead author of a 2026 retrospective study of calcitonin, a hormone drug, as an extra treatment for phantom limb pain after lower leg amputation. Phantom pain, felt in a limb that is no longer there, is hard to treat, so the team reviewed records of patients given at least three days of calcitonin.

From the day before treatment to day seven, average pain intensity fell from 6.41 to 5.24, pain distress fell from 5.85 to 4.81, and reported relief rose. pmc-13271539:
Srinivasan Sanjay writes in 2026 a critical letter about a study of steroid injections for a tuberculosis-linked eye inflammation called serpiginous-like choroiditis. pmc-13271939:
Fangling Zhong and coauthors report in 2026 a case where gout deposits inside the spine combined with a hardened ligament to squeeze the spinal cord. pmc-13272139:
Jieqiong Zeng and coauthors investigate in 2026 an enzyme called heme oxygenase-1 in the immune cells of children with acute Kawasaki disease. A mouse model of the disease, including a version treated with an enzyme blocker, let the team test how the pathway affects heart artery inflammation.
pmc-13272239:

pmc-13272439:

The formulations proved non-toxic to the gut cells in testing.
pmc-13272739:

Tested on three public datasets, the model reached high accuracy across emotion tasks, above ninety percent in each reported test. The authors present it as a strong option for emotion aware computing.
pmc-13273239:

pmc-13273439:

pmc-13273639:

pmc-13273739:

Education, they argue, is the lever that moves practice.
pmc-13273839:

pmc-13274039:

pmc-13274139:

pmc-13275339:

pmc-13275439:

pmc-13275539:

pmc-13275739:

pmc-13276339:

pmc-13276539:

pmc-13276839:

pmc-13276939:

pmc-13278239:

pmc-13279439:

pmc-13279739:

pmc-13279939:

pmc-13280639:

pmc-13280939:

pmc-13281639:

pmc-13282039:

pmc-13282339:

pmc-13282439:

pmc-13282939:

pmc-13283139:

pmc-13283439:

pmc-13284039:
