Gene maps showed stimulation tuned inflammation and pain pathways both ways. Marker-guided, self-adjusting stimulation could make pain care more precise.
pmc-13336939:
Debarani Devi Khumujam and co-authors grow a self-rebuilding catalyst for zinc-air batteries in a 2026 study. Air cathodes need many active sites and fast, reversible oxygen chemistry. The catalyst beat platinum for oxygen intake and iridium oxide for oxygen release, lasting over 5000 cycles in stability tests. pmc-13337839:
Kunfu Wang and a large team build a solar edge AI system for rice pests in a 2026 study. Fast pest control cuts crop losses and chemical use, yet watching large fields by hand is hard. Their prototype spots pests, triggers a trap, and links multiple field nodes.

Training used 1,500 field images of 12 rice pests from paddies in Fujian, China. Lab loop tests and simulated placement in split paddies tested cost and coverage. Early outdoor checks add a first look at performance under real weather and light.
pmc-13338239:
Yuxi Chen and a large team study prostate symptoms, aging complaints, and partner support in a 2026 survey. Enlarged prostate is common after age 50 and overlaps with body, mood, and sexual complaints of aging. A responsive partner might soften that burden, attachment theory suggests.

A total of 412 men aged 50 or older with confirmed enlargement completed symptom and partner scales. Worse prostate symptoms tracked with worse aging complaints in the reported models. Partner responsiveness rose with prostate severity only in the severe group and did not carry the link for moderate cases. Support alone therefore does not explain how prostate burden becomes broader aging strain.
pmc-13338639:
Hayne Cho Park reviewed in 2026 how kidney salt handling controls blood pressure, using rare genetic disorders as natural experiments. Bartter, Gitelman, Liddle, and Gordon syndromes each illustrate a different break in the chain.

Salt wasting disorders show low or normal pressure despite activation of the renin angiotensin system, proving that tubule sodium loss can dominate. Gain of function defects that boost distal sodium uptake raise pressure instead. The review links molecular channels to whole body pressure control and to drug targets for common hypertension.
pmc-13339239:
M. Cassandra Witt and co-authors trace energy sources for surgical treatment of atrial fibrillation in a 2026 review. Bipolar radiofrequency and freezing remain the proven standard with decades of results as reviewed. Both carry heat-related limits and technical demands. Pulsed-field energy, which kills heart cells by electric pulses while sparing neighbors, is the rising option. Early lab and catheter data show fast, deep lesions, setting up surgical adoption questions.
pmc-13339639:
Jayabrata Das and a large team release a dataset of more than 50,000 carbon-nitrogen coupling reactions in a 2026 study. pmc-13339739: Huawen Song and Yanping Liu published a 2026 correction touching only the ethics note of their nursing intern survey on stress and leave-taking. The approval details were wrong as printed. The correct number is E20260410001. It comes from Linfen People's Hospital. Voluntary consent wording stands as restated. All findings stand unchanged.
pmc-13340939:

pmc-13341339:
Jennifer A Pallin and colleagues tracked avoidable hospital stays in 2026 among people with diabetes in Ireland from 2015 to 2024. The decade long picture helps Irish health planners target prevention where stays are rising fastest across the country.
pmc-13341439:
Returning to work after major stroke is the outcome a 2026 nomogram study by Yu Ding's team tries to predict. The cohort covered 350 younger and middle-aged patients with large vessel occlusion treated by endovascular therapy at a Dongguan hospital between July 2018 and July 2025.

pmc-13342139:
Yusuke Yoshida and colleagues tested folic acid doses in 2026 for methotrexate toxicity in rheumatic disease patients. pmc-13344239:

It took in ultrasound exams during 2022 with singleton fetuses, gestational age 24 weeks 0 days to 39 weeks 6 days, biometry measured, and fetal cardiac activity present. They were mean z score near zero, standard deviation of z near one, Kolmogorov Smirnov D statistic near zero, plus close percentile agreement. pmc-13345839:
Tahani H. Alqahtani, Nahed Ahmed Bajenied, and Nawaf H. Alqahtani test classic motivation theory inside Saudi Arabia's public sector in 2026. pmc-13347339:

pmc-13347639:

pmc-13348339:

pmc-13349839:

pmc-13350739:

pmc-13351139:

pmc-13351339:

pmc-13352639:

pmc-13355139:

pmc-13355339:

pmc-13355439:

pmc-13355839:

pmc-13358539:

pmc-13358639:

pmc-13358739:

pmc-13360239:

pmc-13360939:

pmc-13361639:

Four therapy classes were compared, including two modern ones known for heart benefits. Patients without diabetes served as a reference group. pmc-13362039:
Carlo Tremolada and Giulio Alessandri review micro-fragmented fat tissue as a living implant in a 2026 paper. Fat tissue has moved from simple filler to a tool for regeneration. pmc-13363539:

pmc-13365239:

pmc-13369739:

pmc-13370239:

pmc-13370739:

pmc-13371239:

pmc-13371939:

pmc-13374139:

pmc-13374239:

pmc-13374339:
Elinor Coulman and co-authors tested two ways to run a parent course in a 2026 trial. The course, for mums and dads of kids up to age 12, moved to video calls in the virus years. Past proof on video runs next to room runs was thin and mixed.

pmc-13375839:
Aceves-Bueno and colleagues argue that marine conservation thinks too much about space and too little about time, in a 2026 perspective on fisheries closures. pmc-13377339:

pmc-13378039:

It links joined-up leadership, standard pathways, and strong information systems with better use of donated organs and fairer access. Workforce planning and patient-centred practices are also covered. The aim is to help hospitals improve both efficiency and patient outcomes.
pmc-13378239:

Those droplets hold the enzymes in place while letting raw materials reach them and pass between steps. By adjusting the mix of particles, the conditions inside can be tuned for each enzyme chain. The approach was shown with enzymes of interest for making medicines.
pmc-13378339:

pmc-13382239:

pmc-13382439:

pmc-13383439:

pmc-13385139:

pmc-13386939:

pmc-13387739:

pmc-13389439:

pmc-13392439:

pmc-13395439:

pmc-13395839:

pmc-13396239:

pmc-13396739:

pmc-13397639:

pmc-13398639:

pmc-13398739:

pmc-13398839:

pmc-13402939:

pmc-13403639:

pmc-13427439:

pmc-13431239:

pmc-13432439:

pmc-13432839:

pmc-13435439:

The reviewers searched four databases in February 2025 for randomized trials in older adults. Fourteen studies qualified for the review. Balance outcomes ranged from standing tests to full assessment scales, while mobility covered walking speed alone, walking while thinking, and a standard stand and walk test. Study quality was scored with a physiotherapy scale, and evidence strength was graded outcome by outcome. Combined analyses were run where at least three comparable studies existed.
pmc-13470239:
Matheus Santos de Sousa Fernandes tested a play-rich setting in 2026 on lymph node redox and immune balance in healthy adult male mice. Play-rich life, with thinking, sensory, social, and motor play, protects brains, yet its effect on resting lymph node energy use was unclear. Mice lived six weeks in play-rich or standard housing before lymph node and blood tests.

Play-rich life kept energy-cell content while raising both NAD+ and NADH with ratio the same, cut lipid damage, and boosted catalase plus glutathione guards. Most blood signals held steady except IFN-gamma, which fell. Play-rich life thus built a redox-tuned, tough lymph node without broad immune firing or shut-down, a base for disease studies.
pmc-13470939:
Nayereh Baghcheghi and Hamid Reza Koohestani mapped research in 2026 on web overuse and school grades among health sciences students. Evidence on number-based grades was mixed and split, despite rising student reliance on the web. Using Arksey and O'Malley plus PRISMA-ScR methods, the review screened 1,325 records to November 2025 and kept 15 studies.

Web overuse rate ranged from 6% to 84%, with a mostly sideways link to grades through surface learning, school burnout, low mood, anxiety, and body health effects. Risk factors held Type D trait, phone juggling, and bad school times. Long-term and action studies are needed to clarify results and test blocking plans.
pmc-13471539:
Wang and co-authors engineered a nanoparticle that releases its chemotherapy cargo only in the acidic surroundings of a tumor, aiming at drug-resistant esophageal cancer. Their 2026 study built the platform from iron-doped carbon dots carrying doxorubicin plus glucose oxidase, an enzyme that starves and acidifies tumor cells, and tested it in resistant cells and mouse tumors.

The release switch worked sharply: at pH 6.5, mimicking tumor acidity, 60.4% of the doxorubicin escaped, against only 22.7% released at normal body pH of 7.4 in the same tests. Drug loading reached 21.5% for the carbon dots' partner cargo and 16.1% for doxorubicin by weight. The particles also dimmed HIF-1α, a resistance driver unusually high in the squamous type behind over 90% of cases.
pmc-13472039:
Bringhenti and coauthors test how milling speed affects zirconia crown quality. Computer milling steps can change the final fit of ceramic crowns. Fit at edges and bite surface both matter for crown life. The team made crowns with three milling protocols.

Thirty-nine crowns split evenly into slow, normal, and fast groups. A replica method gauged gap thickness under each crown. Edge quality was scored on a severity scale. Bite quality was checked by scope and by size measures. Math tests compared gaps across the three speeds. Results show which speed best balances fit and time.
pmc-13472139:
Keita Ishii and four colleagues reported in 2026 on a rare second lymphoma that appeared seventeen years after a first one. A 67-year-old man had been treated for Epstein-Barr virus positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and stayed in remission after six cycles of R-CHOP chemotherapy. Seventeen years later he developed plasmablastic lymphoma, an aggressive B-cell cancer tied to immune weakness and the same virus, with tumour cells again testing positive for it.

After three cycles of EPOCH chemotherapy brought a partial response, he received his own stem cells in a transplant and reached full remission. Gene sequencing of both tumours found a dominant clone in the later cancer and a small, similar, apparently non-working clone in the earlier sample. The case suggests the second cancer grew from a minor cell line that had quietly persisted. Gene analysis can clarify whether two lymphomas are related.
pmc-13472839:
Zhang and colleagues surveyed hospital environments in Shanghai in 2026 for Acinetobacter baumannii, a germ that causes hard-to-treat infections, comparing drug-resistant and drug-sensitive strains. They collected 1,812 samples from ten medical sites in Pudong during the second half of 2024 and sequenced the genomes of what they found.

They detected 81 strains, and about forty percent resisted carbapenem antibiotics, a last-line drug class. Resistant strains clustered in intensive care units, which supplied over eighty percent of them, and often sat on items patients touch. One clone, ST2, dominated the resistant group, and nearly all resistant strains carried the same resistance gene. Sensitive strains stayed vulnerable to almost every drug tested. The authors urge targeted disinfection and clone tracking in intensive care.
pmc-13472939:
Kaplan and co-authors report SYNCHRONIZE-MASLD, a phase 3 trial of survodutide, a weekly injection hitting two hormone receptors, in adults with obesity and fatty liver disease at risk of progression. Their 2026 randomized study assigned 216 adults, 146 to survodutide 6.0 mg and 70 to placebo, for 48 weeks with liver fat measured by MRI.

Both co-primary endpoints were met. A liver fat cut of at least 30% was achieved by 84.2% of survodutide patients versus 24.3% on placebo in the efficacy analysis, and mean body weight fell 12.2% on the drug against 1.0% on placebo over the trial. The cohort's liver disease was mostly defined by noninvasive tests rather than biopsy, which the authors argue mirrors real clinic populations.
pmc-13473039:
Liu and co-authors built a risk score for Wilms tumor, the commonest childhood kidney cancer, from genes involved in programmed cell death. Their 2026 study mined a national tumor database, screened twelve cell-death patterns, and used machine learning to distill a four-gene model, then checked it against clinical data and single-cell sequencing.

The score split children into high- and low-risk groups with clearly different outlooks: prediction accuracy reached an AUC of 0.820 at one year, 0.721 at three years, and 0.728 at five years in the full cohort. Immune infiltration and drug sensitivity profiles also differed by risk group, hinting at tailored therapy. Overall Wilms survival now exceeds 90% with modern treatment, but the worst subgroups still fall to 30 to 85% at four years.
pmc-13473139:
Zhonghe Li and twelve colleagues surveyed high blood pressure in 2026 among adults in selected townships of Lingcheng District in Dezhou, China. Rates of hypertension keep rising in China, yet awareness, treatment, and control in rural townships remain uncertain. From May to July 2024, trained staff measured blood pressure in 11,600 residents across seven community health centres, after a standard rest. A validated automatic monitor was used, under the 2024 Chinese guideline definitions.

The age-adjusted prevalence reached 32.2 percent, with a further 30.9 percent in the borderline high range. Among people with hypertension, 57.4 percent knew they had it, 50.0 percent were treated, and 38.0 percent had it controlled. Under the stricter 2025 American guideline threshold, prevalence jumped to 57.3 percent and control fell to 14.7 percent. The survey shows real progress at the grassroots, but control still lags far behind what guidelines aim for.
pmc-13473239:
Hill and co-authors pooled the world's data on auto-antibodies against interferons, the immune system's own antiviral alarms, across infectious diseases. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis covered 37 studies including 12,629 people with SARS-CoV-2 infection, the only disease with enough data to pool.

Among COVID-19 patients, pooled seroprevalence of antibodies against interferon alpha or omega was 14% across studies, and the neutralizing subset, the kind that actually blocks the alarm, pooled at 12% of patients. Healthy uninfected controls sat below 1% for the same antibodies, sharpening the contrast. For other infections the crude rates swung from 0.0 to 77.0% between small studies, too scattered to pool, and the authors blame unstandardized testing for much of the noise.
pmc-13473639:
Adrija Ghosh, Purushotam, Chao-Jun Li, and Debasis Banerjee report a nickel-based route in 2026 to build complex carbon chains from plant-derived alcohols. The target shapes, branched olefins and paired double-bond chains, appear in drugs and fine chemicals. Making them with the right twist has long been hard to control. Two different alcohols are joined step by step under ligand-guided nickel action.

The route gave 27 branched olefins with strong control of shape, plus 23 paired-bond chains with even tighter control. Tests with sugar-derived and vitamin-derived alcohols showed the method handles rich starting goods. Labeling studies support a path where the alcohol first loses hydrogen, joins, then regains it. Greener feedstocks could thus feed high-value chemical lines.
pmc-13473939:
Yasufumi Oi and colleagues report a feasibility study, published in 2026, testing group music recreation for people with advanced Parkinson's disease living in care facilities. Voice weakness and swallowing problems are common at this stage, yet rehabilitation evidence for institutionalised patients is scarce, so the team added music sessions to ongoing speech-language therapy.

Twenty-five of thirty-two enrolled patients completed enough of the twelve sessions and both assessments. Voice endurance and a water swallowing test showed small nominal improvements before correction for multiple testing, after which nothing stayed statistically significant. The authors conclude the programme is feasible and worth testing properly in a controlled trial.
pmc-13474839:
Eunsol Seo and co-authors probe gut microbes in newborn breathing distress in 2026, a common problem in late preterm and term babies. Two cohorts were enrolled, one watched in clinic and one used to hunt helpful strains. Stool from the first two days of life was read with gene sequencing. Groups split by whether breathing help with surfactant was given.

Babies with distress who lacked surfactant care showed loss of helpful gut types and growth of risky ones. After surfactant care, gut profiles shifted partway back toward healthy patterns. Candidate helpful strains were grown and tested in a lab gut model and in mice. A tailored probiotic path is argued as plausible, pending trials.
pmc-13476239:
Kai Zhao and co-authors build a network in 2026 to split farm point clouds into single plants. Point clouds from field scans tangle together in dense plantings, which blocks per-plant measures. The method first orders points along a space-filling curve that keeps neighbors close. A state-space model then reads the long ordered line at low cost.

Local patch features and wider graph context feed the sequence model together. Three tasks train at once: naming tissue type, separating plants, and centering each plant. On a public crop data set the method beat prior tools on both naming and splitting scores. Per-plant measures can feed yield and health maps.
pmc-13476439:
Zeeshan Saleem Mufti and co-authors test graph math in 2026 for predicting drug traits across unlike drug families. Ten drugs from seven care areas were drawn as graphs, with atoms as nodes and bonds as links. Neighborhood link counts fed three curve styles to predict nine lab-measured traits. Fit quality was judged by how much trait variance the curves explained.

Graph counts captured core structural facts even across very different drugs. Predictions held up for traits from boiling point to surface tension. Past work usually limited such models to one drug family at a time. Broad-scope graph models could screen new compounds faster.
pmc-13476639:
Brunelli and colleagues studied the pulsatility index in 2026. That index is a Doppler ultrasound measure of resistance in brain blood vessels, and the team asked whether it predicts thinking recovery after a transient ischemic attack or mild stroke. Their cohort included 113 patients, whose blood flow and cognition were tracked over follow-up with standard tests.

Cognitive scores improved over time, with the largest gains on the MoCA screening test appearing during follow-up. A higher pulsatility index at baseline predicted poorer cognitive performance later, while lower vessel resistance pointed the other way. Less severe strokes and better starting cognition also favored recovery. The authors propose the index, split at a threshold used in earlier work, as a simple prognostic marker to guide rehabilitation planning after minor stroke events.
pmc-13478339:
Yan Xu and colleagues present a 2026 mechanistic study of PLOD3, a collagen-processing enzyme, in kidney cancer. Kidney tumors grow in oxygen-poor conditions that fuel aggressive behavior. Screening across several models flagged this enzyme as a major growth driver, and tests confirmed it boosted tumor growth and spread in cells and animals.

Two forces raised enzyme levels: the oxygen sensor HIF-2α and a lactate-based chemical mark on histones. The enzyme then bound a cellular tagging protein called NEDD4 and released its self-block, switching on its protein-destruction activity. That activity destroyed GOT2, an enzyme in glutamine metabolism, rewiring how tumor cells use fuel. The authors map the full chain as a candidate drug target and biomarker source for kidney cancer.
pmc-13478639:
Slawinski and colleagues pooled individual data from four randomized trials in 2026 to untangle how body weight affects colon and rectal cancer survival after chemotherapy. The OCTOPUS analysis covered 7,264 patients with non-spread cancer and traced causal paths from body mass index through dose reductions and toxicity to survival. Doses are often capped in heavier patients out of caution, which may quietly underdose them.

Each five-point rise in body mass index came with a 1.15 percent cut in the average cumulative relative dose patients actually received across the trials. Every five percent more dose, in turn, linked to better survival, at a hazard ratio of 0.94, yet the indirect harm was too small to make weight itself predict worse survival overall. Toxicity did predict worse survival, at a hazard ratio of 1.37, partly because it forced dose cuts of about ten percent.
pmc-13479439:
Imene Mattat and colleagues report a 2026 genome-wide methylation study of date palms grown by tissue culture in Qatar. Cloning palms in the lab produces large numbers of plants, yet some offspring drift from the parent variety through chemical marks on DNA rather than DNA changes. The team compared two major cultivars, Khalas and Kheneizi, against controls grown from offshoots.

Whole genome bisulfite sequencing, the reference method for methylation mapping, found thousands of regions where culture-grown plants differed. Khalas leaned toward losing methylation, while Kheneizi gained slightly more than it lost. One sequence context tended to lose marks while another gained them across both cultivars. Genes overlapping the changed regions were catalogued, giving growers molecular leads for spotting off-type plants early.
pmc-13479739:
ChunZhu Xue and colleagues report a 2026 study comparing two small-cut ways to repair large holes between the heart's upper chambers in adults. Tube-based closure is not always possible, so surgical options with smaller scars matter. Seventy-nine adults operated between 2020 and 2024 were split between a lower mini breastbone incision and a straight incision under the right arm.

All repairs worked, with no deaths, switch-overs to full incisions, redo operations, major leftover shunts, strokes, or low-output problems in either group. Surgery time, bypass time, blood given, breathing tube time, intensive care stay, pain scores, problems, and costs were set side by side. Three-month results round out the picture. The head-to-head helps surgical teams match incision choice to what patients value most, such as pain and looks.
pmc-13479839:
Jaslyn Doshi and coauthors published a 2026 before-and-after study of drug-resistant bacteria carriage in Vietnamese district hospitals around an antimicrobial stewardship program. Southeast Asia is a resistance hotspot, and district hospitals are rarely studied. Four hospitals took part, two urban in Hanoi and two rural in Ca Mau province.

Swabs from patients' noses and digestive tracts were collected in March 2022, just before the six-month stewardship program began, and again in its final two weeks that August. The program bundle included stewardship structures and prescribing support described in the study. Comparing carriage rates across the two surveys tests whether better antibiotic governance can shrink the reservoir of resistant organisms that patients carry silently into and out of hospital.
pmc-13480839:
Mrinal Naskar and co-authors report a 2026 first ranking of how strongly each alcohol group on a sugar offers hydrogen bonds. Sugars bristle with such groups, and their bonding drives how proteins grip sugars and how sugars dissolve, yet group-by-group strengths stayed unmapped. The team built clean model sugars that block teamwork between groups and read bonding strength with infrared light on a scale used in drug design.

Strength swung widely across positions, most sharply for galactose. One glucose group and the galactose tail group led the table, while two other positions trailed. Shape at far-away positions mattered too, which surprised the team. Only the galactose tail group beat a plain ring alcohol. Magnetic scans and modelling tied the order to tugs between electron pull and internal bonds. Drug designers can now weigh sugar groups one by one.
pmc-13482539:
Warkaa Shamkhani and co-authors offer a 2026 framework essay on planning aortic valve care across a whole lifetime, not a single procedure. Catheter valve replacement now often serves as the first valve in patients who may live decades more. The authors argue that the scan taken before the first procedure should guide the opening choice itself, weighing whether a catheter-first path keeps future options open.

Later needs may include reaching the heart arteries again, nesting a second catheter valve, or falling back on surgery. Trials proved early safety across risk levels yet never tested whether the first choice preserves those later doors, and younger patients sat thin in the trial pools. Five-year data already hint at gaps the early trials could not see. Heart teams get a thinking frame, openly not a tested algorithm, for first-valve choices.
pmc-13482639:
Alem Gebremariam and colleagues studied in 2026 leisure-time physical activity and cancer odds in adults with and without cardiometabolic disease. Most activity research covers general populations, leaving the preventive value for adults with heart disease or type 2 diabetes unclear.

Pooling individual data on 598,890 adults aged 35 to 70 from EPIC and UK Biobank, with a median follow-up of 11 years, they tracked a composite of 15 activity-related cancers. Each standard-deviation rise in non-occupational activity tied to lower cancer risk, with hazard ratios of 0.96 without cardiometabolic disease and 0.93 with it. The benefit thus looks equal in both groups, supporting activity guidance for adults with chronic disease too.
pmc-13483739:
Neçirvan Çağdaş Çaltek asks what traits warn of grave harm after big surgery for late-stage ovarian cancer. The 2026 review covers 180 women with stage III or IV disease at one major hospital from May 2020 to late 2024. Grave harm means the worst tier of surgical side effects. Late start of drug care, past 42 days, and length of life are also tracked.

Twenty women, or 11.1 percent, had grave harm after surgery. Bowel surgery and blood top-ups near the time of surgery were both more common in that group. When traits were weighed at once, blood top-ups near surgery were the one clear risk. Links with late drug care and length of life are split by surgery timing in the full text. Teams can use the flag to guard high-risk patients more closely.
pmc-13483839:
Yemane Leake explores what helps and what hinders training child specialists at a teaching hospital in northern Ethiopia. Published in 2026, the descriptive qualitative study interviews all ten first- and second-year pediatric residents at Aksum University hospital in May 2025. An implementation framework organizes the barriers and supports, and a priority matrix turns findings into action steps.

Top-ranked barriers were the lack of a children's intensive care unit and thin diagnostic resources, with further gaps detailed across workplace, program design, and team domains. Residents also named real supports already present in the young post-conflict program. New residency programs in similar settings can use the prioritized list to sequence investments, since fixing everything at once is rarely possible and some gaps block learning more than others.
pmc-13486439:
Michael Acquadro and colleagues interview patients with relentless itching that has no found cause, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The condition, chronic pruritus of unknown origin, is defined by the absence of a skin, body, nerve, or mind explanation. No one had mapped the illness from the patient's side.

Twenty American adults described their signs and daily burdens in long interviews. All had itch, and most named it the worst symptom; raw skin, stinging, burning, and dry rough skin were common too. Day-to-day activities, work, and above all sleep took the hit, with sleep named the worst-hit domain by most. The team folded the findings into a patient-centered model of the disease, linking symptoms to their life effects. They offer it to guide doctors' decisions and to help trial designers pick endpoints that matter to patients.
pmc-13486739:
Junyu Zhang surveys anesthesia staff in Shanghai on crisis teamwork skills. Crisis resource management is the team craft used when surgery goes wrong. This 2026 survey drew 407 valid forms in late 2024. Most staff came from big public hospitals, and most worked in operating rooms. Forms scored how well staff felt they knew the craft, how they viewed it, and how often they used it.

Mean scores for self-rated grasp sat in the mid range. Views of the craft ran warm, and staff said they used it often. A path model links the three scores. Grasp fed both views and use, and views fed use as well. Part of the grasp effect reached use through views. Drill plans should thus shape views, not just teach facts.
pmc-13487339:
Jad Hosri compares two common ear ventilation tubes for children with middle ear disease and finds a lopsided complication pattern. Published in 2026, the retrospective review covers 138 children aged six months to seven years treated at a tertiary center in 2022 and 2023. Records span 268 ears, with 181 receiving fluoroplastic collar button tubes and 87 receiving titanium bobbin tubes.

By the third follow-up visit at roughly seven and a half months, overall complications reached 44.4 percent in titanium ears versus 5.6 percent in fluoroplastic ears. Drainage ran the other way, appearing more often with fluoroplastic tubes at every visit. Clogging, tissue overgrowth, early expulsion, and eardrum perforation fill out the comparison in the full report. Tube model choice trades one problem profile for another, which families deserve to hear before surgery.
pmc-13490739:
Ye Won Jeon and others report two cases of severe chyle leakage after pancreas surgery that resisted all non-operative treatment. In 2026, the case report covers a sixty-six-year-old woman after pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy with vein resection and a sixty-seven-year-old woman after total pancreatectomy. Both suffered persistent, high-output leakage despite conservative care and several programs.

Both women were finally cured by exploratory surgery with multiple lymphatic ligations after before surgery fat loading, which makes leaking channels visible. The authors argue that timely operation can prevent poor feeding and preserve the chance for further cancer therapy. Surgeons facing refractory grade C leaks get a detailed salvage pathway.
pmc-13491439:
Kelsey C Haist and nine colleagues report a 2026 mouse study of Mycobacterium abscessus, a lung bacterium that healthy lungs usually clear. The organism can linger in damaged airways such as those seen in cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis. The team asked whether immune cells that control infection in the air sacs matter equally when infection sits in blocked small airways.

Mice received the bacteria either in the air sacs or inside agar beads that kept infection in the airways. Flow cytometry, imaging, and tissue sections showed the bead model drew more neutrophils and fewer recruited macrophages. Depleting resident alveolar macrophages left early control of air-sac infection impaired, yet bead infection was unaffected. Airway infection therefore creates a different immune setting, where those resident cells matter less.
pmc-13491639:
Olivia Katz and five colleagues investigate in 2026 how often chromosomes swap segments during egg and sperm formation in two pig breeding lines. These swaps, called crossovers, shuffle genes and create new combinations for selection. The boar line and sow line had different selection histories, so the team compared crossover counts and positions across both.

Genomic data covered more than 47,000 boars and 78,000 sows typed at over 20,000 markers. Sows passed on about one more crossover per litter parent than boars, with average counts near twenty-one versus twenty in the two lines. Mothers transmitted more crossovers than fathers in both lines. Parents with the highest counts placed swaps nearer chromosome centers, a pattern the authors say breeders should weigh before selecting on crossover number.
pmc-13491739:
Shan Lan and Zhibin Wu examine in 2026 seasonal swings in blood pressure among 154 patients on long-term hemodialysis, the blood-cleaning treatment for kidney failure. Pressure readings collected between 2018 and 2021 were compared across seasons and split by sex, age, and original kidney disease. The authors also tracked dangerous pressure spikes and drops during dialysis sessions plus heart and brain events.

Pressure ran lowest in summer and highest in winter for everyone. Older patients and men carried higher readings in every season, and patients over sixty showed seasonal swings nearly twice as wide as the youngest group. Cold months brought more pressure spikes during dialysis, more cardiovascular events, and higher mortality. Adjusting for medicines and fluid removal did not erase the pattern, so the authors urge season-aware management for older men especially.
pmc-13491839:
Yuhan Ma and others optimize a chemically defined growth medium for producing glucokinase, an enzyme used in blood glucose testing, in E. coli. In 2026, the study tackles a trade-off: complex media support growth but vary between batches, while simple minimal media are consistent but limit protein yield. High-throughput respiration and growth screening plus machine-learning-guided trials refine the recipe.

The optimized medium raised soluble glucokinase levels thirty-three-fold over the starting recipe, reaching seventy-four percent of complex-media yield at seventy-four percent lower cost. In a 7.5-litre bioreactor it supported dense growth and a titer above 920 milligrams per litre, far exceeding standard media. The recipe offers a cheaper, reproducible route for this and potentially other high-value enzymes.
pmc-13491939:
Zheng Chen and six colleagues characterize in 2026 a fatty peptide made by a soil bacterium that teaches tomato plants to defend themselves against bacterial wilt. The disease, caused by Ralstonia solanacearum, devastates tomato fields worldwide and resists chemicals. Chemical analysis identified the compound as a family of surfactin variants, some with fatty chains never before reported from this Bacillus species.

In pot trials the peptide delayed symptoms by four days and cut final disease levels by roughly a third. It did not kill the pathogen directly in dishes, so protection must run through the plant itself. Defense enzyme activity spiked within two days of treatment. Combined gene and chemistry profiling showed coordinated rewiring of stress hormones, water channels, and pigment pathways, which the authors present as proof of induced systemic resistance worth field testing.
pmc-13492339:
Duperron and four fellow editors present in 2026 a journal issue on how microbes meet new man made taints in soil and water. The field, microbial ecotoxicology, tracks what such taints do to the smallest life, and what microbes do back. The taints span drug waste, care goods, farm sprays, tiny plastics, and germ proof genes. Many of the works were first aired at a 2024 meet in Gothenburg, Sweden.

The issue holds fourteen fresh studies, two pooled reviews, and one survey. Low dose taints star: most works test faint traces, the load wild microbes truly face. Plastics, sprays, metal grains, drugs, and algal toxins each get a lab test. The editors frame the set as a draft plan for taints still to come, like the forever chemicals now in the news. Risk calls for land and water sit at the core.
pmc-13493839:
Feng, Liu, and Gai propose a new way to spot defects in factory photographs, such as scratches, cracks, and missing parts, by working in hyperbolic space. That is a kind of curved geometry that expands rapidly outward. Their 2026 framework learns typical patterns drawn from flawless products and embeds them in that curved space. It then tries to reconstruct each new image guided by the patterns. Where reconstruction fails badly, the system marks a defect and pinpoints its location.

On the widely used MVTec AD benchmark, the method scored near the ceiling on the standard AUROC measure at both whole-image and single-pixel levels. That measure grades how well a detector separates faulty from clean items. The authors say it beat current leading methods across several industrial datasets. They argue the curved space suits defect data because normal products form a hierarchy of variations that flat geometry squeezes together.
pmc-13494539:
Corey H Yu and colleagues describe, in a 2026 methods article, a live fluorescence assay for measuring how ubiquitin moves between enzymes, a step at the heart of targeted protein degradation. New drugs in that field force a cell to tag and destroy harmful proteins, yet labs lack sturdy ways to measure the three-part complexes the drugs create. The assay uses purified parts that glow when close together, so transfer can be watched in real time.

The reaction runs in a single step. It needs no changes to the target protein or the tagging enzyme, so results stay clean and easy to quantify. The team shows the assay can gauge a degrader's grip on its target and on the enzyme, how well the three-part complex forms, and how fast it works. They offer it as a high-throughput tool for finding and tuning degrader drugs and molecular glues.
pmc-13495239:
Yingying Ji and colleagues test, in a 2026 trial, whether pairing brain stimulation with aerobic exercise beats either alone after stroke. Thinking trouble after stroke, above all in planning and focus, is common and lasting. The team enrolled 74 patients with such trouble and split them into three groups: stimulation plus exercise, stimulation alone, or exercise with sham stimulation, over four weeks.

The combined group gained most on executive tests, with better scores, faster responses, and fewer recall errors, and their depression scores fell. Blood markers moved too: growth and messenger chemicals for nerve cells rose, while an excitatory one fell. Rises in two growth factors tracked with faster responses and better general thinking scores. The authors read the pairing as a joined brain-and-body rehab path, though the trial was small and short.
pmc-13495339:
Peter M Waters, Kishore Mulpuri, Brian Scannell, and Steven L Frick write, in a 2026 article, on leading surgical departments for both quick results and long growth. A top surgical leader's core job, they argue, is hiring, growing, and keeping talented people, then melding them into teams that share values while bringing unlike skills. Culture is not a backdrop; each hire should lift it.

Their recipe runs in six moves. Recruit early- and mid-career surgeons whose skills fit present needs and growth plans. Grow their higher skills through mentoring, sponsorship, and coaching. Give them the resources to succeed. Build systems that let surgeons at every stage do lasting, weighty work. Expect and coach professionalism inside a trusting culture. Last, plan for what is coming, not only what is here. The authors frame leadership as program building person by person.
pmc-13495439:
Takashi Kojima, Yingsong Lin, Asahi Hishida, and Tomoaki Nakamura report, in a 2026 study, three-year results for a gentle form of corneal cross-linking in keratoconus. In this disease the cornea thins and bulges forward, blurring sight. Cross-linking stiffens it, yet the standard method strips the surface layer; this custom version works through the intact surface with added oxygen and a tailored pattern.

The team followed 74 patients with 90 treated eyes for at least three years. From year one, uncorrected sight and the steepest cornea measure improved and held. Optical flaws of the cornea eased step by step. The cornea thinned slightly at its peak and thinnest points, a change watched closely. No infections or haze appeared. The authors call the method a possible stabilizer, while asking for randomized trials to weigh it against standard care.
pmc-13499039:
Gemechu Ayana and a large clinical team describe in 2026 a blood clot that formed inside a weakened heart despite prescribed blood-thinning treatment. Their patient was a 65-year-old man with long-standing heart failure, prior heart attack and bypass surgery, kidney disease, and a bulging, scarred tip of the main pumping chamber. Clots in that chamber raise the risk of stroke and other blockages elsewhere in the body.

Scans first found the clot on a routine heart ultrasound. A repeat scan months later showed it again even though a modern oral blood thinner had been prescribed, though the patient reported taking it inconsistently. The authors review evidence on how long thinning treatment should continue and argue for plans tailored to clot shape, heart remodelling, and personal risk rather than one fixed rule.
pmc-13499739:
Raffi Tachdjian and co-authors compare in 2026 how trials of on-demand treatment for hereditary angioedema attacks were designed, since fair comparison across drugs depends on shared rules. The rare genetic disorder causes sudden swelling attacks, and five attack treatments had been approved by mid-2025 on the strength of phase 2 and 3 randomised trials. Their systematic review searched four databases through October 2024 and examined design, attack features, and patient-reported outcome measures.

Twelve trials qualified, nearly all centre-based, where patients had to arrive hours after an attack began, while one home-based trial treated far sooner. Trials differed in minimum attack severity, in rules for rescue medicine and repeat dosing, in when patients were censored from analysis. Relief definitions varied too, with eight trials using time to first relief but six different questionnaires to measure it. The authors urge harmonised definitions before cross-drug claims can be trusted.
pmc-13500039:
Peng Ke and eight co-authors read past cases of a two-step plan to shrink a vast spleen ahead of a stem-cell graft in a marrow scar ill. Their study, from two thousand twenty-six, covers a span of years at one center.

A huge spleen is a chief bar to grafts in this ill: it slows the graft's take and risks its fail. A vein-drug that blocks a growth path, and low rays to the spleen, are each used alone. Proof for their use in chain, in a modern prep plan, was thin. Nine patients got the chain: high-dose drug first, then low rays. All went on to the graft. The team reads how the plan held.
pmc-13500539:
Yi Yang and co-authors present in 2026 a knowledge-guided reasoning system for power grid maintenance that fuses fault records, technical documents, and inspection photos. Grid decisions are high-stakes, yet stitching together such mixed sources well is hard for language models. Their architecture builds a structured knowledge base from over ten thousand maintenance records and retrieves relevant material during reasoning. The model is forced through repeated self-checks on completeness, confidence, and logic, while a vision module flags equipment anomalies in images.

On 120 real fault cases the loop reached far higher output completeness and confidence than single-pass generation in the reported comparison, settling within a few rounds for nearly all cases. Image detection across more than fifteen thousand inspection photos scored strongly and retained most of its performance under occlusion, distance, and bad weather, supporting use within the tested scope.
pmc-13501639:
Lin Zheng leads a sixteen-author team reporting a 2026 study of a plant flavonoid that restores the power of a last-line antibiotic against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The bacterium resists the carbapenem imipenem in many hospitals, so the team tested 2''-O-galloylhyperin, a compound from Pyrola plants, as a helper drug. On its own the compound barely slowed bacterial growth, yet combined with imipenem it cut the antibiotic's minimum inhibitory concentration fourfold against a resistant strain, meeting the formal threshold for synergy.

Citric acid then trapped iron ions, starving electron transfer and raising damaging reactive oxygen species inside the cells. The compound also weakened the resistance enzyme KPC-2 directly. The authors propose this iron-disruption route as a way to rescue carbapenem therapy against multidrug-resistant infections.
pmc-13501839:
Qi Yu leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 cohort study of how metabolic health and body weight, alone and in motion, predict chronic kidney disease. The study followed 7,034 participants sorted into four phenotypes crossing weight with metabolic status: healthy and non-overweight at 35.6 percent, healthy but overweight at 18.3 percent, unhealthy but non-overweight at 17.5 percent, and unhealthy and overweight at 28.6 percent of the cohort at baseline. New kidney disease meant filtration below threshold or protein in the urine across two straight years.

After adjustment, the unhealthy phenotypes carried the risk: hazard ratios of 1.184 for the non-overweight group and 1.420 for the overweight group on that outcome, while staying metabolically healthy and overweight showed no significant link. Change hurt too: people whose healthy overweight status slid into unhealthy territory faced a hazard ratio of 1.649 against those who stayed lean and healthy.
pmc-13504339:
Jing-Lian Chen leads a team reading shifts in gene variant rates across age groups to spot ongoing natural selection in Taiwan, in a 2026 study. Harmful variants tied to disease should thin out in younger cohorts if selection is weeding them. The team used a national biobank with over seventy thousand Han Taiwanese genomes.

After checks for age-linked population mix, 168 variants stood out from neutral drift. Most grew rarer in younger people, a sign of weeding-out selection on disease-linked traits. The set was rich in rare variants and known disease links. At the BRCA1 gene, harmful rare variants under weeding-out sat beside a favored stretch of DNA, which hints at selection flipping over time. Some variants also tied to red cell size and hemoglobin levels.
pmc-13505139:
Bingying Huang and colleagues translated a survey on helplessness in chronic disease into Chinese and tested whether it works well for Chinese patients. The twelve-item survey covers thinking, action, and emotional sides of feeling helpless. They recruited patients in two rounds during 2024 and 2025, and compared scores with established scales for helplessness, anxiety, depression, and confidence in managing illness.

The Chinese version held together well, with strong internal consistency and stable scores when patients were measured again. Factor analysis supported the intended three-part structure. Scores rose alongside anxiety, depression, and general helplessness scores, and fell as confidence in self-management rose, matching what the survey is meant to capture. The authors offer the tool for screening and for tracking patients' mental state during long-term care.
pmc-13507139:
Vishnupriya Kalathil Sahadevan, Abin Thomas, and Umakanta Mishra build, in 2026 work, a production model for greener yarn making that links factories in a circular loop. The model folds in green technology spending, wastewater cleaning, remaking of old garments, and yarn spun from banana stem waste. Two carbon policies are compared inside the math.

A worked example shows the system can stay profitable while cutting harm. Upcycling old garments lifted average profit by about five percent under both policies. A cap-and-trade style policy cut green investment costs more than a carbon tax did in the model. Producer responsibility rules support the loop. Circular links can pay for themselves in this sector.
pmc-13507339:
Chengxiao Zhang, Zeying Chen, Jiaxuan Jiang, Junwen Ouyang, and Kai Hu pool, in 2026 work, eleven studies comparing sutureless, glue-free grafting against stitched grafting in pterygium eye surgery. Pterygium is a fleshy growth creeping over the eye surface, and surgery anchors a patch of the patient's own conjunctiva over the cleared spot. Stitching is slow and irritating, while glue costs money and carries its own risks.

Across 1233 eyes, regrowth rates and overall complications did not differ significantly between methods. Glue-free surgery ran about thirteen minutes faster on average. Its grafts, though, slipped open or pulled back more often, since only natural clotting holds them. Speed favors the new method, with graft security the trade-off to watch.
pmc-13508239:
Tuğçe Erdur, Ahmet Erdur, and Betül Acunaş ask whether being born outside normal working hours harms very premature babies, in 2026 work. Staffing runs thinner at night and on weekends, when on-call teams replace full teams. The single-center study covered 326 babies born between 23 and just under 32 weeks of pregnancy, from 2014 to 2021. Babies were grouped by whether birth fell in weekday daytime hours or in off-hours. Health problems and deaths in hospital were then compared.

Death rates were close between the two groups, with no meaningful difference after counting. Babies born in daytime hours did have mothers with more pregnancy blood pressure problems and placental issues. Low alertness scores at five minutes and severe gut disease predicted death in both groups. The gut finding carried wide uncertainty because cases were few. The authors conclude that birth timing itself did not drive outcomes at their center.
pmc-13508339:
Giuseppe Lanfranchi and three co-authors review what helps and what blocks the adoption of artificial intelligence in health care, in a 2026 systematic review. AI promises gains in efficiency, access, and quality, yet hospitals often stall when moving from pilots to daily use. The review gathers views from clinicians, managers, and patients across the literature. Barriers named include fears for professional autonomy, privacy worries, and gaps in basic infrastructure. Costs, rules, and workplace culture also shape success.

The authors build a single framework linking outside readiness, like regulation and market conditions, to inside readiness in each organization and its users. A recurring snag is the knowledge gap between clinical and IT staff, which weakens planning and trust. Closing that gap is treated as a core fix. The review ends with practical guidance for policy makers, AI vendors, and health institutions at any stage of adoption.
pmc-13508439:
Mingkun Yang and seven co-authors follow mood patterns over time and their link to heart disease in older Chinese adults with metabolic risk, in 2026 work. The group sits in early stages of a combined heart-kidney-metabolic syndrome. Data came from a national aging study running 2011 to 2020, with mood scored at three early waves. Modeling sorted 6,152 people into mood paths. Heart disease and stroke events were then counted over follow-up, with models adjusting for other risks.

Three mood paths emerged: low and steady, moderate and steady, and persistently high symptoms. Heart events struck about one in eight people on the low path, rising to nearly one in four on the high path. The moderate group carried about one third higher risk than the low group after adjustment. The persistently high group carried nearly double the risk. Tracking mood over years, not once, sharpened the warning, the authors say.
pmc-13508639:
Benoît Guillet leads the author group of this 2026 illustrated review of acquired hemophilia A, a rare autoimmune bleeding disorder where the body suddenly makes antibodies against its own clotting factor VIII. It mostly affects older adults and can turn life-threatening without fast care.

Following French national guidance, the review explains that diagnosis rests on a prolonged clotting test, low factor VIII activity, and a measured inhibitor level. Treatment has two arms: stop bleeding with bypassing drugs or a pig-derived factor, and erase the inhibitor with immune-suppressing medicines. A newer antibody drug, emicizumab, may help prevent repeat bleeds. Because relapse and side effects remain risks, the authors require close follow-up for at least two years after remission.
pmc-13510039:
Mohamed E. Suliman and six colleagues published this 2026 study linking two stress systems in chronic kidney disease. One is sugar-damaged proteins called AGEs, acting through their receptor RAGE. The other is peptides from mitochondria, signals the powerhouses release under stress. They measured levels of both systems by ELISA tests in 160 adults with kidney failure awaiting living-donor transplants, and in 80 controls. They looked for correlations and associations.

Patients showed higher AGE levels and higher levels of one receptor form, but a lower AGE-to-receptor ratio, and all three mitochondrial peptides were reduced. One peptide, humanin, stayed linked with AGE levels and the ratio after adjustment. Another, MOTS-c, moved in the opposite direction to AGE levels. The inflammation marker CRP tracked with the ratio, while protein-energy wasting showed no link to either system. The authors read the pattern as two overlapping pathways of glycoxidative and mitochondrial stress.
pmc-13513039:
Muhammad Irfan Zafar, Shaoshan Wang, Qizhi Liu, Jawad Hassan, Talha Shafique, and Yuxian Liu survey night insects across three landscapes in an arid farming region of Xinjiang, China, in 2026 work. Solar ultraviolet traps ran from April to August 2024 in dry shrubland, a horticultural garden, and a riverside vegetation corridor near Kekedala City. DNA barcoding checked species identities.

Traps caught more than sixty-three thousand insects from 83 species. The riverside corridor held the richest community, the garden came next, and dry shrubland held the least. Fifteen crop-damaging species appeared, with cotton bollworms and rhinoceros beetles peaking in high summer. Barcoding found two species never before recorded in China, marking the region as a meeting zone of Central and East Asian faunas. Plant complexity shaped communities more than small weather shifts, though single traps limit firm statistics.
pmc-13513339:
Lyu and colleagues report a 2026 study of a mite that plagues mason bees, key pollinators of spring fruit trees in northern China.  Using two-sex life tables, the team raised mites on four diets: apple pollen, cherry pollen, and bee bread made from each, and tracked development and reproduction.

Cherry pollen strongly promoted mite growth and breeding. Bee bread, the fermented pollen-bee mixture bees store, improved mite fitness further compared with raw pollen of the same plant. The results carry a warning for orchard planning: cherry-heavy orchards may feed the mite best and worsen infestations in mason bee nests. Which foods fuel the pest is key knowledge for orchard planning.
pmc-13513539:
Muhammad Faizal Zulkifli, Jonathan Wee Kent Liew, Meng Li Wong, Lu Deng, and Cheong-Huat Tan show that Aedes aegypti pupae can emerge as adults on merely moist surfaces, in 2026 work. No open water is needed. Pupae were placed in four settings: plain water, moist paper, moist paper over a wet cotton pad, and a double mesh over wet tissue. Common wisdom held that emergence demands an upright pupa at a water surface.

Mosquitoes emerged in every setting with survival of at least ninety percent. Adults from each setting flew and mated as well as water-born ones. Female survival did vary somewhat by the surface used. The quirk already serves a Singapore program that releases millions of bacteria-carrying males to suppress wild populations, where mass rearing gains from drier emergence. The authors say the finding rewrites a basic assumption about this disease-carrying species.
pmc-13514439:
Micaela Berni and eleven colleagues report a 2026 laboratory study of therapeutic magnetic resonance, a magnetic-field stimulation method, applied to mesenchymal stromal cells. Such cells, taken here from bone marrow and fat tissue, can mature into bone and calm immune reactions, which makes them central to regenerative medicine.

Treated cells kept their normal character and stable chromosomes, with no rise in ageing or loss of growth. Bone formation improved: early bone markers switched on sooner and more collagen was laid down than in untreated cultures. The stimulation also lowered reactive oxygen output and curbed the growth of immune cells in mixed cultures, hinting at anti-inflammatory effects. Berni's group presents the method as a safe, non-invasive nudge toward bone repair, while noting that patient trials must come before clinical use.
pmc-13514939:
Vlad Dema heads a ten-author team profiling prostate cancer in young men at a tertiary hospital in Timișoara, western Romania, in a 2026 retrospective review. Prostate cancer is usually a disease of men past seventy, yet diagnoses under fifty-five are rising. Reviewing a decade of records from 2015 to 2024, the team picked out every patient aged fifty-five or younger and charted PSA blood levels, tumour type, grade, and stage.

Seventy of 1,742 prostate cancer patients fit the young group, about four percent, with an average age near fifty-two and most living in urban areas. The usual acinar adenocarcinoma dominated, a minority showed ductal features, and the mean grade sat in the intermediate range. Dema's team concludes that cancer in young men often carries aggressive traits, arguing for attention to inherited risk and joined-up specialist care.
pmc-13515439:
Sanaa Souat and eight colleagues investigate an immune brake called BTLA in glioblastoma, the most lethal common brain tumour, in a 2026 study. Standard immune therapies that release other brakes have disappointed in glioma, so the team asked whether BTLA helps tumours shut immunity down. They studied tumour tissue from a Moroccan cohort of forty-four patients, blood from eight patients with glioblastoma, and two large public gene datasets.

High BTLA levels tracked aggressive features and shorter survival. The marker sat mainly on exhausted T cells and one class of dendritic cell inside tumours. Blood told the same story: T cells marked by BTLA made less interferon gamma, and killer cells carried less of their attack proteins. Souat's team reads BTLA as both a warning sign and a candidate drug target, perhaps best paired with existing brake-release therapies.
pmc-13516239:
Aylin Orhaner, Mehmet Cudi Tuncer, and İlhan Özdemir test a plant compound as a partner for chemotherapy in a 2026 cell study. Triple-negative breast cancer resists treatment and suffers harsh side effects, so the team paired docetaxel with thymoquinone, an active ingredient of black seed. Cancer cells of the MDA-MB-231 line, plus normal skin cells for contrast, received each drug alone and combined.

The pair killed cancer cells in synergy, well beyond either drug solo, and drove far more cells into programmed death. A burst of reactive oxygen inside the cells proved central: mopping it up with an antioxidant partly undid the benefit. Orhaner's team backs wider preclinical work on the pairing.
pmc-13517039:
Aicha Nour Laouameria leads a fifteen-author team building a full pipeline for palladium-103, a radiation source for targeted cancer therapy, in a 2026 study. This isotope fires Auger electrons that dump their energy within nanometres, ideal for killing single cells while sparing neighbours. The team produced it by bombarding rhodium in a cyclotron, then separated it with upgraded dry-distillation gear and recovered the acid with a cotton-assisted trick.

Separation reached well over sixty percent efficiency, with total recovery above eighty percent, beating wet chemistry. Labelled compounds came out over ninety-five percent pure and stayed stable inside mice on SPECT imaging. In a dog whose hormone tumour had spread to the liver, one systemic dose was given. Over twenty-four days its tumours shrank slightly and glucose rose, a hopeful sign for an insulin-making tumour. The authors offer the workflow as a scalable base for trials.
pmc-13517439:
Cayla Bosch and six colleagues squeeze new science out of used rabies test strips in a 2026 Zanzibar study. On Unguja Island, dog rabies persists while testing capacity stays thin, so the true burden hides. The team recovered rabies RNA from spent lateral flow devices, cheap strip tests normally thrown away, and sequenced part of the virus to trace its family tree. They also audited surveillance records from 2016 to 2024.

The island's viruses formed their own distinct branch, an endemic cycle separate from mainland Tanzania strains. Mapping cases against testing rates exposed districts where rabies risk ran high and surveillance ran weakest. Bosch's team argues the strip-recycling trick gives poor regions molecular eyes without new lab gear. Their findings point control teams to the blind spots first, supporting targeted dog vaccination on the road to elimination.
pmc-13517639:
Sung Su Park reports a small dog carrying two neurological diseases at once in a 2026 case study. Months of medicine failed to stop its neck pain and worsening walk. Fresh MRI before surgery then revealed extra brain lesions pointing to a second problem: an immune-driven inflammation of unknown origin.

Park combined both treatments: decompression surgery rebuilt with a titanium mesh plate, plus long-term immune-suppressing drugs. The dog improved and stayed stable for about two years. No spinal-fluid test, tissue proof, or follow-up scan was done, so the inflammation stays presumptive and nobody can split credit between surgery and drugs. The case's lesson is procedural: when signs keep worsening despite treating the known defect, image again before assuming one diagnosis explains all.
pmc-13518239:
Igor S. Aranson and Lev S. Tsimring propose a partial melting theory of group cell motion. In 2026, the theory paper treats a one-cell sheet as a single in space and in time uneven phase bridging a thick liquid and a soft solid with elastic shear response. Shifts follow a melting order gauge tied to scaled shear stress. Group motion drives body shaping, wound healing, and cancer spread.

The model captures solid-like plug flow in tiny-channel paths, side-by-side life of moving and still zones, and solid-body-like spin in round rooms. It explains how one-cell sheets mix liquid and solid actions beyond simple jamming stories. Next steps could cover curved, compliant, or breakable skins, 3D growing tissues, and messenger signals.
pmc-13518739:
Elena Quintanilla, Janire Salazar, Jeroen van de Water, and Teresa Madurell compare bacteria living on a Mediterranean sea fan coral in a marine reserve and in Barcelona's busy seaport in 2026 research. The orange gorgonian Leptogorgia sarmentosa survives in both clean and heavily stressed places, raising the question of whether its microbes help it cope.

The microbe mix varied by site, yet overall variety stayed much the same between seaport and reserve. The main symbiont group Endozoicomonas shifted its mix, and other bacterial groups grew more common in the harbor. Matching records from Cassis and La Spezia showed the same shift. Flexible microbe life, the authors suggest, may help the coral keep working in stressed spots.
pmc-13518939:
James Atterholt, Jeffrey J McGuire, Andrew J Barbour, and Morgan P Moschetti image the buried Gorda slab in 2026 using a fiber-optic cable as a dense seismic sensor array. The slab dives beneath the southern Cascadia Subduction Zone, where the fault interface is deep and quiet, hiding the roughness that steers giant earthquakes.

Their method picks out waves converted at the slab boundary and compares their timing and polarity along the cable at fine spacing. Converted waves also hint that fluids appear and vanish sharply within the slab and the crust above it, sharpening the picture used for earthquake thinking.
pmc-13520339:
Xianglin Yang and colleagues present in 2026 a 12-year-old girl whose long-running unexplained fever turned out to be chronic non-bacterial bone inflammation, a rare immune-driven condition. Fever-led cases are uncommon, since bone pain usually dominates, and the picture can mimic infection or cancer.

Scans showed several inflamed bone areas with strong tracer uptake, raising cancer concern. Cultures, gene-based infection tests and marrow checks found no cause, while a thigh-bone biopsy showed inflammation without infection or tumour. A stepwise drug course starting with naproxen brought improvement. The case warns clinicians to keep this condition in mind during prolonged fever workups in children.
pmc-13521539:

They prepared 60 extracted teeth with standard cavities, filled them with three different composite materials, and loaded them until fracture in a testing machine.

Teeth with fiber posts broke in more favorable ways, meaning breaks dentists can more often repair. More fractures also ran through the filling material itself rather than along its bond. The fiber post groups also showed fewer adhesive and unfavorable failures, and the differences were statistically significant. One material paired with posts gave the best pattern, but the post mattered more than which material was used.
pmc-13522039:
Alshaikh and four co-authors study child eye attention in dental clinics, in work from twenty twenty-six. Dental fear is common in children and can spoil care. Visual distractions in the room may draw the eye away from scary tools, if children actually look at them.

More than a hundred children aged six to twelve took part. A standard fear survey split them into anxious and non anxious groups. Eye tracking recorded where they looked in clinic photos, with and without distractors. Heat maps summed up gaze patterns. Anxious children entered and dwelled on instruments faster without distractors. Results can guide room design that truly calms.
pmc-13522339:
Huajie Ze and colleagues explain in 2026 why seeding layered manganese oxide with copper ions boosts charge storage in water-based pseudocapacitors. Gold-core particles with oxide shells allowed live spectroscopic watching during charge cycles.

Pre-seeded metal ions preserve water trapped between oxide layers. That confined water forms a hydrogen-bond network that eases proton movement, supporting a reversible proton-coupled storage reaction. Similar shifts appeared with cobalt and magnesium seeding. Varying shell thickness separated proton from cation contributions, finding proton storage markedly stronger. Electrolyte tests showed hydroxide movement also improved while proton access stayed open.
pmc-13522439:
Chen and colleagues traced in 2026 how carbon and mercury move together, and apart, through forest ecosystems. Using element ratios, isotope fingerprints, and a global forest data synthesis, the team followed both elements along water-based and solid-based paths from air to soil.

Chen found the mercury-to-carbon ratio stayed nearly fixed in the water path, showing mercury travels in step with dissolved organic carbon. In the solid path, the same ratio rose by nearly a thousandfold from air to soil, as litter and soil matter decayed and left mercury behind. Fallen litter acted as a carbon source yet a mercury sink at once. Living biomass governed joint storage of both. The split picture shows how forests both hold back and redistribute air-borne mercury.
pmc-13522539:
Jihwan Chun and a large team report an antibody engineering study, published in 2026. It improves a malaria-protective antibody called L9. L9 binds a repeated motif on the malaria parasite's surface protein. It protects children for months. It grips weakly when a strain carries fewer copies of the motif. Widely spaced copies also weaken the grip.

The team mutated the antibody systematically. Variants were screened in yeast. Improved versions were found. One was modestly more potent in animal challenge against a Kenyan-strain parasite design. No potency was lost against the normal target. New antibody-to-antibody interactions were also uncovered. They occur between bound copies and widen protection. Next-generation malaria prevention can draw on this.
pmc-13522939:
Shu Matsushita and colleagues examine a correction technique for brain tumor imaging in a 2026 retrospective study using two open datasets totaling seven hundred eighty-seven patients with glioblastoma. Diffusion imaging measures how water moves in tissue, and free water from swelling can distort those values. Maps with and without free-water correction were compared in the bright tumor core and in surrounding altered regions, under two different scan settings.

Corrected values were lower in tumor cores than in surrounding regions in both datasets. Which region changed most after correction flipped between datasets, tracking the different scan settings rather than tumor biology alone. Values with and without correction correlated very strongly. Neither version predicted survival. The authors warn that scan settings must be considered when interpreting the correction in tumor studies.
pmc-13523039:
Joe and colleagues describe an unusual way to publish research: a two-day community symposium built with, not just for, the people the research concerns. Their work studied the sexual health of Black women and their HIV prevention needs across Orange County, Florida, and participants themselves suggested a public event over another journal article. The planning committee mixed HIV organisation staff, communication experts, and community members, including the baker who supplied custom goods, and set shared agreements to work as equals. Providers and residents attended together, hearing results in plain settings rather than lecture halls. The authors walk through committee formation, logistics, and facilitation choices, arguing that community conferences close the gap between findings and practice that academic publishing leaves open.
pmc-13523339:
Guoqing Zhang and collaborators design a personalized thigh bone prosthesis with internal porous architecture in a 2026 engineering study. Conventional prostheses can fit poorly, require excess bone removal, and loosen over time. The design combined shape optimization with a mathematical blending method that smoothly joins solid and porous regions, plus control over pore direction. Printed prototypes were then evaluated mechanically and for fit.

Stress peaked in a half-squat position, and optimization made stress distribution more uniform while cutting weight by more than a third, at a small cost in peak stress and displacement. Printed parts showed clean pore structure, good surface quality, and close fit with matching components. The authors present the prototype as proof of concept for high-performance personalized femoral prostheses.
pmc-13523439:
Zhengwei Wen and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective study on blood markers that might flag leakage at a bowel join after laparoscopic surgery for colorectal cancer. They focus on leakage found after the fifth postoperative day.. The work comes from the First Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University. Three ratios built from routine blood values were tracked on days one, three, and five after surgery.

The sample held 360 patients who had one-stage resections between October 2019 and December 2023. Marker values were higher in the leakage group on days three and five. Rectal tumor location, selected day-three markers, and day-five neutrophil ratios stayed associated with leakage in multivariable work. The day-five neutrophil-to-albumin ratio performed best, although the authors caution that the analysis was exploratory and the markers overlap with each other.
pmc-13523539:
Portillo Avila and colleagues describe a fully guided dental implant case from 2026 in a twenty-five-year-old man born without an upper front side tooth, a condition called maxillary lateral incisor agenesis. Replacing a missing tooth in the visible smile zone demands precise implant placement. The team planned the whole procedure digitally before touching the patient.

They combined a cone-beam CT scan with an intraoral surface scan to design the implant position, then printed a surgical guide that steered the drill during placement. The implant integrated with the bone over six months of healing, a process called osseointegration, and the final crown was fitted successfully. In this single patient, the guided workflow delivered accurate placement with a natural-looking result. The authors present digital guidance as a predictable option for congenitally missing front teeth.
pmc-13524139:
Upadhyay and colleagues present a 2026 case report of sudden eye damage in one forty-year-old man. He developed swelling of both corneas, the clear front windows of the eyes, shortly after a binge of alcohol and marijuana combined with exposure to vehicle exhaust fumes. Because both eyes were affected together and no infection was found, the doctors suspected a toxic injury to the cornea's inner cell layer.

The man's vision measured 6/36 three days after the event, far below normal sharpness, and the team treated the suspected toxic endothelial insult with supportive care. His right eye improved, but the left eye kept endothelial dysfunction, meaning the pump cells that keep the cornea clear did not recover. A corneal transplant, called keratoplasty, was planned for that eye. The authors warn that fumes and binge exposures can permanently damage the corneal endothelium.
pmc-13524939:
Ocak and Akyüz asked whether bone texture on panoramic dental X-rays reflects the depth of a natural hollow under the jaw. That depth matters because deep hollows raise the risk of piercing the jaw's inner plate during implant surgery. Their 2026 retrospective study paired cone-beam computed tomography, a three-dimensional scan, with panoramic images taken within three months in 133 patients.

Ocak measured 229 jaw halves and classed hollow depth into three types from shallow to deep, then computed fractal dimension, a texture complexity score, on matching panoramic regions. Texture scores were higher in the two deeper classes than in shallow jaws, and depth correlated moderately with texture across all sites. The authors stress that the panoramic score cannot replace the three-dimensional scan. It can serve as an early warning cue during review and as a confounder that texture studies in this jaw region must account for.
pmc-13525039:
Hiroto Funahashi and colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, why one hip hurts while the other stays silent in people with dysplasia on both sides and similar socket coverage. Hip dysplasia undercovers the joint, raising pressure and pain risk. Comparing a person's two hips removes many between-person differences.

From 109 surgical patients, thirty-three had one symptomatic hip treated while the other stayed pain-free for at least three years, and eighteen had matched coverage angles on both sides. Symptomatic hips showed greater femoral neck twist and more outward displacement of the femoral head in both cohorts. Socket sector angles differed only in the broader cohort. Adjusted analysis confirmed twist and displacement as factors tied to pain onset, suggesting femoral shape matters once coverage is equal.
pmc-13525739:
Lehrer and Rheinstein asked if a drug for rheumatoid arthritis might also cut the risk of new depression. Their 2026 study used the All of Us health records scheme in the United States. It covered 9,826 adults with the joint disease who had no past record of depression. Of these, 299 took tocilizumab, a drug that blocks a body signal that drives swelling. The rest did not take the drug.

New depression arose in about twenty-two of each hundred who took the drug. In the group that did not, the rate was about thirty-five of each hundred. The gap held when the team weighed age, sex, and race, and when it used time-based checks. The team is careful to say this link does not prove the drug caused the gain. It calls for trials that test the drug for mood in a direct way.
pmc-13527139:
Aritra Das and colleagues propose, in a 2026 study, a hybrid image model for classifying flower growth stages. The task is fine-grained, since early, mid, and full bloom differ subtly and labeled data are scarce. Their framework pairs deep image backbones with graph convolutional networks that reason over a grid of image regions.

A new dataset of 3,889 images covers eight Bangladeshi flower species across three stages, forming twenty-four classes. Systematic trials varied graph depth, node resolution, and how neighboring regions connect. Two hybrid backbones reached ninety-seven percent accuracy, and a transformer backbone jumped from eighty-four to ninety-seven percent once graph processing was added. Grid-based graphs beat nearest-neighbor graphs for stability, and moderate graph depth worked best. Cross-checks on a standard Oxford flower dataset supported generalization.
pmc-13528039:
Haoshen Wu and seven colleagues ask in a 2026 study whether front-view leg alignment can reveal twist alignment in worn knees. They studied 315 legs with end-stage varus knee osteoarthritis, where the leg bows inward. Standing X-rays gave front-view angles. CT scans gave twist measures for the thigh and shin bones. Legs were split into mild and severe bow groups.

Twist measures did not differ between the mild and severe groups. Only shin twist linked with front-view angles, and the links were weak. The tie changed a bit by group but stayed small. The authors conclude front-view readings cannot stand in for twist readings. Surgeons planning knee replacement should order CT when twist matters. Guessing from X-rays risks misplacing parts, they warn.
pmc-13528239:

The system segments each heartbeat trace into twenty classes of waves and rhythms, lead by lead, then combines them into interval measures, a rhythm call, and a median beat. It was trained on nearly two thousand hand-marked ECGs plus many doctor-checked ones.

On an external test set of about thirteen hundred ECGs, wave boundaries drawn by the system matched reference standards closely. Its median beats resembled those from two commercial systems in follow-up tests. Its labeled segments show why it called an interval long or a rhythm abnormal. An open web tool accompanies the study.
pmc-13529639:

Fibroblasts build and remodel that tissue. Together they block drug entry and keep immune cells out. The review gathers lab evidence on breaking the partnership.

Blockers of fibroblast signals slowed tumor growth in preclinical work. Softening the matrix improved drug delivery in models. Tiny engineered particles carried drugs deeper into the stroma. Anti-scarring drugs and immune modulators restored sensitivity to standard treatment in tests. The authors favor combined attacks and stromal reprogramming.
