pmc-13529739:
Haiyin Luo and three colleagues study gusty wind pressure on solar mirror arrays in a 2026 paper. The mirrors, called heliostats, must aim sunlight precisely yet catch wind on big flat faces. Wind tunnel tests ran 130 working conditions. The team mapped how pressure flickers across mirror surfaces. They also tested math for predicting rare extreme gusts.

Pressure behaved in a bell-curve way near the middle below sixty degrees of tilt. Edges broke that pattern as vortices peeled off. Standard peak guessing handled the odd zones poorly. Three extreme-value methods did better, with a Bayesian one giving the tightest ranges. Fit tests confirmed the Bayesian shape matched the data. The authors offer the method for safer mirror design. Storm survival and aiming accuracy both ride on such numbers.
pmc-13530139:
Hui Lichuan and Zhang Hanlin propose in 2026 an active control method that steadies the pantograph pressing against overhead wires on fast trains. At higher speeds the contact force swings widely, hurting power pickup and reliability. Fixed controller settings cope poorly as conditions shift during a run.

Their design tunes a standard regulator through an improved dandelion-inspired search algorithm, with gains that shift smoothly by pantograph position. Simulations at two speeds showed swings in contact force and head movement cut by roughly half versus passive control. Energy use and stability checks rounded out the testing.
pmc-13530739:
Augustin and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 74, a cadaver anatomy study of three stabilizing structures on the outer knee. It is meant to guide where surgeons drill graft tunnels in lateral knee reconstruction. Fixation placed wrong for how a ligament behaves in bending will fail.

The iliotibial band fibers, by contrast, barely changed length, a difference the authors say should individualize tunnel placement.
pmc-13530939:
Yanhong Xiao and colleagues show in 2026 how the cholesterol drug lovastatin kills prostate cancer cells through an iron-driven death route called ferroptosis. Five statin drugs were screened on cancer cell lines, with lovastatin emerging strongest. Tests tracked growth, movement, invasion, iron levels, and cell power stations.

Feeding back the blocked pathway product restored cell survival and calmed stress markers. The results nominate the pathway-to-ferroptosis chain as a treatment target.
pmc-13531739:
Necmiye Keser-Ozturk and colleagues chart severe allergic reactions in 100 children treated at an Istanbul center during 2026 reporting. Records from a full year captured triggers, features, other illnesses, and outcomes for patients up to age 18. Grading of how severe each case was followed the newest world allergy criteria.

Medicines led the trigger list, then food, venom, and unknown causes. Food reactions clustered among outpatients, while drug reactions clustered among inpatients with more coexisting illness. Drug reactions in older children taking many medicines tended to run severe. Nearly all children received muscle-injected adrenaline, yet home rescue pen use before arrival was rare.
pmc-13531839:
Emine Kurt Can and colleagues measure in 2026 how often mothers in eastern Turkey give newborns food or drink before the first breast milk. Such prelacteal feeding denies babies protective first milk. Interviews covered 335 mothers of infants up to two years old at a university hospital during 2023.

About 18 percent reported the practice, most often formula, then sugar water. Lower income, no breastfeeding education, late first feeding, and weak knowledge of first-milk benefits predicted the practice in adjusted models. Schooling, home setting, job status, and antenatal care also mattered. Prenatal teaching is the proposed remedy.
pmc-13532239:
Tian and colleagues isolated in 2026 a virus that infects Staphylococcus aureus germs from a dairy farm environment. Such viruses, called phages, are candidate tools to control the germ, which causes cow udder infections and contaminates dairy food. The team sequenced the phage, named vB_SauL_202595, and tested its killing range, stability, and action in milk and yogurt.

The phage lysed, meaning burst open, about a quarter of 66 tested germ strains, including five highly sensitive ones. Its genome held no antibiotic resistance or major toxin genes, but it carried genes marking it as a temperate phage, one that can hide inside germ DNA. In milk and yogurt it lowered live germ counts and shrank mature biofilms. The authors call it a candidate for dairy biocontrol research only.
pmc-13532439:
Adilet N Toksumakov and a large team report in 2026 on alpha MoO3, a layered crystal, as a material that guides light at very small scales. Most common optical materials respond the same in all directions, which limits control of light. Alpha MoO3 responds in unlike ways along unlike axes, a trait called anisotropy.

The team measured its optical traits from 250 to 1700 nanometres and linked them to a mid-infrared model. Strong contrasts in response helped limit stray light and supported tiny waveguides that guide visible light. Readers learn how one material may serve both infrared and short-wave light tools.
pmc-13532639:
Nicolau Martin-Bassols, Miquel Serra-Burriel, and Kerstin Noelle Vokinger study in 2026 what happens when governments allow copies of patented HIV drugs without owner consent. Such licences aim to improve access for public health needs, yet hard proof of market effects has been scarce. The team used sales and price data from 11 countries for 2002 to 2022.

They focused on 21 HIV drugs that faced at least one such licence. After licences began, retail and hospital sales rose and prices fell by clear margins. Readers should note the study cannot rule out added access through public imports or aid supply.
pmc-13534639:
Ruofei Liu and colleagues identify in 2026 RAD54L as a coordinator of DNA repair in the nucleolus, the cell zone that builds ribosome parts. Heavy gene copying there creates stress and break risk for ribosomal DNA. Cell tests tracked where the protein goes after breaks were cut at those sites.

The protein sits in the nucleolus normally and rushes to repair caps after damage. Without it, repair marks lingered, damage signals rose, and faulty nuclei formed more often. Hybrid RNA-DNA loops also aided repair setup, so the work maps a key guard of genome stability.
pmc-13534739:
Muhammad Irfan and colleagues apply in 2026 machine learning to molecular graphs of two ring compounds used in industry. Number summaries drawn from a graph can predict material traits, yet a fair comparison for these rings was missing. The team computed several indices based on atom links and nearby links for both structures.

Those indices fed models that link molecular shape to measured physical traits. Learning-based fits then judged how strongly each summary tracks real property data across both rings. Readers gain a fast way to estimate traits and a base for models of larger polymer networks in future work.
pmc-13535739:
Biel Garcias and colleagues sequence in 2026 Klebsiella germs from European hedgehogs and compare them with human hospital strains from the same region. The germ causes hospital infections and resists many drugs, and urban hedgehogs meet people and livestock often. Whole-genome reads mapped strain types, resistance genes, and mobile DNA rings.

Hedgehogs carried high resistance levels, including a key enzyme that defeats last-line drugs. Two globally spread hospital clones appeared in both hedgehogs and humans, and shared plasmid types suggest gene spread across settings. Direct transmission was not proven, yet wildlife monitoring is urged.
pmc-13536539:
Veronika Hatlova and colleagues test in 2026 knotless scleral fixation with a durable suture material in rabbit eyes after lens removal. When natural lens support is missing, implants must be stitched to the eye wall, and early hold strength matters. Two knotless patterns were placed in each eye and pull strength was measured over 30 days.

Both patterns needed more force to pull out as days passed, showing growing early stabilisation. The Z pattern ranged slightly higher than the chain pattern across time points. Findings are exploratory yet support further preclinical and clinical checks of both methods.
pmc-13536639:
Ross P. Wohlgemuth and colleagues test in 2026 whether collagenase injections can clear muscle scarring in a mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Scar tissue stiffens muscle and blocks repair, and it is often viewed as hard to reverse. Enzyme shots went into leg muscles of normal and dystrophy-model mice.

The enzyme digested scar matrix well, yet muscle grew weaker with bleeding within a day and a thickened support layer after a week. No functional gain appeared in strength or lab tests. The team urges scar-specific enzymes plus paired therapy work in future trials.
pmc-13538239:
Joseph Amihere Ackah and colleagues compare long-standing high blood pressure with pregnancy-induced high blood pressure in a 2026 systematic review. Both conditions complicate many pregnancies and threaten mothers and babies, yet their timing and course differ. Searches of three databases gathered observational studies, screened for quality and combined in narrative form. Outcomes, risk factors, and diagnostic tools were contrasted across the two conditions.

Major harms in both groups included fetal death inside the womb, slowed fetal growth, low birth weight, and newborn and maternal deaths. Pregnancy-induced pressure often worsened suddenly and severely without close watching, while long-standing pressure favored early steady surveillance. Older age and other illnesses raised risk in both groups. Ultrasound flow checks helped early risk sorting. The authors urge tailored monitoring by condition type.
pmc-13538339:
Shilin You and co-authors review oncolytic virus therapy for liver cancer centered on hepatocellular carcinoma in a 2026 synthesis. Engineered viruses infect and burst tumor cells while sparing normal tissue and waking anti-tumor immunity. Lab and clinical studies across five virus families were weighed for benefit, safety, and delivery hurdles. Special attention went to viruses rebuilt to carry immune boosters or checkpoint blockers.

Herpes and vaccinia viruses showed strong benefit and safety signals, while rebuilt adenovirus and Newcastle disease platforms also showed promise. Better engineering and delivery lifted tumor targeting and immune activation. Standing hurdles include host antiviral defenses clearing the virus, weak delivery to tumors, and choosing the right patients. The authors present virus therapy as a rising partner for standard liver cancer care.
pmc-13538539:
Solomon Oyebisi and colleagues test oil palm stem fibers as concrete reinforcement in a 2026 materials study. Natural fibers promise greener building while easing resource strain. Palm midrib fibers, untreated or soaked in lime solution at varied strengths and times, replaced small shares of concrete volume. Workability plus compression, splitting, bending, bond, and rupture tests ran after curing at three ages.

Lime soaking at a mid strength for a full day gave fibers their best pulling strength. Workability dipped slightly as fiber share rose. Treated fiber lifted compression and splitting strength at low dosage and bending strength at a slightly higher one. Bond strength and rupture resistance beat untreated fiber versions after a month of curing. The authors endorse treated palm fiber for quality sustainable concrete.
pmc-13538639:
Julie Gosez and colleagues model brain electric fields from scalp stimulation in obsessive-compulsive disorder in a 2026 patient-specific study. Response to the stimulation varies widely in treatment-resistant cases. Current direction and strength maps were compared voxel by voxel.

Field strength alone showed no such links, spotlighting direction as the active ingredient. The authors argue that tailoring stimulation to personal anatomy and current direction could sharpen results in psychiatric care.
pmc-13540839:
Zijiao Zhang and six colleagues review, in a 2026 meta-analysis, whether machine learning predicts a first stroke in community primary care better than older statistical models. Stroke prevention depends on spotting high-risk people early in ordinary clinics.

Forty-three studies holding ninety-three models met the criteria. Traditional Cox regression was the commonest approach, and its pooled accuracy matched or beat the machine learning entries, including random forests and gradient boosting. Three quarters of the studies carried a high risk of bias, and applicability to real community care raised concerns in a fifth. The authors conclude that machine learning's clinical value here remains unproven.
pmc-13540939:
Michelle C Paulus and colleagues compare two protein dosing schemes in 2026. The patients were critically ill adults in intensive care. One scheme set protein by total body weight. pmc-13541139:
Ai Cui and six co-authors shared a trial protocol in twenty twenty-six. It tests if a lung-fibrosis drug can prevent radiation injury. The patients have lung cancer. pmc-13541239:

Bench tests produced fields above the design target and heated tumor phantoms to therapeutic temperatures. In a prepared canine cadaver with particles implanted in the brain, imaging signal differences matched later temperature rises at the same spots. A computer simulation of a human glioma treatment suggested clinical feasibility.
pmc-13542939:

pmc-13543539:

pmc-13543639:

pmc-13545139:
Miriam Casares-Lopez and co-authors reported in 2026 on whether tear film tests agree when students new to the task perform them. The authors caution that automated readings cannot replace careful clinical judgment, especially when examiners have little experience.
pmc-13545439:

pmc-13546539:

pmc-13547339:

pmc-13548539:

pmc-13548639:

The team fine-mapped the spots, picked likely causal genes, and checked overlap with known muscle traits. The results show the index has a partly sex-specific gene layout, which may refine how muscle loss is predicted and studied.
pmc-13549339:
Andrey A. Sapronov, Dmitry E. The near-edge part of these spectra reveals an atom's oxidation state and surroundings, and two established programs simulate it, yet their settings are usually adjusted by hand and eye. pmc-13550439:
Julie Bania and colleagues survey urinary tract infections among women's-health patients in Northeast India, in a 2026 tracking study. Nearly nine hundred women took part. The main bacteria resisted several common antibiotics heavily, including two widely used classes. They stayed sensitive to fosfomycin, certain injectables, and stronger reserve drugs. pmc-13550539:

pmc-13550639:

Eight cities besides Shenzhen showed the same pattern in high-risk areas. The authors argue that prevention planning should differ by city and flood level rather than treating the delta as uniform.
pmc-13551139:

pmc-13551839:

Long-term antibody rates were nearly the same in both groups. No one showed signs of fresh infection. Parasite DNA turned up slightly more in patients, yet the gap was not firm. Antibody rates rose with age in both groups. The team concludes that latent infection does not drive this disorder here.
pmc-13551939:

Fast, slow, and resistant starch shares shift with chain mix. The team sums up ways to tune chain length on purpose. Food makers may use those rules for healthier starch.
pmc-13552139:

Forty patients were treated at one Indian medical college. The study window ran about eighteen months. Function scores tracked recovery after the minimally invasive fixation. Patients and surgeons both need realistic recovery expectations.
pmc-13552739:

But the bacteria often resisted penicillin, ciprofloxacin, and tetracycline. pmc-13552939:

Two groups were compared at a liver transplant unit. One aids folks under treatment for cirrhosis itself. The other aids folks who got a liver transplant. Caregivers filled forms and a standard family burden scale. Burden rose for younger caregivers and those with children. Caring for distressed patients and low income also raised it. Women were the most burdened group in the set.
pmc-13556039:

pmc-13556539:

pmc-13557339:

pmc-13558339:

pmc-13558539:

pmc-13558739:

pmc-13559139:

pmc-13560439:

pmc-13562339:

pmc-13562539:

pmc-13563739:

pmc-13563839:

pmc-13564139:

pmc-13569839:

pmc-13571339:

pmc-13572339:

pmc-13573539:

pmc-13575539:

pmc-13576139:

pmc-13576239:

pmc-13576539:

pmc-13576839:

pmc-13578439:

pmc-13578739:

pmc-13579439:

pmc-13579839:

pmc-13580339:

pmc-13580639:

pmc-13582339:

pmc-13585439:

pmc-13586239:

pmc-13588239:

pmc-13589339:

pmc-13589939:

pmc-13590539:

pmc-13590639:

pmc-13591939:

pmc-13592739:

pmc-13593539:

pmc-13593639:

pmc-13594039:

pmc-13595539:

pmc-13596739:

pmc-13598139:

pmc-13600339:

pmc-13602739:

pmc-13607239:

pmc-13607839:

pmc-13608139:
Aydin and seven co-authors published a dental study in twenty twenty-six on how well self-adhesive filling materials seal the gum-side edge of a repair. These newer materials skip a separate glue step, but leaks along the gum line remain a worry.

The team filled one hundred fifty prepared cavities in seventy-five pulled human molars. They compared three surface pre-treatments and five filling materials, including three self-adhesive ones. After heat cycling, they used a fine X-ray scan to measure how far a silver dye crept under each filling. A rinse based on hypochlorous acid cut the leakage for every self-adhesive material. The older soda-based rinse helped only one brand. Standard fillings used with a separate mild glue still sealed best overall. The results point to a simple rinse step that makes the newer materials safer to use.
pmc-13609839:
Xianli Tang and four colleagues build a radio filter whose bandwidth can be dialed continuously without giving up low loss. Phones juggling many bands normally need a shelf of fixed filters, which fights miniaturization. Their design hybridizes acoustic-wave resonators with lumped elements, using a varactor diode to retune a reconfigurable resonator module, in two ladder layouts. Equations derived for both layouts predicted performance before fabrication, and simulations agreed.

Measured results backed the math. The simpler Type I filter tuned its 3 dB fractional bandwidth across a wide span with insertion loss between 1.2 and 2.2 dB. The Type II version, with an extra shunt branch, tuned slightly wider while losing a bit more signal. Both figures beat the 3 to 10 dB losses typical of earlier tunable filters built on low-quality resonators. The authors present the hybrid acoustic approach as a favorable compromise for flexible 5G and 6G front ends.
pmc-13610739:
Maxim I. Suchkov leads a nine-author team testing whether gentle heat treatment makes expressed breast milk safe at home. Several viruses can ride in breast milk, and Holder pasteurization, 62.5 degrees for thirty minutes, is the milk-bank standard balancing safety against nutrition. The team spiked milk from four donors with a panel of RNA and DNA viruses and ran it through a portable home pasteurizer, measuring infectious virus and leftover genomes.

Enveloped RNA viruses, HIV-1, chikungunya, and SARS-CoV-2, dropped below detection. Respiratory syncytial virus did not. Non-enveloped enteroviruses and the DNA viruses tested fell only partly. Two enteroviruses also behaved inconsistently between donors' milk, a reminder that milk composition varies. The authors conclude that home Holder pasteurization is a partial shield, not sterilization. They suggest it could join a future pandemic preparedness toolbox, helping mothers keep breastfeeding through common infections.
pmc-13610939:
Alrahimi and co-authors measure four inflammatory signals in the blood of multiple sclerosis patients in western Saudi Arabia. Middle Eastern data on such markers are scarce. The study enrolled 26 patients and 26 matched healthy controls at one center. Blood tests read IL-6, IL-16, IL-18, and IL-36 levels. Disability was scored by a standard scale and a timed walk. Matched statistical tests compared patients with controls.

Subgroup checks split patients by disease type, duration, and treatment. Correlations tied marker levels to disability scores. No correction for many comparisons was applied, a stated limit. The study seeds regional data for a disease shaped by inflammation.
pmc-13612239:
Monika Drobna-Sledzinska leads a thirteen-author team cataloguing circular RNAs in an aggressive blood cancer in 2026. T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia grows from immature T cells. Circular RNAs, looped molecules that can soak up regulatory microRNAs, are suspects in its machinery. The team fished out RNAs bound to the protein AGO2 in four leukemia cell lines, hunting for circles acting as microRNA sponges.

Circular RNAs were over-represented in the AGO2-bound fraction, 7.3 percent against 3 percent for linear RNAs, and a consistent enriched set emerged. One abundant circle, circN4BP2L2, also ran abnormal in patients. Knocking it down slowed cell proliferation, restored cell-death sensitivity, and shifted key leukemia pathways. Patient tumors with high levels of this circle showed gene-expression features overlapping the knockdown signature. The authors present circN4BP2L2 as a survival-promoting regulator, and the AGO2-bound catalog as a map for further targets.
pmc-13612639:
Marta Maia and colleagues measured severe bleeding around children's kidney transplants and its fallout. Transplant is the preferred treatment for children with kidney failure, yet bleeding rates and risks in this setting were little charted. Their single-centre look-back study covered first transplants from 2008 to 2015, defining severe bleeding by blood loss, transfusion needs, reoperation, or clotting-factor use.

Severe bleeding struck 16 of 218 children, about 7 percent, more often in younger, smaller recipients given kidneys from older living donors at higher graft doses. Low platelet counts after surgery also tracked with bleeding. Five-year graft survival fell to about 63 percent with severe bleeding versus about 92 percent without it. Maia and colleagues flag small-recipient, large-graft mismatch as the key risk.
pmc-13612939:
Natassia Brenman writes about voluntary mental health services in inner-city London and the staff who felt their services were turning into dumping grounds for a system in crisis. Charities in Britain have long provided flexible community care that eases pressure on public clinics and hospitals. Under years of austerity funding cuts, Brenman found through fieldwork at three sites that these groups were stretched well past what they could hold.

Brenman offers the idea of threshold work to explain how staff decide, day by day, who and what they can take in. Staff manage limits in two linked ways: the physical thresholds of their buildings and the shifting line of how unwell a person must be to qualify for help. Readers see how care is shaped as much by doors, rooms, and cut-off points as by goodwill.
pmc-13614439:
Peter Goldie, Michael Bixter, and Suzanne McLaren test a scale for hiding sexual orientation. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses data from nonbinary adults. Hiding who one likes is a stress for many LGBTQ folks.

The scale is short and used in much past research. Its worth for nonbinary folks had not been checked before. Data came from a world sample of a few hundred adults. Tests showed the one part form fit the data well. Scores could be compared across race and orientation groups in part. The scale is judged fit for use here.
pmc-13614639:
Charles J. Gerardo leads a large team testing whether a drug called varespladib, given after antivenom, helps hospital patients bitten by venomous snakes. Snakebite kills an estimated 81,000 to 138,000 people each year and leaves more than 400,000 with lasting disability, mostly in poor regions. Antivenom is the only approved treatment and must be dripped into a vein, so an added drug that blunts venom could save tissue and lives.

In this phase II trial at many centres, patients were randomly assigned in a double-blind design to receive varespladib by vein then by mouth, or a placebo, on top of standard antivenom. Neither patients nor staff knew who got the drug. Trials like this decide whether a promising add-on earns a place in emergency care, where hours matter and stock of antivenom is often short.
pmc-13615039:
Yildiz Ucar, Caner Incekas, Keziban Ucar Karabulut, and Meltem Karacan Golen compare in 2026 how obstructive sleep apnea looks in men and women. They draw on 230 patients diagnosed by overnight sleep studies between 2020 and 2026. The condition, where the airway keeps closing during sleep, was long treated as a mostly male problem. In this group, 68.3 percent were men and 31.7 percent were women.

Women were older at diagnosis and had a higher body mass index. Their average and lowest oxygen levels during sleep were worse, and they showed higher pressure in the lung artery and a weaker heart pumping score. Blood inflammation scores built from white cell types ran higher in men. The contrast suggests women's disease is being caught later, after more harm, and that doctors should not wait for the classic male picture before testing women.
pmc-13615339:
Yue Chen leads a team reviewing how lactate, a by-product of sugar use in cells, and a chemical tag it adds to proteins, called lactylation, steer programmed cell death in human disease. Lactylation was found only recently, and it mirrors a cell's metabolic state while helping control which genes are read. Programmed cell death is the body's orderly way of removing cells under stress, in several distinct forms.

Once treated as separate topics, the two are now shown to be linked: the lactate tag can switch key gene and signal paths that drive various forms of cell death. The review gathers the fresh findings across diseases where this link may matter. Drug hunters gain new targets, since blocking or boosting the tag could change whether diseased cells live or die on cue.
pmc-13616239:
Huanhuan Yang, Yee Sin Ang, Sheng Meng, and Xiao Jiang study double-layer altermagnets. These form a new class of magnetic materials with no overall magnetisation. In double layers, they can turn visible light into electric current in a spin-aware way. Single layers hide their spin splitting, the separation of electron states by spin, behind symmetry rules. Stacking two layers with coupling between them lifts those rules and switches on a current type that was forbidden before.

Using a simplified model of electron orbits, the team showed two current types moving in opposite directions as the layer coupling grows, each ruled by a distinct mechanism. Detailed calculations on a real candidate material, a manganese phosphorus telluride bilayer, backed the predictions. Such light-driven, spin-sorted currents could serve future low-power devices that read information from spin rather than charge alone.
pmc-13616639:
Linzi Williamson and her team work out the pay-back to folk at large of a safe-use site in Saskatoon in Saskatchewan, Canada. Their 2026 study sets a worth on the site. It sits amid hot fights, funds turned down, and shut-downs.

Ends came from talks with twenty-six folk who took part and from files kept by the site. Groups weighed took in users of the site and the folk they love. They took in the wide town, firms, and state kits such as sick bays and the law arm. Cash stand-ins set worth on gains for folk, cash life, and the wild world, with the most low safe grades and bad ends too. The check found each coin put in gave back a grade of four coins and forty-four cents in worth to folk. The team aims to show town gain past tales.
pmc-13618039:
C. Ruth Le Sueur, James F. E. Croft, and Jeremy M. Hutson present a sturdier algorithm for finding bound states in coupled-channel calculations, a workhorse of quantum chemistry and molecular physics. Bound states, the energy levels of weakly joined systems such as van der Waals complexes, appear where a matrix eigenvalue crosses zero. Older search methods were fiddly to program and could lose track of the eigenvalue across an energy range.

Their algorithm tracks the needed eigenvalue of the matching matrix across the full energy span where it exists, making implementations much simpler. They give practical guidance on choosing the matching distance, the point where two halves of the calculation are joined. It should sit in the classically allowed region for every channel of interest, but not too close to a node in the wavefunction. The result is a more robust tool for spectroscopy and weakly bound systems.
pmc-13618839:
Kristina Shkirkova and eight colleagues report a 2026 secondary analysis of the FAST-MAG trial, testing whether a neuroprotectant started by paramedics can bridge stroke patients to clot treatment. The parent phase three trial gave magnesium sulfate or placebo in the field within two hours of symptom onset. This analysis isolates the four hundred one patients who later received thrombolysis after arrival, two hundred fourteen of them magnesium-treated.

The timelines show what prehospital therapy buys: treatment began a median of forty-six minutes after last known well time. Thrombolysis followed at about one hundred fifty minutes, and patients carried a median of ninety-three minutes of study drug exposure before reperfusion. Ninety-day disability did not improve significantly. A subgroup with the most severe strokes hinted at benefit, which the authors label hypothesis-generating only. They frame the contribution as proving the early-exposure model for future protective agents.
pmc-13619039:
Siyi Gong led a 2026 survey across sixteen countries and regions that asked whether long COVID carries early warning signs resembling Parkinson's disease, especially when sleep brings dream-enacting behavior. Past work has hinted COVID-19 may raise Parkinson's risk, but the burden of early features in long COVID was unclear. The team surveyed 11,261 people between May and November 2021, scoring each person's early-feature burden with a set scale.

People with long COVID, numbering 1,155, showed more dream-enacting behavior, smell loss, constipation, and daytime sleepiness. They also showed more dizziness on standing, mood symptoms, bladder trouble, and thinking problems than people who never had COVID or had recovered. Long COVID was tied to a 73 percent higher burden of such features, and new or worsened dream-enacting behavior after infection raised it 38 percent. Readers should note this is survey evidence of symptom burden, not proof that Parkinson's disease itself follows.
pmc-13622339:
Luca Unione and colleagues show that a protein's own letter code can steer the sugar tags it ends up wearing, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Cells decorate many proteins with sugar chains, and the final pattern guides how the protein acts. What sets the pattern, beyond the cell's machinery, was far from clear.

The team studied the tip of the spike protein of the virus that causes COVID-19, made in human cells. To their surprise, some sugar chains ended in a sugar called GalNAc, in several forms. Guessing that nearby charged spots on the protein recruit the enzymes at fault, they swapped four such spots for neutral ones. The mutant protein lost most of its GalNAc-tipped chains and gained plain ones instead, while its folded shape stayed the same. The result proves that local sequence helps decide sugar fate, a point drug makers may use.
pmc-13624039:
R Noah Padgett and colleagues published a 2026 comparison of two one-question measures of how well life is going. They draw on the Global Flourishing Study of more than 200,000 people in twenty-two countries. Surveys need short measures, and the two rivals are a plain life satisfaction question and Cantril's ladder, which asks people to place their life on steps from worst to best.

Both questions were checked against a broad flourishing battery covering happiness, health, meaning, character, financial security, and relationships. Life satisfaction tracked every one of those domains more strongly than the ladder did, and the pattern held in all twenty-two countries. The ladder did lean hardest toward the financial side of life, matching its rung-climbing image. The authors conclude that when only one question fits, the plain satisfaction wording gives the fuller summary of how people judge their lives.
pmc-13625039:
Sintayehu Eshetu Abebaw and Tadla Guadie Feleke gather the research record on how climate change threatens food in Ethiopia. Following standard review rules, they screened the literature and kept 232 studies on climate risks, weak points in the food system, and ways to adapt. Farming there leans on rainfall, which leaves harvests exposed when rains fail or shift.

Drought, heat, and erratic rain stood out as the chief risks, with drought blamed for roughly sixty percent of crop losses in the studies. One degree of warming was tied to a tenth less output of main staple crops, and rural homes lost ground faster than city homes. The reviewers point to hardier farming methods, wider irrigation, and plans fitted to each region.
pmc-13625439:
Souvik Chaudhuri and nine colleagues, publishing in 2026, hunt for early chemical warning signs in community-acquired pneumonia. The infection's course is hard to predict at the door, so the team took blood from seventy patients and thirty-five healthy controls at one center between January and November 2025. A scanning method measured small molecules in the serum, keeping ninety-three for study after cleaning.

Patient blood differed most in a set of organic acids, led by malic acid, and the disturbed pathways covered energy production, amino acid handling, and the body's rust-defense balance. A smaller contrast between sixty intensive care patients and ten milder cases fingered fats, cholesterol, and a vitamin E form. Early metabolic fingerprints may one day help doctors spot which pneumonia will turn severe.
pmc-13626339:
Kate Duchowny and colleagues map where America's essential workers lived during the COVID-19 pandemic. More than fifty-five million people kept working in person while others sheltered, yet little was known about their home neighborhoods. The team linked a national neighborhood database with census survey estimates from 2016 to 2020. Every tract was sorted into five bands by its share of essential workers. Access to food shops, health care, and parks was then compared across the bands.

Tracts dense with essential workers actually held more grocery stores than quieter tracts. The same tracts, though, had significantly fewer health care facilities and less park and green space. The people asked to absorb the most exposure, the authors conclude, went home to places least stocked with the resources that protect health in a crisis.
pmc-13629139:
Kritchavat Ploddi and three colleagues mapped the known methods for building health prediction models. Such models must keep working when moved to new groups of people. Their review searched medical and preprint sources up to August 2023. From over seventeen hundred first hits, it kept eighteen papers on method.

The approaches split into two families. Data-driven ones augment data, blend models, or reweight samples. Knowledge-driven ones rest on causal reasoning. Each family carries its own bets and trade-offs. The review sorts them by aim. Some chase broad reach. Others aim at transport to one target group. The authors call for head-to-head tests on fake and real datasets. They also urge blending the families into more practical toolkits.
pmc-13629539:
Holly A. Caretta-Weyer and nine colleagues attack a hard problem: how residency programmes select trainees. They write with their global collaborative team. They call selection a wicked problem for competency-based education. Selection scores barely predict later success. Dropping clerkship grades has also spawned a shadow trade in chasing publications. That pulls students away from ward learning.

The team ran a creative problem-solving exercise. Eight stakeholders from three lands first designed the worst selection system they could imagine. Many of its features felt grimly familiar. Bias, random calls, metric gaming, and wasted effort all appear in current practice worldwide. Their remedies include social duty in selection. They also urge shared skill frameworks and clear learner handover. Structural options include preference signals or lotteries.
pmc-13630539:
Jin Li and three colleagues built a monitoring framework for drinking water networks that stays trustworthy even when its own sensors lie. Water quality sensors are costly and fault-prone, and a glitching sensor can trigger false contamination alarms or mask a real event, yet most detection methods assume perfect measurements. Their 2026 framework tackles faults and contamination together.

One neural network spots corrupted readings and rebuilds the clean signal, while a second isolates which sensor is faulty, and an explicit check separates sensor-induced wobbles from true contamination signatures. Tested on three realistic networks with simulated chlorine-reactive pollution, exact source pinpointing stayed hard under sparse coverage, but the system narrowed likely source regions well. The authors argue joint modelling is the practical path for real deployments.
pmc-13631239:
Guang Yang and eleven colleagues publish a chromosome-level genome for the White King pigeon, a leading Chinese meat breed, published in 2026. Pigeons have been bred for five thousand years into extraordinary variety, and a clean reference genome is the tool for tracing the genes behind that diversity.

Combining three sequencing technologies, the team assembled a genome of about 1.09 billion bases anchored to twenty-nine chromosomes, then catalogued over twenty-two million single-letter variants and about two and a half million insertions and deletions. Sequencing sixty-four more birds from six Chinese market breeds against the reference showed wide genetic diversity. The dataset is offered as public infrastructure for breeding research and trait genetics.
pmc-13631439:
Tomohiro Nakagawa and seven colleagues published this 2026 case report about a twelve-year-old Japanese boy with a missing piece of chromosome 12. The deleted stretch covers three genes called HNF1A, DHX37, and SETD1B. The boy also had autism, hearing loss, short stature, seizures, and severe learning disability before diabetes appeared at age twelve.

The report traces how each missing gene may explain part of the picture. Loss of HNF1A fits the diabetes, since that gene helps the pancreas release insulin. Loss of SETD1B fits the learning problems, while loss of DHX37 may explain the hormone problem behind his underdeveloped testes. Because the boy could not manage low blood sugar alone, his doctors chose nateglinide plus insulin over the usual sulfonylurea drugs. The case shows why diabetes care must be shaped around a child's wider disabilities.
pmc-13631939:
Seven researchers led by Qiwang Yang tested a therapy that places dissolving thread under the skin at acupuncture points, in mice made obese by diet. The method is used for weight control, but how it works is unclear. Fifty-one mice were split into groups by point choice, with sham and no-treatment controls, over five weeks.

Thread at one leg point raised leptin levels in spinal fluid and eased leptin resistance signals in the brain. Hunger-related brain signals shifted toward fullness. Effects differed by point, and a second belly point alone did less. Food intake dipped briefly in all obese groups. The work maps one path by which the therapy may act.
pmc-13632939:
Vaidotas Marozas and colleagues introduce the ThrombUS+ project, a 2026 Horizon Europe effort to build a wearable system for continuous bedside monitoring of deep vein thrombosis in the lower leg. Clots in deep leg veins can break off and travel to the lungs, causing often fatal pulmonary embolism, yet up to half of cases cause no symptoms. Ultrasound and related tests work in clinics but cannot watch a patient continuously without an operator. The project re-engineers three methods for a wearable device.

Compression ultrasound, electrical impedance plethysmography, and light reflection rheography are combined, with a piezoelectric micropump actuator replacing manual probe pressure and feeding an AI unit that assesses clot risk. Lab tests of individual modules show promise, and large datasets from three clinical studies will train the system. Clinicians get a concept and early progress report, with validation still ahead in a feasibility study and a multicenter trial.
pmc-13633339:
Judit Mari and seven colleagues measured early-onset sepsis and antibiotic use in Hungarian newborns. Sepsis in the first days of life is rare but dangerous, and fear of it pushes doctors toward heavy antibiotic use. The team analyzed the national perinatal registry for 2020 through 2023, covering the country's larger neonatal intensive care units. They counted proven infections, the germs behind them, and antibiotic use.

Proven early sepsis struck about four babies in every ten thousand births, far more often in babies born before thirty-five weeks. Escherichia coli caused a third of cases and group B streptococci about a quarter. A fifth of the babies with E. coli sepsis died, while no streptococcal deaths occurred. Meanwhile nearly two thirds of intensive care babies received antibiotics, usually about five days. The authors call this a first national estimate for their region and urge strategies cutting needless exposure.
pmc-13635239:
Yuhang Luo and a team of co-authors solve the structures of two hepatitis delta virus family ribozymes and pin down how they cut RNA, in a two thousand twenty-six structural biology paper. These self-cleaving RNA enzymes are models for RNA catalysis.

Crystals of ribozymes from a nematode and a bacterial virus showed the family's double-pseudoknot fold, one caught before and after cleavage. A cytosine acts as the general acid, with a pH profile to match. Unusually, the catalytic metal ion behaves as a Lewis acid, binding the attacking oxygen directly rather than tuning acidity. The authors argue this mechanism defines the whole HDV ribozyme class.
pmc-13641439:
How often Americans with advanced kidney failure choose to forgo dialysis, and whether that choice shifted over time, is tracked by Wong and colleagues. National registry data show dialysis starts falling, especially among older adults, yet the registry only counts people who receive dialysis or a transplant, leaving those who decline treatment largely invisible. The team studied more than twelve thousand adults with advanced kidney disease in a large health system between 2012 and 2020.

The share who decided against kidney replacement therapy stayed flat across the study years, at about six percent overall, even as patient numbers and comorbidity rose. That rate sits well below figures reported for veterans and for patients in the United Kingdom and Australia, with the gap widest at older ages. Wong and colleagues suggest that practice culture, health-system design, and access to conservative care, rather than patient need alone, shape who forgoes dialysis.
pmc-13643539:
John D'Angelo and colleagues report the first native transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement in a patient with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries. In this rare condition present from birth, the morphologic tricuspid valve serves the body's main circulation, and its severe leakage can disable the patient.

Their patient was a fifty-nine-year-old woman with symptoms from severe leakage of the systemic tricuspid valve, at high risk for surgery. The heart team went ahead with replacement by catheter, using a Sapien M3 valve. The step wiped out the systemic leakage in full, with no complications, and the patient was much better at the thirty-day check. The case shows the step can be done and can be safe in high-risk patients picked with care.
pmc-13643639:
Emma J Cockcroft and six colleagues present a 2026 mixed-methods study of what helps or blocks physical activity for people with type 1 diabetes in the United Kingdom. Adults answered for themselves, while parents answered for their children, allowing a rare direct comparison.

Among 311 responses, nearly three quarters in both groups reported stigma or negative comments in sport settings. Adults more often cited fear of low blood sugar and low motivation, and they reported far less provider support than parents did for children. Parents flagged untrained coaches more. The authors demand mandatory diabetes education for coaches and teachers plus stronger clinical encouragement.
pmc-13644039:
Zhuyun Sun and eight colleagues present a 2026 diagnostic study building a single test that can tell apart three forms of African swine fever virus, a lethal pig disease devastating the industry. New recombinant strains mixing genotypes I and II have appeared in China and Vietnam.

Their triplex real-time PCR targets one gene per form and detected as few as ten viral copies per microliter. It ignored the parent genotypes and other pig viruses, and repeated runs varied very little. In challenged piglets the test caught virus shedding as early as three days after infection. The authors pitch it for rapid diagnosis and early warning.
pmc-13645539:
Xiaojing Guo and seven colleagues present a systematic review and meta-analysis on breaks in tube feeding for very sick hospital patients. Such breaks are called enteral nutrition interruption. The team searched seven databases through December 2025 and followed standard review guidance. Their subject is how often feeding stops, why it stops, and what harm may follow.

Forty-one studies covering 8,260 patients were pooled, and feeding breaks proved very common across intensive care units. The most frequent causes were airway care, scans, gut intolerance, and surgery or preparation for surgery. Breaks were linked with patients getting less of their planned energy, while links with unit stay and short-term death stayed unclear. The authors call for shared definitions and shorter fasting around procedures.
pmc-13645639:
Deepak Behera and six colleagues report a chemistry advance that makes building cyclopropanes, three-sided carbon rings prized in drug making, both safer and more flexible. Older routes rely on explosive starting materials or work only with narrow partner choices. The team instead uses salts built on thianthrene, a sulfur-containing ring system, as carbene carriers. Carbenes are the reactive one-carbon pieces that form the ring.

These salts let both partners in the reaction vary widely, something earlier methods could not offer. The salts' bulky shape and weak pull on metals explain their strong reactivity, the authors argue. They also proved safe enough to scale up and even to run in solid form by milling. Beyond ring building, the same carriers fed other carbene reactions, which suggests a broad new platform for this branch of chemistry.
pmc-13646139:
Kai Liu, Xiaohu Yang, and Lingti Kong compare side effect reporting patterns for seven Alzheimer's disease drugs in the United States reporting system FAERS. The set covers three newer antibody drugs and four older symptom drugs. Reports ran from early 2004 to mid 2026 and totaled 39,301 valid cases. Four statistical methods hunted for events reported more often than expected, with extra checks for false alarms.

Women and patients over sixty-five supplied most reports. The antibody drugs showed focused signals in nervous system events, above all a brain swelling and bleeding pattern tied to amyloid treatment, plus infusion reactions. Older drugs showed wider, body-spanning patterns, from heart and fall signals to patch-site reactions and confusion. Some signals were absent from the drug labels the team reviewed. The authors stress that reporting patterns flag questions for study, not proven harms.
pmc-13646839:
Olena Les and seven colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, whether blood-thinning drugs deserve a place in treating pulmonary hypertension, the dangerous rise of pressure in the lung arteries. Clotting-driven remodeling of lung vessels is a known part of the disease, which keeps interest in anticoagulants alive. The team weighed trials, observational studies, and pooled analyses across all five disease groups. Survival, clot events, pressure measures, and bleeding were the outcomes tracked.

Evidence hints at a survival benefit only in the idiopathic form of pulmonary arterial hypertension. In disease tied to connective tissue disorders, results looked neutral or worse because bleeding risk climbs. For most other groups, thinners are reserved for standard reasons such as irregular heartbeat or vein clots, except clot-caused disease, where they remain a cornerstone. The authors call for proper trials and disease-specific risk tools before practice can settle.
pmc-13647939:
Daniel Canseco-González and nine colleagues synthesize seven new azide-bearing pyrazole compounds and test them against three fungi that rot crops and ornamentals. Farm antifungals keep losing ground to resistance, so new scaffolds matter. The seven variants differ in the decorations hung on the central ring, and all were made in one high-yielding step from cheap starting materials. Potency was measured against Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, and Alternaria species.

Two compounds led the set against all three fungi. The pattern was clear: a phenyl-type ring at one key position boosted potency sharply, while bare or simple alkyl versions stayed weak. Pairing the best compound with silver nanoparticles doubled its power against one fungus only. Computer docking into a fungal target supported the ranking and showed a snug binding pose. The authors offer the structure rules as a design map for the next round of plant antifungals.
pmc-13648139:
Myong-Hwan Kim and four colleagues report in 2026 on building Korea's first job-exposure matrix for musculoskeletal disorders, conditions affecting muscles, joints, and the back. A job-exposure matrix assigns typical exposure levels to each occupation, letting researchers estimate risk without measuring every worker.

The team drew on five waves of the Korean Working Conditions Survey covering 210,500 workers from 2006 to 2020. For each occupation they rated time spent in repetitive movement, awkward posture, heavy lifting, and prolonged standing, split by upper body, lower back, and legs. Expert agreement was strong for the upper body and back, and higher exposure tracked with more symptoms, supporting the matrix for research and policy.
pmc-13648439:
KanagaVijayan Dhanabalan and seven colleagues map how cells defend themselves against all-trans-retinal, a light-reactive waste product of the visual cycle that damages the retina when it lingers. The enzyme RDH12 normally converts it to a safer form, and the team profiled engineered human cells with and without that protection.

Combining protein and lipid measurements over time, they saw an early stress programme switch on while a key detox arm faded, alongside membrane reshaping and rising iron-handling proteins that favour oxidative chemistry. A drug that blocks ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death, partly rescued the cells. The sequence positions RDH12 as an upstream shield against retinaldehyde toxicity.
pmc-13649439:
Yuxing Zhao and seven colleagues used high-grade scans to compare bone build in obese women who have polycystic ovary syndrome with obese women who do not. Past work on bone density in this hormone disorder clashed, partly since weight itself shifts bone readings. Their groups held 23 obese women with the syndrome, 21 obese women without it, and 24 women of normal weight.

The obese women with the syndrome had denser bone at the wrist and shin than matched obese peers. Yet scans that estimate how much load bone can bear showed no edge in strength for that group. Male hormone levels did not explain the bone gaps. The authors think other traits of the syndrome, such as swelling or insulin issues, may be at play.
pmc-13649739:
Zijun Zhang and ten colleagues built an artificial intelligence system that reads microscope images of the living cornea and writes draft reports, in a study published in 2026. Reading such scans takes rare skill and much time. Their system learned from more than thirty thousand images paired with over four thousand clinic reports.

Automated scores showed strong match with expert reports, and a sorting task hit high accuracy. Eye specialists who graded the drafts gave top marks for flow and safety, with slightly lower marks for support of diagnosis. A question-and-answer mode also scored well on accuracy and lack of harm. Test cases with viral, fungal, and amoeba infections were read well. The authors see wider access to expert-level scans.
pmc-13650339:
Julie Katrine Karstensen led a 2026 Danish cohort study of whether nurse-led heart screening visits change risk factors in people with inflammatory arthritis. These patients face roughly doubled heart disease risk, and European guidance urges planned risk care, yet whether screening programs actually move risk factors was unclear. The team followed 595 patients who attended at least two nurse-led screening visits at the Danish Hospital for Rheumatic Diseases between 2011 and 2015. They compared risk factors across a mean of 683 days.

Smoking and overweight improved clearly between visits, with odds ratios favoring improvement over worsening. Blood sugar, cholesterol, and systolic blood pressure moved in the right direction but not significantly, while waist size and exercise worsened clearly. Care teams get a mixed but useful result: nurse-led screening with motivational talks can shift smoking and weight, while activity and belly fat need stronger strategies.
pmc-13650439:
Eytan Ellenberg led a 2026 study that gives dermatologists a framework for attributing skin cancers to job sun exposure in workers. Outdoor workers face high lifetime ultraviolet doses, yet legal cases need to split blame between job exposure and risk, a different question from population burden. The authors applied a four-step FAIR framework to meta-analyses from 1995 to 2025, adjusting for skin type, sex, and immune status. They split risk with game-theory methods and Monte Carlo models.

Mean occupational shares came to 35 percent for squamous cell carcinoma, 25 percent for basal cell carcinoma, 10 percent for melanoma, and 50 percent for actinic keratosis. The chance of clearing a 20 percent medico-legal threshold reached 85 percent for squamous cell and 75 percent for basal cell cancer. Prevention scenarios cut cases by 10 to 15 percent and costs by 8 to 12 percent. Clinicians and courts get a clear attribution tool, with thresholds that support recognizing work-related skin cancers.
pmc-13650739:
Masuko Katoh and one colleague review two tumor surface targets that arise from gene splicing choices, variants of a sealing protein and a growth factor receptor found mainly on cancer cells. Because healthy tissue largely lacks these exact forms, drug developers treat them as addresses for precision attack.

First-generation antibody drugs against each target now exist, with one combination already approved alongside chemotherapy for stomach and junction cancers. A crowded next generation includes antibody-drug conjugates that deliver poison, two-armed antibodies that also grip immune checkpoints, and engineered immune cells, several posting higher single-agent response rates than the original antibody. Stomach side effects such as nausea are common, since the targets appear in healthy gut lining, though newer engineering softens them for some drugs. The authors look to better diagnostic tests, resistance studies, and combination trials to widen the benefit.
pmc-13651439:
Alexander Muacevic and seven colleagues test whether adding a dental simulation game to a classic calming routine reduces children's pain and anxiety at the dentist. The routine, Tell-Show-Do, explains each step, demonstrates it, then treats, and the trial asked whether letting children rehearse in a game first makes the real visit easier.

Sixty-eight children aged four to ten needing pulp treatment or extraction were randomized; half received the routine alone and half played the simulation game as well. Children in the game group reported clearly lower pain on a faces scale and showed lower pulse rates during treatment. Those pulses are a physiological sign of calmer nerves, while observer-rated pain scores and post-treatment pulses matched between groups. The authors conclude that game-based rehearsal is a worthwhile addition for school-age children, easing both felt pain and anxiety during the procedure itself.
pmc-13652539:
Pedro Pessoa and seven colleagues present REPOP, a method for reading bacterial population sizes from colony counts without overstating the noise. Counting colonies on plates after dilution is a standard lab routine, yet the usual math mixes two kinds of variation. The randomness of drawing a small sample, and real biological differences between populations. The result can make a uniform population look falsely diverse, or hide genuine subpopulations.

REPOP separates those sources by modeling the sampling step itself, so what remains reflects biology rather than arithmetic. The team shows how the correction changes conclusions in cases such as plate counts from worm gut experiments, where hidden subpopulations matter. For microbiologists counting bacteria from soil, water, or animal samples, the method offers cleaner estimates from data they already collect, with no new equipment required.
pmc-13654339:
Kristian Arak and seven colleagues test a simple heart tracing measure that doctors hoped could forecast survival after a major heart attack. Pathologic Q waves on the admission electrocardiogram have long signaled dead heart muscle and worse outcomes in ST-elevation heart attacks. The team asked whether the depth of those waves, measured before emergency artery-opening treatment, could predict who would die in the short and medium term.

Reviewing more than six hundred consecutive patients treated with primary intervention, the researchers compared the deepest and the average Q-wave depth against later mortality. Depth failed as a predictor, a negative result the title states plainly. Negative findings like this one carry practical weight. Since they stop clinicians from leaning on an easy measurement that does not actually sort patients by risk when treatment decisions are urgent.
pmc-13661839:
Yosr Ammar and his team test if shifts in fish groups in the Baltic Sea tell why foul-good paths in eggs of the common guillemot change. Their 2026 study links forms of dioxin-like foul goods to a new shape of the food web.

Foul-good grades hit their top in the nineteen seventies, then fell with new laws, but the fall in guillemot eggs stalled in the nineteen nineties in spite of more cuts. Three spans of fish groups came out: cod and herring led, then sprat, then a stickleback surge. Foul-good paths matched those spans. They fell in a steep way, then held flat, then fell at a slow pace. Heat, salt grade, size of small drift life, and press from fish work drove the fish shifts. The team ends that food web shifts ran up the chain and changed foul-good loads in the sea birds.
pmc-13677639:
Milena Aparecida Ferreira Campos and six co-authors review the gene proof on shape faults in Nellore cattle. Their review, from two thousand twenty-six, pulls the work into one map.

The faults span stance, feet and legs, the navel, coat tint, and the skull and face. They cut yield, ease, and the herd's long life. The team searched three stores for gene studies of pure-bred Nellore herds. Each study's way and flaws were read and weighed. Since the fault forms and ways of work ranged wide, the yield was told as a tale, not a count. The aim is to guide breed picks.
pmc-1395339:
Yuan, Reed, Chen, and co-authors address how to analyse real-time PCR data with sound statistics. PCR is a lab method that copies DNA and tracks its growth as it happens. By 2006 it was used widely across biomedical work, yet agreed ways to treat its data were still missing.

The authors focus on proper handling of uncertainty, giving confidence ranges and tests of whether differences are real. Without such care, small lab noise can be mistaken for a true effect. Their guidance helps researchers report gene activity results that other labs can trust and repeat.
pmc-2588639:
Prince, Adamo, Hamel, and co-authors review how well direct and self-report measures of physical activity agree. Judging whether activity programmes work needs accurate measures of current and changing activity levels. Studies rely either on devices people wear or on what people say they did.

The team searched the literature in a systematic way and compared the two approaches head to head. Agreement turns out to be limited, so the choice of measure shapes study results. Their findings guide researchers to pick measures honestly and warn readers that self-reported activity often runs high.
pmc-2860339:
Schulz, Altman, and Moher present CONSORT 2010, updated guidance for reporting parallel group randomised trials. Clinicians and journals worldwide use the CONSORT statement to lift the quality of trial reports. The 2010 version updates the guideline using new methodological evidence and years of accumulated experience.

A trial report must show how patients were assigned, followed, and counted, so readers can judge bias for themselves. The update keeps that checklist current as trial methods evolve. Journals require CONSORT checklists from authors, making this short statement one of the most influential documents in medical publishing. Journals ask authors to file the checklist alongside their trial report at submission.
pmc-3022639:
Gulliver, Griffiths, and Christensen review barriers and supports for mental health help-seeking in young people. Adolescents and young adults often experience mental disorders, yet they tend not to seek help. Understanding why is the first step toward services young people will actually use.

The team summarised findings from surveys, focus groups, and interviews with young people. Reported barriers include stigma, embarrassment, and poor recognition of problems, while trust and prior good experiences encourage seeking help. Their synthesis gives schools and clinics concrete targets for making support easier to reach.  Stigma kept appearing across countries, marking it as a near-universal obstacle for youth.
pmc-3965039:
Cole, Wang, Fish, and their team described the Ribosomal Database Project in 2013. The project, known as RDP, collects ribosomal RNA gene sequences, a key marker used to name and sort microbes. It aligns those sequences and adds notes about what each one is.

Along with the data, RDP offers tools that let users test their own sequences in the same frame. A lab can compare a new sample with known groups and place it on the tree of microbial life. The resource is widely used in studies of soil, water, and the human gut, where most microbes cannot be grown in a dish.
pmc-5770339:
Fidel Alfaro-Almagro, Mark Jenkinson, and colleagues described brain image processing for UK Biobank in 2018. UK Biobank is a huge health study that invited many past participants back for scans. The imaging covers the brain, heart, and body, plus ultrasound and bone scans.

Their pipeline cleans and checks the first large batch of brain scans in a uniform way. Automated quality checks flag bad scans so analysts can trust the rest. Uniform processing matters because small handling differences can fake results at this scale. The work set the pattern for imaging studies with tens of thousands of people.
pmc-6323939:
Huaiyu Mi, Anushya Muruganujan, Dustin Ebert, and coauthors reported PANTHER version 14 in 2018. PANTHER classifies genes by evolution and function across the tree of life. It groups genes into families and maps them to shared roles.

The update adds many more genomes and a leaner set of ontology terms for quick enrichment tests. Users can ask which functions appear more often than chance in a gene list. Cleaner term sets make those answers easier to read. The resource serves both deep evolution studies and everyday gene-list interpretation in one place.
pmc-8008539:
Matthew Page and colleagues issued the PRISMA 2020 statement in 2021, the updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. A systematic review is only as credible as its report is complete, since readers cannot check steps the authors never described. The 2020 statement modernizes the checklist first published in 2009.

It sets out the items a review should report, covering the question, the search, study selection, results, and the certainty of the evidence. This journal version of the statement carries the same guidance as its sister publications, widening its reach to another readership. Editors, peer reviewers, and authors use the checklist daily, making it one of the most influential short documents in health research.
schoolcraft-algic-researches-vol1-1839:
Henry Rowe Schoolcraft saves the tales of the lakes in Vol. 1 of Algic Researches, out in 1839. Schoolcraft was the state's man midst the tribes round the Great Lakes. His wife's kin gave him tales at first hand. Here he prints them in English: tales of Manabozho, the trickster sire of lore, of beasts that speak, and of how the world was made and marred.

The Algic name is his word for those tribes' stock. The set founds the study of their lore in English. Longfellow drew his famed song from these pages. This tome starts the hoard.
schoolcraft-algic-researches-vol2-1839:
Henry Rowe Schoolcraft ends his hoard of lake tales in Vol. 2 of Algic Researches, out in 1839. The first tome gave the trickster's deeds and the world's birth. Here come grander beasts: the great thunder bird whose wings beat out the storm, and the Weendigo, the gaunt ice giant who eats men in the depth of the cold north woods.

Schoolcraft prints the tales as he heard them, with brief notes. His pair of tomes is the root hoard of Great Lakes lore in English. Fans of myth still mine them. This tome holds their most famed beasts.
scotus-quaestiones-physicorum-de-anima-w:
This Latin volume comes from Luke Wadding's 1639 edition of Duns Scotus. It holds the master's questions on two works of Aristotle: the Physics, all eight books, and the De Anima, on the soul. It adds his logical questions on the Isagoge of Porphyry and on the Categories. Notes by Franciscus Pitigianus and supplements by Hugo Cavellus fill the margins.

Scotus tests Aristotle point by point: motion, place, time, the powers of the soul, and the intellect that thinks. His answers shaped Franciscan teaching for centuries. No English version in the public domain exists. The Wadding text is the form in which the early modern world read the Subtle Doctor on nature and mind.
scotus-quaestiones-quodlibetales-wadding:
John Duns Scotus, the Subtle Doctor of the Franciscans, taught at Oxford and Paris in the years around 1300. His Quodlibetal Questions take up twenty-one disputed points, argued in open session on any topic the crowd might raise. The text here is from Luke Wadding's great edition of the works of Scotus, printed in 1639, with the commentary of Franciscus Lychetus. It is in Latin.

The questions range over God, the will, knowledge, and the fine joints of metaphysics, each split and weighed in the sharp style of Scotus. No English version in the public domain exists. The volume stands as a record of scholastic debate at its most exact and most daring.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5039:
Harry S. Truman gives eight yearly addresses, from January 21, 1946, to January 7, 1953, parted by three stars. The first opens not with the year's state but with the budget. A quarter century back, Truman notes, Congress found it could no longer weigh the money plans of the great offices bit by bit. It called on the president to lay one full executive budget before it instead.

Congress has shown its liking for that way by spreading the budget system and tightening its checks. The bigger and more tangled the federal program grows, Truman argues, the more needful is one budget from the chief. The money plan and the general plan of government cannot in truth be parted. The president bears the charge of urging on Congress one joined set of plans for all the government's work and its paying for it.
stendhal-charterhouse-parma-1839:
Stendhal published The Charterhouse of Parma in 1839, a French novel set in Italy after Napoleon. Fabrizio del Dongo, a young nobleman, rushes to fight at Waterloo but barely grasps what he sees. Back in Parma, he enters the church to gain favor at court. Court intrigue, love, and prison shape his fate.

His aunt Gina schemes brilliantly to protect and advance him. Fabrizio falls in love with Clelia while jailed in a tower. Stendhal wrote the book fast, and its pace feels free and joyful. Critics rank it among the greatest novels ever written. Its mix of war, politics, and love still feels fresh.
the-american-phrenological-journal-and-m: The American Phrenological Journal and Miscellany, 1839. The American journal. This book preserves that periodical. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
the-comedy-of-errors-pg2239: Ephesus runs mad in this edition of Shakespeare's farce: two sets of twins, two Dromios, and a chain of errors that tangles masters and servants. Beatings, arrests, and mistaken wives pile up until the Abbess sorts them out. The fastest farce ever written, breathless with confusion.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-volum: Volume 6 in this second listing of Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer covers chapters XLII to LV, printed at Dublin in 1839. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here. The chapters promise two journeys, a reminiscence of the East, a day in the Phoenix, an adventure in Canada, a courier's passport, and a night in Strasbourg. No chapter text follows, and the numbering clashes with another record also called Volume 6.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Dated August 5, 1897, No. 39 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a premium offer. The premium is a Pocket Kodak camera, for any one who sends four new subscribers. The camera makes a picture one and a half by two inches and weighs only five ounces. It is delivered ready for twelve exposures. Its lens is of the fixed focus type.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
Cervantes' Don Quixote continues in Volume 2, Part 39, Englished by John Ormsby. Chapter sixty-three tells of the mishap that befell Sancho Panza through the visit to the galleys, and the strange adventure of the fair Morisco. Don Quixote turns the enchanted head's reply over and over in his mind.

None of his reflections hits on the secret of the trick. All rest on the promise, taken as certain, of Dulcinea's disenchantment, which he expects soon to see fulfilled. Sancho shares the satisfaction in his own way. Hope built on a stage trick carries the pair to the port, where real ships and real captives will test it.
the-history-of-england-from-the-accessio: Thomas Babington Macaulay wrote The History of England from the Accession of James II. The record shows Volume II of 5, chapters VI to X. Porter & Coates printed it at Philadelphia. The contents outline chapter six in detail. The chapter covers the power of James at its height. It also covers his foreign policy and the standing army. Designs in favor of the Roman Catholic religion follow. The trial of Delamere also appears. Only the title page and contents outline are present here.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Volume 19, No. 535, dated February 25, 1832, visits the Zoological Gardens in Regent's Park. Three engravings show the polar bear, the tunnel, and the monkey cage. The gardens are praised as one of London's most pleasant rational recreations, meaning amusements that also teach.

Paths lined with flowers, shrubs, and young trees lead visitors among animals gathered from almost every country on earth. The writers dwell on the links between familiar and wild creatures. The fireside cat shares a tribe with the lion and the tiger, they observe, while the faithful dog descends from the wolf. Zoology, presented in living form, turns those comparisons into a study anyone can follow.
the-new-lavater-or-and-improved-system-o:
Only a title page, its lettering partly garbled in the scanning, is present here for The New Lavater, so the system itself does not appear. Enough can be read to give the book's full claim. It offers an improved system of physiognomy, meaning the reading of character from faces. The system claims strictly scientific principles. It also claims to fit the present advanced state of anatomical and physiological knowledge.

Practical application to nations, professions, and individuals is promised, with added remarks on phrenology. Accurate engravings illustrate the theories of Dr. Spurzheim and the modern phrenologists. The author signs himself A. Walker, Esquire, lecturer on anatomy. Surrounding scraps of misread type on the leaf are the only other marks these pages offer.
the-winter-s-tale-pg1539: William Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale is represented here by its contents list and cast list alone. The five acts move between Sicilia and Bohemia. King Leontes of Sicilia and King Polixenes of Bohemia head the cast. Perdita, Florizel, Camillo, and the rogue Autolycus also appear. The dialogue of the play does not appear in the pages present.
tob-0039:
After the Cold War, the United States government faced its own record of human radiation research. The Advisory Committee on Human Radiation Experiments issued its final report in 1995. Investigators read secret files and heard testimony about studies run from the 1940s onward.

Patients were injected with plutonium, soldiers were marched near atomic blasts, and prisoners and the sick were exposed, often with no real consent. Thousands of Americans passed through such tests. The committee judged much of the work wrong even by the standards of its day. The report stands as an official apology and a warning about secret science.
tob-10039:
Al-Ghazali, the great eleventh-century Muslim thinker also written Abu Hamid Muhammad, tells his own story in The Confessions. At the height of fame as a teacher, doubt struck him so hard that he could no longer trust what he knew or taught. He left his post and took to wandering as a Sufi seeker.

His account follows that crisis step by step: skepticism, breakdown, travel, and a slow recovery of certainty through lived spiritual practice. Few documents in Islamic literature are so personal about faith and reason. Readers meet a brilliant mind describing, honestly and in his own voice, how it lost and remade itself.
tob-13139:
Paul Carus, an American writer on religion, shaped the Buddha's life into gospel form in 1894. Drawing on the Pali canon, he retells the story in chapters that echo the style of the Christian Gospels. Western readers with no background in Buddhism could thus meet the Buddha on familiar ground.

The narrative follows the prince who leaves his palace, gains enlightenment under the tree, and preaches a path out of suffering. Carus stresses the teaching on craving, compassion, and release from rebirth. Scholars now call the book dated, but it brought thousands of Western readers to Buddhist thought for the first time.
tob-4139:
Volume two of Waite's Paracelsus continues the hermetic and alchemical writings with the Archidoxes and treatises on metals and healing. Readers should note the evidence marks this as a second copy of Waite's edition held in the library. The system of Hohenheim stands entire in its pages.

Paracelsus divides the world among the elements and the three principles, salt, sulphur, and mercury, and builds his cures on that frame. His medicine mixes observation, astrology, and faith in nature's signatures. Verified from the 1919 edition, the volume completes Waite's service: the alchemist-physician's thought, whole, for English readers.
turke-and-gowin-madden-1839:
The Turke and Gowin is a rough northern romance of Sir Gawain, edited by Frederic Madden in 1839. It belongs to the alliterative tradition, the strong verse form of northern England. A strange visitor sets its plot in motion at Arthur's court.

A giant who calls himself the Turk lays a grim challenge before the king and his knights. Gawain takes it up and rides north into a land of odd tests and stranger hosts. The tale is wilder and less polished than the famous Gawain poem. That roughness is part of its charm. It shows the popular edge of the Gawain legend in the late Middle Ages.
un-ga-res-139: Catalogued as General Assembly Resolution 139 and dated by the catalog to 1970, this record gives the number alone, with no subject in its title or notes. That dating sits oddly. The Assembly's low sequential numbers belong to its first years, before the later session-based numbering. What can be stated with care is the form. It is a formal decision of the full Assembly, kept as official record text from the UN's own files. It should be read on its own terms, not through guesswork about its topic.
un-ga-res-39:
Franco's Spain drew the UN General Assembly's sharpest rebuke of its first year in Resolution 39, adopted on 12 December 1946. The text recalls that the peoples of the UN, at San Francisco, Potsdam, and London, had condemned the Franco regime and barred Spain from the UN while it lasted. A Security Council probe in mid-1946 had then weighed what more could be done.

That probe found, without dissent, that the regime was fascist in origin, shape, and conduct. It had been built with much help from Hitler's Germany and Mussolini's Italy. The Assembly assures the Spanish people of warm goodwill, and of a welcome once they can join. For now, the door stays shut.
un-ga-res-a-69-39:
Terror groups seeking mass-kill arms are the fear behind Resolution A/69/39, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the vote of the year before on the same risk. It names the will of states to fight terror, as shown in past Assembly and Security Council texts. The risk of links between terror and weapons of mass destruction, it warns, keeps growing.

Steps by states under the Security Council's 2004 anti-spread vote are noted with care. So is the 2007 start of the world pact against acts of nuclear terror. Tighter guards on atomic goods, agreed in 2005 to the pact on the safety of such goods in transit and store, are welcomed as well.
un-ga-res-a-72-239:
Family farms won a decade of their own under Resolution A/72/239 of the General Assembly. The text looks back with praise on the International Year of Family Farming, kept in 2014. That year raised the standing of family farms, herding, and small plots in the fight for food and good diets. Many lands had since built plans in favor of such farms, with farm teams at home and small loans for small holders.
